children.text: Historical Trauma and the Research Trust Deficit

Recruitment of underrepresented communities into genomic research cannot be separated from the history of exploitation in biomedical research. That history is not ancient — it extends into living memory and continues to shape how communities respond to research recruitment today.

The U.S. Public Health Service Syphilis Study at Tuskegee (1932-1972) enrolled 399 Black men with syphilis and 201 uninfected controls, promising free medical care and burial insurance while deliberately withholding treatment — including penicillin after it became the standard of care in 1947 — to study the natural progression of untreated syphilis. The study ended only when a whistleblower leaked details to the press. Its legacy is a documented, rational distrust of biomedical research and institutions among many Black Americans.

The story of Henrietta Lacks and the HeLa cell line adds another dimension. Lacks was a Black woman whose cervical cancer cells were taken without her knowledge or consent at Johns Hopkins Hospital in 1951. Her cells — known as HeLa cells — became the first human cell line that could be kept alive and grown in the laboratory indefinitely. They have been used in thousands of scientific studies and generated billions of dollars in commercial value. The Lacks family received no compensation and was not informed for decades.

These histories matter for precision medicine recruitment because trust is the prerequisite for participation. When researchers approach Black, Indigenous, or other historically exploited communities with genomic research offers, they are entering those conversations carrying this institutional history — whether or not individual researchers know it or intend it. Effective, ethical recruitment requires community engagement, transparent data governance, and demonstrated benefit to the communities being recruited.

body.analogy: Imagine a bank that, for decades, systematically overcharged customers from a particular neighborhood, denied them loans based on their address, and never faced consequences. Now the bank has new leadership, new policies, and genuinely wants to serve that neighborhood. But residents remember — or their parents remember — and they are not wrong to be cautious. The bank's new good intentions do not erase the institutional memory of harm.
body.bridge: Research institutions that previously exploited communities of color now seek to recruit those communities into genomic research for what they believe are legitimate scientific and equity goals. The skepticism these communities exhibit is not irrational — it is a rational protective response to documented institutional harm. Building trust requires time, transparency, community control over data, and demonstrated reciprocal benefit.
body.concept: Why historical research exploitation creates present-day trust deficits

children.text: Indigenous Data Sovereignty and the CARE Principles

Indigenous communities face a distinct set of concerns around genomic research. Beyond the shared history of exploitation that many minority communities experience, Indigenous peoples have specific legal and political status as sovereign nations, with implications for how data about their members is collected, stored, shared, and used.

Indigenous data sovereignty is the right of Indigenous peoples to govern the collection, ownership, and application of data about their communities. The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance — Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics — provide a framework for how genomic research involving Indigenous communities should be structured. These principles assert that data about Indigenous peoples belongs to and should serve Indigenous peoples, not external researchers or corporations.

Specific cases have illustrated the stakes. The Havasupai Tribe of Arizona participated in a diabetes genetics study at Arizona State University in the 1990s, donating blood samples for that specific purpose. Researchers then used the samples for other studies — including research on schizophrenia, population migration, and inbreeding — without tribal consent. The Havasupai sued, eventually settling in 2010, and the case has since been a touchstone for discussions of Indigenous research ethics.

In Vermont, the Abenaki Nation — Vermont's only state-recognized Indigenous nation — has its own community priorities and sensitivities around research and data governance. Any genomic research initiative seeking to include Abenaki community members must engage tribal leadership as partners, not merely as a recruitment population, and must respect the community's authority to decide whether and on what terms genomic research is appropriate.
LGBTQ+ Populations and Genomic Research Gaps

LGBTQ+ populations — lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and other sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals — represent another group systematically underrepresented in genomic and biomedical research. This is partly a data collection problem: most electronic health records and research databases have not systematically collected sexual orientation or gender identity (SOGI) data, making it impossible to study health disparities that may have genetic or gene-environment interaction components.

LGBTQ+ individuals also have documented higher rates of several conditions with potential genomic components — including depression, anxiety, substance use disorders, and certain cancers — but the research to disentangle genetic from social and minority stress contributions to these disparities is in its infancy. The NIH Sexual & Gender Minority Research Office and the All of Us program's explicit SGM inclusion goals are beginning to address this gap.
Rural Populations and Precision Medicine Access Barriers

Rural populations face a distinct set of precision medicine access barriers that are structural rather than cultural. These include geographic distance from specialized genetic services, limited broadband access needed for telegenetics, provider shortages that mean primary care physicians have little time to engage with genomic complexity, and insurance gaps that make high-cost genomic testing and targeted therapies financially inaccessible.

Rural patients with cancer face documented disparities in receiving tumor genomic profiling — the first step in precision oncology. A study published in JNCI Cancer Spectrum in 2023 found that rural cancer patients were significantly less likely to receive comprehensive genomic profiling than urban patients, even after controlling for insurance status, cancer stage, and cancer type. This means rural patients are less likely to be identified as candidates for targeted therapies they might benefit from.

body.title: Rural and Structural Access Gaps in Precision Medicine

children.text: Vermont-Specific Equity Challenges: Refugee Populations and Rural Geography

Vermont is among the whitest states in the nation by percentage, but it hosts a significant and growing refugee population — particularly in Burlington and surrounding communities — that represents extraordinary genetic and ancestral diversity. Vermont has resettled refugees from Bhutan, Somalia, Democratic Republic of Congo, Bosnia, Sudan, and dozens of other countries.

For refugee populations, precision medicine access barriers multiply. Language barriers complicate genetic counseling, which is inherently nuanced and requires precise communication about probability, uncertainty, and family implications. Reference databases have almost no data from many refugee-origin populations, increasing VUS rates dramatically. Cultural frameworks around fate, family disclosure, and heredity may differ significantly from those embedded in standard genetic counseling practice.

Genetic counselors working with Vermont's refugee communities need cultural competence, access to professional medical interpreters (not family members, who may selectively filter difficult information), and awareness that the Western individualistic framework for genetic decision-making — emphasizing personal autonomy and individual disclosure choices — may not fit the community-oriented decision-making frameworks of many refugee cultures.

body.body: UVMMC's Global Health Program and its associated refugee health clinic provide primary care to Burlington's refugee communities. The program has developed culturally adapted health communication approaches and works with community health workers who share cultural and linguistic backgrounds with patient populations. As genomic medicine becomes more integrated into primary care, these established community relationships represent a critical infrastructure for equitable genomic service delivery.
body.outcome: The Global Health Program model — community health workers as cultural bridges, professional interpreter use, and community engagement in service design — represents a replicable approach for extending precision medicine services to linguistically and culturally diverse populations in rural states.
body.source: UVMMC Global Health Program; Vermont Refugee Health Program Annual Reports
body.title: University of Vermont Medical Center Global Health Program

children.text: What Equitable Precision Medicine Actually Requires

Equitable precision medicine is not simply a matter of increasing diversity in research databases, though that is essential. It requires changes at multiple levels — research design, clinical service delivery, technology development, insurance policy, and community trust-building — working simultaneously.

steps.description: Genomic databases, GWAS studies, and variant interpretation tools must include sufficient representation from all major ancestry groups to ensure that polygenic risk scores and variant classifications are valid across populations — not just European ancestry individuals.
steps.title: Diverse, representative research databases

steps.description: Underrepresented communities must be partners in research design, not merely recruitment targets. This means tribal consultation for Indigenous communities, community advisory boards for other groups, and genuine power-sharing over data governance and benefit distribution.
steps.title: Community-engaged research design

steps.description: Genomic testing and precision medicine therapies must be covered by Medicaid and other public payers at rates that ensure access regardless of income. Inconsistent Medicaid coverage for tumor profiling, targeted therapies, and genetic counseling is a structural equity failure.
steps.title: Insurance coverage and payment reform

steps.description: The genetic counseling workforce must expand dramatically, and telegenetics must be fully reimbursed to extend services to rural areas. Community health workers trained in genomic health communication can extend the reach of genetic counselors in underserved communities.
steps.title: Workforce expansion and telegenetics

steps.description: Genetic counseling and genomic health communication must be available in the languages spoken by patients, with cultural adaptation for communities whose frameworks for understanding heredity, family, and risk differ from the Western individualistic model embedded in standard practice.
steps.title: Culturally and linguistically adapted services

body.title: What Equitable Precision Medicine Requires: A Framework

children.text: The equity failures in precision medicine are not primarily failures of individual prejudice — they are failures of system design. Genomic databases were built with the researchers available, which happened to be primarily from European ancestry academic institutions. Fixing this requires intentional redesign of research infrastructure, not just increased awareness.

body.misconception: The solution to genomic inequity is simply to recruit more diverse participants into existing research frameworks.
body.reality: Recruiting diverse participants into research systems that were not designed with their interests, governance preferences, or data sovereignty in mind replicates historical exploitation in a new form. Equitable genomic research requires restructuring how data governance works — giving communities authority over their data, ensuring benefit flows back to participating communities, and building infrastructure that serves underrepresented populations rather than merely extracting data from them.

body.answer: VUS findings are more common in patients of African ancestry because the databases used to classify variants — such as ClinVar — have been built predominantly from research on European ancestry populations. A variant that has been observed many times in European ancestry individuals may be well-classified as benign or pathogenic; a variant that appears primarily in African ancestry individuals may lack sufficient reference data for classification, resulting in VUS status. This is a limitation of the database, not a feature of the patient's biology. The provider should: (1) explain clearly that VUS does not mean dangerous and is not a basis for preventive surgery; (2) refer to a board-certified genetic counselor for comprehensive counseling; (3) encourage the patient's relatives to be tested, as additional family data can help reclassify variants; (4) inform the patient that VUS classifications are frequently updated as databases improve, and her lab should re-analyze her variants over time; and (5) acknowledge that the higher VUS rate in patients of African ancestry is a systemic inequity in the genomic research infrastructure, not a personal or biological characteristic.
body.hint: Think about what drives VUS classification and how variant databases are constructed.
body.question: A Black woman in Vermont receives BRCA1/2 testing through her OB/GYN after a family history of breast cancer. Her result shows three variants of uncertain significance (VUS). She is devastated and asks whether she should have a prophylactic mastectomy. What should her provider understand about why VUS findings are more common in patients of African ancestry, and how should this be communicated?

body.answer: The CARE Principles require: Collective Benefit — the research must generate direct benefit to the Abenaki community, not just academic publications or commercial applications that flow back to the research institution; Authority to Control — the Abenaki Nation must have genuine authority over how their members' data is collected, stored, analyzed, and shared, including veto power over secondary uses; Responsibility — researchers have an ongoing obligation to the community that extends beyond the data collection period; and Ethics — research must be consistent with the community's own values and governance processes. In practice, a genuine data sovereignty approach would: involve tribal leadership as co-investigators with intellectual property rights, not just as a community advisory board; require that data be stored in systems the tribe controls; require explicit consent for every new use case rather than blanket consent; specify that data cannot be shared with commercial genomics companies; guarantee that research results and benefits flow back to the community; and include community health workers as co-researchers who will remain in the community after the study ends. The Havasupai case specifically teaches that researchers must obtain specific consent for each study use — blanket consent for 'diabetes research' does not authorize use of samples for ancestry, migration, or psychiatric studies.
body.hint: Think about what CARE stands for and what the Havasupai case taught the field about scope of consent.
body.question: A Vermont health system wants to partner with the Western Abenaki community to study genetic factors in type 2 diabetes, which affects the community at elevated rates. Community members have expressed interest in the health question but concern about how their genetic data will be used. What does the CARE framework require of researchers in this situation, and what would a genuine data sovereignty approach look like?

points: More than 78% of GWAS participants have been of European ancestry, making precision medicine less scientifically valid for the 84% of the global population that is not of European ancestry — this is a scientific accuracy problem, not just an ethical concern.

Polygenic risk scores trained on European data perform substantially worse in non-European populations, meaning clinical decisions based on these scores are systematically less accurate for patients of African, Asian, Indigenous, and other non-European ancestry.

Higher rates of variants of uncertain significance in non-European BRCA testing reflect database inadequacy, not biological ambiguity — variant classification databases are built from skewed reference populations.

The Tuskegee syphilis study and the Henrietta Lacks/HeLa cell case are not historical curiosities — they established patterns of research exploitation whose legacy shapes community participation in genomic research today.

Indigenous data sovereignty and the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics) require that research involving Indigenous communities be governed by those communities, not by external institutions.

Economic barriers — inconsistent Medicaid coverage for tumor profiling, targeted therapies, and genetic counseling — mean that precision medicine's benefits are currently distributed along income lines.

Vermont's refugee communities face compounded barriers to genomic equity: language barriers in genetic counseling, near-complete absence of their ancestries in reference databases, and cultural frameworks that differ from the individualistic model embedded in standard genetic counseling.

Equitable precision medicine requires redesigning research infrastructure, not merely recruiting more diverse participants — communities must have authority over their data and receive direct benefit from research participation.

children.text: What Is Value-Based Care?

Value-based care (VBC) is a healthcare delivery model in which providers are compensated based on patient health outcomes rather than the volume of services provided. The core formula is simple: Value = Quality ÷ Cost. In practice, defining, measuring, and aligning incentives around this formula has proven enormously complex.
The Fee-for-Service Problem

Under fee-for-service (FFS) reimbursement, providers are paid for each discrete service rendered — each office visit, procedure, test, and hospitalization generates a claim. This creates a structural incentive to provide more services, regardless of whether additional services improve patient outcomes. The U.S. spends $4.5T annually on healthcare — 17% of GDP — with outcomes rankings 30th or lower among high-income nations on key metrics.
Primary VBC Contract Structures

Five main contract structures have emerged in the shift to value: (1) Pay-for-Performance (P4P) — bonuses or penalties based on quality metric performance. (2) Bundled Payments — single payment for an episode of care across multiple providers. (3) Shared Savings — providers share in savings generated below a benchmark. (4) Shared Risk — providers share in both savings and losses. (5) Global Capitation — fixed per-member-per-month payment regardless of services provided.
Why the Transition Has Been Slow

Despite the ACA's ambitious targets for alternative payment model adoption, the U.S. healthcare system remains predominantly fee-for-service. Several structural forces slow the transition: provider capital constraints preventing care transformation investment, data infrastructure gaps limiting performance measurement, actuarial uncertainty making risk-based contracts financially dangerous for smaller organizations, and commercial payer reluctance to move faster than Medicare.
Module Summary

Value-based care represents a fundamental redesign of healthcare incentives — from rewarding volume to rewarding outcomes. Understanding the contract structures, measurement frameworks, and structural barriers is essential for any healthcare professional navigating today's payment landscape. In Module 2, we examine how shared savings and risk contracts are structured and negotiated.

children.text: One-Sided vs. Two-Sided Risk

In a one-sided risk model, the provider organization shares in savings if performance falls below the cost benchmark, but faces no penalty if costs exceed the benchmark. This asymmetric structure reduces provider financial risk but also reduces incentive intensity — providers have less to lose from poor performance.

Two-sided risk contracts require providers to share in losses when costs exceed the benchmark, in addition to sharing in savings. The stronger financial incentive drives more aggressive care management investment but requires substantial capital reserves to absorb potential losses. Medicare's Enhanced Track ACOs operate under two-sided risk.
Benchmark Methodology

The cost benchmark is the target against which performance is measured. CMS's MSSP benchmark methodology uses a blend of national expenditure trends and the ACO's own historical costs. The blending formula reduces the penalty for ACOs that start from a high-cost baseline (rewarding regression to the mean) while limiting savings for already-efficient ACOs (the 'efficient ACO problem').
Minimum Savings Rate

The minimum savings rate (MSR) is the threshold below which the ACO does not share in savings — a buffer zone protecting CMS from paying savings that fall within normal statistical variation. For smaller ACOs (under 5,000 beneficiaries), the MSR can reach 3.9%, meaning the ACO must reduce costs nearly 4% below benchmark before receiving any payment.
Capitation vs. Shared Savings

Global capitation — a fixed monthly payment per member — represents the most complete transfer of insurance risk from payer to provider. Unlike shared savings, which settles annually, capitation requires monthly cash flow management. Organizations without actuarial infrastructure and adequate reserve capital face significant financial exposure in capitation arrangements.

children.text: Risk Stratification: Finding the Right Patients

Effective care management begins with identifying patients most likely to generate high costs or experience avoidable adverse events. Risk stratification uses claims data, clinical data, and increasingly social determinants information to segment patients into risk tiers. The top 1% of patients by cost typically account for 22% of total spending; the top 5% account for 50%.
Care Team Models

High-performing VBC organizations deploy multi-disciplinary care teams aligned to patient risk tier. Complex patients (top 5% risk) typically receive intensive care management: dedicated care manager (RN or social worker), monthly care manager contact, quarterly physician review, and social needs navigation. Moderate-risk patients (5-15%) receive less intensive monitoring with automated outreach and pharmacist medication management.
Evidence-Based Interventions

The interventions with the strongest evidence for total cost of care reduction in high-risk populations include: transitional care management programs (18-25% 30-day readmission reduction), medication adherence support (12% reduction in diabetes-related hospitalizations), behavioral health integration in primary care (8% total cost reduction in depression-comorbid populations), and home-based palliative care for serious illness patients (31% reduction in ICU utilization in last 6 months of life).
Measuring Care Management ROI

Care management programs typically require 12-18 months before generating measurable cost savings. An HTR model for a 1,000-patient high-risk care management program estimates fully loaded cost of $850,000 annually (1.0 FTE care manager, infrastructure, data). Expected savings from avoidable hospitalization prevention: $1.2-1.8M annually, yielding an ROI of 1.4:1 to 2.1:1.

children.text: The Affordable Care Act created the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) in 2012, establishing ACOs as the central vehicle for Medicare's value-based care agenda. By 2024, over 480 ACOs were participating in MSSP, covering more than 11 million Medicare beneficiaries. After more than a decade of operation, the evidence base is large enough to draw substantive conclusions — and the picture is more nuanced, and in some respects more sobering, than the program's architects anticipated.
MSSP Aggregate Performance: What the Data Shows

CMS publishes annual MSSP results showing aggregate benchmark performance. For performance year 2022, MSSP ACOs collectively generated $2.0 billion in gross savings relative to benchmarks, and $1.8 billion in net savings after shared savings payments to ACOs. Approximately 60% of MSSP ACOs earned shared savings payments. These are non-trivial numbers relative to the program's administrative investment — but they require careful interpretation that the headline figures do not provide.

The aggregate savings figure conceals enormous variation. The top quartile of MSSP ACOs generates the vast majority of savings; the bottom half frequently generates either no savings or incurs losses that erode the aggregate. A 2020 analysis by McWilliams and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that new MSSP ACOs achieved minimal savings in their first 3 years, with meaningful savings concentrated in ACOs that had prior experience in risk-based contracting — particularly those who had previously participated in managed care or commercial ACO programs. Inexperienced organizations entering MSSP largely for the shared savings upside, without the care management infrastructure to generate real efficiency, produced little to no Medicare savings.
Pioneer ACO and NextGen: The Advanced Track Evidence

The Pioneer ACO Model, launched alongside MSSP in 2012 with 32 self-selected advanced organizations, was designed for ACOs with substantial prior experience in coordinated care. Pioneer offered higher shared savings rates and two-sided risk from the start. The CMS evaluation found that Pioneer ACOs generated $385 million in gross savings over 3 years from 2012 to 2015, with average per-beneficiary savings of approximately $300. Importantly, Pioneer ACOs improved on several quality measures including patient experience and preventive care rates. However, 13 of the original 32 Pioneer ACOs dropped out of the model before its conclusion, largely due to the financial risk of two-sided contracts when benchmark methodology produced unfavorable targets — a preview of the rebasing problem that would plague MSSP.

The Next Generation ACO Model (2016-2021) was designed to test even higher risk-reward arrangements, offering up to 80-100% of shared savings for ACOs willing to accept commensurate downside risk. NextGen ACOs were largely drawn from Pioneer graduates and other experienced organizations — the most sophisticated ACO operators in the country. The 2021 evaluation found that NextGen ACOs generated approximately $406 million in net savings to Medicare across the model's life, representing roughly a 1.7% reduction in per-beneficiary spending. This is a meaningful but modest result for organizations operating at the leading edge of ACO capability, suggesting that even the best-equipped ACOs face structural limits on how much cost can be removed from the system through care management alone.
The Benchmark Problem: Why Measuring ACO Savings Is So Difficult

The central methodological challenge in measuring ACO performance is the benchmark — the target spending level against which actual ACO spending is compared. MSSP benchmarks are calculated using 3 years of prior spending for the ACO's attributed beneficiaries, adjusted for risk and national trend factors. This methodology creates several well-documented problems that affect both the measured results and the behavioral incentives facing ACOs.

The rebasing problem is the most consequential. As ACOs improve efficiency, their prior-year spending — the basis for their benchmark — falls, making it progressively harder to generate savings in subsequent contract periods. An ACO that reduces spending by 5% in year 1 faces a lower benchmark in years 4-6, with less room to save relative to a hypothetical world without the ACO. This ratchet effect creates a structural disincentive to sustained improvement and was cited as a primary reason Pioneer ACOs dropped out of the model. Organizations that work hardest to reduce costs are penalized by the benchmark methodology for having done so.

Starting in 2017, CMS introduced a regional component into MSSP benchmarks, blending ACO historical spending with regional fee-for-service spending. This regional adjustment benefited ACOs in high-cost regions (whose benchmarks increased, making savings easier to achieve) and disadvantaged ACOs in already low-cost regions. ACOs in rural, low-cost areas — which may have done more to improve care relative to their baseline than their benchmark scores suggest — can appear to underperform simply because they start from an already-low spending baseline. The regional adjustment, intended to improve fairness, created different fairness problems.

The selection bias problem adds further complexity. ACO beneficiaries are assigned retrospectively based on primary care utilization, creating a population that is healthier-than-average in fee-for-service — patients who have a primary care relationship and use it are less likely to be the highest utilizers. This makes it difficult to separate ACO effects from selection effects in non-experimental evaluations, complicating claims about what the ACO model actually caused versus what would have happened anyway in the attributed population.
BASIC vs. ENHANCED Tracks: Pathways to Downside Risk

The 2019 Pathways to Success rule restructured MSSP into two tracks: BASIC (with a glide path from one-sided to two-sided risk over 5 years) and ENHANCED (two-sided risk from the start, with higher sharing rates up to 75% of savings). CMS's intent was to accelerate the migration of ACOs from one-sided savings-only arrangements toward genuine two-sided risk bearing. The CMMI director at the time, Seema Verma, argued that one-sided MSSP ACOs — which faced no penalty if spending exceeded their benchmark — were providing free money to organizations with favorable benchmarks rather than incentivizing real care transformation.

The Pathways to Success rule drove an initial contraction in MSSP participation — from over 550 ACOs in 2018 to approximately 500 in 2020 — as organizations that had been benefiting from favorable one-sided risk arrangements exited rather than accept downside exposure. This contraction was arguably beneficial in concentrating the program on ACOs with genuine population health management capability, and the program has since grown again as the market has matured.
What High-Performing ACOs Actually Do Differently

Research on ACO performance heterogeneity consistently identifies characteristics of high-performing ACOs that transcend geography and organizational type. A 2023 analysis by Colla and colleagues drawing on MSSP data and ACO survey data found that the strongest predictors of sustained savings include the following.

Robust care management infrastructure: High-performing ACOs invest heavily in embedded care managers, nurses, and social workers who proactively manage high-risk attributed patients between visits. This infrastructure requires upfront investment that takes multiple years to yield savings.

Primary care investment: ACOs that pay primary care physicians above FFS Medicare rates through care management fees, supplemental payments, or risk-sharing bonuses generate stronger alignment and better care coordination outcomes.

Data analytics capability: ACOs that can identify care gaps, risk-stratify their population, and generate actionable analytics for frontline clinicians outperform those operating from claims data alone or relying on lagged CMS data feeds.

Post-acute care management: High-performing ACOs systematically redirect post-acute patients from skilled nursing facilities to home health or home-based therapy. This single intervention — reducing SNF utilization — is the most reliable and largest source of episode cost reduction available to ACOs.

Prior risk-bearing experience: Organizations with experience in Medicare Advantage, commercial capitation, or other risk-based contracts start with population health management infrastructure and organizational culture that new ACOs must build from scratch, often over 3-5 years.
Quality Outcomes in ACOs: The More Consistent Evidence

The ACO quality evidence is more uniformly positive than the savings evidence. Multiple studies have found that MSSP ACO beneficiaries show better performance on preventive care measures, lower rates of avoidable hospitalizations, and better chronic disease management compared to matched fee-for-service controls. A 2018 study in Health Affairs by McWilliams and colleagues found that MSSP ACOs achieved greater reductions in potentially avoidable hospitalizations than non-ACO FFS, with an estimated 7% reduction in hospital admissions for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions — a meaningful improvement in care quality that also has cost implications.

Patient experience scores in ACOs, measured through the CAHPS survey, show modest but consistent improvement over time. ACOs score higher than FFS benchmarks on measures of care coordination, access to care after hours, and provider communication. Readmission rates are lower in ACOs than matched FFS controls in several analyses. These findings suggest that the ACO model is achieving genuine quality improvements — systematizing preventive care, care coordination, and post-acute management — even when the financial savings signal is weak.
CMMI's 2021 Strategic Reset: A Candid Assessment

In 2021, CMMI published a strategic refresh that included an unusually candid assessment of its innovation model portfolio. The report acknowledged that despite more than $10 billion invested in testing alternative payment models since 2010, only a handful of models had generated statistically significant net savings to Medicare. The refresh identified systemic problems: models were too often designed for advanced organizations and failed to scale; financial incentives were insufficient to drive care transformation; and the absence of multi-payer alignment meant that ACOs were managing full clinical responsibility for populations where Medicare was only one of several payers and the ACO's financial stake covered only a fraction of total healthcare costs.

The honest assessment of ACO performance evidence is this: ACOs work better than fee-for-service at the margins for organizations that are already sophisticated at coordinated care, in regions where fee-for-service spending is high relative to the benchmark, and when the benchmark methodology is favorable. For new ACOs, organizations without prior risk experience, and providers in already-efficient markets, the evidence of financial benefit is weak. The quality evidence is more consistently positive, suggesting that the ACO model's most durable contribution may be less about bending the cost curve than about institutionalizing the organizational infrastructure — care management teams, data analytics, post-acute relationships — that is a prerequisite for the more ambitious value-based models that come next in the reform trajectory.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: Over a decade of Medicare Shared Savings Program data reveals a complex, heterogeneous picture of ACO performance: aggregate savings are real but modest, the distribution of results is highly uneven, and the benchmarking methodology contains structural problems that both inflate and limit measured savings. This lesson reviews the MSSP savings track record, Pioneer and NextGen ACO results, the benchmark rebasing problem, what high-performing ACOs actually do differently, and the academic evidence on ACO quality outcomes.
result.title: ACO Performance: What the Evidence Shows

children.text: The ACO model that most healthcare professionals know is the Medicare Shared Savings Program — a federal CMS initiative with nationally standardized rules and a well-documented evidence base. But ACOs have proliferated far beyond Medicare, appearing in Medicaid programs, commercial insurance markets, and multi-payer settings with fundamentally different populations, financing structures, and policy objectives. Understanding how ACOs function outside the MSSP context is essential for healthcare leaders operating in mixed-payer environments, which describes the reality of virtually every health system and physician organization in the country.
Medicaid ACOs: Why They Require a Different Framework

Medicaid ACOs face a fundamentally different operating environment than MSSP ACOs in nearly every relevant dimension. The Medicaid population is younger, poorer, and has higher rates of behavioral health conditions, substance use disorders, unstable housing, and food insecurity than Medicare beneficiaries. Social determinants of health (SDOH) are not peripheral to care management in Medicaid — they are central to whether any clinical intervention will succeed. An ACO that reduces hospital admissions by improving diabetes management faces a categorically different challenge when its attributed population includes people experiencing homelessness or acute food insecurity than when it serves stable, middle-income retirees with intact social support.

Medicaid ACOs are also state-designed rather than federally standardized, meaning there are as many Medicaid ACO models as there are states with Medicaid ACO programs. States typically operate these programs through Section 1115 Medicaid waivers or through their managed care procurement processes. The financial structure varies enormously: some Medicaid ACOs are pure shared savings arrangements similar to MSSP, others operate as capitated managed care organizations with full risk, and still others are hybrid models that layer ACO-style quality accountability on top of existing managed care contracts.
Vermont's OneCare Vermont: The All-Payer ACO Experiment

Vermont's OneCare Vermont represents the most ambitious Medicaid and all-payer ACO experiment in the United States. OneCare is the state's single ACO, operating under the Vermont All-Payer ACO Model — a federal CMMI innovation model approved in 2016 and renewed in 2022 as part of the broader Vermont AHEAD model. OneCare holds a population-based global budget that covers the vast majority of Vermonters across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance within a single accountability structure — an approach with no direct parallel elsewhere in the country.

Under the Vermont model, OneCare receives a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) budget from CMS for Medicare beneficiaries, a Medicaid payment from the State of Vermont, and commercial payments negotiated with Vermont's dominant insurer, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Vermont. The ACO is responsible for managing total cost of care across all payers for its attributed population — approximately 160,000 Vermonters as of 2023 — and must invest a defined portion of its global budget in population health and social determinants initiatives.

Vermont's results have been mixed. CMS evaluations found that the model generated modest Medicare savings in its early years but struggled with attribution methodology challenges and incomplete network participation, since many Vermonters receive care from providers not formally participating in OneCare's network. Vermont's rural geography means that the all-payer alignment that is the model's theoretical strength is harder to achieve in practice. The model has nonetheless invested substantially in community health teams, care management programs, and social determinants initiatives funded through the global budget's population health allocation, creating organizational infrastructure that would not otherwise exist.
Oregon's Coordinated Care Organizations: Regional Global Budgets for Medicaid

Oregon took a fundamentally different approach to Medicaid transformation, creating Coordinated Care Organizations (CCOs) in 2012 through a major Medicaid waiver (House Bill 3650). CCOs are regional, integrated health organizations that receive a global budget for Medicaid beneficiaries in their geographic area and are required to integrate physical health, behavioral health, and oral health into a single organizational accountability structure — a degree of integration that is unusual in American Medicaid and extraordinarily difficult to achieve in practice.

Oregon's CCO evaluation found meaningful early results: emergency department utilization fell 24% between 2011 and 2015, hospitalizations for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions fell significantly, and preventive care rates improved across multiple measures. The global budget structure gave CCOs a strong financial incentive to invest in primary care and social services — if you can prevent an ER visit through upstream intervention, you capture the savings rather than losing revenue from reduced admissions as a hospital would under fee-for-service. The CCO model also gave regional organizations significant latitude to design locally-tailored community health interventions.

Oregon's CCOs have faced challenges in sustaining early performance gains and meeting quality benchmarks in behavioral health — the hardest-to-treat and most resource-intensive population segment. The 2019 CCO 2.0 procurement imposed tighter quality requirements, explicit health equity goals, and greater focus on social determinants. Whether Oregon's model is replicable nationally is debated: it required significant state commitment, substantial federal waiver flexibility, and a political environment unusually favorable to healthcare reform that other states may not share.
Massachusetts MassHealth ACO: SDOH Integration in Medicaid

Massachusetts operates one of the most sophisticated Medicaid ACO programs in the nation, launched in 2018 through a Section 1115 waiver. The MassHealth ACO program offers three participation models: ACO-A (ACOs that partner with managed care organizations), ACO-B (ACOs that subcontract with existing MCOs for administrative services), and ACO-C (Primary Care Clinician ACOs for smaller practices). The program also features a PCMH+ model for patients with complex needs, providing enhanced care management payments and allowing greater flexibility in covered services.

A distinctive feature of Massachusetts's approach is the Flexible Services program, which allows ACOs to spend a portion of their budget on non-traditional services for members with unmet social needs — housing supports, food assistance, and transportation to medical appointments. This is one of the most explicit attempts in American Medicaid to direct healthcare financing toward social services. Early evidence suggests the Flexible Services program is associated with reduced emergency department utilization among targeted high-risk members, though the evaluation challenges are significant given the program's relatively short history.
Commercial ACOs: Blue Cross Total Cost of Care and National Insurer Arrangements

Commercial insurers have developed their own ACO-like arrangements, most commonly structured as total-cost-of-care (TCOC) contracts between health systems and major payers. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts's Alternative Quality Contract (AQC), launched in 2009, is the longest-running and best-studied commercial ACO program in the United States. The AQC provides participating provider groups with a global budget — a fixed PMPM payment for all covered services — plus quality bonuses for performance on a comprehensive quality scorecard covering preventive care, chronic disease management, and patient experience.

Research on the AQC by Song and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that the program generated significant savings — an estimated $256 million over 4 years — with simultaneous quality improvements on multiple measures. The AQC's success has been attributed to several factors: the substantial financial risk on both upside and downside, the long contract terms that allow organizations to invest in care management infrastructure with confidence of multi-year returns, and BCBS Massachusetts's commitment to investing in data sharing and analytics support for participating organizations.

Commercial ACOs face a structural challenge that Medicare ACOs do not: multi-payer fragmentation. A health system operating a commercial ACO with BCBS may simultaneously be in a different arrangement with Aetna, UnitedHealthcare, and Cigna — each with different quality measures, different benchmarking methodology, different data sharing agreements, and different care management expectations. The result is a patchwork of quality programs with potentially contradictory incentives, making it operationally difficult to design care delivery systems around any single model's requirements and limiting the return on infrastructure investment.
Social Determinants and Medicaid VBC: The Unresolved Challenge

The most distinctive and unresolved challenge in Medicaid value-based care is the outsized role of social determinants of health. Research consistently shows that clinical care accounts for only 20-30% of health outcomes, with the remainder driven by social factors including income, housing stability, food security, education, and social support networks. Medicaid enrollees have dramatically higher rates of SDOH risk than commercially insured populations — by definition, since Medicaid eligibility is income-based.

This creates a fundamental design tension in Medicaid ACO architecture: if an ACO is held accountable for total cost of care and quality outcomes for a population whose health is substantially determined by housing instability, food insecurity, and poverty — factors largely outside the ACO's clinical control — then the financial and quality targets may be inherently unachievable without social service investment that healthcare financing does not traditionally support. Some states including Massachusetts and North Carolina have responded by explicitly allowing healthcare dollars to fund social services. But most Medicaid ACOs lack the regulatory and financial flexibility to fully address the social determinants driving poor health outcomes in their populations, leaving a fundamental gap between what ACOs are accountable for and what they have the authority and resources to address.

Medicaid and commercial ACOs represent important extensions of the value-based care framework beyond Medicare, but each faces challenges that MSSP was not designed to address. Population complexity, social determinants, state-level policy variation, managed care integration, and multi-payer fragmentation are not peripheral design considerations — they are central to whether ACO models can generate value in non-Medicare settings. The most promising approaches — Oregon's CCO global budgets, Massachusetts's SDOH-inclusive ACO framework, Vermont's all-payer model — share a common thread: they give accountable care organizations both the financial incentives and the programmatic flexibility to address the full range of factors driving health outcomes for their populations. Where that flexibility is absent, ACOs operating in Medicaid and commercial markets tend to produce more limited results.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: ACO models extend far beyond Medicare, with Medicaid programs in dozens of states and major commercial insurers operating their own accountable care arrangements. The population complexity, state-by-state variation, and social determinants burden of Medicaid ACOs create fundamentally different challenges than MSSP, while commercial ACOs face multi-payer fragmentation that limits the infrastructure investment justification. Vermont's OneCare Vermont, Oregon's Coordinated Care Organization model, Massachusetts's ACO framework, and major commercial total-cost-of-care contracts illustrate the range of approaches and their divergent results.

children.text: When CMS and the broader policy community embarked on bundled payment experimentation in the early 2010s, the theoretical logic was compelling but the empirical evidence was thin. A decade later, there is a substantial body of peer-reviewed research and CMS evaluation data to assess bundled payment's actual effects on spending, quality, and care delivery. The picture that emerges is more heterogeneous than the model's proponents hoped: bundled payments work well in specific clinical contexts — primarily musculoskeletal — but have shown weaker evidence in medical episodes and have raised legitimate concerns about patient selection, spillover effects, and the sustainability of savings over time.
BPCI-Advanced Results: Which Episodes Saved Money

CMS evaluations of BPCI-Advanced through the first several performance years found that the model generated aggregate net savings to Medicare, with results concentrated in a subset of clinical episodes. Lower extremity joint replacement (LEJR) emerged as the clear savings driver: BPCI-A participants managing LEJR episodes consistently generated savings of 2-5% relative to target prices, primarily through reductions in skilled nursing facility (SNF) utilization. Cardiac episodes — major joint replacement, coronary artery bypass graft, cardiac valve procedures — showed more modest savings, while most medical episodes (pneumonia, COPD, sepsis) generated near-zero or negative net savings.

The differential performance across episode types reflects fundamental differences in modifiability. In surgical episodes like joint replacement, post-acute care utilization is the dominant variable: historical SNF use has been high relative to clinical necessity, surgeons have direct influence over discharge destination, and the post-acute spend is large enough that even modest reductions produce meaningful savings. Medical episodes like pneumonia are driven more by acute care intensity and readmission rates — factors more closely tied to underlying clinical complexity and comorbidity burden — making them harder to manage through care coordination interventions alone.
The CJR Mandatory Model: The Cleanest Evidence

The Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model, which randomly assigned geographic markets to mandatory bundled payment participation rather than allowing voluntary self-selection, provides the most internally valid evidence on bundled payment effectiveness. The CJR randomized design eliminates the selection bias that plagues voluntary model evaluations — where the most capable and motivated organizations volunteer — allowing credible causal inference.

The CJR evaluation by Finkelstein, Ji, Mahoney, and Skinner, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018, found that CJR reduced Medicare spending per episode by approximately $812 (about 3.7%), driven almost entirely by reductions in post-acute care spending — specifically, a decline in SNF use and a shift toward home health. Readmission rates did not increase, and patient-reported outcomes on functional recovery and patient experience were not significantly different between CJR and control markets. The quality findings are arguably as important as the savings findings: they suggest that reducing SNF utilization did not harm patients, validating the key premise of post-acute care reduction strategies.

Subsequent analyses of CJR found that savings were concentrated in hospitals that started with high baseline SNF utilization — consistent with the theoretical prediction that bundled payment opportunity is proportional to prior inefficiency. Hospitals that already had low SNF use achieved minimal savings in CJR, while those with SNF utilization rates above 35% achieved the largest reductions. This pattern has important implications for how bundled payment should be designed and where it should be deployed.
Quality Outcomes: Readmissions, Complications, and Patient-Reported Outcomes

One of the central concerns about bundled payment is that financial pressure to reduce episode cost might lead providers to discharge patients too quickly, under-invest in post-acute care, or select healthier patients in the first place. The evidence to date does not strongly support these concerns for joint replacement episodes. Studies of BPCI and CJR consistently find no significant increase in readmission rates, and several find modest reductions in 90-day readmissions consistent with better care coordination during the post-acute period.

Complication rates — including surgical site infections, periprosthetic joint infections, and implant failures — have not shown significant increases in bundled payment environments. Patient-reported outcome studies in joint replacement, including analyses using PROMIS measures and condition-specific instruments like the HOOS and KOOS, have found similar or slightly better functional outcomes at 90 days and 1 year for patients managed under bundled payment compared to matched fee-for-service controls. This evidence, while not definitive, suggests that the cost savings in bundled payment reflect elimination of low-value post-acute care rather than under-treatment of patients who genuinely need it.
Cream-Skimming: The Patient Selection Concern

A persistent concern in bundled payment research is cream-skimming: the practice of preferentially treating low-complexity patients (who generate low episode costs and easy savings) while avoiding high-complexity patients (who generate high episode costs and potential losses). Because bundled payment creates a direct financial incentive for each episode's cost — unlike per-service fee-for-service where each additional service generates revenue — the model could theoretically incentivize patient selection by risk-averse providers.

Several studies have investigated cream-skimming in BPCI and CJR with mixed findings. Analyses by Navathe and colleagues found that some BPCI participants showed shifts in case mix toward lower-complexity patients after joining the model, consistent with selective referral patterns. However, the CJR evaluation, which covers all Medicare joint replacement patients in participating markets regardless of patient complexity, found no evidence of population-level cream-skimming since participation was mandatory. Whether voluntary bundled payment participants systematically avoid complex patients remains an open question with important equity implications.
The Post-Acute Care Reduction Story: Where the Savings Come From

Every rigorous evaluation of bundled payment that finds savings identifies the same mechanism: reductions in skilled nursing facility utilization. Prior to widespread bundled payment, SNF use after joint replacement was substantial and geographically variable in ways that tracked physician and hospital culture rather than clinical need. SNF stays for hip and knee replacement averaged 10-20 days and cost Medicare $15,000-$25,000 per stay — adding 30-50% to total episode costs for patients who were often clinically capable of recovering at home with outpatient therapy.

Under bundled payment, hospitals developed preferred networks of high-quality, lower-cost post-acute providers and implemented clinical protocols for discharge destination. These protocols — typically based on functional assessment criteria developed with physical therapists — identify patients who are clinically appropriate for home discharge and direct them there. Patient education programs (often begun before surgery) address patient and family anxiety about going home, reducing the demand-side pull toward SNF even among patients who could safely recover at home.
Spillover Effects: Do Bundles Change Care for Non-Bundled Patients

One of the more intriguing findings in bundled payment research is the evidence of spillover effects — changes in care delivery for patients not covered by the bundle. Studies of CJR and BPCI found that hospitals participating in bundled payment for joint replacement showed reductions in SNF utilization for other orthopedic and non-orthopedic patients as well, suggesting that the behavioral and organizational changes induced by the bundle generalized beyond the targeted episodes. This spillover effect, if real and durable, would substantially increase bundled payment's return on investment beyond what episode-specific analyses capture.

The mechanism for spillover is organizational: once a hospital has built a preferred post-acute network, trained discharge planners in evidence-based discharge criteria, and engaged surgeons in post-acute utilization management, those capabilities apply across patient populations, not just to bundled payment patients. This suggests that the organizational investment required for bundled payment participation generates value beyond the financial reconciliation — it builds population health management capabilities that have system-wide application.
Why Orthopedics Has Been the Sweet Spot

The concentration of bundled payment savings in orthopedic episodes is not coincidental. Joint replacement sits at an unusual intersection of clinical and financial characteristics that makes it ideal for bundled payment: high volume, clinically predictable, modifiable post-acute utilization, financially meaningful episode costs, engaged specialty surgeons, and meaningful variation in practice patterns that reflects inefficiency rather than clinical necessity. When policy designers look for the next generation of episodes to bundle, they are searching for conditions that share these characteristics — and the list is shorter than the theoretical potential suggests.

Medical episodes like pneumonia, COPD, and heart failure have higher clinical variability, more complex social determinants, greater overlap with other conditions, and fewer clear behavioral targets than surgical episodes. The patient who is readmitted for pneumonia because of poor housing, food insecurity, and inadequate outpatient follow-up is a fundamentally different management challenge than the joint replacement patient being directed from SNF to home health. Bundled payment for medical episodes requires care management capabilities that go well beyond post-acute utilization management — and the evidence suggests that most participating organizations have not yet developed those capabilities sufficiently to generate savings.

The bundled payment evidence base, now over a decade deep, supports a clear conclusion: bundles work well when the following conditions hold — high-volume, clinically predictable episodes; large, modifiable post-acute spend; engaged specialist physicians aligned with episode outcomes; and organizational capacity to manage preferred networks and patient education. When these conditions are absent, the savings are elusive. Future bundled payment design should build on these lessons by identifying episodes with these characteristics, investing in risk adjustment that prevents cream-skimming, building in mechanisms for equity monitoring, and ensuring that savings generated by reducing low-value post-acute care are reinvested in the care coordination infrastructure that makes the model work.

result.summary: The evidence on bundled payment effectiveness is more nuanced than either its advocates or critics suggest. Joint replacement bundles have consistently generated savings driven by post-acute care reduction; cardiac and medical episodes show weaker evidence; and the mandatory CJR model provides the cleanest causal test. This lesson synthesizes BPCI-A results, the CJR evaluation, quality outcome evidence, cream-skimming concerns, and the lessons emerging from over a decade of bundled payment research.
result.title: Bundled Payment Evidence: What the Research Shows

children.text: Bundled payments represent one of the most conceptually elegant reforms in the value-based care toolkit: instead of paying each provider separately for each service delivered during a clinical episode — the hospitalist, the surgeon, the physical therapist, the skilled nursing facility — a single payment covers the entire episode. Any provider that can deliver the same quality of care at lower cost keeps a share of the savings. The logic is compelling: bundled payments create a financial incentive to coordinate care, eliminate redundant testing, and substitute lower-cost post-acute settings for more expensive ones. The reality, as with most VBC models, is more complicated.
What Defines an Episode of Care

An episode of care has three defining characteristics: a clinical anchor event (typically an inpatient hospital admission or a defined outpatient procedure), a time window (how many days before and after the anchor event are included), and a scope of services (which clinical services and care settings fall within the bundle). Each of these design choices has significant consequences for both the incentive structure and the feasibility of the model.

In BPCI-Advanced, the dominant CMS bundled payment model as of 2024, most episodes use a 90-day window post-discharge. This 90-day period captures the acute hospitalization, all post-acute care (skilled nursing, home health, inpatient rehabilitation), outpatient rehabilitation, professional fees, and related readmissions. A hip replacement episode, for example, includes not just the surgery and hospital stay but all follow-up care through 90 days — making the total episode cost potentially two to three times the acute hospitalization cost alone.
Setting the Target Price: Historical Spending Plus a Discount

The target price — the amount Medicare will pay for the entire episode — is calculated from historical claims data for the participating hospital or practice, adjusted for regional trends and case mix. CMS sets the target price by taking 3 years of historical episode spending, risk-adjusting for patient characteristics, applying a national trend factor, and then applying a discount that represents CMS's minimum savings requirement. For BPCI-Advanced, this discount has typically been 3% for most clinical episodes.

The target price calculation is critical to understanding both the opportunity and the risk in bundled payment. A hospital that has historically been efficient in managing post-acute care will have a low target price, giving it less room to generate savings. A hospital with high historical post-acute spending — particularly high skilled nursing facility utilization — will have a higher target price, giving it substantial opportunity to reduce spending below target by shifting patients to home health or outpatient therapy. This asymmetry means that bundled payment participation is most financially attractive for organizations that have historically been inefficient, paradoxically rewarding past waste.
BPCI and BPCI-Advanced: The Model Architecture

The original Bundled Payment for Care Improvement (BPCI) initiative, launched in 2013, was a voluntary pilot that offered four different model variants testing different episode definitions and payment structures. BPCI was notable for being prospective in Model 2 (a single retrospective reconciliation payment) and retrospective in Models 3 and 4. The model attracted hundreds of hospital and physician group participants and generated the evidence base that informed BPCI-Advanced.

BPCI-Advanced, which launched in 2018 and has been extended multiple times, is a voluntary two-sided risk model covering 32 clinical episodes — both inpatient and, uniquely, outpatient procedure episodes. It is considered an Advanced APM under MACRA, meaning qualifying participants earn the 5% APM bonus and are exempt from MIPS reporting. BPCI-Advanced uses retrospective reconciliation: providers continue to receive standard Medicare fee-for-service payments during the performance period, and then CMS reconciles actual episode spending against the target price annually. If actual spending is below target (minus a minimum savings requirement), the participant earns a reconciliation payment. If spending exceeds the target price, the participant owes a repayment.
How Reconciliation Works in Practice

Reconciliation is the financial settlement process at the heart of retrospective bundled payment. For each episode, CMS calculates actual Medicare spending — aggregating all Part A and Part B claims for services falling within the episode definition — and compares it to the target price. The participant (typically a hospital or physician group) receives or pays the difference, subject to stop-loss provisions that cap downside risk at a percentage of the target price. For hospitals operating hundreds of bundled episodes, the reconciliation can be a multimillion-dollar event in either direction.

The 12-18 month lag between episode completion and reconciliation payment creates significant cash flow management challenges. A hospital that improves care coordination in January will not receive reconciliation payments for those episodes until the following year. This lag reduces the direct incentive feedback loop and requires organizations to sustain operational changes before seeing financial confirmation that they are working.
Mandatory vs. Voluntary Participation: The Selection Problem

All current CMS bundled payment models are voluntary, meaning hospitals and physician groups choose whether to participate. This creates a fundamental selection problem: the organizations most likely to volunteer for bundled payment are those most confident they can generate savings — either because they already have low post-acute utilization (giving them little financial opportunity) or because they have substantial post-acute waste and the operational capacity to address it. Organizations that struggle with care coordination, lack data infrastructure, or have poor relationships with post-acute providers are the least likely to volunteer — and arguably the most in need of the model's incentives.

The Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model, launched in 2016, was the first and only mandatory bundled payment model in Medicare history, covering hip and knee replacement in selected geographic markets. CJR's mandatory design was precisely intended to eliminate selection bias and test whether bundled payment could work for organizations that would not have voluntarily chosen it. The CJR evidence is discussed in the next lesson, but the policy lesson is important: voluntary models generate biased evidence about the model's effectiveness across the full distribution of providers.
Gainsharing: Aligning Physicians with Episode Savings

Because the surgeon's clinical decisions — which implant to use, whether to discharge to home vs. SNF, which post-acute provider to refer to — are among the largest drivers of episode cost, aligning surgeon incentives with bundle savings is essential. Gainsharing arrangements allow the hospital or convener entity to share reconciliation payments with the physicians whose decisions drive episode spending. CMS permits gainsharing in bundled payment models, with requirements that payments be proportional to the clinician's contribution to savings and not contingent on the volume or value of referrals that violate the anti-kickback statute's intent.

In practice, gainsharing arrangements vary widely. Some hospitals pay surgeons a flat bonus for completing required episode management protocols (care pathway adherence, patient education, referral to preferred post-acute partners). Others distribute a share of reconciliation savings based on each surgeon's episode volume and cost performance relative to peers. The most sophisticated arrangements provide surgeons with real-time episode cost data — showing them where spending is going during the 90-day window — combined with performance-based payment that rewards cost-conscious care decisions.
Convener Organizations: The Infrastructure Layer

CMS permits convener organizations to serve as the legal participant in BPCI-Advanced on behalf of multiple downstream participants — hospitals, physician groups, or post-acute providers. Conveners handle the administrative burden of model participation (data submission, target price calculation, reconciliation accounting) and provide infrastructure services like care management platforms, post-acute preferred network development, and analytics that individual hospitals may not have the scale to develop independently.

Major convener organizations in BPCI-Advanced include Remedy Partners (acquired by Nuvera), Archway Health, Caravan Health, and several large health systems acting as conveners for their affiliated physician practices. Conveners typically charge a management fee or take a share of reconciliation savings in exchange for their services. This arrangement allows smaller hospitals and physician groups to access bundled payment models without building the full administrative infrastructure independently, expanding the model's reach beyond large academic medical centers.
Which Episodes Are Used Most and Why

Not all clinical episodes are equally amenable to bundled payment, and participation patterns in BPCI and BPCI-Advanced reflect this. The most commonly selected episodes are musculoskeletal — particularly lower extremity joint replacement (hip and knee) — followed by cardiac and cardiac rhythm management episodes, and medical episodes like pneumonia and COPD. Lower extremity joint replacement is the dominant episode for several reasons:

Clinical predictability: The procedure is highly standardized with relatively low intraoperative variation, making episode cost variation attributable to post-acute care decisions rather than surgical complexity.

Large post-acute care spend: SNF utilization after hip and knee replacement has historically been high — often 30-40% of patients — even though evidence consistently shows that healthy patients can safely recover at home or in outpatient rehab settings. This creates a large, modifiable target for cost reduction.

High volume: Joint replacement is among the most common elective procedures in Medicare, giving hospitals enough episode volume to generate statistically stable performance data and meaningful reconciliation payments.

Engaged surgeons: Orthopedic surgeons tend to have strong relationships with their post-acute partners and respond strongly to gainsharing incentives, making physician alignment more achievable than in medical episodes where care is more diffuse.
Relationship to Hospital Coding and DRGs

Bundled payments interact directly with the inpatient DRG payment system. The hospital continues to receive its standard DRG payment for the anchor hospitalization — the bundle does not replace the DRG payment but rather adds a reconciliation layer on top of it. This means that diagnosis coding intensity, which determines which DRG the case maps to, affects both the base payment and the target price calculation. Cases coded to higher-severity DRGs generate higher base payments and higher target prices, creating potential coding dynamics where hospitals have incentives to document patient complexity thoroughly — which may represent legitimate capture of true comorbidity or may represent documentation-driven upcoding.

Risk adjustment in bundled payment target prices uses patient characteristics including age, sex, and the presence of major comorbidities (via CMS's hierarchical condition category model) to adjust target prices. This is designed to prevent hospitals from losing money on complex, comorbid patients whose episodes genuinely cost more than the average. Whether the risk adjustment adequately captures true clinical risk — or whether organizations can game the risk model through diagnosis documentation — is an ongoing concern in bundled payment design.

Bundled payments are technically complex instruments whose success depends on the interaction of target price methodology, episode design, physician alignment, post-acute care strategy, and organizational data infrastructure. The mechanics matter enormously: a well-designed bundle with fair risk adjustment and meaningful gainsharing can align incentives across a fragmented care delivery system in ways that fee-for-service cannot. A poorly designed bundle — with an unfair target price, inadequate risk adjustment, or misaligned physician incentives — generates the appearance of reform while creating perverse incentives around patient selection and coding. Understanding these mechanics is prerequisite to interpreting the evidence on what bundles actually achieve, which the next lesson examines in detail.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: Bundled payments replace per-service billing for a defined episode of care with a single payment covering all services across providers and settings, creating powerful incentives to reduce waste and improve coordination. This lesson explains how episodes are defined, how target prices are set, how BPCI-Advanced and its predecessors work mechanically, how reconciliation functions, and the critical roles of convener organizations, gainsharing arrangements, and post-acute care strategy in determining whether a bundle succeeds or fails.

children.text: Picture a primary care physician seeing 24 patients in a day. Under fee-for-service, she is rewarded for each visit, each test ordered, each referral made. Under value-based care, she is rewarded for something harder to measure but far more important: whether her patients are actually healthier. That shift in incentives changes everything that happens in the exam room.

This module is about the clinical side of the VBC transformation. It is not abstract. The shift shows up in care team huddles, in how discharge plans are written, in how nurses manage phone calls with patients just released from the hospital, and in how a physician spends the last five minutes of every appointment. Understanding these changes is essential for anyone who works in, manages, or influences clinical care.
