body.title: Why Clinical Practice Must Change

children.text: How Payment Models Shape Clinical Decisions

Clinicians do not consciously think 'I am going to order this test because I will get paid for it.' But payment systems create incentive structures that shape behavior in powerful ways. Under fee-for-service, a busy practice survives by filling the schedule. Under value-based care, a practice is rewarded for keeping patients healthy enough that they do not need to come back as often.

body.analogy: Think about two gyms. The first gym charges you every time you visit — the more you visit, the more they earn. They are motivated to have you come back constantly. The second gym charges a flat monthly fee — they earn the same whether you come twice a week or never. But if you quit because you are not getting healthier, they lose your membership. That gym is motivated to actually get you fit.
body.bridge: Fee-for-service is the first gym — providers earn more when you come back. Value-based care is the second gym — providers earn more when you stay healthy and do not need to come back. The incentives point in opposite directions, and that shapes clinical practice in profound ways.
body.concept: How payment models shape clinical behavior

rows.left: Volume of visits and procedures billed
rows.right: Patient outcomes and quality performance scores

rows.left: Reactive — treat flare-ups as they occur
rows.right: Proactive — prevent flare-ups with regular monitoring

rows.left: Lost revenue, little incentive to follow up
rows.right: Care gap — proactively outreach and reschedule

rows.left: Focused on clinical readiness to leave hospital
rows.right: Focused on preventing readmission, including social needs

rows.left: Refer often; no financial cost to over-referring
rows.right: Coordinate care; referrals used when clearly indicated

rows.left: Optimized for throughput — 10 to 15 minute visits
rows.right: Optimized for relationship — longer for complex patients

body.title: Clinical Practice: Fee-for-Service vs. Value-Based Care

children.text: These differences are not just philosophical. They have real operational consequences. A practice moving to value-based contracts must restructure its workflows, hire different staff — care coordinators, community health workers, data analysts — and invest in systems that identify which patients are at risk before they land in the emergency room.
Quality Measures: How Clinical Performance Is Evaluated

In value-based care, clinicians and practices are evaluated on a structured set of quality measures — standardized metrics that assess whether patients are receiving evidence-based care and achieving good outcomes. These come from several sources: the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the National Committee for Quality Assurance, and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.

Quality Measure: A standardized, evidence-based metric used to assess whether patients receive recommended care. Examples: the percentage of diabetic patients with HbA1c under 8.0%, the percentage of patients with hypertension whose blood pressure is controlled, or the percentage of eligible patients who received a colorectal cancer screening.

There are hundreds of quality measures in use across the US healthcare system. For primary care practices in most VBC contracts, a core set of 10 to 20 measures typically drives the bulk of performance-based bonuses or penalties. The most important fall into four categories.

steps.description: Did patients receive recommended screenings and immunizations? Examples: mammography rates, colorectal cancer screening, flu vaccine administration, pediatric well-child visits. These measures track whether clinicians are proactively catching problems early.
steps.title: Preventive Care

steps.description: Are patients with ongoing conditions managed to target levels? Examples: HbA1c control for diabetics, blood pressure control for hypertension patients, statin therapy for cardiovascular patients. These measures track whether care prevents deterioration.
steps.title: Chronic Disease Management

steps.description: Do patients feel heard, respected, and well-informed? Measured via standardized CAHPS surveys. Tracks communication quality, care coordination experience, and overall satisfaction. Poor scores often signal care gaps.
steps.title: Patient Experience

steps.description: Are patients using the ER and hospital for things that could be handled in outpatient settings? Examples: ED visit rate for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions, 30-day readmission rate, potentially preventable admissions. High rates signal gaps in primary care access or management.
steps.title: Avoidable Utilization

body.title: The Four Domains of Clinical Quality in Value-Based Care

body.misconception: Quality measures are just bureaucratic checkboxes that distract from real clinical care.
body.reality: Well-designed quality measures are derived from clinical evidence. A practice that achieves high HbA1c control rates has fewer diabetic patients with amputations, kidney failure, and blindness. The measures exist because doing them consistently saves lives. The legitimate concern is ensuring that measures focus on the right things — and that they do not create perverse incentives of their own.

children.text: The most sophisticated VBC programs now move beyond process measures — did we do the right thing? — toward outcome measures: did the patient get better? Vermont's All-Payer Model tracks outcomes like population-level diabetes prevalence trends and preventable hospitalization rates, not just whether a doctor ordered a hemoglobin A1c test.
Population Health Management: Responsibility Beyond the Appointment

One of the most fundamental shifts in value-based care is moving from patient-by-patient thinking to population-level thinking. Under fee-for-service, a physician's responsibility begins when a patient walks through the door and ends when they leave. Under VBC, a care team is responsible for the health of an entire attributed patient panel — including the people who are not coming in.

body.analogy: A school principal does not just react to students who show up in her office with problems. She monitors attendance rates, tracks which students are falling behind, identifies patterns of absenteeism, and proactively reaches out to struggling families before a student drops out. She manages the entire school population — not just the ones who knock on her door.
body.bridge: Population health management works the same way. A VBC practice does not just treat patients who schedule appointments. It monitors the health status of its entire panel — flagging patients overdue for a screening, whose blood pressure has not been checked in 18 months, or whose recent ER visits suggest they are struggling to manage a chronic condition at home.
body.concept: Population health management

children.text: Population health management requires three things fee-for-service practices rarely had: data, staff, and proactive processes. The data comes from electronic health records and claims. The staff — care managers or medical assistants in expanded roles — conduct outreach to patients who need follow-up. The processes include monthly panel reviews, risk stratification algorithms, and care gap closure protocols.

stats.context: Consistently, the sickest 5% of patients account for roughly 50% of total healthcare spending. VBC practices identify and intensively manage this group. Source: AHRQ.
stats.label: Patients Drive 50% of Costs

stats.context: The CDC estimates that 70% of chronic disease burden is preventable through lifestyle changes and early intervention — exactly what population health management targets.
stats.label: Chronic Disease Is Preventable

stats.context: Patients enrolled in structured care management programs have 3x better adherence to treatment plans and significantly fewer ED visits. Source: Health Affairs, 2022.
stats.label: Impact of Care Management

body.title: Population Health by the Numbers

children.text: Risk stratification is the engine of population health management. Practices use algorithms — built into EHR systems or analytics platforms — to sort patients into tiers based on their likelihood of a high-cost clinical event in the next 6 to 12 months. High-risk patients get intensive care management: regular check-ins, home visits, medication reconciliation. Low-risk patients get preventive outreach: reminders for annual wellness visits and screenings.

body.body: ChenMed operates primary care clinics specifically designed for high-risk Medicare patients. Their model flips the standard formula: instead of seeing 24 patients per day in 15-minute slots, ChenMed physicians see 8 to 10 patients per day for 40-minute visits. Every patient has a dedicated care team. Transportation to appointments is provided. Patients receive monthly wellness visits even when they are feeling fine.
body.outcome: ChenMed patients have 30 to 40 percent fewer hospitalizations and emergency department visits than matched comparison groups. Source: Health Affairs, 2020.
body.source: Health Affairs, 2020; ChenMed internal outcomes reporting
body.title: ChenMed — Intensive Primary Care for High-Risk Seniors

children.text: Care Coordination: The Connective Tissue of Value-Based Care

The US healthcare system was built around specialization. Cardiologists manage hearts. Endocrinologists manage diabetes. Orthopedic surgeons manage joints. This works extraordinarily well for complex procedures and rare conditions. It works catastrophically poorly for the average Medicare patient with five chronic conditions who sees seven different specialists — none of whom talk to each other.

Care Coordination: The deliberate organization of patient care activities and the sharing of information among all participants to achieve safer, more effective care. It includes communication between providers, follow-up after transitions, medication reconciliation, and ensuring patients understand their care plan.

Poor care coordination is expensive and dangerous. When a cardiologist adds a new medication and does not know the patient's nephrologist recently changed a kidney medication, the combination can cause serious harm. When a hospital discharges a patient with instructions to 'schedule a follow-up within a week' but does not help make that appointment, the patient often does not go — and ends up back in the ER within 30 days.

stats.context: Poor coordination — duplicated tests, medication errors, missed follow-ups — costs the US an estimated $27.2 billion annually. Source: Annals of Internal Medicine.
stats.label: Annual Coordination Failure Cost

stats.context: More than half of US adults have at least 2 chronic conditions, requiring active coordination among multiple providers. Source: CDC, 2023.
stats.label: Adults with Multiple Chronic Conditions

stats.context: One in three patients reports experiencing at least one care coordination problem in the past two years. Source: Commonwealth Fund 2022 International Health Policy Survey.
stats.label: Patients Experience Coordination Failures

body.title: The Cost of Poor Care Coordination

children.text: Value-based care fixes this by making coordination an explicit responsibility with a named owner. The care coordinator — often a registered nurse, social worker, or medical assistant in an extended role — serves as the connective tissue between providers, between hospital and home, and between patient and care plan. Their job is to make sure nothing falls through the cracks.

steps.description: Weekly review of the patient panel with the care team. Flag patients overdue for follow-up, those who had a recent hospitalization, or whose risk score changed in the EHR. Decide who gets a proactive outreach call this week.
steps.title: Panel Review

steps.description: When a patient is discharged from the hospital, the coordinator calls within 48 to 72 hours: Did you fill your medications? Do you understand your discharge instructions? Is your follow-up appointment scheduled? Can you get there?
steps.title: Transition Management

steps.description: Ensure that specialist visit notes are shared with the primary care team. Follow up to confirm referrals were completed. Flag conflicting medication orders for physician review.
steps.title: Specialist Coordination

steps.description: At every transition point — admission, discharge, specialist visit — reconcile the patient's complete medication list. Polypharmacy is a leading cause of preventable harm, especially in older adults.
steps.title: Medication Reconciliation

steps.description: Help patients understand their care plan, set personal health goals, and navigate the health system. Activated patients — those who feel confident managing their own health — have significantly better outcomes and lower costs.
steps.title: Patient Activation

body.title: What a Care Coordinator Does in a VBC Practice

body.body: Vermont's Blueprint for Health embeds Community Health Teams in primary care practices across the state. Each CHT includes nurses, social workers, dietitians, and community health workers co-located with or closely partnered with primary care practices. When a practice flags a high-risk patient — perhaps a diabetic with three recent ER visits — the CHT mobilizes. They assess barriers such as no transportation, food insecurity, or depression, connect patients to community resources, and manage follow-up.
body.outcome: Blueprint practices with active CHT partnerships have shown significant reductions in preventable hospitalization rates and improvements in chronic disease management scores compared to non-Blueprint practices. Source: Vermont DVHA Blueprint evaluation reports.
body.source: Vermont Department of Vermont Health Access, Blueprint for Health Annual Reports
body.title: Vermont Blueprint for Health — Community Health Teams

children.text: Reducing Preventable Hospitalizations and Readmissions

Hospitalizations are the single largest driver of healthcare costs. A single inpatient stay for a Medicare patient costs, on average, more than $13,000. Many of those hospitalizations are for conditions that, if managed properly in an outpatient setting, should never have required a hospital bed. These are called ambulatory care-sensitive conditions — uncontrolled diabetes, COPD exacerbations, congestive heart failure, urinary tract infections.

Ambulatory Care-Sensitive Conditions (ACSCs): Medical conditions for which timely and appropriate outpatient care can prevent hospitalization. They include asthma, COPD, congestive heart failure, diabetes complications, and hypertension. High ACSC hospitalization rates signal that primary care access or quality is failing.

Value-based care contracts explicitly target ACSC hospitalization rates as a key performance indicator. A practice with a high ACSC rate is leaving money on the table — and more importantly, leaving patients in harm's way. Hospitalizations carry real clinical risk: hospital-acquired infections, medication errors, delirium in elderly patients, and the deconditioning from days of bed rest.

body.misconception: Keeping patients out of the hospital means denying them care they need.
body.reality: Reducing avoidable hospitalizations is about providing better care earlier — not rationing. A patient with COPD who sees their care coordinator monthly, has a written action plan for exacerbations, and can reach a nurse by phone when their breathing worsens is receiving better care than a patient who sees their doctor twice a year and lands in the hospital every winter. The goal is the right care in the right setting.

children.text: Readmissions are a related but distinct problem. A readmission occurs when a patient returns to the hospital within 30 days of discharge. The national Medicare readmission rate hovers around 15 to 20 percent. CMS began financially penalizing hospitals for excess readmissions in 2013 under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program. Since then, rates have declined — but remain stubbornly high.

steps.description: Use a standardized discharge checklist: review medications, schedule follow-up before discharge, provide written instructions in plain language at a 6th-grade reading level, confirm patient understanding via teach-back method.
steps.title: Structured Discharge Planning

steps.description: A nurse or care coordinator calls within 2 to 3 days of discharge. Confirm the patient is taking medications correctly, understands warning signs, and has a follow-up appointment. Early problem identification prevents crisis.
steps.title: 48 to 72 Hour Post-Discharge Call

steps.description: Patients seen by their primary care provider within 7 days of discharge have significantly lower readmission rates. Schedule this before the patient leaves the hospital whenever possible.
steps.title: Rapid Follow-Up Appointment

steps.description: Medication errors during care transitions are extremely common. Pharmacist-led or nurse-led reconciliation at discharge — comparing the inpatient list to what the patient took before admission — catches dangerous discrepancies.
steps.title: Medication Reconciliation

steps.description: Many readmissions are driven by social factors: no food at home, no transportation to the pharmacy, social isolation causing non-adherence. Transitional care programs that screen for social needs and connect patients to community resources see the largest readmission reductions.
steps.title: Address Social Needs

body.title: Evidence-Based Interventions That Reduce Readmissions

body.answer: Under a VBC contract, this patient represents an open care gap. The practice is responsible for her health outcomes even when she is not actively seeking care. The right response is proactive outreach: a care coordinator calls or sends a letter, offers scheduling assistance including transportation help if needed, and flags her for the team's panel review. If she has barriers to care — cost, transportation, work schedule — the team works to address them. Waiting for her to call is no longer acceptable practice.
body.hint: Think about what 'population health management' means — and who is responsible for patients who are NOT in the office.
body.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has not been seen in your practice in 14 months. Her last HbA1c was 9.2 — well above the target of 8.0. She is not scheduled for an upcoming appointment. Under a value-based care contract, what should happen?

children.text: The New Clinical Team: Roles That Value-Based Care Built

Value-based care has not replaced physicians. But it has radically expanded the clinical team around them. In a well-functioning VBC practice, the physician is the expert clinician and diagnostic mind — supported by a team that handles much of what was once shoved into a 15-minute visit or never done at all.

rows.left: Physician and medical assistant
rows.right: Physician, APP, RN care manager, care coordinator, social worker, CHW

rows.left: Patient calls us when something is wrong
rows.right: We proactively call patients between visits

rows.left: Chart review during the visit
rows.right: Panel management reports, daily risk score reviews, care gap dashboards

rows.left: Answering service or ER
rows.right: Nurse triage line, telehealth, after-hours urgent access

rows.left: Refer to external psychiatry — months of waiting
rows.right: Embedded behavioral health in primary care — same-day or next-day

body.title: The Care Team: Traditional vs. Value-Based

children.text: Advanced Practice Providers — nurse practitioners and physician assistants — play an expanded role in VBC models, often managing the bulk of stable chronic disease visits and wellness exams while physicians focus on complex diagnostic cases. This is team-based care: the right person, for the right patient, at the right time.
Vermont Clinical Programs: Value-Based Care in Action

Vermont is not just talking about value-based clinical care — it has been running the experiment for over a decade. The Blueprint for Health, launched in 2006, was one of the first statewide primary care transformation programs in the country. Every participating practice has undergone a formal practice transformation process: team-based care, patient registries, care coordination, and quality measurement.

Vermont's All-Payer Model, which launched in 2017 and runs through 2029, takes this further. OneCare Vermont — the state's accountable care organization — holds a global budget covering roughly a third of Vermont residents. Practices within OneCare are responsible for the total cost of care for their attributed population. Every preventable hospitalization and readmission is a financial signal that something in the clinical model needs to change.

body.body: Copley Hospital is a 25-bed critical access hospital in Morrisville serving a largely rural population. As a member of OneCare Vermont, Copley participates in population health management for its attributed patients. The hospital invested in a care transition program: every patient discharged is followed by a registered nurse for 30 days post-discharge, and a risk stratification tool identifies patients most likely to be readmitted for intensified outreach.
body.outcome: Copley has maintained readmission rates well below state and national averages for a hospital serving a comparably complex patient population — demonstrating that rural hospitals can achieve VBC goals with the right team structure.
body.source: Vermont DVHA All-Payer Model evaluation, OneCare Vermont reporting
body.title: Copley Hospital — Rural VBC in Morrisville, Vermont

children.text: The Clinical Case for Value-Based Care

For many clinicians, the shift to value-based care feels like an administrative imposition — more metrics to track, more documentation requirements, more meetings. That is a legitimate concern, and it reflects real transition pain. But the underlying logic of VBC aligns more closely with why most clinicians entered medicine than fee-for-service ever did.

Fee-for-service rewarded doing more. It paid well for procedures and poorly for conversations, care coordination, and prevention. It created a system where a physician who spent 45 minutes with a complex elderly patient on 12 medications was paid the same as a physician who spent 10 minutes. It created burnout among clinicians who wanted to practice relationship-based medicine but were trapped on a volume treadmill.

Physician burnout is at crisis levels: 63% of physicians report burnout symptoms, with administrative burden and loss of clinical autonomy cited as primary drivers. VBC, done well, can restore what drew clinicians to medicine: time with patients, team support, and a payment system that rewards doing what is actually right for the patient. Source: AMA National Burnout Survey, 2025.

body.answer: A preventable hospitalization (ambulatory care-sensitive admission) is a hospital stay that could have been avoided with timely outpatient care — like a COPD patient hospitalized for an exacerbation that could have been managed in the clinic with proper monitoring and medication adjustment. A readmission occurs when a patient returns to the hospital within 30 days of being discharged. Both matter under VBC because they represent clinical failures where the care system fell short. Both carry financial consequences: preventable admissions represent waste, and readmissions trigger CMS penalties under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program.
body.hint: Think about timing — one happens before the hospital stay, one happens after.
body.question: What is the difference between a 'preventable hospitalization' and a '30-day readmission,' and why do both matter under VBC contracts?

points: Fee-for-service pays for volume; value-based care pays for outcomes — this distinction reshapes every clinical workflow.
Quality measures in VBC track preventive care, chronic disease management, patient experience, and avoidable utilization.
Population health management means taking responsibility for patients who are NOT in the office — not just those who show up.
Care coordination is a clinical skill and a team function — it prevents the gaps between providers that cause harm and cost.
Preventable hospitalizations and readmissions are the most visible signals of clinical model failure — and the primary financial targets in VBC contracts.
Vermont's Blueprint for Health and All-Payer Model demonstrate that statewide clinical transformation is achievable with measurable results.
Value-based care, done well, can restore the relationship-centered practice that most clinicians entered medicine to provide.
body.title: Key Takeaways — Clinical Practice Under Value-Based Care

result.summary: Value-based care is not just a billing change — it reshapes what happens in every exam room, every hospital ward, and every care team huddle. This module explores how the shift from fee-for-service to value changes clinical workflows, team structures, quality measurement, population health management, and care coordination. If you practice, manage, or support clinical care in any setting, this module explains why the ground is shifting beneath your feet — and what to do about it.
result.title: From Volume to Value at the Bedside: How Value-Based Care Transforms Clinical Practice

children.text: In 2019, a landmark study published in the journal Science made a startling discovery. A widely used commercial algorithm — the kind that decides which patients get enrolled in intensive care management programs — was systematically underestimating the health needs of Black patients. Not by a little. The algorithm assigned Black patients the same risk score as white patients who were, on average, significantly healthier. The practical consequence: Black patients were less likely to be identified for the high-intensity care management they needed.

This module is the culmination of the course — and arguably its most important chapter. Value-based care promises to improve health for everyone by aligning incentives with outcomes rather than volume. But a payment reform that perpetuates or amplifies existing health inequities is not a solution. It is a new version of the same problem. Understanding where VBC fails on equity — and how to fix it — is not optional knowledge for healthcare leaders. It is the central challenge of our generation.
What Health Disparities Actually Look Like

A health disparity is a difference in health outcomes between population groups that is preventable, avoidable, and unjust. It is not just the observation that some groups are sicker than others — it is the recognition that those differences are not random. They reflect systematic disadvantages in access to healthcare, economic stability, education, safe housing, and healthy food.

Health Disparity: A preventable difference in the burden of disease, injury, violence, or opportunity to achieve optimal health between groups defined by race, ethnicity, income, education, disability, geography, or other social characteristics.

stats.context: Black Americans live 3.5 fewer years on average than white Americans. The gap widened to 6 years during COVID-19 due to disparate mortality rates. Source: CDC National Vital Statistics, 2023.
stats.label: Black-White Life Expectancy Gap

stats.context: Black women die from pregnancy-related causes at more than twice the rate of white women — even after controlling for income and education. Source: CDC, 2023.
stats.label: Maternal Mortality: Black vs. White

stats.context: Rural Americans have age-adjusted mortality rates 20% higher than urban Americans — a gap that has widened over the past two decades as rural hospital closures and provider shortages compound. Source: JAMA, 2024.
stats.label: Rural vs. Urban Mortality Gap

body.title: Health Disparities in the United States

children.text: These disparities are not primarily explained by genetic differences or individual health behaviors. The research literature is clear: the most powerful predictors of health outcomes are social and economic — where you live, what you earn, whether your neighborhood has a grocery store, whether you can take a day off work to see a doctor. These are the social determinants of health.
Social Determinants of Health: The 30 to 55 Percent of Outcomes We Rarely Treat

Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age that shape health outcomes. They include: income and wealth, educational attainment, employment quality, food security, housing stability and quality, transportation access, neighborhood safety, and social connectedness. The evidence that SDOH factors account for 30 to 55 percent of health outcome variation — compared to only 10 to 20 percent typically attributed to clinical care — is now firmly established in the research literature.

body.analogy: Imagine a leaky pipe in an apartment building. You can hire the best plumber in the city to mop up the water every day — and they will do excellent work. But if you never fix the pipe, the water keeps coming. Clinical care is the mopping. Social determinants are the pipe.
body.bridge: We spend enormous resources on excellent clinical care — the mopping — while chronically under-investing in the conditions that cause people to get sick in the first place. Value-based care, when designed well, starts asking about the pipe: it screens for food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers, and connects patients to resources that address those root causes.
body.concept: Social determinants versus clinical care

children.text: The most frequently screened SDOH domains in clinical settings are food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers, social isolation, interpersonal violence, and low health literacy. Standardized screening tools — including the Accountable Health Communities tool and the PRAPARE instrument — allow clinical teams to systematically identify SDOH needs during routine visits. But screening alone is insufficient. The critical next step — connecting patients to community resources that address those needs — is where most health systems still struggle.

stats.context: 34% of high-risk VBC patients screen positive for food insecurity. Food-insecure patients have a 2.1x higher risk of preventable hospitalization. Source: AHRQ, 2024.
stats.label: Food Insecurity Prevalence

stats.context: 29% of high-risk VBC patients report transportation barriers to care. Missing appointments due to lack of transportation drives medication non-adherence and delayed diagnosis. Source: AHRQ, 2024.
stats.label: Transportation Barriers

stats.context: Patients experiencing housing instability or homelessness have 4.2x higher risk of preventable hospitalization than stably housed patients. Source: NEJM, 2023.
stats.label: Housing Instability Risk Multiplier

body.title: Social Determinants in VBC Populations

children.text: Three Structural Equity Flaws in Current VBC Design

Value-based care was intended to be an equity intervention — aligning incentives with population health outcomes should, in theory, help the patients who need the most help. The reality is more complicated. Three structural equity problems have been consistently documented in the VBC research literature. Understanding all three is essential for any leader who wants to build VBC programs that advance rather than undermine health equity.

steps.description: Under most ACO attribution rules, providers who serve the most medically and socially complex patients will systematically generate worse performance on standard quality metrics — not because they deliver worse care, but because their patients face compounding barriers outside clinical control. This creates financial pressure to avoid accepting the most vulnerable patients, which is precisely the opposite of what VBC should incentivize.
steps.title: The Panel Selection Problem

steps.description: Standard VBC quality metrics do not adequately account for the social determinants of health that drive 30 to 55 percent of outcome variation. A physician serving a food-insecure, transportation-poor population will show worse HbA1c control rates than a physician serving a food-secure, transportation-rich population — even if the former is a dramatically better clinician. Unadjusted metrics penalize providers for serving high-need populations.
steps.title: The Metric Design Problem

steps.description: The organizations with the greatest ability to invest in care management infrastructure — large health systems, well-capitalized ACOs, urban medical centers — are not the organizations serving the highest-need populations. Rural safety-net providers and Federally Qualified Health Centers serving predominantly low-income and minority populations often lack the capital to build the VBC infrastructure that would most benefit their patients.
steps.title: The Investment Allocation Problem

body.title: Three Structural Equity Flaws in VBC

children.text: The panel selection problem is the most empirically documented. A 2024 study in Health Affairs found that ACOs serving the highest quartile of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — were 2.3 times more likely to exit MSSP within three years than ACOs serving lower proportions of dual-eligible patients. The program's financial structure creates systematic pressure against serving the most vulnerable populations.

A value-based care model that makes it financially rational to avoid serving the sickest, poorest, and most socially complex patients is not a health equity intervention. It is a health equity obstruction wearing the language of reform. Getting the incentives right requires explicit equity design — not just good intentions layered on top of metrics that were built for a different patient population.
SDOH Risk Adjustment: Making the Metrics Fair

The metric design problem — the failure of standard quality metrics to account for social determinants — is the most technically solvable of VBC's equity challenges. SDOH risk adjustment means modifying performance benchmarks to account for the social complexity of the patient population being served, so that providers are compared to peers serving similar populations rather than to the national average.

CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the 2022 MSSP final rule, which introduced a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that increases spending benchmarks for ACOs serving high proportions of patients with low-income subsidy status. This acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively. However, the 3.5 percent adjustment ceiling is widely considered insufficient by health equity researchers — and it uses low-income subsidy status as an imperfect proxy for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation.

rows.left: Low-income subsidy status (proxy for poverty)
rows.right: Area Deprivation Index + Z-code utilization + CHW encounter data

rows.left: Up to 3.5% benchmark increase
rows.right: 8 to 12% adjustment based on SDOH cost impact evidence

rows.left: Medicare enrollment data (limited)
rows.right: EHR SDOH screening data + census social vulnerability index

rows.left: Medicare fee-for-service only
rows.right: All payers including Medicaid and commercial

rows.left: Aggregate performance reporting
rows.right: Disaggregated reporting by race, ethnicity, income, and geography required

body.title: SDOH Risk Adjustment: Current CMS Approach vs. What Researchers Recommend

children.text: CMS has committed to expanding SDOH risk adjustment methodology in the 2026 MSSP final rule, with proposals to incorporate Area Deprivation Index scores, Z-code utilization rates from EHR screenings, and community health worker encounter data as additional adjustment factors. These changes are meaningful but still incomplete. The policy change required to make VBC metrics truly equitable will require sustained advocacy from providers who are experiencing the consequences of inadequate adjustment directly.

body.misconception: If we improve clinical quality across the board, health disparities will naturally narrow.
body.reality: Research consistently shows that quality improvement programs that do not explicitly target disparities can widen them. When a health system improves its overall diabetes control rates, the improvement is often concentrated among the most engaged, most resource-rich patients — while the most vulnerable patients remain unchanged or worsen. Closing disparities requires measuring them separately, targeting interventions at high-disparity populations, and tracking equity-specific outcomes, not just aggregate averages.

children.text: Community Health Workers: The Most Powerful Equity Tool in VBC

Community health workers — frontline public health workers who are typically members of the communities they serve, with lived experience of the social and health challenges those communities face — are emerging as the most powerful equity tool in value-based care. Where clinical care coordinators manage disease processes and care transitions, CHWs address the social and environmental factors that determine whether clinical interventions succeed.

Community Health Worker (CHW): A frontline public health worker who is a trusted member of and has a close understanding of the community being served. CHWs serve as a bridge between health and social services and the communities they serve, reduce cultural and social barriers to care, and provide health education, advocacy, and social support in community settings. They are NOT case managers or care coordinators — the community trust and cultural competence that makes their work effective must be lived, not credentialed.

What makes CHWs distinctive — and irreplaceable — is trust. In communities that have historically had reason to distrust institutional medicine, a CHW who grew up in the neighborhood, speaks the language, and has navigated the same systems can accomplish what no clinical protocol can. They connect patients to food assistance programs, navigate housing resources, provide transportation to appointments, and serve as advocates within a healthcare system that can feel foreign and hostile to those who most need it.

stats.context: A 2024 meta-analysis of 47 RCTs found CHW programs targeting high-risk populations produced an average 22% reduction in preventable hospitalizations. Source: AJPH, 2024.
stats.label: Reduction in Preventable Hospitalizations

stats.context: CHW programs consistently show a 4-to-1 return on investment — the highest ROI of any care management intervention type studied. Source: Health Affairs, 2023.
stats.label: CHW Return on Investment

stats.context: CHW programs targeting high-risk populations show a 31% improvement in chronic disease monitoring completion rates — exceeding care coordinator programs alone. Source: AJPH, 2024.
stats.label: Chronic Disease Monitoring Improvement

body.title: The Evidence for Community Health Workers

children.text: Despite this evidence base, CHW integration into VBC programs has been slower than warranted, primarily because of reimbursement barriers. Most fee-for-service billing structures do not include a direct reimbursement pathway for CHW services, requiring VBC organizations to fund CHW positions out of shared savings or grants. This creates funding fragility — organizations that cannot sustain CHW positions between shared savings payments cycle through workforce disruption that undermines the relationship continuity that makes CHW programs effective.

CMS has taken meaningful steps to address this. The 2024 Medicaid CHW Coverage Rule created a federal minimum standard requiring all state Medicaid programs to provide reimbursement for defined CHW services by 2026. The AHEAD Model's health equity investment fund provides direct CHW program funding in participating states. Vermont, as an AHEAD participant, has an explicit CHW funding stream tied to the All-Payer Model performance requirements.

body.body: Roots Community Health Center in Oakland, California serves a predominantly Black and low-income patient population. Their CHW program places community health workers in every primary care team. CHWs conduct SDOH screenings, make home visits for high-risk patients, connect patients to food and housing resources, attend medical appointments as patient advocates, and provide health education in culturally relevant formats. CHWs are paid employees with full benefits — not volunteers or contractors — reflecting the organization's commitment to workforce stability.
body.outcome: Roots patients with CHW engagement have 40% lower preventable hospitalization rates than demographically matched patients in the surrounding area, and significantly higher rates of completing preventive screenings. Source: Roots Community Health Center outcome reporting, 2024.
body.source: Roots Community Health Center, UCSF Center for Excellence in Primary Care evaluation, 2024
body.title: Roots Community Health Center — CHWs as Clinical Infrastructure

children.text: Rural and Geographic Equity: The Invisible Disparity

Healthcare equity discussions in the United States have historically focused primarily on racial and ethnic disparities — and for important reasons. But a parallel geographic equity crisis receives far less policy attention: the systematic disadvantage faced by rural Americans in healthcare access, provider supply, and health outcomes relative to their urban peers.

Rural Americans are more likely to die from the five leading causes of preventable death — heart disease, cancer, unintentional injury, chronic lower respiratory disease, and stroke. They have fewer physicians per capita, longer travel distances to care, higher rates of uninsurance, and significantly lower rates of receiving recommended preventive services. And they are, as documented in the Technology module, disproportionately outside the VBC system entirely — receiving care under fee-for-service Medicare with its documented incentive failures.

stats.context: Only 23% of rural Critical Access Hospital service areas are covered by an MSSP ACO, compared to 71% of urban hospital referral regions. Rural patients are disproportionately in fee-for-service. Source: CMS, 2025.
stats.label: Rural CAH Areas in MSSP ACOs

stats.context: 138 rural hospitals have closed since 2010, leaving millions of rural Americans further from emergency, obstetric, and inpatient care. Source: Chartis Center for Rural Health, 2025.
stats.label: Rural Hospital Closures Since 2010

stats.context: 62% of rural counties have no psychiatrist — forcing rural residents to travel hours for mental health care or go without. Behavioral health comorbidities are a major driver of preventable hospitalizations. Source: HRSA, 2025.
stats.label: Rural Mental Health Provider Shortage

body.title: Rural Health Equity Gaps

children.text: Vermont's Equity Landscape: Progress and Persistent Gaps

Vermont's All-Payer Model includes an explicit health equity performance requirement — a condition not present in most VBC programs nationally. The AHEAD Model requires participating states to establish measurable health equity goals and report progress annually. Vermont's current equity focus areas include reducing rural-urban disparities in preventive care rates, improving mental health access in rural counties, and addressing the health needs of Vermont's growing refugee and immigrant populations.

Vermont's refugee and immigrant populations — concentrated primarily in Burlington, Winooski, and Rutland — face compounding health equity challenges: language barriers, cultural differences in health-seeking behavior, immigration status concerns, trauma histories from displacement and persecution, and limited familiarity with a healthcare system very different from those in their countries of origin. Vermont's Blueprint for Health has piloted culturally adapted CHW programs for refugee communities, but coverage remains incomplete.

Vermont's Abenaki and other indigenous communities face health disparities that reflect both geographic isolation and historical trauma with healthcare institutions. The legacy of forced assimilation, medical experimentation, and involuntary sterilization programs has created well-founded distrust of the healthcare system that no appointment reminder or care coordinator can overcome. Rebuilding trust with indigenous communities requires sustained, community-led engagement over years — not program cycles.

body.body: Vermont has invested in a public-facing health equity dashboard that disaggregates health outcome data by race, ethnicity, income, and geography — making disparities visible to policymakers, providers, and communities. The dashboard tracks preventable hospitalization rates, chronic disease control metrics, maternal and infant health outcomes, and behavioral health utilization by population group. Vermont is one of only a handful of states with this level of equity data transparency at the state level.
body.outcome: Vermont's equity dashboard has become a policy accountability tool — allowing advocates and legislators to track whether All-Payer Model investments are narrowing identified disparities, and to demand explanations when they are not. Source: Vermont Department of Health, Racial and Ethnic Health Equity Dashboard, 2025.
body.title: Vermont Department of Health — Racial and Ethnic Health Equity Dashboard

body.misconception: Our organization serves everyone equally — we do not have health disparities here.
body.reality: Every healthcare organization serves patients with different outcomes based on race, income, and geography. The question is not whether disparities exist — it is whether you have measured them. Organizations that only report aggregate quality performance systematically miss disparities that are present in the underlying data. If you have not disaggregated your quality metrics by race, ethnicity, and income, you do not know your equity performance. You know your average performance.

children.text: AI Bias in Risk Stratification: Technology as an Equity Threat

The 2019 Science study described at the opening of this module identified a mechanism that explains the algorithmic underestimation of Black patients' health needs: the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health need. Black patients historically had lower healthcare costs — not because they were healthier, but because structural barriers had historically limited their access to care. The algorithm encoded a history of discrimination as a measure of health. The practical consequence: Black patients were significantly less likely to be flagged for high-intensity care management programs.

This problem has been replicated for other demographic groups and other algorithm types. As AI-powered risk stratification tools become increasingly central to VBC care management, the equity risk posed by biased training data becomes increasingly urgent. A healthcare organization that deploys an AI risk model without auditing it for demographic performance disparities is potentially using technology to automate discrimination at scale.

Technology Governance Requirement: Any healthcare organization deploying an AI risk stratification tool in a VBC context has an ethical and, increasingly, a legal obligation to audit the tool for demographic performance disparities before deployment. The audit should examine whether the model's accuracy varies significantly across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic subgroups. If it does, the organization must select a different model, recalibrate it for its specific population, or supplement algorithmic scores with clinical and social worker judgment for populations where the algorithm performs poorly.
Building Equity-Centered VBC: What It Actually Takes

Building a VBC program that genuinely advances health equity rather than performing it in marketing materials requires design choices that are sometimes in tension with the financial optimization logic that drives most VBC strategy discussions. Equity-centered VBC design requires accepting lower short-term shared savings in exchange for serving populations whose care management needs are higher. It requires investing in CHW infrastructure before guaranteed funding arrives. It requires choosing quality metrics that are SDOH-adjusted rather than metrics that produce better scores simply because you serve a more advantaged population.

steps.description: Adopt the CMS Accountable Health Communities screening tool or PRAPARE instrument as a standard clinical workflow for all attributed VBC patients. SDOH data that is not systematically collected cannot be incorporated into risk adjustment, care planning, or community investment decisions. Start with your highest-risk quartile and expand from there.
steps.title: Implement Systematic SDOH Screening

steps.description: Disaggregate all quality metric performance data by race, ethnicity, income level, and geography before reporting aggregate performance. Organizations that only examine aggregate quality scores systematically miss equity disparities present in the underlying data — disparities that will worsen without targeted intervention.
steps.title: Disaggregate Your Quality Metrics

steps.description: If you use AI-powered risk stratification, conduct a demographic equity audit before the next contract cycle. Examine whether the model's accuracy varies by race, income, and geography. If it does, address it — through vendor recalibration, supplemental clinical judgment, or a different tool.
steps.title: Audit Your Risk Stratification Algorithms

steps.description: The CHW ROI evidence and the 2024 Medicaid CHW Coverage Rule make 2026 the right year to build or expand a CHW program. Hire CHWs with lived experience of the specific communities and social challenges your highest-need patients face. Do not hire case managers and call them CHWs.
steps.title: Build a CHW Program Now

steps.description: Advocate explicitly for SDOH risk adjustment in every VBC contract negotiation with payers and in every CMS rulemaking comment you submit. The policy change required to fix the metric design problem will not happen without sustained, evidence-based advocacy from providers who are experiencing its consequences directly.
steps.title: Advocate for SDOH Risk Adjustment

body.title: Five Concrete Steps Toward Equity-Centered VBC

body.answer: Not without disaggregating the data. If the improvement was distributed equally across all demographic groups — white, Black, Latino, low-income, rural — then the organization has genuinely improved equity. But the research literature consistently shows that quality improvement programs that do not explicitly target disparate populations tend to improve aggregate rates by improving outcomes for the most engaged, most resource-rich patients while leaving the most vulnerable behind. If the system's HbA1c improvement was concentrated among higher-income, white patients while control rates for low-income Black and rural patients remained flat or worsened, the aggregate improvement actually reflects a widening disparity. The only way to know is to look at the disaggregated data — and report it publicly.
body.hint: Think about what aggregate statistics can hide.
body.question: A health system reports that its overall HbA1c control rate for diabetic patients has improved from 61% to 74% over three years — a significant achievement. Should leadership declare victory on diabetes equity?

body.answer: The CHW should escalate her observation to clinical and data analytics leadership as a potential algorithmic bias issue — this is exactly the kind of frontline signal that formal AI equity audits are designed to detect. The structural issue is that AI risk stratification models are trained on historical utilization data, and if Black patients in the training dataset historically had lower healthcare utilization due to access barriers — not because they were healthier — the model will have learned to associate lower utilization with lower risk, systematically underestimating the risk of Black patients. This is the bias mechanism identified in the 2019 Obermeyer et al. Science study. The organization should conduct a formal demographic equity audit of the algorithm and report findings to leadership. If the bias is confirmed, the tool must be recalibrated, replaced, or supplemented with clinical judgment for affected populations.
body.hint: Think about the 2019 Science study and how AI models are trained.
body.question: A community health worker in your organization reports that a risk stratification algorithm has been flagging very few Black patients on her panel for high-intensity care management — even patients she knows from clinical experience to be at high risk. What should she do, and what structural issue does this reflect?

children.text: Course Conclusion: What Value-Based Care Can and Cannot Do

Across six modules, this course has examined value-based care through every lens that matters: the economic incentive logic that makes it necessary, the policy architecture that makes it operational, the economics that determine whether it saves money, the technology that makes it analytically possible, the clinical model that determines whether it actually improves patient outcomes, and the equity design requirements that determine whether it works for everyone. The honest conclusion is nuanced but ultimately optimistic.

Value-based care, when designed well, implemented with adequate infrastructure, and evaluated with appropriate equity metrics, produces meaningfully better clinical outcomes than fee-for-service at lower total cost. The fee-for-service system that currently dominates American healthcare is producing the worst outcomes per dollar of any wealthy nation on earth. The most credible available alternative — paying for health rather than for activity — is demonstrably capable of doing better.

What value-based care cannot do, on its own, is eliminate the social determinants of health that account for 30 to 55 percent of outcome variation. It cannot provide affordable housing, food security, safe neighborhoods, or living wages — the most powerful health interventions available at the population level. These are not arguments against value-based care. They are arguments for building it with sufficient ambition, equity intentionality, and long-term commitment to match the scale of the problem it is trying to solve.

Vermont's AHEAD Model participation is the most ambitious attempt in state history to align payment incentives, equity goals, and clinical infrastructure toward a single measurable objective: a healthier population at sustainable cost. Whether it succeeds will depend on the willingness of providers, payers, policymakers, and community organizations to make the hard design choices that equity-centered VBC requires.

points: Health disparities are preventable differences in outcomes between population groups — driven primarily by social determinants, not genetics or individual behavior.
Social determinants of health account for 30 to 55 percent of health outcome variation, yet remain largely outside clinical care delivery.
Three structural equity flaws in current VBC design: the panel selection problem, the metric design problem, and the investment allocation problem.
SDOH risk adjustment is the technical fix for inequitable quality metrics — but the current CMS adjustment is insufficient in magnitude and scope.
Community health workers are the most powerful equity tool in VBC, with a 4-to-1 ROI and 22% reduction in preventable hospitalizations in high-need populations.
AI risk stratification tools can encode and automate historical discrimination — demographic equity audits before deployment are ethically and increasingly legally required.
Disaggregating quality metrics by race, income, and geography is not optional — aggregate improvement can mask widening disparities beneath the average.
Vermont's AHEAD Model equity requirements represent the most ambitious state-level commitment to equity-centered VBC in the country — and a national model worth watching.
body.title: Key Takeaways — Health Equity and Value-Based Care

children.text: Imagine paying a mechanic every time they touched your car — whether or not it ran better afterward. Now imagine that mechanic's salary depended entirely on how many parts they replaced, not on whether your car actually worked. You would quickly end up with a very expensive car that still broke down constantly. This, in essence, is how the United States pays for healthcare.

The US spent $4.5 trillion on healthcare in 2022 — roughly $13,493 per person, and 18.3 percent of the entire national economy. That is more than any other high-income country, by a wide margin. Switzerland, the second-highest spender, dedicates about 11.3 percent of its GDP to health. Germany spends 12.8 percent. Canada spends 12.2 percent.

stats.context: 18.3% of GDP — the highest of any nation on earth. Source: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, 2023.
stats.label: US Healthcare Spending (2022)

stats.context: Behind most peer nations in life expectancy, infant mortality, and chronic disease burden. Source: World Health Organization.
stats.label: US Health Outcomes Ranking

stats.context: JAMA 2019: $760B–$935B per year on unnecessary or low-value care — roughly 1 in 3 dollars spent.
stats.label: Estimated Waste in US Healthcare

body.title: The US Healthcare Spending Paradox

children.text: And yet — despite outspending every peer nation — the US ranks 37th in overall health outcomes according to the World Health Organization. Americans live shorter lives than citizens of 40 other countries. The US infant mortality rate is nearly double that of Finland. Preventable deaths from conditions like diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease occur at far higher rates here than in comparable wealthy nations.
How Did We Get Here? Understanding Fee-for-Service

To understand why America spends so much and gets so little, you need to understand the payment system that drives almost every clinical decision made in the country. That system is called fee-for-service, often abbreviated FFS. Fee-for-service has been the dominant payment model for American medicine since the mid-20th century.

Fee-for-Service (FFS): A payment model in which healthcare providers are paid separately for each service they deliver — each office visit, each test, each procedure, each hospital day. Payment is triggered by doing something, not by whether the patient gets better.

Here is how it works in practice: a physician, hospital, or other provider submits a claim to an insurer — Medicare, Medicaid, or a private insurer — using standardized billing codes called CPT codes. Each code corresponds to a specific service: a visit, a blood draw, an MRI, a surgical procedure. The insurer reviews the claim and pays a set rate for each code. The provider's revenue depends entirely on how many services they bill, not on whether those services helped the patient.

body.analogy: Imagine a restaurant that charged you for every time a server walked past your table — whether they brought food, refilled your water, or just walked by. The restaurant's income would depend not on how satisfying your meal was, but on how many times staff interacted with you. Servers would be incentivized to walk past your table as often as possible, whether you needed anything or not.
body.bridge: In healthcare, this translates into providers ordering more tests, scheduling more follow-up visits, and performing more procedures — because each one generates revenue. Keeping a patient healthy and out of the office is financially penalized under this model.
body.concept: Fee-for-Service Payment

children.text: The Perverse Incentives of Fee-for-Service

The word 'perverse' in economics means an incentive that pushes behavior in the opposite direction from what you actually want. Fee-for-service is full of perverse incentives. Consider what happens when a hospital successfully reduces readmissions by improving care coordination after discharge. Under fee-for-service, that hospital just reduced its own revenue — because each readmission generates thousands of dollars in billing.

Or consider preventive care. A primary care physician who spends an extra 30 minutes helping a diabetic patient understand diet, exercise, and medication adherence may prevent that patient from ever needing a $50,000 hospitalization. Under fee-for-service, the physician is paid a modest office visit fee for those 30 minutes. The hospital that would have done the expensive hospitalization loses revenue. The system as a whole saves money — but the individual providers doing the right thing are financially worse off.

Under fee-for-service, prevention is a cost center, not a revenue source. Providers are paid to treat illness, not to prevent it. This single fact explains more about America's healthcare crisis than almost any other.

stats.context: The largest single category of healthcare waste — driven by billing complexity and multi-payer administrative burden.
stats.label: Administrative Complexity Waste

stats.context: Tests, procedures, and hospital stays that clinical evidence shows don't meaningfully improve outcomes.
stats.label: Overtreatment and Low-Value Care

stats.context: Prices that significantly exceed benchmarks for identical services in other markets.
stats.label: Pricing Failure Waste

body.title: The True Cost of Fee-for-Service Waste (JAMA, 2019)

children.text: Defining Value-Based Care: A Fundamentally Different Approach

Value-based care, sometimes called value-based payment or value-based purchasing, is a healthcare delivery and payment model in which providers are paid based on patient health outcomes rather than the volume of services provided. The key word is 'value' — defined in healthcare as the quality of care delivered divided by the cost of delivering it.

Value-Based Care: A payment and delivery model where providers earn more when they keep patients healthier, improve quality, and reduce unnecessary costs — and earn less when they deliver high volumes of low-quality or unnecessary care. The core formula: Value = Quality / Cost.

This seems like a simple idea — pay for results, not for activity. But implementing it requires solving genuinely hard problems: How do you measure quality? How do you attribute outcomes to specific providers when patients see many doctors? How do you prevent providers from avoiding sick patients to protect their quality scores? How do you account for the fact that some patients have more complex needs than others? These are the questions that value-based payment models are designed to address.

rows.right: Patient outcomes achieved

rows.left: Do more — more visits, tests, procedures
rows.right: Keep patients healthier with fewer interventions

rows.right: Provider shares in savings and losses

body.title: Fee-for-Service vs. Value-Based Care at a Glance

children.text: The Four Main Categories of Value-Based Payment Models

Value-based care is not a single payment model — it is a family of models that shift payment from volume to value in different ways and to different degrees. Think of a spectrum: at one end is pure fee-for-service with no accountability for outcomes; at the other end is full capitation where providers take on complete financial responsibility for a population's health. Most VBC models sit somewhere in between.
Category 1: Pay-for-Performance

Pay-for-performance (P4P) is the simplest form of value-based payment. Providers still get paid fee-for-service for each service, but they receive bonuses for hitting quality targets — or face penalties for missing them. Examples include CMS's Hospital Value-Based Purchasing program, which adjusts Medicare payments to hospitals based on quality scores, and the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) for physicians.
Category 2: Accountable Care Organizations and Shared Savings

Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are networks of doctors, hospitals, and other providers that work together to coordinate care for a defined group of patients. The ACO is given a benchmark spending target. If the ACO spends less than the benchmark while maintaining quality, it shares in those savings. This model keeps the fee-for-service billing infrastructure but adds accountability for total cost of care.

Medicare ACOs generated $1.87 billion in net savings for Medicare in 2022, according to CMS. As of 2024, more than 480 ACOs participate in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, covering over 11 million beneficiaries. Vermont's OneCare Vermont is an ACO that serves both Medicare and Medicaid populations — and is the centerpiece of the state's nationally recognized All-Payer Model.
Category 3: Bundled Payments

Bundled payments group all the costs for a single episode of care — say, a hip replacement surgery plus the 90 days of recovery — into one fixed payment. All providers involved must share that single payment. If they deliver great care efficiently and spend less than the bundle price, they keep the difference. If they spend more, they lose money. This directly incentivizes coordination across the care team.
Category 4: Capitation and Global Budgets

Capitation is the most fundamental shift: providers receive a fixed monthly payment per patient to cover all their care, regardless of how many services that patient uses. The provider takes on complete financial responsibility — called full risk — for the patient's health. If the patient stays healthy and uses few services, the provider keeps the surplus. Global budgets take this idea to the health-system level: an entire hospital or health system receives a fixed annual budget to care for a defined population.

children.text: Vermont: A National Laboratory for Value-Based Care

Vermont is the only state in the nation operating an approved All-Payer Accountable Care Organization Model — a program that brings Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance under a single set of quality and spending targets for the first time in American history. This makes Vermont uniquely important to anyone studying value-based care. What Vermont learns, the nation watches.

The Vermont All-Payer ACO Model was approved by CMS in 2016 and launched in January 2017. At its center is OneCare Vermont, a statewide ACO that contracts with hospitals, physicians, and community organizations across the state. OneCare Vermont currently serves approximately 240,000 Vermonters — nearly 40 percent of the state's population — through its attributed beneficiary program.

body.body: OneCare Vermont launched in 2017 as the operational vehicle for Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model. It serves Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance members under a unified set of quality metrics and spending targets. The organization works with 119 primary care practices, 14 hospitals, and hundreds of community providers across the state to coordinate care for approximately 240,000 attributed Vermonters. Unlike a traditional insurer, OneCare Vermont does not manage claims — instead, it manages the health of a population, investing in care coordination, social services navigation, and community health workers.
body.outcome: In performance years where OneCare met quality targets, Vermont demonstrated lower-than-expected spending growth — a meaningful achievement given Vermont's older, sicker-than-average, and largely rural population.
body.source: Vermont Agency of Administration / CMS All-Payer Model Performance Reports, 2017–2024
body.title: OneCare Vermont: Vermont's Statewide ACO

children.text: The Green Mountain Care Board

Vermont's All-Payer Model is overseen by the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB), a state agency with broad authority to regulate healthcare costs, review hospital budgets, and set statewide health spending targets. The GMCB is one of the most powerful state-level healthcare cost-control bodies in the nation. It reviews and approves hospital budgets every year — meaning hospitals cannot simply raise prices without regulatory approval.

This combination — a statewide ACO (OneCare Vermont) operating under regulatory oversight (GMCB), with a federal partnership (CMS All-Payer Model) — makes Vermont's healthcare system genuinely unique. Understanding how it works, and why it was designed this way, is one of the most valuable things you can learn if you work in Vermont healthcare.

body.body: The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), created by the Affordable Care Act in 2012 and operated by CMS, is the largest ACO program in the world. Participating ACOs take responsibility for the total cost and quality of care for their attributed Medicare beneficiaries. ACOs that spend below their benchmark while meeting quality standards share a portion of savings with Medicare. Those in higher-risk tracks may also face penalties for overspending.
body.outcome: In 2022, Medicare ACOs generated $1.87 billion in net savings for Medicare while serving 11 million beneficiaries. ACOs in higher-risk tracks consistently outperformed lower-risk tracks, demonstrating that meaningful financial accountability improves performance.
body.source: CMS Medicare Shared Savings Program 2022 Performance Year Results, published 2023
body.title: Medicare Shared Savings Program: The Largest VBC Program in the World

children.text: Why This Matters to You, Wherever You Work

If you are a nurse, this transformation changes what your work looks like. Value-based care prioritizes care coordination, discharge planning, chronic disease management, and patient education — all activities that nurses are uniquely positioned to lead. Under fee-for-service, a nurse who prevented a readmission by spending extra time on discharge education was not generating revenue. Under VBC, that same nurse is helping the organization succeed financially.

If you are a hospital administrator, VBC means thinking differently about your budget. Revenue is no longer simply a function of volume. Quality scores, total cost of care for your population, and care coordination infrastructure become central financial drivers. Understanding which patients are at highest risk of expensive preventable events — and investing in keeping them well — becomes essential to financial sustainability.

body.analogy: Transitioning from fee-for-service to value-based care is like converting a city from individual car ownership to a public transit system while everyone is still driving to work. You cannot shut down all the roads at once — you have to build the trains while traffic is still running, convince people the new system is better, and gradually shift incentives until the old system is obsolete.
body.bridge: In healthcare, providers must continue billing fee-for-service while simultaneously building the care coordination, data, and team infrastructure that VBC requires. Organizations that invest in both simultaneously face real financial strain during the transition period — but those that do not invest will be left behind.
body.concept: The VBC Transition

body.misconception: Value-based care means providers just get paid less for doing the same work.
body.reality: VBC redistributes financial incentives — it does not simply cut payments. Providers who deliver high-quality, efficient, well-coordinated care can earn significantly more under VBC than under fee-for-service. The providers who lose money are those who were generating revenue through high volumes of low-value care.

body.misconception: Value-based care is a cost-cutting measure that will hurt patients by rationing necessary care.
body.reality: The evidence shows the opposite: VBC programs consistently improve quality scores, reduce preventable hospitalizations, and increase preventive care rates. The goal is to eliminate waste and low-value care — not necessary care. Patients in high-performing ACOs receive more preventive services, not fewer essential treatments.

children.text: What You Will Learn in This Course

This course has six modules, each building on the last. Module 2 dives into the economics: how money flows through the healthcare system and the mechanics of each major payment model in depth. Module 3 focuses on clinical practice: how VBC changes the daily reality of delivering care. Module 4 examines the policy landscape: the federal programs and Vermont-specific structures that govern the transition. Module 5 covers technology: the data infrastructure that makes VBC possible. Module 6 addresses the most urgent challenge: health equity, and how VBC can be designed to reduce — rather than worsen — the disparities that exist in every healthcare system.

By the end of this course, you will have a sophisticated understanding of one of the most consequential transformations happening in American healthcare. You will understand not just what value-based care is, but why it was designed the way it is, how it plays out in real clinical settings, and what it means for patients, providers, and communities across Vermont and the nation.

The question is no longer whether healthcare should move to value-based payment — it is how fast and how completely. Every major payer, every major health system, and every serious policymaker now agrees that fee-for-service as the dominant payment model is unsustainable. The only debate is about the pace and mechanics of transition.

body.answer: Under fee-for-service, the hospital's revenue decreases — each avoided readmission represents a lost billing opportunity worth thousands of dollars. Under a value-based ACO model, the hospital's financial performance improves — lower spending relative to the benchmark means a larger share of savings, and better quality scores protect or increase future payment rates. This contrast illustrates the core difference between the two systems: FFS rewards volume, VBC rewards outcomes.
body.hint: Think about what generates revenue under each model.
body.question: A hospital reduces readmissions by 15% through an improved discharge education program. Under fee-for-service, what happens to the hospital's revenue? Under a value-based ACO model, what happens?

body.answer: Vermont is the only state operating an approved All-Payer ACO Model — meaning Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance all operate under a single set of unified quality and spending targets. In every other state, these payers operate independently with different rules, creating fragmentation that makes coordinated care harder. Vermont's model, anchored by OneCare Vermont and overseen by the Green Mountain Care Board, attempts to align all payers behind shared goals for the first time in American history.

points: The US spends $4.5 trillion on healthcare (18.3% of GDP) — more than any nation — yet ranks 37th in health outcomes, a paradox driven largely by fee-for-service payment incentives.

Fee-for-service pays providers per service delivered, creating perverse incentives to do more regardless of whether it helps patients. Prevention, coordination, and efficiency are financially penalized.
Value-based care is a family of payment models that pay for outcomes rather than volume — aligning provider incentives with patient health. The core formula: Value = Quality / Cost.
The four main VBC model categories are pay-for-performance, shared savings ACOs, bundled payments, and capitation/global budgets — each shifting more financial risk and accountability to providers.

Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model — the only one of its kind in the US — makes Vermont a national laboratory for value-based care transformation, with OneCare Vermont serving approximately 240,000 Vermonters.
The transition from FFS to VBC requires changes in payment contracts, data infrastructure, clinical workflows, and organizational culture — and is a multi-decade journey, not a single event.
