children.text: After a decade of Medicare ACO experimentation, bundled payments, and quality measurement programs, the US healthcare system has learned a great deal about what value-based care can and cannot achieve in voluntary, programmatic form. The 2021 CMMI strategic refresh — published 10 years after the ACA created CMMI — represented an unusually honest accounting of what had worked, what had failed, and what a more ambitious next decade of VBC reform required. The refresh set a bold target: by 2030, all Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries and most Medicaid beneficiaries should be in an accountable care relationship where a provider takes responsibility for their total cost and quality of care. That goal, and the policy architecture being built to achieve it, defines the current frontier of value-based care in America.
CMMI's 2021 Strategic Reset: The Five Objectives

The 2021 CMMI strategic refresh organized its ambitions around five objectives that reflect the lessons of the first decade. The objectives were: (1) drive accountable care at scale, with the 2030 goal of universal accountable care relationships; (2) advance health equity through every model, with equity built into model design rather than appended as a stratification requirement; (3) support care innovations beyond the hospital, with emphasis on behavioral health, primary care, and home-based care; (4) align payment incentives across payers, recognizing that Medicare-only models fail to capture the full potential of care transformation; and (5) improve quality by changing what is measured, moving toward outcomes and equity metrics. These objectives define the policy agenda that subsequent CMMI models — ACO REACH, Primary Care First, GUIDE — are designed to advance.
ACO REACH: Replacing Direct Contracting with Equity Requirements

The Global and Professional Direct Contracting (GPDC) model, launched by the prior CMS administration in 2020, attracted significant private equity participation and criticism that it would accelerate privatization of traditional Medicare. CMMI redesigned the model as ACO Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health (ACO REACH), launching in January 2023 with two major changes: enhanced equity requirements and modified ownership restrictions intended to limit pure financial entities without provider relationships from dominating participation.

ACO REACH requires all participating organizations to submit a health equity plan documenting how they will identify and reduce health disparities in their attributed population. REACH ACOs must collect social needs data, stratify quality reporting by race and ethnicity, and demonstrate progress on equity metrics over time. The model offers two participation levels: the Global option (accepting 100% of financial risk for total cost of care) and the Professional option (accepting 50% of downside risk, with more limited total cost accountability). ACO REACH allows prospective attribution — beneficiaries are assigned at the beginning of the performance year rather than retrospectively — giving REACH ACOs a more stable, known population to manage.
Primary Care First: Betting on Primary Care

Primary Care First (PCF), launched in 2021 across 26 states, is CMMI's most direct expression of the thesis that investing in primary care capacity is the central mechanism for achieving value in Medicare. PCF replaces per-visit billing for primary care with a flat monthly population-based payment supplemented by a smaller per-visit fee, combined with a performance-based payment for quality and total cost of care outcomes. The PBPM payment is designed to fund care management infrastructure — nurses, care coordinators, behavioral health integration — that cannot be financed through per-visit billing alone.

PCF has two payment adjustments that reflect CMMI's equity commitment. First, a Seriously Ill Population (SIP) payment provides a significantly higher per-patient payment for patients with complex serious illness — recognizing that primary care management of this high-need population is severely undercompensated by standard E&M billing. Second, a Rural/Health Professional Shortage Area bonus increases payments for practices in underserved areas, acknowledging that building primary care capacity in high-need communities requires supplemental investment.
The GUIDE Model: VBC in Dementia Care

The Guiding an Improved Dementia Experience (GUIDE) model, launched in 2024, tests a comprehensive care management approach for Medicare beneficiaries with dementia and their caregivers. Dementia care represents a critical gap in the US healthcare system: approximately 6.7 million Americans have Alzheimer's or related dementia, and the care for these patients — frequently fragmented across multiple specialists and settings, devastating to family caregivers, and prone to avoidable hospitalizations — is among the most expensive and worst-coordinated in Medicare.

GUIDE provides participating organizations with a per-beneficiary-per-month care management payment to fund interdisciplinary care teams, caregiver support services, 24/7 helplines for families in crisis, and respite care. The model explicitly targets caregiver burden — a dimension of care quality entirely absent from traditional clinical quality measurement — and links financial accountability to both patient outcomes (hospitalizations, ED visits, nursing home transitions) and caregiver-reported outcomes. GUIDE represents CMMI's most comprehensive VBC model in a specific disease domain and will generate important evidence about whether comprehensive dementia care management can reduce costs while improving quality of life for patients and caregivers.
Multi-Payer Alignment: The Holy Grail of VBC Scale

The most persistent structural limitation of value-based care models is their payer-specific scope. An ACO that holds Medicare accountable care contracts receives risk-adjusted capitation or shared savings for Medicare beneficiaries — but the same ACO's primary care practices are simultaneously delivering fee-for-service care to Medicaid and commercially insured patients. When a care management nurse invests time in preventing a Medicaid patient's hospitalization, the financial benefit accrues to the Medicaid managed care organization, not to the ACO that employed the nurse. This multi-payer misalignment means that care management investments are financially justified only for the payer population covered by the VBC contract, not for the full patient panel that a practice serves.

Multi-payer alignment — creating accountable care relationships across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance simultaneously for the same provider and geographic population — is the policy mechanism that would resolve this problem. Vermont's all-payer model and Maryland's all-payer hospital rate setting represent the most advanced experiments in multi-payer alignment, but both required years of federal waiver negotiation, state legislative action, and alignment of competing insurer interests that most states cannot replicate. The AHEAD (All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development) model, announced by CMS in 2023, attempts to expand Vermont-style multi-payer accountability to 7 states, with global hospital budgets and Medicare-Medicaid-commercial alignment as the core design.
Voluntary to Mandatory: The Scaling Challenge

CMMI's 2030 goal — all Medicare beneficiaries in accountable care relationships — cannot be achieved through voluntary participation alone. Even optimistic projections for MSSP, ACO REACH, and Primary Care First participation leave tens of millions of Medicare beneficiaries in providers with no accountable care relationship and no VBC payment contract. The math of voluntary adoption has a ceiling: the organizations most motivated and capable have already joined; the remaining providers are either too small, too rural, too specialty-focused, or too risk-averse to participate voluntarily.

Mandatory participation — the approach taken with the CJR bundled payment model — expands coverage but faces intense provider opposition. The politically sustainable path toward scale may require making ACO participation the default for providers above a certain size, with significant administrative simplification to reduce the compliance burden that deters small practices. Geographic market approaches — like the AHEAD model's state-level total cost of care accountability — offer a different path to scale by making all providers in a market subject to aggregate accountability without requiring each to individually contract with CMS.
Private Equity in VBC: One Medical, Oak Street, and ChenMed

The most significant structural development in primary care value-based care over the past decade has not been CMS policy — it has been private equity and technology investment in de novo primary care models built from scratch around value-based payment. Oak Street Health, ChenMed, Iora Health (now One Medical), and CareBridge represent a wave of value-focused primary care organizations that have built their clinical and operational infrastructure around Medicare Advantage capitation from day one, without the legacy fee-for-service revenue that makes transformation difficult for established physician practices.

These organizations have demonstrated that a different primary care model is economically viable: with sufficient capitation, a primary care practice can invest in high-touch care management (lower panel sizes, embedded social workers, care coordinators), longer appointment times, behavioral health integration, and community health worker programs that generate better outcomes and lower total cost of care than traditional high-volume primary care. Amazon's $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and CVS Health's $10.6 billion acquisition of Oak Street Health in 2022-2023 signal that major commercial players believe this model is scalable — though whether massive corporate ownership will preserve the care culture that made these organizations effective is an open question that will take years to answer.
The Equity-First Movement: Designing Accountability for Disparity Reduction

The most important evolution in VBC philosophy since 2020 has been the growing insistence that equity be a primary design objective of payment models, not an afterthought. This represents a shift from the earlier era of VBC, which largely treated health equity as a measurement complexity to be managed (through risk adjustment and stratified reporting) to a vision where reducing racial, socioeconomic, and geographic disparities is an explicit accountability requirement with financial consequences.

Practical manifestations of the equity-first approach include: CMMI's requirement that ACO REACH participants submit and implement health equity plans; CMS's Health Equity Index for Medicare Advantage Stars; the Enhancing Oncology Model's disparity reporting requirements; and North Carolina's Medicaid transformation, which has explicitly tied managed care organization payments to disparity reduction targets. The emerging consensus in VBC policy is that a model that achieves average quality improvement while leaving disparities intact — or worsening them — is not succeeding at its fundamental goal.

The next decade of value-based care will be defined by whether the scaling challenge can be met — whether the innovations demonstrated in voluntary models can be extended to the full Medicare and Medicaid population, including the providers and communities that have not yet been touched by VBC reform. The policy tools exist: ACO REACH, Primary Care First, the AHEAD multi-payer model, and equity-focused accountability frameworks represent a more sophisticated and more ambitious toolkit than anything that existed in 2012. What they require is sustained political will, payment rates sufficient to fund the care management investments that VBC requires, and a commitment to measuring success by equity outcomes — by whether the disparity between the health of affluent and disadvantaged Americans is closing, not merely whether average quality statistics are improving.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: CMMI's 2021 strategic reset set an ambitious goal: every Medicare beneficiary in an accountable care relationship by 2030. Achieving it requires scaling ACO-like arrangements to providers and populations that voluntary models have not reached, making primary care investment the central VBC thesis, designing equity into payment models from the start, and tackling the multi-payer alignment problem that has long been the Achilles heel of value-based care. This lesson surveys the current frontier: ACO REACH, Primary Care First, the GUIDE model, state all-payer experiments, and the private equity-backed direct primary care movement.
result.title: Where VBC Is Heading: Primary Care, Equity and Scale

children.text: Hospital finance in the United States has been built on a simple but perverse logic for over a century: hospitals earn more revenue by treating more patients, performing more procedures, and filling more beds. Fee-for-service hospital payment — whether through Medicare DRGs, commercial per-diem rates, or case rates — rewards volume. This payment structure fundamentally misaligns hospital financial incentives with population health: a hospital that succeeds in preventing hospitalizations through better primary care coordination is reducing its own revenue. A global budget breaks this logic entirely. Under a global budget, a hospital receives a fixed annual revenue allocation — its Global Budget Revenue (GBR) — regardless of how many patients it admits or how many procedures it performs. Maryland has been operating this model for hospitals since 2014, generating the most important evidence in American healthcare on whether inverting hospital incentives can actually improve population health.
Maryland's All-Payer Model: From Per-Admission to Total Cost of Care

Maryland's relationship with alternative hospital payment dates to 1974, when the state established the Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) — a regulatory body with authority to set hospital rates for all payers. Maryland received a federal waiver allowing its all-payer rate-setting system to operate as an alternative to standard Medicare DRG payments, on the condition that Medicare per-admission costs in Maryland grew no faster than the national average. This old waiver system (the 'per-admission model') constrained per-admission costs but did not control total spending — hospitals could earn more by admitting more patients.

In 2014, Maryland and CMS negotiated a fundamental redesign: the Total Cost of Care (TCOC) Model. Under the TCOC Model, Maryland hospitals operate under Global Budget Revenue — a fixed annual revenue amount set for each hospital at the beginning of the year. Hospitals receive their GBR regardless of how many patients they admit: if admissions exceed projected volume, the hospital receives the same GBR (effectively earning less per admission); if admissions fall short, the hospital also receives the same GBR (effectively earning more per admission). This inversion of incentives makes prevention financially beneficial: a hospital that invests in care management programs that reduce avoidable admissions keeps its GBR while reducing the costs of delivering care.
How Maryland Global Budget Revenue Works

Each Maryland hospital's GBR is set annually by HSCRC based on the hospital's prior year revenue, adjusted for approved cost increases, quality performance, and a population health improvement component. The GBR covers hospital inpatient and outpatient services for all payers — Medicare, Medicaid, commercial insurance — at rates set by HSCRC that all payers are required to pay. This all-payer aspect of the model is critical: because every payer pays the same HSCRC-set rates, the hospital cannot make up for a GBR constraint on one payer by increasing volume for another.

Under the global budget, actual patient revenue may diverge from GBR during the year if volume differs from projections. HSCRC reconciles this through periodic adjustments to ensure hospitals ultimately receive their set GBR. If a hospital admits more patients than projected and would otherwise over-earn, HSCRC reduces rates in subsequent periods to claw back the excess. If a hospital admits fewer patients and under-earns, HSCRC increases rates to compensate. The result is stable, predictable annual revenue — a dramatic departure from the volume-dependent revenue volatility that characterizes conventional hospital finance.
Population Health Investment: The GBR Dividend

The most transformative feature of global budget hospital payment is the population health investment opportunity it creates. Under a volume-based payment model, a hospital that diverts patients away from the hospital by investing in community health programs is cutting its own revenue. Under global budget payment, the same investment reduces the cost of serving the allocated patient volume without reducing GBR — effectively creating a margin on every prevented hospitalization. Maryland hospitals have used this mechanism to fund community health workers, care transition programs, food security initiatives, housing navigation, and behavioral health crisis services that would never be financially viable under fee-for-service.

The Maryland TCOC model explicitly sets population health improvement requirements as part of the GBR calculation. Hospitals must demonstrate progress on specific population health metrics — including rates of ambulatory care-sensitive condition hospitalizations, potentially preventable complications, and care coordination measures — or face GBR adjustments. This requirement transforms the hospital from a pure treatment organization into a population health accountable entity, at least for its local service area.
Maryland's Results: What a Decade of Evidence Shows

CMS evaluations of Maryland's TCOC model through 2022 found that the model met its primary financial goal: Maryland's Medicare per capita total cost of care grew more slowly than the national average, generating over $1 billion in cumulative Medicare savings through the model's first several years. Inpatient admissions for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions declined, potentially preventable complications fell, and readmission rates improved relative to national trends. These results provide the strongest available evidence that global hospital budgets can successfully reduce avoidable hospital utilization without harming access or quality.

Quality outcomes in Maryland hospitals have also generally improved under the model. Hospital-acquired condition rates, readmission rates, and mortality rates have improved on several measures, though disentangling the model's contribution from national secular trends and Maryland's specific demographics is methodologically challenging. The COVID-19 pandemic caused significant disruption to hospital utilization patterns and model performance, requiring HSCRC to make substantial GBR adjustments during 2020-2021 to account for pandemic-related admission collapse.
The AHEAD Model: Expanding Beyond Maryland

Building on Maryland's decade of evidence, CMS announced the States Advancing All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development (AHEAD) model in 2022, inviting states to adopt Maryland-style total cost of care accountability structures. The model selected 7 states — Vermont, Maryland (deepening its existing model), Connecticut, Hawaii, Indiana, New Hampshire, and Washington — to implement all-payer total cost of care accountability frameworks combining global hospital budgets with primary care investment requirements and health equity commitments.

Each AHEAD state must establish total cost of care growth targets that apply to Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance spending on hospital services. States must also invest a defined percentage of hospital global budget revenue in primary care and population health, addressing the care coordination gap that global hospital budgets alone cannot close. Vermont's implementation builds directly on OneCare Vermont's existing all-payer ACO framework, adding hospital global budget elements to a pre-existing population health accountability structure.
Implications for Hospital Finance and Strategy

Global budgets create a fundamentally different strategic environment for hospital CFOs and boards. Under volume-based payment, the hospital's financial health depends on maintaining and growing procedural volume, filling beds, and expanding high-margin service lines. Under global budget payment, the hospital's financial health depends on managing the cost of its fixed patient volume efficiently, preventing avoidable utilization, and investing in community health programs that reduce the cost of care delivery without reducing revenue.

This strategic inversion has significant implications for capital allocation. Under fee-for-service, hospitals compete for high-margin elective procedures — cardiac surgery, orthopedics, oncology — and invest capital accordingly in catheterization labs, operating suites, and cancer centers. Under global budget payment, capital investment in inpatient procedural capacity generates capacity that must be kept filled to remain financially rational, potentially working against the population health objectives that global budgets are designed to advance. Maryland hospitals have begun redirecting capital investment toward outpatient and primary care capacity that serves the model's incentives — a structural shift in hospital strategy that would be nearly impossible under conventional payment.
Bond Ratings and Capital Markets Under Global Budgets

Bond rating agencies — Moody's, S&P, Fitch — have generally viewed Maryland hospital global budgets as a mixed financial signal. Revenue predictability is substantially improved under GBR: hospitals know their annual revenue before the year begins, reducing the cash flow volatility that can threaten bond covenants under volume-based payment. This predictability is favorably viewed by rating agencies. However, rating agencies also note that global budgets create the risk of insufficient revenue if cost inflation exceeds GBR growth, and that the model's long-term financial sustainability depends on HSCRC's commitment to setting GBRs that provide adequate operating margins.

Maryland hospital operating margins under the TCOC model have been broadly comparable to national hospital margins, though there is significant variation across individual hospitals. Rural and small community hospitals have faced greater margin pressure under global budgets because their cost structures are less flexible and their ability to substitute population health investment for inpatient volume is more limited in communities with high unmet primary care need. The equity dimension of global budget design — ensuring that the model's financial incentives work for safety-net hospitals as well as large academic medical centers — is one of the central implementation challenges in AHEAD.

Maryland's global budget model represents the most complete inversion of hospital financial incentives available in American healthcare policy. Its decade of results provides credible evidence that hospitals can maintain quality, meet community health needs, and achieve meaningful cost savings under a payment system where their revenue is delinked from their volume. The AHEAD model's expansion to seven states will test whether this model is replicable outside Maryland's unique all-payer regulatory environment. If it succeeds, global hospital budgets could become the foundation of the next generation of value-based care — transforming hospitals from volume-maximizing institutions into community health accountable organizations whose financial interests align, for the first time, with keeping their communities healthy.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: Global budgets for hospitals represent the most radical reimagining of hospital finance in American healthcare: instead of receiving more revenue when they admit more patients, hospitals receive a fixed annual budget regardless of volume. Maryland's All-Payer Model is the world's most advanced real-world test of this concept, and its results over a decade provide important evidence about whether inverting hospital financial incentives can produce population health improvements. This lesson covers Maryland's model history and results, the new AHEAD model expanding to seven states, global budget mechanics, and the implications for hospital strategy and bond finance.
result.title: Global Budgets for Hospitals: Maryland and Beyond

children.text: American healthcare has invested billions of dollars in quality measurement infrastructure over the past three decades. The result is an ecosystem of extraordinary complexity: hundreds of individual measures, maintained by multiple private organizations and government agencies, collected through administrative claims, hybrid abstraction methods, and electronic health records, reported to dozens of programs across CMS, commercial insurers, state agencies, and accreditation bodies. Any serious practitioner of value-based care must understand this ecosystem — not just which measures exist, but how they are constructed, how they are collected, what they actually measure, and why the ecosystem has failed to produce the reliable, actionable quality intelligence its architects envisioned.
NCQA and HEDIS: The Dominant Commercial Quality Framework

The Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set (HEDIS) is maintained by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) and represents the most widely used quality measurement framework in American healthcare. HEDIS comprises approximately 90 measures across 6 domains: effectiveness of care, access and availability of care, patient experience, utilization, health plan descriptive information, and measures addressing disparities. HEDIS measures are used in NCQA health plan accreditation, Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, Medicaid managed care quality requirements, and commercial health plan quality reporting to employers and consumers.

HEDIS measures are constructed from three data sources, each with different characteristics. Administrative data (claims-based) uses medical and pharmacy claims to identify patients who received or failed to receive a specified service. Administrative data has 100% population coverage and low collection cost but is subject to coding completeness variations and cannot capture clinical nuances not reflected in billing codes. Medical record review (abstraction) supplements claims with chart review to identify services not captured in claims — particularly lab values, clinical findings, and services delivered but not billed. Hybrid measures combine claims and medical record data for higher precision at higher collection cost.
Electronic HEDIS (eHEDIS) and EHR Data Submission

NCQA has been progressively expanding electronic HEDIS (eHEDIS) — versions of HEDIS measures calculated directly from structured EHR data rather than claims or medical record abstraction. eHEDIS has the potential to reduce the administrative burden of HEDIS collection while improving data accuracy, since clinical values like HbA1c results and blood pressure readings can be captured directly rather than inferred from billing codes. However, eHEDIS implementation requires standardized data extraction from EHR systems, which remains technically challenging given the diversity of EHR platforms and the inconsistency of structured data entry across clinical workflows.
Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs) and the CMS Quality Framework

Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs) are a parallel quality measure infrastructure developed by CMS and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) specifically for use with certified EHR technology. eCQMs are expressed in Health Quality Measure Format (HQMF), a machine-readable specification that allows EHR systems to calculate measure results automatically from structured clinical data. CMS uses eCQMs in multiple quality reporting programs including the Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) program for hospitals, the Outpatient Quality Reporting (OQR) program, and the MIPS quality category.

The eCQM framework has accelerated with the 2020 CMS Interoperability Rule, which required health plans and providers to implement standardized FHIR-based APIs for data exchange. These APIs enable payer access to EHR clinical data for quality measurement purposes, reducing dependence on claims data and enabling faster, more accurate quality assessment. NCQA's use of these APIs for HEDIS data collection — through the NCQA HEDIS Electronic Reporting project — represents the convergence of the HEDIS and eCQM frameworks toward a common digital infrastructure.
CMS Core Measure Sets: Inpatient, Outpatient, and Primary Care

CMS maintains Core Measure Sets for different care settings that serve as the quality reporting basis for hospital and physician payment programs. The Hospital Inpatient Core Measure Set covers domains including heart failure, pneumonia, venous thromboembolism prevention, stroke care, and perinatal care. The Hospital Outpatient Core Measure Set covers cataract surgery, colonoscopy, and emergency department throughput. The Clinician and Group Core Measure Set covers primary care quality domains including preventive care, chronic disease management (diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression), and care coordination.

CMS aligns these core measure sets with HEDIS and NQF-endorsed measures to the extent possible, but alignment across programs is imperfect. A health system reporting quality to CMS under IQR, to NCQA for health plan accreditation, to commercial payers for VBC contracts, and to state agencies for Medicaid managed care quality requirements may be reporting on dozens of overlapping but non-identical measures to multiple audiences simultaneously — a duplication problem that consumes significant resources without proportionate insight.
NQF Endorsement: The Scientific Legitimacy Process

The National Quality Forum (NQF) is a nonprofit organization that maintains a consensus-based endorsement process for quality measures. NQF endorsement signals that a measure meets scientific standards for importance, scientific acceptability, usability, and feasibility. Endorsed measures receive an NQF number and are considered the gold standard for quality measurement in federal programs. CMS gives preference to NQF-endorsed measures in its quality reporting and payment programs, and NCQA uses NQF endorsement as a credentialing standard for HEDIS measures.

The NQF endorsement process involves technical expert panels, public comment, and steward review — a rigorous procedure that takes 12-18 months per measure. This thoroughness ensures scientific quality but also slows the introduction of new measures in rapidly evolving clinical areas. The NQF process has also been criticized for favoring measures with strong specialty society backing over measures that might be more clinically important but lack organized constituency support.
Process, Outcome, and Structural Measures: The Quality Hierarchy

Quality measures fall into three categories with different strengths and limitations. Process measures assess whether a specific evidence-based clinical action was taken — for example, whether a diabetic patient received an HbA1c test within the measurement year. Process measures are actionable (clinicians know exactly what to do to improve them) and relatively easy to collect, but they measure inputs rather than outcomes and can be gamed by performing the measured process without the broader clinical context that makes it beneficial.

Outcome measures assess whether patients achieved a desired health state — for example, whether a diabetic patient achieved HbA1c control below 8%. Outcome measures reflect what patients actually care about but are influenced by factors outside the provider's control including patient adherence, social determinants, and biological factors. Structural measures assess whether an organization has the infrastructure or capabilities associated with quality care — for example, whether a practice uses an electronic health record or has a formal chronic disease management program.

The quality measurement field has been moving toward outcome measures for two decades, reflecting the recognition that process compliance does not guarantee outcomes. MIPS, Star Ratings, and HEDIS all require at least one outcome measure in their quality reporting frameworks. However, outcome measures require larger sample sizes for reliable measurement, are more sensitive to case mix and social risk, and demand more sophisticated risk adjustment — creating a tension between measurement validity and operational feasibility.
The Measure Proliferation Problem

The quality measurement ecosystem has grown without systematic coordination, resulting in measure proliferation that burdens providers without proportionate information value. A 2019 JAMA analysis estimated that providers in the US face over 600 distinct quality measures across federal, state, and commercial reporting programs. Many of these measures are similar but not identical — measuring hemoglobin A1c with slightly different age cutoffs or different denominator specifications across programs — requiring separate data collection and reporting workflows for technically similar clinical concepts.

The Core Quality Measures Collaborative (CQMC) was established by CMS and major commercial payers to develop aligned measure sets for specific clinical conditions, reducing the measure burden on providers through cross-payer alignment. The CQMC has made progress in aligning measures for oncology, cardiovascular care, and behavioral health, but alignment remains incomplete. The fundamental problem is that each payer has incentive to use measures that reflect well on its plan's enrolled population or that align with its specific quality improvement priorities — creating centrifugal pressure toward differentiation that multi-stakeholder alignment efforts must continuously counteract.
Digital Quality Measures: The Next Generation

CMS and NCQA have both committed to transitioning quality measurement to a fully digital infrastructure — digital quality measures (dQMs) — that would replace claims-based and hybrid collection methods with structured EHR and health information exchange data. A fully digital measure infrastructure would dramatically reduce collection costs, increase measurement frequency from annual to near-real-time, and enable more granular analysis of care patterns than claims-based approaches allow.

The transition to dQMs requires three preconditions that are not yet universally met: standardized structured data entry in EHRs (particularly for clinical values like vital signs, lab results, and medication records), standardized FHIR-based data exchange APIs across all EHR platforms, and quality measure logic expressed in CQL (Clinical Quality Language) that can run against standardized FHIR data models. Progress on all three fronts has been substantial since the 21st Century Cures Act's interoperability provisions took effect, but the transition from a claims-based to a digital quality measurement ecosystem will take years and significant investment to complete.
Equity Stratification: The Missing Dimension

One of the most significant evolution in quality measurement over the past five years has been the growing imperative to stratify quality data by race, ethnicity, language, income, and disability status. Aggregate quality scores can conceal dramatic disparities: a health plan that achieves the 75th percentile on overall HbA1c control may have excellent performance for white, commercially insured members and significantly lower performance for Black, Hispanic, or Medicaid-enrolled members. Without stratified data, these disparities are invisible and therefore unaddressable.

NCQA introduced the Health Equity Accreditation program in 2021 and has been adding demographic stratification to HEDIS measures. CMS required Medicare Advantage plans to report HEDIS and CAHPS results stratified by race and ethnicity beginning in 2024, and has linked equity performance to Star Ratings bonuses. The Enhancing Oncology Model's equity requirements — mandatory SDOH screening and stratified quality reporting — represent the most explicit integration of equity into a CMMI model to date. The field is moving from measuring average quality to measuring the distribution of quality across demographic groups, which is a more demanding and more informative standard.

The quality measurement ecosystem is both indispensable and dysfunctional. It is indispensable because without standardized, systematically collected quality data, there is no objective basis for value-based care payment, quality improvement, or consumer choice. It is dysfunctional because measure proliferation, data collection burden, gaming risk, and equity gaps have made it expensive, administratively burdensome, and only partially informative. The transition to digital quality measures represents the most promising path forward — enabling richer, more frequent, more equitable quality intelligence at lower operational cost — but requires sustained investment in health information infrastructure and regulatory alignment that the market alone will not produce.

result.summary: The American quality measurement ecosystem comprises hundreds of measures maintained by dozens of organizations, collected through multiple data streams, and applied inconsistently across payers and programs. This lesson provides a comprehensive map of the ecosystem: HEDIS and the NCQA, electronic Clinical Quality Measures and their EHR infrastructure, the NQF endorsement process, the progression from process to outcome measures, the measure proliferation problem, the emerging shift toward digital quality measures, and the growing imperative to stratify quality data by equity dimensions.

children.text: When Congress passed the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA) in 2015 with rare bipartisan support, it created the most significant restructuring of Medicare physician payment since RBRVS. The law created two pathways: the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) for physicians who remain in traditional fee-for-service Medicare, and incentivized participation in Advanced Alternative Payment Models (APMs). MIPS was designed as a transitional mechanism — a way to introduce performance-based payment adjustments while most physicians were still operating in fee-for-service arrangements. By 2023, however, MIPS had become a massive compliance exercise that consumed billions of dollars in administrative effort while delivering payment adjustments too small to change behavior and performance scores too inflated to differentiate quality.
MACRA's Architecture: MIPS vs. APMs

MACRA consolidated three legacy CMS quality programs — the Physician Quality Reporting System (PQRS), the Value-Based Payment Modifier, and Meaningful Use — into MIPS, streamlining reporting into a single framework. Simultaneously, it created the APM track: physicians in qualifying Advanced APMs receive a 5% lump-sum bonus on Medicare Part B payments through 2024, transitioning to higher fee schedule updates after 2025. The law was explicit in its intent — the APM track was the destination, MIPS was the on-ramp. CMS projected that most physicians would migrate toward APMs within a decade. That migration has been slower and more uneven than anticipated, with most physicians remaining in MIPS years into the program.

Not all clinicians are subject to MIPS. Physicians below the low-volume threshold — defined as $90,000 or less in Part B allowed charges, 200 or fewer Part B patients, or 200 or fewer covered professional services in a year — are excluded. Small rural practices, new clinicians in their first year of Medicare billing, and clinicians who participate substantially in APMs may also be excluded. In recent years, CMS has exempted an increasing share of eligible clinicians, with roughly 30-40% qualifying for various MIPS exclusions, which itself reflects the program's limited reach into the physician universe.
The Four Performance Categories

MIPS calculates a composite performance score (MIPS Final Score) based on four categories. The weights have shifted over the program's history; for the 2023 performance year the categories and weights were as follows.
1. Quality (30% Weight)

Clinicians select 6 quality measures from a library of hundreds, including at least one outcome measure or a high-priority measure if no outcome measure is applicable to their practice. Quality measures cover domains including preventive care, chronic disease management, patient safety, and patient experience. The quality category score is calculated by benchmarking individual clinician performance against national peer performance on each measure, with scores from 1 to 10 points per measure.

The measure selection flexibility is both a feature and a bug. Clinicians naturally select measures on which they perform well, a phenomenon known as cherry-picking measures. Because each clinician can choose different measures from the library, cross-clinician comparison is severely limited. Studies published in JAMA have shown that MIPS quality scores are more strongly predicted by specialty and measure selection strategy than by independently-assessed clinical quality. A dermatologist and an endocrinologist reporting different measures cannot be meaningfully compared, rendering the quality category a compliance exercise rather than a performance signal.
2. Cost (30% Weight)

The cost category requires no clinician reporting — CMS calculates it entirely from claims data. CMS uses two primary cost measures: Total Per Capita Cost (TPCC), which measures total Medicare spending for attributed beneficiaries across all services, and Medicare Spending per Beneficiary (MSPB), which measures spending in the episode surrounding a hospital admission. Specialty-specific episode cost measures covering conditions like hip and knee replacement, cataract surgery, and ischemic vascular disease have been added over time. Attribution to clinicians for cost purposes follows complex rules that have been criticized for attributing spending to clinicians who have limited control over the care driving costs.
3. Improvement Activities (15% Weight)

The Improvement Activities category is the most flexible of the four. Clinicians attest to completing activities from a menu of over 100 options covering care coordination, beneficiary engagement, patient safety, population management, and behavioral and mental health integration. Activities are weighted high or medium; completing two high-weighted activities or four medium-weighted activities achieves the maximum score. Most clinicians can achieve maximum credit in this category simply by attesting to activities already embedded in their standard practice. Clinicians in PCMHs, rural health clinics, or health professional shortage areas receive automatic full credit, further diluting any performance signal.
4. Promoting Interoperability (25% Weight)

The Promoting Interoperability (PI) category — formerly Meaningful Use and then Advancing Care Information — measures EHR adoption and use. Clinicians must use a 2015 Edition Certified EHR Technology and report on objectives including e-prescribing, Health Information Exchange (HIE) participation, patient access to electronic records, and public health reporting including immunization registry submission. The PI category has the heaviest administrative infrastructure requirements and generates the most hardship exception requests, particularly from small practices and specialists whose clinical workflows do not map cleanly onto electronic information exchange measures.
Payment Adjustments: How Scores Translate to Dollars

MIPS is budget-neutral: the bonuses paid to high performers are funded by penalties on low performers. The maximum payment adjustment in MIPS has scaled up over the program's history: plus or minus 4% in 2019, plus or minus 5% in 2020, plus or minus 7% in 2021, and plus or minus 9% from 2022 onward. An additional exceptional performance bonus of up to 10% extra is available for clinicians scoring above a high-performance threshold, set at 89 points in recent performance years.

The critical problem with budget neutrality in a system with widespread grade inflation is that penalties fall on a thin tail of low performers while bonuses are diluted across the large majority who score well. For the 2021 performance year, approximately 75% of MIPS-eligible clinicians received a positive payment adjustment; only 9% received a negative adjustment. The average positive adjustment was less than 1% of Medicare billings. For a physician billing $400,000 in Medicare annually, a 0.5% positive adjustment represents $2,000 — a trivially small incentive relative to the compliance cost of participation, fundamentally undermining MIPS's behavioral theory of change.
Grade Inflation and the Performance Score Validity Problem

The distribution of MIPS Final Scores has consistently clustered in the high range. In the 2021 performance year, the median score was 89.5 out of 100, and over 30% of eligible clinicians scored above 90. The scoring system rewards reporting completion more than performance excellence: a clinician who reports all required measures receives substantial credit regardless of whether their actual clinical outcomes are superior to peers. The benchmarking methodology uses peer performance distributions, but measure cherry-picking and low data completeness thresholds allow high scores without high performance.

A 2019 JAMA Internal Medicine study by Liao and colleagues found that MIPS scores were poorly correlated with independently measured quality metrics. High MIPS scores did not predict better performance on the CMS Overall Quality Star Rating or on HEDIS measures. The authors concluded that MIPS was measuring reporting compliance rather than care quality. A subsequent 2022 analysis in Health Affairs confirmed these findings, showing that the correlation between MIPS performance scores and patient outcomes was statistically indistinguishable from zero for most conditions.
MIPS Value Pathways: The Reform Within the Reform

Recognizing MIPS's measure proliferation and flexibility problems, CMS introduced MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs) beginning in 2023. MVPs organize a curated set of measures — quality, cost, improvement activities, and PI — around a specialty or clinical condition. Examples include the Rheumatology MVP, the Stroke Care and Prevention MVP, the Anesthesia MVP, and the Preventive Care and Vaccination MVP. By constraining measure choice within a clinically coherent bundle, MVPs aim to enable more meaningful peer comparison, reduce cherry-picking, and produce a quality signal that is more interpretable to patients and purchasers.

MVPs are CMS's attempt to make MIPS serve as a meaningful on-ramp to APMs by aligning measures with the quality frameworks used in specialty-specific Alternative Payment Models. The transition to MVPs is voluntary initially but CMS has signaled intent to deprecate traditional MIPS reporting options over time. Whether MVPs meaningfully address MIPS's fundamental limitations — the small payment adjustments, the administrative burden, the grade inflation — remains contested, since the structural problems are architectural, not just measurement design issues.
Administrative Burden: The Hidden Cost of MIPS Compliance

A 2019 RAND Corporation analysis estimated that the average MIPS-eligible physician practice spent $12,811 per clinician per year on MIPS reporting activities. For small practices, this burden was proportionally larger. A solo primary care physician spending $12,000 annually on MIPS compliance in exchange for a potential $2,000-$4,000 payment adjustment is running a negative expected-value proposition — unless the compliance activities coincidentally generate clinical or operational value independent of the financial incentive, which is rarely their design intent.

The MIPS reporting ecosystem has spawned a cottage industry of vendors — qualified registries, certified EHR vendors, and Qualified Clinical Data Registries (QCDRs) — that help practices navigate reporting requirements. This intermediary layer absorbs resources without directly improving patient care. Small and independent practices are at particular disadvantage: they lack the data infrastructure, analytics capabilities, and compliance staff that large health systems deploy, yet face the same reporting requirements. The resulting consolidation pressure — small practices merging with health systems partly to share MIPS compliance costs — has implications for physician autonomy and market competition that extend well beyond the quality measurement program.
Why MIPS Has Failed to Drive Transformation

The core problem with MIPS as a value-based care mechanism is that it adjusts the price per RVU without changing the underlying volume-based payment model. A physician who scores 95 on MIPS and receives a 1.5% payment bonus is still being paid per encounter, per procedure, per visit. The incentive signal is additive to the fee-for-service signal rather than substitutive of it. Genuine transformation requires payment models that change the fundamental calculus — paying for population health management, care coordination, and outcomes rather than for individual service delivery events. MIPS layers a thin quality and efficiency incentive on top of a volume-based system while leaving the volume-based system intact.

MIPS represents a well-intentioned but structurally limited approach to physician payment reform. Its architects faced a genuine dilemma: disrupting the entire fee-for-service system simultaneously was politically impossible, so MIPS was designed as a soft transition that would maintain most FFS revenue while layering on quality incentives. The result is a system that imposes substantial costs on physicians and health systems, generates data of questionable validity, provides trivially small incentive signals, and leaves the underlying FFS payment model intact. The lesson for value-based care reformers is clear: incremental reforms layered on top of fee-for-service tend to inherit its distortions rather than replace them. Genuine transformation requires moving the center of gravity — from per-service payment to population-based accountability — and MIPS, for all its complexity, does not do that.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: The Merit-Based Incentive Payment System, created by MACRA in 2015, was designed to move Medicare physician payment toward quality and value by adjusting payments based on composite performance scores. In practice, MIPS has generated enormous administrative burden, achieved widespread grade inflation, and failed to drive the structural transformation it promised. This lesson dissects the MIPS architecture, the four performance categories, the payment adjustment mechanics, and the escalating critique that MIPS represents a costly incremental reform that has crowded out more fundamental change.
result.title: MIPS: The Merit-Based Incentive Payment System

children.text: Cancer care accounts for approximately $190 billion in annual US healthcare spending, with costs growing faster than almost any other disease category driven by the proliferation of high-cost targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and increasingly expensive supportive care regimens. For CMS, oncology represents both the most urgent cost challenge and the most complex environment in which to implement value-based care. The Oncology Care Model (OCM), which ran from 2016 to 2022, was the most ambitious attempt in Medicare's history to test episode-based payment in oncology — and its results illuminate both the potential and the hard limits of VBC approaches in cancer.
Why Oncology Is VBC's Hardest Domain

Value-based care in oncology faces structural challenges that do not exist to the same degree in other clinical domains. First, treatment decisions involve profound uncertainty even for expert clinicians: two patients with the same cancer stage and histology can have dramatically different clinical trajectories based on genomic factors, tumor microenvironment, and patient-specific factors that are increasingly well-characterized but still incompletely predictive. Standard risk adjustment models built on claims data cannot adequately capture this biological complexity.

Second, patient expectations in oncology are uniquely powerful. Patients with cancer — and their families — often push strongly for the most aggressive treatment options available, and oncologists experience significant moral pressure to pursue every possible therapeutic avenue. The conversation about treatment goals, including the difficult question of whether a given treatment is likely to extend meaningful life or primarily extend treatment-related suffering, is among the hardest in medicine. Financial incentives are poorly positioned to facilitate these conversations.

Third, drug costs dominate the oncology cost equation in ways that providers have almost no ability to control. A single course of pembrolizumab (Keytruda) for lung cancer can cost $100,000-$200,000 per year. CAR-T cell therapies for hematologic malignancies can cost $400,000-$500,000 for a single treatment course. When drug costs represent 60-80% of oncology episode spending, the total cost of care is driven more by CMS's drug pricing policy and pharmaceutical negotiations than by any provider care management decision.
OCM Design: 6-Month Episodes and MEOS Payments

The Oncology Care Model used 6-month episodes triggered by initiation of chemotherapy — an anchor event that identified patients actively receiving systemic cancer treatment. The episode captured all Medicare spending during the 6-month window: chemotherapy, hospitalizations, emergency visits, physician services, hospice, and supportive care. Target prices were calculated from historical claims data, risk-adjusted for cancer type, stage, and patient demographics, with a 4% discount representing CMS's minimum savings requirement.

A distinctive and important feature of OCM was the Monthly Enhanced Oncology Services (MEOS) payment — a flat monthly fee of $160 per patient during chemotherapy months. This payment was not tied to individual service delivery; it was designed to support care management infrastructure that would not otherwise be reimbursable under fee-for-service. Practices were required to use MEOS funds to provide 24/7 patient access, care navigation, evidence-based treatment planning, and care coordination services. This prospective investment in care management capacity was a more sophisticated approach than typical fee-for-service quality incentives.

OCM participation was voluntary and included both physician oncology practices and hospital outpatient departments. At peak enrollment, approximately 175 practices participated, treating roughly 155,000 Medicare beneficiaries annually. OCM also included a quality performance requirement: practices had to achieve quality thresholds across 12 measures spanning care plan documentation, patient experience, treatment appropriateness, and end-of-life care. Performance below quality thresholds could reduce or eliminate shared savings payments even if cost targets were met.
What Participating Practices Actually Changed

CMS monitoring surveys and qualitative research documented that OCM participation drove genuine operational changes in participating practices. The most consistent changes included: expanding care navigator roles to manage patient calls and symptom monitoring between visits; implementing evidence-based treatment pathways to reduce practice variation; establishing 24/7 access lines to direct symptomatic patients to the oncology office rather than emergency departments; and investing in care planning documentation to meet OCM's quality requirements.

The emergency department reduction was the most financially meaningful operational change across OCM participants. Research by Kline and colleagues found that OCM participation was associated with a 9-14% reduction in emergency department visits among chemotherapy patients relative to matched controls — a meaningful quality improvement (since ED visits represent care failures for oncology patients) that also generated meaningful cost savings. Hospital admission rates also declined modestly. These changes were achievable because they reflected addressable care gaps: chemotherapy patients presenting to EDs for symptoms that could have been managed by oncology practices with the staffing and protocols to handle them.
OCM Results: What the CMS Evaluation Found

The independent CMS evaluation of OCM, conducted by Abt Associates, found that OCM did not generate statistically significant net savings to Medicare in its first several performance periods. Gross savings from reduced utilization (ED visits, hospitalizations, post-acute care) were real and consistent, but these savings were largely offset by the MEOS payments CMS made to participating practices. On net, OCM's financial impact on Medicare was approximately zero — a finding that disappointed proponents who had expected the model to generate substantial savings.

Quality outcomes in OCM were more positive. Participating practices showed improvements in care planning documentation, patient experience scores, and end-of-life care quality indicators including increased hospice use and reduced aggressive care in the last 30 days of life. The improvement in end-of-life care quality — moving patients toward goal-concordant care earlier in terminal illness — is arguably the most important quality achievement in oncology value-based care, with both patient welfare and cost implications that are substantial.
Drug Costs: The Elephant in the Oncology Bundle

The fundamental limitation of OCM as an oncology value-based care model was the inclusion of drug costs in the episode spending calculation. When drug costs represent the majority of total episode spending and those costs are determined by CMS's fee schedule for physician-administered drugs (typically Average Sales Price plus 6%), participating practices have almost no leverage over the largest cost driver. A practice that flawlessly manages care coordination, reduces ED visits, and improves end-of-life care conversations cannot offset the impact of a new PD-1 inhibitor entering the market at $150,000 per year that becomes standard of care during the performance period.

The OCM target price calculation attempted to adjust for new drug approvals and rising drug costs through a trend adjustment, but the methodology was imperfect and created significant financial uncertainty for participating practices. Several large oncology groups withdrew from OCM specifically because they could not manage their financial exposure to drug cost trends that bore no relationship to their care management decisions.
The Enhancing Oncology Model: OCM's Successor

The Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM), which launched in July 2023 as OCM's successor, incorporated several design improvements based on OCM's lessons. EOM narrowed the cancer types covered to 7 high-priority malignancies (breast, lung, prostate, small intestine/colorectal, multiple myeloma, chronic leukemia, and B-cell lymphoma). It increased the Monthly Enhanced Oncology Services payment from $160 to $750 per beneficiary per month to fund more robust care management. It also added explicit health equity requirements — practices must collect and report race and ethnicity data and implement interventions targeting disparities for each episode initiator patient.

EOM also made partial progress on the drug cost problem by excluding very high-cost therapies from the bundle (a carve-out approach) for specified conditions where drug cost variability is driven by treatment selection rather than care management. Whether EOM ultimately generates net savings to Medicare beyond MEOS payments remains to be demonstrated, but the design improvements reflect genuine learning from OCM's decade of operation and represent the most sophisticated oncology VBC model yet designed.

The Oncology Care Model's legacy is complex: it failed to generate the net financial savings its architects hoped for, but it succeeded in demonstrating that systematic care management investment in oncology can reduce emergency utilization, improve end-of-life care quality, and support goal-concordant care. The fundamental lesson is that drug pricing reform is a prerequisite for meaningful financial value in oncology VBC — no care management intervention can save enough through utilization reduction to offset the trajectory of oncology drug costs under current Medicare pricing. The EOM's equity requirements and higher care management payments represent genuine progress, but the model cannot fully succeed until the drug cost problem is addressed through separate policy mechanisms.

result.summary: Oncology is the most complex and expensive domain in which value-based care has been attempted, combining catastrophic cost trajectories, profound clinical uncertainty, patient expectations around treatment intensity, and a drug pricing system largely beyond any single payer's control. This lesson examines the Oncology Care Model (OCM) design and results, the Enhancing Oncology Model that succeeded it, how drug costs complicate oncology bundles, and what the evidence reveals about which aspects of value-based oncology are achievable.

children.text: Understanding ACO payment models, risk adjustment, and quality measurement is necessary but insufficient for practicing value-based care. The operational heart of ACO success is population health management — the set of clinical and organizational processes that identifies high-risk patients, closes care gaps, connects patients to appropriate services, and manages total cost of care at the population level rather than the individual encounter level. This lesson moves from the financial architecture of ACOs to their clinical operating system: how attribution and care gap identification work, how risk stratification organizes care management capacity, what effective interventions look like, and which technology investments support population health management in practice.
Attribution: Who Is in Your ACO Population

Attribution — the process of assigning Medicare beneficiaries to an ACO — determines which patients the ACO is financially and clinically accountable for. MSSP uses claims-based retrospective attribution: beneficiaries are assigned to an ACO based on where they received the plurality of their primary care services (E&M visits with primary care providers) during the performance year. This means the final list of attributed beneficiaries is not known until after the year ends, complicating prospective care management.

ACO REACH uses prospective attribution, assigning beneficiaries at the beginning of the performance year based on prior year utilization patterns. Prospective attribution gives ACOs a defined, stable population to manage from January 1 onward, enabling proactive outreach and care management investment for known individuals rather than reactive interventions for a population that is not fully identified until year end. The tradeoff is attribution accuracy: patients who change their primary care relationships during the year may remain attributed to the ACO even if they are no longer receiving primary care there.

Attribution methodology has important equity dimensions. Claims-based attribution assigns patients who have an established primary care relationship — which correlates with higher income and better access to care. Patients without a primary care relationship — often low-income, underinsured, or facing access barriers — may not be attributed to any ACO, leaving them outside the accountable care framework even though they may have the highest clinical need. Some CMMI models have experimented with alternative attribution methods that include emergency department visits and specialty care utilization for populations with limited primary care access.
Care Gap Identification: Finding What Is Missing

Once attribution establishes who is in the population, care gap identification asks what evidence-based services each attributed patient has not received. HEDIS-based care gap analysis is the foundation: for each attributed patient, an ACO's analytics platform compares clinical criteria (age, sex, diagnosis codes, prior services) against HEDIS measure specifications to identify patients who are eligible for but have not received specific preventive or chronic disease management services.
Common care gap categories in ACO population health management include:
Preventive care gaps: Annual wellness visits, breast cancer screening, colorectal cancer screening, and flu vaccinations for patients who have not received them in the measurement year.

Chronic disease management gaps: HbA1c testing and control for diabetic patients, eye exam completion for diabetics, LDL testing and control for cardiovascular disease patients, and blood pressure monitoring for hypertensive patients.

HCC recapture gaps: Chronic conditions that were documented in prior years but have not been coded in the current year, potentially understating patient complexity and affecting risk-adjusted benchmarks.
Medication adherence gaps: Patients on high-adherence-required medications (statins, antihypertensives, antidiabetics) whose claims suggest non-adherence based on prescription fill patterns.
Risk Stratification: Organizing Care Management Capacity

Care management resources are finite. A population of 10,000 attributed Medicare beneficiaries may include 500 high-risk individuals who account for a disproportionate share of total cost of care, 1,500 rising-risk individuals with early warning signs of high utilization, and 8,000 low-risk individuals who need primarily preventive care outreach. Effective population health management allocates care management intensity proportionally to patient risk — not through intuition but through systematic risk stratification using validated algorithms.

Common risk stratification tiers in ACO population health programs are organized as follows. The highest tier — typically the top 3-5% of the population by predicted cost — are patients with multiple complex chronic conditions, recent hospital admissions, behavioral health comorbidities, and high HCC scores. These patients are typically enrolled in intensive case management programs with dedicated case managers, regular check-in calls, and coordination of care across multiple specialists and settings.

The second tier — rising-risk patients, typically the 10-15% of the population with early indicators of risk escalation — receive disease management programs targeting their primary chronic conditions. This tier is arguably the highest-return investment in population health management: intervening early before high utilization develops can prevent tier-1 escalation, while the cost of the interventions is lower than tier-1 case management. Third-tier patients (the broad middle of the population) receive systematic preventive care outreach — reminders, scheduling support, and health coaching for care gap closure.
Care Management Program Design: What Actually Works

High-performing ACOs invest in multiple evidence-based care management program types. Embedded care managers — registered nurses or licensed social workers placed within primary care practices — are the most consistently evidence-supported intervention. Unlike telephonic care managers operating from a central call center, embedded care managers develop longitudinal relationships with high-risk patients, participate in care team huddles, and have direct knowledge of each practice's patient panel and care protocols.

Community health workers (CHWs) represent an increasingly important component of ACO care management teams, particularly for populations with significant social determinants burden. CHWs — often bilingual, from the community they serve, and with training in health navigation rather than clinical care — excel at connecting patients with community resources, addressing social needs, navigating complex care systems, and building trust with patients who are skeptical of the healthcare system. The evidence for CHW programs in reducing ED utilization and improving chronic disease management has strengthened substantially in the past decade, and CMS has expanded reimbursement for CHW services under several APMs.
Transitions of Care: The 30-Day Window

Hospital-to-community transition management is one of the highest-impact and best-evidenced population health interventions available to ACOs. The 30 days following hospital discharge represent a period of maximum clinical vulnerability: patients are adjusting to new or changed medications, recovering from acute illness, navigating care follow-up appointments, and frequently lacking the knowledge or support to manage their own care safely. The 30-day all-cause readmission rate — a core quality and cost metric — is substantially driven by gaps in transition management.

Evidence-based transition programs — including Eric Coleman's Care Transitions Intervention, Jack Geiger's Project RED (Re-Engineered Discharge), and the BOOST (Better Outcomes by Optimizing Safe Transitions) model — have demonstrated 20-30% reductions in 30-day readmissions when implemented with fidelity. ACO transition programs typically include: post-discharge phone calls within 48-72 hours by care managers; post-discharge primary care appointments within 7 days; medication reconciliation review by a clinical pharmacist or nurse; and identification of social barriers that could impede recovery, particularly transportation to follow-up appointments and medication access.
Technology Enabling Population Health: Analytics, EHR Integration, and Care Gap Dashboards

The ability of ACOs to manage attributed populations effectively depends critically on their data and analytics infrastructure. CMS provides MSSP ACOs with monthly claims data files — lagged by 3-4 months — that form the foundation of population-level analytics. More sophisticated ACOs supplement CMS data with near-real-time clinical data from their EHRs, ADT (admit-discharge-transfer) notification feeds from hospitals and emergency departments, and pharmacy data to create a more complete and timely picture of patient activity.

Population health analytics platforms — from vendors including Arcadia, Health Catalyst, Innovaccer, and Epic's population health module — aggregate these data streams into actionable dashboards that allow care teams to see their attributed population's care gaps, risk scores, and recent clinical events. Care gap dashboards show which patients are missing HEDIS measures, with filters by provider panel, risk tier, geographic area, and demographic group. ADT alerts notify care managers when attributed patients are admitted to or discharged from any hospital or emergency department in real time, enabling proactive transition outreach rather than retrospective review.
Total Cost of Care Reduction: Which Interventions Have the Strongest Evidence
Research on ACO population health interventions consistently identifies the following as having the strongest evidence for total cost of care reduction:

Post-acute care management and preferred networks: Reducing SNF utilization in favor of home health for appropriate patients remains the single largest opportunity for ACO cost reduction, particularly for surgical episodes.
Hospital readmission reduction programs: Evidence-based transition management programs reduce 30-day readmissions by 20-30% with established ROI in most market conditions.

Embedded care management in high-risk patients: Dedicated case managers for the top 3-5% of the attributed population consistently reduce ED and inpatient utilization when programs are implemented with sufficient intensity and longitudinal engagement.

Medication adherence programs: Pharmacist-led medication management programs for high-risk patients on multiple chronic disease medications reduce hospitalizations and improve quality metrics with documented financial return in both commercial and Medicare populations.

Palliative care and advance care planning: Proactive palliative care consultations for patients with serious illness reduce aggressive end-of-life care, improve quality of life, and reduce total cost of care — one of the highest-value interventions in population health management.

Population health management is the operational translation of value-based care payment models into clinical practice. It requires analytics infrastructure to identify and stratify the population, care management programs matched to patient risk levels, technology platforms that bring actionable data to the front line, and organizational culture that treats preventing utilization as a clinical and operational success rather than a revenue failure. The ACOs that consistently generate savings share a common pattern: they have made sustained, multi-year investments in care management infrastructure, they have built physician and staff alignment around population health goals, and they use data systematically to identify and close care gaps rather than relying on episodic quality improvement initiatives. This organizational capability — the ability to manage a defined population's health systematically and continuously — is the most valuable asset in value-based care, and it is built through years of deliberate investment that financial models alone cannot create.
