children.text: For most of quality measurement's history, the question of whether healthcare was working was answered by providers: Did the doctor prescribe the right medication? Was the correct procedure performed? Was the HbA1c checked? These process and surrogate outcome measures tell us whether clinical activities occurred, but they do not tell us whether the patient experienced less pain, returned to work, felt better, or found their treatment worthwhile. Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) — structured, standardized measurements of how patients feel and function, collected directly from patients rather than abstracted from charts — address this fundamental gap. They are the most patient-centered form of quality evidence available, and their use in value-based care is expanding rapidly.
What Patient-Reported Outcomes Are and Why They Matter

A patient-reported outcome is any report of the status of a patient's health condition or health behavior that comes directly from the patient, without interpretation by a clinician or anyone else. PROs can cover a wide range of health domains: symptoms (pain intensity, fatigue severity, dyspnea), function (physical function, cognitive function, social functioning), mental health (depression, anxiety, emotional well-being), treatment adherence and side effects, health-related quality of life, and patient satisfaction with care.

PROs matter for value-based care for several interconnected reasons. First, they measure outcomes that patients actually care about — the FDA's accelerated approval of many oncology drugs is now conditional on PRO evidence that the drug improves symptoms or quality of life, not just tumor response rates. Second, they capture dimensions of health that are invisible to clinical observation: a patient who presents to clinic appearing well but reporting severe fatigue and poor function is a different clinical picture than a patient whose vital signs and lab values are all normal. Third, they enable comparison across interventions, clinicians, and healthcare systems on grounds that patients find meaningful, not just grounds that are administratively convenient.
PROMIS: The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System

PROMIS, developed by the NIH beginning in 2004 and now maintained by Northwestern University's Health Measures organization, is the most comprehensive and methodologically rigorous PRO instrument system available in American healthcare. PROMIS was designed to solve several problems with legacy PRO instruments: they were condition-specific (requiring different instruments for different diseases), they used arbitrary scoring systems that did not allow cross-condition comparison, they were paper-based and administratively cumbersome, and they were developed with limited psychometric rigor.

PROMIS achieves its goals through three key design features. First, it is built on Item Response Theory (IRT) — a psychometric framework that calibrates each individual survey question on a continuous scale, allowing scores from different combinations of questions to be placed on a common metric. Second, it uses Item Banks — large pools of calibrated questions for each health domain — that allow flexible measurement. Third, it implements Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an algorithm selects the most informative questions from the item bank based on the patient's answers to previous questions, achieving precise measurement with typically 4-7 questions per domain rather than the 15-30 questions required by traditional fixed-length instruments.

PROMIS is normed to the US general population with a mean T-score of 50 and standard deviation of 10, meaning a patient with a PROMIS Physical Function score of 40 is approximately one standard deviation below the population mean. This general-population norming allows direct comparison across conditions: a patient with knee osteoarthritis who scores 35 on physical function can be compared to a patient with heart failure or multiple sclerosis on the same scale, enabling cross-condition burden measurement that condition-specific instruments cannot provide.
PROMIS Domains and Clinical Applications

PROMIS maintains validated item banks and short-form instruments for over 70 health domains covering physical, mental, and social health. The most commonly used domains in clinical practice include: Physical Function (assessment of physical activities of daily living and higher-level physical activity); Pain Interference (the degree to which pain disrupts daily activities and participation); Fatigue (the subjective experience of tiredness, weakness, and lack of energy); Depression (mood, affect, and somatic symptoms associated with depressive disorders); Anxiety (subjective fear, apprehension, and tension); and Social Function (ability to participate in social activities and roles).

PROMIS also includes pediatric versions and proxy-report versions (completed by caregivers for patients who cannot self-report), extending its applicability across age groups and clinical populations. Global Health short forms — a 10-item instrument covering physical and mental health global assessments — provide a rapid screening tool that is widely used in population health management contexts.
Condition-Specific PRO Instruments: Complementing PROMIS

While PROMIS provides a universal, comparable measurement framework, condition-specific PRO instruments capture clinical details relevant to specific diseases that generic instruments miss. The Hip disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) are widely used in orthopedic value-based care programs and bundled payment models. The KOOS-12 and HOOS-12, short-form versions, have been incorporated into CMS's bundled payment quality requirements. The PROMIS CAT for Physical Function and the KOOS/HOOS complement each other: PROMIS provides population-comparable scores; KOOS/HOOS captures joint-specific function details that matter for orthopedic management.

In oncology, condition-specific and symptom-specific PRO instruments are essential because cancer treatments produce unique symptom profiles not captured by generic instruments. The FACT-G (Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy - General) and disease-specific variants (FACT-B for breast cancer, FACT-L for lung cancer) are standard in oncology clinical trials and increasingly in routine clinical practice. The FDA's 2021 Project PRO established guidance for PRO instrument selection and collection in oncology drug development, signaling that PROs will become a permanent component of oncology quality assessment.
PRO Performance Measures: From Research to Accountability

A PRO Performance Measure (PRO-PM) is a standardized quality measure based on PRO data that is used to evaluate and compare the performance of healthcare providers or health plans. PRO-PMs move PRO data from individual clinical use (informing care for individual patients) to accountability use (comparing providers or programs). The development of valid, reliable PRO-PMs requires: adequate sample sizes for reliable provider-level measurement, appropriate risk adjustment for case mix (sicker patients report worse outcomes), standardized data collection protocols, and infrastructure for systematic PRO administration and reporting.

CMS has included PRO-PMs in several APM quality frameworks. BPCI-Advanced added KOOS-12 and HOOS-12 PRO-PMs for joint replacement episodes beginning in 2021 — the first inclusion of patient-reported functional outcomes in CMS's bundled payment quality requirements. The Enhancing Oncology Model includes PRO requirements for symptom monitoring. The Comprehensive Primary Care Plus model piloted PRO collection in primary care. These CMS decisions signal that PROs will become a standard component of quality measurement in APMs, though the infrastructure for systematic collection and reporting is still being built.
Digital Health and Real-Time PRO Collection

Digital health technology has dramatically expanded the practical feasibility of PRO collection. Patient portals, smartphone applications, SMS-based surveys, and tablet-based collection in waiting rooms allow PROs to be collected at scale without the paper burden that made systematic collection impractical in busy clinical settings. EHR integration platforms — including APIs connecting PROMIS assessment tools with Epic, Cerner, and other EHR systems — allow PRO results to flow directly into the patient's chart and appear as structured data available for quality measurement and care management.

The most clinically impactful application of digital PRO collection is real-time symptom monitoring in oncology. Studies by Ethan Basch and colleagues published in JAMA and the New England Journal of Medicine demonstrated that weekly web-based symptom monitoring — where patients report symptoms between clinic visits and clinicians receive alerts for concerning symptom escalation — reduced emergency department visits, improved quality of life, and extended overall survival in cancer patients receiving systemic treatment. These results, replicated in multiple studies, have made digital PRO collection a clinical best practice recommendation in oncology, not just a research tool.
Implementation Barriers: Burden, EHR Integration, and Workflow

Despite their clinical and policy value, PROs face significant implementation barriers in routine practice. Patient burden is the most commonly cited: completing multiple PRO instruments at each visit, particularly for patients with multiple chronic conditions who may be asked to complete instruments by multiple providers, creates fatigue and declining response rates over time. Survey optimization — using adaptive testing to minimize questions, selecting domain-specific measures rather than comprehensive batteries, and deploying instruments at clinically appropriate time points — can reduce burden significantly.

EHR integration remains technically challenging despite improvements in interoperability standards. Most EHR systems do not natively display PRO trends in clinically actionable formats — instead, PRO scores appear as discrete data elements or notes that require manual review, rather than trend graphs that show longitudinal change relative to population norms. Workflow integration requires deliberate clinical process design: specifying when PROs are administered, who reviews them, what the clinical response protocol is for concerning scores, and how PRO data informs treatment decision conversations.
Equity Concerns in PRO Collection and Interpretation

PRO collection raises equity concerns that must be addressed for the data to be valid and actionable across diverse populations. Digital PRO collection platforms assume smartphone access, digital literacy, and English proficiency that is not universal. Patients with limited English proficiency, lower digital literacy, or lack of smartphone access systematically have lower PRO completion rates, creating selection bias in the resulting data that may obscure the populations with highest clinical need. PROMIS instruments have been translated and validated in Spanish and several other languages, and some instruments have been validated in low-literacy versions, but coverage across all relevant languages and literacy levels remains incomplete.

Population-level PRO benchmarks may also reflect underlying social inequity rather than provider performance. If a safety-net hospital's patient population reports higher pain scores and lower physical function than a tertiary academic medical center's population, this difference likely reflects socioeconomic and health status differences between populations rather than quality differences between providers. Using unadjusted PRO data for provider accountability without social risk adjustment risks misattributing population health burden to provider quality — the same problem that affects risk adjustment for financial accountability in ACOs.

Patient-reported outcomes represent the most direct measurement of whether healthcare is achieving what patients come to clinicians for: less pain, better function, improved quality of life, and the ability to live according to their values. The methodological infrastructure for valid, reliable PRO collection exists in PROMIS and the growing ecosystem of validated instruments. The digital infrastructure for scalable collection is increasingly available. What remains is the harder work of building clinical workflows that use PRO data in real time, equity-aware collection protocols that serve all patients, and accountability frameworks that use PRO data in ways that improve care rather than creating gaming incentives. PROs are moving from research instrument to clinical standard — the question is how quickly the healthcare system can build the infrastructure to use them well.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) capture what patients themselves experience — pain, function, fatigue, mental health, quality of life — offering a fundamentally different quality signal than clinician-observed outcomes or administrative measures. This lesson covers PROMIS and its computerized adaptive testing approach, condition-specific PRO instruments, the CMS framework for PRO performance measures, digital health opportunities and barriers, equity concerns in PRO collection, and the emerging use of real-time PRO data in care management.

children.text: Risk adjustment is among the most technically complex and financially consequential elements of value-based care payment. At its core, risk adjustment solves a straightforward problem: if you pay every health plan or provider the same amount per patient regardless of patient health status, you create powerful incentives to select healthier patients (whose care is cheap) and avoid sicker patients (whose care is expensive). Risk adjustment neutralizes this adverse selection incentive by paying more for sicker patients and less for healthier ones, making it financially neutral whether a plan or provider serves a sick or healthy population. In practice, CMS's Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk adjustment model is one of the most influential mathematical algorithms in American healthcare — and one of the most gamed.
Why Risk Adjustment Exists: The Adverse Selection Problem

Without risk adjustment, any payment system that pays per-beneficiary creates incentives for providers and plans to preferentially serve low-cost patients. A Medicare Advantage plan that enrolls exclusively healthy beneficiaries can offer rich benefits and low premiums while earning handsome profits; a plan that enrolls chronically ill, high-cost beneficiaries providing equal amounts of capitation would quickly become insolvent. ACO benchmarks set without risk adjustment would systematically favor ACOs serving healthy populations over those serving complex, high-need populations. Risk adjustment attempts to create a level playing field where efficient, high-quality care of sick patients is financially viable.

The theoretical goal of risk adjustment is to predict each individual's expected healthcare costs based on observable health characteristics — demographics and diagnoses — so that payments reflect predicted costs rather than actual costs. An individual with congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and type 2 diabetes has predictably higher costs than a healthy 68-year-old with no documented chronic conditions. The risk adjustment model quantifies this difference and adjusts payments accordingly.
The CMS-HCC Model: Architecture and Logic

The CMS-HCC (Hierarchical Condition Category) model is the risk adjustment system CMS uses for Medicare Advantage payment, Medicare ACO benchmarks, and Part D prescription drug payments. The model was developed in the early 2000s and has been updated multiple times, most recently with significant structural changes in 2024. The CMS-HCC model uses diagnosis codes from the prior year's medical claims (physician, outpatient, and inpatient) to predict the current year's total Medicare spending.

The model maps the approximately 70,000 ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes into 86 Hierarchical Condition Categories (HCCs). The hierarchical structure is critical: when multiple HCCs are clinically related, only the most severe is counted. For example, diabetes with chronic complications (HCC 18) and diabetes without complications (HCC 19) are in the same hierarchy — if a patient has both diagnoses, only HCC 18 is counted, preventing double-counting. The result is a set of mutually exclusive, clinically coherent disease categories that each carry a coefficient representing their incremental predicted cost above the demographic baseline.
RAF Score Calculation

The Risk Adjustment Factor (RAF) score is the output of the CMS-HCC model for each beneficiary. A RAF score of 1.0 represents average expected costs — a hypothetical average Medicare beneficiary. A RAF score of 2.5 means the beneficiary is expected to cost 2.5 times the average — their capitation payment (in Medicare Advantage) or their benchmark contribution (in an ACO) is 2.5 times the baseline rate.

The RAF score is calculated by summing the coefficients for all applicable demographic factors (age, sex, Medicaid dual-eligibility status, disability status) and disease HCC categories. Each HCC has a separately estimated coefficient derived from regression analysis of historical spending data — the coefficient for congestive heart failure (HCC 85) might be 0.34, meaning patients with this diagnosis are predicted to have 34% higher costs than average, holding other factors constant. A patient with congestive heart failure, COPD, and diabetes with complications might have a RAF score of 2.1 from the sum of demographic coefficients (around 0.4 for a 75-year-old female) plus three disease HCC coefficients.
Which Diagnoses Drive the Most RAF: The High-Impact HCCs
Certain HCC categories carry large coefficients that have the most dramatic impact on RAF scores. The highest-impact HCCs in the 2023 CMS-HCC model include:
Septicemia/Shock (HCC 2): Coefficient approximately 1.5 — patients with severe sepsis are predicted to cost 150% more than average.
Lung and Other Severe Cancers (HCC 9): Coefficient approximately 1.2 — active malignancy significantly increases predicted cost.
Congestive Heart Failure (HCC 85): Coefficient approximately 0.34 — one of the most prevalent high-impact conditions.
Chronic Kidney Disease Stage 5 and End-Stage Renal Disease (HCC 136): Coefficient approximately 0.7 — very high-cost population.
Major Depressive, Bipolar, and Paranoid Disorders (HCC 58): Coefficient approximately 0.27 — behavioral health conditions significantly increase total cost of care.
Annual Recalibration: How the Model Evolves

CMS recalibrates the CMS-HCC model periodically using updated Medicare spending data, adding new HCC categories when clinical evidence or spending patterns warrant, removing categories that no longer predict meaningfully, and updating coefficients to reflect changes in treatment costs for specific conditions. The 2024 recalibration, which took effect in the 2024 plan year, was the most significant revision in over a decade: CMS added new HCCs, revised the underlying regression methodology, and adjusted coefficients significantly for several high-volume conditions — resulting in RAF score changes that materially affected Medicare Advantage payment amounts for plans with specific disease mix profiles.
Diagnosis Coding Intensity and Upcoding Concerns

Because the RAF score — and the resulting Medicare Advantage capitation payment or ACO benchmark — depends entirely on documented diagnoses, there is a direct financial incentive to ensure that all applicable HCC diagnoses are coded in every calendar year. This legitimate activity — complete and accurate diagnosis documentation — shades into upcoding when providers document diagnoses that are not genuinely clinically present, document diagnoses at higher severity than clinically warranted, or pursue annual wellness visits primarily for the purpose of refreshing HCC codes rather than delivering clinical value.

The distinction between complete documentation and upcoding is genuinely difficult to draw. Medicare Advantage plans routinely conduct retrospective chart review and home health assessment visits specifically to identify HCC diagnoses that were treated but not coded in claims — an activity that captures legitimate disease burden that claims data misses but that also generates significant increases in RAF scores without any change in patient health status. The OIG has investigated Medicare Advantage coding intensity repeatedly, estimating that MA plans' risk scores exceed what would be expected based on traditional fee-for-service coding by approximately 8-10% — translating to tens of billions of dollars in potentially overstated risk-adjusted payments.
Risk Adjustment and ACO Benchmarks

In MSSP, CMS uses the CMS-HCC model to risk-adjust ACO benchmark calculations. When an ACO's attributed population becomes sicker over time — higher RAF scores in year 3 than year 1 — CMS adjusts the benchmark upward to reflect the expected higher cost of a sicker population. Conversely, if the population becomes healthier (lower RAF scores), the benchmark decreases. This adjustment is designed to ensure that ACOs are evaluated on their efficiency at managing their actual patient population rather than benefiting or suffering from demographic changes in their attributed population.

However, HCC-based risk adjustment in ACO benchmarks creates a perverse incentive: ACOs that improve diagnosis documentation and capture more HCC codes for their attributed patients — an activity CMS encourages as clinically valuable — will see their benchmark increase, making savings harder to achieve. An ACO that invests in HCC recapture (identifying and documenting chronic conditions that were treated but not coded) will have a higher-risk-adjusted benchmark that offsets some of the improved revenue that HCC recapture generates in Medicare Advantage. This tension between the diagnostic coding incentives in MA versus MSSP creates complex strategic challenges for health systems that operate in both environments.
Prospective vs. Concurrent Risk Adjustment: Two Different Signals

There are two fundamentally different approaches to risk adjustment. Prospective risk adjustment uses prior period diagnoses to predict current period costs — the standard CMS-HCC approach. A patient's RAF score is calculated from last year's claims and used to set this year's payment. The advantage is stability and planning: payment is set before the year begins, based on known information. The disadvantage is that new conditions diagnosed during the performance year are not reflected in payment until the following year.

Concurrent risk adjustment uses current period diagnoses to adjust current period payment — so if a patient is diagnosed with cancer in month 3, the payment adjustment reflects that diagnosis from month 3 forward. Concurrent adjustment is more accurate at predicting actual costs but less stable for payment purposes, since payment is adjusted after the year is underway. Concurrent adjustment is used in some commercial risk-sharing arrangements and in certain Medicaid managed care payment models where capitation payments are reconciled after the year based on actual diagnosis mix.
Medicare Advantage Overpayment: The Largest Risk Adjustment Controversy

The most consequential controversy in risk adjustment concerns Medicare Advantage overpayments. Multiple academic studies, MedPAC analyses, and OIG reports have found that Medicare Advantage plans are overpaid relative to what traditional Medicare would spend for the same beneficiaries — estimates range from $12 billion to $25 billion or more annually, depending on methodology. These overpayments arise from two sources: legitimate favorable selection (MA enrollees are healthier than traditional Medicare on dimensions not captured by the HCC model) and improper coding intensity (upcoding that inflates RAF scores without reflecting genuine changes in patient health).

CMS applies a coding intensity adjustment to MA risk scores — a uniform reduction intended to account for the systematic difference between MA coding intensity and traditional Medicare coding intensity. For 2024, this adjustment was -5.9%, meaning MA plans' RAF scores are reduced by 5.9% to offset average coding intensity differences. MA plans and their trade associations have challenged this adjustment as too large; healthcare economists who study MA overpayment argue it is insufficient. The debate over coding intensity adjustment is ultimately a debate about how much of the MA overpayment reflects legitimate clinical documentation versus financial gaming of a risk model.

Risk adjustment and the HCC model are among the most important and least-understood elements of value-based care economics. They determine who is financially accountable for what — and whether that accountability is fair. A risk adjustment model that inadequately captures patient severity punishes providers who care for sicker patients; one that is too easily gamed rewards documentation expertise over care quality. The CMS-HCC model is a sophisticated but imperfect instrument that annual recalibration can improve only incrementally. The larger challenge is that risk adjustment can never perfectly predict individual costs — there will always be legitimate variation in health needs that the model misses, creating residual adverse selection incentives that good VBC policy design must address through other mechanisms.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: Risk adjustment is the mathematical backbone of every value-based care payment model, enabling fair comparison of spending and quality across providers who serve patients with different health needs. The CMS-HCC model and its RAF scores determine billions of dollars in Medicare Advantage payments, ACO benchmarks, and capitation rates — and its complexity creates both gaming opportunities and genuine measurement challenges. This lesson covers HCC model architecture, RAF score calculation, upcoding concerns, prospective versus concurrent adjustment, and Medicare Advantage overpayment controversies.
result.title: Risk Adjustment and HCC Scores: Leveling the Playing Field

children.text: Every time a physician bills Medicare — or most private insurers — the payment they receive traces back to a single number: the relative value unit, or RVU. Introduced in 1992 following the landmark work of William Hsiao and colleagues at Harvard, the RVU-based Resource-Based Relative Value Scale (RBRVS) replaced a chaotic, historically-derived usual and customary fee schedule with a system that was supposed to be rational, reproducible, and fair. Thirty-plus years later, the RBRVS remains the foundation of physician payment in the United States — but its distortions have become so embedded in care delivery that any serious reform of healthcare value requires understanding exactly how it works, and exactly how it fails.
The Anatomy of an RVU

Each physician service is assigned a procedure code under the Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) system maintained by the American Medical Association. For every CPT code, CMS assigns three component RVU values that sum to a total relative value:

Work RVU (wRVU): Reflects the physician time, mental effort, technical skill, and stress involved in the service. This component accounts for roughly 50-55% of total RVUs and is the most politically contested element of the system.

Practice Expense RVU (PE RVU): Covers the overhead costs of delivering the service including staff, rent, supplies, and equipment. It accounts for roughly 40-44% of total RVUs and has both a facility (lower, when the service is delivered in a hospital) and non-facility (higher, when in a physician office) version.

Malpractice RVU (PLI RVU): Reflects the professional liability insurance costs associated with the procedure, typically 3-5% of total RVUs and highest for high-risk procedural specialties like obstetrics and neurosurgery.

Each component is adjusted by a geographic practice cost index (GPCI) that reflects cost-of-living and local input prices in the physician's locality. The Medicare payment formula is then: Payment = [(wRVU x wGPCI) + (PE RVU x PE GPCI) + (PLI RVU x PLI GPCI)] x Conversion Factor. This formula is deceptively simple; its political and economic consequences are anything but.

The Conversion Factor (CF) is a single dollar amount CMS sets each year that translates total RVUs into dollars. For 2024, the CF was set at $32.74 per RVU — down from $33.89 in 2023, a cut that triggered significant physician advocacy. This single number is the lever through which CMS controls total physician spending under Medicare, which makes setting it intensely political. Because Medicare physician payment is budget-neutral by statute, increasing payments for some services requires reducing the conversion factor or reducing payments to others.
How the RBRVS Is Maintained: The AMA/Specialty Society RVS Update Committee

In theory, the RBRVS is a scientifically calibrated system. In practice, the relative values assigned to CPT codes are substantially shaped by the AMA/Specialty Society Relative Value Scale Update Committee — universally known as the RUC. The RUC is a 33-member advisory body on which specialty societies hold strong representation, with primary care consistently underrepresented relative to its share of the physician workforce. When CMS wants to value a new or revised CPT code, it solicits input from the RUC, which conducts surveys of physicians to estimate the typical time and intensity associated with the service. CMS accepts the RUC's recommendations at a rate historically above 85-90%, which critics argue gives procedure-heavy specialties outsized influence over their own payment rates.

The RUC process has drawn sustained criticism from primary care advocates, health economists, and the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC). Because specialists dominate the committee, and because the surveys measure physician perceptions of work rather than objective time-motion studies, the resulting RVU values tend to reflect the profession's historic biases. A 15-minute office visit for diabetes management may generate 1.5 work RVUs; an interventional cardiologist placing a coronary stent may generate 30 or more work RVUs in 90 minutes of procedural time. Whether that 20-to-1 ratio accurately reflects the relative social value, training requirements, or patient impact of these services is a question the RUC process was not designed to answer.
The Undervaluation of E&M: The Core Distortion

The most consequential distortion in the RVU system is the chronic undervaluation of Evaluation and Management (E&M) services — the office visits, hospital rounds, and consultations that constitute the cognitive core of medicine. A new patient office visit of moderate complexity (CPT 99204) generated a total RVU of approximately 3.0 before the 2021 E&M revision. A single colonoscopy (CPT 45378) generated approximately 3.8 total RVUs for roughly the same physician time investment. The physician doing screening colonoscopies at high volume could generate two to three times the annual revenue of an equally trained physician doing complex diabetes or heart failure management.

In 2021, CMS implemented the most significant E&M reform since the system's inception, substantially increasing the wRVUs for office E&M codes and streamlining documentation requirements. Level 4 new patient visits (99204) saw their wRVU increase from 2.43 to 3.17 — a 30% increase. Level 4 established patient visits (99214) increased from 1.50 to 1.92. This reform was partly financed by a reduction in the conversion factor, which meant that proceduralists effectively subsidized the E&M increase through lower per-RVU payments. The reform was directionally correct but insufficient to close a gap that had widened over decades of RUC-dominated valuation.
The SGR Era and the MACRA Fix

From 1997 until 2015, physician Medicare payment was governed by the Sustainable Growth Rate (SGR) formula, a mechanism designed to link aggregate physician spending to GDP growth. When physician spending grew faster than GDP — which it reliably did as volume increased year after year — the SGR formula triggered automatic cuts in the conversion factor. Between 2002 and 2015, the SGR called for cumulative cuts of approximately 30%. Congress overrode these cuts every single year through the so-called annual doc fix, creating enormous policy uncertainty, a growing phantom liability on the federal books, and a pervasive sense among physicians that Medicare payment policy was fundamentally unstable and politically rather than rationally determined.

The Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA) permanently repealed the SGR and replaced it with a new framework. Under MACRA, physicians choose between two tracks: the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) and participation in an Advanced Alternative Payment Model (APM). Both tracks were designed to move payment away from pure volume toward quality and value — but the underlying RVU-based fee schedule remained the payment infrastructure on which both tracks operate. MACRA solved the SGR's annual political crisis while leaving the underlying distortions of the RBRVS system intact.
The wRVU Treadmill: Consequences for Employed Physicians

As hospital systems have acquired physician practices — a trend accelerating sharply since the ACA — most employed physicians are now compensated through wRVU-based productivity formulas. The typical employed physician contract specifies a base salary plus a per-wRVU incentive above a productivity threshold, with total compensation tightly correlated to wRVU output. MGMA data consistently shows that specialist compensation is roughly two to three times primary care compensation when both are driven by wRVU production — a direct reflection of the RVU system's procedural bias embedded in employment contracts.

The wRVU treadmill — the imperative to generate ever-more RVUs to maintain or grow income — has several documented consequences. First, it drives visit compression: physicians see more patients per hour, leaving less time for complex cognitive work, patient education, and care coordination. Second, it incentivizes upcoding — documenting to the highest legitimate level of service to maximize billable RVUs. Third, it creates pressure toward high-RVU procedures even when watchful waiting or lower-intensity care might be clinically equivalent. Fourth, and most perniciously for value-based care, it penalizes physicians who invest time in care coordination, population health activities, and patient outreach that generate no billable codes.

Research by Khullar and colleagues at Weill Cornell has documented that physicians in high-wRVU environments report significantly higher rates of burnout, with primary care physicians experiencing the highest moral distress when productivity targets conflict with relationship-based care. The irony is pointed: the physicians whose work is most essential to value-based care — primary care providers managing complex chronic disease populations — are also those most disadvantaged by the RVU system and most vulnerable to the treadmill dynamic.
How RVU Incentives Distort Care Delivery at the System Level

The RBRVS system creates predictable distortions beyond individual physician behavior. At the system level, the RVU signal shapes specialty workforce decisions across generations of physicians: medical students choosing between internal medicine and cardiology interventional fellowships are, in part, responding to a payment system that will pay the cardiologist three to four times more per clinical hour for the rest of their career. The United States produces dramatically fewer primary care physicians per capita than peer nations — a workforce imbalance that virtually every health policy researcher links to payment disparities rooted in the RVU system.

At the hospital level, service line investment follows RVU revenue. Cardiac catheterization labs, orthopedic surgery suites, and cancer centers generate far more revenue per square foot than primary care clinics or behavioral health departments. Capital allocation systematically favors procedural capacity over primary and preventive care infrastructure. The geographic distribution of these high-RVU services also tends to follow commercially insured patient populations, reinforcing healthcare access disparities between affluent and low-income communities.
Reform Proposals: From Incremental Fixes to Structural Change

Numerous reform proposals have attempted to address the RVU system's distortions at varying levels of ambition. MedPAC has repeatedly recommended time-motion studies to replace RUC survey data as the basis for work RVU valuations. Health economists including the late Uwe Reinhardt argued for a relative value amnesty — a comprehensive re-valuation that would explicitly trade procedural RVU reductions for E&M increases without the constraint of budget neutrality that politically hobbles incremental reform.

CMS Innovation Center models like Primary Care First attempt to partially escape the RVU framework by replacing per-visit E&M billing with flat monthly care management fees for primary care — essentially decoupling primary care revenue from individual visit volume. This represents a meaningful structural shift, but requires primary care practices to accept substantial financial risk during the transition and to build the population health management infrastructure that per-capita payment rewards. The ACA primary care bonus program (2011-2015), which provided a 10% payment increase on primary care E&M services, temporarily reduced the income gap but did not change the underlying RVU values.

The deepest reform — moving toward population-based payment such as capitation or global budgets — would remove per-service payment entirely and make the RVU calculation irrelevant for care delivery decisions. Under capitation, a physician or organization is paid per-member-per-month to manage a population, not per procedure. ACOs, Medicare Advantage plans, and capitated Medicaid managed care organizations operate in this direction, but most physicians remain in fee-for-service RVU-based arrangements for the bulk of their revenue. Until the payment signal changes fundamentally, the wRVU treadmill will continue to shape physician behavior, specialty workforce distribution, and capital investment in ways that systematically undermine the value-based care agenda.

The RVU system is not simply a technical payment mechanism — it is the economic foundation on which the entire architecture of American physician practice is built. Its biases toward procedures and against cognitive care are not accidents; they reflect the political economy of the RUC process and the path dependency of a system that has calcified around historical fee relationships established before modern primary care medicine existed. Any value-based care reformer who does not understand RVUs is working with an incomplete map. The conversion factor, the GPCI, the wRVU threshold in employment contracts, the facility versus non-facility PE rate — these technical details translate directly into physician behavior, specialty choice, and the geography of care. Reforming them is slow, political, and expensive. But without reforming them, every other value-based initiative operates against a persistent structural current.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: The Resource-Based Relative Value Scale (RBRVS) system has governed physician payment for over three decades, yet its internal logic systematically undervalues cognitive and primary care services relative to procedural work. This lesson dissects how RVUs are calculated, how the conversion factor is set, and why employed physicians face a wRVU treadmill that has profound implications for care quality and physician well-being. Understanding the mechanics of RVU-based payment is essential context for every value-based care reform that attempts to change physician behavior.

children.text: Risk adjustment for clinical complexity is widely accepted as a fairness requirement in value-based care payment. Adjusting for patient poverty, race, or social circumstances is far more controversial — a debate that sits at the intersection of health equity, payment policy, and moral reasoning about what healthcare systems can and should be held accountable for. The question is not abstract: it directly affects the financial viability of safety-net hospitals, Federally Qualified Health Centers, and health plans serving Medicaid and dual-eligible populations. And the answer has profound consequences for whether value-based care drives equity improvement or perpetuates existing disparities.
The Core Tension: Fairness vs. Accountability

The case for including social risk factors in risk adjustment is straightforward: social determinants of health — income, housing stability, food security, educational attainment, neighborhood conditions — are among the strongest predictors of healthcare costs and health outcomes. A clinician or health plan serving a population with high rates of food insecurity, unstable housing, and poverty will have worse measured outcomes and higher costs than one serving an affluent population, even if the quality of clinical care is identical or superior. Without adjustment for these factors, payment models systematically penalize providers who serve disadvantaged communities.

The case against social risk adjustment is equally forceful: adjusting for social risk means accepting lower quality targets for providers caring for poor patients. If a safety-net hospital's quality standards are set lower because its patients are poorer, where is the accountability for genuinely improving care for those patients? Adjusted benchmarks may mask systematic quality failures in institutions that serve disadvantaged populations — the very populations for whom quality improvement is most consequential. There is also a race-equity dimension: adjusting for race in risk models could entrench racial disparities in quality standards, treating different quality as acceptable based on patient demographics.
The NASEM 2017 Report: A Framework for Resolution

The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) 2017 report Accounting for Social Risk Factors in Medicare Payment provided the most rigorous framework to date for addressing this dilemma. The report distinguished between two different uses of social risk data in payment: adjusting payment to reflect differences in expected costs (payment risk adjustment), and adjusting performance standards to reflect differences in expected quality outcomes (performance standard adjustment). The NASEM committee concluded that adjusting payment for social risk is appropriate when social factors predict expected costs; adjusting performance standards — holding providers to lower quality targets — is not appropriate because it would entrench disparities.

The NASEM report's key recommendations included: stratify quality reporting by social risk factors to make disparities visible; use social risk data for payment adjustment only when it predicts additional cost beyond clinical risk; invest in building the data infrastructure (collecting SDOH data systematically in claims and EHRs) needed to improve social risk models; and create accountability for reducing disparities rather than just adjusting them away.
Current CMS Policy: Stratified Reporting vs. Direct Adjustment

As of 2024, CMS policy on social risk in payment programs has largely followed the NASEM recommendation to stratify rather than adjust. In MSSP, CMS produces stratified quality reports showing ACO performance separately for dual-eligible and non-dual-eligible beneficiaries, making disparities visible without adjusting the financial targets based on social risk. In the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing program, CMS stratifies hospital quality scores by patient social risk but does not adjust the financial reward-penalty calculations. In Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, CMS has introduced the Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI), which adjusts Star Ratings for plans with high proportions of low-income and dual-eligible enrollees — a partial form of social risk adjustment specific to the Star Rating context.

Critics from the safety-net provider community argue that stratified reporting without payment adjustment is insufficient: making disparities visible is valuable, but if the payment model still penalizes safety-net providers financially for serving disadvantaged populations, visibility alone does not solve the equity problem. The FQHC and community health center community has been particularly vocal about the need for social risk adjustment in quality-linked payment models, arguing that their patient populations' social complexity makes them structurally unable to meet the same performance standards as suburban physician practices serving commercially insured patients.
The Dual-Eligible Population: The Most Challenging Social Risk Context

Dual-eligible beneficiaries — individuals who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid — represent the highest-cost, highest-need population in American healthcare. Approximately 12 million Americans are dually enrolled, representing roughly 15% of Medicaid enrollees but nearly 40% of Medicaid spending, and approximately 20% of Medicare beneficiaries but 35% of Medicare spending. Dual-eligibles have dramatically higher rates of multiple chronic conditions, behavioral health comorbidities, cognitive impairment, functional limitations, and social needs including poverty and unstable housing.

The dual-eligible indicator (DE) is already included in the CMS-HCC model as a demographic risk factor, and dual-eligible status is a criterion for the Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) adjustment in Medicare Part D and for the CAI in Star Ratings. But the DE indicator captures only the administrative status of dual enrollment — it does not capture the degree of social need, housing instability, functional disability, or behavioral health complexity within the dual-eligible population, which varies enormously. A fully-disabled, low-income beneficiary with severe mental illness and unstable housing presents very different care management challenges than a dual-eligible beneficiary who qualified for Medicaid because of modest financial assets with otherwise manageable chronic conditions.
SDOH Z-Codes: A New Data Source for Social Risk Models

ICD-10-CM includes a set of Z-codes (Z55-Z65) that allow clinicians to document social determinants of health in the medical record and in claims data. Z-codes cover domains including: Z59 (Problems related to housing and economic circumstances), Z60 (Problems related to social environment), Z63 (Other problems related to primary support group), and Z64 (Problems related to certain psychosocial circumstances including inadequate food and homelessness). If systematically coded, Z-codes could provide claims-based social risk data that improves risk adjustment models without requiring new data collection infrastructure.

In practice, Z-code utilization is extremely variable and generally low. Studies have found that fewer than 1-2% of Medicare beneficiaries have any Z-code documented in their claims in a given year, despite much higher estimated prevalence of social needs. Systematic barriers include: lack of provider training in Z-code documentation, perceived lack of actionability (documenting food insecurity does not itself connect the patient to food assistance), EHR workflow gaps that do not prompt social needs screening, and uncertainty about whether the information will be used beneficially or result in adverse insurance consequences.
Vermont and Maryland as Policy Laboratories

Several states have taken more direct approaches to social risk adjustment than federal CMS policy permits. Vermont's OneCare Vermont ACO model uses a social risk index based on area deprivation scores, housing instability data, and Vermont's Medicaid enrollment rates to adjust ACO financial targets at the regional level. This approach adjusts the aggregate benchmark rather than individual patient risk scores, partially addressing the safety-net equity concern without requiring individual-level social data.

Maryland's All-Payer Model has included social determinants adjustments in its hospital global budget calculations since the 2014 model update. Maryland hospitals in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas receive higher global budget revenue allocations that reflect the expected higher costs of caring for their populations — an explicit social risk adjustment built into hospital-level payment. Maryland has also invested in community health worker programs and social needs navigation as part of its total cost of care framework, recognizing that social interventions are inseparable from clinical cost management for high-need populations.
Policy Proposals: Equity-Adjusted vs. Equity-Stratified Measurement

The current policy debate has crystallized around two approaches. The equity-stratified approach (current CMS policy) reports performance separately by social risk stratum, maintains common performance standards across all providers, and creates accountability for reducing disparities without adjusting targets. The equity-adjusted approach adjusts financial targets or quality benchmarks for social risk, reducing the financial penalty on safety-net providers while creating a risk that lower standards will be permanently accepted for disadvantaged populations.

A third approach — which some researchers and advocacy organizations are advocating — is to fund social risk management rather than adjust it away. Under this approach, VBC payment models would include explicit supplemental payments for social needs management: care management fees for high-social-risk beneficiaries, population health investment funds for underserved communities, or Medicaid-funded social service integration programs. This approach maintains quality accountability while providing the resources needed to actually address the social determinants that drive disparate outcomes. Whether this approach can generate sufficient political consensus — particularly given the significant budget implications — is the central policy challenge.

The social risk adjustment debate is ultimately a debate about what the healthcare system can and should be held responsible for. Clinical risk adjustment is uncontroversially appropriate: providers cannot control whether their patients have congestive heart failure, so payment must reflect clinical complexity. Social risk adjustment is more contested because social determinants, while also largely outside an individual provider's control, are in principle addressable through healthcare system action — care management, social needs navigation, community investment — even if addressing them requires resources beyond what current payment systems provide. The path forward requires both better data infrastructure for social risk measurement and payment policy that creates accountability for disparity reduction while providing the resources to actually achieve it.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: One of the most contested questions in healthcare payment policy is whether risk adjustment models should incorporate social risk factors — poverty, housing instability, race, neighborhood disadvantage — alongside clinical diagnoses. Adjusting for social risk may perpetuate inequity by holding safety-net providers to lower performance standards; not adjusting punishes providers who serve disadvantaged populations for factors outside their control. The NASEM 2017 report, dual-eligible adjustments, SDOH Z-codes, and state-level experiments offer competing approaches to this unresolved dilemma.
result.title: Social Risk in Risk Adjustment: Should We Adjust for Poverty?

children.text: The most troubling systemic problem with Medicare Advantage Star Ratings is not gaming by high-performing plans — it is the structural disadvantage faced by plans that serve the most vulnerable beneficiaries. Plans with high proportions of dual-eligible and low-income subsidy (LIS) enrollees consistently score lower on Stars than plans serving commercially similar populations, and this performance gap persists even after controlling for many observable quality differences. The financial consequences are substantial: lower Star scores mean lower Quality Bonus Payments, which mean less ability to offer generous benefits, which may make these plans less attractive to the very populations they serve. The equity critique of Star Ratings is not marginal — it goes to the heart of whether a quality payment system can simultaneously reward quality, serve equity, and avoid market segmentation by socioeconomic status.
The Socioeconomic Gradient in Star Performance

Research consistently documents a strong negative association between the proportion of LIS and dual-eligible enrollees in an MA plan and that plan's overall Star Rating. A 2017 analysis by Meyers and colleagues in Health Affairs found that plans in the highest quartile of LIS penetration had average Star Ratings approximately 0.5 stars lower than plans in the lowest quartile, after controlling for plan characteristics. A 2022 MedPAC analysis confirmed this pattern, finding that Special Needs Plans (D-SNPs) — which are designed specifically to serve dual-eligible beneficiaries — scored systematically lower than non-SNP plans on virtually every Star domain.

The mechanisms driving lower Star scores in high-LIS plans are multiple and overlapping. Low-income and dual-eligible beneficiaries have lower health literacy, higher rates of cognitive impairment, greater housing instability, and more limited English proficiency — all of which affect their ability to complete preventive care screenings, adhere to medication regimens, and respond to outreach from plan care coordinators. These are patient-level factors that influence measured quality outcomes but reflect population characteristics rather than plan quality differences.
CAHPS Scores and Health Literacy: The Patient Experience Problem

CAHPS patient experience measures carry 4x weight in the Star Rating calculation — the highest weight of any measure category. Plans serving high proportions of LIS beneficiaries systematically score lower on CAHPS, and this gap is not fully explained by differences in plan quality. Research by Klein and colleagues found that CAHPS response rates and mean scores are significantly lower in low-income populations, with effects that persist after controlling for health status and clinical complexity. The mechanisms include: lower survey literacy (difficulty completing written surveys); response acquiescence bias (some cultural groups systematically avoid extreme response options, pulling scores toward the middle); language barriers (surveys available primarily in English and Spanish); and lower baseline expectations about healthcare interactions that may affect how positive experiences are rated.

The 4x weight on CAHPS measures — intended to prioritize patient experience in Stars — inadvertently amplifies the equity problem. Because CAHPS scores are lower in plans serving disadvantaged populations for reasons partially unrelated to actual care quality, and because these lower scores are multiplied by 4 in the Stars calculation, the equity disadvantage is magnified in the overall Star score. A plan that would otherwise be near the 4-star threshold based on clinical quality measures may fall well below 4 stars once CAHPS-driven underperformance is incorporated with its 4x multiplier.
Medication Adherence Disparities: A Structural Challenge

The three medication adherence measures in Star Ratings — for diabetes medications, renin angiotensin system (RAS) antagonists (for hypertension), and statins — are among the highest-weighted and most consequential measures for overall Star performance. Low-income beneficiaries have consistently lower medication adherence rates than higher-income beneficiaries, driven by cost barriers (even within Part D, cost-sharing creates adherence challenges), transportation barriers to pharmacy access, cognitive and health literacy limitations, and higher rates of comorbid conditions that complicate medication management.

Plans serving high LIS proportions face a structural challenge: the population most in need of medication adherence support is also the population hardest to reach with conventional pharmacy interventions. Text message reminders, patient portal outreach, and pharmacy automatic refill programs are less effective in populations with limited English proficiency, low digital literacy, and unstable phone numbers. Achieving parity in medication adherence outcomes requires more intensive, more expensive interventions — community health worker outreach, in-home medication management, pharmacy benefit design that eliminates cost-sharing for LIS members — that not all plans have the resources or infrastructure to deploy.
The CAI: What It Does and Does Not Fix

The Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI), introduced in 2017, is CMS's primary mechanism for addressing the LIS/DE equity problem in Star Ratings. The CAI applies a positive adjustment to individual measure scores for plans with high proportions of LIS and dual-eligible enrollees, partially offsetting the systematic performance disadvantage. The adjustment is categorical — plans are sorted into groups based on their LIS/DE penetration rate, and each group receives a different adjustment level — rather than a continuous regression-based correction.

The CAI has reduced the Stars gap between high-LIS and low-LIS plans but has not eliminated it. Analyses of post-CAI Star distributions find that D-SNPs and high-LIS plans still perform below average even after CAI adjustment, suggesting that the CAI underadjusts for the true magnitude of the population-driven disadvantage. The categorical adjustment methodology — rather than a continuous model that accounts for the full range of social risk factors — is likely part of the problem: a plan with 70% LIS penetration receives the same categorical adjustment as one with 50%, even though the performance disadvantage may be significantly larger.
CMS Equity Reforms in Star Ratings: 2023 and Beyond

Beginning with the 2023 and 2024 Star Rating cycles, CMS has implemented several equity-focused reforms. CMS added a new Health Equity Index (HEI) reward factor for the 2027 measurement year that provides a Stars bonus for plans that demonstrate improvement in Star measure performance specifically among their disadvantaged enrollee populations — LIS, dual-eligible, disability-based, and racial and ethnic minority subgroups. Plans that reduce disparities in their own member population receive a bonus that can increase their overall Star score by up to 0.4 stars.

CMS has also required MA plans to collect and report HEDIS and CAHPS performance stratified by race and ethnicity beginning in 2024, making plan-level disparities more visible. The stratified reporting requirement is complemented by a requirement for health equity plans — all MA contracts must include plans for how they will address identified disparities in their enrolled population. These requirements represent a meaningful shift from treating equity as a Star Rating adjustment factor to treating disparity reduction as a performance requirement.
Do Star Ratings Incentivize Plans to Avoid Low-Income Enrollees?

The most serious equity critique of the Star Rating system is that its structure creates economic incentives for MA plans to minimize their LIS and dual-eligible enrollment. A plan that serves a high-income, commercially-oriented Medicare population can achieve high Star scores and QBPs more easily than one serving Medicaid-enrolled beneficiaries. If the CAI adjustment is insufficient to fully compensate for the Stars disadvantage, the rational market response is to design benefit packages, choose service areas, and conduct marketing in ways that attract lower-need enrollees and deter higher-need ones.

Evidence on this concern is mixed. Studies have found that some MA plans do appear to design benefits and target marketing in ways that attract healthier enrollees — a practice related to but distinct from the Stars incentive problem. D-SNP plans — which are specifically contracted to serve dual-eligible beneficiaries — have grown significantly in enrollment in recent years, suggesting that the market has found a way to serve this population through specialized plan structures that explicitly address their needs. Whether this specialization is better for equity outcomes than integration of dual-eligible beneficiaries into mainstream MA plans is an open question.
Policy Proposals: Fixing the Star-Equity Problem

Policy proposals for addressing the Star-equity problem range from technical adjustments to fundamental redesign. Technical proposals include: replacing the categorical CAI with a continuous regression-based social risk adjustment that accounts for the full range of social risk factors; applying the HEI reward factor more broadly and with larger financial impact; reducing the CAHPS weight to lower the amplification of the equity disadvantage; and developing alternative CAHPS collection methodologies specifically validated for low-literacy and non-English-speaking populations.

More fundamental proposals would redesign the QBP structure to explicitly fund serving disadvantaged populations — providing higher bonus payments for plans that serve high proportions of LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries regardless of Star score, similar to how DSH payments compensate hospitals for uncompensated care costs. Some researchers argue for developing separate Star Rating benchmarks for D-SNPs versus non-SNP plans, recognizing that the populations are sufficiently different that cross-plan comparison on a common scale is inherently misleading.

The Star Ratings equity problem is a microcosm of the broader tension in value-based care: quality measurement systems designed to improve care can inadvertently penalize the providers and plans that serve the most vulnerable populations, creating market incentives to avoid the patients most in need. The CAI was an important step, the HEI reform is another, and stratified reporting requirements are valuable for transparency. But the deeper problem — that low-income populations have lower measured quality outcomes for reasons partially independent of plan quality, and that the measurement system treats these population-level disadvantages as plan-level performance failures — requires more than incremental adjustment. It requires a fundamental commitment to measuring and incentivizing disparity reduction, not just absolute performance, as the core equity accountability framework.

result.courseTitle: Value-Based Care: From Fee-for-Service to Outcomes
result.summary: Plans serving high proportions of low-income and dual-eligible Medicare Advantage enrollees consistently score lower on Star Ratings even when clinical care quality is comparable, creating a structural equity problem that the Categorical Adjustment Index only partially resolves. This lesson examines the socioeconomic gradient in Star performance, the mechanisms driving lower scores in safety-net plans, the CAI's design and limitations, CMS equity reforms, and the deeper policy question of whether Stars create incentives to avoid serving disadvantaged beneficiaries.

children.text: Medicare Advantage Star Ratings are simultaneously the most powerful quality incentive in American healthcare and one of its most gamed measurement systems. First introduced in 2007 as a consumer information tool, the Star Rating system became a major financial lever when the ACA tied Quality Bonus Payments (QBPs) to Star performance beginning in 2012. Today, plans rated 4 stars or above receive bonus payments worth billions of dollars collectively — creating financial stakes that have made Star Ratings a central strategic priority for every MA insurer and the primary driver of quality improvement investment for most MA plans.
How Star Ratings Work: The Five-Star Framework

Medicare Advantage contracts are rated on a 1-5 star scale based on performance across approximately 40 measures grouped into several domains. The domains and their approximate weights in the overall Star calculation include:
Staying Healthy: Screening and vaccination rates including breast cancer screening, colorectal cancer screening, flu vaccinations, and diabetes monitoring. This domain carries significant weight.

Managing Chronic Conditions: Medication adherence for diabetes, hypertension, and cholesterol medications; controlled blood pressure; HbA1c control; statin use in diabetes. These medication adherence measures are among the highest-weighted measures in the system.

Member Experience: CAHPS measures including getting needed care, getting care quickly, how well doctors communicate, customer service, and overall plan rating. CAHPS measures receive a weight multiplier of 4x in the overall Star calculation.
Member Complaints and Plan Performance: Measures of appeals and grievances rates, disenrollment rates, and CMS audit results.
Health Plan Administration: HRA (Health Risk Assessment) completion rate, care coordination measures, and medication reconciliation after discharge.

For plans that include Part D (prescription drug) benefits, Part D Star measures cover medication adherence, medication safety, and pharmacy quality indicators. The overall contract Star Rating is a weighted average of Part C (medical) and Part D (pharmacy) component ratings.
Cut-Point Methodology: The Annually Shifting Target

Each measure is converted to a 1-5 star score using cut-points determined by the distribution of performance across all MA contracts in that measure. Cut-points are set using cluster analysis — specifically a method that groups plans by natural breaks in the performance distribution — rather than fixed absolute performance thresholds. This means that the cut-point for a 4-star score on breast cancer screening is not fixed at, say, 80%; it shifts each year based on where the natural breaks appear in that year's national performance distribution.

The distributional cut-point methodology has significant implications for plan strategy. As all plans improve on a measure — as happened with medication adherence after MA plans invested heavily in pharmacy intervention programs — the cut-point for a 4-star score also increases, making it progressively harder to maintain a 4-star score on that measure through simple performance improvement. Plans must improve faster than the market to maintain relative standing, creating a perpetual quality arms race that raises overall performance while continuously moving the goalpost.
The Financial Stakes: Quality Bonus Payments and Benefit Design

Plans rated 4 stars or above receive Quality Bonus Payments: an additional 5% of their base Medicare payment (called the benchmark) is added to their effective benchmark, and they receive preferential rebate amounts. For large MA plans serving hundreds of thousands of beneficiaries, a 5% QBP can represent hundreds of millions of dollars annually. MedPAC estimated that total QBPs to MA plans exceeded $10 billion annually by the early 2020s — an enormous financial stake that has made Stars optimization a core business function for every major MA insurer.

The QBP flows through to plan benefit design. Plans that earn QBPs receive higher effective benchmarks, which they can use to offer more generous benefits to enrollees — richer drug formularies, dental and vision coverage, transportation benefits, and lower cost-sharing. This creates a virtuous cycle where high Star plans attract more enrollees with better benefits, increasing the scale over which they can deploy quality improvement investments, potentially further improving Star performance. Conversely, plans that fall below 4 stars face pressure to cut benefits to remain competitive, potentially driving member disenrollment that further destabilizes their quality reporting.
Measure Weighting: Not All Stars Are Created Equal

CMS assigns different weights to different measures in the Star Rating calculation. For 2024, measure weights ranged from 1x to 4x, with the highest weights applied to: CAHPS patient experience measures (4x weight), clinical outcome measures (3x weight), and intermediate outcome measures like blood pressure control and HbA1c control (3x weight). Process measures like preventive screening rates typically carry 1x weight. This weighting structure reflects CMS's policy intent to drive investment toward patient experience and outcomes rather than administrative process compliance.

The 4x weight on CAHPS measures makes patient experience disproportionately influential in overall Star performance, and MA plans have invested heavily in CAHPS optimization. CAHPS scores are based on member surveys measuring experiences with accessing care, provider communication, and overall plan satisfaction. These surveys are administered by third-party vendors and submitted to CMS — but the way plans design their member engagement, manage care coordination, and communicate with members influences CAHPS scores substantially.
The Categorical Adjustment Index: Adjusting for Low-Income Enrollees

CMS introduced the Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI) beginning with the 2017 Star Ratings to address the well-documented disparity in Star performance between plans serving high proportions of dual-eligible and low-income subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries and plans serving lower-need populations. The CAI adjusts individual measure scores upward for plans with high dual/LIS proportions, reflecting that these populations systematically report lower satisfaction, lower medication adherence, and lower preventive care completion rates independent of plan quality.

The CAI is a form of social risk adjustment applied specifically to the Star Rating context. It is designed to prevent the scoring system from systematically penalizing plans that serve disadvantaged populations — a perverse incentive that would drive plans toward cherry-picking healthier, higher-income enrollees. The CAI has been controversial: commercial MA plans argue it creates an unfair advantage for D-SNP (Dual-Eligible Special Needs Plans) and other low-income-serving plans. Advocates for D-SNPs argue the CAI adjustment is too small to fully account for the performance disadvantage these plans face.
How Plans Optimize Star Ratings: Strategy and Gaming

The financial stakes of Star Ratings have spawned an enormous industry of Stars optimization consulting, predictive analytics, and targeted intervention programs. MA plans employ dedicated Stars teams that monitor measure performance throughout the year and deploy interventions to address specific gaps. The most commonly deployed Stars optimization tactics include:

Health Risk Assessment completion campaigns: HRA completion is a direct measure in Stars, and plans deploy outbound calls, in-home visits, and telehealth encounters specifically to complete HRAs for hard-to-reach members.

Medication adherence programs: Plans partner with pharmacy benefit managers to identify non-adherent members and deploy telephonic, mail, and home delivery interventions — particularly for the three medication adherence measures (diabetes, hypertension, statins) that carry high weight and high financial return.

CAHPS survey preparation: Plans identify members who are scheduled to receive CAHPS surveys and ensure those members have positive recent experiences with the plan — directing service recovery efforts toward the CAHPS sample period.

Preventive care outreach: Outbound calls, text messages, and transportation benefits targeting members who have not received breast cancer screening, colorectal cancer screening, or flu vaccinations during the measurement year.
The 2023-2024 Star Wars: COVID Adjustments and Plan Litigation

The 2023 Star Ratings, released in October 2022, triggered unprecedented controversy and litigation. CMS removed COVID-19 adjustments it had applied in prior years to account for pandemic-related performance disruption. Without the adjustments, many plans' scores fell significantly from their 2022 ratings — in some cases dropping from 4 stars to 3.5 stars, crossing the critical threshold that determines QBP eligibility. Several major insurers filed lawsuits challenging CMS's removal of the COVID adjustments, arguing the abrupt change violated administrative law requirements for notice and comment rulemaking.

Federal courts issued injunctions in several cases, and CMS ultimately revised its approach to the COVID adjustment controversy. The litigation highlighted the enormous financial stakes of even small changes to the Star Rating methodology and the intensity of the insurance industry's investment in protecting its Star-linked revenue. It also raised legitimate questions about the stability and predictability of the Star Rating methodology — when plans make multi-year investments in quality improvement based on a given measurement framework, sudden methodological changes can produce perverse results that have nothing to do with actual performance change.

Medicare Advantage Star Ratings represent both the most powerful quality incentive in American healthcare and a cautionary tale about what happens when measurement systems are tied to very large financial stakes without adequate protection against gaming. The Stars system has genuinely improved MA plan quality on measurable dimensions — medication adherence, preventive care completion, and member experience have all improved significantly since QBPs were introduced. But the investment in Stars optimization has also created sophisticated gaming practices that raise questions about whether Stars improvements reflect genuine healthcare improvement or strategic measure management. The annual cut-point adjustments, the measure weighting choices, and the CAI design all involve value judgments about what quality means and who bears the cost of serving disadvantaged populations — judgments that have billions of dollars riding on them.

The five-star system covers approximately 40 measures across clinical quality, patient experience, and operational domains, with cut-points and weights that shift annually and create rich opportunities for strategic gaming. This lesson explains the Star Rating formula, the financial stakes, the CAI adjustment, how plans optimize their Star performance, and the controversial 2023-2024 litigation over COVID-era Star changes.

children.text: What Is an Accountable Care Organization?

An Accountable Care Organization (ACO) is a group of doctors, hospitals, and other health care providers who voluntarily come together to deliver coordinated, high-quality care to Medicare patients. The central premise is that when providers collaborate—rather than operate in fragmented silos—they can prevent unnecessary services, catch problems earlier, and improve outcomes, all while reducing overall spending. Unlike a health maintenance organization (HMO), patients retain full freedom to see any Medicare provider; ACO membership is invisible to the patient unless they are informed.

ACOs operate under Medicare's fee-for-service (FFS) billing system as their baseline. Providers continue to bill and receive standard FFS payments for each service they deliver. On top of that baseline, the ACO is measured against a spending benchmark and a quality scorecard. If the ACO collectively keeps spending below the benchmark and meets quality thresholds, it earns a share of the savings—known as shared savings. If spending exceeds the benchmark, some ACO tracks require the group to pay back a portion of those excess costs, a feature called downside risk or shared losses.

The legal foundation for Medicare ACOs is Section 3022 of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), which amended Title XVIII of the Social Security Act by adding Section 1899 to establish the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP). The MSSP regulations were finalized in November 2011 and became effective January 3, 2012, with the first ACO agreements starting as early as April 1, 2012.

Key Concept: An ACO is not an insurance product and does not require patients to change their behavior. It is a provider-side accountability mechanism—providers take responsibility for the cost and quality of care for a defined patient population while patients continue receiving traditional Medicare benefits.

children.text: How Attribution Works: Assigning Patients to an ACO

Because patients do not enroll in an ACO directly, CMS uses a process called attribution—sometimes called assignment—to determine which patients "belong" to which ACO for measurement purposes. Attribution is based on where a patient receives the plurality of their primary care services. Specifically, CMS examines claims data to identify which ACO-affiliated clinician provided the most primary care evaluation and management visits to a given patient, and that ACO receives credit (and accountability) for that patient.

CMS currently offers ACOs two main attribution approaches. Under prospective attribution, patients are assigned at the start of the contract performance year based on their claims from the prior calendar year. This gives ACOs advance knowledge of their defined population, enabling proactive outreach and care management. Under retrospective attribution, patients are assigned at the end of the performance period based on services used during that year, which typically produces a larger attributed population but reduces the ACO's ability to plan ahead. A hybrid approach—preliminary prospective with retrospective reconciliation—begins with a prospective list that is updated quarterly and finalized retrospectively, balancing planning certainty with accuracy.

Attribution has important financial and clinical implications. Patients who receive no primary care visits during the year may fall out of attribution, creating gaps in accountability for high-need populations. Additionally, specialists and hospitals cannot directly attract attribution—only primary care evaluation and management services count. This design intentionally places primary care physicians at the center of ACO economics, reinforcing their role as care coordinators for the attributed population.
