children.text: Benchmarks: Setting the Spending Target

An ACO's benchmark is the spending target against which its actual expenditures are compared at the end of each performance year. Getting the benchmark right is the single most important technical feature of the MSSP, because an inflated benchmark makes it easy to show savings without actually changing care patterns, while an overly tight benchmark can make participation financially unviable.

The historical benchmark is calculated at the start of each agreement period using the weighted average of risk-adjusted, trended per-capita spending for the ACO's attributed population across the three previous benchmark years. CMS then applies a regional adjustment: the historical benchmark is blended with the average expenditures in the ACO's regional service area, giving partial weight to regional costs. This regional component reduces the incentive to cherry-pick low-cost patients and rewards ACOs that are already efficient relative to their local market.

For new agreement periods beginning January 1, 2024, CMS introduced the Accountable Care Prospective Trend (ACPT)—a fixed projected national spending growth rate—as a third component of the benchmark update factor, creating what is now known as a three-way blended update. The ACPT is blended with actual national and regional FFS spending trends to set the annual benchmark update, reducing the volatility that occurred when benchmarks moved dramatically with pandemic-era utilization swings. Together, these adjustments are designed to make the benchmark a stable, fair, and credible target.

Key Concept: The benchmark is not simply last year's spending. It is a risk-adjusted, regionally-blended, prospectively-trended target. An ACO that starts from a high-cost baseline can earn shared savings even if costs only fall modestly, while an already-efficient ACO must work harder to stay below its benchmark.

body.message: Beating the benchmark shows spending was lower than the target—but that target is not necessarily what spending would have been without the ACO. The Congressional Budget Office's April 2024 review found "mixed results" when comparing ACO spending to counterfactual estimates rather than to program benchmarks. Selection effects—ACOs attracting lower-cost practices—account for some reported savings.
body.title: Common Misconception: Beating the Benchmark ≠ Reducing Spending

children.text: Shared Savings and Shared Losses: The Risk Architecture

When an ACO's actual per-capita spending falls below its benchmark by more than the minimum savings rate (MSR), it qualifies to share in those savings with Medicare. The MSR exists to filter out random statistical variation—small ACOs have higher MSRs because random fluctuation in spending is larger in smaller populations. Conversely, ACOs in downside-risk tracks face a minimum loss rate (MLR): spending must exceed the benchmark by more than the MLR before losses are owed.

The MSSP is organized into tracks with escalating levels of financial risk and reward. The BASIC track allows new ACOs to enter a glide path, starting with upside-only risk in levels A and B, then progressing to limited two-sided risk in levels C through E. The ENHANCED track offers the highest shared savings rate (up to 75 percent of savings) but requires full two-sided risk from day one. Under the "Pathways to Success" redesign finalized in 2018, CMS reduced the maximum time an ACO can remain in upside-only risk from six years to two years for most ACOs, with an extension to three years for low-revenue (typically physician-led) ACOs.

In 2024, two-thirds of MSSP ACOs were operating in the Level E or ENHANCED track, meaning the majority of the program now carries downside risk. This is a marked shift from the program's early years, when nearly all ACOs stayed in upside-only tracks indefinitely. High-risk-track ACOs generated more than two-thirds of all net savings in 2024—$5.4 billion of the $6.6 billion total gross savings—demonstrating that financial accountability correlates with stronger performance.

children.text: Quality Measurement and Its Role in ACO Economics

Shared savings payments are contingent on meeting a quality performance standard—ACOs cannot earn purely by cutting costs. CMS evaluates ACO quality using a composite score drawn from measures spanning preventive care, chronic disease management, patient experience, and care coordination. The quality score gates entry to shared savings: ACOs that fall below the quality threshold receive a reduced share of any savings earned, or may be barred from payment entirely.

In 2024, nearly every ACO in the MSSP met CMS's quality standard, continuing a multi-year trend of high marks on patient experience and preventive care measures. Among ACOs reporting through the CMS Web Interface, the mean percentage of beneficiaries with controlled high blood pressure rose from 77.80 percent in 2023 to 79.49 percent in 2024—a statistically significant improvement. Preventive measures such as influenza vaccination and colorectal cancer screening also showed strong average performance.

The quality-savings linkage is a deliberate policy design: it prevents ACOs from gaming the benchmark through under-provision of care. However, critics note that most ACO quality measures are process-based rather than outcome-based, and that near-universal quality compliance across hundreds of ACOs may reflect measure selection as much as genuine care improvement. CMS has signaled ongoing interest in transitioning toward more outcome-oriented and health-equity-sensitive quality metrics.

body.analogy: Think of an ACO like a restaurant group with a shared kitchen budget. Each chef (provider) still cooks individual dishes (services) and charges per plate (FFS billing). But at year-end, if the whole kitchen spent less than expected AND the food quality scores were high, the restaurant group gets a bonus. The key is that no one chef gets rewarded for cutting corners on ingredients—quality scores make sure the food stays good.
body.concept: ACO shared savings: combining FFS billing with collective accountability

children.text: The ACO Landscape: MSSP, ACO REACH, and ACO PC Flex

The MSSP is the largest Medicare ACO program, but it is not the only one. The ACO Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health (REACH) model, administered by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), is a separate advanced alternative payment model with higher financial risk and more flexibility. ACO REACH launched in 2023, replacing the Global and Professional Direct Contracting (GPDC) model, which itself evolved from the Pioneer ACO Model (2012–2016). In 2023, 132 ACOs participated in ACO REACH, managing care for more than two million Medicare beneficiaries and overseeing $26.6 billion in Medicare Parts A and B expenditures.

The ACO Primary Care Flex (ACO PC Flex) model, launched January 1, 2025, is the newest CMMI initiative. It targets low-revenue MSSP participants—typically smaller, physician-led ACOs—by offering prospective primary care payments (up-front monthly payments rather than retrospective shared savings) to support care management infrastructure that small practices cannot easily finance. This model attempts to solve the capital problem: small practices lack the cash flow to invest in care coordinators, health coaches, and analytics platforms before receiving any savings payments.

Together, these models represent CMS's evolving strategy to move the entire Medicare FFS population—not just commercially insured patients—toward accountable care. The 2025 ACO initiatives announcements from CMS signaled the goal of having every Medicare beneficiary in an accountable care relationship by 2030, though participation remains voluntary and trajectory toward that goal requires continued growth in both ACO numbers and attributed beneficiaries.

body.content:
Within the ACO REACH model, a subset of participants operates as High-Needs Population (HNP) ACOs, specifically designed to serve beneficiaries with complex chronic conditions or serious illness. In performance year 2023, HNP ACOs achieved a 13.3% net savings rate—substantially higher than Standard ACOs (2.8%) or New Entrant ACOs (4.8%).
This performance reflects the financial upside available when organizations master care management for high-cost, high-need patients. HNP ACOs use intensive care models—home visits, palliative care integration, and social needs navigation—that reduce avoidable hospitalizations and emergency department visits for patients who would otherwise drive disproportionately high Medicare expenditures. Source: CMS ACO REACH PY2023 Financial and Quality Performance Results Fact Sheet.

children.text: Why ACOs Expanded Beyond Medicare

The Medicare Shared Savings Program demonstrated that the accountable care concept—providers voluntarily accepting responsibility for the cost and quality of a defined population—could work at scale in a government insurance program. That demonstration triggered rapid interest from Medicaid agencies and commercial health plans, which faced similar problems: fragmented care, avoidable hospitalizations, and payment structures that rewarded volume over value. By the mid-2010s, dozens of states were designing Medicaid ACO programs and commercial insurers were launching parallel contracts with provider networks.

Yet the translation from Medicare to Medicaid and commercial markets is not straightforward. Medicare beneficiaries are older, have stable enrollment, and interact with a single federal payer using standardized rules. Medicaid populations are younger, more diverse, often have complex social needs, and experience high coverage turnover—members can churn on and off Medicaid eligibility multiple times per year, making continuity of attribution and care management extremely difficult. Commercial ACOs face different challenges: multiple competing payers with proprietary data, less standardized quality measures, and the reality that commercial patients may have ACO-like contracts with several plans simultaneously.

Despite these structural differences, the core ACO logic transfers: if providers can reduce avoidable utilization, improve preventive care, and coordinate across settings, both Medicaid programs and commercial payers stand to gain. The mechanisms—attribution, benchmarks, shared savings or shared losses—are adapted but recognizable. This lesson examines how Medicaid and commercial ACO programs have been designed, what the evidence shows about their effectiveness, and what Vermont's own experience illustrates about state-level innovation.

Key Concept: Medicaid ACOs and commercial ACOs share the fundamental ACO architecture—attributed populations, spending benchmarks, and quality-linked payments—but operate in environments with fundamentally different patient populations, payer structures, and data availability compared to the Medicare MSSP.
Medicaid ACOs: State-by-State Innovation

Medicaid is a joint federal-state program, which means there is no single national Medicaid ACO model. Each state that creates a Medicaid ACO does so through its own design, often using Section 1115 demonstration waivers to obtain federal flexibility. States have experimented with widely varying approaches: some run voluntary programs similar to MSSP, others mandate all Medicaid managed care organizations to operate within an ACO framework, and still others create global budget models that blend ACO accountability with capitation payments.

A 2024 scoping review published in collaboration with the Center for Health Care Strategies analyzed 32 studies on Medicaid ACO programs published between 2012 and 2023. The review found mixed evidence overall—Medicaid ACOs showed positive effects on primary care utilization and reductions in avoidable admissions in several states, but cost savings were variable and often dependent on how long the program had been operating and how long patients were attributed. Medicaid ACOs face unique challenges: patient populations with complex social needs, frequent eligibility turnover, and program designs that vary dramatically across states.

Among the key positive findings from the scoping review: Medicaid ACO implementation was associated with an increase in children's likelihood of having a personal doctor or nurse by approximately 4 percentage points, a decline in emergency department visits by approximately 5 percentage points, and increases in specialist care use in some state programs. These are meaningful outcomes for a population that historically has faced significant access barriers. However, cost evidence was weaker, with only a subset of studies documenting actual savings to the state Medicaid program.

children.text: Oregon's Coordinated Care Organizations: The Leading State Model

Oregon's Coordinated Care Organization (CCO) program is widely regarded as the most comprehensive and rigorously evaluated Medicaid ACO model in the United States. Launched in 2012 under an 1115 waiver with substantial initial federal funding, Oregon transformed its entire Medicaid program—the Oregon Health Plan—into a statewide network of CCOs. Each CCO is a regional entity responsible for the physical, behavioral, and oral health of its attributed Medicaid members, operating under a global budget with an annual spending growth cap.

Oregon committed to reducing its Medicaid spending growth rate from 5.4 percent annually to 3.4 percent within three years. Research published in peer-reviewed journals found that the CCO transformation was associated with a 7 percent relative reduction in expenditures across selected services, attributable primarily to reductions in inpatient utilization. Emergency department visit rates fell by 21 percent in the early implementation phase. A Health Affairs study found that these expenditure reductions were attributable to coordinated care organization effects rather than to underlying demographic or economic trends.

The scoping review of Medicaid ACO evidence identified Oregon as showing the most consistently positive results among the nine state programs studied. Oregon's distinctive design elements—mandatory Medicaid enrollment (rather than voluntary), inclusion of mental health and dental services within the global budget (rather than carving them out), community advisory councils with meaningful governance authority, and integration of social determinants of health services—contributed to both its superior performance and the comprehensiveness of its data. As of 2020, the Oregon Health Authority renewed four-year CCO contracts with 15 CCOs, with contracts focusing on behavioral health, health equity, social determinants, and sustainable cost growth.

body.content:
Oregon currently contracts with 15 Coordinated Care Organizations that cover OHP members across the state. Each CCO integrates physical, behavioral, and oral health services under a single global budget, which is capped at a state-specified growth rate. CCOs are governed by community advisory councils that include Medicaid members, community organizations, and local stakeholders.
The Oregon model's inclusion of dental and mental health under the global budget is a critical design feature that most other state programs omit. By integrating these services, Oregon avoids the perverse incentive of carving them out—where behavioral health crises drive hospital admissions that show up as avoidable costs in the physical health budget without accountability. Research found a 7% relative reduction in selected expenditures and a 21% decline in ED visits in the program's early years. Source: CHCS/NIH; Oregon Health Authority.
body.title: Oregon Health Plan CCOs

children.text: Massachusetts MassHealth ACOs: Scale and Integration

Massachusetts launched its Medicaid ACO program in 2018 as part of a Section 1115 demonstration waiver, becoming one of the first states to integrate ACO accountability directly into its Medicaid managed care framework. By June 2023, over 1.3 million MassHealth members—more than half of the program's 2.4 million total—were enrolled in one of 17 MassHealth ACOs. This scale makes MassHealth one of the largest Medicaid ACO programs in the country by attributed population.

An independent evaluation conducted by UMass Chan Medical School found that MassHealth's 2017–2022 Section 1115 demonstration saved Massachusetts more than $500 million over five years while maintaining near-universal health coverage and the lowest uninsurance rate among comparison states. Health outcomes improved in both physical and behavioral health domains. Hospitalization rates were 23 percent lower and emergency department visit rates 13 percent lower among members who received nutrition support services compared to eligible non-participants.

MassHealth's program design included two types of ACOs: Accountable Care Partnership Plans (ACPPs), which are fully integrated ACO-managed care plans combining an ACO with a health plan, and Primary Care ACOs (PCACOs), which are ACOs working with existing managed care organizations. The program also built in a community partner infrastructure—ACO-affiliated organizations providing community health workers, care navigators, and long-term services support—reflecting recognition that social needs are major drivers of Medicaid spending. In September 2022, CMS approved an extension of the MassHealth demonstration waiver through December 2027.

children.text: Commercial ACOs: Private-Payer Accountable Care

Commercial ACOs operate under contracts between provider organizations and private health plans—employer-sponsored insurance, individual market plans, and commercial managed care. Unlike Medicare or Medicaid ACOs, commercial ACOs are governed entirely by private contracts without a regulatory framework, meaning their design varies enormously across payers, markets, and time. The common thread is still the ACO logic: a defined provider network accepts responsibility for a population's total cost of care against a benchmark, with shared savings or shared losses tied to both spending and quality performance.

Commercial ACO growth has been driven by large employers and major health plans seeking to reduce trend growth in healthcare costs. The Health Care Payment Learning and Action Network (HCPLAN) reported that value-based arrangements across all lines of business grew from 41.3 percent of payments in 2022 to 45.2 percent in 2023. Commercial value-based care arrangements specifically grew from 34.6 percent to 39.2 percent in the same period—a 5.1 percentage-point increase in a single year. In 2024, 28.7 percent of all healthcare payments across insurance types came through downside-risk alternative payment model contracts.

Commercial ACOs face distinctive challenges that Medicare and Medicaid ACOs do not. First, multi-payer attribution: a primary care physician attributed to a commercial ACO by one payer may simultaneously be in a Medicare ACO and a Medicaid ACO, with potentially conflicting quality targets and reporting requirements. Second, data opacity: commercial claims data is proprietary and payers often share incomplete claims information with ACO partners, hampering risk stratification. Third, shorter contract terms: commercial ACO contracts often run one to three years, which is insufficient time to see the full financial benefits of care management investments that may take several years to mature.

children.text: Vermont's All-Payer Model: ACOs Across All Insurance Types

Vermont has pursued one of the most ambitious ACO strategies in the United States: an all-payer accountable care model in which a single ACO—OneCare Vermont—accepts responsibility for the total cost of care for Vermonters across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance. Under the Vermont All-Payer ACO Model (VAPCOM), which CMS approved in 2017, OneCare Vermont operates under a global budget that covers attributed patients across all payers, aligning financial incentives in a way that no single-payer ACO can achieve.

The all-payer design directly solves the multi-payer attribution problem that plagues commercial ACOs. When a provider's financial incentives are aligned across all of their patients—not just their Medicare patients or their one commercial contract—clinical behavior can change more consistently and comprehensively. A primary care physician in the OneCare network has the same incentive to prevent avoidable hospitalizations for their Medicaid patient as for their Medicare patient, removing a major source of conflicting financial signals that undermines single-payer ACO models.

Vermont's model has generated considerable national attention and research interest as a proof-of-concept for all-payer ACO design. The state agreed to keep per-capita cost growth below a target rate and to meet annual quality benchmarks across the attributed population. Implementation has been iterative—participation by commercial payers and providers has grown over the years since launch, and the model has been modified through renegotiation with CMS. Vermont's experience offers important lessons about the prerequisites for all-payer ACO success: state political will, a small enough market for coordination to be feasible, and strong primary care infrastructure.

body.analogy: Think of multi-payer ACO fragmentation like a sports referee who has to follow different rulebooks for different players on the same field. A doctor with Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial patients effectively works under three different financial systems simultaneously. Vermont's all-payer model gives everyone the same rulebook, so the referee—and the players—can play a coherent game.
body.concept: All-payer ACO design: why aligning all payers matters

points: Medicaid and commercial ACOs adapt the Medicare ACO model—attributed populations, spending benchmarks, and quality-linked shared savings—to their distinct payer environments, patient populations, and data constraints.

A 2024 scoping review of 32 Medicaid ACO studies found mixed evidence overall, with the strongest findings in primary care access (approximately 4 percentage-point gain in personal doctor rates) and emergency department reduction (approximately 5 percentage-point decline).

Oregon's Coordinated Care Organization program is the best-evidenced Medicaid ACO model, with a 7% relative reduction in expenditures and a 21% drop in ED visits in early implementation; its design integrates behavioral, physical, and oral health under one global budget.

MassHealth (Massachusetts) enrolled over 1.3 million Medicaid members in ACOs by 2023, with an independent evaluation finding $500 million in savings over five years and improved physical and behavioral health outcomes.

Commercial ACO contracts grew significantly, with value-based arrangements representing 45.2% of all healthcare payments across insurance types in 2023, up from 41.3% in 2022, according to HCPLAN data.

Commercial ACOs face unique challenges not present in Medicare or Medicaid programs: multi-payer attribution overlap, proprietary data opacity, shorter contract terms, and the absence of a federal regulatory framework.

Vermont's all-payer ACO model (OneCare Vermont) addresses multi-payer fragmentation by applying a single global budget across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers—one of the most ambitious accountable care experiments in the U.S.

The scoping review of Medicaid ACO evidence identified Oregon as having the most consistently positive results, attributing this partly to the integrated service design that prevents behavioral health and dental carve-outs from undermining physical health cost management.

result.title: ACOs Beyond Medicare: Medicaid and Commercial ACOs

children.text: The Central Question: Do ACOs Actually Save Money?

Since the first Medicare Shared Savings Program ACOs began in April 2012, a persistent and important debate has surrounded a deceptively simple question: do ACOs reduce healthcare spending, or do they merely attract providers who were already efficient? The answer matters enormously for health policy—if ACOs primarily generate shared savings by selecting favorable benchmarks and low-cost patient panels, then the program transfers money to providers without improving efficiency. If they genuinely change care patterns, they offer a scalable path to sustainable Medicare.

The evidence is nuanced and depends critically on how savings are measured. Comparing ACO spending to the program benchmark—the method CMS uses to calculate shared savings payments—consistently shows large, favorable results. But the benchmark is not necessarily what spending would have been in the absence of the ACO. A more rigorous test uses a counterfactual control group of comparable non-ACO providers to estimate the treatment effect. These counterfactual analyses yield more modest, though still generally positive, findings.

Understanding the distinction between benchmark-based and counterfactual-based measurement is essential for interpreting ACO research. This lesson reviews what the program-level data, independent research, and oversight bodies have found about ACO performance across financial outcomes, quality of care, and the variables that predict success.

Key Concept: A benchmark-based savings estimate tells you how far below target an ACO performed. A counterfactual-based estimate tells you whether the ACO changed spending compared to a world where no ACO existed. The two numbers are not the same, and conflating them overstates ACO impact.
Program-Level Results: MSSP Performance Data 2012–2024

CMS publishes annual financial and quality results for the MSSP, and these figures paint an increasingly impressive picture. In performance year 2024, 476 ACOs generated $6.6 billion in total gross savings relative to benchmarks. After accounting for $4.1 billion paid out as shared savings to ACOs, Medicare retained $2.4 billion in net savings—the largest in program history. The per-capita net savings were $241 per attributed beneficiary, up from $207 in 2023. Since the program's inception, ACOs have generated $35 billion in gross savings and $13.6 billion in net savings to Medicare.

The trajectory of program performance has improved markedly as ACOs have matured and taken on greater financial risk. In the program's early years (2012–2014), many ACOs generated little savings and a significant minority exited after failing to earn shared savings payments. By 2024, 75 percent of ACOs earned performance payments—the highest share since the program launched. ACOs in Level E and ENHANCED tracks, which carry two-sided risk, generated $5.4 billion of the $6.6 billion in total gross savings, confirming that downside accountability drives stronger performance.

Quality performance has remained consistently high throughout the program's history. In 2024, nearly every ACO met CMS's quality standard. Mean blood pressure control rates rose from 77.80 percent to 79.49 percent year over year. Long-term trends show consistent improvements in preventive care screening rates, patient experience scores, and chronic disease management metrics. The quality-savings correlation supports the argument that ACOs are not cutting costs by under-delivering care.

children.text: The CBO and Counterfactual Challenge

In April 2024, the Congressional Budget Office published a comprehensive review of Medicare ACO program performance titled "Medicare Accountable Care Organizations: Past Performance and Future Directions." The CBO used counterfactual control groups—comparable providers not participating in ACOs—to estimate how much ACO participation actually reduced spending relative to what would have occurred otherwise. The CBO found "mixed results" across models, with some ACO programs achieving small net savings and others showing small net costs when measured against counterfactuals.

The CBO's more positive findings were concentrated in specific ACO types: physician-led ACOs, ACOs with higher primary care concentration, ACOs that accepted more financial risk (downside-risk tracks), and ACOs in their earlier agreement periods. These characteristics align with the theoretical model of how ACOs should work—primary care-driven coordination, strong financial incentives, and early-stage enthusiasm for change. The finding that physician-led ACOs outperform hospital-system ACOs is particularly notable, given that most large integrated delivery systems initially assumed their scale would be an advantage.

Selection bias is a persistent methodological challenge in ACO research. Practices that choose to form or join ACOs may be systematically different from those that do not—they may already have better care management capabilities, lower baseline utilization, or more motivated clinical leadership. Researchers at Health Affairs and in peer-reviewed literature have documented that post-2017, MSSP composition increasingly shifted toward providers with lower pre-existing spending relative to their region, consistent with providers self-selecting into the program based on expected benchmark favorability.

body.message: ACO benchmarks are designed to accomplish multiple goals—achieving savings, ensuring ACO participation, and managing risk corridor width—and therefore diverge from a pure estimate of what spending would have been without the ACO. Research published in Health Affairs Forefront noted that "All I Do Is Win"—beating the benchmark—does not prove spending was reduced. Policymakers, analysts, and healthcare leaders should treat program-reported savings figures as performance against targets, not proof of equivalent real-world savings.
body.title: Important Caveat: Benchmark ≠ Counterfactual

children.text: What Drives ACO Success? Factors the Evidence Identifies

Across multiple studies and program evaluations, several structural and operational factors consistently predict better ACO financial and quality performance. The most robust finding is that ACOs taking on downside risk—putting their own money at risk if they overspend—significantly outperform upside-only ACOs. Financial accountability changes provider behavior in ways that the prospect of shared savings alone does not. This is why CMS's "Pathways to Success" rule accelerated the timeline for mandatory risk progression.

Physician leadership is a second strong predictor. Physician-led ACOs—those not dominated by a hospital anchor—tend to generate more consistent savings and quality improvements than hospital-anchored ACOs. This may reflect the fact that hospital systems have conflicting incentives: ACO shared savings require reducing hospitalizations, yet admissions revenue is the financial backbone of hospital operations. Physician-led organizations do not face this structural tension. The CBO's 2024 review confirmed that physician-led ACOs are among the most reliably cost-reducing ACO configurations.

Investment in care management infrastructure is a third key predictor. ACOs that deploy dedicated care coordinators, use predictive risk stratification to identify high-cost patients before crises, implement post-discharge follow-up programs, and engage community health workers to address social determinants of health consistently outperform ACOs that layer the ACO contract on top of an unchanged practice model. The evidence suggests that the ACO contract is a necessary but not sufficient condition for savings—the operational transformation matters as much as the financial structure.

children.text: ACO REACH and the Next Generation ACO: Evidence from Alternative Models

The Next Generation ACO (NGACO) model (2016–2021) was designed to test whether ACOs willing to accept full two-sided risk—including capitation-like arrangements—could generate larger net savings than MSSP ACOs. The NGACO model generated $667 million in gross savings across performance years 2016 to 2019. However, after accounting for $909 million in shared savings and other payouts to risk-bearing ACOs, the NGACO model was associated with $243 million in net losses to Medicare over four performance years. CMS terminated the NGACO model after performance year 2021 on these grounds.

The NGACO experience illustrates an important tension in ACO design: higher risk levels attract providers confident in their ability to save, but generous shared savings rates can convert gross program savings into net Medicare costs. The successor ACO REACH model recalibrated this balance, keeping two-sided risk while adjusting the shared savings formula and adding an explicit health equity commitment. In 2023, ACO REACH's 132 participants generated $1.643 billion in gross savings and $695 million in net savings after incentive payments—a net-positive result that justified the program's continuation.

ACO REACH distinguished itself from MSSP through several design features: a total cost of care model (rather than Parts A and B only), a requirement that at least 75 percent of each ACO's governing body consist of participating providers (to prevent private equity capture), and explicit equity benchmarks requiring ACOs to collect and report race, ethnicity, and language data and develop health equity plans. The 2025 announcement of potential NGACO REACH restructuring introduced uncertainty about the model's future trajectory.

body.content:
Aledade is one of the largest physician-focused ACO operators in the United States, providing technology, data analytics, and care management support to independent primary care practices to help them succeed in ACO models. As of 2024, Aledade had grown to support hundreds of practices across dozens of states, participating in both MSSP and ACO REACH.
Aledade's approach exemplifies the physician-led model the evidence favors: independent practices retain ownership and autonomy, while Aledade provides the risk stratification tools, care coordinator training, and claims analytics that individual practices could not afford alone. Their publicly reported results consistently show above-average shared savings rates relative to national MSSP averages, supporting the thesis that physician-led, well-supported ACOs outperform hospital-anchored counterparts. Source: Aledade company publications and NAACOS ACO data.

children.text: Quality Evidence: What ACOs Deliver Beyond Cost

While the financial evidence on ACOs is debated, the quality evidence is more consistently positive. Studies using Medicare claims data and CAHPS surveys show that ACO beneficiaries receive more preventive services, more follow-up care after hospitalization, and report better care coordination experiences than comparable non-ACO patients. ACO quality reporting has yielded year-over-year improvements in blood pressure control, diabetic eye exam rates, tobacco cessation counseling, and influenza vaccination rates—all clinically meaningful outcomes.

A particularly important quality finding involves potentially avoidable hospitalizations. Multiple studies have shown that ACOs reduce ambulatory care-sensitive condition hospitalizations—admissions for conditions like heart failure exacerbation, diabetic ketoacidosis, and asthma that are generally preventable with good outpatient management. Reducing these admissions is clinically valuable, represents genuine care improvement rather than cost-shifting, and aligns with the theoretical mechanism by which ACOs should improve the delivery of care.

Health equity remains a significant unresolved quality challenge. Early analyses found that ACOs were more likely to be located in higher-income, less racially diverse areas, and that attributed populations skewed toward healthier, more educated patients. CMS has responded with quality measures that explicitly stratify results by race and ethnicity, equity bonuses in ACO REACH, and data collection requirements around social risk factors. Whether ACOs can reduce disparities—not just average costs—is now one of the central quality questions in the field.

The best-performing ACOs combine financial accountability (downside risk), physician leadership, care management infrastructure, and equity-focused quality measurement. No single element alone is sufficient—all four must be present for consistently strong performance.

points: ACO performance data must be interpreted carefully: benchmark-based savings (what CMS reports) and counterfactual-based savings (what independent researchers measure) are different numbers, with the latter being more methodologically rigorous.

Selection bias is a persistent challenge: practices that join ACOs may already be more efficient, making it difficult to isolate the true causal effect of ACO participation on spending.

The Next Generation ACO model (2016–2021) produced gross savings but generated $243 million in net Medicare costs after shared savings payments, illustrating the tension between high risk tolerance and program economics.

ACO REACH (launched 2023) addressed NGACO shortcomings with rebalanced incentives, a 75% provider governance requirement, and explicit health equity commitments, generating $695 million in net savings in its first year.

Quality evidence is more consistently positive than financial evidence: ACO beneficiaries receive more preventive care, have fewer avoidable hospitalizations, and report better care coordination than comparable non-ACO patients.

Health equity remains an unresolved quality challenge, with early evidence that ACOs disproportionately served lower-risk, more affluent populations—a gap CMS is actively trying to address through redesigned quality requirements.

This is distinct from the CMS benchmark-based reports, which show large savings because benchmarks are not pure counterfactuals.

children.text: Why ACOs and Population Health Are Inseparable

Everything in this course has assumed a financial reason to manage a population proactively. The Accountable Care Organization (ACO) is the structure that creates that reason. An ACO is a group of providers that agrees to be collectively accountable for the cost and quality of a defined population of patients — and to share in the savings if they keep spending below a benchmark while meeting quality standards.

This is the economic engine. Under fee-for-service, there is no payoff for preventing an avoidable hospitalization — the hospital is paid for the admission. Under an ACO, preventing that admission keeps spending below benchmark and earns shared savings. The ACO flips the incentive so that the proactive, whole-population work this course describes finally pays. ACO strategy IS population health strategy, applied to a financial contract.

And it works at scale. In 2024, the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) — the largest ACO program — had 476 ACOs covering about 10.3 million assigned beneficiaries and generated record net savings of roughly $2.4 billion, the eighth consecutive year of savings. ACOs are no longer an experiment; they are a proven, growing model, and population health is how they succeed.

An ACO is a group of providers accountable for the cost and quality of a defined population, sharing in savings if they beat a spending benchmark while meeting quality. It is the financial engine that makes proactive population health pay — ACO strategy IS population health strategy.
How ACO Economics Work

Three mechanics define an ACO, and all three connect to earlier lessons. First, attribution: patients are assigned to the ACO, usually based on where they get their primary care — this is the "defined population" from the very first lesson. Second, the benchmark: CMS sets an expected spending target for the ACO's attributed population. Third, shared savings: if actual spending comes in below the benchmark AND the ACO meets quality standards, the ACO keeps a share of the difference.

The quality gate matters: an ACO cannot earn savings simply by spending less — it must also hit quality measures (the ACO quality reporting from the Clinical Quality Measurement course), so "savings" cannot come from stinting on care. This is what aligns the financial and clinical goals.

A critical evolution is two-sided risk. Early ACOs took only upside (shared savings with no penalty for overspending). Increasingly, ACOs take two-sided risk — they share in savings but also owe money if they overspend. In 2024, two-sided-risk ACOs generated the large majority of all savings, because real downside risk drives serious population health investment. Risk is the engine: the more an ACO has at stake, the harder it works the population health levers.

body.title: How an ACO Earns Shared Savings

children.text: The Strategic Levers

How does an ACO actually beat its benchmark? Not by denying care, but by reducing avoidable, low-value utilization — the high-cost events that add little clinical benefit. The primary targets are preventable inpatient admissions, avoidable emergency department visits, and destabilizing care transitions. Every lever in this course points at these.

The strategy is built on the population health toolkit: risk-stratify the attributed population to find the high-risk and rising-risk patients; deploy care management to those tiers; run chronic-disease programs (diabetes, heart failure, hypertension) to prevent the complications that drive admissions; integrate behavioral health; close care gaps for quality; and use transitional care and remote monitoring to prevent readmissions. The ACO is where all the previous lessons combine into one financial strategy.

Two ACO-specific levers deserve emphasis. Post-acute care management: a huge share of avoidable spending is in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and other post-acute care, so top ACOs build preferred, high-quality SNF networks and manage length of stay and readmissions there. And primary care investment: top-performing ACOs have markedly higher primary-care utilization — one analysis found about 2.5 times the PCP service use of the MSSP average — because strong primary care prevents the downstream expensive events. ACOs that invest in primary care and post-acute management win.

children.text: The Leakage Problem

A distinctive ACO challenge is "network leakage" — attributed patients getting care outside the ACO's network. Leakage hurts an ACO two ways: it loses visibility into the patient's care (the out-of-network data blind spot from the data-infrastructure lesson), and it loses the ability to manage cost and quality for care it does not control. Out-of-network utilization can seriously derail an ACO's savings.

The data bears this out: costs are higher for ACOs whose patients see primary care physicians outside the ACO's network. When a patient's care fragments across providers the ACO cannot coordinate, avoidable duplication, gaps, and high-cost events multiply — exactly the fragmentation population health exists to fix, now with direct financial consequences.

Managing leakage is therefore a core ACO strategy: building strong primary-care relationships so patients stay in-network, establishing preferred specialist and post-acute networks, and using data (including ADT alerts and predictive analytics) to detect and respond to leakage. This is the financial expression of the whole course's theme — fragmented care is bad care and expensive care, and keeping the patient within a coordinated, accountable network is how an ACO delivers better outcomes at lower cost.

body.message: When attributed patients get care outside the ACO's network, the ACO loses both visibility (the out-of-network data blind spot) and control over cost and quality — and its costs rise. Strong primary care relationships, preferred networks, and leakage-detection analytics are essential, because uncoordinated out-of-network care directly erodes shared savings.
body.title: Leakage Quietly Destroys ACO Savings

children.text: Where the Course Comes Together

The ACO is where this entire course resolves into a coherent business strategy. Each earlier lesson is a lever an ACO pulls: data infrastructure gives the ACO visibility into its attributed population; risk stratification and prediction target its limited resources; care gap closure earns the quality gate; chronic-disease and behavioral programs prevent the complications that drive cost; care management and patient engagement deliver the interventions; and leakage management keeps it all coordinated.

This also clarifies why population health and value-based payment are inseparable, as the first lesson claimed. Population health is the operational method; the ACO (and value-based contracts generally) is the payment model that rewards it. Neither works alone: value-based payment without population health capability just shifts risk onto unprepared providers; population health without value-based payment has no business case. Together, they form the model.

The strategic takeaway for any provider entering value-based care is that succeeding as an ACO is not about a single trick — it is about systematically building the full population health stack and pointing it at avoidable utilization, while keeping patients coordinated within the network and meeting quality. The ACOs that win are the ones that do population health well. The next lesson goes deeper into the financial discipline of managing the total cost of care that underlies all of this.

body.content:
A successful two-sided-risk MSSP ACO invests heavily in primary care (driving PCP utilization well above average), risk-stratifies its attributed population, and deploys care managers to the high-risk and rising-risk tiers. It runs diabetes, heart-failure, and behavioral-health programs, uses ADT alerts for transitional care, and builds a preferred high-quality SNF network to cut avoidable post-acute spending.
The result: fewer preventable admissions and readmissions, strong quality scores, and shared savings earned by keeping its defined population healthier and better coordinated — population health as financial strategy.

The ACO flips the fee-for-service incentive: preventing avoidable events now pays, making it the financial engine for proactive population health.
In 2024, MSSP had 476 ACOs covering ~10.3M beneficiaries and generated record net savings of ~$2.4 billion, an eighth straight year of savings.
ACO economics rest on attribution, a spending benchmark, and a quality gate; two-sided (downside) risk drives the majority of savings because real risk drives serious investment.

ACOs win by reducing avoidable utilization (preventable admissions, ED visits, bad transitions) using the full population health toolkit, plus post-acute/SNF network management and primary-care investment (top ACOs ~2.5x PCP use).
Network leakage — patients getting out-of-network care — destroys visibility, control, and savings, so keeping patients coordinated in-network is a core ACO strategy.
The ACO is where the whole course resolves: population health is the operational method and value-based payment (ACOs) is the model that rewards it — neither works without the other.

This flipped incentive is exactly what makes the proactive, whole-population work of population health financially worthwhile — ACO strategy is population health strategy.

children.text: Quality as a Gate on Savings

Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are groups of providers who take collective responsibility for the cost and quality of a population of patients. If they keep spending below a benchmark, they can share in the savings. But there is a catch built into the design: an ACO cannot simply cut costs and pocket the difference. It must also prove it delivered good care.

That proof comes through quality reporting. In the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) — the largest ACO program — quality performance is the gate that determines whether, and how much, an ACO actually gets to keep of any savings it generates. Score too low on quality, and savings shrink or disappear regardless of how much money was saved.

This makes ACO quality reporting fundamentally different from public reporting or even MIPS. Here, quality measurement is wired directly into a shared-savings contract: it is the safeguard that prevents "savings" from being achieved by stinting on care.

In the Medicare Shared Savings Program, an ACO must meet a quality performance standard to qualify for and keep shared savings. Quality reporting is the gate that ensures cost savings did not come at the expense of care.
The APM Performance Pathway

MSSP ACOs report their quality through a specific channel called the APM Performance Pathway (APP). The APP was designed to align ACO quality reporting with MIPS, so an ACO's quality work satisfies both its Shared Savings Program obligations and the MIPS requirements of its clinicians at once.

For 2024, ACOs had a transitional choice. They could report the legacy CMS Web Interface set of 10 measures, or the newer APP measure set of three clinical quality measures submitted electronically. Those three APP measures are familiar ones from elsewhere in this course: diabetes HbA1c poor control, depression screening and follow-up, and controlling high blood pressure.

On top of those, ACOs must administer the CAHPS patient-experience survey, and CMS calculates additional measures directly from administrative claims data. So even the "three-measure" APP option is really a blend of clinician-reported measures, a patient survey, and claims-based measures — combining several measure types we have already studied.

children.text: eCQMs, MIPS CQMs, and Medicare CQMs

A subtle but important wrinkle in ACO reporting is the "collection type" — how the same measure's data is gathered. ACOs can report their APP measures as eCQMs, MIPS CQMs, or Medicare CQMs, and the difference is about which patients are included.

eCQMs and MIPS CQMs are reported on the ACO's entire all-payer, all-patient population — every patient regardless of insurer. Medicare CQMs, by contrast, are MIPS CQMs reported only for the ACO's eligible Medicare fee-for-service population. Medicare CQMs were introduced as a more attainable bridge for ACOs not yet able to pull all-payer data from every practice's EHR.

This distinction matters because all-payer reporting is technically demanding: it requires aggregating standardized clinical data across many practices and EHR systems for patients with every kind of insurance. The collection-type options reflect a real-world tension between the aspiration of comprehensive, all-payer digital measurement and the practical limits of today's data infrastructure.

children.text: The Quality Performance Standard
Reporting the measures is only half the requirement; an ACO must also perform well enough to meet the quality performance standard. This standard is what links the quality score to the dollars.

The standard is defined relative to national benchmarks expressed as percentiles. In recent years, an ACO could meet it by scoring at or above roughly the 30th or 40th percentile (depending on the year) on its measures, with a lower floor (around the 10th percentile) on at least one outcome measure. Beginning in 2025 and beyond, the standard generally requires reaching at least the 40th percentile across the MIPS quality performance category scores.

An ACO that meets the standard is eligible for its full earned share of savings; one that falls short sees its savings reduced or forfeited. The percentile design means the bar is relative — ACOs are effectively measured against each other, so the standard rises as the field improves.

children.text: Where ACO Reporting Is Headed

ACO quality reporting is in active transition, all in the direction of fewer, more meaningful, fully digital measures. The legacy 10-measure Web Interface is being retired in favor of the APP. Starting in 2025, CMS introduced the "APP Plus" measure set, which grows the APP to six measures (a mix of eCQMs/Medicare CQMs, an administrative-claims measure, and the CAHPS survey) and expands further in later years.

The throughline is the shift toward electronic, all-payer digital quality measurement — pulling measures directly from EHRs across an ACO's whole patient population rather than from a sampled Medicare subset or manual abstraction. That is exactly the digital-measures future the next lessons of this course explore.

For now, the key takeaway is structural: in an ACO, quality measurement is not a report card on the side — it is a contractual gate on real money. The measures, collection types, and percentile standards all exist to ensure that when an ACO claims savings, it has earned them without shortchanging patients.

The trajectory is clear: retire the old Web Interface, consolidate on the APP, and push ACOs toward electronic, all-payer quality measurement.

children.text: The Problem With Spreading Overhead by Formula

The traditional cost-allocation methods covered earlier — step-down allocation, ratios of cost to charges — share a common weakness: they spread overhead using broad averages and formulas rather than tracing it to what actually drives it. They answer "what share of administration should radiology bear?" with a tidy ratio, but that ratio may bear little relation to how much administrative work radiology truly causes. For decades this was good enough, because hospitals were paid for volume and didn’t urgently need precise costs. Value-based care changed that calculus entirely.

Activity-based costing (ABC) is the response. ABC is an approach to costing that traces resource consumption to activities, and activities to cost objects (such as a patient, a procedure, or a service). Instead of assuming overhead spreads evenly, ABC asks what activities a service actually requires — scheduling, registration, the procedure itself, recovery, billing — and assigns the cost of each activity based on how much of it the service consumes. The result is a far more accurate picture of what a given episode of care truly costs.

The most influential refinement, designed specifically to make ABC practical in healthcare, is time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC). It has become the leading method for answering the question that value-based care makes unavoidable: when a hospital is paid a single bundled or capitated amount, does that payment actually cover the cost of delivering the care?

Key Concept: Activity-based costing (ABC) traces resource use to specific activities and then to cost objects (patients, procedures), rather than spreading overhead by broad averages. Time-driven ABC (TDABC) simplifies this by costing the actual time each step of care consumes.
How Activity-Based Costing Works

The core idea of ABC is that activities, not departments, consume resources — and products or services consume activities. Rather than asking "how much did the radiology department spend?", ABC asks "what activities happen in radiology, what does each cost, and how many of each does a given patient require?" A chest X-ray and a complex interventional procedure may occur in the same department, but they consume vastly different activities; ABC captures that difference where average-based methods blur it.

Traditional ABC, however, earned a reputation for being expensive, slow, and hard to maintain. Mapping every activity and continuously surveying staff about how they spend their time proved impractical for organizations as complex as hospitals. This implementation burden is precisely why the original ABC method, despite its conceptual appeal, was adopted unevenly — it was more commonly used in narrower settings like laboratories than across whole hospitals.

body.message: Classic activity-based costing is conceptually superior to formula-based allocation but notoriously resource-intensive to build and maintain — requiring detailed activity mapping and ongoing staff time surveys. That practical burden, not a flaw in the logic, limited its spread in healthcare and motivated the time-driven version.
body.title: ABC’s Accuracy Came at a Cost

children.text: Time-Driven ABC: The Healthcare Breakthrough

Time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC) was created by Robert Kaplan and Steven Anderson at Harvard Business School to simplify and modernize ABC, and it was brought squarely into healthcare when Kaplan and Michael Porter laid out a seven-step approach for applying it in clinical settings in 2011. TDABC’s elegance is that it reduces the entire costing problem to just two parameters: the capacity cost rate (the cost per unit of time for a given resource — a nurse, an operating room, an MRI) and the time each activity in the care pathway requires.

In practice, a multidisciplinary team builds a process map that follows the patient through the complete care cycle — from scheduling and check-in, through the procedure and recovery, to follow-up and billing. For each step, they estimate the time consumed and multiply it by the capacity cost rate of the resources used. Summing across all steps yields the total cost of treating that patient for that condition. By prioritizing accuracy over false precision and requiring far fewer resources than classic ABC, TDABC made activity-based costing finally feasible at the scale of a hospital.

body.title: The Logic of Time-Driven ABC

children.text: TDABC has now been applied across the full range of care — primary, secondary, acute, tertiary, and long-term — and to procedures as varied as colonoscopy, aortic valve replacement, and carpal tunnel release. Because it produces patient-specific, activity-level costs, it gives leaders something formula-based allocation never could: a defensible, granular answer to what each step of care actually costs, and where in the pathway the money is going.
Why It Matters for Value-Based Care

The rise of TDABC in healthcare is inseparable from the rise of value-based care. Implementing value-based initiatives depends on cost-assessment methods that produce high-quality cost information, and TDABC is increasingly used to fill that cost-information gap. When a hospital accepts a bundled payment for a joint replacement or a capitated rate for a population, it can no longer hide imprecise costing behind fee-for-service billing — it must know, step by step, what the care costs to know whether the payment is sustainable.

TDABC also does something subtler: it turns costing into an improvement tool. By revealing the time and cost of each step in a care pathway, it exposes waste — idle equipment, redundant steps, bottlenecks — that can be removed without harming patients. A systematic review found that TDABC contributed to value-based initiatives, especially through cost-saving findings, in the studies that applied it for that purpose. One published example used TDABC specifically to reduce idle time in an interventional radiology suite, converting cost transparency directly into efficiency.

body.content:
In a pilot analyzing colonoscopy, aortic valve replacement, and carpal tunnel release, clinicians used TDABC to map the true cost of each procedure’s full care cycle.

The value of the exercise was not just a more accurate number — it was visibility. Seeing exactly where time and money were consumed let teams identify steps that added cost without adding value, compare their costs against the bundled payments they received, and target specific improvements. This is the core promise of TDABC for value-based care: it measures the denominator (cost) in the value equation of outcomes-over-cost, making true value measurable for the first time.
body.title: TDABC as a Value Platform

children.text: The Barriers — and the Honest Verdict

Despite its promise, TDABC is far from universally adopted, and the reasons are instructive. Resource and operational constraints loom large: hospitals facing unpredictable payment environments and competing priorities (like major electronic-health-record implementations) struggle to invest in building costing systems. Organizational barriers — resistance to change, the difficulty of collecting accurate data, and the need for continuous training — slow adoption further. And methodological gaps remain: TDABC still struggles with allocating shared support-department costs, and its ability to directly inform bundled-payment rates is not yet well established.

Even the seemingly simple step of estimating staff time at each point in the process map remains resource-intensive in practice. These are not reasons to dismiss TDABC, but they explain why a method praised in the literature for two decades is still spreading unevenly across real hospitals. The path forward, researchers agree, requires further methodological standardization, genuine workforce engagement, and tighter integration with the decisions hospitals actually make.

body.analogy: Traditional cost allocation is like splitting a group restaurant bill evenly regardless of what each person ordered — fast, but unfair to the person who had only a salad. Time-driven activity-based costing is like an itemized receipt that follows each diner’s actual order. It takes more effort to produce, but it finally shows who truly cost what — which is exactly what you need when someone else (a bundled payer) is paying a fixed amount for the whole table.
body.concept: TDABC vs. formula-based cost allocation

children.text: The honest verdict is that activity-based costing, and TDABC in particular, represents the most accurate available answer to hospital finance’s hardest question — what does care actually cost? — while remaining genuinely difficult to implement well. For a hospital moving into value-based contracts, that trade-off increasingly tilts toward adoption: the cost of not knowing your costs rises sharply the moment your revenue is fixed. Understanding ABC and TDABC is therefore understanding both the destination of hospital cost accounting and the real-world friction on the road to it.

Time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC), created by Kaplan and Anderson and brought into healthcare via Kaplan and Porter’s 2011 seven-step approach, simplifies ABC using just two parameters: the capacity cost rate and the time each activity requires.
TDABC works by mapping the full patient care pathway, estimating the time each step consumes, and multiplying by each resource’s capacity cost rate to produce a patient-specific, activity-level cost.

TDABC has been applied across all care settings and many procedures (colonoscopy, aortic valve replacement, carpal tunnel release), giving leaders a defensible answer to what each step of care truly costs.

TDABC is central to value-based care because fixed payments (bundles, capitation) require knowing true costs, and it doubles as an improvement tool by exposing waste and idle capacity in care pathways.
Adoption barriers are real: resource and operational constraints, resistance to change, data-collection difficulty, unresolved support-cost allocation, and resource-intensive staff-time estimation.

children.text: CMS released preliminary AHEAD Model Year One performance data in January 2026, covering Maryland’s established Total Cost of Care program and the four initial AHEAD states: Vermont, Colorado, Connecticut, and New York. The data creates a clear bifurcation between hospitals that invested in care coordination infrastructure before entering the model and those that did not.
The Bifurcation: Who Is Winning and Who Is Absorbing Risk

Among rural hospitals in AHEAD states, 34% generated net shared savings in Year One, with an average positive variance of $1.4M against their total cost of care benchmark. These hospitals shared three characteristics: they had implemented a care transitions program at least 24 months before AHEAD entry, they had risk-stratified their Medicaid populations using SDOH data, and they had renegotiated at least one commercial payer contract to align incentives with the AHEAD benchmark.

The 41% of rural AHEAD participants that reported downside risk exposure in Year One averaged a negative variance of $880,000. The primary driver was higher-than-benchmarked specialist utilization—patients who previously had no primary care relationship presenting with advanced chronic disease and requiring expensive specialty workups. This is a predictable first-year effect that dissipates in Year Two as care coordination begins to intercept high-cost events.
The hospitals generating savings in AHEAD Year One had been building care coordination capacity for two to three years before entry. The model rewards preparation, not just participation.

body.title: AHEAD Year One Financial Performance: Rural Hospital Cohort

children.text: The Care Coordination Investment Calculus

For rural hospitals currently evaluating AHEAD entry in the 2027 enrollment window, the data suggests a minimum 18–24 month preparation period before assuming performance risk. The investment threshold for a viable care coordination program—typically one full-time care coordinator per 500 high-risk attributed patients—runs between $280,000 and $420,000 annually for an average rural hospital population. Against potential shared savings of $1.4M, this is a strong return, but it requires upfront capital that many distressed rural hospitals do not have.

CFO ALERT: RHT program states offer care coordination infrastructure grants that can offset 40–60% of the upfront investment required before AHEAD entry. Check your state’s RHT funding allocation before assuming self-funding is the only path.

children.text: The first cohort of rural hospitals to deploy AI clinical decision support tools at operational scale—primarily through RHT program infrastructure grants and partnerships with Texas’s Lone Star AI Network and Vermont’s digital transformation program—has completed 12–18 months of production deployment. The data challenges both the optimist and pessimist narratives about AI in rural healthcare settings.
What the Real-World Data Shows

Across 14 rural deployments analyzed in a pre-publication report shared with HRSA in December 2025, AI clinical decision support tools demonstrated statistically significant improvements in three areas: sepsis early warning (average 4.2-hour earlier intervention, 12% mortality reduction in the pilot cohort), medication reconciliation error detection (31% reduction in discharge reconciliation errors), and preventable readmission risk flagging (18% reduction in 30-day readmissions for flagged patients who received care coordination follow-up).

The AI tools that are working in rural hospitals are doing one thing well and doing it quietly. The ones that are failing are trying to do everything and generating so much noise that clinicians have learned to ignore them entirely.

body.title: AI CDS Performance Across 14 Rural Hospital Deployments

children.text: The Alert Fatigue Problem Is Real and Solvable

The readmission risk flagging deployment had the highest alert fatigue rate (41%) and the highest clinician override rate (38%) in the cohort. The root cause, in 10 of the 14 sites, was model calibration: the tools had been trained on urban hospital populations with different baseline risk distributions and had not been recalibrated to the rural patient population before deployment. Sites that invested 90 days in local model recalibration before going live showed alert fatigue rates below 15%.

The human-in-the-loop requirement is not a temporary limitation pending better AI—it is an architectural feature of safe AI deployment. Rural hospitals that treated AI CDS outputs as recommendations requiring clinical judgment outperformed those that attempted to automate responses to AI alerts. The former group showed 22% better outcomes on the primary metrics; the latter showed AI tools being disabled by frustrated clinicians within six months.

DEPLOYMENT CHECKLIST: Before activating any AI CDS tool in a rural hospital, complete four steps: (1) local model recalibration on 12 months of your own patient data, (2) alert threshold setting with clinical leadership (not vendor defaults), (3) override tracking workflow to capture clinician reasoning, (4) 90-day alert fatigue audit with defined escalation if false positive rate exceeds 20%.

What is the training data composition—what % is rural/CAH population? How will local recalibration be supported?
What is the vendor’s alert threshold methodology and can it be adjusted post-deployment?
What override tracking and model feedback mechanism is built into the product?
What SLA covers alert fatigue rate monitoring and remediation if thresholds are exceeded?

This analysis examines outcomes from 14 rural AI deployments across six states, with particular focus on alert fatigue rates, clinician override patterns, and the workflow design choices that separate effective deployments from counterproductive ones.

children.text: Clinical decision support (CDS) has been championed as one of the most powerful tools in the healthcare system's drive toward safer, higher-quality, more efficient care. Hospitals spend millions implementing CDS platforms, regulators embed CDS requirements into meaningful-use and quality-reporting programs, and health IT vendors advertise outcomes that sound almost too good to be true. But what does the peer-reviewed evidence actually say? The honest answer is nuanced: in some domains CDS delivers clear, measurable benefit; in others the evidence is thin, mixed, or actively cautionary.

This lesson cuts through the marketing and the hype to examine what systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and large observational studies have found. Understanding where CDS works, where it struggles, and why is not an academic exercise — it is the foundation for deploying CDS responsibly and getting real results for patients.
The Research Landscape: What Systematic Reviews Tell Us

The body of research on CDS is large but uneven. The landmark 2012 systematic review by Bright and colleagues, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, remains one of the most comprehensive analyses ever conducted. Searching MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science through January 2011, the authors identified randomized trials of electronic CDS implemented in real clinical settings. Their core finding: CDS consistently improved health care process measures — particularly those related to ordering preventive services — but the evidence for improvements in actual clinical outcomes (mortality, morbidity, readmissions) was far thinner and more variable.

The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) has funded multiple evidence reports on the topic. The 2012 report "Effect of clinical decision-support systems: a systematic review," cited by AHRQ's PSNet, echoed the Bright findings and highlighted a critical methodological problem: most studies evaluating CDS are conducted at large academic medical centers with custom-built systems and dedicated informatics teams. These settings are not representative of the community hospitals, small practices, and federally qualified health centers that constitute most of American healthcare. Generalizability of CDS evidence is therefore a persistent and under-acknowledged weakness.

When researchers parse the literature by clinical domain, two distinct tiers emerge. Medication safety — including drug-drug interaction checking, dosing alerts, and allergy screening — has a relatively robust evidence base accumulated over decades. Preventive care reminders (vaccinations, cancer screenings, chronic disease monitoring) have a solid if modest evidence base. Diagnostic decision support — helping clinicians reach the right diagnosis — has a much weaker, more contested evidence base. Understanding this tiered landscape is the first step toward deploying CDS where it is most likely to help.

children.text: Where CDS Clearly Works: Medication Safety and Preventive Care

The strongest evidence for CDS effectiveness is in medication safety. Drug-drug interaction (DDI) checking, allergy alerts, and dosing support have been built into electronic health record platforms since the 1990s, giving researchers decades of data. A 2021 AHRQ rapid report summarizing evidence from randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews found that computerized provider order entry paired with medication-related CDS was associated with reduced medication errors at a moderate strength of evidence, and with prevention of adverse drug events at a low-to-moderate strength of evidence. One frequently cited early RCT demonstrated a 55 percent reduction in non-intercepted medication errors when a CPOE-with-CDS system was compared to paper-based ordering.

Preventive care reminders represent another domain with a solid evidence base. A review of 33 controlled studies found that CDS reminder systems led to an average 13 percent improvement across six preventive care procedures, with pneumococcal vaccination showing the largest gain at 17.2 percent. A separate review of 16 randomized controlled trials found an overall 77 percent increase in preventive procedures when computerized reminder systems were used, though this figure reflects relative improvement from often-low baseline rates. CDS reminder prompts for HPV vaccination, influenza immunization, colorectal cancer screening, and osteoporosis screening have all shown statistically significant improvements in ordering rates in published trials.

Dosing alerts for renally cleared medications represent a particularly well-studied CDS intervention. Patients with chronic kidney disease or acute renal failure are at elevated risk of drug toxicity when standard doses are prescribed without adjustment. CDS tools that fire an alert when a clinician orders a renally dosed drug for a patient with a low estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) have been shown to reduce inappropriate prescribing and associated adverse events. The mechanism is straightforward: the clinical rule is well-defined, the EHR data needed to evaluate it (serum creatinine, weight, age) is reliably present, and the correct action (dose reduction or drug switch) is unambiguous. These conditions — clear rule, reliable data, unambiguous action — are the template for CDS that works.
