children.text: When You Disagree With the Denial

Not every denial is correct. Payers deny claims that should have been paid — for incomplete information they could have requested, for "medical necessity" the documentation actually supported, or simply in error. When a provider believes a denial is wrong, the remedy is the appeal: a formal request that the payer reconsider its decision.

Appeals are the back-end's tool for fighting denials, distinct from simply correcting and resubmitting. You resubmit when the claim had a fixable error; you appeal when you believe the claim was correct and the denial was not. Appeals are more formal, more documentation-heavy, and governed by strict deadlines and levels.

The most striking fact about appeals is how underused they are relative to how often they work. Only about 11.5 percent of denied Medicare claims are ever appealed — yet most appeals succeed. That gap represents enormous recoverable revenue left on the table simply because providers do not pursue it.

An appeal is a formal request that a payer reconsider a denial believed to be wrong. Strikingly, only ~11.5% of denied Medicare claims are appealed — yet most appeals succeed, meaning huge recoverable revenue goes unpursued.
The Levels of Appeal

Appeals proceed through escalating levels, and you generally must exhaust each internal level before moving to the next. A first-level appeal is the initial formal request asking the payer to reconsider, reviewed by insurance-company personnel. The payer typically has a defined window (often around 30 days) to respond.

If the first-level appeal is denied, a second-level appeal triggers another internal review — usually by a different medical reviewer who did not participate in the original decision — supported by additional evidence and stronger documentation. Only after exhausting internal appeals can a provider (or patient) usually request an external review by an Independent Review Organization (IRO), a neutral third party whose decision the payer must honor.

Each level raises the bar and the independence of the reviewer. The internal levels give the payer a chance to correct itself; the external review removes the decision from the payer entirely. This escalation structure exists for commercial and ACA-plan appeals, and a parallel (more elaborate) structure governs Medicare.

body.title: Escalating Levels of Appeal

children.text: The Medicare Five-Level Process

Medicare has its own, formally defined five-level appeals process that is worth knowing because Medicare is so large. Level 1 is Redetermination by a Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC); Level 2 is Reconsideration by a Qualified Independent Contractor (QIC); Level 3 is a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ); Level 4 is review by the Medicare Appeals Council; and Level 5 is judicial review in federal district court.

Each level has strict deadlines. A redetermination must be requested within 120 days of the initial determination; a reconsideration within 180 days of the redetermination notice, with the QIC having 60 days to decide. Miss a deadline and the appeal right is generally forfeited — the same unforgiving clock that governs timely filing governs appeals.

In practice, the vast majority of cases resolve early: over 90 percent of Medicare Advantage appeals are settled at Level 1 or Level 2, with only about 2 to 3 percent reaching an ALJ hearing. This means a well-prepared first- or second-level appeal is where most recoverable revenue is actually won — the higher levels are rare and reserved for the hardest cases.

body.title: The Five Levels of Medicare Appeal

children.text: Winning an Appeal: Documentation and the Peer-to-Peer

Appeals are won on evidence. The core of any appeal is a clear, specific appeal letter that states exactly why the claim should be paid, paired with as much supporting documentation as possible — the medical records, physician statements, and clinical evidence that establish the case. A missing physician statement or an incomplete record can sink an otherwise valid appeal.

For clinical denials (especially medical necessity), a powerful tool is the peer-to-peer review: the treating physician speaks directly with a physician reviewer at the payer to argue the clinical case. It is requested by the provider and, for some denials, must be completed quickly. A peer-to-peer can overturn a denial before a formal written appeal is even needed, because it lets two clinicians resolve a clinical disagreement directly.

The recurring theme is that appeals reward preparation and specificity. A generic "please reconsider" letter rarely works; an appeal that cites the specific policy, attaches the exact documentation that rebuts the denial reason, and addresses the CARC code head-on is what succeeds. This is also why good documentation (the earlier lesson) pays off twice — once in preventing the denial, and again in winning the appeal if one happens.

body.content:
A payer denies an inpatient admission as "not medically necessary." Rather than file a written appeal immediately, the hospital requests a peer-to-peer review, and the admitting physician speaks directly with the payer's physician reviewer to explain the clinical picture that justified admission.
The reviewer, hearing the clinical reasoning directly, overturns the denial — resolving it faster than a formal multi-level appeal and recovering the full payment.

children.text: Payer Relations and the Bigger Picture

Appeals are one front in a broader, ongoing relationship between providers and payers. Beyond individual appeals, strong payer relations involve tracking each payer's denial and reversal patterns, escalating systemic problems (a payer denying a whole category of valid claims), and using contract terms — prompt-payment clauses, dispute-resolution provisions — to hold payers accountable.

The data from appeals feeds back into this relationship. If a particular payer consistently denies valid claims that are then overturned on appeal, that pattern is leverage — in contract renegotiation, in regulatory complaints, and in operational pushback. Appeals are not just claim-by-claim recovery; in aggregate they are evidence about payer behavior.

The practical bottom line connects back to the opening fact: because most appeals succeed but few are filed, building real appeal capacity — clear ownership, deadline tracking, strong documentation, and routine use of peer-to-peer — is one of the highest-return investments in the back end. An organization that appeals diligently recovers revenue its peers abandon. With denials worked and appealed, the cycle turns to posting the payments that do come in — the subject of the next module.

body.message: Most appeals succeed, yet only a small fraction of denied claims are ever appealed (~11.5% in Medicare). Failing to appeal valid denials abandons revenue that would very likely be recovered. Track appeal deadlines, build strong documentation, and use peer-to-peer reviews — diligent appealing recovers what competitors write off.

children.text: The Money Still Owed

After claims are submitted, paid, and posted, there is always a residual: money that has been billed but not yet collected. That outstanding balance — owed by payers and patients — is accounts receivable (AR). Managing AR is the back-end discipline of systematically chasing that unpaid money until it is collected or appropriately written off.

AR management matters because billed revenue is not collected revenue. A claim can be perfectly submitted and still sit unpaid for weeks because the payer is slow, the claim got stuck, or no one followed up. AR is where revenue goes to wait — and where, without active management, it quietly ages, becomes harder to collect, and eventually dies as bad debt.

The core insight driving all of AR management is that money gets harder to collect the older it gets. Collectibility within the first 60 days runs high — around 90 percent — but once an account passes 90 days, the probability of ever collecting falls dramatically, toward half or less. Time is the enemy, which is why AR is organized entirely around age.

Accounts receivable (AR) is billed-but-uncollected revenue owed by payers and patients. The central truth of AR management: money gets harder to collect the older it gets — collectibility is ~90% within 60 days but falls sharply past 90 days.
Days in AR: The Headline Number

The single most important AR metric is Days in Accounts Receivable — the average number of days it takes to collect after billing. The calculation is straightforward: Total Accounts Receivable divided by Average Daily Charges (total charges over a period divided by the number of days in that period). The result is "how many days of billing is currently sitting uncollected."

Lower is better. The widely used benchmark is to keep Days in AR under 40 (per HFMA and MGMA norms), with leading organizations under 30. A rising Days in AR is one of the earliest warning signs that something is wrong upstream — claims are being denied, delayed, or not followed up — because all of that backs up into uncollected receivables.

Days in AR is powerful precisely because it is a summary number that reflects the health of the whole cycle. You cannot fix it directly; you fix it by fixing the things that feed it — cleaner claims, faster denial work, diligent follow-up. It is the thermometer, not the disease.

children.text: Aging Buckets: Organizing AR by Time

Because age determines collectibility, AR is organized into "aging buckets" — groupings of receivables by how long they have been outstanding. The standard buckets are 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91-120, and 120+ days, each showing the dollar amount sitting in it. The AR aging report is the back-end's primary worklist and dashboard.

The aging report instantly reveals the shape of the problem. A healthy AR profile is weighted toward the youngest buckets, with little money in 90+ days. When dollars pile up in the older buckets, it signals that claims are getting stuck and not being worked — and that revenue is sliding toward the point of no return. High performers keep less than about 15 percent of total AR in the 90+ day bucket.

Aging buckets also separate the two kinds of AR: insurance (payer) AR and patient AR. They behave differently — patient balances are generally harder and slower to collect, so a higher tolerance for older self-pay AR is normal. Reading the aging report means looking not just at totals but at where the money sits, who owes it, and which buckets are growing.

body.title: Standard AR Aging Buckets

children.text: The Follow-Up Process

AR follow-up is the systematic work of tracking unpaid claims and balances, contacting payers or patients to resolve them, correcting errors, resubmitting claims, and filing appeals when needed. It is the active, hands-on chasing that turns aged receivables back into cash — and it is organized around the aging buckets.

Effective follow-up assigns staff to specific buckets — someone focused on accounts approaching 60 days, another on the 90-plus accounts — and prioritizes the worklist by both age and dollar value. The principle mirrors denial prioritization: work the highest-value and most time-sensitive accounts first, and document every payer call and response so the follow-up has a trail.

Cadence matters. Most organizations review AR reports at least weekly for operational follow-up, because catching a stuck claim at 35 days and resolving it is vastly better than discovering it at 95 days when it is half-uncollectible. The discipline is to keep accounts moving down toward resolution before they age into the low-collectibility buckets — proactive follow-up rather than reactive cleanup.

children.text: Why Speed Wins

The throughline of AR management is that speed wins, because of the collectibility curve. An account worked in the 31-60 bucket is highly collectible; the same account left to reach 120+ days may be worth a fraction of its face value, even though nothing about the underlying claim changed. The decline is not about the claim's validity — it is purely about elapsed time.

This is why the youngest buckets deserve attention too, not just the old ones. Preventing a claim from aging is cheaper and more effective than rescuing it after it has aged. Strong AR management is therefore front-loaded: catch and resolve issues early, keep the aging report weighted young, and reserve heroic recovery efforts for the genuinely hard cases.

Eventually, some AR is uncollectible and must be written off — but that decision should be deliberate, based on real recovery probability, not the accidental result of neglect. Well-managed AR keeps Days in AR low, the 90+ bucket small, and write-offs intentional. What remains after payer AR is worked is the patient's portion — which is its own distinct challenge, and the subject of the final lesson in this module: patient collections.

body.message: Collectibility falls with age regardless of whether the claim is correct — ~90% within 60 days, dropping sharply past 90 days. Letting accounts drift into older buckets destroys recoverable revenue. Work AR proactively and weekly to keep it young; do not wait until accounts are nearly uncollectible.
body.title: Aged AR Loses Value Even If the Claim Is Valid

children.text: What Are the ASAM Criteria?

The ASAM Criteria, published by the American Society of Addiction Medicine, are the most widely used set of standards for assessing people with substance use disorders and matching them to the right intensity of treatment. They answer a question that confronts every clinician at intake: given this particular patient, what level and setting of care do they actually need?

Before standardized criteria existed, placement decisions were often driven by what a program happened to offer, by reimbursement rules, or by guesswork — a patient who needed intensive treatment might be sent to a weekly outpatient group, while someone who could safely be treated at home might be admitted to a costly residential bed. The ASAM Criteria replaced this with a structured, clinical approach to matching patients to care.

The criteria are revised periodically; the Fourth Edition was released in 2023. Many state Medicaid programs and commercial payers require the use of the ASAM Criteria for substance use disorder placement, which is why understanding them matters not just clinically but for how addiction treatment is authorized and paid for.

The ASAM Criteria, from the American Society of Addiction Medicine, are the national standard for assessing substance use disorders and matching patients to the appropriate intensity and setting of treatment. The Fourth Edition was released in 2023.
The Six Assessment Dimensions

The heart of the ASAM Criteria is a multidimensional, biopsychosocial assessment. Rather than looking only at the substance or the amount used, the clinician evaluates the whole person across six dimensions, each capturing a different factor that affects what kind of treatment a patient needs and where it should be delivered.

The six dimensions, in their long-standing form, are: (1) acute intoxication and withdrawal potential; (2) biomedical conditions and complications; (3) emotional, behavioral, or cognitive conditions and complications; (4) readiness to change; (5) relapse, continued use, or continued problem potential; and (6) recovery and living environment. Each dimension is given a risk rating, and together they paint a picture of the patient’s needs and risks.

This multidimensional view is what makes the criteria powerful. Two people with the same diagnosis can need very different care: one with severe withdrawal risk and an unstable living environment may need a 24-hour setting, while another who is medically stable, motivated, and supported at home can succeed in outpatient care. The dimensions surface those differences systematically. (The Fourth Edition updated the dimension labels — for example, foregrounding psychiatric and cognitive conditions and person-centered considerations — but the underlying biopsychosocial logic is the same.)

children.text: The Levels of Care

The assessment leads to a placement recommendation along a continuum of care intensities. The ASAM Criteria describe broad levels of care running from Level 0.5 to Level 4, with higher numbers indicating more intensive services and more clinical supervision. Each broad level contains sublevels for finer matching.

Level 0.5 is early intervention — for people with risky use who do not yet meet full criteria for a disorder. Level 1 is outpatient treatment, generally fewer than nine hours of service per week for adults, delivered while the person lives at home. Level 2 is intensive outpatient or partial hospitalization — more hours per week for those needing structure but not residential care.

Level 3 is residential treatment, provided in a structured setting staffed 24 hours a day, with sublevels ranging from clinically managed low-intensity to higher-intensity residential care. Level 4 is medically managed intensive inpatient care, with daily physician oversight and 24-hour nursing — the most intensive setting, used for example when withdrawal is medically dangerous. Patients can move up or down this continuum as their needs change.

children.text: Matching the Patient to the Right Level

The purpose of the criteria is patient–treatment matching: using the multidimensional assessment to recommend the least intensive level of care that can safely and effectively meet the patient’s needs. This avoids both under-treatment (placing someone in a level too weak to help them) and over-treatment (using a costly, restrictive setting a person does not need).

Crucially, placement is meant to be dynamic, not a one-time label. As a patient stabilizes, they should step down to less intensive care; if they deteriorate, they should step up. The criteria envision a continuum that patients move along over time, with treatment planning driven by ongoing reassessment of the six dimensions rather than a fixed program length.

This is a sharp departure from the old "one program fits all" approach and from arbitrary fixed stays (such as the historic "28-day rehab"). Care should follow the patient’s clinical needs as measured across the dimensions — which is exactly what payers are trying to enforce when they require ASAM-based placement.

body.content:
Two patients both have a severe opioid use disorder. One is in dangerous withdrawal, has unstable housing, and a co-occurring psychiatric crisis — the dimensions point toward a medically managed (Level 4) or high-intensity residential (Level 3) setting.
The other is medically stable, highly motivated, and lives with a supportive family — the same diagnosis, but the dimensions support outpatient (Level 1) or intensive outpatient (Level 2) care. The ASAM assessment, not the diagnosis alone, drives the placement.
body.title: Same Diagnosis, Different Levels

children.text: Why the ASAM Criteria Matter

The ASAM Criteria matter because they bring consistency, clinical rigor, and accountability to a field that long lacked them. They give clinicians a common language for placement, give patients a better chance of landing in care that fits their needs, and give payers an objective basis for authorizing treatment.

Their adoption by state Medicaid agencies and commercial insurers also reflects a broader shift toward treating addiction like other chronic medical conditions — with standardized assessment, a defined continuum of care, and movement between levels based on clinical status. The next lesson examines two of the most important specific settings on this continuum: opioid treatment programs and office-based opioid treatment.

For anyone working in or analyzing addiction treatment, fluency with the six dimensions and the levels of care is foundational. It is the framework that connects "this person has a substance use disorder" to "this is the care they should receive and where."

body.message: ASAM levels are not permanent labels. The criteria are designed for patients to step up or step down along the continuum as repeat assessments of the six dimensions show their needs changing — not for fixed, one-size-fits-all program lengths.

children.text: How Common Are Behavioral Health Conditions?

"Behavioral health" is an umbrella term that covers both mental health conditions — such as depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia — and substance use disorders involving alcohol, opioids, and other drugs. These conditions are not rare or marginal. They are among the most common health problems Americans face, touching tens of millions of households every single year.

The federal government measures this burden each year through the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), conducted by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA). In 2023, an estimated 58.7 million adults aged 18 or older — 22.8%, or roughly one in five — experienced any mental illness in the past year. Of those, 14.6 million adults (5.7%) had a serious mental illness, meaning a condition that substantially interfered with major life activities.

Substance use disorders are nearly as widespread. Among people aged 12 or older, 48.5 million had a substance use disorder in 2023. Behavioral health conditions are, in short, a normal part of the population’s health profile — not an edge case the health system can treat as optional.
Behavioral health = mental health conditions + substance use disorders. In 2023, about 1 in 5 U.S. adults had any mental illness, and 48.5 million people aged 12+ had a substance use disorder.

children.text: The Treatment Gap: Prevalence Is Only Half the Story

High prevalence would matter less if most people who needed care received it. They do not. The defining feature of the U.S. behavioral health system is a large and persistent treatment gap — the distance between the number of people who have a condition and the number who actually get treated for it.

Of the 58.7 million adults with any mental illness in 2023, 27.1 million did not receive any mental health treatment in the past year — roughly 46% went untreated. The gap is even more dramatic for substance use: of the 48.5 million people aged 12 or older with a substance use disorder, only 15.6% (about 7.1 million) received any substance use treatment, leaving 85.4% — more than 41 million people — without care.

These gaps are not driven by a single cause. Surveys consistently identify cost, lack of insurance coverage, stigma, not knowing where to go, workforce shortages, and a belief that one should handle problems alone. Understanding behavioral health burden therefore means looking past raw prevalence to the systemic failure to connect people with effective treatment.

children.text: The Human Toll: Mortality and Lost Years of Life

Untreated behavioral health conditions are lethal. In 2023, more than 49,000 people in the United States died by suicide. Suicide was the 11th leading cause of death overall that year, but it ranked as the second leading cause of death for Americans aged 10–14, 15–24, and 25–44 — meaning that for young and working-age people, few things kill more.

The toll extends far beyond suicide. People living with serious mental illness die substantially earlier than the general population — estimates commonly range from roughly 10 to more than 20 years of life lost. Critically, the majority of these excess deaths are not from the psychiatric condition itself but from preventable physical illnesses such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and cancer, compounded by smoking, limited access to medical care, and the side effects of some medications.

This is why behavioral and physical health cannot be treated as separate problems. A person with schizophrenia is far more likely to die of a heart attack that went unmanaged than of anything directly psychiatric. The burden of behavioral health is, in large part, a burden of fragmented care — a theme that runs through the rest of this course.

When Conditions Overlap: Co-Occurring Disorders

Mental health conditions and substance use disorders frequently travel together. In 2023, an estimated 20.4 million adults had a mental illness co-occurring with a substance use disorder in the past year, and 6.8 million had a serious mental illness alongside a substance use disorder.

Co-occurring disorders (sometimes called "dual diagnosis") are clinically harder to treat and historically have fallen between the cracks of a system that separated mental health care from addiction care. A person seeking help for depression and an alcohol use disorder might once have been told to "get sober first" before addressing the depression — a sequencing that often left both conditions untreated.

Modern best practice is integrated treatment that addresses both conditions at the same time, in the same setting, by a coordinated team. The scale of co-occurrence — more than 20 million adults — is one of the strongest arguments for the integration models this course explores.

children.text: The Economic Burden

Beyond the human cost, behavioral health conditions impose an enormous economic burden. A 2024 study by economists affiliated with Yale and the National Bureau of Economic Research estimated that mental illness costs the U.S. economy roughly $282 billion every year — a drag comparable in size to an average economic recession.

That figure is not mostly hospital bills. The study attributed about $83 billion to the direct costs of treatment, roughly $10 billion to years of life lost to suicide, and the largest share — about $189 billion — to reduced work productivity. In other words, the cost of untreated and undertreated behavioral illness shows up in lost wages, missed work, and diminished output far more than in clinical spending.

This matters for policy. If most of the economic damage comes from lost productivity rather than treatment, then investing in access to effective care is not simply a cost — it can be an investment that pays back through healthier, more productive people. The economics reinforce the clinical case for closing the treatment gap.

children.text: You Cannot Manage the Body Without the Mind

A population health program focused only on physical disease will hit a wall, because mental and physical health are deeply intertwined. Depression makes diabetes harder to control; anxiety drives ER use; serious mental illness shortens lifespan dramatically, largely through untreated physical disease. The chronic-disease programs from the last two lessons cannot fully succeed without addressing behavioral health.

The comorbidity is the rule, not the exception. A patient with diabetes, hypertension, and depression is a common population health profile — and the depression is not a side issue. Untreated depression undermines the self-management (diet, activity, medication adherence) that diabetes and hypertension control depend on. Treating the behavioral health condition often improves the physical ones, and vice versa.

Yet behavioral health has historically been siloed — separated from medical care by different systems, providers, payment, and even buildings. Patients fall through the gap between them. Behavioral health integration is the work of closing that gap, bringing mental health care into the medical setting where most patients are actually seen. It is essential infrastructure for population health.

Mental and physical health are inseparable: untreated depression undermines chronic-disease self-management, and behavioral health has historically been siloed from medical care. Integration brings mental health care into the medical setting where patients are actually seen.
The Collaborative Care Model

The gold-standard approach to behavioral health integration is the Collaborative Care Model (CoCM), developed at the University of Washington in the 1990s. It is, by a wide margin, the most evidence-backed integration model: more than 90 randomized controlled trials, beginning with the landmark IMPACT trial published in 2002, have shown it more effective than usual care for depression, anxiety, and other conditions.

CoCM works through a defined three-role team. The primary care provider (PCP) leads overall care and prescribes. A behavioral health care manager (typically a licensed clinician) does the hands-on work — regular check-ins, brief evidence-based interventions, tracking the patient, and coordinating. And a psychiatric consultant provides expert guidance, reviewing the caseload with the care manager and advising on treatment, without needing to see every patient directly. This structure lets one psychiatrist effectively support a large population — solving the chronic shortage of psychiatric access.

Note how purely this is a population health model: it is team-based (not physician-only), it operates on a caseload/registry, the scarce specialist (psychiatrist) is leveraged across many patients via consultation, and it lives inside primary care where patients already are. CoCM is population health applied to mental health.

body.title: The Collaborative Care Team

children.text: Measurement-Based Care: Treat to Target

A defining principle of CoCM — and a direct bridge to the quality-measurement and care-gap themes of this curriculum — is measurement-based care. Rather than treating depression by impression, CoCM uses a validated, quantitative measure to track each patient and treat toward a specific goal, just as a diabetes program treats toward an A1c target.

The standard tool for depression is the PHQ-9, a nine-item questionnaire scored 0 to 27. The care manager administers it at regular intervals, and the team treats "to target" — for example, aiming for a PHQ-9 score of 10 or lower, or a 50 percent reduction. If a patient is not improving on the measure, the team escalates: adjusts medication (with psychiatric-consultant input), changes the intervention, or intensifies follow-up. The number drives the action.

This is profound because it brings the rigor of chronic-disease management to mental health. Just as you would not manage hypertension without measuring blood pressure, CoCM does not manage depression without measuring symptoms — and it does not accept "no improvement" passively. Measurement-based, treat-to-target care is a large part of why CoCM outperforms usual care: it systematically catches and acts on patients who are not getting better.

body.content:
A primary care patient screens positive for depression and is enrolled in collaborative care. The behavioral health care manager administers the PHQ-9 at baseline (score 18, moderately severe) and re-measures every few weeks.
When the score has not improved after several weeks, the care manager reviews the case with the psychiatric consultant, who recommends a medication change. The team tracks the PHQ-9 down toward the target (≤10) — actively escalating rather than waiting, which is exactly why measurement-based collaborative care beats usual care.
body.title: PHQ-9 Treat-to-Target in Action

children.text: Making It Sustainable: Payment

A model is only sustainable if it can be paid for, and a major barrier to behavioral health integration was historically the lack of reimbursement for the care-manager and consultation work that happens outside a face-to-face visit. CMS addressed this by creating specific billing codes for the Collaborative Care Model.

The CoCM codes — CPT 99492 (initial month, ~70 minutes), 99493 (subsequent month), and 99494 (additional time), plus G2214 — let a practice bill for the time the behavioral health care manager and psychiatric consultant spend managing a patient in coordination with the billing provider. This created a financial pathway for the team-based, between-visit work that CoCM depends on.

This matters for population health generally: the proactive, team-based, between-visit work that defines the whole field (care management, monitoring, coordination) only scales when there is a way to pay for it. The CoCM codes are one example of payment evolving to support population health activities; chronic care management (CCM) and remote monitoring (RPM) codes are others. Where payment follows, programs become sustainable rather than grant-dependent pilots.

A real-world note: a single complex patient — say, with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and depression — may be served by several of these programs at once (collaborative care for the depression, chronic care management and remote monitoring for the physical conditions), all coordinated in one care plan. Integration is what keeps that from being three disconnected efforts.
Why Integration Is Population Health

Behavioral health integration is not a niche add-on to population health — it is core to it, for three reasons. First, the comorbidity: behavioral health conditions cluster with and worsen the expensive physical conditions population health targets, so ignoring them caps how much a program can achieve. Second, the cost: patients with untreated behavioral health conditions are disproportionately high utilizers, exactly the high-risk group risk stratification surfaces.

Third, the model fit: CoCM is population health in microcosm — registry-based, team-based, measurement-driven, specialist-leveraged, embedded in primary care, and increasingly payable. Everything this course teaches about managing physical chronic disease applies to behavioral health through CoCM, and the two reinforce each other when managed together.

The practical takeaway is that a serious population health program must integrate behavioral health from the start — screening for depression and anxiety as routinely as it checks blood pressure, building a collaborative care team, treating to target with validated measures, and billing the available codes to sustain it. The next module turns from disease-specific programs to the care management roles and models that deliver all of this work across conditions.

body.message: Managing physical chronic disease while ignoring co-occurring depression or anxiety caps results, because untreated behavioral health undermines self-management and drives utilization. The evidence-based fix is integration — the Collaborative Care Model with measurement-based, treat-to-target care embedded in primary care — not referring patients off to a disconnected mental health silo.

children.text: Why How We Pay Shapes the Care We Get

Health care follows the money. The way behavioral health services are paid for determines, more than almost anything else, what care actually gets delivered — and for decades the dominant payment method has worked against good behavioral health care. Understanding payment is therefore essential to understanding why integration and access remain so hard, even when the clinical models exist.

The traditional method is fee-for-service: a provider bills for each discrete, face-to-face service and is paid per unit. Fee-for-service rewards volume — more visits, more billable procedures — but it does not pay for many of the activities that make behavioral health care effective: care coordination, case management, peer support, crisis response, and the between-visit follow-up that keeps patients engaged. Those activities are often uncompensated or undercompensated.

The result is a system that structurally underinvests in exactly the services people with behavioral health conditions need most. This lesson examines how value-based payment aims to fix that, and looks at the leading concrete example: the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic.

Fee-for-service pays per face-to-face service and rewards volume — but it underpays for care coordination, case management, peer support, and crisis response, the very activities that make behavioral health care work.
Fee-for-Service vs. Value-Based Payment

Value-based payment (VBP) is the broad alternative to fee-for-service. Instead of paying for the volume of services, value-based models tie payment to the value of care — its quality, outcomes, and total cost. Value-based payment can take many forms, from bonuses for hitting quality targets, to bundled payments for an episode of care, to capitation (a fixed amount per patient per month regardless of the number of visits).

The appeal for behavioral health is direct: if a clinic is paid for keeping a population healthy rather than for each billable visit, it gains the flexibility — and the financial incentive — to invest in care coordination, follow-up, and team-based care that fee-for-service never rewarded. Value-based payment aligns the money with the goal of actually helping patients improve.

But behavioral health has lagged the rest of medicine in adopting value-based payment. Structural barriers — fragmented funding streams, the lack of a single dominant payer, limited data infrastructure, and small provider organizations without the capital to take on financial risk — have all slowed the shift. Behavioral health providers often lack the resources that large hospital systems used to move into value-based contracts.

children.text: The CCBHC Model: A Payment-Driven Reform

The most important behavioral health payment reform of the past decade is the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic (CCBHC) model. It was created by Section 223 of the Protecting Access to Medicare Act of 2014 — based on the Excellence in Mental Health Act — and launched as an eight-state Medicaid demonstration that began operating in 2017.

The defining feature of a CCBHC is its payment method: instead of fee-for-service, CCBHCs are reimbursed through a Prospective Payment System (PPS) — a rate calculated from the clinic’s actual cost of delivering a required, comprehensive set of services. Critically, that cost basis includes the services fee-for-service neglects: care coordination, case management, peer and family support, and 24/7 crisis response. States can also add quality bonus payments, layering a value-based incentive on top of the cost-based rate.

In exchange for this enhanced, flexible payment, CCBHCs must meet federal certification standards — including providing a comprehensive range of services (such as crisis services available 24/7, outpatient mental health and substance use treatment, case management, peer supports, and primary care screening) and offering routine outpatient care within 10 business days. The model essentially says: we will pay you adequately to deliver real, comprehensive care, and in return you must actually deliver it.

children.text: A Growing National Model

The CCBHC model has expanded well beyond the original eight states. The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act created a pathway to add new states to the Medicaid demonstration on a recurring basis, and in June 2024 the federal government announced ten additional states joining the demonstration, including Vermont. Many other states have adopted the model outside the formal demonstration through Medicaid state plan amendments or grants.

Evidence and policy momentum have both grown: expansion of CCBHCs has been associated with increased access to mental health and substance use care, and the model enjoys notable bipartisan support — relatively rare in health policy. Its combination of guaranteed comprehensive services and adequate, flexible payment has made it a leading template for reforming the behavioral health safety net.

Vermont’s inclusion in the 2024 cohort connects this national reform to the state-specific systems covered next in this course. Vermont already has a distinctive community behavioral health infrastructure (its Designated Agencies) and opioid treatment system (Hub-and-Spoke); CCBHC funding is a new layer atop that foundation.

The recurring expansion, enabled by the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, reflects strong bipartisan support for paying behavioral health clinics for comprehensive, coordinated care rather than fee-for-service volume.

children.text: Payment Reform as the Engine of Better Care

The thread connecting this lesson to the rest of the course is that good clinical models need good payment models to survive. The Collaborative Care Model needed Medicare billing codes to spread. Integrated care needs payment for coordination. And comprehensive community behavioral health needs something like the CCBHC prospective payment to fund the services fee-for-service ignores.

Value-based payment is not a panacea — it brings its own challenges around measurement, risk, and the capacity of small providers — and behavioral health still trails the rest of medicine in adopting it. But the direction is clear: aligning payment with outcomes and comprehensive care is widely seen as essential to closing the behavioral health treatment gap.

For anyone analyzing behavioral health policy, the key question to ask of any reform is: how does it pay for the care, and does that payment reward the activities that actually help patients? Payment design is not a back-office detail — it is one of the most powerful levers for improving behavioral health care.

Good clinical models need good payment models to survive. Fee-for-service starves coordination and crisis care; value-based and prospective payment are how the system learns to fund what actually works.

children.text: Where Genomic Knowledge Comes From

Every clinical genomics application in this course — interpreting a variant, calculating a risk, matching a drug — depends on knowledge that had to be discovered somewhere. That somewhere is, increasingly, the biobank. Biobanks are the engine of population genomic research, the resource that turns raw human genetic variation into the knowledge clinicians use. Understanding them explains where genomic medicine's evidence base actually comes from.

A biobank is a large, secure repository of biological samples (like blood and saliva) from volunteer participants who consented to donate them for research, along with the genomic data derived from those samples and — crucially — linked to the participants' health records, lifestyle data, and environmental exposures. It is the combination that gives biobanks their power: genomes connected to real health outcomes across large populations.

This linkage is what enables discovery. With a genome alone, you cannot learn what a variant does; with hundreds of thousands of genomes linked to lifelong health data, patterns emerge — which variants associate with which diseases, drug responses, and traits. Biobanks are how the field moves from individual sequences to generalizable knowledge.

A biobank is a large repository of consented biological samples and genomic data, linked to participants' health, lifestyle, and environmental data. That linkage of genomes to real outcomes at population scale is what generates the knowledge clinical genomics depends on.
The Major Biobanks

A handful of national biobanks dominate the landscape, each holding genomic and health data on hundreds of thousands of people. The UK Biobank is a landmark — about 500,000 participants with whole-genome sequence data plus more than 10,000 variables including imaging, physical measurements, activity tracking, and lifestyle questionnaires, all linked to health records. It has become a globally used resource powering thousands of studies.

In the United States, the NIH All of Us Research Program has enrolled over 500,000 participants and is generating clinical-grade whole-genome sequence data. Internationally, programs like Singapore's PRECISE, Biobank Japan, and Korea's National Project of Bio-Big Data are building comparable resources. Together these initiatives are generating unprecedented volumes of high-resolution genomic data integrated with deep clinical and environmental information.

A critical difference between them is diversity, which foreshadows a major equity issue. UK Biobank participants are roughly 88 percent white — even somewhat over-representing white participants relative to the UK population. All of Us, by explicit design, prioritizes recruiting from populations historically underrepresented in genomic research. This matters enormously because genomic knowledge derived from a non-diverse cohort applies less well to everyone else — the foundation of the "diversity deficit" the equity lessons address.

children.text: What Biobanks Discover: GWAS and Polygenic Risk

The signature discovery method enabled by biobanks is the genome-wide association study (GWAS). A GWAS scans the genomes of large numbers of people, comparing those with a condition (or trait) to those without, to find genetic variants statistically associated with it. With biobank-scale data, GWAS have identified hundreds of thousands of variant-trait associations across virtually every common disease.

These associations feed a powerful tool: the polygenic risk score (PRS). Most common diseases (heart disease, diabetes, many cancers) are not caused by a single gene but by the combined small effects of many variants. A PRS sums up the effects of those many variants into a single score estimating a person's genetic predisposition to a condition — fundamentally different from the single-gene, high-penetrance variants of the hereditary-conditions lesson.

Polygenic risk scores are an emerging frontier of precision medicine — potentially identifying people at elevated risk for common diseases before symptoms, enabling earlier prevention. But they carry serious caveats: they are probabilistic (a high score is elevated risk, not destiny), their communication to patients is challenging, and — critically — they perform far worse in populations underrepresented in the biobanks they were derived from. A PRS built mostly on European-ancestry data is less accurate for everyone else, which is exactly why biobank diversity matters so much.

body.content:
Researchers run a genome-wide association study across a biobank of hundreds of thousands of people, finding the many variants associated with coronary heart disease. They combine those variants' effects into a polygenic risk score.
A person's PRS can then estimate their genetic predisposition to heart disease, potentially flagging high-risk individuals for earlier prevention. But because the underlying GWAS was conducted mostly in European-ancestry participants, the score is markedly less accurate for people of other ancestries — a direct consequence of biobank composition.

children.text: Consent and the Ethics of Biobanking

Biobanks raise distinctive ethical challenges, starting with consent. Because biobank data is used for countless future studies that cannot all be specified in advance, participants typically sign "broad consent" — agreeing to let their samples and data be used for a wide range of future research purposes, rather than consenting to each specific study. This enables the open-ended discovery biobanks are built for.

Broad consent is ethically contested. It trades the specificity of traditional informed consent (where you know exactly what you are agreeing to) for the practical flexibility research needs. Critics note that biobank consent documents can frame research narrowly (in terms of disease and treatment) while obscuring the full range of lawful uses — raising questions about whether participants truly understand what they agreed to. Maintaining public trust requires transparency about how data is actually used.

Other ethical questions include return of results (if a biobank discovers something clinically important about a participant, does it tell them? — practices vary), data governance and privacy (these are vast repositories of the most personal data imaginable), and benefit sharing (do participants and their communities benefit from discoveries made with their data?). These connect directly to the next lessons on genetic privacy law (GINA) and consent and equity — biobanks are where many of those issues become concrete at scale.

body.message: Biobank participants typically give "broad consent" for unspecified future research, since the studies cannot all be known in advance. This enables open-ended discovery but means participants do not know exactly how their data will be used — and consent documents can obscure the full range of uses. Maintaining trust depends on transparency, and the model raises ongoing questions about return of results and benefit sharing.
body.title: Broad Consent Trades Specificity for Flexibility

children.text: Why Biobanks Matter for Clinical Genomics

Biobanks close the loop of clinical genomics. The interpretation bottleneck from earlier lessons — knowing what a variant means — is solved largely by biobank-scale data: a variant seen across hundreds of thousands of people with known health outcomes becomes interpretable (recall the GA4GH data-sharing lesson, which exists partly to pool exactly this kind of data). Biobanks are the source of the knowledge that makes individual genomic results meaningful.

They are also where the future of precision medicine is being built — polygenic risk scores for common diseases, new drug-gene associations, novel disease genes, and the multi-omics research of a later lesson. The clinical applications of tomorrow are being discovered in the biobanks of today. And they make vivid the equity stakes: because discovery happens in these cohorts, who is in them determines who benefits from the resulting knowledge.

The takeaway is that clinical genomics rests on a research foundation, and biobanks are that foundation. They generate the evidence, raise the central ethical questions of consent and trust, and embody the diversity problem that determines whether genomic medicine serves everyone or only the populations who were studied. The next two lessons take up the policy and ethics — genetic privacy and discrimination protections (GINA), and consent and equity — that the rise of biobanks and clinical genomics makes urgent.

children.text: Who Is Actually Responsible When a Hospital’s Finances Fail?

When a hospital makes a disastrous financial decision — overbuilds, mismanages its debt, or quietly slides toward insolvency — the question of accountability eventually lands in one place: the board of directors. Hospital executives run the institution day to day, but the board holds ultimate responsibility for its financial health and its faithfulness to its mission. Understanding board financial oversight is understanding the last line of defense in hospital finance, and the legal duties that make board service a serious obligation rather than an honorary title.

This responsibility is rooted in the concept of fiduciary duty — the legal obligation to act in the best interest of the organization and the community it serves. For the governing board of a nonprofit hospital, the fundamental fiduciary duty is to ensure the organization’s fidelity to its core mission, and all board members are liable and accountable for their actions. A board member who rubber-stamps management without genuine scrutiny is not fulfilling a ceremonial role poorly; they are breaching a legal duty.

For nonprofit hospitals especially, this oversight carries public weight. These organizations hold billions in tax-exempt assets and enjoy tax exemptions justified by their community benefit. The board is the body that holds the institution to that bargain — ensuring the hospital is financially sound enough to survive and mission-driven enough to deserve its privileged status. Board financial oversight sits at the intersection of finance, law, and public trust.

Key Concept: A hospital board holds ultimate fiduciary responsibility for the organization’s financial health and mission. Fiduciary duty — the legal obligation to act in the organization’s best interest — makes board members accountable and liable for their oversight, not merely advisory.
The Three Fiduciary Duties

Fiduciary duty is traditionally broken into three components, and every board financial decision can be tested against them. The duty of care requires board members to exercise reasonable care and diligence — to stay informed and understand the financial reports, budgets, strategic initiatives, and risks that materially affect the organization, and to make decisions thoughtfully rather than carelessly. A director who never reads the financials or asks a probing question has failed the duty of care regardless of good intentions.

The duty of loyalty requires board members to put the organization’s interests ahead of their own — avoiding conflicts of interest and never using their position for personal gain. This is why hospitals require conflict-of-interest policies and disclosures: a board member who steers a contract to their own company, even if the deal seems fair, violates the duty of loyalty. The duty of obedience requires the board to ensure the organization stays faithful to its mission and complies with the law, including the obligations that underpin its tax-exempt status.

Loyalty: self-dealing or undisclosed conflicts
Obedience: straying from mission or breaching legal/tax obligations

children.text: The Board’s Core Financial Responsibilities

Fiduciary duty translates into a concrete set of financial responsibilities. A hospital board has six core financial duties: to specify financial objectives, to review and align management’s financial plan with those objectives, to enhance the organization’s creditworthiness, to ensure capital is effectively allocated, to monitor financial performance, and to verify the financial statements. Notice how these map onto earlier lessons — creditworthiness ties to the debt-financing and bond-rating material, and capital allocation to the capital-planning material. The board is the body that governs all of it.

The most important ongoing duty is monitoring financial performance — and here the duty of care has a sharp, practical edge. Genuine oversight requires reviewing actual financial statements, not summaries or verbal updates: the treasurer’s report should always include the current balance sheet and income statement so the board can see the institution’s true position. A board that accepts a reassuring slide saying "finances are fine" has not exercised oversight; one that reviews the statements, tracks the ratios from Module 1, and questions variances has.

children.text: The Tools of Oversight: Committees, Audits, and Form 990

Boards cannot exercise oversight on instinct; they rely on structures and documents. The most important structure is the audit committee — and best practice, drawn from the principles of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, holds that if a tax-exempt hospital lacks a separate audit committee, it should establish one composed of members completely independent from management who receive no consulting or advisory fees. The audit committee oversees independent external audits, internal controls, and risk, providing the board an objective check on management’s financial reporting. Other Sarbanes-Oxley-inspired practices include auditor independence (periodic rotation), whistleblower protection, and document-retention policies.

The central oversight document for a nonprofit hospital is the IRS Form 990, the annual information return that publicly discloses the organization’s finances, governance, and compensation. Board review of the Form 990 before filing has long been a best practice — and the IRS itself has concluded that nonprofits with a board review process are more likely to be in compliance with tax laws. For hospitals specifically, Schedule H reports the Section 501(r) policies covered earlier: community health needs assessments, financial assistance, emergency care, and billing and collection practices. The 990 is where the board’s stewardship of the tax-exempt bargain becomes public and auditable.

Modern boards increasingly rely on dashboards and reporting tools that present real-time financial and compliance data, letting them track the key ratios and metrics continuously rather than quarterly. But tools do not replace judgment. The IRS scrutiny of nonprofit hospitals’ tax-exempt status has intensified, and a board that cannot demonstrate active, documented oversight of both financial performance and community-benefit obligations exposes the institution to real regulatory and reputational risk.
Why Governance Determines Destiny

It is tempting to treat board governance as a formality far removed from the real work of running a hospital. The evidence says otherwise: board configuration and oversight practices are associated with hospital financial performance. Boards that include financial expertise, meet regularly, review actual statements, maintain independent audit committees, and conduct honest self-assessments tend to govern stronger institutions. Weak boards — disengaged, conflicted, or financially illiterate — preside over weaker ones. Governance is not separate from finance; it is the mechanism that steers it.

body.analogy: A hospital board is like the flight crew’s oversight of an aircraft. Management flies the plane day to day, but the board is responsible for ensuring the instruments are accurate, the fuel reserves are adequate, the route is sound, and the airline’s rules and the law are followed. A board that simply trusts the pilot and never checks the gauges is not being polite — it is abdicating the very responsibility that justifies its existence, and everyone on board bears the consequences.

children.text: The duties also create a structural tension the board must manage: the same body responsible for financial soundness is responsible for fidelity to a charitable mission, and these can pull against each other. A board fixated only on margins may neglect community benefit and the duty of obedience; a board fixated only on mission may let the institution slide toward insolvency, failing the duty of care. Good board financial oversight holds both — keeping the hospital financially viable precisely so it can fulfill its mission, recognizing that an insolvent hospital serves no one.

This is why board financial oversight is the right capstone for the governance side of hospital finance. Every concept in this course — margins and ratios, payer mix, cost accounting, capital and debt, value-based payment — ultimately rolls up to a board that must understand it well enough to govern it. The board does not need to be expert in every detail, but it must be diligent enough to ask the right questions, independent enough to get honest answers, and loyal enough to act on them in the organization’s and community’s interest. When hospital finance fails, it is most often because that oversight failed first.

Fiduciary duty has three components: the duty of care (stay informed and decide diligently), the duty of loyalty (avoid conflicts of interest and self-dealing), and the duty of obedience (uphold the mission and comply with the law).
Good intentions do not satisfy fiduciary duty — these are legal standards measured by conduct, so failing to review actual financials or disclose a conflict is a breach regardless of sincerity.

Genuine oversight requires reviewing actual financial statements (balance sheet and income statement in the treasurer’s report), not summaries or verbal reassurances.

children.text: From Capability to Care

This course has covered what genomic medicine can do — diagnose rare disease, predict risk, guide drug choice, screen newborns and prospective parents, and push toward a multi-omics, AI-assisted future. But capability is not the same as care. A health system can have access to all of this technology and still fail to deliver it to patients, because the hard part of genomic medicine is not the science — it is the implementation. This final lesson is about turning genomic capability into a functioning clinical program.

This matters because the gap between what genomics can do and what most patients actually receive remains large. The technology has advanced faster than health systems' ability to use it. Building a precision-medicine program means solving a set of practical problems — workflow, the electronic health record, workforce, reimbursement, and equity — that determine whether genomic medicine reaches real patients or stays trapped in research and specialty centers.

Encouragingly, the field is maturing: by 2026, a large majority of surveyed health systems (around 76 percent) report having formal precision-medicine programs. But building one well requires understanding the specific barriers and how leading programs overcome them. This lesson synthesizes the course into the practical question every health-system leader faces: how do we actually do this?

Capability is not care — a health system can have all the genomic technology and still fail to deliver it. The hard part of genomic medicine is implementation: workflow, EHR integration, workforce, reimbursement, and equity. By 2026 ~76% of surveyed health systems report formal precision-medicine programs.
The Electronic Health Record Problem

A foundational and underappreciated barrier is the electronic health record. Genomic results are useless if clinicians cannot find and act on them at the point of care. Yet in most health systems, genomic data is poorly integrated: results are often stored as static PDF reports that a clinician must hunt for, rendering them effectively invisible during a time-pressured visit. A cancer-risk variant buried in a PDF from two years ago does no good if the physician never sees it when it matters.

The technical roots of this problem connect directly to the interoperability themes of the broader HTR curriculum: genomic data does not flow cleanly across systems, and there is semantic misalignment across standards like HL7 FHIR and SNOMED CT. The fragmentation that plagues health-data exchange generally is especially acute for genomic data, which is voluminous, complex, and not well represented in legacy EHR structures. Solving genomic care requires solving genomic data integration.

The strategic response is clinical decision support (CDS) — building genomic information into the EHR so that it actively surfaces at the right moment. Rather than expecting a clinician to remember a patient's pharmacogenomic profile, a well-designed system alerts the prescriber automatically when they order a relevant drug (recall the pharmacogenomics lesson). This makes genomic data actionable in the workflow rather than buried in it, and it is a central focus of leading programs precisely because it determines whether genomic data changes care at all.

children.text: Workforce and Workflow

The second major barrier is the workforce. Genomic medicine done well depends on expert interpretation and counseling, but the availability of genetic testing has far outstripped the supply of trained genetic counselors and genetics specialists. There are simply not enough experts to personally counsel every patient who could benefit from genomic testing. This bottleneck is structural — you cannot train genetic counselors fast enough to meet the demand that cheap sequencing has created.

Programs address this in several ways. Clinical decision support (again) helps non-specialist clinicians interpret and act on genomic results without needing a geneticist for every case. Education raises the genomic literacy of primary-care and specialist physicians (the purpose of courses like this one). And new care models — pharmacist-led pharmacogenomics services, telegenetics, and triage systems that route the complex cases to scarce specialists while handling routine results otherwise — extend limited expertise across more patients. The goal is to scale genomic expertise without requiring a specialist in every room.

Workflow integration ties this together. Genomic medicine fails when it is bolted onto clinical practice as extra work; it succeeds when it is built into existing workflows so that the right information and the right action happen at the right time without heroic effort from busy clinicians. The three recurring barriers that stall programs — cost, lack of reimbursement, and workflow complexity — are all, at root, about fitting genomics into the realities of clinical practice rather than expecting practice to bend around genomics.

body.message: Cheap sequencing has created demand that the supply of genetic counselors and geneticists cannot meet — you cannot train specialists fast enough. Programs scale expertise through clinical decision support (so non-specialists can act), clinician education, and new care models (pharmacist-led PGx, telegenetics, triage). Genomic medicine succeeds when built into existing workflows, not bolted on as extra work for busy clinicians.
body.title: Testing Has Outstripped the Genetics Workforce

children.text: Reimbursement, Value, and Where to Start

The third barrier is economic: cost and reimbursement. Genomic testing and the staff time to explain it cost money, and reimbursement has historically lagged, partly due to demands for proof of clinical utility. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem — payers want evidence of value before paying, but generating that evidence requires doing the testing. Sustainable programs must navigate the reimbursement landscape and build the economic case deliberately.

The good news is that the economic evidence is increasingly favorable, especially for pharmacogenomics. Cost-effectiveness analyses of pharmacogenomic clinical decision support have found it cost-effective — one analysis reported an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of about $39,477 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY), well under the common $100,000/QALY willingness-to-pay threshold. Many CPIC-guided pharmacogenomic interventions are cost-effective or even cost-saving by avoiding adverse drug reactions and ineffective prescriptions. This is why pharmacogenomics is often where health systems start.

Indeed, the practical wisdom for building a program is to start where the value is clearest and the workflow simplest. Leading programs prioritize high-impact, well-evidenced applications first — pharmacogenomics (immediate prescribing impact, growing evidence base, CDS-friendly), oncology (where genomic testing is already standard of care), and maternal-fetal/reproductive health. Starting with focused, high-value use cases builds the infrastructure, evidence, and clinician confidence to expand, rather than trying to do everything at once. Begin narrow and prove value, then broaden.

body.content:
A health system launching precision medicine does not begin by sequencing everyone. It starts with pharmacogenomics: building clinical decision support so that when a clinician prescribes a drug with a known gene-drug interaction, the system automatically flags the patient's relevant genetic result.
This is high-value (preventing adverse drug reactions), evidence-backed (cost-effective at roughly $39,477/QALY, often cost-saving), and workflow-friendly (the alert fires at the moment of prescribing). Succeeding here builds the EHR infrastructure, clinician trust, and economic case to expand into oncology, reproductive health, and beyond. Start narrow; prove value; broaden.
body.title: Where a Program Starts

children.text: Bringing It All Together

Building a precision-medicine program is the synthesis of everything in this course. The technical lessons (sequencing, variant interpretation, pharmacogenomics, risk) define the capabilities. The ethics-and-policy lessons (consent, secondary findings, GINA and privacy, equity) define the framework within which those capabilities must operate. The population-screening lessons (newborn screening, carrier screening) model genomics at scale. And the frontier lessons (multi-omics, AI) point to where the program must be ready to grow. A real program weaves all of these together into something that actually reaches patients.

Above all, equity must be designed in, not bolted on. The diversity deficit means genomic tools work less well for underrepresented populations; a program that ignores this will deliver worse care to exactly the patients already facing disparities. Responsible program-building means actively considering who the program serves, ensuring access across populations, interpreting results with appropriate caution where the evidence base is thin, and not letting AI and automation silently amplify existing biases. A precision-medicine program that widens disparities is a failure, however advanced its technology.

The closing message of this course is that genomic medicine is no longer a future promise — it is a present reality that health systems can and increasingly do deliver. But delivering it well requires more than technology. It requires integrating genomic data into the EHR so it is actionable, scaling expertise through decision support and education, building the economic and reimbursement case starting with high-value applications, and designing for equity throughout. The clinicians and leaders who understand both the science and the implementation are the ones who will turn the extraordinary capabilities of genomics into better care for real patients. That is the work — and you are now equipped to do it.

children.text: Reading the Evidence: What "Success" Means in Bundled Payment Research

Evaluating bundled payment programs is harder than it appears. The central question — "do bundles save money and improve care?" — demands three separate answers: Do they reduce total episode spending? Do they reduce spending in a way that generates net savings to Medicare after reconciliation payments? And do they maintain or improve the quality of care delivered? These are distinct tests, and a program can pass one while failing another. Most rigorous research now distinguishes between gross episode savings (reductions in FFS claims) and net Medicare savings (what remains after reconciliation bonuses are subtracted).

The methodological challenge is defining the counterfactual. What would those patients have cost if the bundle had never existed? Researchers typically compare bundle participants to matched comparison hospitals or use difference-in-differences designs that control for pre-existing trends. Both approaches can be confounded by the selection effect: providers who voluntarily enter bundled payment programs are not a random sample — they tend to be larger, more integrated, and already more cost-efficient than non-participants. Any evaluation that does not rigorously account for this self-selection risk will overstate the program's causal impact.

With those caveats in mind, the body of evidence on bundled payments is substantial and growing. The strongest evidence comes from surgical episodes — joint replacements, spine procedures, cardiac procedures — where episode costs are large, post-acute care is a known driver of variation, and the bundle gives providers a clear lever to pull. Evidence for medical episodes (pneumonia, heart failure, sepsis) is much weaker and in some cases negative, reflecting the inherent difficulty of coordinating care for patients with complex, unpredictable trajectories.

Net Medicare savings = gross episode spending reduction minus reconciliation payments made to participants. A model can achieve gross savings (claims go down) while generating net losses (bonuses paid out exceed the savings). Evaluations that report only gross savings overstate program value to the federal government.
Surgical Episodes: Where Bundles Work Best

The most consistent evidence for bundled payment effectiveness comes from lower-extremity joint replacement — hip and knee arthroplasty. Multiple independent studies evaluating BPCI and the mandatory Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model found that participation was associated with significant reductions in episode spending, driven primarily by shifts in post-acute care utilization: fewer discharges to skilled nursing facilities and inpatient rehabilitation, shorter SNF stays when they do occur, and lower readmission rates.

A landmark NEJM study evaluating the first two years of the CJR mandatory model found statistically significant episode cost reductions without deterioration in mortality, readmission, or patient-reported function. Analyses of BPCI orthopedic episodes found per-episode spending declines averaging roughly $1,166, with the reductions concentrated in SNF costs. Importantly, these quality-neutral cost reductions suggest that prior fee-for-service spending included avoidable post-acute utilization that could be eliminated without harming patients.

Cardiac procedures show similarly strong results. Bundled payment programs for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) have demonstrated cost reductions through shorter ICU stays, earlier extubation protocols, and standardized cardiac rehabilitation pathways. The BPCI program for major cardiac procedures generated savings across participating sites, with the highest-performing hospitals combining aggressive clinical protocol standardization with strong post-discharge follow-up programs.

children.text: Medical Episodes: The Mixed and Negative Evidence

The picture for medical episode bundles — heart failure, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sepsis — is considerably less encouraging. A rigorous study published in JAMA Internal Medicine evaluating BPCI Model 2 participation for heart failure found that hospital participation was not associated with improvement in process-of-care quality measures, nor with reductions in 30-day or 90-day risk-adjusted all-cause mortality or readmission rates. In other words, the bundle had no detectable effect on either cost or quality for this high-volume condition.

Why do medical episodes respond so differently? Several structural factors explain the divergence. First, medical episodes have much higher cost variance — a heart failure patient can cost $8,000 or $80,000 depending on comorbidities and complications that are difficult to predict or control at admission. Surgical episodes have more predictable cost trajectories, making target prices more accurate and financial risk more manageable. Second, post-acute care is a less dominant cost driver for medical episodes, meaning providers have fewer high-leverage levers to pull to reduce spending.

Third, medical episodes require cross-specialty coordination that is structurally harder to achieve. A joint replacement bundle centers on an orthopedic surgeon who acts as the natural care captain. A heart failure bundle involves hospitalists, cardiologists, primary care physicians, pharmacists, and home health agencies — all of whom need to function as a coordinated team across settings they have historically operated in silos. Building those relationships requires organizational trust and shared workflows that take years to develop and are not financially motivated by the bundle alone.

body.content:
A study published in early 2024 analyzing BPCI participation for heart failure episodes found that bundled payment participation was not associated with improved quality performance or outcomes on key measures including 30-day and 90-day readmission and mortality rates. The researchers concluded that bundled payment models may be most effective for surgical and procedural conditions where post-acute care costs are predictable and reducible, rather than complex medical conditions with highly variable trajectories.
This evidence is consistent with CMS's own evaluation findings and has informed the design of subsequent models, which have increasingly focused on high-cost surgical procedure types with clearer care pathways and more concentrated provider accountability.
body.title: BPCI Heart Failure Episode — PubMed Study (2024)

children.text: BPCI Advanced: Evaluation Findings Across Five Model Years

CMS has published multiple annual evaluation reports for BPCI Advanced, providing the most detailed longitudinal evidence available on a voluntary federal bundled payment program. Through Model Year 5 (ending 2022), BPCI Advanced generated approximately $344 million in gross savings — a roughly 4% reduction in episode spending compared to the risk-adjusted target price benchmark. Per-episode spending declined by an average of $1,014. Readmission and mortality rates remained stable, satisfying the quality non-inferiority threshold built into the model.

Participation patterns in BPCI Advanced reveal the selection dynamics that complicate evaluation. The model has consistently attracted high-volume orthopedic and cardiac programs at large academic medical centers and community hospitals with strong surgical volumes. These institutions already invested in care coordination prior to joining the program and were better positioned to achieve savings from day one. The Penn LDI evaluation noted that physician group practice participation in BPCI Advanced was lower than hospital participation, and that future models need to better engage PGPs if savings are to be extended to the physician setting.

The fourth annual CMS evaluation report (2023) confirmed that savings persisted through the later model years but that per-episode savings rates were compressing over time — consistent with the "ratchet effect" where target prices are adjusted downward as participants demonstrate efficiency. High-performing participants reported that maintaining savings required continuous investment in care coordination and protocol improvement, not a one-time transformation. This finding has important implications for program sustainability and the transition from voluntary to mandatory models.

children.text: What Predicts Success in a Bundled Payment Program?

Research consistently identifies a cluster of organizational characteristics that distinguish high-performing bundled payment participants from those who exit or underperform. Surgeon or specialist engagement is the single most consistent predictor of success. When the physician who performs the procedure is an active partner in designing the episode care pathway — not merely a recipient of hospital-imposed protocols — adoption is faster, variance is lower, and cost reductions are more durable. Programs that treat bundled payment as a finance problem rather than a clinical quality initiative rarely succeed.

Strong post-acute networks are the second predictor. High performers develop preferred relationships with a small set of SNFs and home health agencies, share patient-level data with those partners, and create clear discharge criteria that minimize unnecessary institutional post-acute stays. Facilities that discharge patients to a broad, undifferentiated network of post-acute providers lose the ability to standardize care in the 90-day tail of the episode — where cost variation is highest and provider accountability is most diffuse.

Data infrastructure matters more than most institutions anticipate before joining a bundle. Participants need near-real-time visibility into their episode claims to identify which patients are generating outlier costs and why. Providers who wait for quarterly claims reports to understand their performance cannot make mid-episode course corrections. Successful participants invest in analytics platforms that flag high-cost patterns early — unexpected readmissions, unusually long SNF stays, duplicate imaging — so care managers can intervene before costs accumulate beyond the target.
