children.text: Limitations and Open Questions in the Field

Despite the growing body of evidence, several important questions remain unresolved. The most significant is generalizability: can the savings demonstrated by self-selected high performers in voluntary programs be replicated across a broader, less-selected population of hospitals forced to participate in mandatory models? Early evidence from the CJR mandatory model is cautiously optimistic — savings were achieved across a heterogeneous set of hospitals — but TEAM's mandatory extension to five episode types beginning in 2026 will provide the most definitive test yet.

Equity concerns are a second open question. Research has found that bundled payment programs may inadvertently disadvantage safety-net hospitals that serve higher proportions of low-income patients with complex social needs. These patients have higher post-acute care needs and face barriers — transportation, housing instability, medication access — that make care coordination harder and episode costs higher. Standard risk adjustment does not fully account for social determinants of health, potentially making target prices systematically under-set for safety-net populations.

The interaction between bundles and other value-based care models is also poorly understood. A hospital simultaneously participating in an ACO and BPCI Advanced for overlapping patient populations faces complex attribution rules and potentially conflicting incentives. CMS has worked to align these models, but providers operating in multiple value-based contracts simultaneously need sophisticated analytics to understand how their performance in one program affects their financial exposure in another. As the value-based care ecosystem matures, managing this portfolio complexity will become a core healthcare administration competency.

body.message: Many news reports and even some policy briefs describe bundled payment "savings" without clarifying whether those figures are gross (before reconciliation payments to providers) or net (after payments). Programs that reduced episode claims but paid out bonuses exceeding the reduction — as was the case in some early BPCI surgical episodes — technically lost money for Medicare even while appearing successful. Always ask: savings to whom, measured how?

result.title: Bundled Payment Evidence: What the Research Shows

children.text: What Is an Episode-Based Bundled Payment?

A bundled payment — also called an episode-based payment — collapses the dozens of separate claims that Medicare or a commercial payer would ordinarily process for a single clinical event into one aggregated target price. Instead of a hospital billing for the inpatient stay, a surgeon billing separately for the procedure, a post-acute facility billing for its days, and a home health agency billing for visits, the payer holds all of those costs up against a single benchmark. If the team delivers the episode for less, providers share in the savings; if spending exceeds the target, they owe the difference back.

The logic is straightforward: fee-for-service rewards doing more — more tests, longer stays, more specialist consults — because each service generates a separate payment. Bundling inverts that incentive. A provider who reduces an unnecessary post-acute day or avoids a preventable readmission keeps part of the savings rather than losing revenue. Quality guardrails prevent providers from cutting corners to hit their target: readmission rates, mortality, and patient-experience scores are tracked, and poor quality can disqualify a participant from receiving any reconciliation payment.

Bundled payments sit in the middle of the value-based care spectrum. They are more aggressive than pay-for-performance bonuses, which layer small incentives onto an otherwise unchanged fee-for-service chassis, but less comprehensive than capitation, which hands a provider a fixed monthly sum to cover all care. Bundles concentrate accountability on a defined clinical episode — a joint replacement, a cardiac procedure, a chemotherapy course — making them easier to attribute to specific providers and easier to price than a full-population capitation arrangement.

An episode of care is a clinically meaningful window of time tied to a specific health event — typically an inpatient anchor stay or a qualifying outpatient procedure, plus a defined follow-up period (most commonly 90 days) during which related care is included in the bundle.

children.text: The Mechanics: How a Bundle Is Structured

Every bundled payment model defines three core elements: the anchor event that starts the clock, the episode window, and the care that is included or excluded. In the CMS Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced) model — the largest ongoing federal voluntary bundled payment program — an episode begins either with an inpatient admission identified by a Medicare Severity-Diagnosis Related Group (MS-DRG) code, called the Anchor Stay, or with a qualifying outpatient procedure in a hospital outpatient department, called the Anchor Procedure. The episode ends 90 days after the patient is discharged or the procedure is completed.

The financial engine is retrospective reconciliation. Medicare continues to pay providers their ordinary fee-for-service claims throughout the episode — nobody waits for a single check. At the end of each six-month performance period, CMS totals all non-excluded Medicare claims for each participant's episodes and compares that aggregate with the pre-set target price. If spending is below the target, the participant earns a reconciliation payment (shared savings). If spending exceeds the target, the participant owes a repayment amount. CMS provides preliminary target prices before each model year begins so participants can plan care-delivery changes in advance.

Target prices are calculated from historical Medicare claims data for that clinical episode type in the participant's market, risk-adjusted for patient complexity, and trended forward with a discount rate (the "haircut") that represents the savings Medicare expects to achieve. The haircut ensures the program generates net savings for the federal government even after reconciliation payments are made to high-performing participants.

body.title: How a BPCI Advanced Episode Flows

children.text: Who Participates and What They Are Accountable For

Under BPCI Advanced, two entity types can participate: acute care hospitals (ACHs) and physician group practices (PGPs). A hospital participating as an ACH is accountable for the full 90-day episode cost for every eligible patient admitted. A PGP participates as an episode initiator — responsible for managing costs during the episode triggered by the group's physicians. This distinction matters: hospitals have more leverage over post-acute placement, while physician groups have more direct influence over care protocols and follow-up intensity.

The 35 BPCI Advanced clinical episodes span eight clinical service line groups: cardiac care, cardiac procedures, gastrointestinal surgery, gastrointestinal care, neurological care, medical and critical care, spinal procedures, and orthopedics. Participants do not have to take on all 35 — they can select the episode types where they have the most clinical volume, existing care-coordination infrastructure, and confidence in their ability to manage costs. This flexibility encourages participation but also creates selection effects: hospitals tend to choose episode types where they already perform well.

Quality measurement is built into the financial settlement. BPCI Advanced tracks Medicare Spending per Beneficiary (MSPB) composite quality scores and requires participants to submit quality data. Low quality scores can reduce or eliminate reconciliation payments, ensuring that cost-cutting does not come at the expense of patient safety. Participants are also encouraged — but not required — to engage post-acute providers (skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies) as downstream episode partners who share in savings and absorb a portion of any penalties.

children.text: The Target Price: How CMS Sets the Benchmark

Setting an accurate target price is the most technically demanding element of any bundled payment program. If the target is too high, providers collect windfall payments without changing behavior. If it is too low, providers lose money on every episode regardless of efficiency gains, and they exit the program. CMS attempts to thread this needle by using three to five years of historical fee-for-service claims for the specific episode type in the participant's region, then applying risk adjustments and a discount that ensures the government retains savings.

The target price methodology for BPCI Advanced uses a blend of national and regional data, adjusted for the case-mix complexity of the participant's patient population using hierarchical condition categories (HCCs). High-severity patients receive higher target prices; straightforward cases receive lower ones. CMS also applies a "stop-loss" and "stop-gain" corridor: no single episode can swing the reconciliation more than a defined dollar cap in either direction, protecting both participants and Medicare from extreme outlier cases.

Because target prices are anchored to historical spending, participants who have already reduced episode costs through prior efficiency work start with a lower baseline — a phenomenon sometimes called the "ratchet effect." As participants reduce costs over time, CMS lowers the target price in subsequent model years, requiring continuous improvement just to maintain savings. This dynamic has led some high-performing participants to exit voluntary programs voluntarily once their baseline is compressed, a structural tension that mandatory models are designed to overcome.

body.analogy: Think of the target price like a par score in golf: it is based on what a skilled player should need to complete the hole, adjusted for the difficulty of the terrain (patient complexity). Finishing under par earns savings; going over means you owe the difference. And once you consistently shoot par, the course committee lowers the expected score next season.

children.text: Care Transformation: What Providers Actually Change

The practical care changes driven by bundled payments cluster around three levers: post-acute placement, length of stay, and readmission reduction. Post-acute care — skilled nursing facilities, inpatient rehabilitation, home health — is the single largest driver of episode cost variation for surgical procedures. A hip replacement patient discharged to a skilled nursing facility costs Medicare roughly twice as much over 90 days as the same patient discharged directly home with home health support. Bundled payment participants therefore invest heavily in standardized discharge criteria, preferred SNF networks, and home health partnerships.

Clinical pathway standardization is the second major lever. When a hospital takes on risk for a hip replacement episode, it has a powerful financial incentive to create and enforce a standard care protocol: pre-operative patient optimization (weight, hemoglobin, diabetes control), standardized implant selection, evidence-based rehabilitation protocols, and scheduled follow-up calls. These protocols reduce variance — the expensive outlier cases that blow up episode budgets — and often improve clinical outcomes simultaneously.

Readmission prevention rounds out the triad. A 90-day episode means that any readmission within three months of the initial procedure falls inside the bundle and adds directly to the participant's cost. Participants invest in post-discharge nurse navigator programs, 24/7 patient hotlines, medication reconciliation, and remote monitoring to catch warning signs before they become emergency department visits. These infrastructure investments require upfront capital, which is part of why BPCI Advanced pays preliminary reconciliation payments — to fund the care-coordination capabilities that drive savings.

body.content:
Analyses of BPCI Advanced performance in lower-extremity joint replacement (one of the highest-volume episodes in the model) found that per-episode spending declined on average by $1,014 — approximately a 4% reduction — by Model Year 5, generating an estimated $344 million in total program savings. Quality metrics including readmission and mortality rates remained stable, indicating that cost reductions were achieved without compromising patient safety.
Participants who succeeded shared common characteristics: strong surgeon engagement, standardized implant formularies, disciplined SNF referral networks, and nurse navigator programs for post-discharge monitoring. Hospitals that treated bundled payments as a physician engagement strategy — rather than a finance department exercise — consistently outperformed those that did not.

children.text: The Future of Bundled Payments: From Voluntary to Mandatory

CMS has moved decisively toward mandatory bundled payment models after learning that voluntary programs attract a self-selected group of already-efficient providers. The Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model — launched in 2016 as a mandatory program in randomly selected metropolitan statistical areas — was the first federal mandatory bundle and provided critical evidence that bundles can generate savings at scale without quality deterioration. CJR saved Medicare an estimated $63 million between 2016 and 2018.

The next generation mandatory model is the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), finalized by CMS to launch on January 1, 2026, and run through December 31, 2030. TEAM will require approximately 741 acute care hospitals in selected Core-Based Statistical Areas to accept financial risk for five surgical episode types: lower extremity joint replacement, surgical hip femur fracture treatment, spinal fusion, coronary artery bypass graft, and major bowel procedure. Unlike BPCI Advanced's 90-day window, TEAM episodes end 30 days after discharge, reflecting a sharper focus on the immediate post-acute transition.

Commercial payers have also accelerated their own bundled payment programs independently of CMS. Large self-insured employers — working through coalitions like the Pacific Business Group on Health — negotiate direct bundle contracts with hospital systems for high-volume procedures. The multi-payer environment creates both opportunity (providers can amortize care-coordination infrastructure across multiple payers) and complexity (different episode definitions, target price methodologies, and quality metrics across each payer relationship). Standardization of episode definitions across payers remains one of the field's central operational challenges.

body.message: Bundled payments cover a specific clinical episode, not a patient's entire care. A patient under a bundled payment arrangement for a knee replacement still receives fee-for-service payment for unrelated conditions like diabetes management or a subsequent cardiac event. Do not confuse episode-based bundles with full-risk capitation or population-based payment models, which cover all care for a defined patient population.

result.title: Episode-Based Bundled Payments: How They Work

children.text: Paying for an Episode, Not a Service

A bundled payment sits conceptually between fee-for-service and the population accountability of an ACO. Instead of paying separately for the surgeon, the hospital stay, the rehab facility, and every follow-up visit, a bundle holds providers accountable for the total cost of a defined clinical episode — for example, a hip replacement and everything that happens in the 90 days after it.

The mechanics are usually retrospective. Providers keep billing fee-for-service throughout the episode, then at the end Medicare reconciles total spending against a predetermined target price. If actual spending came in under the target and quality held, the providers keep the difference; if it ran over, they may owe Medicare back.

Bundling targets a specific weakness of fee-for-service: fragmentation. When no one is accountable for the whole episode, costs leak — especially into post-acute care, where discharge decisions vary enormously. A bundle gives providers a direct financial reason to coordinate the entire arc of care.

A bundled payment sets a single target price for a whole episode of care (often 90 days). Spending is reconciled against that target: beat it with good quality and keep the savings; exceed it and potentially repay. The episode — not the individual service — becomes the unit of accountability.
The CMS Innovation Center (CMMI)

Most of Medicare’s bundled-payment and value-based experiments come from one place: the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), known as the CMS Innovation Center. It was created by Section 3021 of the Affordable Care Act in 2010 with a specific mission — to test new payment and delivery models that could reduce spending while preserving or improving quality.

CMMI has a powerful and unusual authority: if a model is certified by the actuary to lower spending without harming quality (or improve quality without raising spending), the Secretary of HHS can expand it nationally without an act of Congress. That ability to scale successful models is what makes CMMI Medicare’s primary engine of payment innovation.

CMMI is also why models can be made mandatory in selected regions. Voluntary models suffer from selection bias — only providers who expect to benefit join — so CMMI sometimes requires all hospitals in chosen markets to participate, producing cleaner evidence about whether a model actually works.

body.content: Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced), launched in 2018, let participants take accountability for 90-day episodes across a menu of medical and surgical conditions, with target prices based partly on their own historical spending. It was the first episode model to include an outpatient surgical condition (spine surgery). Like other episode models, it billed fee-for-service throughout and reconciled spending against the target price at the end of each episode.
body.title: BPCI Advanced

children.text: CJR: Testing Mandatory Bundles

The clearest test of bundled payment was the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model, which ran from April 2016 through December 2024. CJR was mandatory for hospitals in selected metropolitan areas and covered hip and knee replacements — high-volume, high-cost procedures with notoriously variable post-acute spending.

The results validated the core theory. A rigorous evaluation found CJR reduced institutional spending per joint-replacement episode by roughly $812 (about a 3 percent relative decrease), driven largely by a meaningful drop in patients being discharged to costly post-acute facilities instead of home. Critically, CMS found no adverse effects on quality — complication rates, mortality, readmissions, and ED use did not worsen.

CJR demonstrated that a well-designed bundle could squeeze out wasteful post-acute spending without harming patients. Its success directly shaped the next generation of mandatory models, proving that the lever to pull in episode payment is usually post-acute care.

children.text: From CJR to TEAM

The lessons from CJR fed directly into its successor: the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), a mandatory episode-based payment model launching in January 2026. TEAM expands the bundled-payment approach beyond joint replacement to five surgical episode categories and adds enhanced protections for safety-net hospitals.

TEAM reflects how Medicare’s thinking has matured. It is mandatory (for cleaner evidence and broader impact), it spans multiple procedures (not just one), and it explicitly builds in equity safeguards to avoid penalizing hospitals that serve disadvantaged patients — addressing a recurring critique of earlier value programs.

TEAM also illustrates the cumulative nature of payment reform: each model learns from the last. CJR proved bundles work for joint replacement; TEAM extends that proof across more surgeries while patching the equity gaps the earlier models exposed.

body.message: Voluntary models attract providers who expect to win, biasing results. Mandatory models like CJR and TEAM require everyone in selected markets to participate, which gives CMS cleaner evidence about whether a payment model truly works — but also generates strong provider pushback.
body.title: Mandatory models produce better evidence

children.text: CMMI’s Mixed Track Record

For all its importance, CMMI’s overall record is sobering and politically contested. In roughly 14 years it has launched more than 50 models, but a 2023 Congressional Budget Office analysis found that only six produced statistically significant savings — and none exceeded about $220 million in annual savings. Factoring in CMMI’s operating budget, its net budgetary impact has been only marginally negative.

Very few models have cleared the high bar required for national expansion. To date, only the Diabetes Prevention Program and the Pioneer ACO model met the statutory criteria, and even the Pioneer ACO model was never fully folded into permanent Medicare. Many promising-looking models simply did not save money once rigorously evaluated.

This record is essential context, not a footnote. It shows that paying for value is genuinely hard — good ideas frequently fail to deliver net savings — and it fuels ongoing debate about how CMMI should be reformed. But the standouts, like CJR’s bundled-payment success, are exactly why Medicare keeps testing, refining, and occasionally scaling new models.
CMMI’s history is a humbling lesson: most payment experiments do not save money — but the few that do, like mandatory bundles, point the way for the rest of the system.

children.text: Measuring Care From the Patient's Seat

Clinical measures like HEDIS tell you what was done to and for a patient. But they cannot tell you what the care felt like from the patient's side — whether their doctor listened, whether they got help quickly, whether anyone explained their medications. Capturing that perspective is the job of CAHPS.

CAHPS — the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems — is a program run by the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ). It began in 1995 to build the scientific understanding of patient experience as part of advancing safe, patient-centered care. CAHPS is not a single survey but a family of rigorously developed, standardized surveys.

Each CAHPS survey is designed for a specific setting — hospitals, health plans, clinician practices, dialysis facilities, and more. To carry the CAHPS name, a survey must be approved by the CAHPS Consortium overseen by AHRQ, which is what guarantees the surveys are scientifically sound and comparable across organizations.

CAHPS is AHRQ's family of standardized surveys, launched in 1995, that measure patient experience. Each survey targets a specific care setting and must be approved by the AHRQ-overseen CAHPS Consortium.
Experience Is Not Satisfaction

The single most important concept in CAHPS is a distinction that is easy to miss: patient experience is not the same as patient satisfaction. The two terms are often used interchangeably, but CAHPS deliberately measures experience, not satisfaction.

A satisfaction question asks how happy a patient was — a subjective rating that depends heavily on expectations. An experience question asks whether something that should happen in care actually happened, and how often. Instead of "How satisfied were you with communication?" CAHPS asks "During this hospital stay, how often did doctors explain things in a way you could understand?"

This framing matters because experience questions are actionable and fair. "How often did nurses treat you with courtesy and respect?" points to a specific, improvable behavior, and it is far less swayed by whether a patient simply liked their food or their room. By anchoring on concrete events rather than feelings, CAHPS produces data that organizations can actually act on.

children.text: HCAHPS: The Hospital Survey

The most consequential member of the CAHPS family is HCAHPS — the Hospital CAHPS survey — the first national, standardized, publicly reported survey of patients' hospital experiences. It exists to let patients and the public compare hospitals on experience using the same questions everywhere.

HCAHPS has a long development pedigree. Beginning in 2002, CMS partnered with AHRQ to develop and test it; it was endorsed by the National Quality Forum in 2005, implemented in October 2006, and its results were first publicly reported in March 2008. That careful, multi-year development is why HCAHPS scores are treated as credible enough to drive payment.

The survey organizes its questions into composite topics that reflect the core of the hospital experience: communication with nurses, communication with doctors, responsiveness of hospital staff, communication about medicines, discharge information, care transition, the hospital environment (cleanliness and quietness), and an overall hospital rating.

children.text: When Experience Affects Payment

HCAHPS is not just informational — it has real financial teeth. Results are publicly reported on Medicare's Care Compare website and feed directly into the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) program, which redistributes a portion of Medicare payments based on performance.

The weight is significant: patient-experience measures from HCAHPS make up a substantial share of a hospital's Value-Based Purchasing score. That means how patients answer questions about communication, responsiveness, and discharge can swing a hospital's Medicare reimbursement by meaningful amounts each year.

Tying payment to patient experience was a deliberate policy choice: it signals that how care is delivered — not just whether the clinical box was checked — is part of quality. It also raised the stakes for getting the measurement right, because money now rides on the numbers.

body.content:
HCAHPS results are publicly posted on Care Compare and built into Hospital VBP, which redistributes a percentage of Medicare payments based on performance.
Patient-experience scores form a large portion of each hospital's VBP score, so consistent shortfalls in, say, communication or responsiveness can translate into real reductions in Medicare reimbursement — making patient experience a board-level financial issue, not just a satisfaction metric.
body.title: HCAHPS in Hospital Value-Based Purchasing

children.text: Making the Comparison Fair

Comparing hospitals or plans on patient experience is only fair if the comparison accounts for differences that have nothing to do with quality. CAHPS surveys therefore apply adjustments before results are publicly reported.

Two adjustments are central. Patient-mix adjustment accounts for differences in the kinds of patients each organization serves — factors like age, education, and health status that are known to influence how people answer experience questions, independent of the care's quality. Mode adjustment accounts for the fact that people respond differently depending on whether they were surveyed by mail, phone, or another method.

These adjustments are the experience-survey analog of risk adjustment for clinical outcomes. Without them, a hospital serving an older or sicker population could look worse purely because of who it treats, not how well it treats them. The adjustments are what make a hospital's publicly reported scores a fair basis for comparison — and for payment.

body.message: Publicly reported CAHPS scores are patient-mix and mode adjusted precisely because raw responses are influenced by who answered and how they were surveyed. Comparing unadjusted scores across organizations can be misleading — always use the adjusted, reported figures.

children.text: Deciding What to Build and What to Buy

The previous lesson established that hospitals plan major investments through a fixed capital budget, where every department’s request competes for limited dollars. This lesson is about how those decisions actually get made — and constrained. Capital planning sits at the intersection of three forces: the financial analysis that tells a hospital whether an investment will pay off, the strategic judgment about what the institution needs to fulfill its mission, and the government regulation that, in many states, determines whether the hospital is even allowed to make the investment at all.

These three forces pull in different directions. Pure financial analysis favors the projects with the best returns. Strategic and mission considerations may favor projects with modest financial returns but high community value. And in much of the country, a state regulator wielding "certificate of need" authority can block a project entirely, regardless of how attractive it looks on the hospital’s spreadsheet. Capital planning is the discipline of navigating all three.

Key Concept: Capital planning combines financial analysis (NPV, IRR, payback, profitability index), strategic and mission-driven prioritization, and — in many states — Certificate of Need (CON) regulatory approval to decide which long-term investments a hospital pursues.

children.text: Certificate of Need: The Regulatory Gatekeeper

Certificate of Need (CON) programs are state laws that require health care providers to obtain government approval before making major capital investments — building or expanding facilities, adding beds, or acquiring expensive equipment. Their stated purpose is to restrain health care facility costs and allow coordinated planning of new services and construction, on the theory that unchecked duplication of expensive services (every hospital buying its own proton-beam machine) drives up total spending. Currently, 35 states and Washington, D.C. operate CON programs, with enormous variation among them.

The dollar threshold that triggers CON review reveals how differently states approach this. In New York, projects by general hospitals exceeding $30 million require a CON; in Iowa, projects over just $1.5 million do. Thresholds are typically lower for non-hospital providers like ambulatory surgery centers than for hospitals. The practical effect is that the same capital project — say, a new surgery center — might sail through unregulated in one state and require a months-long, contestable approval process in another.

CON laws are genuinely controversial, and the evidence is mixed and politically charged. Critics point to research suggesting hospital charges are about 5.5% lower five years after a state repeals CON, and that per-capita hospital expenditures run about 20.6% higher in CON states — arguing the laws protect incumbents and stifle competition. Defenders argue CON prevents wasteful duplication and protects rural and safety-net providers from being undercut. The result is an active reform landscape: in 2024, Georgia advanced reforms exempting certain single-specialty ASCs from review, and New York proposed raising its hospital CON threshold from $15 million to $30 million.

body.message: In a CON state, a hospital cannot simply decide to build based on financial merit. It must first determine whether the project triggers CON review and, if so, win regulatory approval — a process competitors can oppose. A capital plan that ignores CON can be dead on arrival no matter how strong its projected return.
body.title: CON Is the First Question, Not an Afterthought

children.text: The Financial Analysis: Will the Investment Pay Off?

For projects that clear regulatory hurdles, hospitals apply rigorous capital-budgeting techniques to judge financial merit. The most important is net present value (NPV), which measures the dollar profitability of a project by discounting its expected future cash flows back to today’s dollars and subtracting the initial investment. A positive NPV means the project is expected to create value after accounting for the time value of money; a negative NPV means it destroys value. NPV is the gold standard because it answers the question that matters: will this investment make the hospital better off in real terms?

Several companion metrics fill out the picture. Internal rate of return (IRR) expresses a project’s return as a percentage, making it easy to compare against the hospital’s cost of capital. Payback period measures how long it takes to recoup the original investment — intuitive and useful for gauging risk, but flawed because it ignores both long-term profitability and the time value of money. Profitability index (PI) measures return per dollar invested, which is especially valuable when capital is scarce because it ranks projects by efficiency of capital use, not just total return.

body.title: Core Capital-Investment Metrics

children.text: Beyond the Numbers: Strategic and Mission Scoring

If hospitals funded only the highest-NPV projects, they would look very different — and would likely violate their missions and obligations. Many essential investments have modest or even negative financial returns: replacing a failing fire-safety system, meeting a new regulatory mandate, building behavioral health capacity, or upgrading the electronic health record. A purely financial ranking would starve these in favor of profitable service-line expansions. So hospitals deliberately incorporate non-financial criteria into capital decisions.

The standard tool is project scoring — a ranking technique that combines financial metrics with non-financial factors such as patient safety, regulatory compliance, quality improvement, strategic alignment, and community need. Each request is scored across these dimensions, allowing a high-need safety project with poor financials to compete fairly against a high-return revenue project. This is how hospitals reconcile the spreadsheet with the mission: the NPV matters, but it is one input among several, not the sole verdict.

body.content:
Imagine a hospital weighing two capital requests of equal cost. Project A is a new orthopedic suite with a strong positive NPV and a three-year payback. Project B is a replacement HVAC and electrical system with no revenue at all — pure cost.

On financial metrics alone, Project A wins easily. But a scoring model that weights safety, regulatory compliance, and operational risk will likely rank Project B higher, because a failing electrical system threatens the entire facility. The orthopedic suite generates money; the infrastructure keeps the hospital legally open and physically safe. Good capital planning funds both in the right order — and project scoring is how that judgment is made explicit and defensible.
body.title: How Two Requests Compete

children.text: Putting Capital Planning Together

Effective capital planning braids the three strands into a single disciplined process. First, the regulatory screen: does the project trigger CON review in this state, and can approval be won? Second, the financial analysis: what are the NPV, IRR, payback, and profitability index, and how do they compare to other requests competing for the same limited budget? Third, the strategic and mission scoring: how does the project rank on safety, compliance, quality, community need, and strategic fit? Only a project that survives all three screens — or is deliberately funded despite weak financials for strategic reasons — earns a place in the capital budget.

body.analogy: Capital planning is like a family deciding on a major home investment. First they check whether local zoning even permits it (the CON regulatory screen). Then they run the numbers — will the addition raise the home’s value more than it costs (NPV)? Finally they weigh things money can’t capture: a wheelchair ramp for an aging parent may have terrible "ROI" but tops the list because the need is real. Hospitals do exactly this, just with stakes in the tens of millions.
body.concept: The three screens of capital planning

children.text: The discipline matters because capital decisions are largely irreversible and shape a hospital for decades. A building, once built, must be staffed and maintained for its lifetime; a technology, once bought, locks in service contracts and training. As the prior lesson showed, these capital choices flow into the operating budget as depreciation and operating costs for years. A hospital that chases high-NPV projects while neglecting infrastructure, or that lets mission override financial reality entirely, will eventually find its capital decisions undermining its solvency.

In the value-based-care era, capital planning is also shifting. Investments increasingly favor projects that support population health, care coordination, data infrastructure, and outpatient and community settings — rather than simply adding inpatient beds and procedure rooms. The metrics stay the same, but the strategic scoring evolves: a project that lowers total cost of care and keeps patients healthy may rank higher than a revenue-maximizing inpatient expansion that a fee-for-service hospital would have prized. Understanding capital planning means understanding not just the tools, but how a changing payment landscape changes what a hospital should choose to build.

children.text: The Single Number That Makes Managed Care Work

Everything about Medicaid managed care hinges on one number: the capitation rate — the fixed amount per member per month (PMPM) that a state pays an MCO to cover a defined population’s care. Set that number too high, and the state wastes taxpayer money and overpays plans for little benefit. Set it too low, and plans cannot deliver adequate care, may cut corners or avoid sick members, and could exit the market entirely. The entire promise of managed care — budget predictability with adequate care — depends on getting this number right. This lesson explains how that number is actually built.

Capitation rate-setting is a technical, actuarial discipline, but its logic is comprehensible and its stakes are enormous. Because the rate determines both the state’s spending and the plans’ resources, federal law surrounds it with a strict requirement: actuarial soundness. Rates cannot be a political guess or a budget target imposed from above; they must be developed by qualified actuaries according to professional standards and certified to CMS. Understanding actuarial soundness and the rate-development process is understanding the financial heart of Medicaid managed care.

The governing rule is 42 CFR 438.4, the federal regulation on actuarial soundness, supported by detailed annual CMS rate development guides. Together they define what a sound rate is, how it must be built, and how it must be documented — turning a single PMPM figure into a rigorously justified calculation.

Key Concept: A Medicaid capitation rate is the fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment to an MCO. Federal law (42 CFR 438.4) requires rates to be "actuarially sound" — projected to cover all reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs for the population and services, developed by qualified actuaries and certified to CMS.

children.text: What "Actuarially Sound" Means

Actuarial soundness is the legal and professional standard that governs every Medicaid capitation rate. Under the regulation, actuarially sound capitation rates are those projected to provide for all reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs required under the contract and for the operation of the plan, for the covered time period and population, developed in accordance with generally accepted actuarial principles and practices. In plain terms: the rate must realistically cover what it actually costs to care for the population, plus the legitimate costs of running the plan — no more, no less.

Two features of this standard matter. First, rates must be developed and certified by qualified actuaries, professionals bound by actuarial standards of practice — not set by political fiat. This is a safeguard against states lowballing rates to fit a budget, which would undermine care, and against plans inflating rates beyond justified costs. Second, the standard is forward-looking and population-specific: it asks what the defined population will reasonably cost in the coming period, which requires projecting from historical experience into the future.

body.message: Actuarial soundness is not just a technicality — it is the guardrail that keeps rates honest. It prevents states from setting rates so low that plans must skimp on care or flee the market, and prevents rates so high that taxpayers overpay. The requirement that a qualified actuary certify the rate is what gives that guardrail teeth.
body.title: Soundness Protects Both Sides

children.text: Building the Rate: Base Data, Trend, and Adjustments

How does an actuary actually build a sound rate? The process, outlined in federal rules (42 CFR 438.5(b)), follows a logical sequence. It begins with base data: identifying and developing base utilization and price data from the actual experience of the Medicaid population (or a similar population) — essentially, what did it cost to provide care to these people recently, drawn largely from the encounter data discussed in earlier lessons. This historical experience is the foundation everything else builds on.

Next comes trend: the actuary develops and applies trend factors to project the base data forward, accounting for how costs will change due to medical inflation, shifts in utilization, new treatments, and price growth. A rate for next year cannot simply repeat last year’s costs; it must anticipate where costs are heading. After trending, the actuary applies adjustments — for changes in covered benefits, eligibility, program design, and special considerations for individuals with chronic illness, disability, ongoing needs, or catastrophic claims. Finally, the rate must account for the plan’s non-medical costs: an administrative load (the cost of running the plan) and a risk margin (compensation for bearing financial risk).

body.title: How a Capitation Rate Is Built

children.text: The result is not a single statewide number but a set of rates organized into rate cells — rate groupings specific to eligibility category, age, gender, locality or region, and optionally diagnosis or health status. Rate cells matter because different populations cost vastly different amounts: a healthy child costs far less than an elderly person with disabilities. By setting a distinct rate for each cell, the system pays plans appropriately for whatever mix of members they actually enroll — and reduces (though does not eliminate) the incentive to cherry-pick, a problem addressed more directly by risk adjustment in the next lesson.
Rate Ranges, MLR Targets, and Certification

Rate development does not always produce a single point; states may develop and certify a range of capitation rates per rate cell, as long as the certification identifies and justifies the assumptions, data, and methodologies for both the upper and lower bounds. But the range is bounded: the upper bound of a rate range cannot exceed the lower bound multiplied by 1.05 — a maximum 5% range. Separately, the rules permit a state to move up to 1.5% in either direction from the certified rate without notifying CMS, a figure CMS chose because it is generally not more than the risk margin in a typical rate-setting process. These guardrails prevent rate ranges from becoming a backdoor for arbitrary rate-setting.

The rate must also align with the medical loss ratio standard from earlier lessons. The certified rates must target an MLR of at least 85%, meaning the rate is built so that at least 85 cents of every dollar is expected to go to medical care and quality rather than administration and profit; states may target a higher MLR if they choose. This links rate-setting to the MLR requirement covered in its own lesson — the rate is constructed with the MLR floor in mind, and the MLR is then measured against actual experience.

Finally, none of this is valid until certified. CMS uses "rate certification" to mean both the actuary’s letter attesting that the rates are actuarially sound and meet federal requirements, and all the supporting documentation — the actuarial report, data, memos, and workbooks behind it. CMS reviews this certification before approving the rates, and only approved rates can be paid with federal matching funds. The certification is the formal proof that the single PMPM number rests on a rigorous, documented, professionally sound foundation.
Why Rate-Setting Is the Make-or-Break Function

Capitation rate-setting is where the abstract promise of managed care meets hard arithmetic. Every other element of the program — network adequacy, quality, care management — depends on plans having enough money to deliver, and not so much that the program is wasteful. Get the rate right, and plans can build real networks and manage care well while the state controls spending. Get it wrong in either direction, and the whole edifice wobbles: underfunded plans skimp or exit, overfunded plans pocket the difference, and either way the public interest suffers.

body.analogy: Setting a capitation rate is like a city setting the fixed annual fee it pays a contractor to maintain all its parks. Set it from real data on what upkeep actually costs (base data), adjusted for rising wages and materials (trend) and for how many parks and how big (rate cells and adjustments), plus a fair amount for the contractor’s overhead and risk. Pay too little and the parks go to seed; pay too much and taxpayers are fleeced. And a qualified, independent estimator (the actuary) must certify the number is honest before the city signs the check.
body.concept: How Medicaid capitation rates are built

children.text: This is also why rate-setting connects to so much else in the course. The base data comes from encounter data, whose accuracy the contract and oversight lessons emphasized. The rate cells set the stage for risk adjustment, the next lesson’s subject, which refines payment for the actual health of enrolled members. The 85% MLR target ties to the MLR lesson that follows. And the actuarial soundness requirement is itself a Part 438 mandate from the federal-framework lesson. Rate-setting is the financial hub where data, regulation, and the other operational pieces converge into the payment that drives the entire system.

For the student, the key insight is that the capitation rate is neither a guess nor a negotiation in the ordinary sense — it is a regulated, actuarial calculation built from real experience, projected forward, adjusted for population and program, and certified by professionals. The discipline of actuarial soundness exists precisely because the number is so consequential. When you understand how a Medicaid capitation rate is set, you understand how a state turns its budget into adequate care for millions of people — and why so much regulatory care surrounds that single PMPM figure.

points: A Medicaid capitation rate is the fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment to an MCO, and federal law (42 CFR 438.4) requires it to be "actuarially sound" — projected to cover all reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs for the population and services.

Actuarial soundness requires rates to be developed and certified by qualified actuaries per generally accepted actuarial principles, protecting against rates set too low (forcing skimping or market exit) or too high (wasting taxpayer money).

Rates are built in a sequence: start with base utilization and price data from actual experience (largely encounter data), apply trend factors to project forward, make adjustments for benefit/eligibility/program changes and high-need members, and add administrative load and risk margin.
Rates are organized into rate cells specific to eligibility category, age, gender, region, and optionally health status, so plans are paid appropriately for the mix of members they enroll.

States may certify a range of rates per cell, but the upper bound cannot exceed 1.05× the lower bound (a 5% maximum range), and a state may move ±1.5% from the certified rate without notifying CMS (roughly the typical risk margin).
Certified rates must target a medical loss ratio of at least 85%, linking rate-setting to the MLR requirement, with states free to target a higher MLR.
A rate is valid only when certified — the actuary’s attestation plus all supporting documentation — which CMS reviews before approving rates for federal matching funds.

Rate-setting is the financial hub of managed care: it draws on encounter data, sets the stage for risk adjustment, ties to the MLR standard, and determines whether plans can deliver adequate care while the state controls spending.

children.text: Turning Risk Into a To-Do List

Risk stratification tells you who needs attention; predictive analytics sharpens who is about to need it. But "this patient is high-risk" is not yet an action. Care gap analysis is what turns risk into a concrete, closeable list of specific things to do for specific patients — it is where population health becomes operational.

A care gap is, simply, a missed service: a clinical service a patient is due for, based on guidelines and quality measures, that has not happened. A diabetic patient overdue for an eye exam. A 55-year-old who has never had a colonoscopy. A heart-failure patient not on a guideline-recommended medication. Each gap is a precise, actionable item — find it, close it.

This is the workhorse activity of day-to-day population health. While risk models and dashboards set strategy, care gap closure is the relentless operational grind that actually improves measured quality and outcomes: identify every open gap across the panel, and systematically close them.

A care gap is a needed clinical service a patient is due for but has not received. Care gap analysis turns abstract risk into a concrete, closeable to-do list — the workhorse operational activity of population health.
Care Gaps and Quality Measures

Care gaps are defined against quality measures — most prominently HEDIS, the standardized measure set from the National Committee for Quality Assurance (covered in depth in the Clinical Quality Measurement course). A quality measure defines what should happen for a population; a care gap is the missing piece for an individual patient measured against it.

The relationship is precise. Recall that a HEDIS measure has a denominator (everyone eligible for the service) and a numerator (everyone who received it). A care gap is exactly the difference: an eligible patient in the denominator who is NOT yet in the numerator. Closing a gap moves that patient into the numerator and raises the measure rate. Care gap analysis is, in effect, HEDIS improvement done one patient at a time.

Gaps span the full range of measures: cancer screenings, immunizations, chronic-disease management (like comprehensive diabetes care, which bundles HbA1c testing, blood pressure control, eye exams, and nephropathy screening), behavioral health follow-up, and more. As open gaps accumulate across a population, measured quality falls; closing them is how the population's quality scores rise.

children.text: The Closure Workflow

Identifying gaps is necessary but useless without a workflow to close them. Care gap closure is an end-to-end process: identify patients overdue for services, reach out to them, schedule appointments, deliver the service, and document it so the gap actually registers as closed. Each step can fail, so each needs deliberate design.

Two workflow moments are especially high-leverage. The first is pre-visit planning: before a patient's scheduled visit, the team reviews their open gaps and pre-populates them so the provider can address them during the visit they are already having. The second is point-of-care alerts: surfacing a patient's open gaps in the EHR while the provider is with them. Evidence shows pre-visit gap alerts increase in-visit gap closure by about 34 percent — catching the patient who is already in the building is far easier than chasing one who is not.

For gaps that cannot be closed during an existing visit, proactive outreach campaigns reach patients who are not coming in — the whole-population behavior that defines population health. The mechanics matter: outreach that includes a direct scheduling link converts roughly three times better than outreach asking patients to call the office. Reducing friction is as important as sending the reminder.

children.text: Why Closing Gaps Pays

Care gap closure is not just good medicine — it is directly tied to revenue and reputation through quality programs. Closing gaps improves HEDIS scores, UDS measures (for community health centers), and CMS Star Ratings, all of which feed value-based contract revenue and quality bonuses (the MIPS, ACO, and Star Ratings mechanics from the Clinical Quality Measurement course).

This creates a powerful alignment: the same activity that improves a patient's health — getting them their overdue screening or controlling their chronic disease — also raises the organization's quality scores and earns it more under value-based payment. Care gap closure is one of the cleaner places in health care where doing right by the patient and doing well financially point in the same direction.

Note the honest tension, though: because gaps are tied to bonuses, there is a risk of "teaching to the test" — chasing the measured gaps while ignoring unmeasured needs. Good programs treat gap closure as a floor (the minimum, guideline-based care everyone deserves) rather than the ceiling of what they do for patients. The metric is a means to better health, not the end in itself.

children.text: Doing Gap Analysis Well

Effective care gap analysis rests on the foundations from earlier lessons. It needs solid data infrastructure (a gap is only real if the data is complete — out-of-network care the EHR cannot see can create false gaps for services that actually happened). It uses risk stratification to prioritize (close the highest-risk patients' gaps first). And it depends on accurate documentation and coding so closed gaps actually register.

The operational best practices are concrete: maintain an up-to-date registry of open gaps, run daily huddles and pre-visit planning so the team knows each day's gap opportunities, surface point-of-care alerts to close gaps during existing visits, and run frictionless outreach (direct scheduling links) for the patients who are not coming in. Automation increasingly handles the identification and outreach at scale.

The throughline is that care gap analysis is where population health's strategy meets daily execution. The risk models and predictions point the way, but it is the steady, systematic closing of specific gaps for specific patients — visit by visit, outreach by outreach — that actually moves a population's health and quality scores. The next module turns to the chronic-disease programs where much of this gap closure concentrates.

children.text: The People Who Do the Work

The first half of this course built the analytic machinery of population health — data, risk stratification, prediction, care gaps, and disease-specific programs. But analytics do not call patients, coordinate their care, or help them manage at home. People do. This lesson is about those people: the care managers, and the models that organize their work.

Care management is the hands-on, relationship-based core of population health — the human layer that turns a risk score into actual help for a real person. A care manager is the team member who takes responsibility for guiding a defined set of high-risk patients: coordinating their care across providers, helping them navigate the system, supporting their self-management, and intervening proactively before problems escalate.

This is where the proactive, whole-population philosophy becomes a job. The risk stratification lesson identified who needs intensive attention; care management is who delivers it. Understanding the roles, the program types, and the structural models is understanding how population health actually reaches patients.

Care management is the hands-on, relationship-based core of population health: a care manager takes responsibility for guiding a defined set of high-risk patients — coordinating care, supporting self-management, and intervening proactively. Analytics identify who needs help; care managers deliver it.
Who Care Managers Are

Care managers come from varied backgrounds, and the mix matters because different patients need different expertise. The most common is the registered nurse (RN) care manager, who handles the clinical work — medication management, disease education, symptom monitoring, coordinating with physicians. RNs are the backbone of complex and chronic care management.

But care management is a team, not a single role. Social workers address the social and behavioral barriers — housing, benefits, mental health, family situations — that often drive a patient's health more than the clinical issues. Community health workers (the subject of a later lesson) bring trusted, culturally-concordant connection to the community and help with on-the-ground barriers. Pharmacists manage complex medication regimens. The right team for a population mixes these roles.

The key principle is matching the role to the need. A patient whose diabetes is uncontrolled because of a complex insulin regimen needs an RN or pharmacist; a patient whose diabetes is uncontrolled because they cannot afford food or get to appointments needs a social worker or community health worker. Effective care management deploys the whole team and routes each patient to the role that addresses their actual barrier.

children.text: Types of Care Management

Care management is not one program but several, distinguished by the population and the time horizon. Chronic Care Management (CCM) is ongoing support for patients with two or more chronic conditions expected to last at least a year — the steady, month-to-month work of keeping chronic disease controlled. Medicare reimburses it: CPT 99490 covers 20 minutes of clinical staff time per month for care planning and oversight.

Complex CCM serves patients needing more intensive management, with codes (99487, plus add-on 99489) covering 60+ minutes per month and moderate-to-high-complexity decision-making. Transitional Care Management (TCM) is the time-limited, high-intensity work in the 30 days after a hospital discharge — the post-discharge follow-up that prevents readmissions (connecting to the heart-failure and ADT-alert lessons). And complex (intensive) care management targets the highest-risk, highest-cost patients with hands-on, often in-person support.

These programs each have their own reimbursement, eligibility, and intensity, but they share a logic: match the program to the patient's risk tier and situation. A stable two-chronic-condition patient gets CCM; a patient just discharged from the hospital gets TCM; the complex apex patient gets intensive care management. This is the risk pyramid translated into staffing and programs.

body.title: Types of Care Management

children.text: Caseload: The Central Design Variable

The single most important operational decision in care management is caseload — how many patients one care manager is responsible for. It is the dial that trades off intensity against reach, and getting it wrong wastes the whole program. Too high, and the care manager cannot meaningfully help anyone; too low, and the program is too expensive to scale.

Caseloads vary enormously by intensity. A typical RN care manager handling high-risk patients carries roughly 50 to 150 patients. But the range is wide: a purely telephonic, light-touch program might run as high as ~500 members per care manager, while intensive in-person case management for the most complex patients might be as low as ~25 to 1. The intensity of the intervention determines the caseload, not the other way around.

The factors that set the right caseload include the clinical and social complexity of the patients, the care manager's experience, the available social supports, the setting, and the target outcomes. The discipline is to match caseload to the population's needs: the highest-risk apex patients need small caseloads and intensive attention; the broader rising-risk tier can be served with larger caseloads and lighter touch. This is, again, the risk pyramid driving resource allocation.

children.text: Embedded vs. Centralized Models

Beyond who and how many, there is a structural question: where does the care manager sit? Two models dominate. In the embedded (practice-based) model, the care manager is part of the primary care team — physically and organizationally inside the practice, working alongside the physicians and their patients. In the centralized model, care managers work from a central hub (often a health plan or a system-level team), independent of any one practice's workflow.

Each has trade-offs. Embedded care managers build trust with both physicians and patients, integrate into the clinical workflow, and benefit from warm hand-offs and shared knowledge — evidence suggests embedded models are generally better adopted into practice. Centralized models offer efficiency, consistency, specialized expertise, and easier scaling across many practices, but can feel disconnected from the front-line care team.

Many organizations blend the two — embedded care managers for the highest-touch work where relationship and workflow integration matter most, centralized teams for scalable, telephonic, or specialized functions. There is no single right answer; the choice depends on the population, the organization's structure, and the resources available. The throughline is that care management is the human engine of population health, and how you staff, size, and structure it determines whether all the upstream analytics actually translate into better care. The next lesson turns to what care managers and patients actually do together: care planning and patient engagement.

body.message: A care manager given 300 of the most complex patients cannot meaningfully help any of them; one given 25 light-touch patients is wasted capacity. The caseload must match the intervention intensity and patient complexity — small for intensive in-person work, larger for telephonic light-touch — or the program fails on either impact or cost.

children.text: The Patient Does Most of the Work

A profound truth sits beneath all of population health: patients manage their own health almost all of the time. A person with diabetes spends maybe a few hours a year with clinicians and the other ~8,760 hours managing the disease themselves — choosing what to eat, whether to take medications, when to check glucose, how to respond to symptoms. The care team is a small fraction of the equation; the patient is the rest.

This reframes the care manager's job. It is not to manage the patient, but to help the patient manage themselves more effectively. The two tools for doing that are the care plan (the shared roadmap of what the patient and team will do) and patient engagement (the work of getting the patient to actively participate). Without these, even the best analytics and care managers produce instructions the patient ignores.

This is also where many population health programs quietly fail. They identify the right patients, assign a care manager, and create a plan — then the patient does not follow it, because the plan was made for them rather than with them, or because they lack the knowledge, confidence, or means to act. Engagement is the difference between a plan on paper and a change in health.

Patients manage their own health almost all the time; the care team is a small fraction. The care manager's job is to help patients manage themselves — through a shared care plan and genuine patient engagement, not instructions handed down.
The Person-Centered Care Plan

A care plan is the shared roadmap for a patient's care — but the crucial word is "shared." A person-centered care plan is developed WITH the patient, not for them, and reflects not just what is clinically optimal but what the patient is actually willing and able to do given their preferences and real-life constraints.

Its core components are goals and action steps that the patient and care manager set together. Crucially, the goals should be the patient's goals, expressed in terms that matter to them — "be able to play with my grandchildren" or "stop having to take insulin" — not just clinical targets. A plan anchored in what the patient cares about gets followed; one that lists only the clinician's targets often does not.

The mechanism for building such a plan is shared decision-making: the clinician and patient collaborate, with the clinician explaining options, benefits, risks, and tradeoffs in plain language, and the patient contributing their preferences, values, and constraints. The final plan reflects both clinical evidence and what the patient will realistically do. A person-centered plan also unifies medical and behavioral health into one document rather than separate, disconnected plans — connecting to the integration lesson.

children.text: Patient Activation and the PAM

Patients differ enormously in their readiness to manage their own health, and meeting them where they are is essential. The key concept is "patient activation" — a patient's knowledge, skills, and confidence to manage their own health and care. It is distinct from engagement: engagement is what a patient does; activation is the underlying capacity that makes engagement possible.

Activation is measurable. The Patient Activation Measure (PAM), developed by Judith Hibbard, is a validated 13-item survey that scores a patient and places them in one of four levels: Level 1 (may not yet believe their role is important), Level 2 (lacks confidence and knowledge to act), Level 3 (beginning to take action), and Level 4 (maintaining healthy behaviors even under stress). Knowing a patient's activation level lets the team tailor its approach.

Why it matters: more-activated patients have better health outcomes and care experiences, and tailoring support to activation level improves results. A Level 1 patient who is overwhelmed needs small, confidence-building steps and basic education, not a complex 10-point self-management regimen that will only set them up to fail. A Level 4 patient can take on more. Treating every patient identically ignores the single biggest predictor of whether the plan will work.

children.text: Engagement Techniques That Work

Engagement is a skill, and several evidence-based techniques make it work. The first is motivational interviewing (MI): a collaborative, non-judgmental communication style that helps patients find their own motivation to change, rather than being lectured. MI is especially effective for behavior change in chronic illness, and brief versions are adapted for short clinical encounters.

The second is the teach-back method: after explaining something, the clinician asks the patient to explain it back in their own words, revealing and correcting misunderstandings on the spot. Teach-back improves health literacy and knowledge retention among patients with chronic disease, and it is far more effective than simply asking "do you understand?" (to which patients almost always say yes).

Underlying both is attention to health literacy — the patient's ability to obtain, understand, and use health information. Much of what clinicians say is not understood, and a plan a patient does not understand is a plan they cannot follow. Plain language, teach-back, and meeting patients at their activation level are how a care plan crosses the gap from the clinician's mind into the patient's actual behavior.

body.content:
A care manager explains a new insulin regimen, then says: "I want to make sure I explained that clearly — can you walk me through how you'll take your insulin tomorrow morning?" The patient's explanation reveals they think they only take it when they feel symptoms.
The care manager corrects the misunderstanding on the spot. Without teach-back, that error would have gone home with the patient — a "plan" that would have failed silently. Asking "do you understand?" would have gotten a "yes" and missed it entirely.
body.title: Teach-Back in a Diabetes Visit

children.text: Why This Is the Linchpin

Care planning and patient engagement are the linchpin where all the upstream population health machinery either pays off or stalls. The data found the right patient; risk stratification flagged them; the care manager reached them; a disease program defined the evidence-based care. But none of it changes the patient's health unless the patient actually does something different — and that depends entirely on a plan they own and an engagement that activates them.

This is why the best programs treat engagement as a core competency, not an afterthought. They measure activation (PAM), tailor to it, build plans around patient goals, communicate with teach-back and plain language, and use motivational interviewing to spark intrinsic motivation. They recognize that a beautifully evidence-based plan the patient ignores is worth nothing, while a modest plan the patient embraces changes their trajectory.

The humbling, central lesson is that population health ultimately runs on the patient's own choices, repeated thousands of times between visits. Everything the system does is in service of supporting those choices. Get the engagement right and the analytics, care management, and disease programs all bear fruit; get it wrong and they are expensive machinery producing plans no one follows. The remaining lessons turn to the value-based contracts that pay for all of this, the equity lens that ensures it reaches everyone, and the measurement that proves it works.

body.message: Care plans built around clinical targets and handed to patients routinely fail. Plans must be built WITH patients around THEIR goals, tailored to their activation level, and communicated so they actually understand (teach-back, plain language). The most evidence-based plan is worthless if the patient does not own it or cannot follow it.

children.text: Billing for What You Actually Did

A service can be delivered flawlessly, documented thoroughly, and coded correctly — and still never get billed. The step that prevents that catastrophe is charge capture: the process of recording every billable service, procedure, supply, and medication a patient received so it ends up on the claim. If charge capture fails, the work was done for free.

Charge capture is the bridge between the clinical event and the financial claim. After the diagnosis and procedure are coded, charge capture ensures those coded services — plus the supplies and drugs used — are formally recorded as charges in the billing system. It answers a deceptively simple question: did we actually bill for everything we did?

The answer, distressingly often, is no. Missed charges are one of the most common and most invisible forms of revenue loss, because nothing alerts you to a charge that was never entered. Unlike a denial, which is at least visible, a missed charge simply never appears — silent, lost revenue.

Charge capture is the process of recording every billable service, procedure, supply, and medication so it reaches the claim. A service that is not captured is never billed — silent, invisible lost revenue.
The Chargemaster: The Master Price List

Charge capture rests on the chargemaster, also called the Charge Description Master (CDM). The chargemaster is the organization's master database of every billable item and service, mapping each one to its code, price, department, and applicable modifiers. It is, quite literally, the backbone of the revenue cycle — every charge that gets captured is pulled from it.

Because the chargemaster defines what can be charged and at what price, errors in it propagate everywhere. An outdated code, a missing item, or an incorrect price in the CDM produces wrong or rejected charges across thousands of claims. Maintaining the chargemaster — keeping codes current, prices accurate, and items complete — is an ongoing revenue-integrity discipline of its own.

Charge entry is the specific administrative step where finalized codes and their fees from the chargemaster are entered into the billing system, creating the line items that form the claim. In some settings this is automated from the EHR; in others it is manual. Either way, charge entry is where the chargemaster's data becomes an actual charge on a patient's account.

children.text: How Charges Get Lost

Missed and inaccurate charges arise in several recurring ways. A procedure may be documented but never billed. Ancillary services (a lab, an imaging study) may become disconnected from the encounter. Supplies and implants may be used but never linked from the usage log to the claim. Charges on the hospital (facility) claim may contradict those on the professional (physician) claim.

A particular problem is the "late charge" — a charge that arrives after the claim has already been submitted. Late charges either get dropped entirely (lost revenue) or force a costly claim correction. High-volume, supply-heavy, and ancillary-dependent departments (the OR, the ED, infusion, cath lab) are the classic hotspots where charges slip through.

The defense is charge reconciliation: systematically comparing what was documented against what was charged, ideally on a daily basis, to catch missing charges before the claim goes out. Daily reconciliation is a recognized best practice precisely because charge capture is a major, ongoing source of revenue leakage that must be actively hunted, not assumed.

body.message: Unlike a denial, a charge that was never entered triggers no alert — it simply never appears. This makes missed charges one of the most insidious revenue leaks. Daily charge reconciliation against documentation is the main defense, especially in supply-heavy areas like the OR, ED, and infusion.
body.title: A Missed Charge Is Invisible

children.text: The Scale of the Leak

The financial stakes of charge capture are larger than they first appear. The Healthcare Financial Management Association reports that up to 1 percent of a health system's net charges are lost to charge-capture leakage, and broader estimates put annual losses in the range of 1 to 3 percent of net revenue.

One percent may sound small until you apply it to a large organization's revenue — for a health system, it can mean millions of dollars vanishing every year, invisibly, into uncaptured charges. Because the loss is silent and recurring, it often goes unnoticed for years, which is exactly what makes it so damaging.

Conversely, fixing charge capture is one of the highest-ROI activities in the revenue cycle. Organizations that implement robust charge-capture systems commonly recover a meaningful share of previously lost revenue in the first year — money that was always earned but never collected. The point is not to bill more than was done; it is to bill for all of what was done.

children.text: Capturing Charges Well

Strong charge capture combines process and technology. On the process side: daily charge reconciliation, regular charge-capture audits, a well-maintained chargemaster, and clear accountability for charge entry in every department. On the technology side: EHR-integrated charge capture that records charges at the point of care, and automated tools that flag missing, duplicate, or inconsistent charges.

Automation is increasingly powerful here. Modern revenue-cycle software uses algorithms and machine learning to detect likely missed charges, and natural language processing can read clinical documentation to surface billable services that were documented but never coded or charged — directly attacking the "documented but not billed" leak.

But charge capture must always stay tethered to documentation and compliance. Capturing a charge for something that was not documented or not done is not revenue recovery — it is fraud. The goal is integrity: bill for everything actually performed and documented, and nothing else. That integrity link between documentation and charges is exactly the territory of the next lesson, on documentation requirements and compliance.

The OR is a classic charge-capture hotspot: a single surgery involves the procedure, anesthesia, implants, instruments, and consumable supplies, each a potential charge that must be linked back to the encounter.
When supplies and implants used in the case are not captured from the usage log onto the claim, the organization loses real money on high-cost items — which is why supply-heavy departments get the most intensive charge reconciliation and audit attention.

children.text: The $5,000 MRI That Nobody Pays $5,000 For

A hospital lists an MRI at $5,000. A commercial insurer pays $1,200 for it. Medicare pays perhaps $500. A cash-paying patient might be quoted $3,200. The uninsured patient who never negotiates gets billed the full $5,000. Same machine, same scan, same hospital — four wildly different prices, none of which has much to do with what the scan actually costs to perform. Welcome to the strangest pricing system in the American economy, governed by a document called the chargemaster.

The chargemaster — formally the charge description master (CDM) — is a comprehensive listing of every billable item and service a hospital offers, each paired with a price and standardized billing codes. Every blood test, surgical supply, medication dose, room-day, and procedure has its own line item, and a large hospital’s chargemaster can contain tens of thousands of entries. The price attached to each item is called the gross charge or "list price."

Understanding the chargemaster is the key to one of hospital finance’s most important distinctions: the difference between what a hospital charges (gross revenue) and what it actually collects (net revenue). Confusing the two leads to wildly wrong conclusions about hospital finances — and the gap between them is where almost all the action in hospital revenue lives.

Key Concept: The chargemaster (CDM) is a hospital’s master list of every billable item and its gross charge (list price). Gross charges are the starting point for billing, but they are not what the hospital actually collects — net revenue is.
