children.text: The Contract Is Where Promises Become Obligations

Once a state selects its MCOs through the procurement covered in the last lesson, it translates the winning proposals into a binding contract. That contract — often hundreds of pages long — is the single most important operational document in Medicaid managed care. It converts the federal requirements of 42 CFR Part 438 and the state’s own priorities into specific, enforceable obligations the plan must meet. If the procurement is where the state chooses its partners, the contract is where it defines exactly what those partners must do.

Three categories of contract requirements form the operational backbone of every Medicaid MCO contract: network adequacy (ensuring enrollees can actually access providers), quality assurance (ensuring the care is good), and reporting (ensuring the state can see what the plan is doing). These three threads run through the entire relationship, and each is anchored in federal regulation. Together they are how a state holds a risk-bearing private plan accountable for serving a vulnerable public population.

Understanding these requirements matters because they are the mechanism that addresses the central tension of managed care. A capitated plan has an incentive to spend less — which could mean a thin network, skimpy care, or hidden problems. Network, quality, and reporting requirements are the contractual counterweights: they force the plan to maintain real access, demonstrate real quality, and show the state real data.

Key Concept: An MCO contract converts federal rules and state priorities into binding obligations across three core areas — network adequacy (access), quality assurance (good care), and reporting (transparency) — backed by enforcement tools like sanctions and liquidated damages.
Network Adequacy Requirements

The first pillar is network adequacy: the contract must require the plan to maintain a provider network sufficient to deliver the covered services. Under 42 CFR 438.68, states must develop and publish quantitative time-and-distance standards for a defined set of provider types — primary care (adult and pediatric), OB/GYN, behavioral health, adult and pediatric specialists, hospitals, pharmacy, and pediatric dental — plus additional types as CMS determines. The 2024 final rule layered appointment wait-time standards on top of these, as the federal-framework lesson described, so adequacy is now judged by both geography and timeliness.

Crucially, network adequacy is not just about counting providers. In setting standards, states must consider factors such as providers’ ability to communicate with limited-English-proficient enrollees, accommodation of disabilities, the availability of triage or screening lines, and the use of telemedicine and other innovative technologies. This reflects a recognition that a "provider in the network" is only meaningful if a real enrollee — who may have a disability, speak limited English, or live far from care — can actually reach and use them. The contract embeds these considerations as binding requirements.

To verify adequacy, states require plans to support a Network Adequacy and Access Assurances Report (NAAAR), documenting an analysis that supports the assurance that each plan’s network is adequate. Combined with the secret-shopper surveys from the federal-framework lesson, this gives the state both the plan’s self-reported network data and an independent test of whether that network functions in practice — closing the gap between paper networks and real access.
Quality Assurance Requirements

The second pillar is quality assurance. The contract must require the plan to participate in the state’s quality apparatus, which federal rules build around several components. Each state contracting with managed care plans must draft and implement a written quality strategy for assessing and improving the quality of care (42 CFR 438.340). Within that, each plan must operate a Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program, undergo external quality review (EQR) by an independent organization, and meet accreditation and reporting requirements.

These requirements work together as a system. The state’s quality strategy sets the overall direction and goals. Each plan’s QAPI program is its internal engine for measuring and improving care. External quality review provides an independent, expert assessment of each plan’s performance — the subject of its own lesson later in this course. And quality measure reporting (including HEDIS, also covered later) generates the data that feeds all of it. The contract binds the plan into this entire structure, making quality not optional but a condition of payment.

body.message: Because a capitated plan profits by spending less, there is a risk it could cut corners on care. The quality strategy, QAPI, external quality review, and measure reporting exist precisely to detect under-provision and force improvement — turning "good care" from a hope into a measured, enforceable obligation.
body.title: Quality Requirements Counter the Skimping Incentive

children.text: Reporting Requirements and Enrollee Protections

The third pillar is reporting — the data flow that lets the state see what its plans are doing. The centerpiece is the requirement under 42 CFR 438.66 that each state submit to CMS, no later than 180 days after each contract year, a Managed Care Program Annual Report (MCPAR) on each program. That report must assess, at minimum, each plan’s financial performance (including medical loss ratio), the quality and timeliness of encounter data, enrollment and benefit changes, a summary of grievances, appeals, and state fair hearings, network adequacy and access, and performance on quality measures. The MCPAR is essentially the state’s annual accountability ledger for managed care.

Two reporting streams deserve special note. Encounter data — the information about every item or service an enrollee receives under the contract — is the managed care equivalent of fee-for-service claims data, and it is essential for rate-setting, quality measurement, and oversight; the timeliness and accuracy of encounter data is itself a monitored requirement. And appeals and grievances data give a direct window into enrollee experience: enrollees can appeal service denials and file grievances about any dissatisfaction, and since 2022 states must report certain appeals and grievance data to CMS annually, so the state can spot a plan that is denying too much care.

These reporting requirements connect to enforcement. Federal rules require states to maintain a monitoring system spanning administration, appeals and grievances, claims, enrollee materials, finance and MLR, information systems and encounter data, marketing, medical and utilization management, program integrity, network management, quality improvement, and LTSS delivery. When monitoring reveals problems, contracts give states enforcement tools: monetary penalties, corrective action plans, suspension of new enrollment, and liquidated damages — predetermined monetary penalties written into the contract for specific failures. These are the teeth behind the requirements.

body.title: The Three Pillars of an MCO Contract

children.text: Why the Contract Is the Heart of Oversight

Everything a state can require of a plan after the contract is signed must be in the contract. This makes contract design enormously consequential — it is the state’s last and best chance to exercise leverage. A weak contract with vague standards and few reporting requirements leaves the state with little ability to hold a plan accountable; a strong contract with clear, measurable, enforceable requirements gives the state real oversight. Because the relationship runs for years, the quality of the contract determines the quality of the accountability for the entire contract term.

body.analogy: An MCO contract is like the franchise agreement behind a restaurant chain. The franchisee (the plan) runs the day-to-day operation, but the agreement dictates the standards it must meet — the menu it must offer (covered services), the locations it must staff (network adequacy), the inspections it must pass (quality review), and the sales reports it must file (reporting). If a location skimps, the franchise agreement’s penalty clauses (sanctions and liquidated damages) are what let headquarters force a fix. A vague agreement means a chain that can’t control its own restaurants.
body.concept: How the MCO contract enables oversight

children.text: The three pillars also illustrate how managed care’s components interlock. Network adequacy without reporting would be unverifiable; quality requirements without enforcement would be toothless; reporting without standards to measure against would be meaningless. The contract weaves them together: it sets the standards (network and quality), requires the data to verify them (reporting), and attaches the consequences for failure (sanctions). Each pillar depends on the others, and the contract is what binds them into a coherent system of accountability.

This lesson sets up the rest of the course in a direct way. The monitoring and oversight lesson that follows explains how the state actually uses the reporting and enforcement provisions established here. The rate-setting module explains how the financial terms — including the encounter data and MLR provisions referenced above — are calculated. The network adequacy and quality lessons go deeper into those specific contract requirements. The contract is the hub; the operational details radiate out from it. Master what the contract requires, and you understand the structure within which all of Medicaid managed care operates.

points: The MCO contract converts federal rules (42 CFR Part 438) and state priorities into binding, enforceable obligations, organized around three core pillars: network adequacy, quality assurance, and reporting.

Network adequacy requirements (438.68) include quantitative time-and-distance standards for specified provider types plus 2024 appointment wait-time standards, and must consider LEP communication, disability accommodation, and telehealth.
States require network assurance documentation (the NAAAR) and, combined with secret-shopper surveys, verify that paper networks deliver real access.

Quality assurance requires a state quality strategy (438.340), a plan QAPI program, external quality review by an independent organization, and accreditation/measure reporting — a system that exists to counter the skimping incentive of capitation.

Reporting centers on the Managed Care Program Annual Report (MCPAR) under 438.66, due within 180 days of the contract year, covering financial performance/MLR, encounter data, enrollment/benefit changes, grievances and appeals, network adequacy, and quality measures.

Encounter data (the record of every service an enrollee receives) is the managed care equivalent of claims data and is essential for rate-setting, quality, and oversight; appeals and grievances data (reported to CMS annually since 2022) reveal enrollee experience and over-denial.

Federal rules require a broad state monitoring system, and contracts provide enforcement teeth — monetary penalties, corrective action plans, enrollment suspension, and liquidated damages (predetermined penalties for specific failures).

Because anything the state can require after signing must be in the contract, contract design is the state’s key point of leverage — a strong, measurable contract enables real oversight for the entire multi-year term.

children.text: The Gap Between Billed and Collected

In the previous lesson, we saw that a hospital’s gross charges (what it bills at chargemaster prices) are far higher than its net revenue (what it actually collects). This lesson dissects exactly where that money goes. The difference between what a hospital bills and what it keeps is not one thing — it is three distinct categories, each with its own cause, accounting treatment, and policy significance: contractual adjustments, charity care, and bad debt.

Confusing these three is one of the most common errors in hospital finance, and it leads to badly wrong conclusions. A contractual adjustment is a planned discount the hospital agreed to. Charity care is care the hospital chose to give away to those who cannot pay. Bad debt is money the hospital expected to collect but never received. They look similar on a statement — all three reduce gross charges down toward net revenue — but they mean completely different things about the hospital and its patients.

Getting the distinctions right matters enormously. They determine how a hospital reports its finances, whether a nonprofit meets its community-benefit obligations, how much "uncompensated care" the sector claims, and how aggressively a hospital pursues patients for unpaid bills. This is where hospital finance, tax law, and medical-debt policy all intersect.

Key Concept: Three different write-downs separate gross charges from net revenue. Contractual adjustments are agreed payer discounts (not uncompensated care). Charity care is free/discounted care for those who cannot pay. Bad debt is expected payment that was never received. Charity care + bad debt = uncompensated care.

stats.context: The median hospital uncompensated-care rate rose from 6.4% to 8.7% in the first half of 2023 alone — up by roughly a third in six months (industry data)

children.text: Contractual Adjustments: The Discount You Agreed To

A contractual adjustment (or contractual allowance) is the difference between a hospital’s gross charge and the amount a payer is contractually obligated to pay under its negotiated rate. If a hospital bills $5,000 for a procedure and the insurer’s contract says it will pay $1,200, the $3,800 difference is a contractual adjustment. Crucially, this is not money the hospital ever expected to receive — it is the discount baked into the contract the hospital signed.

This is the single most important point about contractual adjustments: they are not uncompensated care. The IRS is explicit that charity care excludes contractual adjustments with third-party payors, self-pay or prompt-pay discounts, and the gap between Medicare/Medicaid revenue and cost. A contractual adjustment simply reflects the reality that chargemaster prices are fiction and negotiated rates are the truth. By far the largest portion of the gap between gross and net revenue is contractual adjustments — and it represents a planned discount, not a loss or a charitable act.

body.message: Hospitals (and headlines) sometimes describe the gap between inflated chargemaster prices and negotiated payments as money "lost" or "given away." It is neither. A contractual adjustment is a discount off a fictional list price the hospital itself set artificially high — not a charitable contribution and not uncompensated care.
body.title: Contractual Adjustments Are Not "Losses"

children.text: Charity Care vs. Bad Debt: Intent Is the Dividing Line

Once contractual adjustments are set aside, the remaining unpaid amounts fall into two categories that look identical on a balance sheet but differ entirely in meaning. The dividing line is intent and expectation. Charity care is free or discounted care provided to patients who are unable to pay and who meet the hospital’s specified income and asset criteria. The hospital never expected payment — it deliberately provided the care for free or at a reduced cost to those in need.

Bad debt is the opposite: it represents services for which the hospital expected payment but never received it. Bad debt arises when patients who could potentially pay — or who never applied for financial assistance — simply do not pay their bills, whether because they cannot, will not, or never engaged with the billing process. The same unpaid $2,000 hospital bill is charity care if the patient qualified for and received financial assistance, but bad debt if the patient simply never paid and never applied.

left.label: Charity Care
points: Hospital never expected payment
Patient qualifies under income/asset criteria
Deliberately provided free or discounted
Counts toward nonprofit community benefit
Reflects the hospital’s charitable mission

right.label: Bad Debt
points: Hospital expected payment but did not collect
Patient may not have applied for assistance
Results from non-payment, not a granted discount
Treated as a credit loss, not charity
Often reflects gaps in screening or collections

body.title: Charity Care vs. Bad Debt

children.text: Together, charity care and bad debt make up uncompensated care — the overall measure of hospital care for which no payment was received from patient or insurer. This is the number the hospital industry cites to demonstrate the burden of serving the uninsured and underinsured. Note what it excludes: contractual adjustments and the Medicare/Medicaid shortfall are not part of uncompensated care, which is why precise definitions matter so much in debates about hospital finances.
Why the Distinction Has Legal Teeth: Section 501(r)

For nonprofit hospitals, the line between charity care and bad debt is not just an accounting nicety — it is a legal obligation tied to their tax exemption. Under Internal Revenue Code Section 501(r), enacted as part of the Affordable Care Act, tax-exempt hospitals must establish a written financial assistance policy (FAP) and a separate written policy for emergency medical care. The FAP must spell out the eligibility criteria for charity care, how patients apply, and how the hospital distinguishes charity care from bad debt.

Section 501(r) goes further, imposing concrete patient protections. It limits the amounts a hospital can charge financial-assistance-eligible patients for emergency or medically necessary care (they cannot be billed more than the amounts generally billed to insured patients), and it restricts "extraordinary collection actions" — such as lawsuits, wage garnishment, or reporting to credit agencies — until the hospital has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient qualifies for financial assistance. A hospital that fails these requirements risks its tax-exempt status.

body.content:
Imagine a uninsured patient treated in the ER who never fills out a financial-assistance application. If the hospital simply sends the bill to collections, the unpaid amount becomes bad debt — and the patient may face aggressive collection actions.

If instead the hospital screens the patient and determines they would have qualified for financial assistance (sometimes called "presumptive eligibility"), the same care is reclassified as charity care. The dollars written off are similar, but the meaning is opposite: one is a failure of process that harms a vulnerable patient and inflates bad debt; the other fulfills the hospital’s charitable mission and its 501(r) obligations. This is why screening patients for assistance is both an ethical and a financial priority.
body.title: Why "Presumptive Charity" Matters

children.text: The Bigger Picture: A Rising Burden

These categories are not static — they move with the economy and with policy. Uncompensated care has been an enormous and growing burden: U.S. hospitals accumulated nearly $745 billion in uncompensated care costs between 2000 and 2022. And it can spike fast: in the first half of 2023, the median hospital uncompensated-care rate jumped from 6.4% to 8.7% — a roughly one-third increase in just six months — as pandemic-era coverage protections unwound and more patients lost insurance.

The strain falls unevenly. Rural and safety-net hospitals, which serve disproportionate numbers of uninsured and low-income patients, absorb the most uncompensated care while having the fewest commercial patients to offset it. As uncompensated care rises, these facilities are forced to cut services, delay investments, or close — exactly the institutions whose communities can least afford to lose them. The 2025 Medicaid DSH cuts, discussed in the payer-mix lesson, land directly on top of this rising uncompensated-care burden.

body.analogy: Think of a hospital’s billed charges as a restaurant tab. The contractual adjustment is the standing discount the regular customer’s membership card always applies — expected and agreed. Charity care is the meal the owner deliberately comps for someone who clearly can’t pay. Bad debt is the diner who quietly walks out without paying a bill the owner fully expected to collect. All three reduce the till, but only a careless bookkeeper would record them the same way.
body.concept: Contractual adjustments vs. charity care vs. bad debt

children.text: For the student of hospital finance, the lesson is precision. When you see that a hospital "wrote off" a large sum, the first question is always: which kind of write-off? A mountain of contractual adjustments is normal and meaningless as a measure of charity. A large charity-care figure may reflect genuine community benefit. A swelling bad-debt figure may signal a broken financial-assistance process or a community losing insurance. Three numbers that look alike tell three completely different stories — and knowing which is which is the mark of someone who actually understands how hospitals get paid, and how they don’t.

points: The gap between a hospital’s gross charges and net revenue comes from three distinct categories: contractual adjustments, charity care, and bad debt — each with a different cause and meaning.
A contractual adjustment is the agreed difference between the chargemaster price and a payer’s negotiated rate; it is a planned discount, NOT uncompensated care and NOT a loss.

Charity care is care the hospital never expected to be paid for, provided free or discounted to patients who meet income/asset criteria; bad debt is care the hospital expected payment for but never received.
The dividing line between charity care and bad debt is intent and expectation — the same unpaid bill can be either, depending on whether the patient qualified for and received financial assistance.
Charity care plus bad debt equals uncompensated care; this measure excludes contractual adjustments and the Medicare/Medicaid payment shortfall.

IRC Section 501(r) requires tax-exempt hospitals to maintain a written financial assistance policy (FAP), limit charges to FAP-eligible patients, and restrict extraordinary collection actions until they determine assistance eligibility.

Screening patients for assistance ("presumptive eligibility") can reclassify bad debt as charity care — fulfilling the charitable mission and 501(r) obligations rather than subjecting vulnerable patients to aggressive collections.

Uncompensated care is large and rising — nearly $745 billion from 2000–2022, with the median rate jumping from 6.4% to 8.7% in the first half of 2023 — and it falls hardest on rural and safety-net hospitals.

children.text: The United States healthcare apparatus is less a system and more a collection of disconnected silos operating under conflicting incentives. While we lead the world in medical innovation and per capita spending, we trail significantly in population health outcomes. This paradox is not accidental; it is the structural result of three colliding forces: Economics, Policy, and Technology.
1. The Economic Engine: Incentivizing Volume Over Value

The fee-for-service (FFS) model remains the bedrock of American healthcare economics, despite decades of attempted reform. FFS fundamentally misaligns provider revenue with patient health. In this model, a healthy patient is a lost revenue stream, while a chronically ill patient represents a recurring financial asset. This economic gravity pulls the entire system toward intervention rather than prevention.
Key Insight: Until the economic architecture rewards the absence of disease as lucratively as its treatment, systemic insolvency remains a mathematical certainty.

children.text: 2. Policy: The Lag Between Legislation and Reality

Policy in the US is often reactive rather than proactive. Regulatory frameworks struggle to keep pace with the rapid evolution of care delivery models and digital health capabilities. The fragmentation between federal mandates (CMS) and state-level insurance regulations creates a compliance labyrinth that drains resources from patient care to administrative overhead.

children.text: 3. Technology: The Promise and the Silo

Technology is often touted as the savior of healthcare, yet without interoperability, it acts as an accelerant for fragmentation. Electronic Health Records (EHRs) were designed for billing, not clinical insight. While AI offers hope for administrative efficiency, its deployment is currently hampered by data governance issues and a lack of standardized integration protocols.

children.text: From "What Does Care Cost?" to "Which Care Makes Money?"

The previous lesson established that hospitals must allocate overhead to know the full cost of care. This lesson takes the next step: using cost information to answer the questions that actually drive hospital strategy. What does a single case — one knee replacement, one heart catheterization, one delivery — cost the hospital? And which clinical service lines are financially carrying the institution versus quietly draining it? These are the questions that determine where a hospital invests, what it markets, and sometimes what it stops doing altogether.

Two analytical tools answer them. Cost-per-case analysis estimates the cost of treating an individual patient or procedure. Service-line analysis aggregates those cases into clinical lines — cardiology, orthopedics, obstetrics, oncology — and measures the financial contribution of each. Together they turn the abstract idea of "cost" into concrete management decisions, and they reveal a truth that surprises many: a hospital’s busiest services are not always its most profitable, and its profitable services are not always the ones it promotes.

Key Concept: Cost-per-case analysis estimates what treating one patient or procedure costs the hospital. Service-line analysis aggregates cases into clinical lines (e.g., cardiology) to measure each line’s financial contribution — guiding investment, growth, and divestment decisions.

stats.context: Orthopedic surgeons generate an average of roughly $2.7 million in annual revenue for their affiliated hospitals — among the highest of any specialty (industry analyses)
stats.label: Orthopedic Surgeon Hospital Revenue

stats.label: Hip Replacement Margin Gap

children.text: How Hospitals Estimate Cost Per Case

There is no single perfect way to cost an individual case; hospitals use several methods that trade accuracy against effort. The simplest is the ratio of cost to charges (RCC): a department divides its total cost by its total charges to get a ratio (say, $40 million in cost against $100 million in charges equals 0.4), then multiplies a case’s charges by that ratio to estimate its cost. RCC is fast and useful for high-level departmental monitoring, but because it applies a single average ratio to every case, it is unreliable for individual case-level decisions.

A more refined approach is RVU-based costing, which uses relative value units — standardized measures of the resources (physician time, staff time, equipment, supplies) a procedure consumes. The hospital divides total expenses by total RVUs to get a cost per RVU, then multiplies by the RVUs assigned to a given procedure. This better reflects relative resource intensity, though it can misstate cost when local workflows or patient mix differ from the national averages embedded in the RVU scale. The most precise (and most labor-intensive) method is microcosting, which tallies the actual individual resources consumed by a specific case.

steps.description: Multiply a case’s charges by the department’s cost-to-charge ratio. Fast and good for high-level monitoring; too crude for case-level decisions.
steps.title: Ratio of cost to charges (RCC)

body.title: Three Common Cost-Per-Case Methods

body.message: RCC and similar average-based methods apply one ratio across every case, masking the real variation in resource use. They are fine for monitoring trends but dangerous for deciding whether a specific procedure or contract is profitable — that requires methods that reflect actual case-level resources.
body.title: Don’t Use Average Ratios for Specific Decisions

children.text: Contribution Margin: The Service-Line Workhorse

Once cases can be costed, the central tool for comparing them is contribution margin. Contribution margin measures the profitability of a case or service exclusive of indirect costs — that is, revenue minus the variable (direct) costs of providing the care, before subtracting overhead like administration, capital depreciation, and the cost of charity care. For a hospital paid a fixed amount per DRG (diagnosis-related group), contribution margin is calculated by comparing the case-related variable costs against the DRG payment for that case.

The reason contribution margin, rather than full cost, is the preferred tool for comparing treatments within a service line is subtle but important. Overhead is largely fixed and will be incurred whether or not a particular case is performed. So when deciding whether one more procedure is worth doing — or which procedures to grow — what matters is whether its revenue exceeds the additional variable cost it triggers. A procedure with a positive contribution margin helps cover the hospital’s fixed overhead even if, after full overhead allocation, it appears only marginally profitable.

The numbers vary enormously by procedure and market. One analysis found contribution margins running thousands of dollars higher in concentrated (less competitive) hospital markets — about $5,259 higher for angioplasty, $4,123 for total knee replacement, $5,889 for total hip replacement, and $7,931 for lumbar spine fusion — than in competitive markets, reflecting the pricing power that comes with market concentration. The same procedure can be a financial winner or a loser depending on the payment rate, the patient’s payer, and the hospital’s cost structure.
Which Service Lines Carry the Hospital?

Aggregate the contribution margins across a clinical line and you get service-line profitability — the financial scorecard hospital executives live by. The pattern is consistent across American hospitals: procedure-heavy specialties such as cardiovascular surgery, interventional cardiology, orthopedics, and neurosurgery consistently rank among the most profitable, while services like primary care, behavioral health, and obstetrics often run thin or negative margins despite being essential. An orthopedic surgeon generating around $2.7 million in annual hospital revenue illustrates why these lines command so much strategic attention.

This profitability is exactly what funds the rest of the hospital. Positive contribution margins on orthopedic and cardiac procedures — especially for privately insured patients — are used to subsidize less remunerative procedures and patient groups, from money-losing behavioral health to charity care. Service-line analysis thus reveals the internal cross-subsidy that mirrors the payer-mix cross-subsidy: a handful of profitable lines keep the doors open for the mission-driven but unprofitable ones.

body.content:
A community hospital might assume its high-volume emergency department or its busy primary care clinics are financial pillars, simply because they are always full.

Service-line profitability reporting often overturns that assumption: those high-activity areas may carry thin or negative margins, while a lower-volume cardiac or orthopedic line quietly generates most of the contribution to margin. Leaders who assume a service line is profitable based on volume, referrals, or "downstream revenue" frequently find those assumptions don’t survive scrutiny — high activity does not guarantee positive margin. This is why CFOs insist on actual margin data rather than volume as the basis for strategy.
body.title: Why Volume Can Deceive

children.text: Turning Analysis Into Strategy — Carefully

With reliable cost-per-case and service-line data, leadership can make deliberate choices: grow the service lines with strong margins, invest in the staff and equipment that expand them, scrutinize lines that consume heavy resources for little contribution, and renegotiate or restructure money-losing arrangements. The purest financial logic says concentrate on the profitable lines and shed the unprofitable ones. Many hospital strategies — the marketing push behind a new orthopedic institute, the expansion of a cardiac program — flow directly from this analysis.

body.analogy: A hospital’s service lines are like a grocery store’s departments. The store may sell mountains of low-margin staples like milk and bread (the high-volume ED and primary care), but it earns its real profit on the prepared foods and specialty items (cardiac and orthopedic procedures). A manager who judged each department only by how many customers it served would mismanage the store; the one who tracks margin by department knows which aisles fund the rest — and which loss leaders are worth keeping anyway.
body.concept: Service-line profitability analysis

children.text: But pure financial logic runs straight into the hospital’s mission and obligations. The unprofitable service lines — behavioral health, obstetrics in rural areas, primary care, charity care — are often the ones a community most needs and, for nonprofit hospitals, the ones their tax-exempt community-benefit obligations require. A hospital that shed every money-losing line would betray its purpose and likely its legal standing. Service-line analysis must therefore inform strategy without dictating it; the goal is a sustainable portfolio, not the elimination of everything that loses money.

There is also a methodological humility required. As the previous lesson showed, overhead allocation is judgment, so a line’s "profitability" depends partly on how costs were assigned. Good analysts distinguish contribution margin (clean, based on variable costs) from fully allocated margin (which carries allocation assumptions), and they incorporate downstream and total-cost-of-care effects rather than viewing each line in isolation. Done well, cost-per-case and service-line analysis are among the most powerful tools in hospital finance. Done carelessly, they can justify abandoning exactly the care a community depends on — which is why the numbers must always be read alongside the mission.

points: Cost-per-case analysis estimates what treating one patient or procedure costs; service-line analysis aggregates cases into clinical lines to measure each line’s financial contribution and guide strategy.

Common cost-per-case methods trade accuracy for effort: ratio of cost to charges (RCC) is fast but crude, RVU-based costing reflects relative resource intensity, and microcosting is most accurate but labor-intensive.
Average-ratio methods like RCC are appropriate for high-level monitoring but unreliable for specific case- or contract-level decisions, which require methods that capture actual resource use.

Contribution margin — revenue minus variable (direct) costs, before overhead — is the preferred tool for comparing treatments, because fixed overhead is incurred regardless and a positive contribution margin helps cover it.
Procedure margins vary widely by market and payer; contribution margins ran thousands of dollars higher in concentrated markets (e.g., ~$5,889 for total hip replacement) than in competitive ones.

Procedure-heavy lines (cardiovascular surgery, interventional cardiology, orthopedics, neurosurgery) are consistently most profitable, while primary care, behavioral health, and obstetrics often run thin or negative margins.
Profitable lines internally cross-subsidize unprofitable but essential ones; high volume does not guarantee positive margin, so strategy should rest on actual margin data, not activity.

Service-line analysis must inform but not dictate strategy — unprofitable lines are often mission-critical and required by nonprofit community-benefit obligations, and "profitability" depends partly on overhead-allocation judgment.

children.text: Deciding What the Plan Is Responsible For

When a state contracts with an MCO, one of the most consequential design decisions is also one of the least visible: exactly which services the plan is responsible for. It would seem obvious that a comprehensive plan should cover everything, but Medicaid programs routinely pull certain services out of the MCO contract and manage them separately. These decisions — to "carve in" or "carve out" a benefit — shape how care is delivered, how it is coordinated, and whether a member’s care is unified or fragmented across multiple systems.

The terminology is simple. A carve-in is a service that remains within or is integrated into the MCO’s responsibility — the plan provides it and is paid (through capitation) to cover it. A carve-out is a service removed from the MCO benefit package — the plan neither provides it nor receives payment for it, and the state manages that service through a separate arrangement, such as a limited-benefit plan or fee-for-service. Every Medicaid managed care program is, in effect, a set of decisions about which benefits to carve in and which to carve out.

These decisions carry real stakes for members and for the system. Carve-outs can bring specialized expertise to complex services but risk fragmenting a person’s care across disconnected plans; carve-ins promise integration and "whole-person care" but depend on the MCO actually coordinating well. This lesson examines which services are commonly carved out, the strong recent trend toward carving them back in, and the surprisingly mixed evidence on whether integration delivers.

Key Concept: A carve-in keeps a service within the MCO’s capitated responsibility; a carve-out removes it, so the plan neither provides nor is paid for it and the state manages it separately. The mix of carve-ins and carve-outs defines the scope of each MCO contract and how integrated a member’s care is.

stats.context: About 23 states carve behavioral health into their MCOs, with another 17 using mixed "carve-up" approaches — reflecting a strong shift toward integration (industry analyses)
stats.label: Carve In Behavioral Health

stats.context: 28 states and DC carve pharmacy into their MCOs, while 7 states carve prescription drugs out (KFF / AHIP)

children.text: What Gets Carved Out — and Why

A handful of services are carved out far more often than others, and they share a common trait: they are specialized, distinct from general medical care, and historically managed through their own systems. The services most frequently carved out of Medicaid managed care are behavioral health (mental health and substance use), dental, pharmacy, and non-emergency medical transportation (NEMT). Behavioral health is the most commonly carved-out service of all, reflecting a long history of separate mental health systems and specialized provider networks.

The rationale for carving out is real. A specialized service may benefit from a vendor with deep, focused expertise — a behavioral health organization that understands serious mental illness, a dental plan with a dedicated dentist network, a transportation broker that manages rides. Carving out lets the state contract with an entity built specifically for that service, rather than expecting a general medical MCO to manage something far outside its core competence. When done well, a carve-out delivers specialized management that a comprehensive plan might handle poorly.

But carve-outs come at a cost: fragmentation. When a member’s behavioral health is managed by one entity, their physical health by another, their pharmacy by a third, and their transportation by a fourth, no single organization sees the whole person. A patient with serious mental illness and diabetes may have their psychiatric care and their diabetes care managed by entities that never communicate. This fragmentation is precisely the problem that the integration movement, discussed next, aims to solve.

left.label: Carve-In (Integrated)
points: Service stays within the MCO’s capitation
One plan responsible for the whole person
Easier coordination across physical and other care
Depends on the MCO actually integrating care
Aligned with "whole-person care" goals

right.label: Carve-Out (Separate)
points: Service removed from the MCO benefit package
Managed by a specialized vendor or fee-for-service
Brings focused expertise to complex services
Risks fragmenting a member’s care across systems
Requires deliberate cross-system coordination

body.title: Carve-In vs. Carve-Out

children.text: The Trend: Carving Back In

Over the past decade, the dominant trend has been to carve services back in — to integrate them into comprehensive MCOs in pursuit of "whole-person care." The shift in behavioral health is striking: the number of states with behavioral health carve-in arrangements grew rapidly, more than quadrupling in a single recent year, and today roughly 23 states carve behavioral health into their MCOs, with another 17 using mixed "carve-up" approaches. Meanwhile, primary "horizontal" behavioral health carve-outs to separate care-management organizations have declined — from about 13 states in 2011 to roughly 9 — driven by a clear policy preference for integration.

Pharmacy shows the same integrationist tilt: 28 states and the District of Columbia carve pharmacy into their MCOs, compared with just 7 that carve prescription drugs out. The logic behind carving in is intuitive and powerful — when one plan is responsible for all of a member’s care, it has both the information and the financial incentive to coordinate across physical health, behavioral health, and pharmacy, treating the person as a whole rather than a collection of disconnected benefits.

This integration goal connects directly to the financial model. A fully capitated MCO responsible for the whole person internalizes the trade-offs: it benefits financially when better behavioral health care reduces avoidable medical admissions, or when managing medications prevents hospitalizations. Under carve-outs, those savings flow to a different entity — a version of the "wrong pocket problem." Carving in aligns the incentives so that one plan profits from coordinating the member’s total care, which is the theoretical heart of the whole-person-care argument.
Does Integration Actually Work?

Given the strength of the carve-in trend, one might expect clear evidence that integration improves care. The reality is more humbling. Research on whether carve-in models deliver better outcomes is genuinely mixed. Some studies have found that access to and utilization of services was not better at integrated MCOs compared to carve-out models, finding no consistent association between integration and claims-based measures of utilization and quality. In other words, simply putting a benefit inside the MCO contract did not, by itself, produce better care.

Yet other evidence is more encouraging. In New York and Oregon, behavioral health integration led to higher use of both behavioral and physical health outpatient services among individuals with serious mental illness and those with milder behavioral health needs — suggesting integration can improve access when implemented well. The divergence points to a crucial lesson: the outcome depends not on the contracting structure alone, but on how the integration is actually executed.

body.message: Putting two benefits in the same MCO contract (financial integration) does not guarantee that the administration and delivery of care are actually coordinated (clinical integration). States seeking real integration must pair the contracting change with investments in workforce, data analytics, and performance oversight — otherwise a carve-in is integration in name only.
body.title: Financial Integration Is Not Clinical Integration

children.text: Designing the Benefit Package

For a state Medicaid program, the carve-in/carve-out decision is a balancing act with no universally right answer. Carving in offers the promise of coordinated, whole-person care and aligned incentives, but only if the MCO genuinely integrates the service rather than administering it in a silo. Carving out offers specialized expertise and focused management, but at the risk of fragmenting the member’s experience. The right choice depends on the service, the state’s MCO capabilities, the strength of specialized vendors, and how much the state is willing to invest in making integration real.

body.analogy: Carve-ins and carve-outs are like deciding whether one general contractor handles your entire home renovation or you hire separate specialists for plumbing, electrical, and roofing. The single contractor (carve-in) can coordinate everything and is accountable for the whole project — but only if they actually manage the subtrades well. Hiring separate specialists (carve-out) gets you deep expertise in each area, but now someone has to make sure the plumber and electrician don’t work at cross-purposes. Neither is automatically better; it depends on the contractor’s coordinating skill.
body.concept: Carve-in vs. carve-out benefit design

children.text: Two requirements cut across the decision regardless of structure. First, care coordination: whether a service is carved in or out, states and plans are responsible for coordinating care across delivery systems so the member does not fall through the cracks. Second, behavioral health parity: federal rules require that behavioral health benefits be covered on par with medical benefits, a requirement that applies however behavioral health is structured. These obligations mean that even a carve-out cannot be an excuse to ignore a service or treat mental health as second-class.

This lesson opens the benefits-and-network module by defining the scope of what an MCO actually manages. The next lessons build on it: network adequacy standards apply to the services a plan covers, and provider credentialing concerns the providers a plan must contract with for those covered benefits. The carve-in/carve-out decision is logically first because it determines the boundaries of the plan’s responsibility — everything else in benefit and network management operates within the scope these decisions set.

points: A carve-in keeps a service within the MCO’s capitated responsibility, while a carve-out removes it so the plan neither provides nor is paid for it and the state manages it separately.

The services most commonly carved out are behavioral health (the most frequent), dental, pharmacy, and non-emergency medical transportation — specialized services historically run through their own systems.
Carve-outs bring specialized vendor expertise but risk fragmenting a member’s care across disconnected entities that may never communicate.

The dominant decade-long trend is to carve services back in for "whole-person care": about 23 states now carve in behavioral health (with 17 mixed "carve-up" approaches), horizontal BH carve-outs fell from ~13 states in 2011 to ~9, and 28 states plus DC carve in pharmacy versus 7 that carve it out.

Carving in aligns incentives by making one capitated plan responsible for the whole person, so it benefits financially from coordinating across physical, behavioral, and pharmacy care (avoiding a "wrong pocket" problem).

The evidence that integration improves outcomes is mixed — some studies found no utilization/quality advantage for integrated MCOs, while New York and Oregon saw higher outpatient service use after behavioral health integration.
Financial integration (same contract) is not the same as clinical integration (coordinated delivery); real integration requires investments in workforce, data analytics, and performance oversight.

Regardless of structure, states and plans must coordinate care across delivery systems and comply with behavioral health parity, and the carve-in/carve-out decision sets the scope within which network adequacy and credentialing then operate.

children.text: Why a Crisis System Is Needed

A behavioral health crisis — a suicidal emergency, a psychotic episode, an overdose, or acute distress — demands an immediate response. Yet for decades the United States lacked a dedicated system to provide one. When someone was in a mental health crisis, the default responders were too often the police and the emergency department: settings designed for crime and physical trauma, not for psychiatric emergencies.

The consequences of this default were serious. People in crisis ended up in jail or in long emergency-department "boarding" waits, sometimes escalating an encounter that should have been de-escalated, and occasionally with tragic outcomes when armed police responded to someone who needed care rather than confrontation. The recognition that mental health crises require a mental health response — not a law-enforcement or generic-medical one — is the foundation of the modern crisis continuum.

This connects directly to the burden described at the start of this course: with tens of thousands of suicide deaths each year and tens of millions of people living with behavioral health conditions, a functioning crisis system is not a luxury. It is a core piece of the safety net, and building one has become a major national priority.

A behavioral health crisis requires a behavioral health response. For decades the U.S. defaulted to police and emergency departments; the modern crisis continuum is built on the principle that mental health emergencies need mental health responders.
The Crisis Continuum: Three Pillars

SAMHSA’s National Guidelines for Behavioral Health Crisis Care define what a complete crisis system looks like, organized around three essential elements — often summarized as "someone to contact, someone to respond, and a safe place for help." Together these three pillars form a continuum that can meet a person wherever their crisis is.

The first pillar, someone to contact, is a crisis line: a number a person can call, text, or chat any hour of the day to reach trained crisis counselors — the role 988 now fills nationally. The second, someone to respond, is mobile crisis teams: trained behavioral health responders (rather than police) who can come to the person in the community to assess and de-escalate on-site. The third, a safe place for help, is crisis receiving and stabilization services: places a person can go for short-term care instead of an emergency department or jail.

The power of the continuum is that the three pillars work together. A 988 counselor can dispatch a mobile crisis team; a mobile team can bring someone to a crisis stabilization facility; and stabilization can connect the person to ongoing treatment — all without defaulting to police or the ED. SAMHSA updated these national guidelines in 2025, reflecting new research and emerging best practices for a coordinated crisis system.

body.title: The Three Pillars of the Crisis Continuum

children.text: 988: The National Crisis Line

The centerpiece of the contact pillar is 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. In July 2022, the United States transitioned the older ten-digit National Suicide Prevention Lifeline to the simple, three-digit 988 — an easy-to-remember number analogous to 911, but for behavioral health crises. It provides free, confidential, 24/7 support for people in suicidal, mental health, or substance-use crises, by call, text, or chat.

988 is not a single call center but a national network of more than 200 local and state crisis centers, supported by SAMHSA. Routing calls to local centers helps connect people to resources in their own community. The transition to 988 was explicitly framed by SAMHSA as a first step toward a fully transformed crisis care system — the contact pillar that the response and stabilization pillars are meant to build around.

Demand has been substantial and growing. Since its July 2022 launch, 988 received roughly 16.5 million contacts — about 11.1 million calls, 2.9 million texts, and 2.4 million chats — with monthly volume rising over time and text and chat growing especially fast. Importantly, the vast majority of contacts are resolved on the line: more than 98% of calls are handled without dispatching emergency services, underscoring that most crises can be defused through skilled conversation.

children.text: Does It Work? Early Evidence

The system is young, but early evidence is encouraging. The national answer rate for 988 calls, texts, and chats rose substantially after launch — to around 91% — while wait times fell, meaning more people in crisis are actually reaching a counselor quickly. Higher answer rates matter because an unanswered crisis line is no help at all.

Most strikingly, research has begun to link 988 to reduced suicide. A study published in JAMA found that after the launch of 988, suicide deaths among adolescents and young adults dropped about 11% compared with projected rates, and that the states with the largest increases in answered calls saw the largest declines in suicide rates. While more research is needed, this is exactly the kind of population-level signal the system was built to produce.

These results reinforce the core lesson of the whole crisis continuum: when people in crisis can reach skilled help immediately, outcomes improve. The contact pillar is necessary but not sufficient on its own — its full promise depends on the response and stabilization pillars being built out so that 988 can connect callers to in-person help when a phone call is not enough.

children.text: Building Out the Continuum — Including in Vermont

A crisis line only works if there is somewhere to route people who need more than a phone call. That is why states are working to build out the response and stabilization pillars — mobile crisis teams and crisis receiving facilities — to complement 988. In Vermont, this builds directly on the infrastructure covered earlier in this course: the Designated Agencies have long provided community crisis services, giving the state an existing local foundation on which to connect 988 to in-person care.

The crisis continuum is also where many threads of this course converge. It depends on integration (linking crisis care to ongoing treatment), on payment reform (funding mobile teams and stabilization, which fee-for-service neglects), on the community-based providers like Vermont’s Designated Agencies, and on treating behavioral health emergencies with the seriousness given to physical ones — the parity principle in action.

The transformation is far from complete. Funding, workforce, and the uneven build-out of mobile crisis and stabilization services remain real challenges, and 988’s long-term financing is an ongoing policy question. But the direction is clear and increasingly evidence-backed: a coordinated crisis continuum, anchored by 988, that responds to behavioral health emergencies with care rather than handcuffs.

body.message: 988 is the contact pillar, but a crisis line is only as good as what it can connect people to. Without robust mobile crisis teams and crisis stabilization facilities — the response and "safe place" pillars — callers still risk defaulting to the emergency department or police. Building the full continuum is the unfinished work.
body.title: A Line Is Only the Beginning

children.text: No Health System Can Do This Alone

The recurring lesson of this entire course is that most of what produces health happens outside the health care system — in housing, food, neighborhoods, education, and social conditions. That fact has an unavoidable implication: a health system, no matter how well-run, cannot fix those upstream conditions by itself. Hospitals do not build housing, run food banks, operate transit systems, or fund early childhood education. The organizations that do those things live in other sectors entirely.

This is why cross-sector partnership is not an optional add-on to equity work but a structural necessity. Closing disparities requires health systems to work with community-based organizations, social-service agencies, public health departments, housing authorities, schools, and local government — each of which controls levers the health system does not. The hard part is that these sectors have different funding streams, cultures, timelines, and data systems, which makes genuine collaboration difficult.

This lesson covers how that collaboration is structured: the models that connect health care to community resources, the financing and legal mechanisms that fund cross-sector work, and the named programs that show what works and what is hard. The goal is to move from the abstract idea that "we should partner" to a concrete understanding of how partnerships are actually built and sustained.

Most health is produced outside health care, so health systems cannot close disparities alone. Cross-sector partnership with community, social-service, public-health, and government organizations is a structural necessity, not an add-on.
The Accountable Health Communities Model

The most ambitious federal test of cross-sector partnership was the CMS Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Model, which ran from 2017 to 2023. Its theory was simple and directly tied to the SDOH evidence in this course: systematically screen Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries for health-related social needs — housing, food, transportation, utilities, and interpersonal safety — and connect those with needs to community resources, then measure whether doing so reduced cost and utilization.

The model was built around "bridge organizations" — twenty-eight diverse entities, including community-based organizations, hospitals, health systems, payers, and health information exchanges, that coordinated screening and referral across sectors in their communities. In its assistance track, some beneficiaries were randomly offered navigation services to help them actually connect with resources, allowing a rigorous evaluation. Over its life, AHC organizations screened more than one million beneficiaries — a genuinely large-scale test.

The results were instructive and mixed. In the assistance track, the evaluation found reductions in total expenditures and unplanned inpatient readmissions, with Medicaid expenditures down about 3% and Medicare about 4% for beneficiaries who received navigation. These were meaningful but modest effects, and a central lesson was that screening and referral alone are not enough if the community resources people are referred to do not have the capacity to meet the need. AHC demonstrated both the promise and the limits of the screen-and-refer approach.

body.content:
AHC was CMS's flagship cross-sector demonstration: screen Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries for five core social needs and connect them to community resources through 28 "bridge organizations." It screened over one million beneficiaries.
In the randomized assistance track, beneficiaries who received navigation showed reduced total expenditures and unplanned readmissions — Medicaid spending down ~3%, Medicare ~4%. A key lesson: referral only works if community resources have the capacity to meet the identified needs, so investing in community capacity matters as much as screening.

children.text: Connecting the Sectors: Referral Networks and Infrastructure

For cross-sector partnership to function day to day, health care and community organizations need a shared way to connect patients to services and track what happens. This is the same closed-loop referral infrastructure introduced in the SDOH screening lesson — platforms like Unite Us and findhelp that link clinical settings with community-based organizations, route electronic referrals, and report back whether the patient was actually served.

These platforms matter for partnership because they create the connective tissue that makes collaboration operational rather than aspirational. Without shared infrastructure, a "partnership" is often just a list of phone numbers and a hope that patients follow through. With it, a clinic and a food bank can function as parts of a single coordinated network, with visibility into whether referrals close. The infrastructure does not replace relationships, but it makes the relationships scalable.

Crucially, this infrastructure also begins to address the capacity problem that AHC surfaced. By tracking referral outcomes across a network, it makes visible where community resources are overwhelmed or missing — which is the information needed to direct investment toward building community capacity rather than just generating more unfulfilled referrals. Partnership infrastructure, used well, is both an operational tool and a planning instrument.

children.text: Financing Cross-Sector Work: Community Benefit

Partnerships need money, and one of the most significant funding levers is the community benefit obligation that nonprofit hospitals carry. Most US hospitals are tax-exempt 501(c)(3) organizations, and in exchange for that exemption they are required to provide community benefit. The Affordable Care Act sharpened these requirements considerably, turning a vague expectation into specific, enforceable obligations.

Under Section 9007 of the ACA (codified as Internal Revenue Code Section 501(r)), every tax-exempt hospital must conduct a Community Health Needs Assessment (CHNA) at least once every three years, with input from people representing the broad interests of the community, including public health expertise — and must adopt an implementation strategy describing how it will address the priority needs identified. Hospitals report their community benefit spending and compliance on IRS Form 990, Schedule H. The requirements have teeth: a hospital that fails to conduct its triennial CHNA can face a $50,000 excise tax.

For equity work, the CHNA process is a major opportunity. It legally requires hospitals to systematically assess community needs in partnership with community voices, and to commit to addressing them — which is essentially a mandate for cross-sector engagement. Health systems that treat the CHNA as a genuine planning process, rather than a compliance checkbox, can use it to direct community benefit dollars toward the social conditions and community partners that actually move equity. It is one of the clearest places where law, financing, and cross-sector partnership converge.

children.text: What Makes Partnerships Succeed

Cross-sector partnerships are easy to announce and hard to sustain. The evidence and experience point to a few factors that separate durable, effective partnerships from press-release collaborations. The first is genuine shared power and trust, especially with community-based organizations. Health systems are large and well-resourced; community organizations are often small and close to the community. Partnerships fail when the health system treats community partners as subcontractors rather than equals — and when it extracts data and effort without sharing resources and decision-making.

The second is sustainable financing for the community side. The AHC lesson — that referrals fail when community capacity is lacking — generalizes: a health system that refers patients to an underfunded food bank or housing agency without investing in that organization's capacity is setting the partnership up to fail. Effective partnerships move money, not just referrals, toward the community organizations doing the upstream work, whether through community benefit dollars, contracts, or shared-savings arrangements.

The third is shared data and aligned goals. Partners need compatible ways to share information (within privacy rules), common definitions of success, and the patience to work across the very different timelines and cultures of health care, social services, and government. None of this is easy, which is exactly why cross-sector partnership is genuinely hard work rather than a slogan. But because the upstream conditions that drive disparities live outside health care, this hard work is unavoidable for any organization serious about equity.

body.message: A common failure mode is the health system extracting data and referrals from community-based organizations while controlling all the resources and decisions. Durable partnerships require shared power, shared data, and shared money — investing in the capacity of community partners rather than offloading work onto under-resourced organizations and expecting them to absorb it.

children.text: How Hospitals Pay for the Big Things

A new hospital tower can cost hundreds of millions of dollars. A major system-wide electronic health record can run into the billions. No hospital pays for investments of this scale out of its annual operating surplus — the thin margins covered in earlier lessons make that impossible. Instead, hospitals borrow, and the dominant way they borrow is by issuing bonds. Understanding debt financing — how hospitals issue bonds, how credit ratings determine what they pay, and how covenants constrain what they do afterward — is essential to understanding how hospitals fund their futures.

For nonprofit hospitals, debt financing comes with a powerful advantage rooted in their tax status. Because they are 501(c)(3) charitable organizations, they can issue tax-exempt (municipal) debt — bonds whose interest is exempt from federal (and often state) income tax for the investor. That tax exemption lets investors accept a lower interest rate, and nonprofit hospital borrowers save, on average, an estimated 2 percentage points on their borrowing compared to taxable bonds or bank financing. On a $300 million bond, two points is enormous, and those savings ultimately lower the cost of care.

But borrowing at attractive rates is not automatic. A hospital must convince investors it will repay, and the entire machinery of credit ratings and bond covenants exists to price and police that risk. The story of hospital debt financing is the story of how a hospital’s financial health — the ratios from earlier lessons — translates directly into the cost and availability of the capital it needs to survive.

Key Concept: Nonprofit hospitals fund major investments primarily by issuing tax-exempt (municipal) bonds, saving roughly 2 percentage points versus taxable financing. Credit ratings determine the interest rate they pay, and bond covenants impose ongoing financial requirements they must meet.

children.text: Tax-Exempt Bonds: The Workhorse of Hospital Capital

When a nonprofit hospital issues a bond, it is borrowing from investors who buy the bonds and receive interest payments over time, with the principal repaid at maturity. These are typically issued through a state or local financing authority, which is what gives them their tax-exempt, "municipal" character. The proceeds fund capital projects — and in recent years, new issuance has gone primarily toward renovation and expansion of existing facilities and growth opportunities, especially ambulatory (outpatient) expansion that reflects care moving out of inpatient settings.

The municipal hospital bond market is cyclical and revealing. After three years of declining volume, 2024 saw a large rebound, with healthcare bond issuance jumping more than 100% year over year as hospitals returned to the capital markets to fund delayed projects. This rebound signals both pent-up capital needs from years of deferred investment and enough financial recovery for hospitals to take on new debt — connecting directly to the rising capital-expenditure trends discussed in the budgeting lessons.
Credit Ratings: The Price of Trust

Before a hospital can sell bonds at a good rate, it must be rated. The three major credit rating agencies — Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s (S&P), and Fitch — evaluate a hospital based on the likelihood that it will default on its debt, examining metrics like its cost structure, local demographics, and payer mix, alongside the financial ratios covered earlier (operating margin, days cash on hand, debt service coverage). The rating they assign is a letter grade that investors use to judge risk.

The most important dividing line is investment grade. Bonds rated BBB- or higher by S&P and Fitch, or Baa3 or higher by Moody’s, are investment grade; anything below is "speculative" or "junk." This line matters enormously because many institutional investors are restricted to investment-grade securities, so a hospital that falls below it loses access to a huge pool of buyers. The rating directly sets the interest rate: a higher rating signals lower risk, so investors accept lower returns, and the hospital borrows more cheaply.

Ratings move, and the direction has been worrying. In 2024, the three agencies collectively issued 95 downgrades against just 37 upgrades — an improvement over 2023’s 116 downgrades and 33 upgrades, but still a lopsided picture. Many downgrades reflected ongoing expense pressure that outpaced revenue growth, even as patient volumes recovered and reliance on contract labor declined. Each downgrade is more than a label: it tangibly raises the hospital’s future borrowing costs and signals deteriorating financial health to the entire market.

body.message: When a hospital’s rating falls, investors demand more return for the added perceived risk, pushing up interest rates on new debt, widening spreads, and triggering more restrictive terms and reserve requirements. A drop below investment grade can be severely detrimental — sharply limiting access to capital and harming even existing bondholders.
body.title: A Downgrade Is Expensive — Especially Below Investment Grade

children.text: Covenants: The Strings Attached to Borrowing

Lending a hospital hundreds of millions of dollars is risky, so bondholders protect themselves with covenants — contractual promises the hospital must keep for as long as the bonds are outstanding. The two most common financial covenants come straight from the ratios covered earlier. A debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) covenant requires the hospital to maintain enough cash flow to cover its principal and interest payments, with minimums often ranging from 1.10 to 1.25. A days cash on hand covenant requires the hospital to keep a minimum liquidity cushion, often in the range of 40 to 80 days.

These covenants are typically consolidated through a master trust indenture, a financing structure that pools the credit of multiple nonprofit entities into an "obligated group" and consolidates all financial covenants into a single document used across the system’s bond issues. The structure lets a health system borrow on the combined strength of its members. Privately placed bonds held by banks often carry more stringent covenants than publicly issued bonds under a master indenture — but they offer the flexibility of negotiating directly with the lender if trouble arises.

children.text: Breaching a covenant is serious. A covenant default can trigger remedies ranging from penalty rates to, in the worst case, acceleration — the lender demanding immediate repayment of the entire balance. Because the consequences are so severe, hospitals approaching a covenant breach must take aggressive early action: cutting costs, raising liquidity, or negotiating waivers and amendments with bondholders or banks before the breach occurs. Covenant management is a core discipline of hospital treasury operations, not a back-office afterthought.
Why Debt Financing Ties the Whole Course Together

Debt financing is where nearly every concept in hospital finance converges. The financial ratios from Module 1 are not academic — they are literally the inputs rating agencies use and the thresholds covenants enforce. A hospital’s payer mix and operating margin shape its rating; its days cash on hand is both a liquidity measure and a covenant requirement; its debt service coverage determines whether it can borrow more. The abstract idea of "financial health" becomes concrete the moment a hospital tries to raise capital.

body.analogy: A hospital borrowing through bonds is like a homebuyer getting a mortgage. The credit rating is the credit score: a better score means a lower interest rate and access to more lenders. The tax exemption is like a special low-rate program only certain buyers qualify for. The covenants are the mortgage terms — keep your income above a threshold, maintain insurance — and breaking them can let the bank call the loan. Just as a homebuyer’s whole financial life shapes their mortgage, a hospital’s entire financial profile shapes its access to capital.
body.concept: Hospital bonds, ratings, and covenants

children.text: This convergence creates a powerful feedback loop, for better or worse. A financially strong hospital earns a high rating, borrows cheaply, invests in facilities and technology that strengthen it further, and easily meets its covenants. A struggling hospital gets downgraded, borrows expensively (if at all), cannot fund the investments that would improve its position, and risks breaching covenants — accelerating its decline. Debt financing can be a ladder up or a spiral down, and which one depends on the fundamentals built in every prior lesson.

For the student of hospital finance, debt financing is the capstone of the capital side of the field. It shows why margins, liquidity, and coverage ratios matter beyond the financial statements: they determine whether a hospital can afford to build, expand, and modernize — or whether it is locked out of the capital markets precisely when it most needs them. Mastering bonds, ratings, and covenants means seeing how a hospital’s past financial performance becomes the constraint and the engine of its future.

Healthcare bond issuance rebounded sharply in 2024 (up more than 100% year over year), with proceeds going largely to renovation, expansion, and ambulatory (outpatient) growth.

The three major rating agencies — Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch — assess default risk using cost structure, demographics, payer mix, and financial ratios, assigning a credit rating that sets the hospital’s borrowing cost.
Investment grade (BBB-/Baa3 or higher) is the critical threshold; falling below it cuts off access to many institutional investors and sharply raises borrowing costs.
Rating trends have been negative: agencies issued 95 downgrades versus 37 upgrades in 2024, driven by expenses outpacing revenue, and each downgrade raises future borrowing costs.

Bond covenants impose ongoing requirements — commonly a debt service coverage ratio (often 1.10–1.25 minimum) and days cash on hand (often 40–80 days) — frequently consolidated via a master trust indenture and obligated group.
Breaching a covenant can trigger penalty rates or acceleration (demand for immediate full repayment), so hospitals must act aggressively and early to cut costs, raise liquidity, or negotiate waivers.
Debt financing ties the whole course together: the financial ratios are the very inputs rating agencies use and covenants enforce, creating a feedback loop that can be a ladder up or a spiral down.

children.text: Knowing Why Isn't Enough

The previous lesson explained why claims are denied. But understanding root causes does nothing for revenue unless an organization actually works the denials it receives — and, just as importantly, learns from them to prevent the next ones. That requires a structured denial management workflow: a repeatable system for handling denials, not a pile of rejected claims someone gets to eventually.

The stakes of not having one are alarming. By industry estimates, somewhere between 35 and 65 percent of denied claims are never reworked at all — not appealed, not resubmitted, just abandoned. That is earned revenue, already worked for and delivered, simply written off because no one got to it in time or at all. A weak denial workflow is one of the largest silent revenue losses in health care.

A denial workflow turns that around. As one practitioner put it bluntly: if you are not tracking denials by type, payer, date received, and appeal outcome, you do not have a denial management workflow — you have a "hope-and-resubmit" strategy. This lesson lays out what a real workflow looks like.
A denial management workflow is a repeatable system to work and learn from denials. Without one, 35-65% of denied claims are never reworked — earned revenue abandoned simply because no one got to it.
The IMMP Framework

A useful structure for the workflow is the IMMP framework — Identify, Manage, Monitor, and Prevent. It captures the full lifecycle: catch the denial, work it, track the outcome, and feed the lessons back upstream to stop it recurring. The framework's power is that it links the tactical (working today's denials) to the strategic (reducing tomorrow's).

Identify means promptly catching every denial as remittances come in and categorizing each by root cause — administrative errors (missing info, authorization), clinical denials (medical necessity, coding), and technical rejections (electronic submission problems). Manage means routing each denial to the right person to correct, resubmit, or appeal it. Monitor means tracking outcomes — what was recovered, what was lost, which payers and reasons dominate.

Prevent is the part that actually shrinks the denial rate. It uses the patterns from Monitor to fix the upstream process responsible — registration training, authorization workflow redesign, coding education. Without Prevent, a team is on a treadmill, working the same denials forever; with it, the denial volume itself falls over time.
