children.text: Reconciliation: Making Sure It All Matches

Posting and reconciliation are related but distinct. Posting records the payment; reconciliation is the broader quality-control step that verifies everything matches afterward. The most fundamental reconciliation is deposit matching — confirming, ideally daily, that the money actually deposited in the bank (the EFT or checks) matches the remittances posted in the system.

Deposit matching catches a whole class of problems: a remittance posted but the money never arrived, money deposited but not posted, or amounts that do not tie out. Until the posted payments reconcile to the bank deposits, the organization cannot trust its own revenue numbers. This is the financial-integrity backbone of the back end — the point where the books are proven to reflect reality.

Reconciliation also includes payment variance analysis: checking that what was paid matches what the payer contract said should be paid. This is exactly the underpayment detection from the payer-contracts lesson, and payment posting is where it operationally happens — as each payment posts, it can be compared to the expected reimbursement, and any shortfall flagged for recovery.

body.message: Posting records a payment; reconciliation proves it is correct. Skipping reconciliation — especially daily deposit matching of posted remittances against actual bank deposits — means the organization's revenue figures may not reflect reality, with money posted-but-not-received or received-but-not-posted going undetected.
body.title: Posting Is Not Reconciliation

children.text: Why Accurate Posting Matters

Payment posting is deceptively high-stakes because everything downstream depends on it being right. A key metric is the posting accuracy rate — the percentage of audited postings with no errors in patient, claim, amount, or adjustment. Wrong posting distorts patient balances (billing patients the wrong amount), corrupts AR (making accounts look paid or unpaid incorrectly), and breaks the KPIs that drive management decisions.

Accurate posting is also the trigger point for back-end follow-up. As payments post, the system should automatically route exceptions: underpayments flagged for recovery, denials sent to the denial workflow, and remaining patient balances queued for patient billing. Posting is not just record-keeping — it is the dispatcher that hands each claim's outcome to the right next process.

In short, payment posting closes the loop on the payer side of each claim: it records the truth, reconciles it against the bank and the contract, and dispatches the leftovers (denials, underpayments, patient balances) to be worked. Once the payer has paid and posted, what remains is the unpaid balance — which leads directly into the next two lessons on accounts receivable management and patient collections.

children.text: The Rulebook Behind Every Medicaid Managed Care Contract

Medicaid is a federal-state partnership: states run their programs, but they do so within rules set by the federal government, and they receive federal matching dollars only if they follow those rules. For managed care, the master rulebook has a name worth memorizing: 42 CFR Part 438. This section of the Code of Federal Regulations governs Medicaid managed care organizations and defines what states must require of the plans they contract with — from network adequacy to financial standards to quality and beneficiary protections.

Understanding Part 438 is essential because it is the framework within which everything else in this course operates. When a state writes an MCO contract, sets capitation rates, defines network standards, or oversees plan performance, it is implementing requirements that ultimately trace back to Part 438. The companion rules for the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) live at 42 CFR Part 457, applying parallel managed care protections to CHIP enrollees. Together, these regulations are the federal floor for Medicaid and CHIP managed care.

This framework is not static. In 2024, CMS substantially updated it through a major final rule, raising the bar on access, finance, and quality. This lesson covers both the enduring structure of Part 438 and the significant 2024 changes that now shape how states must manage their managed care programs.

Key Concept: 42 CFR Part 438 is the federal regulation governing Medicaid managed care, setting the rules states must follow for network adequacy, finance (including MLR), quality, and beneficiary protections. CHIP managed care is governed by the parallel 42 CFR Part 457.

stats.context: If a state sets a minimum MLR for its managed care plans under Part 438, it must be equal to or higher than 85 percent (42 CFR 438.8)

children.text: What Part 438 Requires

Part 438 is organized around the state’s responsibilities as the entity contracting with private plans. Its core requirements span the operational territory this course will explore. On network adequacy, a state that contracts with a managed care plan must develop and enforce network adequacy standards, including quantitative standards for specified provider types. On finance, it governs how capitation rates must be actuarially sound and sets the rules for the medical loss ratio. On quality, it requires quality assessment and improvement programs and external review. And throughout, it establishes beneficiary protections — enrollment, grievances and appeals, and access to care.

A central financial requirement is the medical loss ratio (MLR). Part 438 provides that if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its plans, that minimum must be equal to or higher than 85 percent, and the MLR must be calculated and reported each year by the plan. The MLR — covered in depth in its own lesson — ensures that at least 85 cents of every capitation dollar goes toward medical care and quality rather than profit and administration. States have been required to submit summary MLR reports to CMS since rating periods beginning July 1, 2017.

Part 438 also imposes detailed network adequacy requirements at section 438.68. States must develop quantitative network adequacy standards for certain provider types covered under the contract, and states whose contracts cover long-term services and supports (LTSS) must develop quantitative standards for LTSS provider types as well. These requirements exist to ensure that the promise of a "network" is real — that enrollees can actually reach the providers their plan claims to offer.
The 2024 Final Rule: Access, Finance, and Quality

In 2024, CMS issued one of the most significant updates to the managed care framework in years. The "Medicaid and CHIP Managed Care Access, Finance, and Quality" final rule (CMS-2439-F) was published May 10, 2024, and became effective July 9, 2024. It advances CMS’s efforts to improve access to care, quality and health outcomes, and health equity for Medicaid and CHIP managed care enrollees — and it applies to both Part 438 (Medicaid) and Part 457 (CHIP). The rule is best understood through its three named pillars: access, finance, and quality.

The most concrete and consequential changes are on access. For the first time, the rule sets specific, enforceable appointment wait time standards: enrollees must be able to get a routine appointment within 15 business days for primary care (adult and pediatric) and for OB/GYN services, and within 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use services. These are national floors that translate the abstract idea of "network adequacy" into a measurable patient experience — how long someone actually has to wait to see a provider.

On finance, the rule addresses state directed payments and reduces some state burdens while specifying MLR requirements and adding standards for "in lieu of services and settings" (ILOS) — alternative services like housing or nutrition supports that plans can offer in place of traditional covered benefits. On quality, it establishes a quality rating system for Medicaid and CHIP managed care plans, a kind of consumer-facing report card. Together these pillars push the framework from process requirements toward measurable outcomes and transparency.

children.text: Enforcement: The Secret Shopper

A standard means nothing without enforcement, and the 2024 rule pairs its access requirements with a specific monitoring tool: the secret shopper survey. States must use annual secret shopper surveys to determine plan compliance with the appointment wait time standards and to assess the accuracy of electronic provider directories. A secret shopper survey involves a third party posing as an enrollee and attempting to schedule an appointment with a provider listed in the plan’s directory — testing whether the network is real and accessible in practice, not just on paper.

The methodology is specified to make the results meaningful. The surveys must use a random sample, cover all areas of the state served by the plan, and reach a statistically valid sample of providers for the wait-time tests. Crucially, the results must be submitted to CMS and posted on the state agency’s public website — building in transparency and accountability. This directly targets the long-standing problem of "ghost networks," where provider directories list doctors who are not actually accepting new Medicaid patients or who cannot be reached.

body.message: For decades, network adequacy was judged on paper — a plan could list thousands of providers while enrollees struggled to get appointments. The secret shopper survey tests the directory against reality, exposing "ghost networks" and inaccurate listings, and forcing plans to maintain networks that actually deliver timely care.
body.title: Why the Secret Shopper Matters

children.text: Why the Framework Matters

It is easy to dismiss regulatory citations like "42 CFR Part 438" as bureaucratic detail, but the framework is where the public interest in Medicaid managed care is actually protected. Recall the central tension from earlier lessons: capitation gives plans a financial incentive to under-provide care and avoid expensive members. Part 438 and its CHIP counterpart are the legal counterweight — the binding rules that require plans to maintain adequate networks, spend most of their capitation on care, meet quality standards, and treat beneficiaries fairly. Without this framework, managed care would be risk transfer with no guardrails.

body.analogy: If a Medicaid MCO contract is the lease on an apartment, 42 CFR Part 438 is the housing code behind it. The lease sets the specific terms between landlord and tenant, but the housing code sets the floor no lease can fall below — working heat, safe wiring, a real door that locks. The 2024 rule is like the code being updated to add a new requirement that the heat actually reach a measured temperature, with inspectors (secret shoppers) sent to verify it. The code is what makes the lease’s promises enforceable.
body.concept: How the federal framework backs managed care contracts

children.text: The framework also illustrates the federal-state dynamic that runs through all of Medicaid. The federal government sets the floor through Part 438; states build on top of it through their own contracts, which can be more demanding but not less. This is why two states’ Medicaid managed care programs can look quite different while both complying with the same federal rules — and why a major federal rule change, like the 2024 update, ripples through every state’s program at once, forcing contract amendments, new monitoring, and new reporting nationwide.

For the rest of this course, Part 438 is the connective tissue. The procurement and contracting lessons implement its requirements; the rate-setting and MLR lessons implement its financial standards; the network adequacy and quality lessons implement its access and quality provisions; and the oversight lesson implements its monitoring and enforcement expectations. When you encounter a specific operational requirement later, it is worth asking where it traces back to in the federal framework — because almost always, the answer is here.

Part 438 requires actuarially sound capitation rates and provides that any state-mandated minimum medical loss ratio must be at least 85 percent, reported annually by each plan.
Network adequacy requirements (section 438.68) require states to set quantitative standards for specified provider types, including LTSS provider types when LTSS is covered.

The 2024 "Access, Finance, and Quality" final rule (CMS-2439-F, effective July 9, 2024) significantly updated the framework across three pillars — access, finance, and quality — for both Medicaid and CHIP.
The rule established first-of-their-kind appointment wait-time standards: 15 business days for primary care and OB/GYN, and 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use services.
It also addressed state directed payments, added standards for in lieu of services and settings (ILOS), and established a new quality rating system (a public report card) for managed care plans.

Enforcement relies on annual secret shopper surveys — a third party posing as an enrollee to test appointment availability and directory accuracy — with results reported to CMS and posted publicly to expose "ghost networks."

The framework is the legal counterweight to capitation’s under-provision incentives, sets a federal floor states can exceed but not fall below, and is the connective tissue linking procurement, rate-setting, network, quality, and oversight throughout this course.

children.text: The Birth of Fee-for-Service: A 1965 Bargain With Medicine

When President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965 on July 30, Medicare and Medicaid were created to extend health coverage to elderly and low-income Americans. To win the cooperation of organized medicine — particularly the American Medical Association, which had fiercely opposed government health insurance — the law was structured around a simple payment principle: physicians would be paid a fee for each service they delivered, just as they billed private patients. Fee-for-service (FFS) was not a deliberate policy choice so much as a political accommodation to secure physician participation.

When Medicare services formally began on July 1, 1966, more than 19 million Americans age 65 and older enrolled in the program. Physician payments were based on "customary, prevailing, and reasonable" (CPR) charges — essentially whatever a doctor had historically charged. This created an immediate structural problem: every new claim submitted at a higher charge raised the future benchmark, producing a ratchet effect that drove spending upward with no automatic governor.

For the first two decades, policymakers treated the escalating costs as a managed problem rather than a systemic one. Various fee schedule updates, assignment rules, and charge limits were layered on top of CPR without fundamentally questioning the underlying incentive architecture. By the 1980s, it was clear that the "more services = more revenue" logic was deeply embedded in American healthcare finance — and that it was not going away without deliberate reform.

Key Concept: Fee-for-service is a payment model in which a provider receives a separate, discrete payment for each individual service rendered — a visit, a test, a procedure, a prescription. Volume, not value, drives revenue under this model.

children.text: How Fee-for-Service Distorts Clinical Incentives

The defining feature of fee-for-service is that it pays providers for activity, not outcomes. A surgeon who performs an operation is paid regardless of whether the patient recovers well or poorly. A primary care physician who spends 45 minutes counseling a patient on lifestyle changes to prevent diabetes earns less than a specialist who performs a 15-minute procedure. A hospital that discharges a patient quickly — reducing the episode cost — earns less than one that extends the stay. In each case, the financial incentives and the clinical incentives point in opposite directions.

This misalignment is not a flaw in individual physician character; it is the predictable output of a well-functioning incentive system pointed in the wrong direction. When volume is the revenue driver, rational economic actors — hospitals, physician groups, imaging centers — respond by increasing volume. This dynamic is widely documented. A survey published in JAMA Internal Medicine found that physicians themselves reported approximately 20% of overall medical care as unnecessary, including 22% of prescriptions, 25% of tests, and 11% of procedures.

The consequences extend beyond wasteful spending. Overutilization exposes patients to real harms: unnecessary surgeries carry surgical risk, excessive imaging involves radiation exposure, and over-prescription of antibiotics contributes to antimicrobial resistance. Fee-for-service also systematically under-incentivizes prevention, care coordination, and the management of chronic disease — precisely the areas where the U.S. population most urgently needs investment, given rising rates of diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease.

children.text: Overutilization: The $750 Billion Problem

The scale of waste in fee-for-service medicine is staggering and well-documented. A landmark 2012 analysis by the Institute of Medicine (now the National Academy of Medicine) estimated that the United States wasted roughly $750 billion out of $2.6 trillion in annual healthcare spending — approximately 30% of all health expenditures. That analysis identified six categories of waste: unnecessary services, inefficient care delivery, excess administrative costs, inflated prices, prevention failures, and fraud. Unnecessary services — a direct product of FFS incentives — was the single largest category.

More recent estimates have adjusted the figures but not the conclusion. Overtreatment and low-value care are estimated to cost approximately $200 billion annually in the United States. These are not edge cases or outlier events; they are the normal output of a system designed to pay for doing more. The geographic variation in Medicare spending — a well-studied phenomenon — illustrates this clearly: regions with more FFS-driven care often show higher spending but not better health outcomes than lower-spending peers.

Defensive medicine — the practice of ordering additional tests or procedures primarily to guard against malpractice liability rather than for clinical necessity — compounds the problem. Physicians practicing under FFS are simultaneously incentivized by payment and by fear of liability to order more. The result is a system with two powerful engines pushing utilization upward and few structural forces pulling it back.

body.analogy: Imagine paying a taxi driver by the mile, then asking them to recommend the best route across town. They might genuinely believe the longer route is better — more scenic, fewer lights — but the meter is also running in their favor. In fee-for-service medicine, providers have the same structural conflict: the payment system rewards more care, even when the right clinical answer is less.

children.text: The Outcomes Paradox: Spending More, Getting Less

The United States spends more on healthcare than any other country on Earth — by a significant margin. In 2023, the U.S. spent approximately $14,885 per capita on health, compared to an OECD average of $5,967. That is more than two-and-a-half times the average spending of other wealthy nations. And yet, by nearly every population health measure, the U.S. performs poorly relative to its peer countries.

U.S. life expectancy was 78.4 years in 2023 — 2.7 years below the OECD average and nearly 4 years shorter than the average among comparable high-income nations (82.5 years). The U.S. performs worse than the OECD average on 77% of health status indicators, including obesity rates (43% in the U.S. versus 26% OECD average) and opioid mortality (223 per million in the U.S. versus 30 per million OECD average). The fee-for-service structure contributes to this paradox by over-investing in acute, high-intensity intervention while systematically under-investing in the primary and preventive care that drives population health.

This mismatch between spending and outcomes is not inevitable. Countries that organize care around primary care-centered, capitated or globally budgeted payment models consistently achieve better population health at lower cost. The evidence from international comparison does not indict American physicians or hospitals — it indicts the payment architecture that shapes how those physicians and hospitals behave.

body.content:
Vermont launched the nation's first statewide All-Payer Accountable Care Organization (ACO) model in 2018, moving the state's major payers — Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurers — toward value-based payment simultaneously. Rather than paying providers separately for each service, the model provides a single, globally-negotiated budget for a defined population. Vermont has historically had one of the highest rates of primary care utilization in the nation, contributing to better health outcomes relative to its spending level.
The model demonstrates that shifting the payment architecture — not just layering quality bonuses onto FFS — is what produces durable change in care delivery patterns.
body.title: Vermont All-Payer ACO Model

children.text: Early Attempts to Fix the System: Managed Care and the SGR

Policymakers began serious attempts to constrain FFS-driven spending in the 1980s and 1990s. The most influential structural response was managed care — health maintenance organizations (HMOs) and preferred provider organizations (PPOs) that used capitation, utilization review, and gatekeeping to moderate volume. Managed care did succeed in slowing spending growth through the mid-1990s, but a political and consumer backlash against restricted access and coverage denials led Congress to pass patient protection legislation and effectively defanged many of managed care's cost-control mechanisms by the early 2000s.

For Medicare, Congress attempted a different fix with the Sustainable Growth Rate (SGR) formula, enacted as part of the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. The SGR tied aggregate physician payment updates to GDP growth, theoretically preventing physician spending from outpacing the broader economy. In practice, it failed. When physician spending exceeded the SGR target, the formula required automatic fee cuts — often exceeding 20% — that Congress consistently overrode with emergency "doc fix" legislation rather than allow payments to fall. By 2015, the proposed SGR-driven cut was 21.2% — an amount both politically and practically impossible to implement.

The SGR experience illustrated a fundamental truth: you cannot fix a volume-driven payment system by threatening to reduce the per-unit price when volume rises, because those whose livelihoods depend on that volume will always find a way to reverse the cuts. The only durable solution is to restructure the underlying payment model — to make it financially neutral or advantageous to deliver less but better care. That insight became the foundation for the value-based care movement.

children.text: Why FFS Persists Despite Its Flaws

Given the weight of evidence against fee-for-service, a reasonable question is why it remains the dominant payment model in American healthcare. The answer involves entrenched financial interests, administrative complexity, and the genuine difficulty of measuring "value" in health. Provider organizations that have built their revenue models, staffing levels, and capital investments around FFS volume face existential risk in a rapid transition to different payment structures. Hospitals whose margins depend on high-acuity inpatient admissions cannot easily restructure overnight.

There is also the measurement problem. Value-based payment requires robust quality metrics, attribution methodologies (to determine which provider is responsible for a patient's outcomes), risk adjustment (to avoid penalizing providers who care for sicker patients), and data infrastructure capable of tracking patients across settings over time. These systems are expensive to build, slow to validate, and contested in their design. FFS, by contrast, is administratively simple: the claim defines the service, the fee schedule defines the payment, and the transaction is complete.

Despite these barriers, the trajectory is clear. CMS has set explicit targets for moving Medicare toward value-based payment, and the commercial insurance market has followed. Understanding why FFS fails — at the level of incentive structure, not just cost — is the essential first step toward understanding why every major reform initiative of the past 15 years has been an attempt to move away from it.

body.message: Fee-for-service is sometimes confused with "privatized" healthcare, but it is actually the dominant payment model within both public (Medicare, Medicaid) and private insurance programs in the United States. The problem is not who pays, but what behavior the payment incentivizes. Both public and private FFS payers face the same volume-driven cost dynamic.

children.text: The Next Step Beyond eCQMs

The previous lesson showed how eCQMs pull quality data directly from EHRs — a big advance over claims and manual chart abstraction. But eCQMs have a limitation: they are tightly bound to a single EHR's data, and they rely on older technical standards. The next evolution, which CMS is actively driving the entire field toward, is the digital quality measure, or dQM, built on the modern FHIR standard.

CMS defines a digital quality measure as a measure that uses standardized digital data from one or more sources, captured and exchanged via interoperable systems, with standards-based specifications and code packages, computable in an integrated environment without additional effort. The key phrases are "one or more sources" and "without additional effort" — dQMs are meant to draw from many data sources and run automatically.

This matters because it is not a niche technical update — CMS has set the strategic goal of transitioning all the quality measures in its reporting programs to dQMs. Everyone working in quality will be living in a dQM world; this lesson explains what that means.

A digital quality measure (dQM) uses standardized digital data from one or more interoperable sources, with standards-based specifications, computable automatically. CMS's goal is to transition all its quality measures to dQMs.
What Makes a dQM Different From an eCQM

eCQMs and dQMs both use digital data and interoperability standards, so the line between them can blur. The clearest distinction is the breadth of data sources. An eCQM is generally tied closely to EHR data — it measures what is in the electronic health record. A dQM can pull standardized digital data from many sources: EHRs, claims, registries, and even patient-generated health data.

This multi-source capability is powerful. Recall the recurring problem of care gaps that are not really gaps — a service happened but the EHR didn't capture it. A dQM that can also see claims and registry data has more places to find evidence of care, producing a more complete and accurate picture than an EHR-only eCQM.

The other key difference is the underlying technology. eCQMs were built on the Quality Data Model (QDM); dQMs are built on FHIR — the same modern, web-based interoperability standard used across health IT — which makes the data far easier to exchange and combine across systems.

children.text: The FHIR Standards Stack

A FHIR-based measure rests on a specific stack of standards, and the names are worth knowing because they appear constantly in this space. The foundation is FHIR Release 4 (R4), the version of the interoperability standard most measures build on.

On top of FHIR sit two implementation guides. The Quality Improvement Core (QI-Core) defines the data profiles — it replaces the old QDM as the model for representing clinical data, and it is built directly on FHIR resources (including US Core). The Quality Measure Implementation Guide (QM IG) describes how to represent the measure itself using FHIR's Clinical Reasoning module. Notably, Clinical Quality Language (CQL) — the same logic language used in eCQMs — carries forward to express measure logic in dQMs.

So the transition is evolutionary, not a clean break. CMS's first operational step is converting existing QDM-based eCQMs into "FHIR eCQMs" that use QI-Core and the QM IG. From there, measures can expand to the multi-source dQM vision. CQL remains the logic language throughout, which preserves much of the existing measurement know-how.

children.text: Why CMS Is Pushing dQMs

CMS is not adopting dQMs for technology's own sake. The motivations are the same pain points that have run through this whole course. First, reduced burden: if measures compute automatically from interoperable data "without additional effort," providers spend less time on manual abstraction and submission.

Second, better data and accuracy: drawing from multiple standardized sources captures care that any single source would miss, addressing the care-gap and free-text problems that limit eCQMs. Third, speed: FHIR's real-time, API-based exchange supports the dream of near-real-time quality insight rather than the retrospective, year-end picture that plagues HEDIS-style reporting.

Fourth, interoperability and alignment: because dQMs use the same FHIR standard as patient access APIs, payer data exchange, and the broader health-IT ecosystem, quality measurement stops being a separate data silo and becomes part of one connected data fabric. That alignment is the strategic prize.

children.text: The Reality: A Hard, Ongoing Transition

The dQM vision is compelling, but getting there is a multi-year, difficult transition. Targets have shifted, and the practical reality is that providers, vendors, and CMS are all working through a long migration: converting measures, upgrading EHRs to support the FHIR standards, building the data pipelines, and validating that FHIR-based measures produce correct, comparable results.

The same data-quality dependency from the eCQM lesson applies with full force here. A dQM that can pull from many sources is only as good as the standardized data those sources provide. If the underlying FHIR data is incomplete or inconsistently coded, a more sophisticated measure simply computes a wrong answer more efficiently. Multi-source data also raises new challenges around de-duplication and reconciling conflicting records.

For anyone in the field, the practical posture is to understand where the puck is going — FHIR-based, multi-source, automated, near-real-time measurement — while recognizing that today's reporting still leans heavily on eCQMs and even legacy methods. The dQM is the destination; the journey is the work of this decade. That is exactly why the next lesson tackles the foundation everything here depends on: EHR data quality.

Multi-source data also introduces de-duplication and reconciliation challenges.

children.text: The Question Every Other Lesson Has Been Building Toward

Every concept in this course — payer mix and margins, cost accounting, capital and debt, value-based payment, governance — ultimately serves a single question: can this hospital survive? Financial sustainability is the capacity of a hospital to remain financially viable over the long term while continuing to fulfill its mission. It is not a single metric but a condition: enough margin to reinvest, enough liquidity to weather shocks, enough access to capital to modernize, and a business model durable enough to withstand a relentlessly changing landscape. This capstone lesson examines the forces threatening that sustainability today and the strategies hospitals are using to defend it.

The central threat is deceptively simple and increasingly severe: expenses are growing faster than revenue. In 2025, hospital expenses increased by 7.5% — over twice the rate of growth in hospital prices over the same period. When the cost of providing care rises faster than the payment for it, margins compress, and for many hospitals, health systems, and medical groups, margin pressure in 2026 is more intense than at any point in the last decade. The thin margins documented throughout this course are now being squeezed harder than ever.

This is not a temporary post-pandemic hangover; it is a structural challenge driven by labor and drug costs, an aging population shifting payer mix toward government programs, and looming federal funding cuts. Understanding financial sustainability means understanding both why the pressure is mounting and what separates the hospitals that will adapt from those that will close.

Key Concept: Financial sustainability is a hospital’s capacity to stay viable long-term while fulfilling its mission — requiring adequate margin, liquidity, and capital access. The defining threat today is expense growth outpacing revenue growth, compressing already-thin margins.

children.text: The Expense Squeeze

The first force eroding sustainability is cost growth across the board. Recent data shows the squeeze in detail: labor expenses grew about 4.9%, non-labor expenses 6.4%, and drug expenses 6.8% year over year — with non-labor and drug costs surging fastest. Labor, as the cost-accounting lessons established, remains the largest single expense, but the broad-based rise across supplies, pharmaceuticals, and services means hospitals cannot cost-cut their way out through any single lever. Total expenses rising 5.4% against gross operating revenue rising only 3.9% captures the bind: the gap between the two lines is where margin disappears.

These costs are largely outside the hospital’s direct control. Drug prices are set by manufacturers; wage levels are set by competitive labor markets and persistent clinical workforce shortages; supply costs reflect global pressures. Because so much of the cost base is fixed or externally driven, and because (as earlier lessons showed) hospitals cannot quickly shed fixed costs when revenue softens, the expense squeeze translates almost directly into margin erosion. Year-to-date operating margins around 2.0% (with system allocations) as of late 2025 leave almost no cushion against further cost shocks.

body.message: Because expense growth is broad-based and largely externally driven — labor, drugs, supplies all rising — no single cost cut restores sustainability. Hospitals that treat cost control as the entire strategy, rather than pairing it with revenue diversification and payment-model change, tend to manage decline rather than reverse it.
body.title: You Cannot Cut Your Way to Health Alone

children.text: The Payer and Policy Threat

The second force is the deterioration of the revenue side, driven by payer mix and federal policy. As the population ages, more patients shift into Medicare; as economic and coverage conditions change, more shift into Medicaid or become uninsured. Both trends move the payer mix toward the below-cost government payers analyzed in earlier lessons, eroding the commercial cross-subsidy that hospital finances depend on. In one nationwide survey of healthcare finance professionals, 66% cited government funding and Medicaid cuts as a leading concern — the single most pressing worry on the revenue side.

That worry has a concrete cause. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) is projected to cut roughly $911 billion in federal Medicaid and CHIP spending over ten years, with about $155 billion of that falling on rural areas, alongside the DSH cuts covered in the payer-mix lesson. Medicaid work requirements and tightened eligibility are projected to increase the uninsured population, adding uncompensated care just as supplemental payments shrink. For hospitals with heavy government payer mixes, this is a direct, multi-year hit to revenue with no obvious replacement.

Nowhere is the threat more acute than in rural communities. Nearly half of rural hospitals already operate with negative margins, more than 100 rural hospitals have closed or converted in the last decade, and modeling suggests proposed Medicaid policies could cut rural safety-net hospitals’ net operating income by roughly 25–28%. For these institutions, financial sustainability is not an abstraction — it is the difference between a community having a hospital and not having one. Mechanisms like state-directed payments and provider taxes have become critical lifelines.
Strategies for Sustainability

Faced with this squeeze, hospitals are pursuing several strategies, and the strongest combine them rather than relying on any one. The first is operational excellence and disciplined cost control — but elevated from a finance-department task to a board-level strategic initiative, treating "operational rigor" and getting at the expense lines as a core competency rather than a one-time cost-cutting drive. This is cost management as an ongoing discipline informed by exactly the cost-accounting tools covered earlier.

The second is revenue diversification, especially the shift toward outpatient care. Outpatient revenue has been growing far faster than inpatient — rising 7.2% versus 3.5% in one recent month — as care migrates to ambulatory settings and hospitals build outpatient, ambulatory surgery, and service-line capacity to capture it. The third is the development of value-based enterprise models and strategic partnerships, positioning the organization to be paid for keeping populations healthy rather than depending solely on volume that is increasingly capped by government payers. Together these reflect a hospital trying to reshape both its cost base and its revenue base for a different future.

children.text: The Synthesis: Why Sustainability Ties It All Together

This lesson is the capstone of hospital finance because sustainability is where every prior concept converges. The thin margins and ratios from Module 1 define how little cushion exists. The payer mix and reimbursement realities from Module 2 explain why revenue is under threat. The cost accounting from Module 3 is the toolkit for the expense discipline sustainability demands. The capital and debt strategy from Module 4 determines whether a hospital can fund its transformation. The value-based finance of Module 5 offers the most promising path to a durable model. And the governance of the prior lesson is what steers all of it. Sustainability is not a topic alongside the others — it is what the others add up to.

body.analogy: A hospital’s financial sustainability is like a household living on a fixed income whose bills keep rising. Cutting spending helps but cannot fully close the gap; the household also needs new income sources and must adapt to a changing world. The ones that endure are not those that simply economize, but those that restructure — finding new revenue, controlling costs continuously, and adjusting their whole way of living to the new reality. Hospitals that merely cut, without reshaping revenue and payment, are economizing their way toward the exit.
body.concept: Hospital financial sustainability

children.text: The stakes of getting this right could not be higher, because a hospital is not just a business. When a hospital fails financially, a community loses access to care, jobs, and often its largest employer — which is why financial sustainability and mission are inseparable rather than opposed. A hospital cannot serve its community if it cannot keep its doors open, and it does not deserve to keep its doors open if it abandons its community in pursuit of margin. The art of sustainable hospital finance is holding both truths at once: remaining financially viable precisely so the mission can endure.

Looking ahead, the pressures are intensifying — margin compression at decade-high levels, hundreds of billions in Medicaid cuts phasing in, an aging population, and relentless cost growth. But the path forward is visible in the strategies the strongest organizations are already pursuing: rigorous cost discipline, diversified and outpatient-weighted revenue, genuine movement toward value-based payment, and disciplined capital stewardship under engaged governance. The hospitals that master the full toolkit this course has assembled — and have the discipline to apply it as their landscape shifts beneath them — are the ones that will still be standing, and still serving their communities, when the next decade of change arrives.

Because cost growth is broad-based and largely externally driven, no single cost cut restores sustainability — hospitals that rely on cost-cutting alone tend to manage decline rather than reverse it.

The revenue side is threatened by payer-mix shifts toward below-cost government payers and by federal policy: the OBBBA cuts an estimated $911 billion in Medicaid/CHIP over 10 years (~$155B rural), and 66% of finance professionals cite government cuts as a leading concern.

Rural hospitals are most at risk — nearly half operate with negative margins, 100+ have closed or converted in a decade, and proposed Medicaid policies could cut rural safety-net net operating income by ~25–28%.

Sustainability strategies combine operational excellence (cost control as a board-level competency), revenue diversification (faster-growing outpatient care), value-based enterprise models, and disciplined capital/partnership strategy.

Sustainability is the capstone of hospital finance because it integrates every prior concept — margins, payer mix, cost accounting, capital and debt, value-based finance, and governance all converge on whether the hospital survives.

Financial viability and mission are inseparable: a hospital cannot serve its community if it closes, but should not survive by abandoning its community — sustainable hospital finance means staying viable precisely so the mission can endure.

children.text: Food Insecurity Is a Clinical Problem

Food insecurity — limited or uncertain access to enough food for an active, healthy life — affects a large and growing share of Americans. According to the USDA, in 2023 about 13.5% of US households (18.0 million households) experienced food insecurity at some point during the year, and roughly 47 million people lived in food-insecure households, including nearly 14 million children. Both figures rose from 2022 and reached their highest levels in years.

For clinicians, food insecurity is not merely a social misfortune; it has direct, measurable clinical consequences. It is associated with worse control of diabetes and hypertension, higher rates of depression and anxiety, and more hospital admissions. The mechanism is intuitive: a patient who cannot reliably afford or access fresh produce, lean protein, and whole grains cannot follow the diet their chronic disease requires, no matter how good their medication regimen is.

There is also a cruel feedback loop with cost. Food-insecure patients sometimes face a "treat or eat" tradeoff, rationing medications to pay for food or skipping food to afford prescriptions. The result is worse disease control, more complications, and higher downstream medical costs — which is precisely why "food is medicine" has moved from slogan to a serious area of clinical intervention and payment reform.

Food insecurity is a clinical issue with measurable effects on diabetes, hypertension, mental health, and hospitalization. In 2023, ~47 million Americans — including nearly 14 million children — lived in food-insecure households.
Screening for Food Insecurity

Because food insecurity is often invisible and stigmatized, identifying it requires deliberate screening rather than assumption. The good news is that effective screening can be extremely brief. The Hunger Vital Sign, a validated two-item tool, asks whether in the past 12 months the household worried food would run out before there was money to buy more, and whether food bought did not last. An affirmative answer to either item flags food-insecurity risk.

Two questions are short enough to fit into nearly any clinical workflow — intake forms, rooming questions, or a patient portal. The brevity matters: a tool that takes thirty seconds is far more likely to be used consistently than a long questionnaire, and consistency is what surfaces the patients who need help. Food-insecurity items are also embedded in the broader SDOH tools covered earlier, such as PRAPARE and the CMS AHC tool.

As with all SDOH screening, the rule holds: do not screen without a plan to respond. A positive food-insecurity screen should connect to something concrete — a referral to SNAP enrollment assistance, a food pharmacy, a produce prescription, or a medically tailored meal program, depending on the patient's needs and the resources available.

body.content:
Developed by researchers at Children's HealthWatch and validated against the longer USDA food-security module, the Hunger Vital Sign is a two-question screen: (1) "Within the past 12 months we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more," and (2) "Within the past 12 months the food we bought just didn't last and we didn't have money to get more."
A response of "often true" or "sometimes true" to either statement identifies a household at risk for food insecurity. Its brevity has made it one of the most widely adopted social-needs screens in clinical settings, including pediatrics.
body.title: The Hunger Vital Sign

children.text: Medically Tailored Meals: The Strongest Evidence

Among "food is medicine" interventions, medically tailored meals (MTMs) have the strongest evidence base. These are fully prepared, home-delivered meals designed by registered dietitians for a patient's specific medical condition — renal-appropriate meals for kidney disease, low-sodium meals for heart failure, controlled-carbohydrate meals for diabetes. They target the sickest, highest-cost patients, for whom diet is directly entangled with disease control.

The clinical and economic results are substantial. In a widely cited study by Berkowitz and colleagues, receiving medically tailored meals was associated with a 49% reduction in inpatient admissions, 72% fewer skilled-nursing-facility admissions, and about 16% lower total health care costs compared with similar patients who did not receive them. The effects concentrate where they should: among high-need patients whose conditions are most diet-sensitive.

Modeling work has extended these findings to a national scale. A study published in JAMA Network Open by researchers at Tufts University's Friedman School estimated that a nationwide medically tailored meal program for eligible patients could avert roughly 1.6 million hospitalizations and save insurers on the order of $13.6 billion annually. These are projections, not guarantees, but they explain why payers and Medicaid programs are increasingly willing to cover MTMs.

children.text: Produce Prescriptions and Food Pharmacies

A second family of interventions tries to improve diet quality more broadly. Produce prescription programs let clinicians "prescribe" vouchers or debit-style cards redeemable for fruits and vegetables at grocery stores or farmers markets. Food pharmacies — grocery-style spaces inside clinical settings where food-insecure patients can select free healthy food — pursue the same goal through a different channel.

The evidence on produce prescriptions is genuinely promising but more mixed than for medically tailored meals, and honesty about that matters. Several evaluations have found meaningful improvements: a large Tufts-led analysis reported modest A1c reductions (around 0.3 percentage points) along with reduced food insecurity and improved diet, and some physician-supported programs have reported larger A1c drops of roughly a full point. But at least one randomized clinical trial found that a produce prescription subsidy alone did not significantly improve A1c or health care utilization at twelve months.

The likely explanation is that program design matters enormously. Produce prescriptions paired with nutrition education, navigation support, and clinician involvement appear more effective than a subsidy handed out in isolation. The takeaway for practice is not "produce prescriptions don't work" or "they cure diabetes" — it is that food-as-medicine interventions need to be designed and evaluated carefully, with realistic expectations and attention to the wraparound supports that make them effective.

body.message: It is tempting to claim produce prescriptions reliably produce clinically large A1c reductions. The evidence is mixed: some studies show modest benefits (~0.3 to ~1.0 point A1c), but a randomized trial found a subsidy alone did not improve outcomes at 12 months. Present these programs as promising and design-dependent — not as proven, uniform A1c reducers.
body.title: Do not overstate the produce-prescription evidence

children.text: SNAP and the Limits of Clinical Programs

No clinic-based food program can match the scale of the federal nutrition safety net. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) is by far the largest food-security intervention in the United States, reaching tens of millions of people. For most food-insecure patients, helping them enroll in or maintain SNAP benefits is the single highest-impact food intervention a care team can facilitate — yet many eligible people are not enrolled, often due to administrative barriers and stigma.

This points to an important strategic principle: clinical food programs and public benefits are complements, not substitutes. A medically tailored meal program serving a few hundred of the sickest patients does not reach the thousands of food-insecure people in a health system's broader population. Screening that routinely connects patients to SNAP, WIC, and local food resources scales in a way that a boutique meal program cannot.

It also means that food-as-medicine work is inseparable from policy. The reach of the nutrition safety net depends on eligibility rules, benefit levels, and enrollment processes set by federal and state policy. Health systems serious about food insecurity therefore work on two fronts at once: deploying targeted clinical interventions for their highest-need patients, and helping the broader population access the public programs built for exactly this purpose.

children.text: Data Is Necessary but Not Sufficient

The previous lesson made the case for high-quality REaL data and stratified measurement. But producing a beautiful dashboard that displays a disparity is not the same as closing it. The history of health equity work is littered with organizations that mistook measurement for progress — that invested heavily in identifying gaps and then stalled, treating the dashboard as a destination rather than a starting point.

Health systems that actually reduce disparities share a recognizable pattern. They move deliberately from data (the gap exists and here is its size) to root-cause analysis (why does it exist) to targeted intervention (a specific change aimed at the specific cause) to accountability (someone owns the result and is measured on it). Each step is necessary; skipping any one is where most efforts fail.

This lesson is about that pipeline: how to turn a stratified disparity finding into a structured equity action plan, choose interventions that fit the root cause, set measurable targets, and build the organizational accountability that determines whether the gap actually narrows. The tools are not exotic — they are ordinary quality improvement methods, applied with an equity lens.

Identifying a disparity is the beginning, not the end. The systems that close gaps move from data to root-cause analysis to targeted intervention to accountability — and most failures happen when one of those steps is skipped.
The Equity Action Cycle

A practical way to structure disparity reduction is as a cycle that mirrors standard quality improvement but begins with stratified data. The first step is to identify and quantify the gap: take a meaningful measure — say, postpartum follow-up visits — stratify it by race, ethnicity, and language, and name the size of the gap between the highest- and lowest-performing groups. A precise gap ("an 18-point Black-white difference") is far more actionable than a vague concern.

The second and most-often-skipped step is root-cause analysis. A gap in postpartum follow-up could stem from scheduling barriers, transportation, appointment availability, language-discordant communication, or distrust — and each cause implies a completely different intervention. Disaggregating the gap further (Where does it appear? At scheduling? In no-show rates? In which clinics?) tells you what is actually broken. Choosing an intervention before understanding the cause is how organizations waste effort on changes that do not move the gap.

Only then does the cycle proceed to designing a targeted intervention, setting a specific time-bound improvement target, and measuring against it on a regular cadence — iterating if the gap is not closing. This is deliberately the discipline of quality improvement: treat a disparity exactly like any other quality defect, with a named owner, a measurable target, and a feedback loop, rather than as a values aspiration without a mechanism.

children.text: Choosing Interventions That Fit the Cause

The reason root-cause analysis matters so much is that interventions are not interchangeable. An intervention that fixes a transportation barrier does nothing for a gap driven by language discordance, and vice versa. The art of disparity reduction is matching a specific, evidence-based change to the specific cause the analysis revealed.

The toolkit is well established. For access and follow-up gaps: community health worker outreach to the affected population, reminder calls and messages in the patient's preferred language, same-day or extended-hours appointments, and transportation support. For communication gaps: professional interpreter services and language-concordant scheduling and care. For trust gaps: partnership with trusted community organizations and culturally concordant staff. Each maps to a category of root cause.

A critical design principle is to target the intervention to the gap population without stigmatizing them. Disparity reduction often means giving more — more outreach, more support — to the group that is behind, which is exactly the equity-over-equality logic from the start of this course. Universal interventions (a change applied to everyone) sometimes widen gaps, because the already-advantaged take them up faster; targeted interventions aimed at the lagging group are usually what actually closes a disparity.

body.content:
Mass General Brigham used stratified data to identify clear inequities in its own care: lower colorectal cancer screening rates among patients of color and patients with limited English proficiency, and racial and language disparities across diabetes outcome measures.
Rather than stopping at the finding, its Chief Medical Officer for Health Equity organized targeted responses — culturally and linguistically tailored screening-awareness campaigns, mobile Community Care Vans bringing screenings and chronic-disease services into underserved neighborhoods, and equity goals embedded in its strategic plan. It illustrates the full pipeline: stratify, find the gap, analyze who is missed, and deploy interventions aimed at that population.
body.title: Mass General Brigham — Targeted Disparity Reduction

children.text: Disparity Dashboards: Making Gaps Visible and Owned

The operational home for this work is increasingly the disparity dashboard — a tool that displays key quality and outcome measures stratified by race, ethnicity, language, and other equity-relevant factors, in a form leaders and frontline teams can act on. A 2023 framework published in The Lancet Digital Health evaluated the literature on disparity dashboards and laid out principles for using them to drive improvement rather than just display data.

A good disparity dashboard does more than show gaps; it assigns them. It makes a specific gap visible to a specific owner with a specific target, and it tracks movement over time so that progress (or its absence) is unambiguous. The difference between a dashboard that drives change and one that gathers dust is whether the numbers on it are tied to accountable owners and time-bound goals — the same discipline as any effective performance management.

Dashboards also surface the aggregate trap in real time. By always showing measures stratified rather than in aggregate, they prevent the comfortable illusion that a good overall number means equitable care. A clinic that sees its colorectal screening gap on the dashboard every month cannot un-see it — which is precisely the point.

children.text: Accountability: The Factor That Separates Progress From Stagnation

Across the literature on health systems that make measurable equity progress, one factor recurs above all others: accountability tied to leadership. Systems that close gaps consistently link senior-leader performance goals — and, increasingly, compensation — to measurable equity outcomes. When the CEO's and chief medical officer's reviews include a specific equity target, the organization predictably allocates resources, attention, and urgency to meeting it.

The National Academy of Medicine has been explicit on this point: holding the CEO accountable against clear, quantifiable equity goals is described as an essential governance duty, and modifying executive compensation so that a meaningful portion is tied to equity metrics is a key lever. This is not symbolic. Compensation and performance review are how organizations signal what genuinely matters, and equity work that lacks that signal tends to remain a values statement that competes — and loses — against everything that is measured and rewarded.

The contrast is stark and well documented. Organizations that treat equity as a values commitment without accountability rarely produce measurable improvement; organizations that wire it into goals, dashboards, and compensation do. The lesson for anyone doing this work is that the technical pipeline — data, root cause, intervention, target — only delivers when it sits inside an accountability structure that makes closing the gap someone's actual job.

body.message: A published equity statement, a diversity committee, and a dashboard are not enough on their own. The evidence is consistent: measurable disparity reduction requires tying specific, quantifiable equity goals to senior-leadership performance and compensation. Without that accountability, equity work competes against everything that is actually measured and rewarded — and usually loses.
body.title: Values statements without accountability rarely close gaps

children.text: Two Forces Shaping What Comes Next

Having built up the full machinery of Medicaid managed care across this course — delivery models, federal rules, procurement, rate-setting, networks, quality, and value-based payment — we close by looking forward. Where is this system heading? The answer is shaped by two powerful forces pulling in different directions. One is aspirational: a sustained movement toward "whole-person care" that addresses the social factors driving health, not just medical services. The other is fiscal and political: looming federal cuts and enrollment losses that threaten to reshape the program’s scale and strain its finances. The future of Medicaid managed care lies in the tension between these two forces.

The whole-person-care movement reflects a genuine intellectual shift. There is growing recognition that medical care alone cannot produce health when a person lacks stable housing, adequate food, reliable transportation, or employment — the social determinants of health (SDOH). Medicaid managed care, with its capitated, population-focused structure and (via Section 1115) its flexibility to fund non-traditional services, has become a leading vehicle for acting on this recognition. The direction of travel is toward MCOs that address the whole person and their social context, not just their diagnoses.

But that aspiration now collides with a harsh fiscal environment. Major federal Medicaid cuts and policy changes are projected to shrink enrollment and squeeze financing precisely as states aspire to do more. Understanding the future of Medicaid managed care means holding both realities at once — the expansive vision of whole-person care and the contractionary pressure of cuts that could undermine it.

Key Concept: The future of Medicaid managed care is shaped by two forces — an aspirational shift toward whole-person care addressing social determinants of health (SDOH), and a fiscal/political shift toward major federal cuts and enrollment losses that threaten the program’s scale and finances.

children.text: Whole-Person Care: The Aspirational Direction

The defining aspiration of modern Medicaid managed care is whole-person care — integrating physical health, behavioral health, services for intellectual and developmental disabilities, pharmacy, and social supports into a single coordinated approach centered on the member rather than fragmented by service type. This is the through-line connecting many earlier lessons: the carve-in trend toward integration, MLTSS coordination for complex members, and value-based payment all point toward treating the whole person rather than a collection of disconnected benefits.

Increasingly, that integration extends beyond clinical care to social needs. Medicaid managed care organizations are using Medicaid funds to address social determinants of health, supporting members’ broader needs including housing, nutrition, and employment, in recognition of the adverse health impacts of unmet social needs. The mechanisms are ones this course has already covered: Section 1115 demonstrations (the HRSN waivers), "in lieu of services and settings" (ILOS) authority from the 2024 final rule, and value-based arrangements that reward keeping people healthy. Together they let plans pay for a food prescription or a housing navigator when those interventions improve health more than another clinical visit would.

Effective whole-person care depends on partnership and infrastructure. Plans are increasingly partnering with community-based organizations to connect members with critical resources, recognizing that an MCO cannot itself provide housing or food but can fund and coordinate with the organizations that do. Key elements of doing this well include member- and community-centeredness, structured programming, and realignment of the delivery system. Some states are even beginning to integrate SDOH factors into risk adjustment, so plans serving members with greater social needs are paid appropriately — extending the risk-adjustment logic from clinical conditions to social circumstances.

children.text: The Fiscal and Political Headwinds

Against this expansive vision stand serious headwinds. Recent federal law (H.R.1, also discussed as OBBBA in the hospital-finance course) is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by roughly $911 billion — about 14% — over a decade, and to increase the number of uninsured people by around 7.5 million, with impacts varying widely by state (spending cuts ranging from about 4% to nearly a fifth of federal Medicaid spending in some states). These are not marginal adjustments; they represent a structural contraction of the program’s federal financing.

The enrollment effects are projected to be large and are already beginning. Since the enactment of H.R.1, net Medicaid enrollment has already declined by over a million members, and overall enrollment is projected to fall by 9 to 10 million between 2027 and 2028 — with managed care plans losing roughly 7 million members. The drivers include work reporting requirements and more frequent (six-month) eligibility redeterminations beginning January 1, 2027, which research consistently shows cause eligible people to lose coverage through administrative churn, not just genuine ineligibility.

These pressures cascade through the system in ways this course has mapped. As enrollment falls and financing tightens, the Medicaid segment’s profitability is projected to deteriorate sharply — with segment EBITDA expected to turn negative in 2025–2026. Providers, already reimbursed below fee-for-service levels in many cases, face reduced or stagnant rates alongside more uninsured patients, pressuring them to cut staff and services or close — a particular threat to rural and safety-net providers. The network adequacy, payer-mix, and sustainability problems from earlier lessons all intensify under fiscal contraction.

body.message: Whole-person care asks Medicaid managed care to do more — addressing housing, food, and social needs. Federal cuts and enrollment losses push it to do less, with shrinking budgets and fewer members. How states and plans navigate between this expansive vision and contractionary pressure will define Medicaid managed care for the rest of the decade.
body.title: The Core Tension of the Coming Years

children.text: What States and Plans Are Prioritizing

Facing these crosscurrents, states and advocates are converging on a set of priorities for the years ahead. The top concerns identified for Medicaid managed care include enrollment oversight (ensuring that eligible people are not wrongly disenrolled amid redeterminations and work requirements), network adequacy (keeping real access as financing tightens), benefit design (deciding what to cover when budgets shrink), and MCO accountability (holding plans to their obligations even under fiscal stress). These priorities are, notably, the very subjects of this course — the machinery built to govern managed care becomes more important, not less, when the program is under strain.

The 2024 final rule’s quality rating system, the strengthened network adequacy and secret-shopper requirements, the tightened MLR and directed-payment oversight — all of these accountability tools take on heightened significance in a contracting environment. When budgets are ample, oversight catches occasional problems; when budgets are cut and plans face negative margins, the temptation to under-provide care, thin networks, and avoid expensive members grows, and robust oversight becomes the main protection for vulnerable enrollees. The future will test whether the accountability framework this course described can hold under real fiscal pressure.

body.analogy: Medicaid managed care’s future is like a household that has finally decided to invest in long-term health — better food, a safer home, preventive care (whole-person care) — just as its income is cut. The wisest response is not to abandon the vision but to protect the investments that actually keep people well and out of expensive crises, while watching spending carefully. The danger is that under financial stress, the household cuts exactly the preventive investments that would have saved money later. States face the same choice: whether cuts fall on the whole-person investments that improve health or are absorbed without gutting them.
body.concept: Navigating between vision and fiscal constraint

children.text: Conclusion: Where the Course Has Led

This final lesson completes a journey that began with a simple question: why do states pay private plans to manage Medicaid, and how is that arrangement governed? The answer unfolded across the course. States moved to managed care chiefly for budget predictability; they choose among delivery models that transfer different amounts of risk; they operate within the federal framework of 42 CFR Part 438; they select plans through procurement, pay them through actuarially sound risk-adjusted capitation bounded by medical loss ratios, require adequate networks and credentialed providers, measure quality through HEDIS, oversee performance through external review, and increasingly push value-based payment and whole-person care. Every piece exists to capture managed care’s benefits while guarding against its central risk: that a plan paid a fixed amount will under-serve the vulnerable people who depend on it.

The future will stress-test that entire structure. Whole-person care represents Medicaid managed care reaching toward its highest ambition — using its capitated, population-based design to address the social roots of health, not just treat illness. The fiscal and political headwinds represent the constraint within which that ambition must be pursued. The same tools that govern managed care in good times — risk adjustment, network standards, quality measurement, MLR floors, oversight — are what will protect enrollees if the cuts arrive as projected. The machinery is not bureaucratic overhead; it is the safeguard that determines whether managed care serves its members or fails them when money is tight.

For the student who has worked through this course, the enduring lesson is that Medicaid managed care is neither inherently good nor bad — it is a powerful financial and delivery structure whose outcomes depend entirely on how well it is designed, paid, and overseen. It can deliver coordinated, whole-person care to tens of millions, or it can become risk transfer with thin networks and under-provided care. The difference lies in the operational details this course has covered. As Medicaid managed care moves into a future of expansive vision and fiscal pressure, those details — the rates, the rules, the networks, the measures, the oversight — will determine whether the system honors its purpose: caring for the people who have nowhere else to turn.

points: The future of Medicaid managed care is shaped by two opposing forces: an aspirational shift toward whole-person care addressing social determinants of health (SDOH), and major federal cuts and enrollment losses that threaten the program’s scale and finances.

Whole-person care integrates physical health, behavioral health, IDD services, pharmacy, and social supports around the member, extending beyond clinical care to address housing, nutrition, and employment.

Plans address social needs through Section 1115 HRSN waivers, "in lieu of services" (ILOS) authority, value-based arrangements, community-based partnerships, and emerging SDOH-informed risk adjustment.
Recent federal law (H.R.1/OBBBA) is projected to cut federal Medicaid spending ~$911 billion (~14%) over a decade and raise the uninsured by ~7.5 million, with impacts varying widely by state.

Medicaid enrollment is projected to decline 9–10 million between 2027 and 2028 (MCOs losing ~7 million), driven by work reporting requirements and six-month redeterminations starting January 1, 2027, with declines already underway.

Fiscal pressure cascades through the system: Medicaid-segment profitability is projected to turn negative in 2025–2026, and providers face below-FFS rates plus more uninsured patients, threatening staff cuts and rural/safety-net closures.

States and advocates prioritize enrollment oversight, network adequacy, benefit design, and MCO accountability — the very machinery of this course — which becomes more important under fiscal strain because the incentive to under-provide grows.

The enduring lesson is that Medicaid managed care is neither inherently good nor bad; its outcomes depend on how well it is designed, paid, and overseen — the operational details that determine whether it delivers whole-person care or becomes risk transfer that fails vulnerable members.

children.text: Consent for a Test That Sees Everything

Ordering a single-gene test is relatively simple to consent for: the patient agrees to look at one thing. But genome and exome sequencing is fundamentally different — it reads vastly more than the reason the test was ordered. A sequencing test ordered to diagnose a child's seizures also, incidentally, contains information about that child's risk of inherited cancer, heart disease, and dozens of other conditions. This is what makes informed consent for genomic sequencing uniquely challenging.

The core issue is that the test generates information the patient did not ask for and may not want. Informed consent for sequencing therefore cannot be a simple "do you want this test?" — it must address what additional information might surface, whether the patient wants to receive it, and what the implications could be. The breadth of sequencing turns consent into a genuine conversation about uncertainty and choice.

This lesson covers two of the most important ethics-and-policy issues in clinical genomics: how to handle the unexpected information sequencing reveals (secondary findings, and the consent that must precede them), and the diversity-and-equity deficit that determines whether genomic medicine serves everyone or mainly the populations who have been studied. Both are practical realities clinicians and programs must confront, not abstract debates.

Genome and exome sequencing reads far more than the reason it was ordered — so informed consent must address what unexpected information might surface and whether the patient wants it. This lesson covers secondary findings, the consent that precedes them, and the diversity deficit at the heart of genomic equity.
Secondary Findings and the ACMG List

When sequencing is performed for one reason, it can reveal medically important information unrelated to that reason — for example, a cancer-predisposition variant found during testing for an unrelated condition. The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) addressed this by publishing a recommended list of genes for which laboratories should actively look for and report such "secondary findings," because the conditions are serious and medically actionable (something can be done to prevent or treat them).

The current list, ACMG SF v3.2, includes 81 genes, and is now updated annually. The genes were chosen because variants in them cause conditions that are clinically actionable — for example, hereditary cancer syndromes (like BRCA1/BRCA2), cardiovascular conditions, and others where early knowledge enables prevention or surveillance. The logic is that if sequencing happens to reveal a high-risk, actionable variant, the patient benefits from knowing, even though that was not why the test was ordered.

Importantly, patients can typically opt out of receiving secondary findings — the choice is theirs. Secondary findings are returned through the ordering clinician, who places the result in the context of the patient's clinical picture and family history (echoing the genetic-counseling theme of earlier lessons). The model balances the value of actionable information against the patient's right not to learn things they did not seek.
