children.text: The Heart Failure Readmission Problem

Heart failure population health centers on a specific, high-stakes event: the hospital readmission. Heart-failure patients decompensate — fluid builds up, symptoms worsen — and end up back in the hospital, often within 30 days of a prior discharge. With a national 30-day readmission rate around 25 percent and each readmission costing many thousands of dollars, preventing readmissions is where the clinical and financial stakes concentrate.

Readmissions are also a quality-and-payment focal point: the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (from the Clinical Quality Measurement course) penalizes hospitals for excess heart-failure readmissions, so reducing them improves both patient outcomes and the bottom line. The key insight is that many heart-failure readmissions are preventable with timely intervention — they result from a gradual decompensation that, if caught early, can be managed at home instead of in the hospital.

Two interventions dominate. Transitional care — structured follow-up in the vulnerable post-discharge window (the ADT-alert-driven outreach from the data-infrastructure lesson, medication reconciliation, an early follow-up visit) — directly attacks the readmission risk. And remote patient monitoring (RPM) catches decompensation before it becomes a crisis.

children.text: Remote Patient Monitoring

Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is the signature heart-failure intervention and a powerful example of population health technology. Patients are equipped with connected devices — most importantly a scale, because a sudden weight gain signals fluid retention and impending decompensation — plus blood-pressure cuffs. Readings transmit automatically to the care team, which is alerted to abnormal values via a dashboard.

The logic is anticipation, the same theme as predictive analytics: a heart-failure patient who gains several pounds over a few days is decompensating, and a phone call to adjust their diuretic can prevent a hospitalization that is still days away. RPM converts the invisible gradual decline into a visible, actionable signal — catching the problem in the window where a cheap intervention works.

The evidence is strong. Remote monitoring programs have cut heart-failure 30-day readmission rates roughly in half — one program reported a 10 percent readmission rate versus the ~25 percent national rate — and reduced monthly costs substantially for monitored Medicare heart-failure patients. RPM is increasingly reimbursed and increasingly standard for high-risk heart-failure populations, exactly because the math is so favorable: a modest monitoring cost prevents a very expensive readmission.

children.text: Common Threads and the Bigger Picture

Hypertension and heart failure management share the population health DNA seen throughout this course. Both rely on registries and risk stratification to find and prioritize patients; both use home monitoring and continuous data rather than sporadic office visits; both depend on team-based care (pharmacists, nurses, care managers) rather than physician visits alone; and both aim to intervene early, in the cheap window, before a costly event.

And like diabetes, both are equity issues. Hypertension prevalence and control, and heart-failure outcomes and readmissions, are unequally distributed — worse among several racial and ethnic groups and lower-income communities, driven by access, the social determinants, and structural factors. A cardiovascular program that does not address these disparities will improve the average while leaving the gap, so equity-aware design (the focus of a later module) is essential.

The strategic point is that these chronic-disease programs are where population health delivers its clearest return: well-controlled hypertension prevents strokes, heart attacks, and heart failure downstream; prevented heart-failure readmissions save large, immediate costs. They are concrete proof that the proactive, data-driven, team-based, whole-population approach works — and they set up the next lesson, behavioral health integration, which addresses a dimension of health that profoundly affects these very conditions.

body.message: Hypertension and heart failure change continuously, but office visits are occasional snapshots. Programs that rely only on periodic visits miss the silent rise in blood pressure or the gradual fluid buildup that precedes a crisis. Continuous data — home BP monitoring, RPM weight tracking — plus team-based response is what actually achieves control and prevents readmissions.

children.text: The Most Widely Used Measure Set in America

HEDIS — the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — is the most widely used set of health-plan performance measures in the United States. Stewarded by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), it is reported by commercial, Medicaid, and Medicare Advantage plans covering the large majority of insured Americans.

HEDIS matters because its results are everywhere. They feed NCQA health-plan accreditation and ratings, Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, and many state Medicaid oversight programs. Because the specifications are standardized and audited, a plan's breast-cancer-screening rate in one state can be compared directly with another plan's across the country.

NCQA updates HEDIS each "measurement year" (MY), adding, revising, and retiring measures as evidence changes. The current set includes more than 90 measures, giving plans and regulators a broad, comparable picture of performance across the spectrum of care.

HEDIS is NCQA's standardized set of 90+ health-plan performance measures, updated annually by measurement year. Its results drive accreditation, Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, and Medicaid oversight.
The Domains of Care

HEDIS organizes its measures into domains so that performance can be understood by category rather than as a jumble of individual metrics. The set spans roughly six domains covering the breadth of plan performance.

The domains include Effectiveness of Care (the largest, covering preventive and chronic-disease care like screenings and diabetes control), Access/Availability of Care, Experience of Care, Utilization and Risk-Adjusted Utilization, Health Plan Descriptive Information, and measures collected through electronic clinical data systems. The Effectiveness of Care domain is where most of the familiar clinical measures live.

This organization maps neatly onto the Donabedian framework and the IOM aims: effectiveness and access measures are largely process-oriented, experience measures capture patient-centeredness, and utilization measures help detect underuse and overuse. The domains let a plan see not just whether it is doing well, but in which dimension of quality.

children.text: How a HEDIS Measure Is Calculated

At its core, almost every HEDIS measure is a rate: a numerator divided by a denominator. The denominator is the eligible population — the members who could have received the service in question. The numerator is the subset of those members who actually received it (or met the clinical target). The rate is simply numerator ÷ denominator.

Defining the denominator precisely is most of the work. NCQA specifies an "eligible population" using age, gender, diagnosis, and enrollment criteria, then subtracts denominator exclusions — members for whom the service would not be appropriate. HEDIS commonly excludes people in hospice or palliative care, those with advanced illness or frailty, and long-term nursing-home residents, because the measured service may not benefit them.

Two other rules shape the denominator. A continuous enrollment requirement specifies how long a member must have been enrolled (with only small allowable gaps) before they count, so a plan is not judged on members it barely covered. And measures define a precise measurement window for when qualifying events and services must occur.

children.text: Where the Data Comes From

A measure is only as good as the data feeding it, and HEDIS uses three collection methods. The administrative method relies entirely on claims and encounter data the plan already has — it is cheap and complete but captures only what was billed. If a service happened but was not coded on a claim, administrative data misses it.

The hybrid method addresses that gap by combining administrative data with manual review of a random sample of medical records — traditionally 411 members — to find services that were delivered but not captured in claims. Hybrid measurement is more accurate but labor-intensive and expensive, requiring trained abstractors to pull data from charts.

The third and increasingly important method is the Electronic Clinical Data Systems (ECDS) method, which draws structured clinical data directly from EHRs, registries, and health information exchanges. NCQA is steadily moving measures to ECDS reporting to capture richer clinical detail without manual chart abstraction — a key step in the broader transition to digital quality measures.

children.text: A Worked Example: Controlling High Blood Pressure

Consider one of the best-known HEDIS measures, Controlling High Blood Pressure (CBP). It assesses adults 18 to 85 years of age who have a diagnosis of hypertension and whose blood pressure was adequately controlled during the measurement year.

The denominator is members aged 18 to 85 with a hypertension diagnosis (identified on at least two different dates of service within the specified window) who meet enrollment criteria, minus the standard exclusions. The numerator is the subset whose most recent representative blood pressure reading was below 140/90 mm Hg — both systolic under 140 and diastolic under 90. If multiple readings occur on the same day, the lowest systolic and lowest diastolic values are used.

This single measure shows why HEDIS specifications are so detailed: the age range, the two-diagnosis requirement, the exact blood-pressure threshold, and the rule for choosing among same-day readings are all spelled out precisely. That precision is exactly what makes one plan's CBP rate genuinely comparable to another's — and it is why HEDIS measures cannot be calculated casually from rough data.

body.content:
Denominator: adults 18-85 with a hypertension diagnosis on at least two service dates, meeting enrollment rules, minus exclusions.
Numerator: those whose most recent representative BP reading is <140/90 mm Hg.
A plan that controls blood pressure in 700 of 1,000 eligible hypertensive members reports a CBP rate of 70%. The precise, standardized definition is what makes that 70% comparable across plans nationwide.

children.text: How We Actually Measure Whether a Plan Delivers Good Care

Throughout this course, the requirement that managed care plans deliver "quality" care has appeared again and again — in the contract, in the federal framework, in external quality review. But quality is meaningless unless it can be measured in a standardized, comparable way. How do you actually tell whether one plan delivers better diabetes care than another, or whether a plan is screening children appropriately? The dominant answer in American health care is HEDIS — the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — and for Medicaid specifically, a set of mandatory Core Set measures built largely on it.

HEDIS is the closest thing health care has to a universal report card for health plans. Managed by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), it defines standardized measures so precisely that a plan in Vermont and a plan in Texas calculate "the percentage of diabetics whose blood sugar is controlled" exactly the same way — making their results genuinely comparable. More than 235 million people are enrolled in plans that report HEDIS, and more than 90% of health plans use it. For Medicaid, HEDIS measures and the federal Core Sets are how states judge plan quality, hold plans accountable, and drive improvement.

This lesson explains what HEDIS is, how the data is collected and audited, how benchmarks turn raw rates into judgments, and how the mandatory Medicaid Core Sets layer specific reporting requirements on top of HEDIS. It is the measurement engine behind the quality requirements established earlier in the course.

Key Concept: HEDIS (Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set), managed by NCQA, is a set of precisely standardized quality measures that let health plans be compared on the same basis. Medicaid plans report HEDIS measures and the mandatory federal Core Sets, which became required for all states starting in 2024.

children.text: What HEDIS Measures and How

HEDIS includes more than 90 measures organized across six domains of care: Effectiveness of Care, Access/Availability of Care, Experience of Care, Utilization and Risk-Adjusted Utilization, Health Plan Descriptive Information, and measures collected through electronic data. The measures span the full range of what good care looks like — childhood immunizations, cancer screenings, diabetes and blood pressure control, postpartum care, behavioral health follow-up, and many more. Each is defined with technical precision: exactly which patients are in the denominator, what counts as the numerator, and how to calculate the rate.

The precision is the entire point. Because HEDIS specifies measures so exactly, results are comparable across plans, states, and time — the foundation of any meaningful quality judgment. The data comes from several sources: most HEDIS data is collected through insurance claims, medical charts, and surveys. Clinical measures use either an administrative methodology (drawing purely on electronic records like claims and pharmacy data) or a hybrid methodology (combining administrative data with a sample of medical-record review to capture care that claims miss). The choice of method affects both the accuracy and the cost of measurement.

HEDIS also pairs with CAHPS — the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems surveys — which capture the patient experience dimension (the patient-reported experience measures, or PREMs, distinct from the clinical outcomes HEDIS emphasizes). Together, HEDIS (largely clinical process and outcome measures) and CAHPS (experience) give a fuller picture of a plan’s performance than either alone, and both feed the plan ratings and benchmarks discussed below.
Audit and the Measurement Year

Numbers a plan reports about itself are only trustworthy if they are verified — the same self-reporting conflict that motivated external quality review. HEDIS addresses this through a formal audit. HEDIS results must be audited by an NCQA-approved auditing firm before they can be publicly reported, conducted by Certified HEDIS Compliance Auditors who follow NCQA standards. The audit includes an assessment of the plan’s information-systems capabilities and an evaluation of compliance with HEDIS specifications — confirming that the plan calculated the measures correctly rather than in a self-flattering way.

HEDIS uses specific timing language worth understanding. The Measurement Year (MY) is the calendar year in which the care was delivered; the audit and reporting happen the following year. So MY 2024 measures care provided during 2024, audited and reported in 2025. Plans submit their final, locked rates through NCQA’s Interactive Data Submission System (IDSS), and the audited results are captured in Final Audit Reports (FARs). This MY/reporting-year structure is why HEDIS results always lag the care they describe by roughly a year.

body.message: An unaudited HEDIS rate is just a plan’s claim about itself. The NCQA-approved compliance audit — validating the data systems and the calculation — is what turns a self-reported number into a trustworthy, comparable result. This audit also feeds the mandatory performance-measure validation that external quality review organizations conduct.
body.title: Audit Is What Makes the Numbers Mean Anything

children.text: Benchmarks: Turning Rates Into Judgments

A HEDIS rate by itself — say, 58% of diabetics with controlled blood sugar — means little without context. Is 58% good or bad? Benchmarks supply the answer by showing how a plan compares to others. NCQA’s Quality Compass provides national, state, and regional HEDIS and CAHPS benchmarks, along with plan-level results, so a plan can see where it stands against peers and competitors. Benchmarks transform an isolated number into a judgment: a rate at the 90th percentile is excellent; one at the 25th percentile signals a problem.

Percentiles are the key tool. Organizations analyze performance against the 25th, 50th (median), 75th, and 90th percentiles to understand where they fall in the distribution and how much room they have to improve. A state can set a contractual quality threshold at, say, the 50th percentile, requiring plans to perform at least as well as the national median. This is how benchmarks become accountability: by attaching consequences (in contracts, ratings, or payment) to where a plan’s HEDIS rates land relative to peers.

These measures also feed broader rating and payment programs. NCQA’s HEDIS measures are used for health plan ratings and payment programs including CMS Star Ratings, state Medicaid quality reporting, and many alternative payment and value-based care programs. A single HEDIS rate can thus ripple outward — informing a plan’s public rating, its standing in a state’s quality strategy, and even its payment under value-based arrangements. This is why plans invest enormous effort in HEDIS performance: the measures are consequential far beyond the report itself.
The Medicaid Core Sets

For Medicaid specifically, HEDIS connects to a parallel federal requirement: the Medicaid and CHIP Core Sets of Health Care Quality Measures. These are standardized measure sets — the Adult Core Set, the Child Core Set, and a Behavioral Health Core Set — that CMS and states use to measure the quality of care delivered to the roughly 78 million Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries. Many Core Set measures are HEDIS measures, calculated following HEDIS specifications, which is why HEDIS reporting and Core Set reporting are tightly intertwined for Medicaid plans.

A major change took effect recently: starting in 2024, reporting of the Child Core Set and the behavioral health measures on the Adult Core Set became mandatory for all states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the territories, with the first round required to be submitted and certified by December 31, 2024. Before this, much Core Set reporting was voluntary and uneven; the mandate creates, for the first time, a consistent national picture of Medicaid quality. States submit state-level data annually, and CMS publicly publishes measures reported by at least 25 states that meet data-quality standards — building transparency and cross-state comparison.

body.analogy: HEDIS is like a standardized exam for health plans. Just as the SAT defines each question precisely so a score in one state means the same as in another, HEDIS defines each measure so "diabetes control rate" is calculated identically everywhere — making plans comparable. The NCQA audit is the proctor ensuring no one cheats on their own score. Benchmarks (percentiles) are the score report showing how you rank against everyone else. And the Medicaid Core Sets are like a required subset of that exam that every state must now take and report.
body.concept: How HEDIS standardizes quality measurement

children.text: This lesson is the measurement backbone of the care-management-and-quality module and connects to much that came before. The performance-measure validation that EQROs perform (from the oversight lesson) largely validates these HEDIS and Core Set measures. The quality requirements written into MCO contracts are largely defined in terms of HEDIS rates and benchmarks. And the value-based purchasing covered in the next module ties plan and provider payment to performance on exactly these measures. HEDIS is not a standalone report — it is the common currency of quality that flows through contracting, oversight, and payment alike. Master HEDIS and the Core Sets, and you understand how "quality" stops being a slogan and becomes a measured, audited, benchmarked, and consequential number.

points: HEDIS (Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set), managed by NCQA, is a set of precisely standardized quality measures that make health plans comparable on the same basis; over 90% of U.S. plans use it.

HEDIS includes more than 90 measures across six domains (effectiveness, access/availability, experience, utilization/risk-adjusted utilization, descriptive information, and electronic data), each defined with exact numerator/denominator specifications.

Data is collected via administrative methodology (claims and electronic records) or hybrid methodology (administrative data plus medical-record review), and HEDIS pairs with CAHPS surveys to capture patient experience.

HEDIS results must be audited by NCQA-approved Certified HEDIS Compliance Auditors before public reporting, verifying data systems and correct calculation — the safeguard that makes self-reported rates trustworthy.
HEDIS uses the "Measurement Year" (MY) for the year care was delivered, audited and reported the following year via NCQA’s IDSS, so results lag the care by about a year.

Benchmarks (via NCQA’s Quality Compass) and percentiles (25th, 50th, 75th, 90th) turn isolated rates into judgments and accountability, and HEDIS measures feed CMS Star Ratings, state Medicaid reporting, and value-based programs.

The Medicaid/CHIP Core Sets (Adult, Child, Behavioral Health) measure quality for ~78 million beneficiaries and draw heavily on HEDIS specifications; the Child Core Set and Adult behavioral health measures became mandatory for all states in 2024 (first submission due December 31, 2024).
HEDIS is the common currency of quality across the course — EQROs validate these measures, contracts define quality in their terms, and value-based purchasing ties payment to performance on them.

children.text: From Scorekeeping to Improvement

Calculating HEDIS rates is only half the job. A breast-cancer-screening rate of 68 percent is a scorecard, not an improvement. The real value of HEDIS comes from using the data to find where care is falling short and then systematically closing those shortfalls — turning measurement into action.

For health plans, HEDIS performance is not optional housekeeping. Results drive NCQA accreditation, Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, Medicaid oversight, and performance-based payments. A plan that lets its rates drift loses accreditation standing, Star bonuses, and contract leverage — so improving HEDIS scores is a core operational discipline, not a once-a-year reporting exercise.

This lesson covers how organizations actually move HEDIS numbers: by understanding the data-timing problem, finding and closing "care gaps," enriching their data, and benchmarking against peers to know where to focus.

HEDIS quality improvement means using measure results to find and close gaps in care — not just reporting a score. For plans, HEDIS performance drives accreditation, Star Ratings, Medicaid oversight, and payment.
The Care Gap: The Unit of Improvement

The central concept in HEDIS improvement is the "care gap" (also called a gap in care). A care gap is an eligible member who has not yet met a measure's numerator requirement — for example, a woman due for a mammogram who has not had one, or a diabetic member with no recorded eye exam this year.

Improving a HEDIS rate is, mechanically, the work of closing care gaps: getting each open member the needed service (and getting it documented) before the measurement window ends. Every gap closed moves a member from the denominator-only group into the numerator, raising the rate.

Plans generate "gap-in-care reports" that list, member by member, which measures are still open. These reports are then routed to care managers and to the member's providers, who do the outreach — scheduling the overdue screening, ordering the lab, or confirming a service already happened. The care gap is the actionable unit that connects a statistic to a specific person and a specific next step.

children.text: The Data Lag Problem

HEDIS improvement is shaped by an awkward timing problem: HEDIS data collection is largely retrospective. Plans rely heavily on claims, and claims arrive weeks or months after care is delivered. By the time a gap shows up in the data, the measurement year may be nearly over and the window to act is closing.

This creates the classic "year-end chase," where plans scramble in the final months to close gaps and abstract charts before hard deadlines — supplemental data submission and medical-record review both end on fixed dates after the measurement year. Gaps not closed and documented before those deadlines simply count against the plan, even if the member was actually eligible to be compliant.

The better answer is year-round, proactive gap monitoring rather than a reactive year-end sprint. Plans increasingly use near-real-time dashboards and alerts that flag open measures as soon as data arrives, so outreach happens continuously. Effective gap closure, as practitioners put it, starts not with today's data but with yesterday's performance — acting early instead of waiting for the retrospective picture to settle.

body.message: Because HEDIS data is retrospective, gaps surface late and plans scramble before fixed deadlines for supplemental data and chart review. Relying on a year-end chase guarantees some genuinely eligible members are missed; year-round monitoring is the fix.
body.title: The Year-End Chase Is a Symptom, Not a Strategy

children.text: Better Data: Supplemental and Standardized

A huge share of "missed" care is not actually missed — it happened but never made it into the plan's claims data. Closing that visibility gap is where supplemental data comes in: structured clinical data pulled from electronic health records, health information exchanges, and data aggregators to capture services that claims alone do not show.

Supplemental data is especially powerful for measures that need clinical values rather than just a billing code — blood pressure readings for the hypertension measure, A1c results for diabetes control. Those numbers live in the EHR, not on a claim. By ingesting and normalizing this data to national standards and HEDIS value sets, plans can credit care that was genuinely delivered, raising numerator accuracy without chasing a single chart by hand.

This is also why the field is moving from manual hybrid chart abstraction toward electronic clinical data systems (ECDS) reporting. Richer, standardized electronic data both improves measured performance and cuts the administrative burden of the year-end chase — a theme that connects directly to the digital quality measures covered later in this course.

body.content:
A plan's claims might show a diabetic member had an office visit but not record an A1c result, leaving the diabetes-control measure open. Pulling the actual A1c value from the practice's EHR via a data feed or HIE can close that gap — the care happened, it just was not on a claim.
Normalizing such clinical data to HEDIS value sets lets plans credit real care, improve numerator accuracy, and reduce reliance on labor-intensive manual chart review.
body.title: Supplemental Clinical Data Closing Gaps

children.text: Benchmarking: Knowing Where to Push

With limited time and staff, a plan cannot work every measure equally hard. Benchmarking tells it where the opportunity is greatest. NCQA's Quality Compass is the standard tool: it provides national, regional, and state benchmarks for each HEDIS and CAHPS measure, plus plan-level results for competitor analysis.

Quality Compass reports performance at percentiles — commonly the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th — so a plan can see not just its own rate but where that rate falls in the distribution. A measure sitting at the 25th percentile is a bigger improvement opportunity (and a bigger accreditation/Star risk) than one already at the 90th.

Used well, benchmarking turns improvement into a focused, data-driven exercise: identify the measures lagging peers, target the care gaps within them, deploy outreach and supplemental data, and re-measure against the benchmark. The formal mechanics of running those improvement cycles — Plan-Do-Study-Act and the Model for Improvement — are covered later in this course; HEDIS data is what feeds them.

children.text: The Germline Side of Disease

The previous lesson covered somatic genomics — acquired changes in a tumor. This lesson turns to the germline side: inherited variants present from conception in every cell, which raise the risk of disease and can be passed to children. Hereditary conditions are where genomics intersects most directly with families, prevention, and difficult personal decisions.

The distinguishing feature of a germline finding is that it is not just about one patient. Because the variant is inherited, it has implications for the patient's relatives — and a result in one person can prompt testing across an entire family. This family dimension makes hereditary genetics fundamentally different from most of medicine, which treats one patient at a time.

And critically, many hereditary conditions are actionable: knowing a person carries a high-risk variant lets them and their clinicians intervene to prevent the disease or catch it early. A germline result is not just a label — it is a chance to change the future, for the patient and for relatives who share the variant. That actionability is what makes hereditary genetics so valuable.

Hereditary conditions arise from inherited (germline) variants present from conception. Because they are inherited, a result affects the whole family — and because many are actionable, knowing about them lets patients and relatives prevent disease or catch it early.
Major Hereditary Cancer Syndromes

More than 50 hereditary cancer syndromes have been described, but two dominate clinical practice. Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer (HBOC) syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in BRCA1 or BRCA2. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, and carriers face dramatically elevated cancer risk — women with BRCA variants have roughly a 65-74 percent lifetime risk of breast cancer and a substantially elevated risk of ovarian cancer.

HBOC's prevalence varies by population: the BRCA carrier frequency is roughly 1 in 500 in the general population but about 1 in 40 in people of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry — a reminder that genetic risk is unevenly distributed and that ancestry matters in risk assessment.

The other major syndrome is Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer), caused by defects in DNA mismatch-repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM). It is highly penetrant and autosomal dominant, and it accounts for roughly 1-3 percent of all colorectal cancer cases, plus elevated risk of endometrial and other cancers. Note the connection to the oncology lesson: Lynch-related tumors are often mismatch-repair deficient / MSI-high — the same molecular feature that makes them responsive to tumor-agnostic immunotherapy. Germline and somatic genomics intertwine.

children.text: The Central Role of Genetic Counseling

Hereditary genetic testing should rarely happen without genetic counseling, because the results carry weight far beyond a typical lab value. Genetic counselors help patients understand whether testing is appropriate, what the possible results mean (including the ACMG categories and the dreaded variant of uncertain significance), the implications for relatives, and the emotional and practical consequences of knowing.

Counseling matters because a germline result is life-altering in ways a routine test is not. A positive predictive result tells a healthy person they carry substantial future risk — information that affects family planning, relationships, mental health, and major medical decisions. A negative result must be interpreted carefully (does it rule out the family's known variant, or just the common ones?). And a VUS leaves the patient in genuine uncertainty. Pre-test and post-test counseling helps patients make informed choices and cope with the answers.

Counseling also addresses the family dimension. A counselor helps the patient understand who among their relatives is at risk, how to share the information, and how relatives can pursue their own testing. This is delicate — it involves disclosing genetic information across a family, with all the privacy, relationship, and ethical complexity that entails (the subject of later lessons on GINA and consent). The genetic counselor is the professional who navigates all of this, which is why their role is central to hereditary genetics.

This is also a workforce reality: there are far fewer genetic counselors than the demand created by cheap, widespread testing, which is part of why models like counselor-supported primary care and telegenetics are growing.
Management: Turning Knowledge Into Prevention

The point of identifying a hereditary risk is to act on it, and for many syndromes there are well-established, effective interventions. For BRCA carriers, the management toolkit has three levers: enhanced screening (earlier, more frequent, more intensive surveillance — e.g., breast MRI in addition to mammography), chemoprevention (risk-reducing medications such as tamoxifen), and risk-reducing surgery (such as prophylactic mastectomy or removal of the ovaries and fallopian tubes).

For Lynch syndrome, management centers on intensive colorectal surveillance — frequent colonoscopy starting at a young age, which can catch and remove precancerous polyps before they become cancer — along with surveillance for the other associated cancers. These are not hypothetical benefits: enhanced surveillance and risk-reducing interventions in high-risk carriers measurably reduce morbidity and mortality.

The key concept underlying management is penetrance — the probability that someone with a variant will actually develop the associated disease. Penetrance is rarely 100 percent; a BRCA variant confers high but not certain risk. This is why management is about risk reduction and vigilance, not certainty, and why the choices (especially irreversible surgery) are deeply personal and require careful, individualized counseling weighing the patient's specific risk, values, and life stage.

children.text: Cascade Testing: From One Patient to a Family

The most powerful — and most underused — feature of hereditary genetics is cascade testing: when a person (the "proband") is found to carry a pathogenic variant, that information cascades to their at-risk relatives, who can then be tested. Because these conditions are autosomal dominant, each first-degree relative (parent, sibling, child) has a 50 percent chance of carrying the same variant.

Cascade testing is extraordinarily high-value because it turns one diagnosis into prevention for a whole family. Relatives who test positive can pursue the same risk-reducing surveillance and interventions before they ever get sick; those who test negative are reassured and spared unnecessary screening. The CDC recognizes this by designating cascade testing for Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer, Lynch syndrome, and familial hypercholesterolemia as "Tier 1" genomic applications — meaning the evidence for population-level benefit is strongest for these.

Yet cascade testing is consistently underutilized — many relatives of identified carriers never get tested, due to barriers in communication, access, cost, and the difficulty of sharing genetic information within families. Closing this gap is a major opportunity (and an equity issue, since barriers fall unevenly). The broader lesson is that hereditary genetics is uniquely leveraged: each identified carrier is a doorway to preventing disease across an entire family tree. Counsel well, manage with the appropriate prevention, and cascade to relatives — that is the full cycle of hereditary genetic care, and it sets up the policy and ethics lessons on protecting the genetic information all of this generates.

Cascade testing is CDC Tier 1 but badly underutilized.

children.text: What Is the 21st Century Cures Act?

The 21st Century Cures Act — officially H.R. 34 — is one of the most consequential pieces of health legislation enacted in the United States in the past decade. President Barack Obama signed it into law on December 13, 2016, capping a multi-year, bipartisan effort to modernize the country's biomedical research enterprise, overhaul the federal mental health system, and drag the healthcare information technology sector into a genuinely interoperable future. The law passed by overwhelming margins — 392 to 26 in the House on November 30, 2016, and 94 to 5 in the Senate on December 7, 2016 — a rarity in an era of polarized legislating that underscores how broadly supported its core goals were across party lines.

At its core, the Act is best understood as three distinct but interlocking policy packages bundled into a single statute. The first package dramatically accelerates biomedical research by creating a dedicated NIH Innovation Account funded at $4.976 billion over ten years, with sub-appropriations targeting cancer, the brain, and precision medicine. The second package reforms the nation's fractured mental health delivery system by incorporating the long-stalled Helping Families in Mental Health Crisis Act and committing $1 billion in opioid crisis grants to states. The third package — and arguably the most operationally far-reaching — mandates true electronic health information interoperability, prohibits "information blocking," and requires federally certified EHR systems to offer open, standards-based APIs that patients can use to access their own records at no cost.

The total authorized funding across all three packages reaches $6.3 billion, making the Cures Act not just a policy milestone but a substantial investment in infrastructure. Critics at the time noted that authorization does not guarantee appropriation — Congress still had to fund the accounts annually — but supporters argued that the ring-fenced NIH Innovation Account structure created a more durable funding mechanism than ordinary discretionary spending, insulating flagship research programs from year-to-year budget battles.

The 21st Century Cures Act (H.R. 34, 2016) is a tripartite law that (1) funds landmark biomedical research through a dedicated NIH Innovation Account, (2) restructures federal mental health and substance use programs, and (3) mandates open, interoperable health IT through binding prohibitions on information blocking and requirements for FHIR-based patient access APIs.

children.text: Research Funding: Cancer, Brain, and Precision Medicine

The centerpiece of the Cures Act's research agenda is the NIH Innovation Account, a dedicated fund that sits outside the normal appropriations process and is designed to provide predictable, multi-year financing for three flagship initiatives. This structural choice was deliberate. Biomedical research programs that require sustained investment — building tissue banks, running decade-long longitudinal cohorts, funding research consortia — have historically been vulnerable to the unpredictability of annual appropriations. The Innovation Account attempts to solve that problem by giving Congress a framework to pre-commit funding over a ten-year window, even if the actual dollar transfers still require annual appropriation action.

The three flagship initiatives funded through the NIH Innovation Account each represent a different dimension of the federal research agenda. The Cancer Moonshot, later formally renamed the "Beau Biden Cancer Moonshot" in honor of Vice President Biden's son who died of brain cancer in 2015, received $1.8 billion to accelerate cancer prevention, detection, treatment, and data sharing. The BRAIN (Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies) Initiative received $1.5 billion to map neural circuitry at unprecedented resolution and develop new tools for treating neurological and psychiatric conditions. The Precision Medicine Initiative — which later became the All of Us Research Program — also received $1.5 billion to build a national cohort of one million or more participants whose genomic, environmental, and lifestyle data would inform individually tailored treatments.

Beyond the three research flagships, the Act also invested $1 billion in opioid grants to states — a recognition that the opioid crisis ravaging communities across the country required not just more research but immediate, on-the-ground infrastructure to expand treatment access and improve prescription drug monitoring. The FDA provisions of the Act further accelerated the pipeline from research bench to patient bedside through new approval pathways for breakthrough devices and a framework for using real-world evidence from electronic health records and claims databases in post-market studies. Taken together, the research title of the Cures Act represents the most ambitious single legislative investment in biomedical science since the National Cancer Act of 1971.

The Cancer Moonshot was named for Beau Biden, son of then-Vice President Joe Biden, who died of glioblastoma multiforme at age 46 in May 2015. Vice President Biden personally championed the initiative and led the White House Cancer Moonshot Task Force before the Cures Act codified and funded it.

The NIH Innovation Account works differently: the Cures Act established the account in statute and authorized specific annual transfer amounts for each year from FY2017 through FY2026. This means Congress pre-committed to a funding trajectory in the authorizing legislation itself, rather than leaving each year's level entirely to the appropriations process. While actual transfers still require appropriations action, the statutory schedule creates a strong expectation — and a political baseline — that provides more stability for grantees, university research programs, and NIH program officers than traditional year-by-year discretionary spending would allow.

children.text: Mental Health and the Opioid Crisis

The mental health title of the Cures Act represented the culmination of years of work by Representative Tim Murphy (R-PA), a clinical psychologist who had spent much of his congressional tenure fighting for what he called "evidence-based mental health care." His Helping Families in Mental Health Crisis Act, introduced in multiple sessions of Congress, was incorporated nearly wholesale into the Cures Act after years of stalling. The legislation's core insight was that the federal mental health bureaucracy had become fragmented, underfunded, and disconnected from the evidence base — funding peer support and awareness programs while failing to adequately support the clinical treatment and hospital-based care that severe psychiatric illness actually requires.

The most structurally significant change in the mental health title was the creation of a new Assistant Secretary for Mental Health and Substance Use within the Department of Health and Human Services — a position that elevated mental health policy to the same bureaucratic level as other major health domains. The legislation also reorganized the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), tightened requirements around evidence-based practices, and expanded the ability of states to use Assisted Outpatient Treatment (AOT) — court-ordered community-based care for individuals with severe mental illness who have a history of treatment non-adherence. Privacy rule clarifications in the Act also made it easier for providers to share mental health information with family members in crisis situations.

The $1 billion in opioid state grants represented one of the federal government's most direct financial interventions in the opioid crisis up to that point. The grants were authorized over two fiscal years and structured to flow through a formula-based allocation process that weighted states' burden of opioid overdose deaths and the capacity of their existing treatment infrastructure. States were required to submit plans demonstrating how funds would be used for evidence-based interventions — including medication-assisted treatment (MAT) expansion, prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) improvements, and naloxone distribution — rather than general public awareness campaigns.

Patients do not receive grants; states and local health agencies do. This distinction matters because it means the grants improve the system's ability to deliver care without replacing the insurance coverage and Medicaid financing that actually pays for individual treatment episodes.

children.text: Information Blocking: The New Prohibition

Of all the provisions in the 21st Century Cures Act, the information blocking prohibition has proven to be the most disruptive to established business practices in the health IT industry. For years, critics argued that EHR vendors, hospitals, and health information exchanges were intentionally making it difficult — or prohibitively expensive — for patients and providers to access, exchange, or use electronic health information. The Act addressed this directly by making "information blocking" a federal offense subject to civil monetary penalties. The statutory definition is deliberately broad: any practice by a regulated actor that is likely to interfere with access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI) — unless the practice falls within one of eight defined exceptions.

The Cures Act subjects three categories of actors to the information blocking rules. Health IT developers of certified health information technology (the EHR vendors themselves) are covered. Health information exchanges (HIEs) and health information networks (HINs) are covered. And healthcare providers — hospitals, physician practices, clinics — are covered. This tripartite scope was intentional: Congress recognized that information blocking could originate at any node in the health IT ecosystem, not just at the vendor level. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule, published May 1, 2020 in the Federal Register and effective June 30, 2020, fleshed out the specific regulatory definitions that give the statute operational meaning.

Enforcement of the information blocking rules began April 5, 2021 — the date when actors could first be formally reported to the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) of HHS for suspected violations. As of February 2026, OIG had received nearly 1,600 complaints, reflecting the breadth of perceived violations across the industry. Active enforcement actions began in September 2025. For health IT developers and HIEs/HINs, penalties can reach up to $1 million per violation — a figure large enough to create genuine compliance pressure even for the largest vendors. Healthcare providers face a different enforcement mechanism: disincentives established under a July 2024 final rule, which can affect Medicare reimbursement rates and meaningful use attestation.

Information blocking is defined as any practice by a covered actor (health IT developer, HIE/HIN, or healthcare provider) that is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage access, exchange, or use of electronic health information — unless the practice qualifies under one of the eight regulatory exceptions established by ONC.

points: Charging excessive fees to access or export patient data that are not cost-based
Deploying non-standard or proprietary interfaces that prevent third-party apps from connecting
Including contract "gag clauses" that prevent customers from disclosing interoperability limitations
Delaying responses to API queries without technical justification
Conditioning data access on the purchase of additional vendor products or services

right.label: The 8 Regulatory Exceptions (Permitted Practices)
points: Privacy Exception — practices required to protect patient privacy under applicable law
Security Exception — practices necessary to protect the security of EHI
Preventing Harm Exception — practices needed to prevent endangerment of patients or others
Infeasibility Exception — practices technically or legally not feasible to perform
Health IT Performance Exception — routine system maintenance and downtime
Licensing Exception — reasonable and non-discriminatory licensing of IP
Content/Manner Exception — responding in a different form or manner than requested
Fees Exception — charging reasonable, cost-based fees for access or export

children.text: Interoperability: FHIR APIs and Patient Access

The interoperability mandates in the Cures Act translate its broad policy goals into specific, enforceable technical requirements. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule — published May 1, 2020 and effective June 30, 2020 — requires that all ONC-certified health IT systems support FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) Release 4.0.1 as the technical standard for patient-facing access APIs. FHIR R4 is a specification published by HL7 International that defines how healthcare data should be structured and exchanged using modern web standards — RESTful APIs, JSON, and OAuth 2.0 authentication. By mandating FHIR R4 specifically, ONC locked in a single, vendor-neutral standard that any compliant application can connect to, regardless of which EHR system a hospital uses.

The minimum data set that must be accessible through the FHIR API is defined by the United States Core Data for Interoperability version 1 (USCDI v1), which includes clinical notes, laboratory results, medications, allergies, immunizations, vital signs, demographics, and care team members. Patients have the right to access this data through any SMART on FHIR-compatible application of their choosing, at no cost, without the provider or EHR vendor being able to block or restrict that access. The Act also mandated the development of the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) — a nationwide governance framework that establishes the legal, technical, and policy rules for how health information networks can share data across organizational and geographic boundaries.

The combined effect of the FHIR mandate, the information blocking prohibition, and TEFCA is to create — for the first time — a coherent federal framework for nationwide health data exchange. Before the Cures Act, the health IT landscape was a patchwork of proprietary interfaces, regional health information organizations with incompatible standards, and contractual barriers that prevented patients from exercising meaningful control over their own records. After the Act, any certified EHR system must publish a standards-based FHIR API, attest that it is not engaging in information blocking, and — as TEFCA networks mature — participate in a national exchange framework. The transformation is still in progress, but the legal architecture is now in place.

body.analogy: Requiring all certified EHRs to support FHIR Release 4.0.1 is like mandating the USB-C connector standard for all consumer electronics: once every device uses the same port, any compliant cable or accessory works with any device — no proprietary adapter needed. Before FHIR R4 was mandated, each EHR vendor had its own proprietary API (or no API at all), so a patient-facing app had to build a separate integration for each vendor. The standard port means the app only needs to be built once.
body.concept: FHIR R4 Mandate as the USB-C Standard for Health Data

body.content: Epic Systems — the largest EHR vendor in the United States, used by roughly 35% of U.S. hospitals — built its "App Orchard" ecosystem directly in response to the Cures Act interoperability mandates. App Orchard is a marketplace where third-party developers publish SMART on FHIR applications that connect to Epic's FHIR R4 API. Patients at Epic-using hospitals can authorize any App Orchard application — or any SMART on FHIR app they choose — to receive their health data via the standard API. Competitors like Oracle Health (Cerner) and Meditech built comparable API ecosystems. The result is that the Cures Act effectively forced the entire certified EHR market to open its data layer to patient-authorized third-party applications, creating the infrastructure for a generation of consumer health apps.

children.text: FDA Provisions and Real-World Evidence

The FDA title of the Cures Act addresses a set of long-standing criticisms of the regulatory pathway from medical innovation to patient access. The Act created or strengthened several mechanisms designed to accelerate the availability of breakthrough products while maintaining safety standards. The Breakthrough Device Designation program — building on the existing Breakthrough Therapy designation for drugs — allows novel medical devices that provide more effective treatment or diagnosis of life-threatening or irreversibly debilitating conditions to receive priority FDA review, with more frequent interaction between developers and FDA reviewers during the development process. The Act also expanded expanded access (compassionate use) pathways, making it easier for patients with serious conditions to access investigational products outside of clinical trials.

Perhaps the most forward-looking FDA provision in the Cures Act is the real-world evidence (RWE) framework. Traditional drug and device approval relies on randomized controlled trials — expensive, time-consuming, and often conducted on patient populations that do not reflect the diversity of real-world patients. The Cures Act directed FDA to develop a framework for using real-world data — including data from electronic health records, insurance claims databases, patient registries, and wearable devices — to support regulatory decisions, including post-approval studies and, in some cases, new indications for already-approved products. The Act also clarified the regulatory status of software as a medical device (SaMD), explicitly excluding certain low-risk wellness and administrative software from FDA oversight while preserving the agency's authority over clinical decision support tools that could cause patient harm if they malfunctioned.

points: The 21st Century Cures Act (H.R. 34) was signed December 13, 2016, with near-unanimous bipartisan support (392–26 House, 94–5 Senate), authorizing $6.3 billion across three policy pillars: research funding, mental health reform, and health IT interoperability.

The NIH Innovation Account ($4.976B over 10 years) funds three flagship research programs: the Cancer Moonshot ($1.8B), the BRAIN Initiative ($1.5B), and the Precision Medicine Initiative ($1.5B), with an additional $1B in opioid grants to states.

The Act incorporated the Helping Families in Mental Health Crisis Act (Rep. Tim Murphy), created the Assistant Secretary for Mental Health and Substance Use, and restructured SAMHSA around evidence-based practices.

Information blocking — any practice by a health IT developer, HIE/HIN, or provider that interferes with access to electronic health information — is now a federal offense with penalties up to $1 million per violation for developers and HIEs; providers face Medicare reimbursement disincentives.

Eight regulatory exceptions exist to the information blocking prohibition, covering privacy, security, harm prevention, infeasibility, IT performance, licensing, content/manner, and reasonable cost-based fees.

The ONC Cures Act Final Rule (effective June 30, 2020) mandates FHIR Release 4.0.1 as the standard for patient access APIs and USCDI v1 as the minimum data set — giving patients a legally enforceable right to their health data through any authorized app, at no cost.

FDA provisions established the Breakthrough Device Designation, expanded real-world evidence frameworks for regulatory decisions, and clarified that low-risk wellness software is excluded from FDA medical device oversight — shaping the entire digital health regulatory landscape.

ONC administers the certification program and receives complaints, but it is OIG that investigates and adjudicates penalties. CMS administers the provider disincentive process established by the July 2024 final rule. The FTC has no information blocking enforcement authority under the Cures Act.

children.text: Why Quality Measurement Matters

Healthcare quality in the United States has long been characterized by profound variation. The Institute of Medicine's landmark 2001 report "Crossing the Quality Chasm" catalogued the gap between the care Americans receive and the care they should receive, organizing the challenge around six dimensions: care should be safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable. Two decades later those six aims remain the organizing principle behind virtually every major quality measurement program in the country — including those run by CMS, NCQA, and The Joint Commission. The persistent variability in clinical outcomes across hospitals, health plans, and geographic regions is both the problem quality measurement was designed to expose and the reason it continues to expand.

Measurement is the prerequisite for improvement. A health system cannot reliably close a gap it cannot see. Quality measures translate abstract aims — "be safer," "be more equitable" — into specific, reportable rates that clinicians, administrators, payers, and policymakers can act on. A 30-day readmission rate tells a hospital CEO that something is breaking down in care transitions. A low rate of A1C testing in diabetic patients tells a health plan that its network may not be providing guideline-concordant care. Without these concrete signals, improvement efforts are speculative rather than targeted. Quality measurement converts clinical ambition into operational data.

The stakes are no longer purely clinical — they are financial. Federal payment programs now link reimbursement directly to measured quality performance. The Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) adjusts Medicare payments to individual clinicians based partly on how well they score on quality measures. Hospital Value-Based Purchasing ties a portion of inpatient reimbursement to performance on clinical, safety, and patient experience measures. The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program penalizes facilities with excess readmission rates. As the healthcare system shifts from volume to value, the ability to measure, report, and improve on quality measures has become a core business competency for every provider organization.

CMS defines quality measures as "tools that help measure or quantify healthcare processes, outcomes, patient perceptions, and organizational structure and/or systems that are associated with the ability to provide high-quality health care and/or that relate to one or more quality goals for health care — effective, safe, efficient, patient-centered, equitable, and timely care."

children.text: The Donabedian Framework: Structure, Process, Outcome

In 1966, Avedis Donabedian published "Evaluating the Quality of Medical Care" in the Milbank Memorial Fund Quarterly — now considered one of the most cited articles in public health history. Donabedian proposed that quality could be assessed through three interconnected lenses: the structure in which care is delivered, the processes of care that occur, and the outcomes that result. His framework gave healthcare a vocabulary for measurement that had previously been missing, and it remains the conceptual backbone of virtually every quality program in use today, more than fifty years after its publication.

Structure refers to the context in which care is delivered: the physical facilities, the equipment available, the qualifications and number of staff, how financing is organized, and whether the organization uses an electronic health record. Structure measures are often the easiest to collect but the least directly tied to patient outcomes. Process measures capture the transactions between patients and providers — whether a diabetic patient had their hemoglobin A1C tested, whether a patient with hypertension was prescribed an ACE inhibitor, whether a smoker received cessation counseling. Because they describe actions that clinicians take (or fail to take), process measures are highly actionable. Outcome measures capture the ultimate effects on health: 30-day readmission rates, in-hospital mortality, hospital-acquired infections, patient satisfaction scores.

Donabedian's framework implies a causal chain: better structure enables better processes, and better processes produce better outcomes. That logic underpins all modern quality improvement programs. But the chain has real limits. Structure does not guarantee good process — a well-equipped hospital can still deliver inconsistent care. Process does not guarantee good outcomes — sometimes the right care is delivered and the patient still deteriorates due to disease complexity. And outcomes are influenced by factors entirely outside the health system, including socioeconomic conditions and patient behavior. This is why high-quality measurement programs typically balance all three dimensions rather than relying on outcomes alone.

body.analogy: Think of structure as a kitchen, process as the recipe followed, and outcome as the dish that arrives — you need all three to understand why a meal was good or bad.

children.text: HEDIS: The Health Plan Quality Standard

The Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — universally known as HEDIS — is maintained by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) and is the most widely used health plan quality tool in the United States. Health plans use HEDIS to measure performance across dozens of clinical domains including preventive care, chronic disease management, behavioral health, and maternal health. Results are used for NCQA accreditation, public reporting through Quality Compass, and value-based contracting with employers, Medicaid agencies, and Medicare Advantage sponsors. As of the MY2023/2024 ratings cycle, approximately 227 million Americans are enrolled in health plans that report HEDIS results to NCQA — a scale that makes it unlike any other quality dataset in American healthcare.

HEDIS data is collected through three methods depending on the measure. Administrative data — claims and encounter records — is the most efficient source and sufficient for many measures. Supplemental data allows plans to incorporate information from provider EHRs and labs that does not appear in claims. The hybrid method combines administrative data with targeted medical record review for a random sample of eligible members, providing higher accuracy for measures where claims alone are insufficient. The MY 2024 State of Health Care Quality Report includes national averages for 90 quality measures covering clinical care and patient satisfaction, giving plans, purchasers, and regulators a comprehensive national benchmark.

NCQA's 2024 Health Plan Ratings are calculated as a weighted average of HEDIS clinical quality scores and CAHPS patient experience scores, plus bonus points for accreditation status. Plans use these ratings for marketing differentiation, member retention, and to satisfy contractual requirements from large employers and government programs. For Medicaid managed care plans and Medicare Advantage organizations, HEDIS performance can directly affect premium revenue through quality bonus payments, creating powerful financial incentives to invest in the care gaps HEDIS measures reveal. Vermont's Medicaid managed care and ACO programs rely on HEDIS as a core performance framework for their quality improvement portfolios.
227 million Americans are in plans that report HEDIS — making it the most widely used healthcare quality tool in the country.

children.text: Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs)

Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs) represent a fundamental shift in how quality data is collected. Traditional clinical quality measures (CQMs) required manual abstraction — a trained person reviewing paper charts or PDF-based records to find the information needed to calculate a rate. That process was expensive, slow, and prone to inter-rater variability. eCQMs are specified in a standard electronic format, with logic written using Health Quality Measure Format (HQMF) and expressed against standard clinical terminologies — SNOMED CT for clinical findings, LOINC for laboratory and clinical observations, ICD-10 for diagnoses, and RxNorm for medications. Data is extracted automatically from EHR systems, eliminating manual review for the bulk of reporting.

CMS uses eCQMs across multiple programs: the Medicaid Promoting Interoperability Program, the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program (formerly Meaningful Use), the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS), and Alternative Payment Models (APMs). A critical operational advantage of eCQMs is coverage: because they run against structured EHR data for all applicable patients, eCQMs automatically meet MIPS's 75% reporting frequency threshold — a requirement that is administratively burdensome when using traditional chart-abstracted measures. This near-complete patient coverage also makes eCQM rates more statistically reliable than sample-based results, giving CMS and providers a more accurate picture of actual performance.

The next evolution of eCQMs is FHIR-based quality reporting. The HL7 FHIR standard — the same infrastructure driving patient access APIs and interoperability mandates — is now being applied to quality reporting. FHIR-based quality measures (sometimes called "digital quality measures" or dQMs) use FHIR resources and Clinical Quality Language (CQL) to define measure logic that can execute against FHIR-compliant EHR data. This approach promises to reduce the gap between care delivery and quality reporting, enabling near real-time feedback and making it feasible to expand measurement into clinical domains that were previously too complex or costly to abstract manually.
eCQMs extract data directly from EHRs in a standard electronic format — eliminating the manual chart abstraction that traditional CQMs required, reducing both cost and human error.

children.text: CMS Quality Reporting Programs: MIPS, IQR, and VBP

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services operates the largest portfolio of quality reporting programs in American healthcare. For individual clinicians, the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) is the primary vehicle. MIPS consolidates quality, improvement activities, promoting interoperability, and cost into a composite score that adjusts each clinician's Medicare Part B payments upward or downward. In 2024, the Quality performance category accounts for 30% of the MIPS final score — the single largest component. CMS finalized 198 quality measures available for MIPS reporting in 2024 (173 traditional CQMs plus 58 eCQMs), added 11 new measures, and removed 11 others. Clinicians must report on a minimum of 6 quality measures, including at least one outcome or high-priority measure.

For acute care hospitals, the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) Program is the foundational reporting vehicle. IQR is a pay-for-reporting program: hospitals that do not successfully report face a reduction in their annual payment update. But IQR data also feeds directly into programs with more direct payment consequences. The Hospital Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) Program uses IQR-reported measures to calculate a Total Performance Score that can either increase or decrease inpatient Medicare payments. The Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program (HACRP) uses safety and infection measures to identify the worst-performing hospitals, which receive a 1% payment reduction on all Medicare discharges. Together these programs create a layered financial accountability structure for hospital quality.

The movement toward value-based payment has fundamentally changed how provider organizations think about quality measurement. When quality scores were used only for public reporting, the financial consequences of poor performance were reputational. Now they are direct and material. A large hospital system subject to HRRP penalties, HACRP reductions, and VBP adjustments simultaneously can see millions of dollars in annual payment impact from quality performance. This has driven significant investment in quality improvement infrastructure — care management teams, data analytics platforms, population health systems, and transitional care programs — all justified in part by the financial return on improving measure performance.

children.text: Quality Measurement and Health Equity

Aggregate quality scores can obscure profound inequities hidden within the average. A health system may achieve a respectable overall 30-day readmission rate while Black or Hispanic patients at the same institution face rates two to three times higher. A health plan may report strong HEDIS scores on diabetes care while patients with limited English proficiency receive far lower rates of A1C testing and retinal exams. When quality measurement programs report only aggregate rates, they cannot detect — and therefore cannot address — these disparities. Stratifying quality measures by race, ethnicity, preferred language, and socioeconomic status is the methodological prerequisite for an equitable quality improvement agenda.

Both CMS and NCQA have made explicit commitments to embed equity stratification into their quality measurement frameworks. NCQA has developed HEDIS equity measures and is expanding stratified reporting requirements. CMS's Universal Foundation for quality measurement, launched as part of its National Quality Strategy, includes health equity as a core domain and is incorporating race and ethnicity stratification into MIPS and Medicaid reporting. The practical challenge is data: stratified quality reporting requires that EHRs and health plans collect accurate, complete, and standardized race, ethnicity, and language data — a requirement that remains inconsistently met across the industry. Health information exchanges like Vermont's VITL play a growing role in aggregating this data across provider organizations to enable population-level equity analysis.

body.message: A hospital may have an excellent average 30-day readmission rate while having much higher rates for Black or Hispanic patients. children.text: Two Philosophies of Payment

For most of the twentieth century, fee-for-service was the unchallenged foundation of American healthcare finance. Hospitals billed for admissions, physicians billed for office visits, and laboratories billed for every test they ran. The logic was straightforward: you perform a service, you get paid for it. As healthcare grew in complexity and cost, however, that logic began to reveal a profound structural flaw. The United States now spends approximately 18 percent of its gross domestic product on healthcare — more than any other high-income nation — yet ranks well below peers on life expectancy, avoidable mortality, and access to primary care. The spending and the outcomes were moving in opposite directions, and the payment system was at least partly responsible.

The volume-to-value shift began in earnest with the Affordable Care Act of 2010, which created the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI) and charged it with testing alternative payment models at scale. The underlying premise was that if you change what you pay for, you change what providers do. Instead of rewarding every procedure and encounter, value-based models reward providers for keeping patients healthy, reducing unnecessary hospitalizations, and coordinating care across settings. Changing the payment architecture, in other words, was seen as the most reliable lever for changing clinical behavior.

The stakes could not be higher. Medicare and Medicaid together cover more than 160 million Americans and account for the largest single share of national health expenditure. How CMS structures its payment models shapes what every hospital, physician practice, and post-acute facility does in practice. Understanding the difference between fee-for-service and value-based care — not just in theory but in operational detail — is essential for anyone working in health informatics, policy, or administration.

Fee-for-Service (FFS): A payment model in which providers receive a separate reimbursement for each individual service, procedure, or encounter they deliver. Payment rates are set prospectively (e.g., via Medicare's physician fee schedule or DRG-based inpatient rates) and are independent of whether the service improves the patient's health. The incentive is to deliver more services, not better outcomes.

children.text: How Fee-for-Service Works — and Why It Creates Problems

In a fee-for-service system, every billable interaction has a code. Physicians use Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes to document what they did; hospitals use Diagnosis-Related Groups (DRGs) for inpatient stays and Ambulatory Payment Classifications (APCs) for outpatient services. Each code maps to a payment rate set by a prospective payment system. Medicare's physician fee schedule converts CPT codes into relative value units (RVUs) — composite measures of physician work, practice expense, and malpractice cost — then multiplies by a conversion factor to produce a dollar amount. More RVUs mean more revenue; no RVUs mean no revenue. Prevention, care coordination, and phone calls that keep patients out of the hospital generate few or no billable events under traditional FFS.

The perverse incentive chain that FFS creates is well documented. A cardiologist who orders an echocardiogram generates revenue; a primary care physician who spends forty minutes counseling a diabetic patient on lifestyle changes may barely cover overhead. Surgical specialties that perform high-RVU procedures are systematically better compensated than primary and preventive care, which contributes to specialist shortages in rural areas and underinvestment in chronic disease management. Studies suggest that up to 30 percent of FFS spending may be attributable to low-value or unnecessary services — imaging ordered out of habit, procedures performed on patients unlikely to benefit, hospitalizations that could have been avoided with better outpatient management.

Fragmentation is FFS's other structural legacy. Because each provider bills independently, specialists and primary care physicians have little financial incentive to communicate or coordinate. A patient with heart failure, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease may see five separate specialists who each optimize for their own domain without a unified treatment plan. Hospital readmissions — often preventable with proper discharge planning and follow-up — generate additional admissions revenue under FFS rather than creating a financial penalty. This architecture does not fail by accident; it produces exactly the behaviors the payment system rewards.

body.analogy: Fee-for-service is like paying a mechanic by the part they replace, not by whether the car runs — the incentive is to find more parts to replace, not to fix the root problem.
body.concept: FFS payment incentivizes volume of services rather than patient outcomes, just as paying per repair part incentivizes more replacements rather than a well-functioning vehicle.

body.message: Under FFS, a provider who avoids an unnecessary hospitalization actually loses revenue. The system penalizes prevention and efficiency because neither generates a billable event. A well-coordinated care team that keeps a high-risk patient out of the emergency department is financially punished relative to one that admits the same patient for observation.

children.text: The Value-Based Care Spectrum

Value-based care is not a single payment model — it is a spectrum ranging from modest quality bonuses layered on top of FFS to full capitation in which providers receive a fixed monthly payment per patient regardless of how many services they deliver. The common thread is that provider payment is linked, in some way, to quality metrics, outcome measures, or total cost of care benchmarks. The degree of financial risk the provider accepts varies dramatically across the spectrum, and that risk level largely determines how strongly the model changes provider behavior.

Pay-for-performance (P4P) sits at the low-risk end. Providers continue to receive FFS base payments but earn small bonuses — or face small penalties — based on performance on quality metrics such as HbA1c control rates, cancer screening adherence, or patient experience scores. Because the adjustments are typically small relative to total revenue, P4P alone has a limited effect on clinical practice. Shared savings models, like Medicare ACOs, occupy the middle of the spectrum: providers take responsibility for a defined population and share in any savings achieved versus a spending benchmark, with more advanced tracks adding downside risk. Full capitation — common in staff-model HMOs and some Medicaid managed care contracts — places the full utilization risk on the provider organization, creating the strongest incentive to invest in prevention and care management.

CMS has structured its Alternative Payment Model (APM) framework to encourage providers to move along the spectrum toward greater accountability. The Quality Payment Program designates certain two-sided risk models as Advanced APMs; clinicians who meet participation thresholds in Advanced APMs earn a 5 percent incentive bonus (applicable to payment years 2020 through 2024) and are exempt from the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) reporting requirements. By 2026, a record 82.8 percent of MSSP ACOs were in Advanced APM tracks — evidence that the financial incentives are working to push providers toward greater risk-sharing.
