children.text: The Medicare Shared Savings Program: ACOs in Action

The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), launched in 2012 under the Affordable Care Act, is the largest value-based care program in the United States by beneficiary count. MSSP allows groups of physicians, hospitals, and other providers to form Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) and accept accountability for the total cost and quality of care for an attributed population of Traditional Medicare beneficiaries. Attribution is largely based on primary care utilization: beneficiaries are assigned to the ACO whose primary care clinicians they see most frequently. The ACO is then measured against a benchmark — an estimate of what CMS would have spent on that population absent the ACO — and earns or owes a share of the difference.

The financial mechanics of MSSP are designed to balance risk and reward. ACOs in upside-only tracks (BASIC Level A/B) can earn up to 40–50 percent of savings above the minimum savings rate but owe nothing if they spend above benchmark. ACOs in two-sided tracks (BASIC Level E and ENHANCED) earn a higher savings share — up to 75 percent — but also owe a portion of losses. Benchmarks are updated annually and incorporate regional spending trends to prevent ACOs in low-cost markets from being penalized for historical efficiency. Quality performance gates apply: ACOs must meet minimum quality standards to receive shared savings, and quality scores affect the savings rate they earn.

Performance year 2024 produced the most compelling evidence yet that MSSP works at scale. With 476 ACOs caring for approximately 10.3 million Traditional Medicare beneficiaries, the program generated $4.1 billion in shared savings for participating ACOs and $2.4 billion in net savings for Medicare — the highest figures since program inception in 2012. Seventy-five percent of ACOs earned performance payments, and only 16 ACOs owed shared losses totaling $20.3 million. The results suggest that the MSSP model, particularly as ACOs mature and move into two-sided risk, is delivering meaningful reductions in total cost of care while maintaining or improving quality.
In 2024, MSSP ACOs earned $4.1 billion in shared savings while Medicare net-saved $2.4 billion — the best results since the program launched in 2012.

children.text: Hospital Value-Based Programs: VBP, HRRP, and HACRP

CMS applies value-based care logic to hospitals through three interlocking payment adjustment programs that together create significant financial stakes for quality performance. Unlike voluntary ACO participation, these hospital programs are mandatory for most Medicare-participating acute care hospitals. They operate by modifying the DRG-based inpatient prospective payment that hospitals would otherwise receive — rewarding strong performers and penalizing hospitals with poor quality metrics, high readmission rates, or elevated rates of hospital-acquired conditions.

The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), launched in fiscal year 2013, has been particularly influential in reshaping hospital behavior around care transitions. By penalizing excess 30-day readmission rates for six specific conditions — acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, elective hip and knee replacement, and coronary artery bypass graft surgery — HRRP created a direct financial incentive to invest in discharge planning, medication reconciliation, post-acute follow-up, and community-based transitional care programs. Hospitals that previously regarded readmissions as additional revenue now face up to a 3 percent penalty on all Medicare inpatient discharges, not just those related to the penalized conditions.

The combined effect of these three programs is to create a multi-domain quality accountability framework for hospitals. VBP evaluates safety, clinical outcomes, efficiency (Medicare spending per beneficiary), and patient experience; HRRP focuses on post-discharge outcomes for high-risk conditions; HACRP targets patient safety events during the hospital stay itself. Together, they represent CMS's attempt to make hospital payment sensitive to the full arc of a patient's care — from admission through recovery — rather than rewarding the volume of services delivered during the inpatient episode alone.

steps.description: CMS withholds 2% of Medicare payments from all participating hospitals and redistributes based on quality performance across four domains: safety, clinical outcomes, efficiency (Medicare spending per beneficiary), and patient experience (HCAHPS). children.text: The Road Ahead: Challenges and Progress

Despite more than a decade of VBC expansion, significant barriers remain. Attribution methodology — determining which patients are accountable to which provider — remains contested and can produce misalignment between clinical relationships and financial accountability. Small and independent practices often lack the data infrastructure, care management staffing, and actuarial expertise needed to participate meaningfully in risk-bearing arrangements. Rural providers face population sizes too small to generate statistically stable quality or cost measurements. And the transition from FFS to VBC requires providers to invest upfront in care coordination infrastructure before the downstream savings materialize — a cash flow challenge that has slowed adoption among safety-net and critical access hospitals.

CMS's stated goal is to have all Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship by 2030, with a parallel goal of moving all Medicaid beneficiaries into value-based arrangements through state partnerships. As of 2024, roughly half of providers remain outside meaningful value-based arrangements, and the pace of transition has been uneven across specialties and geographies. The record MSSP results in 2024 — and the milestone of 82.8 percent of MSSP ACOs in Advanced APM tracks by 2026 — suggest the trajectory is positive, but reaching the 2030 goal will require sustained policy commitment, technical assistance for smaller providers, and continued refinement of benchmark-setting methodologies to ensure that efficiency gains are genuinely rewarded rather than competed away in future benchmark resets.
"The fee-for-service system rewards doing more, not doing better. The transition to value-based care is fundamentally about realigning financial incentives with patient health."

children.text: Why Governance Matters in Health Information Exchange

Health information exchange (HIE) is the electronic sharing of clinical data across organizations — hospitals, clinics, labs, pharmacies, insurers, and public health agencies — to improve care coordination and reduce redundancy. But technology alone cannot make exchange work. Without shared rules about who can access what data, when, and for what purpose, even the most sophisticated interoperability infrastructure collapses into a tangle of liability disputes, privacy violations, and clinical mistrust. Data governance is the backbone of every functioning HIE.

The core problem is fragmentation. Health data is generated and stored across thousands of unconnected systems, each with its own policies, data models, and access controls. When a patient sees a specialist, visits an emergency department in another state, or fills a prescription at a retail pharmacy, their data rarely follows them automatically. Without a governance framework — legal agreements, defined roles, audit trails, breach response plans — organizations have no basis for trusting that data received from another institution is accurate, appropriately de-identified, or used for legitimate purposes.

Effective HIE governance requires three interlocking frameworks to coexist: legal (what entities are permitted to share under which laws), technical (what standards and systems enable the exchange), and ethical (what uses are appropriate given patient expectations and societal values). Data sharing agreements (DSAs) are the primary legal instrument that ties these frameworks together for every participating organization.

Data Sharing Agreements (DSAs) are the legal foundation of any HIE. A DSA is a formal contract between participating organizations that codifies which entities are authorized to access the exchange, defines their roles and responsibilities, specifies what categories of data can be shared, establishes the conditions and permitted purposes for sharing, and assigns accountability for security, breach response, and compliance. Every organization that joins an HIE signs a DSA — no DSA, no access.

children.text: HIE Governance Models: Centralized, Federated, and Hybrid

There is no single governance architecture for HIEs. Organizations choose among three primary models — centralized, federated, and hybrid — each representing a different answer to the fundamental tension between data access speed and privacy risk. The model chosen shapes everything downstream: how quickly clinicians can retrieve records, how breaches are contained, how audits are conducted, and how much infrastructure investment is required upfront.

In a centralized model, a single governing organization stores and controls all data in a shared repository. This enables fast queries across all participants and simplifies auditing and compliance oversight, since there is one place to look. The trade-off is concentration of risk: a breach at the central repository exposes data for every patient in the network. Centralized HIEs also require significant upfront infrastructure investment and place substantial trust — and legal liability — in the governing entity. In a federated model, data stays at each provider site. When a query is sent, it travels to each node and data is returned on-demand. This distributes risk — a breach at one hospital does not expose records from others — and eliminates a single point of failure, but it makes cross-network queries slower and more complex, and demands strong interoperability standards at every node.

The hybrid model attempts to capture advantages of both. Common services — query routing, provider directories, consent management — are centralized, while clinical data remains at each provider. Many real-world HIEs have converged on hybrid architectures as governance complexity and privacy expectations have grown. Texas offers a prominent example of how a hybrid model can operate at a statewide scale.

children.text: TEFCA: A National Governance Framework

For decades, health information exchange in the United States was a patchwork of local and regional efforts — each with its own rules, technical standards, and participating organizations. A clinician in Boston could not easily retrieve records from a patient's prior care in Phoenix because the HIEs in those regions operated under incompatible governance frameworks. The 21st Century Cures Act of 2016 directed the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) to address this fragmentation by establishing a national framework for trusted exchange. The result was TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement.

ONC published version 1 of TEFCA on January 19, 2022. A subsequent Common Agreement v1.1 was published in November 2023. Version 2.0 was released on April 22, 2024, and added mandatory FHIR-based transaction support — marking a pivotal shift from older document-based exchange toward modern API-driven interoperability. TEFCA operates through Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs): large-scale networks that sign the Common Agreement, agree to operate under shared technical and policy rules, and serve as the on-ramps for providers and health systems seeking nationwide exchange capability. Participation in TEFCA is voluntary, but any organization seeking TEFCA-based exchange must connect through a QHIN.

ONC does not administer the Common Agreement directly. Instead, ONC contracted with The Sequoia Project to serve as the Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE). The Sequoia Project develops and updates the Common Agreement, reviews and designates QHIN applicants, and monitors ongoing compliance. This structure — a public mandate executed through a nonprofit RCE — is a deliberate governance design that keeps the federal government at arm's length from day-to-day network operations while maintaining public accountability.

TEFCA's Common Agreement establishes the technical infrastructure model and governing rules for different health information networks to securely share clinical information — all under commonly agreed-to rules of the road. It sets baseline standards for privacy, security, patient matching, and exchange behaviors that all QHINs and their participants must follow, regardless of which QHIN they connect through.

children.text: Patient Consent: Opt-In, Opt-Out, and Everything In Between

One of the most consequential governance decisions any HIE must make is how to handle patient consent. Two primary models have emerged: opt-in and opt-out. In an opt-in model, a patient must affirmatively consent — sign a form, click a checkbox, or verbally agree — before their protected health information (PHI) is included in the HIE. In an opt-out model, patient data is included automatically upon enrollment with a participating provider, and the patient must take active steps — submitting an online form, calling a help line, or mailing a request — to have their records excluded.

HIPAA sets a federal floor for health information privacy but does not dictate which consent model HIEs must use. States have broad authority to impose stricter requirements, and consent models vary considerably across the country. Some states mandate opt-in; others permit opt-out; some allow community-wide consent — a single consent that covers all future sharing with all HIE participants in a community or state, reducing per-encounter administrative burden. The result is a patchwork that complicates cross-state exchange and creates compliance challenges for health systems operating in multiple jurisdictions.

The trade-offs between opt-in and opt-out are real and well-documented. Opt-out models produce more complete datasets: when participation is the default, a larger and more representative population of patients appears in the HIE, supporting more reliable quality measurement and population health analytics. Opt-in models give patients stronger control over their data, but the patients who engage are systematically different from those who do not — often more health-literate, more trusting of the healthcare system, and more likely to have established primary care relationships. This selection bias can distort clinical and quality data, making opt-in HIEs less useful for understanding outcomes across the full population.

body.analogy: Choosing between opt-in and opt-out is like choosing between a library that only lends books to people who fill out a membership form (opt-in) versus one that gives access to all residents automatically unless they specifically decline (opt-out) — the first is more respectful of individual choice; the second serves more people but requires residents to know the system exists and how to leave it.

children.text: 42 CFR Part 2: Special Protections for Substance Use Disorder Records

42 CFR Part 2 is a federal regulation that governs the confidentiality of substance use disorder (SUD) patient records held by federally assisted programs. It was enacted in an era when SUD stigma was — and in many contexts remains — so severe that patients refused to seek treatment if they believed their records could be used against them in employment, child custody, or criminal proceedings. Part 2's protections are intentionally stricter than HIPAA: they restrict disclosures that HIPAA would otherwise permit, and they apply a higher bar for consent before SUD treatment records can be shared with any external entity, including other treating providers.

The 2024 SAMHSA final rule, issued February 16, 2024 and effective April 16, 2024, made the most significant changes to Part 2 in decades. The most important change aligned Part 2 more closely with HIPAA's treatment, payment, and operations (TPO) framework: patients can now give a single consent covering all future TPO disclosures of their SUD records, eliminating the prior requirement to obtain consent for each individual disclosure. This change was designed to reduce the administrative friction that had made Part 2 records difficult to integrate into electronic health records and HIE data flows. SAMHSA provided a two-year implementation window; enforcement began February 16, 2026.

Despite the 2024 simplifications, several critical protections remain unchanged. SUD counseling notes — analogous to HIPAA's psychotherapy notes — still require a separate, distinct patient consent and cannot be shared under the general TPO consent. When a HIPAA-covered entity receives Part 2 records with TPO consent, it can redisclose that information under HIPAA rules for most purposes — but cannot use the information in any legal proceeding against the patient without a separate court order. And without any patient consent or court order, Part 2 programs cannot disclose any information identifying a person as having or having had a SUD, even in emergencies, with only narrow exceptions. HIEs and EHR vendors must implement technical segmentation to ensure Part 2 records do not travel with general clinical data under standard HIPAA-based consent.

The 2024 SAMHSA final rule (effective April 2024, enforcement February 2026) allows a single TPO consent for future SUD record sharing — eliminating the prior requirement to get consent for each individual disclosure — but SUD counseling notes still require a separate consent, and records can never be used in legal proceedings against the patient without separate authorization.

children.text: Data Ethics and Secondary Use of Health Data

Secondary use refers to using EHR records, claims data, or HIE data for purposes beyond the direct care of the patient who generated that data — including clinical research, quality improvement, public health surveillance, and commercial analytics. Secondary use is not inherently unethical; it is, in fact, how most clinical knowledge is generated. But it raises persistent ethical tensions: the patient whose data is used in a research study did not consent to that specific study. The health system that shares data for a quality improvement initiative may not have disclosed that use to patients at the time of their care. The commercial analytics company that licenses claims data may use it in ways patients would find surprising or objectionable.

The ethical framework for secondary use rests on five stewardship principles that health information governance bodies, IRBs, and data custodians have converged on over the past two decades. These principles — purpose limitation, data minimization, transparency, accountability, and patient access and correction rights — do not eliminate the tension between research benefit and privacy protection, but they provide a structured basis for evaluating whether a proposed secondary use is justifiable. Studies consistently show that patients broadly support the use of their data for research and quality improvement, but they want to know who is using it, for what purpose, and with what safeguards. Trust is the currency of secondary use; when it is lost — through data breaches, opaque data sharing practices, or commercial uses patients did not anticipate — patients opt out, data completeness declines, and the system loses the population-level insights that motivated secondary use in the first place.

The ethical use of health data requires building and maintaining patient trust — not just technical safeguards. Patients broadly support research use of their data, but they want transparency about who uses it and for what.

children.text: What Are Health Disparities and Why Do They Persist?

Health disparities are preventable differences in the burden of disease, injury, violence, or opportunities to achieve optimal health experienced by socially disadvantaged groups. These differences are not random — they follow predictable patterns tied to race, ethnicity, income, geography, language, and disability status. Where a person is born, how they grow up, where they work and live, and how they age shape their health in ways that dwarf the influence of clinical care.

The data make the pattern unmistakable. In 2023, Black Americans had a life expectancy of 74.0 years — 4.4 years less than White Americans (78.4) and 7.3 years less than Hispanic Americans (81.3). Black infants died at a rate of 10.9 per 1,000 live births in 2023, more than twice the White rate of 4.5. Black maternal mortality reached 50.3 deaths per 100,000 live births — 3.5 times the White rate of 14.5 — and the gap is not closing.

These gaps persist not because of biological differences between groups, but because of cumulative structural disadvantages: income, neighborhood, education, environmental exposure, and unequal treatment within the healthcare system itself. Understanding their root causes is the first step to closing them.

Health disparities are differences in health outcomes between groups that are avoidable, unnecessary, and unjust. Health equity is the state in which every person has a fair and just opportunity to attain their highest possible level of health — regardless of race, income, zip code, or language.

children.text: The Five Domains of Social Determinants of Health

Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age — and the broader forces shaping those conditions: economic policies, social norms, political systems, and community infrastructure. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Healthy People 2030 framework organizes SDOH into five domains that interact and reinforce one another.

Economic stability is the most studied domain: poverty limits access to nutritious food, safe housing, and preventive care — driving chronic disease rates up and life expectancy down. Education shapes health literacy, employment options, and earning potential throughout life. Neighborhood and built environment determines whether people have access to grocery stores, safe places to exercise, clean air and water, and transportation to healthcare appointments. Social and community context — including discrimination, incarceration, and social cohesion — affects mental health, stress physiology, and health behaviors.

Health care access and quality is the fifth domain — and while it is what most people think of when they think of healthcare disparities, it is only one of five. Expanding coverage and reducing clinical bias matters enormously, but it cannot alone close gaps rooted in poverty, housing instability, or neighborhood disinvestment.

children.text: Racial and Ethnic Disparities: The Evidence

Racial and ethnic health disparities in the United States are among the most well-documented and persistent in the developed world. They exist across nearly every health condition — cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, mental health, and maternal and infant health — and they exist even after controlling for income and insurance status, pointing to systemic and structural factors including discrimination in care delivery.

Black maternal mortality illustrates the depth of the problem. In 2023, Black women died from pregnancy-related causes at a rate of 50.3 per 100,000 live births — compared to 14.5 for White women. This 3.5-fold disparity persists across income levels and education levels: Black women with college degrees experience higher maternal mortality than White women without them. Research consistently identifies delayed or inadequate care, implicit bias among providers, and preterm birth driven by chronic stress as key mechanisms.

The Hispanic paradox — whereby Hispanic Americans have lower mortality than White Americans despite lower average income and insurance coverage — illustrates that SDOH operate differently across groups. Strong family cohesion, lower smoking rates, and immigration selection effects partially explain this pattern. Understanding the paradox is important: it demonstrates that SDOH are not simply about income, and that protective factors in culture and community can buffer against adverse exposures.

body.content: In 2023, the CDC reported that Black women died from pregnancy-related causes at 50.3 per 100,000 live births — 3.5 times the White rate of 14.5. The gap did not improve between 2022 and 2023 despite overall U.S. maternal mortality declining. Studies find that even among college-educated Black women, maternal mortality exceeds that of White women without college degrees. Causes include implicit bias in pain management, later diagnosis of complications, higher rates of preeclampsia driven by chronic stress (weathering hypothesis), and systemic underinvestment in maternal care in majority-Black communities. (Source: CDC NCHS Maternal Mortality Report, February 2025)

children.text: SDOH and Health IT: Screening, Data, and Action

Addressing SDOH requires knowing where individual patients stand — which means screening for food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers, social isolation, and financial strain during clinical encounters. Organizations like NACHC, PRAPARE (Protocol for Responding to and Assessing Patients' Assets, Risks, and Experiences), and AHC (Accountable Health Communities) have developed validated SDOH screening tools now used across thousands of clinical sites.

The challenge is what happens after screening. Identifying that a patient lacks stable housing is only useful if there is a referral pathway to a housing resource — and a closed-loop system to confirm whether the referral was acted on. Community-based organizations, 211 resource networks, and social care platforms like Unite Us and findhelp are working to build those closed-loop connections between clinical and social care.

CMS has prioritized SDOH data collection at the system level. Beginning in January 2023, CMS started collecting optional race and ethnicity data from Medicare Advantage enrollment forms. CMS also finalized the collection of race/ethnicity data through issuers' EDGE servers beginning with 2023 benefit year data. The goal is to stratify quality measures by race, ethnicity, and language — making disparities visible in reporting programs so health plans and providers are accountable for closing them.

children.text: CMS Strategy and the Road to Equity

CMS has made health equity a formal pillar of its strategic plan. The agency's equity strategy centers on five priorities: expanding the collection of standardized demographic and SDOH data; identifying and reducing disparities in Medicare and Medicaid; building capacity in underserved communities; engaging in community partnerships; and closing the gap in cultural and language access to care.

In quality reporting, CMS is moving toward requiring stratification of HEDIS, MIPS, and other measures by race, ethnicity, and language — making it impossible for plans and providers to submit aggregate scores that mask disparities. The logic is simple: if a health plan serves 100,000 members and reports a 90% diabetes control rate, but the rate is 95% for White members and 75% for Black members, the aggregate score obscures a 20-percentage-point gap that requires action.

body.message: Collecting race, ethnicity, and language data is necessary but not sufficient. The goal is not better reporting — it is closing the gaps the data reveals. Systems that collect demographic data but do not analyze it by subgroup, do not set disparity-reduction targets, and do not hold leaders accountable are performing equity theater, not achieving health equity.

children.text: Defining Value in Healthcare

What does "value" mean in healthcare? The simplest formulation — popularized by Harvard's Michael Porter — is Value = Outcomes / Cost. High-value care delivers meaningful, evidence-based clinical benefit relative to its cost and risk to the patient. Low-value care is the inverse: interventions where cost or risk exceeds the likely benefit. But value is not just about money — it is about whether care actually improves or risks patient health.

The scale of low-value care in the United States is staggering. The Institute of Medicine's landmark 2012 report "Best Care at Lower Cost" estimated that approximately 30% of US health spending in 2009 — roughly $750 billion — was wasted. That waste included unnecessary services, excessive administrative costs, fraud, and inflated prices. More recent estimates place annual spending on low-value care at $100 billion to $700 billion depending on what is counted. Up to 40% of Medicare beneficiaries receive at least one low-value service per year.

The consequences are not just financial. Unnecessary services expose patients to real harm — radiation from imaging, surgical complications, drug side effects, healthcare-associated infections, and the cascade of follow-up tests triggered by false-positive results. A healthcare system that provides more care than is needed is not just wasteful; it is actively dangerous.

High-value care = meaningful clinical benefit relative to cost and risk. Low-value care = interventions where cost or harm exceeds likely benefit. The goal is not to spend less — it is to spend on care that works.

children.text: What Makes Care Low Value?

Low-value care is not always obvious. It ranges from blatantly wasteful services — antibiotics for viral infections, routine pre-operative testing before low-risk surgery — to subtler overuse driven by habit, anxiety, or financial incentive. JAMA research estimated that $12.8 to $28.6 billion could be saved annually by targeting the most common low-value services alone.

The IOM identified six categories of healthcare waste: unnecessary services (overuse beyond evidence), inefficiently delivered services (care that could be done better or cheaper), excess administrative complexity, inflated prices, missed prevention opportunities, and fraud and abuse. Unnecessary services — the clinical waste category — is the most directly actionable through clinical behavior change, but it is also the hardest to reduce because it requires changing the habits of individual providers.

A concrete example: more than 200,000 unnecessary back surgeries took place over a three-year period, costing Medicare more than $1.9 billion, according to the Lown Institute. The evidence shows that most patients with chronic low back pain do better with physical therapy and conservative management than with surgery — yet the financial incentive for surgery, combined with patient expectations, drives continued overuse. Imaging without clear clinical indication, routine urine cultures in asymptomatic patients, and repeat imaging for stable findings are other common offenders documented in Choosing Wisely recommendations.

children.text: Choosing Wisely: A National De-Implementation Campaign

In 2012, the ABIM Foundation and Consumer Reports launched the Choosing Wisely campaign — the highest-profile national effort to reduce low-value care through clinical engagement rather than regulatory mandate. The campaign launched with nine specialty societies offering 45 recommendations about tests and treatments that clinicians and patients should question. By 2023, more than 80 specialty societies had joined, producing over 700 recommendations spanning imaging, laboratory testing, medications, and procedures. The campaign has since spread to more than 30 countries.

Each Choosing Wisely recommendation is generated by a specialty society based on evidence that a particular service is frequently ordered, has significant cost or risk, and is often not necessary given current clinical evidence. Examples include: don't order routine imaging for uncomplicated low back pain; don't prescribe antibiotics for non-specific upper respiratory infections; don't perform routine pre-operative tests for low-risk procedures. Importantly, the recommendations are framed as starting points for conversation — not prohibitions.

The evidence on Choosing Wisely's impact is mixed but instructive. Active interventions — clinical decision support alerts, audit and feedback, educational outreach, leadership engagement — reduced overuse in 65% of studies. Simply disseminating the recommendations without an active change strategy produced reductions in only 13% of studies. The lesson: awareness alone does not change behavior. Sustained de-implementation requires targeted strategies matched to the local barriers driving the overuse.

body.content: Antibiotic prescribing for acute respiratory infections is one of the most documented cases of low-value care. More than 40% of antibiotic prescriptions for respiratory infections in primary care are estimated to be unnecessary — contributing to antimicrobial resistance and patient harm from side effects. Multiple Choosing Wisely lists from the AAFP, ACIP, and infectious disease societies recommend against prescribing antibiotics for viral pharyngitis, bronchitis, and sinusitis without bacterial confirmation. Health systems using clinical decision support prompts tied to these recommendations have shown 20–30% reductions in unnecessary antibiotic prescribing in primary care. (Source: ABIM Foundation / Choosing Wisely)
body.title: Choosing Wisely — Antibiotic Overprescription

children.text: Barriers to Reducing Low-Value Care

Knowing that a service is low-value does not automatically stop it from being ordered. Research on barriers to de-implementation consistently identifies a cluster of factors that make it difficult for clinicians — even those who understand the evidence — to stop providing unnecessary care.

Patient expectations and requests are the most commonly cited barrier: 85% of primary care physicians in a multinational survey identified patient expectations as a challenge, and 83% cited direct patient requests for tests or treatments. Clinicians also fear medical error (81%) — the anxiety that the one patient they do not image or test will be the one who has something serious. Time pressure (81%) and fear of under-diagnosis (79%) round out the top barriers. These are not irrational fears; they reflect the asymmetry of accountability in medicine, where doing too much is rarely penalized and doing too little can result in lawsuits.

System-level factors compound individual barriers. Fee-for-service payment rewards volume — ordering more generates more revenue, even when the additional care provides no benefit. Fragmented care means that multiple providers order overlapping tests without visibility into what has already been done. Electronic health records that make ordering easy but provide no feedback on cumulative cost or redundancy also contribute to overuse.

children.text: High-Value Care in Practice

High-value care is not simply cheap care — it is care that delivers the right outcome for the right patient at the right time, with evidence supporting both the clinical benefit and the cost-effectiveness. Many of the highest-value interventions in medicine are also among the least expensive: blood pressure control, cholesterol management, colorectal cancer screening, smoking cessation, and vaccination. These interventions prevent enormous amounts of downstream disease, hospitalization, and premature death.

The CMS Million Hearts Cardiovascular Disease Risk Reduction Model demonstrated this principle at scale. The model paid providers to systematically measure patients' cardiovascular risk using a validated tool, and to intensify treatment for high- and medium-risk beneficiaries. The result was reduced first-time heart attacks and strokes — without increasing total care costs. The program exemplifies value-based care logic: invest in evidence-based prevention upstream to avoid expensive acute events downstream.

body.analogy: High-value care is like maintaining a car on schedule — oil changes, tire rotations, brake checks. It seems like spending money on something that isn't broken. But it prevents the catastrophic breakdown that costs ten times more and strands you on the highway. Low-value care is like buying expensive fuel additives based on a TV commercial — you spend real money for no proven benefit, and you might damage the engine.
body.concept: High-Value vs. Low-Value Care Logic

children.text: The highest-value interventions in American medicine — controlling blood pressure, managing diabetes, screening for cancer, vaccinating against flu and pneumonia — are also among the most underprovided. The US simultaneously over-provides low-value services and under-provides high-value ones, producing the worst of both worlds: excess cost and avoidable harm.

points: High-value care delivers meaningful clinical benefit relative to its cost and risk; low-value care is care where cost or harm to the patient exceeds likely benefit.
The IOM estimated roughly $750 billion — about 30% of US health spending in 2009 — was waste, with unnecessary services being the most directly reducible category.
Up to 40% of Medicare beneficiaries receive at least one low-value service per year; annual low-value spending estimates range from $100 billion to $700 billion.

The Choosing Wisely campaign, launched by the ABIM Foundation in 2012, produced more than 700 specialty society recommendations on overused services; active interventions based on those recommendations reduced overuse 65% of the time.

The top barriers to de-implementing low-value care are patient expectations (85%), patient requests (83%), fear of medical error (81%), and time pressure (81%) — requiring both cultural and structural change, not just education.
Effective de-implementation strategies include clinical decision support alerts, audit and feedback, shared decision making, payment reform, and prior authorization — and work best in combination.
The US simultaneously over-provides low-value care and under-provides high-value preventive care — indicating that the solution is not simply spending less, but spending on what works.

children.text: What Is HIPAA and Who Does It Cover?

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) is the foundational federal law governing the privacy and security of health information in the United States. Enacted by Congress and signed into law on August 21, 1996, HIPAA established national standards that apply to specific categories of organizations — not to every business that handles health data.

HIPAA applies to three categories of "covered entities": health plans (insurers, HMOs, Medicare, Medicaid), health care clearinghouses (organizations that process health data between nonstandard and standard formats), and health care providers who transmit health information electronically in connection with HIPAA-covered transactions. The regulatory definitions are codified at 45 CFR § 160.103.

A covered entity is any health plan, health care clearinghouse, or health care provider that transmits protected health information electronically. Only covered entities — and their business associates — are directly subject to HIPAA requirements.

body.message: HIPAA does not apply to all organizations that handle health data. An employer holding employee wellness program data, a fitness app tracking your steps, or a friend sharing health information is generally NOT a covered entity and is not bound by HIPAA. This is a frequent source of public confusion.
body.title: Common Misconception

children.text: Protected Health Information: What HIPAA Actually Protects

HIPAA protects "Protected Health Information" (PHI) — any individually identifiable health information created, received, maintained, or transmitted by a covered entity. PHI encompasses information in any format: paper records, electronic records (ePHI), and oral communications.

The law identifies 18 specific categories of identifiers that, when linked to health information, make that information PHI. These include names, geographic data smaller than a state, all date elements directly related to an individual (except year alone), phone numbers, fax numbers, email addresses, Social Security numbers, medical record numbers, account numbers, certificate/license numbers, URLs, IP addresses, biometric identifiers (fingerprints, voiceprints), full-face photographs, and any other unique identifying number or code.

The 18 HIPAA identifiers define PHI. Health information with ALL 18 identifiers removed is considered "de-identified" under the Safe Harbor method and is no longer subject to HIPAA Privacy Rule protections.

body.analogy: Think of PHI like a sealed envelope: the health data inside is the letter, and the 18 identifiers are the name and address written on the outside. Covered entities can share the letter contents in certain ways, but must protect the sealed envelope — the combination of identity and health information.
body.concept: Protected Health Information (PHI)

children.text: The Privacy Rule: Patient Rights and Permissible Disclosures

The HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164) establishes the standards for when covered entities may use or disclose PHI, and what rights patients hold over their own health information. The Privacy Rule was finalized in 2002 and has been updated several times since.

The Privacy Rule permits — without patient authorization — uses and disclosures for treatment, payment, and health care operations (collectively "TPO"). Beyond TPO, covered entities may disclose PHI for specific public interest purposes: public health reporting, research with proper oversight, law enforcement, and national security. All other disclosures generally require written patient authorization.

These cases resulted in settlements ranging from $3,500 to $200,000, signaling that patient access violations — not just large data breaches — carry real enforcement risk.

children.text: The Security Rule: Protecting Electronic PHI

The HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR §§ 164.302–318) applies specifically to electronic protected health information (ePHI). It requires covered entities and business associates to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI.

The Security Rule uses a "required vs. addressable" structure: required specifications must be implemented; addressable specifications must either be implemented or the entity must document why an equivalent alternative measure was used. This flexibility allows organizations of different sizes and complexity to tailor their security programs.

children.text: Business Associates and the BAA Requirement

A "business associate" is any person or organization that performs functions or activities on behalf of a covered entity that involve the use or disclosure of PHI. Common examples include cloud storage vendors, billing companies, EHR software vendors, and legal firms handling patient records.

HIPAA requires covered entities to enter into a written Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with each business associate before sharing PHI. The BAA must specify permitted uses, require the business associate to safeguard PHI, require reporting of breaches and security incidents, and set terms for termination. Under the 2013 Omnibus Rule, business associates became directly liable for HIPAA Security Rule compliance — not just contractually obligated.
A covered entity that shares PHI with a vendor without a signed BAA is already in violation of HIPAA — even if no breach has occurred. The BAA must be in place before PHI is shared.
HITECH Act and Breach Notification

The Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act, enacted as part of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, significantly strengthened HIPAA. HITECH expanded HIPAA reach to business associates, increased civil monetary penalties, and created the Breach Notification Rule.

Under the Breach Notification Rule, covered entities must notify affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovering a breach of unsecured PHI. If a breach affects 500 or more individuals, the covered entity must also notify HHS and prominent media outlets in the affected region.

The Privacy Rule establishes seven core patient rights, including the right to access and amend health records, and permits disclosures for treatment, payment, and health care operations without patient authorization.

children.text: Why Healthcare Needs Data Standards

Healthcare generates vast amounts of data — lab results, medication orders, diagnoses, vital signs, imaging reports — across thousands of incompatible software systems. Without common data standards, a lab result from one hospital cannot be reliably interpreted by a different hospital's EHR, and a patient's medication list cannot flow automatically from a physician's office to a pharmacy. Standards are the shared language that allows different healthcare systems to exchange, interpret, and act on information consistently.

Health Level Seven (HL7) International, founded in 1987 as an ANSI-accredited, not-for-profit standards organization, became the primary body responsible for healthcare data exchange standards in the United States and globally. The name "Health Level Seven" refers to Layer 7 — the application layer — of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model. HL7's standards now underpin virtually every electronic clinical workflow, from patient admission to lab ordering to claims submission.

Two generations of HL7 standards dominate the landscape today: HL7 Version 2 (v2), the workhorse of hospital systems since 1987, and FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), the modern API-based standard that is rapidly becoming the foundation for patient access, interoperability regulations, and digital health innovation. Understanding both — how they work, how they differ, and how they coexist — is essential for anyone working in health IT.

HL7 International is an ANSI-accredited, not-for-profit standards developing organization that provides a framework of international standards for the exchange, integration, sharing, and retrieval of electronic health information. It was founded in 1987 and its standards are now implemented in healthcare systems across 50+ countries.

children.text: HL7 Version 2: The Original Healthcare Messaging Standard

HL7 v2 was first released in October 1987 and became the dominant standard for real-time clinical data exchange in hospitals. It uses a pipe-delimited text message format where data elements are separated by the | character, sub-components by ^, repeating values by ~, and sub-sub-components by &. While this seems archaic by modern standards, it was revolutionary in 1987 — enabling the first automated exchange of admission, discharge, lab, and order data between disparate hospital systems.

HL7 v2 messages are organized into message types that correspond to clinical events. ADT messages (Admit, Discharge, Transfer) communicate patient movement and demographics — a new admission sends an ADT-A01, a discharge sends an ADT-A03. ORM messages carry orders from the ordering system to the fulfilling department (lab, pharmacy, radiology). ORU messages return results — an ORU-R01 carries lab results, vital signs, or radiology reports back to the ordering clinician. Every message contains segments — MSH (message header with sender, recipient, timestamp, and message type), PID (patient demographics), and type-specific segments like OBR (observation request) and OBX (observation result).

Despite being nearly 40 years old, HL7 v2 remains deeply embedded in healthcare IT. It is present in 95% of US healthcare organizations and installed in 35+ countries. Complex HL7 v2 integration projects typically take 3–6 months to implement due to the high degree of local customization — every hospital implements v2 slightly differently, with local Z-segments and non-standard field usage, creating integration complexity that FHIR was specifically designed to eliminate.

body.content: When a clinician orders a blood glucose test in a hospital EHR, an ORM^O01 message travels from the EHR to the laboratory information system (LIS). When the lab completes the analysis, the LIS sends an ORU^R01 message back to the EHR containing the patient ID, the test ordered (LOINC code in OBR), and the result value, units, and reference range (in OBX segments). This exchange — invisible to the clinician — happens in seconds and relies entirely on HL7 v2 message parsing. In a large academic medical center, thousands of these messages flow per hour, 24 hours a day.
body.title: HL7 v2 in Action: Lab Result Delivery

body.message: Despite being called a 'standard,' HL7 v2 is notorious for implementation variation. Two hospitals can both claim HL7 v2 compliance while implementing the same fields in incompatible ways. Z-segments (custom extensions) are common, field optionality is high, and there is no enforced terminology binding. This is why interface engines (Mirth Connect, Rhapsody) exist — to translate between the many dialects of v2 spoken by different systems.
body.title: v2 Is Not Truly Standardized

children.text: FHIR: The Modern Healthcare API Standard

Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR, pronounced "fire") is HL7 International's next-generation standard, designed from the ground up for the web era. Where HL7 v2 sends messages in response to clinical events, FHIR exposes data through RESTful APIs — the same technology that powers websites, mobile apps, and cloud services. A FHIR server makes clinical data available as discrete, addressable resources that any authorized application can retrieve using standard HTTP requests.

FHIR organizes clinical information into modular resource types — Patient, Observation, Encounter, Condition, MedicationRequest, DiagnosticReport, Immunization, AllergyIntolerance, and many more. Each resource has a defined structure and is accessible at a predictable URL. For example, to retrieve patient 123's blood pressure readings, a developer sends a standard HTTP GET request: GET /Observation?patient=123&code=55284-4 — and receives a JSON bundle of matching Observation resources. FHIR R4 (v4.0.1, released in 2019) is the current implementation baseline, mandated by both the ONC Cures Act Final Rule and the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Rule.

FHIR's developer-friendly design dramatically reduces integration time. Where HL7 v2 projects take 3–6 months, FHIR implementations for equivalent scope often complete in 6–12 weeks. Standard JSON libraries, HTTP clients, and FHIR reference implementations (HAPI FHIR in Java, Microsoft Azure Health Data Services, Google Cloud Healthcare API) provide off-the-shelf tooling. Epic's FHIR APIs alone process over 1 billion transactions per month — a scale that reflects both the standard's adoption and the explosive growth of patient-facing apps and third-party integrations built on top of it.

body.analogy: Think of HL7 v2 as the postal system — it delivers messages from one place to another, and has been doing so reliably for decades. FHIR is like the internet — instead of mailing documents, you query a live database using a URL, and get back structured data in real time that any app can use. Both carry health information; only one was designed for the world of smartphones and APIs.

children.text: SMART on FHIR: Secure App Integration

SMART on FHIR (Substitutable Medical Applications, Reusable Technologies) is the standard framework for securely connecting third-party applications to EHR data via FHIR. It builds on OAuth 2.0 — the same authorization protocol used by Google, Facebook, and most major web platforms — and adds healthcare-specific scopes and launch context so that apps know which patient is being viewed and what data they are authorized to access.

SMART supports two launch modes. In an EHR Launch, the app is opened from within an active EHR session — the EHR passes the app a launch token containing the current patient ID, encounter ID, and FHIR server URL. The app uses this context to immediately display relevant patient data without requiring a separate login. In a Standalone Launch, the app opens independently (e.g., a patient-facing mobile app) and prompts the user to authenticate and select a patient context. SMART scopes control exactly what data the app can access — patient/Observation.read gives read-only access to a specific patient's observations, while user/MedicationRequest.write allows the app to create medication orders on behalf of a clinician.

SMART on FHIR has enabled the emergence of healthcare app ecosystems. Epic's App Orchard and Oracle Health's (formerly Cerner) App Market host thousands of third-party clinical apps — decision support tools, specialty workflows, patient engagement platforms, and analytics dashboards — all connecting to EHR data through SMART on FHIR without requiring custom point-to-point integrations. This shift from proprietary interfaces to open, standards-based app platforms is one of the most significant structural changes in health IT driven by FHIR adoption.

children.text: Regulatory Mandates and the Road Ahead

FHIR's rise from technical standard to regulatory requirement was driven by federal policy. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule, published May 1, 2020 and effective June 30, 2020, requires certified EHR developers to publish FHIR R4-based APIs at no cost to patients and authorized third parties. EHR developers must also attest that they will not engage in information blocking — refusing to share data through these APIs. Failure to comply exposes developers to penalties of up to $1 million per violation enforced by the HHS Office of Inspector General.

The CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F) complements ONC's rule on the payer side. It requires CMS-regulated payers — Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA Marketplace plans — to implement a FHIR R4 Patient Access API covering claims, encounters, and a defined clinical data subset (USCDI v1). Payers must also implement a Provider Directory API and a Payer-to-Payer exchange mechanism. TEFCA's Common Agreement v2.0, released April 2024, added mandatory FHIR-based transaction support as a condition for QHINs, bringing FHIR into the national exchange infrastructure.

HL7 v2 and FHIR are not competitors — they are complementary. v2 remains the backbone of high-volume, real-time hospital transactions (admissions, lab orders, results) and will not be replaced overnight. FHIR is the standard for API-driven innovation: patient apps, payer-to-payer exchange, quality reporting, and clinical decision support. Most health systems today run both in parallel.

children.text: The Integration Problem in Healthcare

A typical large academic medical center operates dozens of clinical and administrative systems — an EHR, a laboratory information system (LIS), a radiology information system (RIS), a picture archiving and communication system (PACS), a pharmacy system, a billing system, a patient portal, and more. Each was built by a different vendor, speaks a different data format, and was designed without knowledge of the others. Making them work together is the core challenge of healthcare integration architecture.

Poor integration has real clinical and financial consequences. A lab result that doesn't reach the ordering physician in time delays treatment. A medication list that doesn't follow a patient from hospital to pharmacy causes adverse drug events. A prior authorization status that can't be retrieved electronically triggers phone calls and fax loops that cost physicians' offices enormous time. Analysts estimate that a lack of interoperability costs the US healthcare system over $30 billion annually in avoidable inefficiencies — administrative overhead, unnecessary duplicate testing, and delayed clinical decisions.

Healthcare integration architecture is the discipline of designing the connections between these systems — choosing the right patterns, technologies, and standards to make data flow reliably, securely, and consistently. Three major architectural patterns have evolved over the past 40 years: point-to-point integration, hub-and-spoke (interface engine), and API-based architectures using modern standards like FHIR. Each represents a different trade-off between simplicity, scalability, and flexibility.

Healthcare integration architecture defines how disparate clinical and administrative systems exchange data — reliably, securely, and at scale. Getting it right is not just a technical problem; it is a patient safety and operational efficiency imperative.

children.text: Point-to-Point: The Spaghetti Problem

The simplest integration approach is point-to-point: every system that needs to talk to another system gets a direct, custom connection. When a hospital has 5 systems, this is manageable — 10 connections. When a health system has 50 systems, point-to-point requires up to 1,225 custom connections. When systems are updated, every connection touching that system must be retested and potentially rebuilt. This exponential growth in complexity is called "spaghetti integration" — the architecture looks like a bowl of tangled noodles, and it becomes impossible to change anything without breaking something else.

Point-to-point integrations also create deep technical dependencies. If the lab system changes its patient ID format, every system connected to the lab — the EHR, the radiology system, the billing system — must update its interface simultaneously. Coordination across vendors at that scale is extremely difficult, and failed or mismatched updates cause data errors that can ripple into clinical decisions. The lack of a central routing or transformation layer means there is no single place to apply a fix or policy change.

Despite its problems, point-to-point integration remains common in healthcare — particularly among smaller organizations and for specific use cases where two systems have a single, stable connection that has worked for years. Legacy point-to-point interfaces are frequently the last to be migrated during enterprise integration modernization projects, because they are deeply embedded in workflows and the risk of touching a working interface is perceived as high.

body.message: With point-to-point integration, the number of interfaces grows as a function of the square of the number of systems: 5 systems = 10 interfaces; 10 systems = 45 interfaces; 50 systems = 1,225 interfaces. Every interface is a custom build, a maintenance liability, and a potential point of failure. This is why organizations that start with point-to-point inevitably hit a wall and are forced to adopt a hub-based or API-based architecture.
body.title: The n×(n-1)/2 Scaling Problem

children.text: Hub-and-Spoke: The Interface Engine Model

The hub-and-spoke model solves the scaling problem by introducing a central integration engine — the hub — that all systems (the spokes) connect to. Instead of each system needing to know how to communicate with every other system, each system only needs one connection to the hub. The hub handles all protocol translation, message transformation, routing logic, and delivery. A hospital with 50 systems needs only 50 connections in a hub-and-spoke model instead of 1,225. The hub is the single place where integration logic lives, where problems are diagnosed, and where changes are made.

Interface engines — the software that implements the hub — are specialized middleware platforms designed for healthcare data exchange. They ingest HL7 v2 messages (ADT, ORM, ORU), transform them between formats, apply routing rules (e.g., send all lab results for Cardiology patients to the Cardiology dashboard), and deliver them to destination systems. They also handle error management, message acknowledgment (ACK/NAK), retry logic, and audit logging — critical functions in a healthcare environment where a missed lab result can be a patient safety event.

The dominant interface engine platforms in the US market are Mirth Connect (now NextGen Connect), Rhapsody, Corepoint, Iguana (iNTERFACEWARE), and Cloverleaf (Infor). Mirth Connect was the most widely deployed open-source integration engine — but on March 19, 2025, NextGen Healthcare announced that Mirth Connect 4.6 would transition to a closed-source proprietary license. Version 4.5.2 is the last freely available open-source release. Two open-source forks emerged in response: BridgeLink (from Innovar Healthcare) and the community-governed Open Integration Engine. Rhapsody is consistently rated Best in KLAS for clinical data integration among large health systems.

body.title: Point-to-Point vs Hub-and-Spoke Integration

children.text: Modern API-Based and Event-Driven Architecture

The rise of FHIR has enabled a third architectural paradigm: API-based integration, where systems expose standardized endpoints rather than sending messages through a central engine. In a FHIR-native architecture, a lab system publishes Observation resources via a FHIR API; an EHR subscribes to those resources and displays them in the clinical workflow; a patient app pulls the same data via SMART on FHIR. No custom interface engine is required for simple read queries — the API is the interface.

For more complex workflows — particularly those requiring asynchronous processing, guaranteed delivery, and high throughput — modern healthcare architectures layer event-driven infrastructure on top of FHIR APIs. Message brokers like Apache Kafka and RabbitMQ decouple producers from consumers: a patient admission event is published to a Kafka topic and consumed by multiple downstream systems (care management, analytics, scheduling) independently. Cloud-native platforms — AWS HealthLake, Azure Health Data Services, Google Cloud Healthcare API — provide managed FHIR servers with built-in scalability, security, and compliance.

In practice, most health systems today operate hybrid architectures. HL7 v2 over TCP/IP (MLLP protocol) continues to handle high-volume real-time hospital transactions — ADT feeds, lab results, radiology orders — because these workflows are stable, well-tested, and running on existing infrastructure. FHIR APIs layer on top to enable patient-facing applications, payer data exchange, quality reporting, and third-party app integration via SMART on FHIR. The interface engine (Rhapsody, Mirth, etc.) bridges the two worlds, translating v2 messages into FHIR resources when needed.

children.text: Building a Reliable Integration: Key Principles

Regardless of the architecture pattern chosen, successful healthcare integration depends on a set of engineering principles that apply across approaches. The first is guaranteed message delivery: in healthcare, a message that is dropped — a lab result, a medication order, an ADT — can cause patient harm. Interface engines must implement acknowledgment (ACK/NAK) protocols, retry queues, and dead-letter handling so no message is silently lost.

The second principle is idempotency: the same message delivered twice should not create duplicate records in the destination system. Patient demographics sent twice should update, not create a second patient. Lab results retransmitted after a failure should not create duplicate result entries in the EHR. Designing integrations to handle duplicates gracefully requires either deduplication logic at the interface engine or at the receiving system — ideally both.

The third principle is observability: every message that enters and leaves the integration layer should be logged with enough metadata — sender, recipient, message type, patient ID, timestamp, status — to reconstruct what happened during a clinical incident. When a physician says "the lab result never arrived," the integration team needs to be able to trace the message's journey in minutes, not hours. Comprehensive audit logging is not optional in healthcare IT — it is a regulatory requirement under HIPAA and a patient safety imperative.

The three non-negotiable principles of healthcare integration engineering: (1) Guaranteed delivery — no message silently lost; (2) Idempotency — duplicate messages don't create duplicate records; (3) Observability — every message traceable from source to destination. Systems that violate any of these principles will eventually cause a patient safety event or a compliance failure.

body.content: CommonWell Health Alliance is a not-for-profit trade association of health IT companies that built a national patient identity and record-locator infrastructure on top of member EHR systems. Rather than centralizing clinical data, CommonWell uses a federated record-locator model: member organizations enroll patients and register their record locations; when a clinician requests a patient's records, CommonWell queries the network and returns document links from all participating sites. As of 2024, CommonWell's network connects thousands of sites across the US, enabling cross-organizational patient record access without requiring a central data repository. This real-world deployment illustrates how large-scale healthcare integration can be achieved through federated architecture and common governance standards rather than a single monolithic hub.

children.text: Start Here: The Simple Idea

Before any of the laws, standards, or acronyms, health information exchange rests on one simple, human idea: your health information should be able to follow you. When you go from your primary care doctor to a specialist, to the emergency room, to the pharmacy, the people caring for you should be able to see the relevant parts of your story — your medications, allergies, recent tests, and diagnoses — without you having to remember and repeat everything yourself.

Health Information Exchange — almost always shortened to HIE — is the electronic sharing of health-related information between authorized organizations. The federal Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) defines it as the electronic exchange of health care information across organizations within a region, community, or hospital system. That is the whole concept. Everything else in this course is detail layered on top of it.

Note that "HIE" is used two ways, and both are fine. It can mean the activity — exchanging information — or the organization that makes the exchanging possible (as in "the state HIE"). Context tells you which one someone means.

Health Information Exchange (HIE) is the electronic sharing of a patient's health information between authorized organizations, so that critical information can follow the patient across the places they receive care.
The Problem HIE Solves: A Fragmented System

To understand why HIE exists, picture the problem it was built to fix. American health care is delivered by a vast, disconnected patchwork of independent hospitals, clinics, labs, pharmacies, and specialists. Historically, each kept its own records in its own system, and those systems did not talk to each other.

The result was fragmentation: your records sat in silos scattered across every place you had ever been seen. A specialist might not know what your primary care doctor prescribed; an emergency room might have no idea about your allergies; the same blood test might be ordered three times because no one could see it had already been done. Care was being delivered with an incomplete picture.

This fragmentation persisted partly because providers compete with one another and partly because their software came from different vendors that were not designed to interoperate. HIE is the deliberate effort to bridge those silos so that information can move with the patient even when the organizations do not share a common owner or a common software system.

body.analogy: Imagine moving to a new city and discovering that your bank, your old landlord, and your employer all keep your records on paper in locked filing cabinets that only they can open — and none of them will mail copies to anyone. Every time you need to prove something, you start from scratch. HIE is like giving all the trustworthy parties a secure, shared way to look up exactly the records they need, when they need them.
body.concept: Why a fragmented health system needs information exchange

children.text: The Three Ways Information Is Exchanged

Not all exchange looks the same. The ONC describes three basic forms of HIE, and almost everything you will encounter fits into one of them. Learning these three is the single most useful mental model for the whole field.

The first is directed exchange (sometimes called "push"). One provider securely sends specific information directly to another — for example, a primary care doctor sending a referral and recent labs to a specialist, or a hospital sending a discharge summary to a patient's regular physician. It is point-to-point, like secure email between care providers.

The second is query-based exchange (sometimes called "pull"). Here a provider searches for and requests information about a patient from other organizations — for example, an emergency room looking up a newly arrived, unconscious patient's medication and allergy history from wherever that data lives. The third is consumer-mediated exchange, where patients themselves access, manage, and direct the sharing of their own health information.

children.text: Why It Matters: The Benefits

HIE is not technology for its own sake — it changes care in concrete ways. With a fuller picture of a patient, providers can avoid ordering tests that were already done elsewhere. Among physicians who use HIE, about 8 in 10 report that it reduces duplicate test ordering, and studies have linked HIE use to fewer repeat CT scans, ultrasounds, and chest X-rays.

Safety improves too. Access to a patient's medication history, allergies, and potential drug interactions helps providers avoid dangerous prescribing errors and adverse drug events. And in emergencies — where a patient may be unable to speak for themselves — the ability to pull critical history quickly can directly improve the speed and accuracy of care.

The most consistently reported benefits, though, are about coordination. Surveyed physicians most often cite improved care quality (around 84 percent) and better care coordination (around 83 percent) as the payoffs of HIE. When information follows the patient across providers and settings, the whole care team can work from the same page.

children.text: How We Got Here, and What HIE Looks Like Today

For decades, exchange barely happened because most records were on paper and the few electronic systems were islands. The turning point was the HITECH Act of 2009, which authorized billions of dollars to drive the adoption and "meaningful use" of electronic health records — and explicitly pushed providers toward exchanging information across organizational boundaries, not just digitizing their own files.

Once records were electronic, networks emerged to connect them. Today HIE happens through regional and statewide HIE organizations and through large national networks. For example, the eHealth Exchange provides connectivity for dozens of regional and state HIEs and a large majority of U.S. hospitals, while organizations like CRISP operate shared HIE services across several states. More recently, a federal framework called TEFCA is knitting these networks together through certified "Qualified Health Information Networks" (QHINs) so they can exchange with one another nationwide.

You do not need to memorize those names yet — later lessons cover the laws, standards, and architecture in depth. The goal of this first lesson is simply to leave you with the core picture: HIE exists to let trustworthy information follow the patient across a fragmented system, it happens in three basic ways, and it makes care safer and better coordinated. Everything that follows builds on that foundation.

CRISP operates as a nonprofit data utility supporting statewide and district HIEs across several states. These are real, working examples of the organizations that make day-to-day exchange possible.

children.text: Why Patient Identity Matters

Every clinical decision depends on being confident that the data being viewed belongs to the right patient. When a physician reviews a medication list, orders a blood transfusion, or interprets a lab result, they must be certain the record in front of them is for the person sitting across from them. Patient identity — uniquely identifying each individual and correctly linking all their records — is the foundation on which every other health IT function depends.

The consequences of patient identity failures are severe. Duplicate patient records — two or more separate records created for the same patient — affect 5 to 10 percent of all stored records in most hospitals, and up to 20 percent in multi-facility health systems. A 2018 Black Book survey found that duplicate records cost hospitals an average of $1,950 per patient in rework, redundant testing, and claims denials. More critically, duplicate records are estimated to contribute to nearly 2,000 preventable deaths per year, and patient identification errors account for approximately 70 percent of adverse patient outcomes.

The most dangerous MPI error is an overlay — when two different patients’ records are merged into a single record. The result is a composite chart that contains data from two people: the first patient may receive a medication they are allergic to (because the allergy was in the second patient’s record), or receive a blood transfusion of the wrong type. Overlays are extremely difficult to detect and correct once they occur, because there is no obvious signal that something is wrong — the chart looks complete and internally consistent.

A Master Patient Index (MPI) is the enterprise system that uniquely identifies each patient and links all their records across clinical and administrative systems. Without a reliable MPI, a health system cannot safely exchange, aggregate, or analyze patient data.

children.text: What Is a Master Patient Index?

A Master Patient Index (MPI) is a centralized database that serves as the authoritative patient identifier repository for a healthcare organization. When a patient registers at a hospital, the MPI checks whether a record already exists for that person. If it does, the new encounter is linked to the existing record. If not, a new record — with a unique patient identifier (UPI), a non-changing alphanumeric key — is created. Every subsequent encounter, lab result, medication record, and clinical note is linked to that UPI, creating a longitudinal patient record across the organization’s systems.

An Enterprise Master Patient Index (EMPI) extends the concept across multiple organizations or facilities. Where an MPI serves a single institution, an EMPI identifies, links, and manages unique patient identities across disparate systems in a health system, an HIE, or a multi-state network. The EMPI is what makes it possible to say “this record from Hospital A and this record from Hospital B belong to the same person” — even when the two records were created with slightly different demographic information.

The MPI/EMPI does not store clinical data — it stores identity data. Its output is a set of record links and a master identifier that can be used to retrieve the correct clinical records from each contributing system. In an HIE, the EMPI is paired with a record-locator service (RLS): the EMPI finds that patient Jane Smith at Hospital A is the same as Jane J. Smith-Williams at Clinic B, and the RLS then queries both organizations for her clinical records and presents them to the requesting clinician.

body.analogy: A Master Patient Index is like the Social Security Administration’s database — not the agency that pays your benefits or issues your passport, but the authoritative system that assigns you a unique number, verifies your identity, and ensures that all records associated with you are correctly linked. In healthcare, the MPI plays the same role: not storing the medical records themselves, but ensuring all records point to the right person.

children.text: How Patient Matching Works

Patient matching — determining whether two records belong to the same individual — is the core function of the MPI. It sounds simple, but it is surprisingly difficult. Names are misspelled, abbreviated, or changed (marriage, divorce). Dates of birth are transposed. The same patient may have registered under a nickname at one facility and a legal name at another. Social Security numbers are frequently withheld or incorrectly entered. No single identifier reliably and uniquely identifies a patient across all settings in the US.

Two primary algorithmic approaches are used: deterministic matching and probabilistic matching. Deterministic matching requires an exact match on all specified fields — if the SSN, last name, and date of birth all match exactly, the records are linked; if any field differs, they are not. It is fast and highly precise but fails whenever data entry errors, name changes, or missing fields are present. Probabilistic matching assigns statistical weights to each data element based on how discriminating that element is; it calculates a composite match score and declares a match if the score exceeds a defined threshold. Probabilistic matching handles minor data variations — nickname vs. legal name, transposed birth year digits — but can produce false positives if thresholds are set too loosely.

Modern EMPIs use a hybrid approach: deterministic matching for high-confidence cases (exact SSN + exact DOB + exact last name), probabilistic matching for borderline cases, and referential matching for ambiguous records. Referential matching compares patient demographics against a large external reference database — such as credit bureau records or driver’s license data — to resolve identities with higher confidence. Vendors including Verato offer referential matching as a service integrated with hospital EMPIs. Name fuzzy-matching algorithms like Soundex and Jaro-Winkler are used to catch phonetic variants: “Smith” and “Smyth”, “Katherine” and “Catherine”, “Jose” and “José.”
