children.text: Why Housing Is a Clinical Variable

Of all the social determinants, housing has perhaps the most direct and measurable relationship to health. Housing instability — whether eviction risk, overcrowding, unsafe conditions, or outright homelessness — degrades health through many channels at once: exposure to the elements, interrupted medication and treatment, inability to store food or insulin, untreated chronic disease, violence, and relentless stress. It is difficult to manage diabetes, heart failure, or a mental illness without a stable, safe place to sleep.

The numbers are stark. People experiencing homelessness in the United States have an average age of death around 48 years — more than two decades shorter than the general population — and mortality rates three to six times higher than housed peers. They rely heavily on emergency departments and inpatient care because the structural barriers to primary and preventive care are so high. Housing instability is not a backdrop to their health problems; it is a primary driver of them.

For a health system operating under value-based contracts, this population is often the most expensive and hardest to manage. A chronically unhoused patient with several conditions can cycle through the emergency department dozens of times a year. From both a moral and a financial standpoint, treating that patient's medical conditions while ignoring their homelessness is treating the symptom and leaving the cause untouched.

Housing instability is a primary driver of poor health, not a side issue. People experiencing homelessness die roughly 26 years earlier than the general population and use emergency and inpatient care at far higher rates.
The Cost Logic: Why Housing Can Save Money

There is a compelling economic argument layered on top of the moral one. The highest-utilizing unhoused patients generate enormous, largely avoidable costs through repeated emergency visits, inpatient stays, and complications of conditions that could be managed in stable settings. For these patients, the cost of doing nothing is not zero — it is very high, just paid through the most expensive part of the system.

This is the core insight behind treating housing as a health intervention: providing stable housing to a high-need individual can reduce their use of crisis care enough to partly or fully offset the cost of the housing itself. The savings are not guaranteed for every person, and the strongest effects concentrate among the highest utilizers, but the logic has held up well enough to attract serious investment from payers and health systems.

Two cautions matter. First, the business case is strongest for the chronically homeless with high medical utilization, not for everyone with a housing need — the math does not work the same way across the whole population. Second, framing housing purely as cost savings can be a trap: if a program does not produce net savings, that does not make it a failure, because reducing avoidable death and suffering has value independent of the spreadsheet.

children.text: Housing First: The Evidence-Based Model

The dominant evidence-based approach is Housing First. Its premise is a reversal of older "treatment first" models: rather than requiring a person to achieve sobriety, complete treatment, or demonstrate "housing readiness" before earning housing, Housing First provides permanent housing immediately and unconditionally, then wraps supportive services around the person in their new home.

The rationale is both humane and pragmatic. Expecting someone to resolve addiction or serious mental illness while sleeping on the street or in a shelter inverts the order in which recovery actually happens — stability comes first, and it makes everything else more achievable. Removing the preconditions also stops screening out the very people with the most acute needs, who are least able to clear a readiness bar.

The evidence is strong, particularly for chronically homeless people with serious mental illness or substance use disorders. Randomized controlled trials find Housing First produces dramatically higher housing retention than treatment-as-usual — in one trial, 73% of Housing First participants were stably housed at one year versus 31% of the comparison group. A 2021 comparison found Housing First decreased homelessness by 88% and improved housing stability by 41% relative to Treatment First, and the model is consistently associated with reduced hospitalization and emergency department use.

body.content:
Housing First has been tested in multiple randomized controlled trials, including large multi-site studies in the US and Canada (such as the At Home/Chez Soi trial). The defining results: people offered immediate, unconditional permanent housing with supports stay housed at far higher rates than those in treatment-first programs — about 73% versus 31% stably housed at one year in one US trial.
A 2021 comparative analysis found Housing First reduced homelessness by 88% and improved housing stability by 41% versus Treatment First, and trials consistently show reduced use of hospitals and emergency departments. Housing First is now endorsed as a best practice for ending chronic homelessness, even for people who are actively using substances.
body.title: Housing First — Randomized Trial Evidence

children.text: How Health Systems and Medicaid Pay for Housing

Recognizing housing as health care, payers and health systems have built mechanisms to fund housing-related services — with an important boundary. Federal Medicaid dollars generally cannot pay for "room and board" (rent itself) as an ongoing benefit, but they can increasingly pay for the services that help people find and keep housing.

In November 2023, CMS released a Medicaid and CHIP Health-Related Social Needs (HRSN) Framework that, through Section 1115 demonstration waivers, allowed states to cover a defined menu of housing supports: housing transition and navigation services, tenancy-sustaining services such as eviction prevention and tenant-rights education, one-time moving costs, and home modifications — plus, for specific high-need populations, up to six months of transitional rent and up to six months of nutrition services. By early 2024, several states had approved demonstrations under this framework.

This policy area is in flux and worth tracking. In March 2025, the federal administration rescinded the November 2023 HRSN guidance and framework, stating it would review state requests to cover health-related social needs on a case-by-case basis under existing statute rather than the standardized framework. The underlying authority to use 1115 waivers for housing supports remains, but the standardized national framework that had accelerated adoption was withdrawn — a reminder that the financing of housing-as-health-care depends on shifting federal policy.

children.text: What This Means in Practice

For frontline clinical teams, the practical implications start with screening: identifying housing instability through SDOH screening and documenting it (Z59 codes capture housing and economic problems). A patient flagged as unstably housed or homeless should trigger a referral pathway — to a housing navigator, a community partner, or a medical respite program — not just a note in the chart.

Medical respite deserves special mention. It provides short-term residential care for people experiencing homelessness who are too ill to recover on the street but do not need a hospital bed. Respite programs reduce inappropriate emergency department use and readmissions by giving patients a safe place to heal — a concrete, fundable intervention that sits squarely at the intersection of housing and health care.

At the system level, some health systems have gone further and invested directly in affordable housing as a population-health strategy, treating it as a way to reduce their most expensive utilization while improving outcomes. Whether through direct investment, Medicaid-funded services, or community partnerships, the throughline is the same: a system that treats housing as outside its lane is leaving one of the most powerful health levers untouched.

The exact scope depends on each state's waiver and current federal policy, which changed in 2025.

children.text: The Moonshot That Started It All

Clinical genomics did not appear overnight; it grew out of one of the largest scientific endeavors in history — the Human Genome Project (HGP). Understanding this history matters because it explains both how far genomics has come and why it is only now becoming a routine part of medicine: the technology had to get dramatically cheaper first.

The HGP was an international effort, launched in 1990, to determine the complete sequence of the roughly 3.2 billion base pairs of human DNA and to map all the genes — the first reading of "nature's complete genetic blueprint for a human." It was the world's largest collaborative biological project, involving researchers across the US, UK, France, Japan, China, and others.

It was declared complete in April 2003 — actually ahead of schedule — at a total cost of about $2.7 billion. That single number frames the entire story: sequencing one human genome cost billions of dollars and took over a decade of global effort. For genomics to enter the clinic, that cost had to fall by a factor of millions. Remarkably, it did.

The Human Genome Project (1990-2003, ~$2.7 billion, international) produced the first complete human DNA sequence. Its staggering cost is the key to the story: genomics could only become clinical once sequencing got radically cheaper.
The Plummeting Cost of Sequencing

The defining trend of modern genomics is the collapse in the cost of sequencing a genome. The National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) has tracked this carefully: from about $95 million per genome in 2001, to roughly $1,000 by 2014 (the famous "$1,000 genome" milestone), to around $200 to $600 today, with vendors now claiming a $100 genome.

To appreciate how extraordinary this is, compare it to Moore's Law — the benchmark for how fast computing costs fall. Sequencing costs did not just keep pace with Moore's Law; they outpaced it dramatically, falling roughly 2,000 times faster than the Moore's Law baseline in the period after 2008. There is no precedent in technology for a cost curve this steep.

The inflection point was 2008, when "next-generation sequencing" (NGS) arrived. NGS replaced the older, slow Sanger method with massively parallel sequencing — reading millions of DNA fragments at once instead of one at a time. This is what broke the cost curve, producing the steepest decline between roughly 2007 and 2011. NGS is the technology that made clinical genomics economically possible, and it underlies nearly every genetic test used today.

children.text: Why Cost Changed Everything

The plummeting cost is not just a fun statistic — it is the entire reason genomics is becoming clinical. At $2.7 billion per genome, sequencing was a once-in-history research achievement. At $95 million, it was still pure research. At $1,000, and now a few hundred dollars, sequencing a patient's genome becomes a feasible clinical test — comparable in cost to other diagnostic workups.

This cost collapse transformed what is possible. It enabled population-scale research (the biobanks of a later lesson), routine tumor sequencing to guide cancer therapy, pharmacogenomic testing to personalize prescriptions, expanded newborn and carrier screening, and direct-to-consumer genetic testing. None of these were viable when a genome cost millions; all became possible as the price fell into the clinical range.

The trajectory also reframes "precision medicine" itself. The vision — tailoring care to an individual's genetic makeup — was articulated for decades, but it was economically fantastical until sequencing became cheap. The cost curve is what turned precision medicine from an aspiration into an emerging reality. When you read about a genomic application in this course, the cheap-sequencing curve is the enabling condition underneath it.

children.text: The Hidden Costs and the Real Bottleneck

There is an important caveat to the "$200 genome" headlines. That figure largely reflects the cost of the sequencing chemistry (the "consumables") alone. The full cost of clinical genome sequencing also includes sample processing, the heavy computational work of analyzing the data, expert interpretation of what the variants mean, reporting, and long-term data storage. The all-in clinical cost is considerably higher than the headline sequencing price.

This points to where the real bottleneck has shifted. Generating the raw sequence is now cheap and fast; the hard, expensive part is interpretation — turning billions of letters into a clinically meaningful answer about what a patient's variants actually mean (recall the ACMG classification and the VUS problem from the previous lesson). The challenge of genomics has moved from "can we read the DNA?" (solved) to "can we understand what it means?" (still hard).

This is why the rest of this course focuses heavily on interpretation, data standards, decision support, and clinical workflows rather than on sequencing itself. The sequencing problem is largely won; the value now lies in making sense of the data and acting on it appropriately. The cheap-genome era created an avalanche of genomic data, and the field's central work is now turning that data into better care.

Real clinical genome testing also costs sample processing, computational analysis, expert interpretation, reporting, and data storage — and the bottleneck has shifted from reading DNA (now cheap) to interpreting what variants mean (still hard and expensive). Don't mistake the consumables price for the total cost of clinical genomics.
body.title: The "$200 Genome" Is Not the Clinical Cost

children.text: Where Clinical Genomics Stands Now

The arc from the HGP to today is a story of a research moonshot becoming everyday medicine, driven by an unprecedented cost collapse. Genomics has moved from a $2.7 billion, decade-long international project to sequence one genome, to a routine test that can be ordered for a cancer patient, a baby, or someone choosing a medication. That transition, compressed into about two decades, is one of the fastest technology-to-medicine translations in history.

But the work is unfinished in important ways. Interpretation remains hard, especially for variants of uncertain significance and in populations underrepresented in genomic databases (an equity issue explored later). The infrastructure to integrate genomic data into clinical care — data standards, EHR integration, decision support — is still maturing. And the policy and ethical frameworks (privacy, consent, non-discrimination) are still catching up. Cheap sequencing solved the first problem; the field is now working through the harder ones that follow.

The takeaway is that you are entering clinical genomics at a pivotal moment: the technology is finally cheap and powerful enough to be clinical, but the systems, interpretation, and policy to use it well are still being built. The rest of this course covers exactly those frontiers — the tests, the clinical applications, the data infrastructure, and the ethics — that turn cheap sequencing into genuinely better, more equitable care.

Sequencing the first human genome took the Human Genome Project 13 years and ~$2.7 billion. Today, a clinical lab can sequence a patient's genome for a few hundred dollars in sequencing cost, often within days.
That is a cost reduction of roughly a millionfold in about two decades — a decline so steep it outpaced Moore's Law by ~2,000x after 2008. This single comparison explains why genomics is only now becoming a routine part of medicine.

children.text: The Language That Turns Care Into a Bill

A claim is not written in English — it is written in codes. To bill for care, the clinical encounter must be translated into standardized codes that payers recognize, and getting those codes right is the heart of the mid-cycle. Medical coding is the language that converts what happened in the exam room into something an insurer can adjudicate and pay.

There are three primary code sets, and the easiest way to keep them straight is by the question each answers. ICD-10 codes answer "why" — the diagnosis or reason for care. CPT codes answer "what" — the procedure or service performed. HCPCS Level II codes answer "what else" — the supplies, drugs, equipment, and services CPT does not cover.

Every claim weaves these together: a diagnosis (why) that justifies a procedure (what), plus any supplies or drugs (what else). Understanding these three code sets — who maintains them, what they cover, and how they connect — is foundational to everything downstream in billing.

Three code sets carry a claim: ICD-10 (the diagnosis — "why"), CPT (the procedure or service — "what"), and HCPCS Level II (supplies, drugs, and equipment — "what else"). Together they translate an encounter into a billable claim.
ICD-10: The Diagnosis Codes

ICD stands for the International Classification of Diseases, developed by the World Health Organization as the global standard for reporting diagnoses. The U.S. uses a clinical modification called ICD-10-CM for diagnoses — the codes physicians use to report why a patient was seen, submitted on claims to explain why care was provided.

ICD-10-CM in the U.S. is maintained by the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). There is also a separate, distinct code set — ICD-10-PCS — used specifically for inpatient hospital procedures; its codes are seven characters, with each character an "axis" specifying details of the procedure. Do not confuse the two: ICD-10-CM is diagnoses (everywhere), ICD-10-PCS is inpatient procedures (hospitals).

The single most important role of ICD-10 codes in billing is establishing medical necessity. Payers want proof that a procedure was justified by the patient's condition, and the diagnosis code is how that justification is communicated. A procedure that is not supported by an appropriate diagnosis will be denied as not medically necessary, no matter how well it was performed.

children.text: CPT: The Procedure and Service Codes

CPT stands for Current Procedural Terminology. CPT codes describe the services that providers and facilities deliver — surgeries, office visits, consultations, diagnostic tests. Where ICD-10 codes describe the "why," CPT codes describe the "what." CPT is maintained and copyrighted by the American Medical Association (AMA), whose CPT Editorial Panel decides additions, deletions, and revisions.

CPT codes are five characters, mostly numeric and always beginning with a number. A heavily used category is Evaluation and Management (E/M) codes, which describe office and hospital visits. For example, CPT 99204 is a Level 4 evaluation-and-management visit for a new patient, requiring moderate medical decision-making or 45 minutes of total time.

CPT coding is where much of a claim's dollar value is set, because the procedure code largely determines reimbursement. It is also where some of the most consequential errors and compliance risks live — selecting a higher-level code than the documentation supports ("upcoding") or a lower one ("downcoding") — topics the documentation-compliance lesson takes up next.

A practical note: CPT codes are often paired with two-digit "modifiers" that add detail (e.g., that a procedure was bilateral, or distinct from another service the same day). Modifiers are small but mighty — a missing or wrong modifier is a frequent denial cause.
HCPCS Level II: Everything Else

HCPCS (the Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System) has two levels. Level I is essentially CPT. Level II — what people usually mean by "HCPCS codes" — covers the products, supplies, and services that CPT does not: certain drugs and biologicals, ambulance services, and durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (collectively "DMEPOS").

HCPCS Level II codes are maintained by CMS and have a distinctive format: a single letter followed by four digits — which is how you tell them apart from numeric CPT codes at a glance. A well-known subset is the "J-codes," which identify drugs administered other than by mouth, such as injectable and infused medications.

HCPCS Level II matters because a lot of real cost lives in supplies and drugs. An infusion clinic, a DME supplier, or an ambulance service depends on accurate HCPCS coding to be paid for the products it provides. Omitting or miscoding these is direct lost revenue, the same way a missed CPT charge is.

children.text: How the Codes Work Together

The codes are not independent — they must link coherently on a claim. The diagnosis (ICD-10) must support the procedure (CPT) it is paired with, demonstrating medical necessity. The supplies and drugs (HCPCS Level II) must be consistent with the procedure and diagnosis. A claim is essentially an argument: "this diagnosis justified this procedure, which used these supplies."

When the links break, the claim is denied. A procedure code with an unrelated diagnosis triggers a medical-necessity denial. A drug J-code without a supporting diagnosis or procedure looks unjustified. This is why coding is a skilled profession: certified coders read the clinical documentation and select codes that are not just individually correct but coherent together and fully supported by the record.

Finally, the bedrock rule of coding is that the code must reflect what was actually documented and done — no more, no less. Coding what was not documented is fraud; failing to code what was documented is lost revenue. That balance, and the documentation that underpins it, is the subject of the next lesson. For now, the key is that these three code sets are the alphabet of the entire claim — master them and the rest of billing becomes legible.

body.message: Individually correct codes are not enough. The diagnosis (ICD-10) must justify the procedure (CPT), and supplies/drugs (HCPCS) must fit both. A procedure unsupported by an appropriate diagnosis is denied as "not medically necessary" — coding is about coherent, documented linkage, not isolated code accuracy.
body.title: Codes Must Link, Not Just Exist

points: Medical coding translates a clinical encounter into standardized codes payers can adjudicate; three code sets dominate.
ICD-10-CM codes report the diagnosis ("why"), are maintained by the CDC/NCHS, and establish medical necessity for procedures.
ICD-10-PCS is a separate 7-character code set for inpatient hospital procedures — distinct from ICD-10-CM diagnoses and from CPT.
CPT codes describe the procedure or service ("what"), are maintained by the AMA, are five characters starting with a number, and include E/M codes like 99204.
HCPCS Level II codes cover supplies, drugs, and DMEPOS ("what else"), are maintained by CMS, and use a letter-plus-four-digits format (e.g., J-codes for injectable drugs).
CPT codes often carry two-digit modifiers that add detail; a missing or wrong modifier is a common denial cause.
The codes must link coherently — the diagnosis must justify the procedure — and must reflect exactly what was documented and done, no more and no less.

body.explanation: CPT codes describe what was done and largely drive reimbursement; ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes describe why and establish medical necessity. Payers require that a procedure be justified by an appropriate diagnosis — a CPT code not supported by a relevant ICD-10 code is denied as not medically necessary. Supplies and drugs are captured by HCPCS Level II codes.

children.text: The Breakdown of the Hydraulic Model

In standard health economics, cost-shifting operates on a 'hydraulic' principle: as government reimbursement rates (Medicare/Medicaid) fall below the marginal cost of care, hospitals raise prices for private commercial insurers to cross-subsidize the loss. Bhattacharya notes that this model relies heavily on a firm's market power and a balanced payer mix. However, the Oliver Wyman report indicates a structural failure of this mechanism in Vermont. Due to demographic aging, the ratio of commercially insured patients in rural areas has plummeted. The remaining commercial base is too small to absorb the 'tax' required to cover the widening gap between Medicaid reimbursement and fixed hospital operating costs.

body.title: The Solvency Gap: Payment-to-Cost Ratios (2024)

children.text: Fixed Costs and the Volume Trap

Rural hospitals are characterized by high fixed costs relative to variable costs. The inability to cost-shift effectively leads to an immediate solvency crisis because revenue is largely fixed by government fee schedules, while inflation drives up input costs (labor, technology). Unlike standard competitive firms that would exit the market when Average Total Cost exceeds Price, rural hospitals are 'essential utilities' constrained by Act 167 mandates to remain open. This creates a disconnect between economic reality and policy mandate, forcing hospitals to consume reserves to survive.
The arithmetic of cost-shifting fails when the commercial population drops below 35%. You cannot balance a system-wide deficit on a vanishing tax base.

children.text: The Problem Medicare Had to Solve

For Medicare’s first 18 years, hospitals were paid retrospectively for whatever it cost them to treat a patient. This cost-based reimbursement was, in the words of analysts, a "nearly risk-free world" for hospitals: the more services they delivered and the longer patients stayed, the more Medicare paid. There was no built-in reason to be efficient.

Predictably, costs spiraled. Cost-based payment rewarded volume and length of stay, not value, and Medicare hospital spending grew faster than the program could sustain. By the early 1980s, policymakers concluded the incentives themselves had to change.

The solution was a prospective payment system — pay a fixed, predetermined amount per case based on the patient’s diagnosis, set in advance. If a hospital treats the patient for less, it keeps the difference; if it spends more, it absorbs the loss. This single change shifted financial risk from Medicare onto hospitals and rewired the incentives of American hospital care.

Prospective payment means the price is set before the care is delivered, based on the patient’s diagnosis — not on the hospital’s actual costs. Efficiency becomes the hospital’s reward; inefficiency becomes its loss.

children.text: What Is a DRG?

The unit of payment under the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS) is the Diagnosis-Related Group, or DRG. DRGs were developed at Yale University in the early 1970s by Robert Fetter and John Thompson as a way to classify hospital cases into clinically similar groups that consume similar resources.

The core idea is patient classification by "case mix." Instead of paying for each test, drug, and bed-day, Medicare assigns each inpatient stay to a single DRG based on the principal diagnosis, procedures performed, complications, comorbidities, age, and discharge status. Each DRG carries a relative weight reflecting how resource-intensive that type of case is on average.

Medicare uses a refined version called MS-DRGs (Medicare Severity DRGs), which account for the severity of illness through complication and comorbidity tiers. For fiscal year 2025, CMS uses a total of 773 MS-DRGs. A high-weight DRG such as a major organ transplant pays far more than a low-weight DRG such as a simple medical admission.

body.content: In the early 1970s, Robert B. Fetter, Ph.D., and John D. Thompson, MPH, at Yale University built the first operational set of Diagnosis-Related Groups to relate the types of patients a hospital treats to the costs it incurs. A decade later, Congress adopted their classification system as the backbone of Medicare’s national prospective payment system — turning an academic case-mix tool into the engine of U.S. hospital reimbursement.
body.title: Yale University and the Birth of DRGs

children.text: How a DRG Payment Is Calculated

The base IPPS payment for a case is, at its heart, a multiplication: a standardized base payment rate multiplied by the DRG’s relative weight. The base rate is split into a labor-related share and a non-labor share, and the labor share is adjusted by the local area wage index so that hospitals in high-cost labor markets receive more.

On top of that base payment, Medicare adds several adjustments. Teaching hospitals receive an Indirect Medical Education (IME) add-on tied to their resident-to-bed ratio. Hospitals serving many low-income patients receive a Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) add-on. And unusually expensive cases can qualify for outlier payments once costs exceed a high threshold.

The combined formula means two hospitals treating the identical DRG can be paid different amounts based on where they are, whether they teach, whom they serve, and whether the case became catastrophically expensive — but the starting point is always the same: base rate times relative weight.

children.text: How IPPS Changed Hospital Behavior

Because a hospital now earns a fixed amount per DRG regardless of how long the patient stays, IPPS created powerful pressure to reduce length of stay and eliminate unnecessary days and tests. After 1983, hospitals intensified their scrutiny of length of stay, and average inpatient stays fell substantially across the system.

IPPS also made accurate clinical documentation and coding financially critical. Since the DRG assignment — and thus the payment — depends on documented diagnoses, complications, and comorbidities, hospitals invested heavily in coding, case management, and clinical documentation improvement programs.

The same incentives carry risks regulators watch closely: "upcoding" (assigning a higher-paying DRG than warranted) and premature discharge ("quicker and sicker"). These concerns are exactly why Medicare layered on quality and readmissions programs in later decades — covered later in this course.

body.message: A fixed payment per DRG rewards efficiency but can incentivize premature discharge and upcoding. Medicare’s later quality programs — like the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program — exist partly to counterbalance these inpatient-payment incentives.
body.title: The downside of paying per case

children.text: Why IPPS Still Matters

IPPS was the first large-scale demonstration that changing how you pay providers changes how they deliver care. It proved that Medicare’s purchasing power could reshape behavior across thousands of hospitals at once — a lesson that underpins every later payment reform.

The prospective-payment logic spread far beyond hospitals. Medicare went on to build prospective payment systems for skilled nursing facilities, home health, inpatient rehabilitation, and more — each applying the same principle of paying a predetermined amount per episode or unit of care rather than per service.

And the DRG concept itself became foundational to bundled payments and value-based care. Once you can define and price a discrete episode of care, you can begin holding providers accountable for the cost and quality of that whole episode — which is precisely where Medicare payment policy has been heading ever since.
The 1983 shift to DRG-based prospective payment proved a principle that still drives reform today: change how you pay, and you change how care is delivered.

children.text: Why Individual-Record APIs Are Not Enough

Standard FHIR REST APIs are brilliant for the single-patient interaction: a clinician clicks into a chart, the app fires a GET /Patient/{id}/$everything, and within seconds the full record arrives. That model works perfectly at the bedside. It falls apart, however, the moment you need data on thousands or millions of patients simultaneously. A payer managing a Medicare Advantage panel of 500,000 members cannot issue half a million sequential HTTP requests to compute a single quality measure. Network latency alone would make the job take days, and the server on the other end would almost certainly throttle or block the traffic long before completion.

Population health analytics, value-based care reporting, actuarial modeling, public health surveillance, and clinical research all share a common requirement: access to cohort-level data in bulk. Quality measure programs such as HEDIS require health plans to assemble longitudinal records spanning years of encounters, lab results, prescriptions, and diagnoses for every enrolled member. Doing that record-by-record through a patient-facing API is not just slow — it is architecturally wrong. The data pipeline breaks down at scale.

Payer-to-payer data exchange introduces a second pressure point. When a member switches insurance plans, the incoming payer must receive the full claims and clinical history for that member from the prior payer. Under CMS rules finalized in 2024, impacted payers must support this exchange via FHIR APIs and must provide data going back five years. Doing that for thousands of concurrent member transitions demands a purpose-built bulk mechanism, not patient-by-patient REST calls. Bulk FHIR was designed precisely for these scenarios, enabling server-side export jobs that run asynchronously and deliver data as downloadable files.

children.text: The Bulk FHIR Specification: How It Works

The normative standard is the HL7 FHIR Bulk Data Access Implementation Guide, currently at version 2.0.0 (STU 2), published by HL7 International and available at hl7.org/fhir/uv/bulkdata/. The specification builds on top of FHIR R4 and defines three export endpoints that correspond to different scopes of data. The Group/$export endpoint exports all FHIR resources for members of a named Group resource — the most common use case for payer populations and clinical cohorts. The Patient/$export endpoint exports resources for all patients on the server. The System/$export endpoint (sometimes written /$export) exports every resource in the system regardless of patient linkage, useful for operational data migrations.

The protocol follows an asynchronous kick-off pattern. The client sends a GET or POST request to the chosen export endpoint with the HTTP header Prefer: respond-async. The server immediately returns an HTTP 202 Accepted response — it does not start streaming data yet. Crucially, the 202 response includes a Content-Location header whose value is a polling URL. The client then polls that URL at regular intervals (using exponential back-off as recommended by the specification) until the server returns a 200 OK response with a JSON manifest listing the completed output files. Each output file contains resources of exactly one FHIR type — for example, all Patient resources in one file, all Condition resources in another.

The output format is NDJSON — Newline Delimited JSON — with the MIME type application/fhir+ndjson. NDJSON serializes each FHIR resource as a single line of compact JSON with no internal whitespace, separated from the next resource by a newline character. This design enables streaming parsers to process files line by line without loading the entire document into memory, making it practical to handle files that contain millions of resources. Analytics platforms, data warehouses, and research data pipelines can ingest NDJSON files directly into columnar storage engines such as Apache Parquet or BigQuery without additional transformation overhead.

steps.description: Client sends GET [base]/Group/{id}/$export with header Prefer: respond-async and optional parameters like _type (resource types to include) and _since (date filter). Server responds 202 Accepted with Content-Location header pointing to a status URL.

steps.description: Client polls the Content-Location URL. Server returns 202 (still in progress) with optional X-Progress header, or 200 OK (complete) with JSON manifest of output files. Client should use exponential back-off; server may include Retry-After hints.
steps.title: Status Polling

steps.description: The 200 OK body is a JSON object with fields: transactionTime, request (original URL), requiresAccessToken (boolean), output (array of file descriptors), and error (array of error file descriptors for any resources that failed to export).

body.analogy: Think of bulk FHIR like ordering a freight shipment rather than buying items one by one at a store counter. You place a single order (kick-off request), the warehouse assembles your pallet in the background (server builds NDJSON files), you check the tracking number periodically (status polling), and then you pick up the whole shipment at once (file download). Walking into the store and buying 500,000 items individually would be absurd — yet that is exactly what individual FHIR REST calls require at population scale.

children.text: Regulatory Drivers: CMS and ONC Requirements

Bulk FHIR moved from a promising technical idea to a federal mandate through two landmark rules. The ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule, published in May 2020, required certified health IT developers to support the HL7 FHIR Bulk Data Access IG (v1.0.0, STU 1) as part of their certification criteria. Specifically, the rule mandated support for the Group/$export operation, enabling population-level data extraction from electronic health records. The compliance deadline for certified EHR systems was December 31, 2022, meaning that since January 2023, any CEHRT-certified system must support bulk export of USCDI data elements for defined patient groups.

On the payer side, CMS issued the Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F) in 2020, requiring Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP agencies, and QHP issuers to implement FHIR-based Patient Access APIs. The subsequent CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), published February 2024, extended these requirements and introduced mandatory Payer-to-Payer Bulk Data Exchange. Under CMS-0057-F, impacted payers must implement a FHIR-based payer-to-payer API that uses Bulk FHIR to transfer clinical data, claims and encounter data, and prior authorization records for members transitioning between plans. Payers must exchange data covering the prior five years of a member's history. The enforcement deadline for this requirement is January 1, 2027.

The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) adds a third layer of momentum. ONC's FHIR Roadmap for TEFCA Exchange version 2 charts a four-stage path toward full FHIR adoption across Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs). Stage 2 — requiring QHIN-facilitated FHIR API exchange — was completed in 2024. Stage 3, piloting QHIN-to-QHIN FHIR exchange, is targeted for 2025 pilot implementation. While TEFCA does not yet mandate bulk FHIR specifically, its FHIR roadmap creates the network infrastructure through which bulk transfers between organizations will eventually flow. TEFCA-connected QHINs are expected to support bulk exchange as the framework matures toward end-to-end FHIR exchange in Stage 4.

Non-compliance can result in civil monetary penalties.

children.text: Real-World Use Cases: From Quality Measures to Research

The most prominent active initiative involving Bulk FHIR in 2024 and 2025 is the NCQA Bulk FHIR Quality Coalition. The National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) — the organization that administers HEDIS, the industry-standard quality measurement program — launched the coalition to perform end-to-end testing of regulated FHIR data using digital HEDIS measurement as the real-world test case. Representatives from CMS and the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy (ASTP, formerly ONC) participate as observers. The coalition brings together cohorts of health plans, Data Aggregator Validation (DAV)-certified data partners, and technology vendors to build FHIR data pipelines from clinical and claims data, then test those pipelines against HEDIS-specific FHIR Implementation Guides.

HEDIS electronic measures represent a paradigm shift in quality reporting. NCQA has converted the lengthy HEDIS Volume 2 measure specifications into Clinical Quality Language (CQL), enabling automated, consistent computation directly against FHIR data rather than relying on manual chart abstraction, fax-based data collection, or proprietary extracts. A Bulk FHIR pipeline for HEDIS measurement works as follows: a health plan kicks off a Group/$export against a network provider's FHIR server for its enrolled members, receives NDJSON files containing claims (via CARIN Blue Button FHIR IG) and clinical data (via US Core FHIR IG), and runs CQL measure logic against the combined dataset. NCQA aims to transition HEDIS reporting to fully digital measures by 2030, and Bulk FHIR is the foundational data transport layer for that transition.

Research platforms represent a third major use case. Academic medical centers and research networks use the HL7 Da Vinci Payer Data Exchange (PDex) Implementation Guide alongside Bulk FHIR to build longitudinal patient datasets for clinical trials, retrospective cohort studies, and machine learning model training. The combination of Group/$export with _type filtering (limiting exports to specific resource types) and _since date parameters enables incremental data updates — a research platform can pull only the new encounters and lab results since its last extract, keeping a population dataset current without re-downloading the entire history. This incremental export pattern dramatically reduces server load and network transfer volumes while maintaining dataset freshness.

body.content: When a Medicare Advantage member switches plans on January 1, the incoming payer must request five years of historical data from the prior payer. Under CMS-0057-F, the prior payer's Payer-to-Payer Bulk API must return: US Core clinical data (conditions, medications, allergies, procedures), claims and encounter data with financial fields excluded, and active and pending prior authorization records. The data is exported as NDJSON via Group/$export for the cohort of transitioning members, transferred securely, and ingested into the incoming payer's care management systems — enabling continuity of care without gaps in clinical context.

children.text: Implementation Challenges and Security Considerations

Authentication for Bulk FHIR is handled by the SMART Backend Services Authorization specification, defined within the SMART App Launch IG (currently v2.2.0) and referenced by the Bulk Data Access IG. Unlike user-facing SMART on FHIR apps, bulk clients operate without a human in the loop — there is no browser redirect or login screen. Instead, the client registers its public key (as a JSON Web Key Set, or JWKS) with the authorization server, then uses an asymmetric key pair to sign a JWT assertion. The authorization server validates the JWT against the registered public key and issues a short-lived OAuth 2.0 bearer token. This token is then presented with each bulk export request. The entire flow requires TLS 1.2 or higher for all connections.

Large file handling presents engineering challenges that developers frequently underestimate. A bulk export for a payer with millions of members can produce tens of thousands of NDJSON files totaling hundreds of gigabytes or more. Servers must implement file expiration policies (the Bulk Data IG notes files may be deleted after retrieval), and clients must download files promptly — implementations commonly expire export files after 24 to 72 hours. On the client side, NDJSON files must be streamed and processed line by line rather than loaded entirely into memory. Parallelizing downloads across multiple files, using S3-compatible object storage as a landing zone, and employing streaming ETL pipelines are standard patterns for production bulk FHIR consumers.

Privacy risks at population scale are qualitatively different from single-patient access. A bulk export grants access to the records of thousands or millions of individuals simultaneously, meaning a misconfigured authorization scope or a compromised client credential exposes an entire population's data in a single breach. De-identification requirements apply when bulk FHIR data is used for research under an IRB protocol: HIPAA Safe Harbor de-identification must remove all 18 specified identifiers, or Expert Determination must certify re-identification risk below defined thresholds. Rate limiting is equally important — servers enforce HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses when clients exceed agreed traffic levels, and production systems must implement tenant-specific rate limits to prevent any single bulk consumer from degrading service for others. Security best practices recommend regular audits of registered backend service credentials and rotation of asymmetric key pairs on a defined schedule.

body.message: Unlike single-patient APIs where a misconfigured scope exposes one record, a bulk FHIR scope error exposes an entire population simultaneously. Organizations must implement least-privilege scoping (e.g., system/Patient.read rather than system/*.read), audit all registered backend service credentials regularly, and monitor export job logs for anomalous access patterns. SMART Backend Services credentials should be treated with the same security controls as privileged database accounts.

points: Standard FHIR REST APIs require one request per patient — impractical for populations of thousands or millions. Bulk FHIR solves this with a single async kick-off that exports entire cohorts as downloadable NDJSON files.

The HL7 Bulk Data Access Implementation Guide (v2.0.0, STU 2) defines three export endpoints: Group/$export for defined cohorts, Patient/$export for all patients, and System/$export for all server resources.
The async kick-off pattern returns 202 Accepted immediately. Clients poll a status URL until they receive a 200 OK with a JSON manifest listing NDJSON output files ready for download.

NDJSON (application/fhir+ndjson) encodes one FHIR resource per line, enabling streaming parsers to process files without loading them entirely into memory — critical for files containing millions of resources.

The ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule mandated that certified EHRs support Bulk FHIR (Group/$export) for USCDI data elements by December 31, 2022. CMS-0057-F requires payer-to-payer Bulk FHIR data exchange by January 1, 2027.
NCQA's Bulk FHIR Quality Coalition is actively using bulk exports as the data pipeline for digital HEDIS measurement, targeting full digital quality reporting by 2030.

SMART Backend Services authorization — using asymmetric JWT key pairs and OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow — provides the system-to-system authentication layer required for Bulk FHIR, with no human user in the loop.

Privacy and security risks are amplified at population scale: a single misconfigured bulk credential can expose millions of records. Least-privilege scoping, credential rotation, and rate limiting are non-negotiable safeguards.

The response also includes a Content-Location header with the URL the client must poll to check progress — 200 OK only arrives when the export files are fully ready for download.

children.text: What Is the Clinical Document Architecture?

The Clinical Document Architecture (CDA) is an HL7 document markup standard that uses XML to define the structure, encoding, and semantics of clinical documents for the purpose of exchange. HL7 CDA Release 1 was approved as an ANSI standard in November 2000, and the far more widely adopted Release 2 achieved ANSI approval in May 2005 and later became an ISO standard in 2009. CDA Release 2 remains the foundation of nearly every structured clinical document exchanged in the United States today — from hospital discharge summaries sent to primary care physicians, to the care summaries that flow between EHR systems at care transitions.

A CDA document is divided into two logical regions: a header and a body. The header is the administrative and provenance layer — it identifies the patient, the author, the organization that created the document, the type of encounter, and the legal custodian. The body carries the clinical content itself. Inside the body, content is organized into nested sections, and each section must contain a narrative block — a chunk of human-readable text that any browser can render without special software. This design principle is fundamental to CDA's philosophy: a CDA document must always be renderable by a human, even if the machine-processable entries inside it cannot be decoded.

Below the narrative block sits an optional entries layer. Entries encode the same clinical facts in machine-readable form using coded vocabularies — SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, and ICD. A receiving system that cannot interpret the entries can safely ignore them and render only the narrative. A system that can parse them gains structured, computable data. This dual-layer design — human-readable narrative plus machine-processable entries — was innovative for its time and is what separates CDA documents from simple PDF attachments or plain-text discharge summaries. It is the architectural decision that made CDA durable enough to underpin two decades of US health information exchange policy.

body.analogy: Think of a CDA document like a legal contract with attached exhibits. The contract body (the narrative block) is written in plain English so any lawyer or judge can read it. The exhibits (the structured entries) contain the same information in a precise, machine-indexable format that automated systems can search and process. You can act on the contract using only the narrative — but the exhibits make automation possible.

children.text: C-CDA: The Consolidated Implementation Guide

The base CDA standard defines the document framework but deliberately leaves the clinical content largely unconstrained. This flexibility created a proliferation of competing, incompatible CDA implementation guides across US states, health systems, and specialty societies. By the early 2010s, a physician receiving a CDA document might find that allergies were coded in one section in one system, a completely different section in another, and not coded at all in a third. The Consolidated CDA — C-CDA — was HL7's answer to this fragmentation. The S&I Framework, coordinated by the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC), drove the consolidation of seven previously separate CDA implementation guides into a single, nationally harmonized specification.

C-CDA defines a specific set of document types, each with required sections, required coded entries, and vocabulary bindings. The core document types include: the Continuity of Care Document (CCD), which aggregates a patient's full longitudinal health record for transfer between providers; the Discharge Summary, limited to information generated at the point of hospital release; the Progress Note, used for ongoing encounter documentation in inpatient or outpatient settings; the History and Physical (H&P); the Consultation Note; the Operative Note; the Procedure Note; the Diagnostic Imaging Report; the Referral Note; the Transfer Summary; and the Care Plan. Each document type is governed by a template that specifies which sections are required, which are optional, and which data elements inside each section must be present in both narrative and coded form.

C-CDA 2.1, published in 2015, has been the regulatory cornerstone of US interoperability requirements for nearly a decade and has seen only errata updates since its publication. C-CDA 3.0 merged the 2.1 guide with the C-CDA Companion Guide, added enhancement requests, and incorporated USCDI V4 alignment. However, the HL7 community moved quickly: C-CDA 4.0 has been published as the current normative version, and C-CDA 5.0 is in active ballot. The regulatory adoption of C-CDA 2.1 expired as a standalone certification basis on January 1, 2026, marking a transition to newer versions aligned with the US Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) requirements.

children.text: CDA in Meaningful Use and CEHRT

The C-CDA standard did not become ubiquitous through organic market adoption. It was mandated. Meaningful Use Stage 2, finalized by CMS and ONC in 2012, required eligible professionals and eligible hospitals to electronically exchange summary care records using C-CDA for every transition of care and referral where feasible. The specific regulatory hook was 45 CFR 170.314(b)(2), which required EHR technology to create, display, and transmit C-CDA documents as a precondition of certification. ONC's CEHRT (Certified EHR Technology) program embedded C-CDA compliance at the product level — no certification meant no Meaningful Use incentive payments.

The 2015 Edition certification criteria, published in the Federal Register in October 2015, extended and refined the C-CDA requirements. Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(1), "Transitions of Care," certified health IT had to both create and receive C-CDA documents. Receive was the harder requirement — it forced vendors to parse and incorporate incoming C-CDA data into their systems, not merely generate outbound documents. This bidirectional mandate pushed every major EHR vendor to invest in C-CDA production and consumption, creating the foundation for today's national clinical document exchange infrastructure through networks like CommonWell, Carequality, and the eHealth Exchange.

The role of ONC in C-CDA adoption cannot be overstated. ONC coordinated the original consolidation effort through the S&I Framework, funded testing infrastructure at the Standards Implementation and Testing Environment (SITE), and published Companion Guides to clarify ambiguous requirements in the base specification. ONC also funded the C-CDA Scorecard — a free online tool at site.healthit.gov that allows providers and vendors to submit a C-CDA document and receive an automated quality score highlighting deviations from best practices. The interplay between regulatory mandate and publicly funded tooling is what transformed C-CDA from a technical specification into infrastructure.

children.text: The Transition to FHIR: C-CDA vs. FHIR Documents

HL7 FHIR has emerged as the preferred API framework for modern health data exchange, and it is reasonable to ask: does FHIR make C-CDA obsolete? The honest answer is nuanced. FHIR and C-CDA were designed for different primary use cases. C-CDA excels at producing a complete, human-readable clinical document — a discharge summary or care summary that can be rendered in a browser, signed by a physician, and attached to a patient record. FHIR excels at granular, API-driven retrieval of specific clinical resources: a patient's current medications, a single lab result, or a list of active problems. These are complementary, not competing, capabilities.

The FHIR community recognized this complementarity and created two bridges. The first is the C-CDA on FHIR Implementation Guide (currently version 1.2.0 STU 1, based on FHIR R4, with version 2.0.0 in continuous build development). This guide defines FHIR profiles on the Composition resource that map directly to C-CDA document types — CCD, Discharge Summary, Progress Note, and others. The second bridge is a wrapping approach: a C-CDA document can be referenced via a FHIR DocumentReference resource, allowing FHIR-native systems to discover and retrieve C-CDA documents without requiring full conversion. Both strategies support incremental migration rather than a hard cutover.

C-CDA will not disappear quickly. Tens of thousands of EHR installations generate and consume C-CDA documents daily, and the regulatory infrastructure — CEHRT certification, Carequality, eHealth Exchange — remains organized around C-CDA payloads. Replacing it requires not just updating software but rewriting certification criteria, retesting vendors, renegotiating network participation agreements, and retraining implementation teams. Realistically, C-CDA will coexist with FHIR for at least a decade. The trajectory is clear — FHIR is the direction of travel — but the journey is long, and C-CDA remains the workhorse of clinical document exchange in the United States today.

children.text: Real-World C-CDA Implementation: Quality, Validation, and Common Pitfalls

Despite two decades of standardization effort, production C-CDA documents frequently suffer from quality problems that impair interoperability. Research has documented that real-world system-generated C-CDA documents regularly contain data represented inconsistently or incompletely. Common failure patterns include: missing coded entries despite a narrative section being present; misuse of null flavors (the XML mechanism for representing unknown or unavailable data) to mask absent data rather than convey its true status; section templates applied to incorrect content types; date and time precision errors; and vocabulary codes that are valid in isolation but semantically incorrect in context. Studies have found that automated tools identify approximately thirteen times more issues than schematron validation alone — meaning that passing basic schema validation is a floor, not a ceiling.

The primary validation stack for C-CDA has three layers. First, XML schema validation confirms that the document is well-formed and matches the CDA XML schema. Second, schematron validation applies the business rule constraints defined in the C-CDA implementation guide — for example, that a CCD must contain a Problem section, or that every Medication Activity entry must include a route code. Third, the ONC SITE C-CDA Scorecard goes beyond schema and schematron to assess best practices: are LOINC codes used for lab results instead of local codes? Are date-times recorded with appropriate precision? Are section templates applied correctly? The Scorecard generates a quantitative grade and a detailed issue report that implementers can act on.

In addition to the free SITE tooling, EHR vendors seeking CEHRT certification must submit to testing through ONC-Authorized Testing Laboratories (ATLs). The two largest ATLs in the US are Drummond Group and ICSA Labs. Both test C-CDA creation and reception as part of the 45 CFR 170.315(b)(1) Transitions of Care criterion. Real-world implementation teams also rely on the Lantana Group's Schematron Validator and the NIST CDA Validation tool hosted at cda-validation.nist.gov. A mature C-CDA implementation practice includes automated validation in the document generation pipeline — not just during certification testing — so that quality problems are caught before documents reach receiving systems.

body.content: When a patient is discharged from an acute care hospital, the hospital EHR must generate a C-CDA Discharge Summary or Continuity of Care Document. This document must contain — in both narrative and coded form — the discharge diagnosis (ICD-10-CM coded), the reconciled medication list (RxNorm coded), allergy list (SNOMED CT coded), pending follow-up instructions, and any referrals. The document is transmitted via Direct Secure Messaging or a network like Carequality to the receiving primary care provider's EHR. The receiving system must parse the C-CDA, reconcile the medication list against the patient's existing record, and flag any discrepancies for the physician to review. If the sending system used local codes instead of RxNorm, the receiving system cannot perform automated reconciliation — the document arrives but the computable value is lost.

children.text: What CEHRT Is and Why It Exists

Certified EHR Technology — universally shortened to CEHRT — is the federally defined standard that an electronic health record system must meet before it can be used to satisfy the requirements of Medicare and Medicaid quality and incentive programs. The term sounds bureaucratic, but the concept is straightforward: the federal government will not pay clinicians or hospitals for demonstrating "meaningful use" of a health IT system unless that system has been independently tested and found to meet a published set of technical criteria. CEHRT is the stamp that says the system passed.

The legal foundation for the entire certification machinery is the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act — the HITECH Act — which was signed into law on February 17, 2009, as part of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act. HITECH authorized the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) to establish a certification program and directed the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to tie billions of dollars in EHR incentive payments to the use of certified technology. Without HITECH, there would be no certification program; without the certification program, there would be no agreed-upon baseline for what an EHR must do.

ONC published its first set of certification criteria in the 2011 Edition Final Rule, establishing the inaugural CEHRT definition to support Meaningful Use Stage 1. The program has gone through multiple editions since — 2014 Edition, 2015 Edition, and the landmark 2015 Edition Cures Update — each ratcheting up the technical bar as the healthcare system's expectations for data sharing and interoperability evolved. Today, CEHRT is not merely an eligibility checkbox for incentive payments; it also underpins the 21st Century Cures Act's information-blocking prohibitions and the Promoting Interoperability performance category inside CMS quality payment programs.

children.text: The 2015 Edition Cures Update Requirements

The single most consequential regulatory update to the certification program arrived on May 1, 2020, when ONC published the "21st Century Cures Act: Interoperability, Information Blocking, and the ONC Health IT Certification Program" Final Rule in the Federal Register (85 FR 25642). This rule — commonly called the Cures Act Final Rule — substantially upgraded the 2015 Edition certification criteria and created what is now known as the 2015 Edition Cures Update. Developers of certified health IT were required to meet the new API standards and provide them to customers by no later than May 2, 2022.

The headline technical requirement introduced by the Cures Update is a standardized API for both single-patient and population-level data services, built on HL7 FHIR Release 4 (FHIR R4). Specifically, certified products must implement the FHIR US Core Implementation Guide, the FHIR Bulk Data Access Implementation Guide for population-level queries, and the HL7 SMART Application Launch Framework Implementation Guide so that third-party applications can authenticate and retrieve data securely. These three implementation guides together form the technical spine of modern app-based interoperability in U.S. healthcare.

Alongside the API requirement, the Cures Update mandated support for the United States Core Data for Interoperability Version 1 (USCDI v1) as the minimum data set. USCDI v1 defines 52 individual data elements organized into 16 data classes — covering patient demographics, allergies and intolerances, medications, laboratory results, vital signs, clinical notes, care team members, health concerns, immunizations, implantable devices, patient documents, problems, procedures, provenance, smoking status, and unique device identifiers. Any CEHRT system must be able to expose all of these data classes through its FHIR API. The Cures Update also required an Electronic Health Information (EHI) export function, allowing patients or their authorized representatives to download a complete export of their entire record — not just the USCDI subset.

body.content: Before the Cures Update, a hospital could use a 2015 Edition-certified EHR that supported only proprietary or HL7 v2 interfaces for data exchange. After the update, that same hospital's vendor was required to ship a FHIR R4-based patient-facing API, a bulk data export endpoint for population analytics, and an EHI export tool — all tested against specific implementation guides. This meant that a patient could, for the first time, connect a smartphone app directly to their hospital's EHR using the same open standards their bank uses for account aggregation.

children.text: ONC-ATLs and the Certification Testing Process

Before any product can appear on the Certified Health IT Product List (CHPL) at chpl.healthit.gov, it must be tested by an ONC-Authorized Testing Laboratory (ONC-ATL) and then certified by an ONC-Authorized Certification Body (ONC-ACB). These are separate but often overlapping roles. The three established ONC-ATLs are Drummond Group, ICSA Labs, and SLI Compliance — a division of Gaming Laboratories International. In 2023, Leidos joined as a fourth ONC-ATL, adding capacity to a process that had at times created bottlenecks for vendors racing to meet regulatory deadlines.

Testing at an ONC-ATL is methodical and criterion-by-criterion. The lab works through each applicable certification criterion in 45 CFR § 170.315, running the vendor's software against standardized test procedures and test data to verify conformance. For the FHIR API criterion, this includes executing specific API queries, validating FHIR resource structures, testing SMART App Launch sequences, and verifying that the bulk data export endpoint returns well-formed FHIR bundles. Passing the lab tests earns a "test report," which the vendor then submits to an ONC-ACB — such as Drummond Group or SLI Compliance, which hold dual ATL and ACB status — for final certification and listing on the CHPL.

Certification is not a one-time event. ONC-ACBs conduct ongoing surveillance — both reactive, triggered by complaints or anomalies, and random-sample surveillance — to verify that certified modules continue to function as certified in real-world deployments. If an ONC-ACB finds a non-conformity, the developer must correct it within a defined remediation period. At the program level, ONC itself can initiate Direct Review under 45 CFR § 170.580 if it has reasonable belief that a developer has violated a Condition or Maintenance of Certification. Severe or uncorrected violations can result in suspension or termination — decertification — of one or more modules, with the status publicly visible on the CHPL so that providers can see when a product they rely on is under corrective action.

children.text: CEHRT in CMS Quality Programs

The most direct way most clinicians encounter CEHRT requirements is through the Promoting Interoperability (PI) performance category inside the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS). MIPS is CMS's consolidated quality reporting framework under MACRA, and the PI category carries a weight of 25 percent of a clinician's total MIPS final score. To report PI, a clinician must attest to using CEHRT and must provide their EHR's CMS EHR Certification ID (CEHRT ID) — a unique identifier visible on the CHPL — as part of their submission.

The 2024 PI performance category is organized around four objectives: Electronic Prescribing, Health Information Exchange, Provider to Patient Exchange, and Public Health and Clinical Data Exchange. Each objective contains required and optional measures. The Electronic Prescribing objective includes the e-Prescribing measure and the Query of Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) measure. The Health Information Exchange objective includes measures for sending and receiving care summaries. The Provider to Patient Exchange objective focuses on enabling patients to access their data via API-enabled apps. Under Public Health and Clinical Data Exchange, Immunization Registry Reporting and Electronic Case Reporting are required; Public Health Registry Reporting, Clinical Data Registry Reporting, and Syndromic Surveillance Reporting are optional bonus measures worth up to 5 additional points.

Clinicians must also provide four required attestations as part of their PI submission: an attestation that they have not taken actions to limit or restrict the compatibility or interoperability of their CEHRT; an ONC Direct Review attestation; a Security Risk Analysis measure confirmation; and a Safety Assurance Factors for EHR Resilience (SAFER) Guides attestation. The maximum attainable PI score is 105 points — the extra 5 come from optional bonus measures — but the score is capped at 100 for final MIPS weighting purposes. Advanced APM participants are generally excluded from MIPS reporting requirements but often must still use CEHRT to qualify for the Advanced APM bonus.

body.analogy: Think of the CEHRT ID on a PI attestation like the VIN number on a car title. The car still has to pass a safety inspection (ONC-ATL testing), be registered (CHPL listing), and have its registration current (ongoing surveillance). Without a valid VIN matching current registration, you cannot legally operate the vehicle in programs that require one — just as a clinician cannot claim PI credit without a valid, active CEHRT ID.
body.concept: CEHRT ID in MIPS PI reporting works like a vehicle VIN: it uniquely identifies the certified product and proves the regulatory requirements are met.

children.text: What Certification Does NOT Guarantee

CEHRT certification is a necessary condition for participating in federal quality programs — but it is emphatically not a sufficient condition for real-world interoperability or safe, usable software. This distinction matters enormously in practice. Certification testing occurs in a controlled lab environment with standardized synthetic data, scripted workflows, and idealized network conditions. A vendor's software might pass every criterion in the lab and still behave very differently when deployed in a busy emergency department with legacy infrastructure, thousands of active patient records, and staff under time pressure.

Research published in peer-reviewed literature confirms this usability gap. Studies have found that EHR certification testing does not accurately represent actual use by clinicians in their clinical environment, and that vendor-reported usability scores are based on test cases that do not resemble real clinical scenarios. The testing environment lacks variables such as task interruptions, increased noise levels, concurrent alerts, and other stressors that characterize real clinical settings. Poorly designed screen layouts, redundant workflow sequences, and alert fatigue are documented consequences — all of which survived the certification process untouched.

ONC acknowledged this gap and, through the Cures Act Final Rule, created a Real World Testing requirement. Health IT developers certified under the program must annually submit Real World Testing plans describing how they will demonstrate interoperability and functionality in actual production environments — not just in the lab. However, a 2025 study published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association found that developers were not presenting results in meaningful ways with appropriate context, suggesting that Real World Testing as currently implemented falls short of providing genuine transparency. ONC and the authorized certification bodies have been called on to more closely inspect report quality and impose clearer metric requirements.

body.message: A CHPL listing tells you a product met the federal technical bar on the day it was tested. It does not tell you whether the product is easy to use, whether it will interoperate with your specific trading partners, or whether it will perform reliably at scale. Procurement decisions should include real-world reference checks, usability testing with actual clinical staff, and review of the vendor's Real World Testing results on CHPL.

children.text: The Policy Origin: CMS-9115-F and the Interoperability Mandate

On May 1, 2020, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services published the landmark Interoperability and Patient Access final rule, formally known as CMS-9115-F. The rule arrived amid a pandemic, yet it represented years of policymaking work aimed at dismantling one of the most persistent barriers in American healthcare: the inability of patients to easily obtain and move their own health data. For decades, insurance claims, encounter records, and clinical results sat locked inside payer systems, accessible only through cumbersome request processes. CMS-9115-F changed the legal landscape fundamentally by requiring regulated payers to open standardized, secure digital doors directly to patients and the applications patients choose.

The rule applies to a broad set of federally regulated payers: Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations, Medicaid Fee-for-Service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Fee-for-Service programs, CHIP managed care entities, and issuers of Qualified Health Plans (QHPs) on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges. This scope is intentional — together these programs cover hundreds of millions of Americans, and establishing a uniform standard across them creates the critical mass needed to make patient-facing data exchange a market reality rather than a pilot curiosity. Notably, large commercial plans sold outside the exchanges were not directly captured, a gap that some states have moved to close through their own legislation.

The technical standard chosen by CMS was HL7 FHIR Release 4.0.1, the then-current version of the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources specification. FHIR R4 provides a REST-based API architecture with well-defined resource types, enabling developers to build consumer applications without requiring bespoke integrations for each payer. CMS recognized implementation complexity created by the COVID-19 pandemic and exercised enforcement discretion through July 1, 2021, at which point active enforcement of the Patient Access API and Provider Directory API requirements began in earnest. Missing either deadline was not a technicality — CMS signaled it would use existing program oversight authorities, including corrective action plans and, for Medicare Advantage, contract termination.

children.text: What the Patient Access API Must Expose

The Patient Access API is not a single data dump — it is a structured set of FHIR resource endpoints that collectively give a member a longitudinal view of what their insurance plan knows about them. CMS-9115-F identified three primary categories of data that must be available: claims and encounter information (including cost data such as provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing), clinical data including laboratory results when maintained by the payer, and formulary and coverage data. The CARIN Alliance for Blue Button Implementation Guide (CARIN IG) was explicitly endorsed by CMS as the recommended specification for the claims and encounter data layer, defining profiles for the Patient, Coverage, and ExplanationOfBenefit FHIR resources that form the foundation of every compliant implementation.

The clinical data requirement is where many payer implementations have stumbled. CMS requires that payers expose data classes and elements aligned with the U.S. Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) standard, as reflected in the US Core FHIR Implementation Guide. This means exposing resources such as MedicationRequest, Condition, Procedure, and CareTeam — data elements that can logically be derived from claims even when payers do not hold provider-sourced clinical records. CMS-0057-F (the 2024 successor rule) escalated the bar by requiring conformance with USCDI v3, a step up from the USCDI v1 that most CMS-9115-F implementations targeted. In practice, fewer than 30 percent of evaluated payer APIs made clinical resources fully available, illustrating how the clinical data tier remains the most challenging compliance frontier.

Access to this data is member-authorized and flows through the OAuth 2.0 SMART App Launch protocol, which allows a member to grant a third-party application permission to retrieve their records directly from the payer's FHIR server. The application receives a token scoped to that member's data, and the payer must return the applicable FHIR resources without filtering or degrading the data. CMS explicitly prohibits payers from using the app registration process as a competitive gatekeeping mechanism — registration must be open to any legitimate developer, and delays or denials without documented security justification constitute compliance violations.

children.text: Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange: From CMS-9115-F to CMS-0057-F

One of the most ambitious provisions of the original CMS-9115-F was the requirement that payers exchange data with each other when a member transitions between plans. The vision: when you switch from one insurance plan to another, your new insurer automatically receives up to five years of your claims, encounter, and clinical history from your prior insurer — reducing redundant testing, filling dangerous care gaps, and enabling your new care team to understand your complete medical story from day one. However, implementation challenges proved severe. On December 8, 2021, CMS announced enforcement discretion on the payer-to-payer provisions of CMS-9115-F, acknowledging that the member-mediated authentication model outlined in the original rule was not well-suited for business-to-business data transfers.

The 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F), published January 17, 2024, resolved these tensions with a redesigned Payer-to-Payer API framework. Under CMS-0057-F, payers are no longer required to use patient-mediated SMART App Launch authentication for payer-to-payer exchanges — CMS recognized that "protocols requiring user level credentials managed by the payer are generally not appropriate for business-to-business data exchanges." Instead, the new model requires that when a member enrolls in a new plan, the receiving payer must collect the member's opt-in consent and information about former or concurrent plans, then — within one week of receiving both — request the required data from identified prior payers. The full Payer-to-Payer API compliance deadline under CMS-0057-F is January 1, 2027.

The technical vehicle for payer-to-payer exchange is the Da Vinci Payer Data Exchange (PDex) Implementation Guide, which CMS recommends as the specification for this API. PDex defines how payers package FHIR resources — including claims, USCDI clinical data, and prior authorization history — into standardized bundles that receiving payers can ingest. A critical feature of PDex is its provenance framework, which preserves the chain of custody for clinical information as it moves across payer boundaries. The data scope is substantial: up to five years of adjudicated claims and encounters (excluding provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing), data classes aligned with USCDI, and prior authorization information excluding drug authorizations. Plain-language educational resources explaining the Payer-to-Payer API to members must also be provided, underscoring that member trust and informed consent are foundational to the design.

body.analogy: Imagine every time you moved to a new city, your entire medical file automatically transferred to your new doctor's office before your first appointment — without you having to carry a folder of records or repeat your history from scratch.
body.concept: The Payer-to-Payer API aims to create the same seamless longitudinal data continuity when members change insurance plans, ensuring new payers and providers start with a complete picture instead of a blank slate.
