children.text: The Provider Directory API: Making Network Data Trustworthy

Alongside the Patient Access API, CMS-9115-F required covered payers to implement a publicly accessible, FHIR R4-based Provider Directory API. The purpose is straightforward but long-elusive: give consumers, providers, and app developers reliable, machine-readable information about which clinicians and facilities participate in a given insurance network. The implementation guide endorsed by CMS for this purpose is the Da Vinci PDEX Plan-Net IG, currently at version 1.2.0 (published February 25, 2025). Plan-Net defines FHIR profiles for the key entities in a provider network: Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organization, OrganizationAffiliation, HealthcareService, InsurancePlan, Endpoint, and Location. Together these resources allow a third-party application to answer questions like "Which cardiologists in Burlington, Vermont accept my Blue Cross plan?"

Provider directory accuracy has been a chronic industry problem, and the No Surprises Act — which took effect January 1, 2022 — added regulatory teeth by creating a 90-day attestation cycle. Health plans must verify all provider details at least once every 90 days, including physician name, specialty, address, phone number, and network participation status. Inaccurate directories create concrete patient harm: a member who selects an in-network provider based on a stale directory and then receives an unexpected out-of-network bill has experienced both a financial injury and a failure of the information infrastructure that was supposed to protect them. CMS reinforced this with Medicare Advantage-specific requirements for annual attestation of directory accuracy through the HPMS MPF Provider Directory module, adding a formal accountability mechanism to what had previously been an honor-system process.

Despite mandatory requirements, the state of provider directory FHIR APIs as of 2024 remains uneven. Many payers have struggled to maintain accurate Practitioner-to-Plan relationships — one of the most frequently cited deficiencies in API audits. The core challenge is organizational: provider directory data is collected through credentialing, contracting, and roster processes that often exist in siloed systems. Surfacing this data through a coherent FHIR API requires not only technical integration work but also operational governance to ensure that roster updates flow promptly into the API. CMS-0057-F introduced a Provider Access API — distinct from the public-facing Provider Directory API — that allows providers to query payer data about their own patients, with a separate compliance deadline of January 1, 2027.

body.message: A "ghost network" occurs when a provider appears in an insurance directory but is no longer accepting new patients, has left the network, or has moved locations. Studies have found error rates exceeding 40 percent in some commercial plan directories. The Provider Directory API requirement creates a machine-readable surface for auditing — but the data quality it reflects is only as good as the operational processes feeding it.
body.title: Ghost Networks: A Persistent Patient Safety Problem

body.content: A developer querying a compliant Plan-Net endpoint can retrieve a PractitionerRole resource that bundles the practitioner's NPI, specialty taxonomy code, the specific InsurancePlan network they participate in, their office address as a Location resource, accepted patient telephones, and the network's HealthcareService offerings — all in a single structured FHIR response. This is the machine-readable equivalent of the printed directory booklet, updated continuously rather than annually.

children.text: Adoption, Enforcement, and the Gaps That Remain

More than four years after the July 2021 enforcement date, the Patient Access API landscape reflects the messy reality of federal mandates meeting real-world implementation complexity. Industry analysis published in November 2024 by Flexpa found that nearly half of targeted payer endpoints still lacked a live, conformant Patient Access API, and that actual member usage — the number of API calls being made by consumers through third-party apps — numbered in the hundreds per plan rather than the thousands that would indicate mainstream adoption. The contrast with established health information networks is stark: Carequality moves approximately 940 million clinical documents per month through provider-initiated queries, while patient-mediated FHIR pulls via the Patient Access API are orders of magnitude smaller.

CMS enforcement has been measured rather than aggressive. The agency uses existing program oversight mechanisms — annual survey instruments for Medicare Advantage, the QHP certification process for Marketplace plans, and state-level oversight for Medicaid and CHIP — rather than a centralized enforcement unit issuing fines. Enforcement actions can escalate from corrective action plans to public reporting of violations and ultimately to contract termination for Medicare Advantage organizations, but documented cases of termination specifically for Patient Access API non-compliance remain rare. CMS did, however, signal a new accountability lever: starting January 1, 2026, impacted payers must annually report Patient Access API usage metrics to CMS (first report due March 31, 2026), creating a transparency mechanism that will enable comparative assessment of engagement across plans.

Perhaps the most consequential unresolved gap is the privacy protection asymmetry for data that leaves the payer system. When a member authorizes a third-party app to receive their health data through the Patient Access API, that data exits the HIPAA regulatory perimeter. Most third-party health apps are not covered entities and are not bound by HIPAA — they are instead subject to the Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits deceptive practices but does not constrain how a company may use or monetize health data as long as its privacy policy discloses those practices. This creates a scenario where a member's complete insurance claims history — a detailed proxy for their medical conditions, prescriptions, and provider relationships — could lawfully be sold to data brokers or used for targeted advertising, with the only safeguard being whatever terms the app's privacy policy contains. The ONC and FTC have flagged this gap repeatedly, but as of mid-2025 no federal legislation has closed it comprehensively.

The state-level response has begun to fill some voids. California's SB 1419, effective January 1, 2025, and Tennessee's SB 2012, effective May 2024, extended Patient Access API-style requirements to commercial plans sold outside the federally facilitated exchanges — populations not covered by CMS-9115-F. These state actions are early indicators that interoperability mandates may eventually reach all lines of business, not just government-program-adjacent markets. Meanwhile, the January 2027 deadline under CMS-0057-F for the full suite of new APIs — Payer-to-Payer, Provider Access, and Prior Authorization — represents the next major wave of compliance pressure that will test whether payers can scale from partial Patient Access API conformance to a comprehensive interoperability architecture.

children.text: What This Means for Vermont's Health Ecosystem

Vermont's health system occupies a distinctive position in the national interoperability landscape. The state operates a unified Health Information Exchange (Vermont HIE/VHIE) and has long pursued All-Payer Model ambitions that require rich data flows between payers, providers, and the state itself. For Green Mountain Care Board-regulated payers and the Vermont Health Connect marketplace, the CMS-9115-F and CMS-0057-F requirements overlay on top of existing state data-sharing expectations. Vermont Blue Cross Blue Shield, MVP Health Care, and Medicaid managed care organizations operating in the state are all subject to the federal Patient Access API mandates and must maintain conformant FHIR endpoints serving members.

The practical implication for Vermont consumers is significant but still largely unrealized. A Vermont resident enrolled in Medicaid or a Marketplace plan today has the legal right to connect any SMART-on-FHIR application to their payer's Patient Access API and retrieve their complete claims history, formulary information, and available clinical data. Yet awareness of this right is minimal, and the ecosystem of trustworthy, Vermont-specific health management apps built on these APIs is nascent. Closing the gap between legal entitlement and consumer benefit requires not just API compliance but also member education, app vetting frameworks, and policy clarity on downstream data use protections that Vermont could model through state-level privacy legislation.

For healthcare organizations and technologists building on Vermont's health platform, the Patient Access API represents an underutilized data source. Aggregating member-authorized payer data alongside provider-sourced clinical data from the VHIE creates the longitudinal health record that care coordination programs need but have historically lacked. Population health analytics, care gap identification, and medication reconciliation all improve meaningfully when claims data — the most complete record of what services a member actually received — is available alongside clinical documentation. The CMS-0057-F Payer-to-Payer API will further amplify this by ensuring that members who transition between Vermont plans or arrive in Vermont from out of state bring their prior history with them automatically.

The Patient Access API is not an IT project. It is a patient rights framework built on top of an IT standard. The goal is not API uptime — it is a Vermont where every resident can walk into any healthcare encounter with their complete insurance and clinical history in hand.

The Payer-to-Payer API carries up to five years of claims, encounters, USCDI clinical data, and prior authorization history, using the DaVinci PDex IG for packaging and provenance.

The Da Vinci PDEX Plan-Net IG (current version 1.2.0, February 2025) defines the FHIR-based Provider Directory API, which the No Surprises Act reinforced with mandatory 90-day data attestation cycles.
Actual member adoption of third-party apps connecting to Patient Access APIs remains low — hundreds of pulls per plan versus hundreds of millions of provider-initiated transactions monthly.

Health data shared through the Patient Access API exits HIPAA protections once received by a non-covered third-party app; FTC oversight covers only deceptive practices, leaving a significant privacy gap.
Starting March 31, 2026, payers must report annual Patient Access API usage metrics to CMS — creating the first systematic transparency tool for measuring real-world engagement.

This IG defines profiles for the Patient, Coverage, and ExplanationOfBenefit FHIR resources that form the backbone of every compliant payer implementation. The PDex IG serves a different but related role — it is recommended for the Payer-to-Payer API context, particularly for provenance tracking when data moves between plans.

children.text: The Consent Baseline: What HIPAA Allows Without Patient Authorization

Before examining consent models in health information exchange (HIE), it is essential to understand what the law already permits without any patient signature. The HIPAA Privacy Rule, codified at 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164, establishes a baseline under which covered entities — hospitals, physicians, health plans, and their business associates — may use and disclose protected health information (PHI) without obtaining patient consent or authorization for three overarching categories: Treatment, Payment, and Health Care Operations, collectively known as TPO. These exceptions are not loopholes; they are deliberate design choices reflecting Congress's intent to allow the healthcare system to function efficiently while still protecting sensitive data from non-clinical misuse.

Under the Treatment exception, a primary care physician can share a patient's medication history with a referring cardiologist without asking the patient to sign anything first. Under the Payment exception, a hospital can send a patient's diagnosis codes and procedure records to a payer for claim adjudication. Under Health Care Operations, a hospital quality team can review records to evaluate outcomes without triggering authorization requirements. The minimum-necessary standard still applies to Payment and Operations disclosures — meaning only the PHI reasonably necessary to accomplish the purpose should be shared — but Treatment disclosures carry no such restriction, recognizing that a treating clinician may need the full clinical picture.

This federal floor does not stop states from enacting stronger protections. Many states have enacted "super-HIPAA" statutes that require explicit written consent even for some TPO disclosures, particularly for mental health records, HIV/AIDS status, genetic information, and reproductive health data. Vermont, for instance, imposes strict confidentiality requirements on HIV-related records beyond what HIPAA mandates. Maryland and Connecticut have similarly robust mental health privacy laws that restrict disclosure for treatment coordination unless the patient has consented in writing. These state variations create a patchwork that HIE operators must navigate carefully: a network spanning multiple states must honor the most restrictive applicable law, which often means building consent workflows even when HIPAA alone would not require them.

children.text: Key principle: HIPAA is a floor, not a ceiling. States may — and frequently do — require stronger patient protections. HIE networks operating across state lines must determine which jurisdiction's law governs each disclosure and build their consent architecture accordingly.
Opt-In vs. Opt-Out: Definitions, Trade-offs, and State Variation

The central policy question for any HIE is whether patient data flows into the network by default — with patients able to withdraw — or only after patients affirmatively agree to participate. These two approaches, opt-out and opt-in respectively, represent fundamentally different theories of patient autonomy and administrative practicality. In an opt-out model, patients are enrolled automatically and must actively contact the HIE or their provider to restrict sharing. In an opt-in model, the patient must affirmatively sign a consent form before any records are accessible through the network. Each model carries meaningful trade-offs for data completeness, care coordination, and administrative burden.

Research published in the American Journal of Managed Care found that hospitals located in states with opt-in consent policies were 7.8 percentage points more likely than hospitals in opt-out states to report regulatory barriers to health information exchange. This gap illustrates the operational weight of opt-in consent: providers must manage consent tracking for every patient, consent forms expire, patients move, and the administrative cost compounds across millions of encounters. By contrast, opt-out models produce more complete network data because the default is inclusion. The trade-off is that patients who never read the enrollment notice may not realize their records are being shared, raising autonomy concerns — particularly among historically marginalized communities with legitimate reasons to distrust data sharing.

State policies vary considerably. New York uses a consent-to-access model through its Statewide Health Information Network (SHIN-NY) in which patients must sign a consent form for each provider who wishes to access their records — giving patients granular control but creating administrative complexity. California does not have a statewide statutory mandate, but most California HIE organizations have implemented opt-out mechanisms that allow data sharing by default while honoring patient withdrawal requests. Texas legislation frames HIE participation as "voluntary," placing it outside a strict opt-in or opt-out classification. Beyond binary models, some HIEs have moved toward granular consent, where patients can say yes to sharing their diabetes records but no to sharing their mental health records — a more patient-centered approach that requires significantly more sophisticated technical infrastructure.

body.content: Some HIEs now offer patients a tiered consent menu rather than a single on/off switch. A patient might permit their primary care records and lab results to be shared broadly, while restricting mental health visit notes to only their psychiatrist, and blocking substance use disorder records entirely from the HIE. This granular model respects the eleven sensitive data categories recognized in health data privacy frameworks — including genetics, mental health, substance use, and sexual/reproductive health — and more closely reflects patient preferences. Research shows that 82.5% of patients consider mental health information sensitive and 64.1% want choices about sharing sensitive records with providers, underscoring demand for granular control.

children.text: 42 CFR Part 2: The Special Rule for Substance Use Disorder Records

No federal regulation creates more friction in health information exchange than 42 CFR Part 2, the Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records rule. Originally enacted in the 1970s to encourage people with addiction to seek treatment without fear that their records could be used against them in criminal proceedings or by employers, Part 2 has historically imposed requirements far stricter than HIPAA's TPO framework. Under the pre-2024 regime, substance use disorder (SUD) treatment records could not be disclosed — even to other treating physicians — without a patient-signed consent form that named the specific recipient, the specific purpose, and had an expiration date. A patient treated at an opioid treatment program could not have those records automatically shared with their cardiologist even in an emergency without a valid consent in place.

On February 8, 2024, the Department of Health and Human Services published a Final Rule modifying 42 CFR Part 2, implementing changes Congress required in the 2020 CARES Act. The rule took effect on April 16, 2024, with a compliance deadline of February 16, 2026. The 2024 Final Rule makes four landmark changes. First, it allows a single patient consent to cover all future uses and disclosures for treatment, payment, and health care operations — eliminating the need to name every specific recipient. Second, it aligns Part 2 breach notification requirements with HIPAA's Breach Notification Rule. Third, it grants Part 2 patients new rights to request an accounting of disclosures and to request restrictions on certain disclosures, mirroring rights already available under HIPAA. Fourth, it replaces Part 2's criminal-only penalties with HIPAA-aligned civil and criminal enforcement authority, administered by HHS Office for Civil Rights.

Despite these improvements, the consent segmentation challenge for HIEs remains significant. Even under the 2024 rule, Part 2 records require consent before they can flow through an HIE — the single-consent mechanism helps, but HIE platforms must be able to identify which records originated from a Part 2 program and apply the appropriate controls. Historically, many HIE vendors simply blocked all exchange of SUD records to avoid compliance exposure, meaning a patient's treatment for opioid use disorder was invisible to the emergency department treating that same patient for an overdose. Implementing Part 2-compliant segmentation requires labeling records at the source, propagating those labels through the exchange infrastructure, and enforcing access rules at the point of query — a technically demanding sequence that most legacy HIE platforms were not built to support.

body.message: A common compliance mistake is assuming that a HIPAA-compliant HIE automatically handles 42 CFR Part 2 records correctly. It does not. Until a provider's HIE platform explicitly implements Part 2 consent tracking and record segmentation, the safest default is to exclude SUD records from HIE exchange entirely — which means care gaps. The 2024 Final Rule alignment helps, but technical implementation remains the bottleneck.
body.title: Do Not Conflate HIPAA and Part 2

children.text: FHIR Consent Resource and Digital Consent Management

The emergence of HL7 FHIR as the dominant interoperability standard has introduced a structured, computable mechanism for expressing consent: the FHIR Consent resource. Available since FHIR Release 3 and substantially refined in R4 and R5, the Consent resource can encode a wide range of privacy policies in machine-readable form. The resource's core structure begins with a base decision — either permit or deny — and then layers in provisions that represent exceptions to that decision. Each provision can be scoped by data category, purpose of use, actor (the individual or organization authorized to access), date range, and security label. Nested sub-provisions allow for arbitrarily complex policy trees: a patient could grant broad access to a care team but exclude a specific data category or specific provider role.

The HL7 Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) Implementation Guide, published by the HL7 Security Working Group, extends this capability by defining how security labels should be applied to individual FHIR resources based on their sensitivity classification. The DS4P IG specifies the sec-label-basis extension, which records which policy or regulation drove the label assignment — allowing a system to know, for instance, that a MedicationRequest resource carries a Part 2 label because it originated from a certified opioid treatment program. The sec-label-related-artifact extension can then point to the specific consent directive that authorizes a disclosure, creating an auditable chain from consent to data release. Packages for both R4 and R4B are available, and the SAMHSA-sponsored Consent2Share (C2S) open-source platform was built on this specification to demonstrate feasibility.

The technical challenges of enforcing granular consent at scale in production FHIR APIs are considerable. First, consent must be checked at query time — not just at ingestion — meaning every FHIR API call must be evaluated against the patient's current consent record before any data is returned. Second, consent records themselves can change: a patient revokes consent, updates a provision, or grants new access. The HIE's query engine must either maintain a consent cache that is updated in near real-time or query the authoritative consent store synchronously, adding latency. Third, many clinical workflows generate bulk queries — document queries, summary patient records, care gap analyses — and applying row-level consent filtering to millions of records requires purpose-built data access control infrastructure that most EHR vendors have not yet standardized. The FHIR Consent resource provides the grammar; building a scalable enforcement engine is the engineering work the industry is still completing.

body.analogy: Think of the FHIR Consent resource as a sophisticated key-ring management system. Each consent provision is like a copy of a key that grants access to a specific room (data category) in a building (the patient record). The base decision sets whether the default is "all doors locked" (deny) or "all doors open" (permit), and each provision adds or removes specific keys. The DS4P security labels are like the room labels on each door. The enforcement engine is the security guard who checks every key against every door at every entry point — in real time, at scale.
body.concept: FHIR Consent provisions map data access rules in a machine-readable hierarchy, but enforcement requires an active policy decision point at every API query.

children.text: The Path to Standardization: TEFCA, ONC, and Consent Interoperability

The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA), administered by ONC and operated through the Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE), represents the federal government's most ambitious attempt to create a national, interoperable HIE fabric. TEFCA's architecture is built around Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) — large-scale networks that interconnect regional HIEs, provider networks, payers, and public health agencies under a single governance framework and set of technical standards. As of 2024, Common Agreement Version 2.0 was published in the Federal Register on May 1, 2024, with updated standard operating procedures released in August 2024 to support new exchange purposes including public health and benefit determination.

TEFCA's consent approach rests on the concept of Exchange Purposes (XPs). Every data request transmitted through TEFCA must identify the lawful purpose for which it is made — Treatment, Payment, Health Care Operations, Public Health, Benefits Determination, or Individual Access Services. For Individual Access Services, entities must obtain express consent from the individual before providing access. For other exchange purposes, TEFCA relies on the applicable federal and state laws that already govern those disclosures — meaning HIPAA's TPO framework applies to Treatment, Payment, and Operations queries, while state law may layer additional requirements. TEFCA does not yet impose a unified national consent standard, and state-level variation remains a significant interoperability barrier within the network of networks. A QHIN receiving a Treatment query from a provider in a state with opt-in HIE consent requirements must still honor those requirements even if the data originates in an opt-out state.

ONC's Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) initiative, launched as a pilot program in October 2011, laid the conceptual and technical groundwork for what is now the HL7 DS4P Implementation Guide. The initiative demonstrated that metadata tags could be used to label sensitive data categories and enforce selective sharing across organizational boundaries. SAMHSA's Consent2Share platform — an open-source consent management and data segmentation tool — was built on DS4P specifications and designed to integrate with existing EHR and HIE systems. For production-grade consent management, organizations including CommonWell Health Alliance, Carequality, and regional HIEs have been developing or procuring consent management platforms capable of storing, evaluating, and enforcing patient consent decisions at the speed required for real-time clinical exchange. The convergence of TEFCA governance, FHIR R4 APIs, and DS4P security labels is creating the technical foundation for a national consent interoperability layer — but full standardization across all fifty states remains a multi-year effort.

TEFCA Common Agreement Version 2.0 was published May 1, 2024, with updated SOPs released August 2024. Every TEFCA query must declare an Exchange Purpose; Individual Access Services require express patient consent. State law still governs consent requirements for Treatment, Payment, and Operations queries within QHIN networks.

children.text: On December 13, 2016, President Obama signed the 21st Century Cures Act into law. The legislation was one of the most sweeping health information technology reforms in the United States since the HITECH Act of 2009, and its interoperability provisions — concentrated in Title IV — set off a regulatory cascade that would reshape how hospitals, insurers, app developers, and patients exchange electronic health information for years to come.

Yet the law itself was only the opening act. The actual requirements that providers and health IT vendors had to meet came primarily through two landmark final rules published simultaneously on May 1, 2020: the ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (85 FR 25642) and the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F). Together these rules translated congressional intent into specific, enforceable mandates around APIs, data standards, and a new federal prohibition called information blocking. Understanding what each layer of this legal framework actually requires — and what it does not — is essential for anyone working at the intersection of health policy, technology, or clinical care.

This lesson walks through the five pillars of the interoperability framework created by the Cures Act: the legislative architecture of Title IV, the information blocking prohibition and its exceptions, the FHIR API mandates and certification requirements, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) that aims to create a network of networks, and finally the real-world impact measured since enforcement began — including the significant gaps that remain.
Title IV: The Legislative Architecture

The 21st Century Cures Act spans 362 pages and covers topics ranging from cancer research to mental health to drug approvals. Title IV, however, is exclusively focused on health information technology. It contains four major sections — 4001 through 4004 — that together define the statutory framework for interoperability and information blocking. Section 4001 directed ONC to establish an annual strategy for using health IT to reduce burden on clinicians. Section 4002 updated the certification program for electronic health records, requiring that certified technology not block information sharing. Section 4003 directed ONC to develop a Trusted Exchange Framework for nationwide interoperability. And Section 4004 — the most consequential from a compliance standpoint — formally prohibited information blocking and established penalties for violations.

What makes Title IV unusual in federal health IT law is the breadth of entities it covers. Prior federal health IT legislation primarily targeted providers participating in federal programs and the EHR vendors serving them. Title IV extended new legal obligations to health information exchanges (HIEs), health information networks (HINs), and health IT developers far beyond the narrow scope of EHR certification. The law also created a definition of interoperability that set a new standard: health IT should enable the secure exchange and use of health information without special effort on the part of the user. That phrase — without special effort — became a touchstone in subsequent regulatory debates.

Congress also gave ONC explicit authority to update the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI), a standardized set of health data elements that must be supported by certified systems. USCDI Version 1, which became the baseline for the Cures Act final rules, defined 16 data classes including patient demographics, clinical notes, laboratory results, medications, vital signs, and provenance information. Subsequent versions have expanded these requirements, with USCDI v3 adding social determinants of health data elements and v4 incorporating additional clinical data.

children.text: The Information Blocking Prohibition: Section 4004 in Detail

Section 4004 of the Cures Act created an entirely new category of federal health care violation: information blocking. The statute defines information blocking as a practice that is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI), and that the actor knows — or should know — is likely to have that effect. Unlike HIPAA, which regulates what information must be protected, the information blocking prohibition regulates practices that unnecessarily restrict what information can flow.

The law identifies three categories of regulated actors: health IT developers of certified health IT; health information exchanges and health information networks (HIEs/HINs); and health care providers. The knowledge standard differs by actor type. For health IT developers and HIEs/HINs, the standard is whether they know or should know that a practice is likely to interfere with EHI access. For providers, it is a slightly higher bar — the provider must actually know that the practice is unreasonable. The definition of EHI itself was phased in: initially limited to data elements in USCDI v1, and then expanded by October 2022 to encompass the full scope of a patient's designated record set as defined under HIPAA.

ONC established eight regulatory exceptions that, when met, mean a practice does not constitute information blocking. These are: (1) Preventing Harm — blocking is permitted when it substantially reduces a genuine risk of harm to a patient or third party; (2) Privacy — compliance with state or federal privacy laws or patient-requested restrictions; (3) Security — protecting against threats to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of EHI, but only when applied consistently and non-discriminatorily; (4) Infeasibility — technically or organizationally impossible to fulfill a specific request; (5) Health IT Performance — system maintenance or upgrades requiring temporary unavailability; (6) Content and Manner — responding in an alternative manner when a request is unreasonable in its scope; (7) Fees — charging market-based, cost-related fees for access, applied uniformly; and (8) Licensing — conditions on licensing interoperability interfaces, subject to fair terms requirements. Between April 2021 and May 2023, ONC received 708 complaints alleging information blocking — 79% filed by or on behalf of patients, with health care providers named as the alleged actor in 80% of cases.

children.text: FHIR APIs and CEHRT Requirements: The Technical Mandate

The ONC Cures Act Final Rule's most technically consequential provision was the creation of a new certification criterion for standardized APIs using HL7 FHIR Release 4 (FHIR R4). This criterion — codified at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(10) — requires that certified EHR technology (CEHRT) support application programming interfaces that allow both individual patients and authorized third-party apps to access health data programmatically, without special effort, and at no cost to the patient. The standard chosen was not arbitrary: FHIR R4 had emerged from a multi-year HL7 standards development process and had already seen significant industry adoption before it became mandatory.

The ONC rule established two distinct API use cases. The first is the Patient Access API: a single-patient, read-only API that allows patients to authorize third-party applications — including smartphone health apps — to retrieve their records from their provider's EHR. The second is the Provider Access API and Bulk Data Access: population-level data export capabilities that allow authorized entities to retrieve records for multiple patients simultaneously. SMART on FHIR, a companion specification that ONC also endorsed, provides the authorization and authentication layer that allows apps to plug into EHRs much as apps plug into a smartphone operating system. By 2024, more than 250 certified products from over 200 health IT developers had implemented the Bulk Data Access API criterion.

The CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Rule (CMS-9115-F) extended parallel FHIR API requirements to payers — specifically Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care organizations, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plans in the Federally Facilitated Marketplace. These payers were required to implement a FHIR R4-based Patient Access API making claims, encounter data, and clinical data (conforming to USCDI v1) available to members. CMS also required payers to implement a Provider Directory API, enabling providers to verify network information programmatically. Data had to be available from January 1, 2016 forward for all current enrollees. A subsequent CMS rule — CMS-0057-F, the Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule published in January 2024 — added prior authorization exchange via FHIR APIs, with compliance deadlines extending to 2026–2027.

body.analogy: Think of FHIR R4 as the USB-C standard for health data. Before FHIR mandates, every EHR vendor used a proprietary connector — a health app had to build a custom integration for Epic, another for Cerner, another for Athena. FHIR R4 creates one universal port. Once a vendor certifies to the standard, any authorized app can plug in without custom development.

children.text: TEFCA: Building the Network of Networks

Section 4003(b) of the Cures Act gave ONC a specific mandate: publish a Trusted Exchange Framework — a common set of principles that all health information networks should follow — and a Common Agreement that health information networks could sign to participate in nationwide, query-based exchange. The resulting initiative, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA), took several years to develop through public comment and stakeholder engagement. ONC published TEFCA's foundational documents in January 2022, and in December 2023 reached the pivotal milestone of designating the first Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) — the organizations that anchor TEFCA's exchange infrastructure.

TEFCA operates through a three-tier governance structure. At the top is ONC, which sets policy. Below ONC is the Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE) — currently the Sequoia Project — which manages the Common Agreement, handles QHIN applications, and oversees technical standards through the QHIN Technical Framework (QTF). At the operational level are the QHINs themselves: large health information networks that sign the Common Agreement and agree to exchange data with one another under shared rules for patient identity matching, authentication, and performance. As of early 2024, eight organizations had been designated as QHINs: eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, Health Gorilla, Konza, MedAllies, Kno2, CommonWell Health Alliance, and eClinicalWorks. CommonWell alone serves more than 37,000 provider organizations and more than 244 million unique individuals.

The transformative promise of TEFCA is query-based exchange at national scale. Before TEFCA, a clinician at a hospital in Vermont wanting to access records from a hospital in Texas faced a patchwork of bilateral agreements, network memberships, and technical barriers. TEFCA creates a single on-ramp: join any QHIN, and you can query any other QHIN's participants under the shared rules of the Common Agreement. TEFCA defines five exchange purposes: Treatment, Payment, Health Care Operations, Public Health, and Individual Access Services (IAS) — the last being a critical pathway for patients to access their own data. In August 2024, Carequality — one of the largest existing interoperability frameworks in the country — announced alignment with TEFCA, signaling a broad industry convergence around this infrastructure.

body.content: A patient is admitted to a Vermont hospital after a car accident. The treating physician needs medication history from the patient's primary care practice in Florida. Under TEFCA: (1) The hospital's EHR, as a participant in a Vermont-based QHIN, sends a Treatment-purpose query to the TEFCA network. (2) The TEFCA infrastructure routes the query to any QHIN whose participants include the Florida practice. (3) The Florida QHIN returns the patient's medication list, problem list, and allergy information in FHIR R4 format. (4) The Vermont EHR displays the results — no phone calls, no fax, no bilateral agreement required. The entire exchange occurs under the legal and technical governance of the Common Agreement.

children.text: Real-World Impact and What Remains Unfinished

Since the information blocking prohibition took effect in April 2021 and the FHIR API certification deadlines began hitting in late 2022, measurable change has occurred in the health IT landscape. Patient access to health data through third-party apps has expanded dramatically. ONC's 2023 data showed that just 5% of certified EHR products — in market penetration terms — had satisfied the full Cures Update API criteria, yet those 5% supported approximately 66% of inpatient users and 77% of ambulatory users nationwide, because the criterion was adopted by the dominant market players early. More than 250 certified products now support the Bulk Data Access API. Payers subject to CMS-9115-F have stood up Patient Access APIs, giving millions of Medicaid and marketplace enrollees machine-readable access to their claims and clinical data for the first time.

Despite this progress, significant gaps persist. First, provider directory accuracy remains a chronic problem. CMS required payers to publish Provider Directory APIs, but the underlying data in those directories — which provider is in network, what their practice address is, what specialties they offer — is notoriously inaccurate. Studies have found error rates exceeding 50% in payer directories, undermining the value of the API mandate. Second, consent portability is largely unsolved. TEFCA's Common Agreement governs what QHINs can share with one another, but patient consent preferences expressed in one system — say, a request not to share behavioral health records — are not reliably honored when records travel across TEFCA or between EHR systems. Third, data quality and completeness vary widely. A FHIR API can return a medication list that is months out of date, or clinical notes that were never coded into structured data. The Cures Act mandated access to data, not the accuracy or completeness of that data.

Ongoing rulemaking is attempting to address some of these gaps. ONC's Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability (HTI-1) final rule, published in December 2023, codified TEFCA requirements and expanded USCDI to v3. A subsequent HTI-2 rulemaking proposed additional standards and strengthened API transparency requirements. HHS also proposed new provider disincentive rules for information blocking by health care providers — a separate track from OIG enforcement — which would allow CMS to exclude information-blocking providers from meaningful use incentive programs or Medicare payment bonuses. The cumulative effect of these rules, if fully implemented, would represent the most comprehensive federal interoperability infrastructure the United States has ever had. Whether it will deliver seamless, patient-centered health data exchange in practice remains an open question.

body.message: A common misconception is that FHIR API mandates override HIPAA privacy rules. They do not. HIPAA governs what information covered entities must protect; the Cures Act governs practices that unreasonably block access. When a patient authorizes a third-party app to receive their records through a FHIR API, the provider is permitted to share those records despite HIPAA — but HIPAA still applies to how the receiving app handles that data if it is a covered entity or business associate. The two frameworks intersect but do not cancel each other.
body.title: HIPAA still governs privacy — FHIR does not override it

points: The 21st Century Cures Act was signed December 13, 2016; its core interoperability and information blocking rules were published May 1, 2020, in two simultaneous final rules from ONC (85 FR 25642) and CMS (CMS-9115-F).
Title IV, Section 4004 prohibits information blocking — practices that knowingly and unreasonably impede EHI access — by three actor types: health IT developers, HIEs/HINs, and health care providers.

ONC established eight exceptions to the information blocking prohibition (preventing harm, privacy, security, infeasibility, health IT performance, content and manner, fees, licensing); meeting an exception means a practice is not information blocking.
Both ONC and CMS mandated HL7 FHIR Release 4 as the required API standard: ONC for certified EHRs, CMS for Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace payer Patient Access APIs.

TEFCA — directed by Section 4003 — is a voluntary nationwide framework connecting Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) under a Common Agreement; eight QHINs were designated by early 2024, enabling query-based exchange at national scale.

OIG's civil monetary penalty rule took effect September 1, 2023, allowing fines up to $1 million per information blocking violation for non-provider actors; provider disincentives are a separate HHS track.

Significant gaps remain: provider directory inaccuracy, lack of cross-system consent portability, and variable data quality undermine the promise of FHIR-enabled access even where APIs are technically compliant.

Ongoing rulemakings — including HTI-1 (Dec 2023), the CMS Prior Authorization Rule (Jan 2024), and proposed provider disincentives — are layering additional requirements on top of the original 2020 rules.

body.explanation: The Cures Act's information blocking prohibition applies to three categories of actors: health IT developers of certified health IT, health information exchanges and networks, and health care providers. Individual patients are the intended beneficiaries of the law, not regulated actors subject to its prohibitions. Patients exercising their right to access their own records — including through third-party apps authorized via FHIR APIs — are explicitly protected by, not constrained by, the information blocking framework.

children.text: Who Owns Health Data? The Legal Reality

One of the most persistent misconceptions in American health care is that patients "own" their medical records. The intuition is understandable — the information is about the patient, generated in service of the patient, and feels intensely personal. Yet federal law does not grant patients ownership of the documents or data in their medical record. What HIPAA actually confers is a right of access — the right to inspect and obtain copies of protected health information held in a covered entity's "designated record set." The covered entity — the hospital, physician practice, or health plan — retains custody and legal control of the originals. This distinction between access rights and ownership rights has profound consequences for every downstream governance question about who can use, sell, or delete health data.

State law adds another layer of complexity. Medical records statutes vary considerably across jurisdictions. Some states grant patients a stronger right to compel disclosure, set shorter response deadlines, or cap the fees providers may charge for copies. A handful of states have begun experimenting with broader patient rights language, but none has fully codified patient ownership in the property-law sense. Meanwhile, EHR vendor contracts routinely include clauses that assert the vendor's right to de-identify and aggregate data from the platform for product improvement, benchmarking, or sale — rights that providers often unknowingly sign away during procurement negotiations. The practical result is a three-way tension among the patient's access interests, the covered entity's custody rights, and the technology vendor's contractual data claims.

The HIPAA Privacy Rule's right of access has been actively enforced. HHS Office for Civil Rights ran a dedicated Right of Access Initiative beginning in 2019, resolving dozens of cases against covered entities that delayed, denied, or overcharged patients seeking their own records. Penalties ranged from thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars. The message was clear: while patients may not "own" their data in a legal sense, covered entities are obligated to make it swiftly and affordably available. The confusion between access and ownership persists because in practical terms the distinction rarely matters to a patient who simply wants their lab results — but it matters enormously to anyone designing governance policy, setting data licensing terms, or building a secondary-use research program.

body.message: HIPAA gives patients the right to obtain copies of their health records, but the covered entity retains legal custody. Patients cannot unilaterally delete their records from a provider's system or prevent a provider from retaining the data for legally required periods.
body.title: Access Right ≠ Ownership

children.text: Data Stewardship Roles and Frameworks

Governance frameworks clarify accountability by separating three related but distinct roles: the data owner, the data steward, and the data custodian. These roles, codified in the DAMA International Data Management Body of Knowledge (DAMA-DMBOK), now in its second edition with a third edition under active community development begun in 2025, provide a globally recognized vocabulary for assigning responsibility without conflating technical capability with policy authority. In healthcare, where the stakes of data misuse include regulatory penalties, patient harm, and reputational damage, clearly delineated roles are not administrative overhead — they are a patient safety mechanism.

The data owner is typically a senior executive or department head who bears ultimate accountability for a specific data asset — for example, the Chief Medical Officer who owns the clinical data domain, or the CFO who owns the revenue cycle dataset. The data owner defines the strategic policy: who may access the data, under what conditions, for what purposes, and with what retention schedule. The data steward is the operational role, often filled by a health information manager or clinical informaticist, who translates those policies into day-to-day practice — reviewing data quality exceptions, resolving identity-matching disputes, and serving as the business contact when a downstream team needs access. The data custodian is the technical role, typically an IT professional responsible for the infrastructure that stores, moves, and secures the data — managing encryption, backup schedules, access logs, and disaster recovery. None of these three roles is interchangeable; collapsing them into one person or one title is a governance anti-pattern that healthcare organizations frequently pay for during audits or breaches.

The American Health Information Management Association (AHIMA) published its Information Governance Principles for Healthcare (IGPHC) framework, organizing health information governance around eight principles: accountability, transparency, integrity, protection, compliance, availability, retention, and disposition. These principles apply not just to the EHR but to every information asset in the enterprise — claims data, scheduling systems, research databases, and even the informal data shadows created in spreadsheets and email attachments. AHIMA's emphasis on organization-wide scope was deliberate: data governance failures often occur precisely in the "shadow IT" spaces that formal governance programs ignore.

children.text: Organizational Data Governance Programs

Translating governance frameworks into organizational reality requires structures that span clinical, operational, and technical domains. Most mature health systems establish a Data Governance Council — a cross-functional body with representation from clinical informatics, health information management, IT security, compliance, finance, and increasingly, patient experience teams. The council's charter defines its decision rights: which decisions require council approval (data sharing agreements, secondary-use policies), which can be delegated to domain stewards (data dictionary updates, access request approvals), and which are escalated to the executive team (breach response, vendor data-rights disputes). Without a formal charter, governance councils tend to become advisory bodies with no enforcement power — capable of producing policies that nobody follows.

Two foundational capabilities underpin any serious governance program: the data dictionary and master data management (MDM). A data dictionary is a centralized catalog that defines every data element in the enterprise — its name, definition, permitted values, source system, owner, and data classification. Without a data dictionary, different departments routinely use the same term to mean different things ("admission date" in the EHR versus "admission date" in the financial system are often calculated differently), generating inconsistencies that corrupt analytics and reports. Master data management addresses the complementary problem of patient identity integrity — ensuring that John H. Smith born 3/4/1962 in the EHR is correctly recognized as the same person as John Harold Smith born 3/4/1962 in the claims system. Poor patient matching generates duplicate records, which can lead to clinicians treating the wrong patient's history.

Patient identity integrity is not merely an operational inconvenience — it is a clinical safety issue. Duplicate or overlaid medical records are classified as a type of healthcare-acquired patient safety event. Health systems with mature governance programs invest in probabilistic matching algorithms, regular duplicate detection runs, and clear escalation paths when a potential overlay is discovered. Governance programs also extend to the contract review process: before a new technology vendor is onboarded, governance policies should require a review of data-rights clauses to ensure the organization is not inadvertently granting the vendor rights to patient data that exceed the minimum necessary standard or conflict with the organization's own data use agreements.

children.text: TEFCA and National Governance Infrastructure

Individual health system governance programs, however mature, cannot solve the governance problem at the national scale. Health data routinely crosses organizational and state boundaries as patients seek care from multiple providers, insurers process claims, and public health agencies monitor disease trends. The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) is the federal government's framework for governing nationwide health information exchange. Authorized under the 21st Century Cures Act, TEFCA establishes a set of common policies, technical requirements, and legal obligations that all participants in the network must follow as a condition of participation. The Common Agreement, now at Version 2.1 (published November 2024, updated January 17, 2025), is the legally binding document that governs relationships among the Recognized Coordinating Entity, Qualified Health Information Networks, and their downstream participants.

The Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE) role is the linchpin of TEFCA's governance structure. ONC selected The Sequoia Project, a non-profit public-private collaborative, as the RCE in 2019 following a competitive process. In August 2023, ONC renewed The Sequoia Project's contract for a further five years, confirming its ongoing role in developing, implementing, and maintaining the Common Agreement and the QHIN Technical Framework. The Sequoia Project works with ONC's Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy (ASTP) to update governance documents, onboard new QHINs, and operate the RCE Directory Service that allows QHINs to locate and route messages to other participants in the network. This governance structure — a federal agency setting overall policy while a private non-profit manages operational implementation — is intentionally designed to balance government accountability with the flexibility of private-sector execution.

Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) are the operational nodes of the TEFCA network. They must meet rigorous technical and governance standards, complete a formal onboarding and designation process overseen by the RCE, and sign the Common Agreement before they can exchange data under TEFCA. As of late 2025, eleven QHINs had been designated, including CommonWell Health Alliance, eHealth Exchange, Epic's Carequality network, Kno2, MedAllies, eClinicalWorks (designated January 2025), Surescripts Health Information Network (designated April 2025), and Oracle Health (designated November 2025). TEFCA exchange is constrained to lawful purposes defined in the Common Agreement — individual treatment, payment, health care operations, public health, benefits determination, and a small set of other permitted purposes. Using the network for marketing, selling data, or other non-enumerated purposes is a material violation of the Common Agreement.

body.content: Every TEFCA query must be tagged with one of the defined Exchange Purposes. A clinician looking up a patient's medication history uses XP: Treatment. A health plan verifying a claim uses XP: Payment. A state health department tracking influenza cases uses XP: Public Health. This tagging requirement is not bureaucratic overhead — it is the governance mechanism that limits data use to the purpose for which the exchange was authorized, and it creates an audit trail that the RCE and ONC can use to detect misuse.

children.text: Patient Data Rights: Access, Correction, and Portability

The patient data rights landscape has expanded significantly since the original HIPAA Privacy Rule took effect in 2003. The ONC's 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (effective April 2021, with full scope expanded October 2022) codified the information blocking prohibition, making it unlawful for healthcare providers, health IT developers, and health information networks to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information except under specific enumerated exceptions. As of October 6, 2022, the information that must not be blocked encompasses all electronic protected health information in the designated record set — not just a limited subset of structured data. Enforcement includes civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation for health IT developers and networks, with CMS-administered disincentives for providers (effective July 31, 2024) such as reduced payment adjustments under the Merit-based Incentive Payment System.

State legislatures have moved to fill gaps that federal law leaves unaddressed, particularly for consumer health data held by non-HIPAA entities — fitness apps, period trackers, direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies, and wellness platforms. Washington State's My Health MY Data Act (HB 1155), signed by Governor Jay Inslee on April 27, 2023, was the first U.S. law to specifically regulate consumer health data outside HIPAA's scope. The Act requires regulated entities to obtain consumer consent before collecting or sharing consumer health data, prohibits geofencing around healthcare facilities, grants consumers the right to delete their health data, and — critically — includes a private right of action allowing individuals to sue for violations. Geofencing prohibitions took effect July 23, 2023; full compliance obligations for large entities began March 31, 2024.

The Federal Trade Commission has pursued parallel authority over non-HIPAA health data through the Health Breach Notification Rule (HBNR). In April 2024, the FTC finalized significant amendments to the HBNR (effective July 29, 2024) that expanded the rule's scope to clearly cover health apps and connected devices, even those that do not interact with a HIPAA-covered entity. The revised rule defines "breach of security" to include unauthorized disclosures — not just hacking events — and requires covered entities to notify the FTC simultaneously with individual notifications for breaches affecting 500 or more people, within 60 days of discovering the breach. Taken together with Washington's My Health MY Data Act and similar state laws under development in other jurisdictions, the regulatory landscape for consumer health data is rapidly converging toward a HIPAA-like accountability regime for previously unregulated actors.

body.message: Apps and platforms that collect health data but do not qualify as HIPAA covered entities or business associates are no longer in a regulatory vacuum. The FTC HBNR amendments and state laws like Washington's My Health MY Data Act impose real obligations and enforcement risk. Organizations in this space should conduct a data mapping exercise and review their consent, sharing, and breach notification practices against both federal and applicable state requirements.

children.text: What Are FHIR Implementation Guides?

FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is often called "the language of modern healthcare data," but a language alone is not enough. Two systems can both speak FHIR and still be unable to exchange data usefully if they use different resource structures, terminology codes, or workflow expectations. This is where Implementation Guides — IGs — come in. An IG is a formal, published specification that narrows the broad flexibility of FHIR into precise, agreed-upon rules for a specific use case. It defines which resources must be supported, which data fields are required versus optional, which code systems to use, and how the API calls should flow between systems.

HL7 International publishes FHIR IGs through a rigorous multi-stage process. A project team drafts the IG, submits it for community ballot as a "Standard for Trial Use" (STU), receives and reconciles hundreds of public comments from implementers, vendors, and regulators, and then publishes a revised version that reflects real-world feedback. Only after sustained, demonstrated implementation does a specification mature toward Normative status. This process ensures that IGs are not just theoretical documents — they are living standards shaped by the engineers, clinicians, and payers who actually build and operate systems against them.

Two HL7 FHIR Accelerator programs have produced the most influential IGs in the payer-provider space: the Da Vinci Project and the Gravity Project. An Accelerator is a structured program inside HL7 that brings together industry stakeholders to build and test IGs faster than the traditional standards process alone allows. Each Accelerator has a specific domain focus, a governing structure, and a commitment to testing in real pilots before declaring work complete.

body.analogy: Think of FHIR as the English language and an Implementation Guide as a legal contract written in English. Both parties understand the words, but the contract specifies exactly which terms mean what, what must be delivered by when, and what happens when something goes wrong. Without the contract, two fluent English speakers can still talk past each other.
body.concept: FHIR is flexible by design; IGs add the constraints that make interoperability precise and reliable.

children.text: The Da Vinci Project was founded in 2019 as an HL7 FHIR Accelerator with a specific mandate: accelerate FHIR adoption in value-based care by solving the most painful payer-provider data exchange problems. The project started with twenty-two founding member organizations and has grown to more than sixty industry-leading payers, providers, and health IT vendors. Its work is organized into use cases — discrete problem statements — each of which produces its own Implementation Guide and reference implementation. CMS's prior authorization interoperability mandates, finalized in the 2024 CMS-0057-F rule, cite Da Vinci IGs directly as the required technical standards.

The Gravity Project has a different origin and a different focus. It was initiated in November 2018 by the Social Interventions Research and Evaluation Network (SIREN) at the University of California, San Francisco, in collaboration with EMI Advisors LLC of Bethesda, Maryland. With initial funding from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, SIREN launched Gravity in 2019 as a national collaborative effort to develop structured data standards for social determinants of health (SDOH). Where Da Vinci attacks billing and authorization friction, Gravity attacks a different gap: the absence of standardized, machine-readable codes for the social conditions — food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers — that drive as much as 80 percent of health outcomes but are almost never documented in a form that clinical systems can act on.

children.text: Key Da Vinci IGs: PDex, PAS, CRD, and DTR

Da Vinci has published more than a dozen Implementation Guides. Four have become the centerpiece of federal interoperability mandates and real-world payer-provider integrations: the Payer Data Exchange IG (PDex), the Prior Authorization Support IG (PAS), the Coverage Requirements Discovery IG (CRD), and the Documentation Templates and Rules IG (DTR). Together these four IGs address the most administratively burdensome touchpoints in the American healthcare system: sharing a patient's longitudinal record when they switch payers, submitting and adjudicating prior authorization requests in near real-time, and ensuring that providers surface payer coverage rules inside their own EHR workflow before ordering a service.

The Payer Data Exchange IG (PDex), currently at version 2.1.0 (STU2.1) with version 2.2.0 in continuous development, defines the FHIR API surface that enables two critical data flows. First, payer-to-payer exchange: when a patient changes health plans, the new payer can call the old payer's PDex API to retrieve the patient's complete clinical history as FHIR resources conforming to US Core profiles. Second, payer-to-provider exchange: providers can call a payer's PDex endpoint to retrieve administrative and claims-derived clinical data about a patient, eliminating fax-based information requests. PDex has been updated to align with both US Core 6.1.0 and 7.0.0, enabling compliance with both CMS-0057-F and the ONC HTI-1 rule simultaneously.

The Prior Authorization Support IG (PAS), at version 2.1.0, defines a FHIR-based API workflow that replaces traditional X12 278 prior authorization transactions. Under PAS, a provider's EHR submits a FHIR Claim resource — bundled with all required supporting documentation — to the payer's PAS endpoint. The payer's system evaluates the request, potentially in real-time using clinical decision support, and returns a ClaimResponse resource. The entire round-trip can happen in seconds for straightforward cases, compared to the 72-hour or multi-day waits that characterize traditional PA processes. CMS-0057-F identifies PAS IG version STU 2.0.1 as the normative standard for the Prior Authorization API that covered payers must implement by January 1, 2027.

children.text: Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), currently at version 2.1.0, is the upstream trigger in the Da Vinci burden-reduction workflow. It leverages CDS Hooks — a standard for embedding clinical decision support into EHR workflows — to allow payers to inject coverage information at the exact moment a clinician is making a treatment decision. CRD answers the question "Does this patient's plan require prior authorization for this service?" before the order is finalized, not after. This timing is critical: it is far more efficient to surface a coverage requirement during the ordering workflow than to discover a PA is needed only after a claim is denied.

Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), at version 2.1.0, is the companion to CRD. Where CRD identifies what is required, DTR provides the mechanism for gathering it. DTR uses SMART on FHIR to launch a payer-curated questionnaire application inside the provider's EHR. Using CQL (Clinical Quality Language) logic, the app queries the patient's FHIR records to pre-populate answers wherever the data already exists, surfacing only the truly missing information to the clinician. CMS has established its own Document Requirements Lookup Service (DRLS) — which combines CRD and DTR functionality — specifically for Medicare Fee-for-Service programs, validating the architecture at the federal level.

children.text: Da Vinci in Regulation: How CMS-0057-F Codified These IGs into Law

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule — formally CMS-0057-F — was published in January 2024 and represents the most consequential federal interoperability mandate since the 2020 CMS and ONC interoperability rules. The rule applies to Medicare Advantage organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plan issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges. Collectively, these plans cover the majority of Americans with government-sponsored or exchange-based coverage.

CMS-0057-F establishes a two-phase compliance timeline. The first phase took effect January 1, 2026: covered payers must now respond to standard prior authorization requests within 7 calendar days and to expedited requests within 72 hours; they must include specific, structured reasons for any denial; and they must begin publicly reporting prior authorization metrics, with the first annual reports due March 31, 2026 covering calendar year 2025 data. These provisions are not FHIR-specific — they are operational requirements that any payer must meet regardless of their technology approach. However, they create enormous pressure for automation, because manual PA processes cannot reliably meet 72-hour response windows at scale.

The second phase — and the one that directly references Da Vinci IGs — takes effect January 1, 2027. By that date, covered payers must have four FHIR-based APIs live and in production: a Patient Access API (based on PDex), a Provider Access API (also based on PDex), a Payer-to-Payer API (PDex again), and a Prior Authorization API based on Da Vinci PAS IG version STU 2.0.1. This is a landmark moment in U.S. healthcare standards history: for the first time, a specific named private-sector Implementation Guide — developed by a multi-stakeholder coalition, not a government body — is cited by name in a federal rule as a required technical standard. The Da Vinci Project's architecture has, in effect, become federal infrastructure.

CMS-0057-F requires covered payers to implement the Da Vinci PAS IG (STU 2.0.1) as the technical standard for their Prior Authorization API by January 1, 2027 — making Da Vinci specifications enforceable federal requirements for Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and exchange plans.

The compliance landscape is challenging. Survey data from WEDI (Workgroup for Electronic Data Interchange) from late 2025 found that many payers were still in early stages of implementation for the Prior Authorization API specifically, with readiness varying widely across plan types and sizes. Smaller plans and state Medicaid agencies face particularly steep technical lift, as they may lack the internal engineering capacity to build FHIR API infrastructure from scratch. This has driven a cottage industry of FHIR platform vendors offering turnkey compliance solutions built on top of the Da Vinci specifications.

The regulation also reflects a broader policy strategy: rather than CMS building and mandating its own proprietary technology, the agency is leveraging privately developed, community-consensus standards that have already been tested in real implementations. This approach reduces the risk of government-mandated technology failures and creates a market-driven path to adoption — payers who implement Da Vinci IGs well will have a competitive compliance advantage, which accelerates the overall ecosystem. In mid-2025, more than fifty major health insurers voluntarily committed to targeting at least 80 percent real-time electronic prior authorization approval rates by 2027, reflecting the industry's recognition that FHIR-based PA is not just a regulatory requirement but a genuine operational efficiency driver.

body.content: Regence BlueCross BlueShield and MultiCare Connected Care became early proof that Da Vinci's architecture works at production scale. They launched what was described as the nation's first scalable FHIR-based prior authorization system using Da Vinci specifications. The results were dramatic: 94 percent of prior authorization inquiries received an immediate response — meaning the request was either approved or determined to require no PA at all — within seconds of submission. Clinicians at MultiCare could make requests directly from within their EHR, and the authorization decision flowed back into the same workflow without phone calls or faxes. At HIMSS 2025, MultiCare's Anna Taylor and Regence's Heidi Kriz presented this outcome as a benchmark for what standards-based prior authorization can achieve in practice.
body.title: Regence and MultiCare: The Nation's First Scalable FHIR Prior Authorization System

children.text: The Gravity Project: Putting Social Determinants of Health into FHIR

Social determinants of health — the conditions in which people are born, live, learn, work, and age — are estimated to drive 80 percent or more of health outcomes, yet they have historically been invisible to clinical information systems. A clinician might know that a patient's diabetes is poorly controlled, but unless food insecurity is documented in a structured, coded field, the health system has no way to connect that clinical problem to its social cause, refer the patient to a food pantry, or measure whether that referral reduced hospitalizations. The Gravity Project exists specifically to close that gap.

Gravity's approach is rigorous and consensus-driven. For each SDOH domain, a multi-stakeholder work group assembles the evidence base for how that condition should be defined, screened for, and documented. The group then works with SNOMED CT International, Regenstrief Institute (which stewards LOINC), and the ICD-10 Coordination and Maintenance Committee to create or curate the actual codes that represent each concept. This is painstaking work — getting a new concept into SNOMED CT or LOINC can take 12 to 18 months — but it ensures that Gravity's value sets are grounded in internationally recognized, maintained terminology systems rather than local codes that fragment data across organizations.

The Gravity SDOH Clinical Care Implementation Guide, currently at version 2.3.0 (STU 2.3, generated May 2025 and based on FHIR R4), defines FHIR profiles, value sets, and workflows for the full SDOH care cycle: screening a patient for social needs, documenting findings as FHIR Observations and Conditions, creating FHIR ServiceRequests for community referrals, and tracking the status of those referrals through FHIR Tasks. Version 3.0.0 is currently in ballot as of early 2026, with expanded domain coverage and improved alignment with the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI).

children.text: The SDOH domains covered by the Gravity IG span far beyond the two most commonly discussed. Food insecurity and housing instability were the first domains completed — the Gravity Project completed its initial food insecurity and housing data identification work before expanding. The current IG includes value sets and profiles for transportation insecurity, utility insecurity (inability to pay for heat, electricity, or water), educational attainment barriers, employment and financial strain, social isolation, intimate partner violence, and digital access barriers, among others. Each domain has a corresponding set of screening questions (mapped to LOINC panel codes), condition codes (mapped to SNOMED CT and ICD-10), and intervention codes for referrals.

State health systems and Medicaid programs are now formally recognizing Gravity standards. Washington State's 2025 FHIR Infrastructure Roadmap named the Gravity SDOH Clinical Care IG as a core interoperability standard for community and clinical data exchange. New York sought to leverage Gravity standards for exchange of SDOH screenings between clinical systems and community-based organizations like Unite Us and FindHelp, ensuring that FHIR-compliant screenings could be ingested by social care platforms in real-time. Colorado's vendor contracts for its statewide social care platform explicitly require Gravity-aligned terminology and FHIR-based exchange. These state-level mandates are creating the network effects that transform a voluntary standard into a de facto requirement.

body.content: A patient comes in for a diabetes follow-up. The nurse administers the LOINC-coded AHC HRSN screening panel (LOINC panel code 96777-8) inside the EHR. The patient screens positive for food insecurity. The EHR creates a FHIR Observation with LOINC code 88122-7 ("Within the past 12 months, we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more") and a FHIR Condition with SNOMED CT code 733423003 ("Food insecurity"). The care coordinator creates a FHIR ServiceRequest for a food pantry referral, which is transmitted via Task to the community-based organization's FHIR endpoint. When the referral is fulfilled, the CBO updates the Task status, and the EHR receives a structured confirmation — all without a fax machine or a phone call.
