children.text: Implementation Reality: Adoption, Challenges, and What Comes Next

Real-world adoption of both Da Vinci and Gravity IGs is accelerating but uneven. On the Da Vinci side, the Regence-MultiCare prior authorization pilot is no longer an outlier — it is a benchmark. The Da Vinci Trebuchet pilot program organizes multi-organization cohorts to test specific IGs in production environments, with 2026 cohorts already forming. CMS's regulatory deadline of January 1, 2027 for FHIR-based PA APIs is creating real urgency across the industry. Roughly 65 percent of EHR transactions on Epic systems achieved electronic prior authorization by 2025, with ePA transaction volumes nearly doubling from 2023 to early 2025.

The barriers to full PAS IG adoption are real and multi-layered. Technical complexity is one factor — implementing a compliant FHIR Claim submission endpoint that correctly handles all PAS workflow states (pended, approved, denied, modified) requires significant engineering investment. Organizational alignment is another: the PAS workflow requires both the EHR vendor and the payer platform to implement complementary sides of the same API, which means bilateral negotiations that take time. Smaller regional health plans and safety-net providers face resource constraints that make in-house implementation difficult. And despite a January 2027 deadline, WEDI's 2025 surveys found that a meaningful share of covered entities had not yet begun implementation work for the Prior Authorization API specifically.

ONC has provided an important tool to support PAS adoption: the Da Vinci Prior Authorization Support Test Kit, launched on Inferno (the federal FHIR testing platform). This test kit allows implementers to validate their PAS implementations against the IG's conformance requirements before going live, reducing the risk of interoperability failures in production. The existence of an authoritative, publicly available test kit is a meaningful maturity signal — it means the IG has progressed from specification to executable, testable infrastructure.

body.message: CMS-0057-F's January 1, 2027 API implementation deadline applies to Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, CHIP managed care, and exchange plans. Plans that fail to meet requirements face potential compliance action. The prior authorization operational requirements (72-hour expedited, 7-day standard response) already took effect January 1, 2026. Organizations that have not begun their Da Vinci PAS implementation should treat this as an urgent priority, not a future concern.
body.title: The 2027 Deadline Is Not a Soft Target

children.text: On the Gravity side, the implementation picture is more heterogeneous. Major EHR platforms including Epic have built SDOH screening and documentation modules that align with Gravity value sets, making it easier for health systems to capture structured SDOH data. But the harder problem — closing the referral loop with community-based organizations — remains a work in progress. CBOs typically lack the technical capacity to build FHIR endpoints, so interoperability between clinical systems and the social care sector depends on intermediary platforms like Unite Us, FindHelp, and Aunt Bertha that can translate between FHIR and the APIs those organizations actually use. States like New York and Colorado are addressing this through explicit vendor contract requirements, creating the contractual obligation that drives technical investment.

Looking ahead, both projects have substantial roadmaps. Da Vinci is expanding into clinical data exchange between providers and payers for value-based care performance measurement, and is developing IGs for attachments — the structured clinical documents that support claims adjudication. Gravity is developing version 3.0 of its SDOH Clinical Care IG with expanded domain coverage and is pursuing deeper integration with the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) — the federally required minimum dataset for EHR certification. As SDOH data elements enter USCDI and EHR certification criteria, Gravity's approach shifts from voluntary best practice to the floor that every certified EHR must support. That normative shift, once complete, will make structured social needs documentation as routine as recording a blood pressure.

children.text: Why De-identification Matters

Every time a patient visits a clinic, fills a prescription, or receives a laboratory result, that encounter generates data — and that data contains some of the most sensitive details a person can share about themselves. The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) defines Protected Health Information, or PHI, as any individually identifiable health information that is created, received, maintained, or transmitted by a covered entity or its business associates. The scope is deliberately broad: PHI covers information in any format, whether electronic, paper, or spoken, if it relates to a person's physical or mental health, the provision of care, or payment for that care.

The tension in modern healthcare data is acute. On one side, patients have a legitimate expectation that the intimate details of their medical histories will not flow freely through the world. On the other side, researchers, public-health officials, health systems, and software developers need large, representative datasets to answer important questions — how does a new treatment perform across different demographic groups? What risk factors predict hospital readmission? How can an EHR be tested without exposing real records? De-identification is the legal and technical bridge that allows health data to move across this tension without dissolving the privacy protection that patients deserve.

The regulatory stakes have also increased sharply. The 21st Century Cures Act and the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Rule have accelerated data sharing mandates across payers, providers, and health information networks. As more data flows through APIs and exchanges, the volume of PHI potentially exposed to secondary use has grown exponentially. Getting de-identification right is no longer a compliance checkbox — it is a foundational requirement for operating responsibly in a connected health system.

children.text: HIPAA's Two De-identification Methods

HIPAA's Privacy Rule, codified at 45 CFR § 164.514(b), provides two legally recognized pathways for de-identifying health information. Once either pathway is satisfied, the resulting data is no longer considered PHI and is no longer subject to HIPAA's use and disclosure restrictions. Choosing the right pathway depends on the resources available, the level of statistical rigor required, and the downstream use of the data.

The first and most commonly used method is Safe Harbor. Under Safe Harbor, a covered entity must remove all 18 categories of direct identifiers specified in the regulation: (1) names; (2) geographic subdivisions smaller than a state, including street address, city, county, precinct, and ZIP codes, with a narrow exception for three-digit ZIP codes serving populations greater than 20,000; (3) all date elements other than year that are directly related to an individual, plus ages over 89 which must be aggregated into a single "90+" category; (4) telephone numbers; (5) fax numbers; (6) email addresses; (7) Social Security numbers; (8) medical record numbers; (9) health plan beneficiary numbers; (10) account numbers; (11) certificate and license numbers; (12) vehicle identifiers and serial numbers including license plates; (13) device identifiers and serial numbers; (14) web URLs; (15) IP addresses; (16) biometric identifiers including fingerprints and voice prints; (17) full-face photographs and comparable images; and (18) any other unique identifying number, characteristic, or code. The entity must also have no actual knowledge that the remaining information could identify an individual. Safe Harbor is rules-based and requires no special statistical expertise, making it widely accessible.

The second method is Expert Determination. Here, a qualified statistician or other expert applies generally accepted principles of statistical and scientific methods to analyze the data and concludes that the risk of identifying any individual is very small. The regulation does not define "very small" numerically, leaving this to professional judgment. The expert must document their methods and findings so that the covered entity can justify the conclusion if challenged. Expert Determination is more flexible than Safe Harbor — it can retain ZIP codes or date elements that Safe Harbor would require removing — but it demands rigor, resources, and defensible documentation. Most large academic medical centers and research consortia rely on Expert Determination when they need richer geographic or temporal granularity in their datasets.

children.text: Re-identification Risks: The Limits of De-identification

De-identification is a risk-reduction strategy, not a guarantee of permanent anonymity. This distinction matters enormously, and a series of landmark empirical studies has demonstrated just how porous the anonymity of seemingly de-identified data can be when an adversary has access to even modest amounts of auxiliary information.

The most cited demonstration came from computer scientist Latanya Sweeney in 1997. The state of Massachusetts had released medical encounter data for approximately 135,000 state employees with obvious identifiers — names, addresses, and Social Security numbers — removed. Sweeney obtained the publicly available Cambridge, Massachusetts voter registration list, which contained name, address, date of birth, sex, and ZIP code for each voter. By linking the two datasets on the combination of five-digit ZIP code, date of birth, and sex, she was able to uniquely identify the medical records of then-Governor William Weld — demonstrating that the combination of these three "non-identifying" fields was sufficient to pinpoint an individual. Her subsequent analysis of the 1990 U.S. Census showed that 87 percent of the American population could be uniquely identified by ZIP code, date of birth, and sex alone. This trio of fields, none of which appears on HIPAA's Safe Harbor list except for detailed dates, illustrates the concept of quasi-identifiers: attributes that are individually innocuous but collectively identifying.

A decade later, in 2008, Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov of the University of Texas at Austin published "Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets," applying their methodology to the Netflix Prize dataset — a collection of 100 million movie ratings submitted by approximately 500,000 anonymous subscribers that Netflix released for a machine-learning competition. Narayanan and Shmatikov showed that by knowing just a few of a subscriber's movie ratings and approximate dates, an adversary could cross-reference the Netflix data with publicly available Internet Movie Database (IMDb) reviews to uniquely identify that subscriber's record with high confidence. The attack worked even when the adversary had imprecise or partial knowledge, and it succeeded even when some ratings were deliberately perturbed as a privacy defense. The Netflix study crystallized a broader principle: sparse, high-dimensional data is extraordinarily difficult to anonymize because each data point narrows down the set of plausible individuals so rapidly.

body.analogy: Imagine you are given a jigsaw puzzle with most pieces removed, but you can still recognize the full picture. De-identified data is like a puzzle with the corner pieces removed — it looks incomplete, but someone with a second puzzle box (auxiliary data) can fill in just enough to reconstruct the original image.
body.concept: Re-identification works by combining a de-identified dataset with auxiliary external data — each additional piece narrows the field of candidates until a single individual is identified.

body.message: DNA sequences present a categorical re-identification risk that goes beyond quasi-identifiers. Even a partial genome can be matched against public genealogical databases (such as GEDmatch) to identify an individual or their relatives. The HIPAA Safe Harbor rule requires removing "biometric identifiers" but does not explicitly enumerate genomic sequences, creating an interpretive gap. Any organization sharing genomic data should treat it as permanently identifiable regardless of accompanying metadata removal.
body.title: Genomic Data Cannot Be Truly De-identified

body.content: k-anonymity, introduced by Sweeney in 1998, is a formal privacy model that requires every record in a dataset to be indistinguishable from at least k-1 other records with respect to all quasi-identifier fields. A dataset with k=5 guarantees that any re-identification attempt narrows the adversary's target to a pool of at least five people. Higher k values offer stronger protection but reduce analytical utility because they require more generalization (e.g., replacing exact age with an age range). Extensions such as l-diversity and t-closeness address additional attack vectors where k-anonymity alone is insufficient, such as when all records in a k-anonymous group share a sensitive attribute value.
body.title: The k-Anonymity Framework

children.text: Synthetic Data: A Different Privacy Approach

Where de-identification tries to protect real patients by removing or generalizing information that could identify them, synthetic data takes an entirely different approach: it generates entirely fictional records that statistically resemble a real population without corresponding to any actual individual. If no real person's data is present in the dataset, there is no real person to re-identify. This philosophical shift — from "hide the individual" to "replace the individual" — makes synthetic data an increasingly attractive option for certain use cases.

There are two broad families of synthetic data generation. Statistical synthesis methods model the marginal and joint distributions of variables in a real dataset and then draw new records from those distributions. These approaches, which include techniques such as multiple imputation and Gaussian copulas, can preserve complex correlations between variables such as the relationship between age, diagnosis codes, and medication lists. Generative model approaches use machine learning — particularly generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders — to learn the underlying structure of a dataset and generate new samples that are statistically realistic but do not directly copy any training record. Generative models are more powerful but also more difficult to validate and more susceptible to memorization attacks, in which the model effectively reproduces a real training record.

The most widely used open-source synthetic patient generator in health IT is Synthea, developed by MITRE Corporation. Synthea simulates the entire medical history of synthetic patients from birth to death using probabilistic disease models, clinical guidelines, and demographic data drawn from public sources. It generates output in standard formats including HL7 FHIR and C-CDA, and MITRE has made one million synthetic patient records freely available for download. Synthea has been adopted across health IT development, FHIR API testing, clinical decision support validation, machine learning model training, and healthcare education — any context where a realistic but risk-free patient dataset is needed. Because Synthea records are built from models rather than real encounters, they carry no HIPAA obligations and require no IRB approval for use.

body.message: Synthetic data, however realistic, reflects the model used to generate it — not ground truth. Statistical associations that were not captured in the generation model will be absent from the synthetic dataset. Rare events and edge cases are often underrepresented. For regulatory submissions, clinical trial analysis, or population health surveillance that requires legally defensible results from real-world evidence, synthetic data is a supplement, not a replacement, for appropriately governed access to real patient records.

children.text: Governance Framework: When to Use What

Selecting the right privacy-preserving approach requires matching technical options to regulatory context, research purpose, and organizational risk tolerance. HIPAA provides a tiered framework for research data use that maps roughly to increasing levels of identifiability — and increasing governance requirements.

Fully de-identified data, produced by either the Safe Harbor or Expert Determination method, falls outside HIPAA entirely. Organizations can share, publish, or sell de-identified data without patient authorization, data use agreements, or IRB oversight under HIPAA (though state law and institutional policy may impose additional requirements). This is why de-identification is so valuable for large-scale data sharing initiatives: once data crosses the de-identification threshold, the regulatory friction drops substantially. However, as the re-identification literature demonstrates, fully de-identified data still carries residual risk — particularly when the data is rich in quasi-identifiers or when it will be merged with other datasets.

Between identified data and fully de-identified data sits the Limited Data Set, defined at 45 CFR § 164.514(e). A Limited Data Set retains certain geographic and date elements — city, state, ZIP code, and dates of admission, discharge, service, birth, and death — that Safe Harbor would require removing. Because a Limited Data Set still contains PHI, it must be protected: any disclosure requires a Data Use Agreement (DUA) executed between the covered entity and the recipient. The DUA must specify permitted uses and disclosures (limited to research, public health, and health care operations), identify who may access the data, require the recipient to implement appropriate safeguards, prohibit re-identification, and obligate reporting of any unauthorized use or disclosure. Limited Data Sets are a practical middle ground for research that needs geographic precision or temporal patterns but does not require full patient-level identification.

For research that requires identified data — full medical record numbers, individual diagnoses, and linked longitudinal records — covered entities must obtain patient authorization or qualify for an IRB waiver of authorization under 45 CFR § 46.116. The IRB evaluates whether the research could practicably be conducted without the waiver, whether it poses minimal risk, and whether it includes adequate privacy safeguards. In practice, large health systems and academic medical centers maintain dedicated data governance committees that evaluate data requests, classify the appropriate tier, and require data use agreements or IRB documentation before any data leaves the institution.

An emerging alternative to any form of data sharing is federated learning — a machine-learning paradigm in which model training occurs locally at each data-holding institution, and only model updates (gradients or parameters) are shared across sites rather than the underlying patient data itself. Programs such as the PCORnet national patient-centered clinical research network and the NIH's National COVID Cohort Collaborative (N3C) have pioneered federated and enclave-based approaches that allow multi-institutional analyses without requiring any institution to export its raw patient records. These architectures fundamentally reframe the privacy problem: instead of asking "how do we safely share data?", they ask "how do we bring computation to the data?"

children.text: Governance Rule of Thumb: Match the data tier to the analytical need. If ZIP code precision is not required for the research question, use Safe Harbor de-identification and eliminate the DUA burden. If it is required, use a Limited Data Set with a DUA. children.text: The Burden Problem: Physicians Spend More Time on EHRs Than on Patients

When the electronic health record was introduced into American medicine, it arrived with a promise: replace error-prone paper charts with a searchable, shareable digital record that would improve care quality and save time. Decades later, the promise has been only partially kept. The digital record exists — but the time savings never arrived. Instead, a mountain of peer-reviewed evidence now documents one of the most consequential unintended consequences in modern medicine: physicians routinely spend more hours each day interacting with their EHR than they spend in face-to-face contact with patients. This is not hyperbole — it is a measurable, replicated finding that is reshaping how health systems think about clinician well-being and workforce sustainability.

A landmark time-motion study by Sinsky and colleagues, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that for every hour physicians spent in direct clinical face time with patients, they spent nearly two additional hours on EHR and desk work. Subsequent research has only deepened this picture. A 2024 study published in the Annals of Family Medicine found that for every 8 hours of scheduled patient visits, primary care physicians logged 5.3 additional hours in the EHR — 2.1 of those hours devoted exclusively to clinical documentation. Overall, physicians today report spending roughly 13 hours per week on indirect patient care tasks such as order entry, documentation, and referral management, within a 57.8-hour reported workweek. That math leaves precious little time for the human encounter that drew most physicians to medicine in the first place.

What is perhaps most striking is what happens after clinic hours. Researchers coined the term "pajama time" to describe the hours physicians spend in the EHR at home, after their clinical day has technically ended. A study in the Annals of Family Medicine found that primary care physicians spent approximately 86 minutes — nearly an hour and a half — on the EHR after clinic hours every day. Among upper-year family medicine residents, nearly one-third report spending three or more additional hours per day on after-hours EHR work. This chronic overflow of documentation into personal time has been directly linked to burnout, reduced professional satisfaction, and lower examination performance. The AMA's 2024 national burnout survey of nearly 18,000 physicians across 43 states found that 43.2 percent of physicians reported at least one burnout symptom — and ineffective EHR systems ranked among the most consistently cited sources of occupational stress.

The carpenter is technically productive — paperwork is real work — but the building is going up slower, and the carpenter is exhausted. children.text: Root Causes: Poor Design, Alert Fatigue, and Fragmented Data

Understanding why EHRs consume so much physician time requires looking beneath the surface of the software itself. Most commercial EHR systems were not designed with usability as the primary objective — they were designed to fulfill billing and compliance requirements, and the clinical workflow was often an afterthought. As a result, physicians routinely navigate dozens of screens, click through cascading dropdown menus, and manually enter data that could theoretically be auto-populated if systems communicated with one another. Poor interoperability is at the heart of this problem: when a patient arrives from another health system, their prior lab results, imaging reports, and medication lists frequently do not follow them. The physician or their staff must manually re-enter that information, dramatically extending visit preparation time and increasing the risk of transcription errors.

One of the most pervasive and dangerous documentation behaviors to emerge from EHR design failures is copy-forward documentation — the practice of copying a prior note into the current encounter and editing only minimally. A 2022 analysis of over 100 million EHR notes found that 50.1 percent of all text in clinical notes was duplicated from prior documentation on the same patient. As many as 90 percent of clinicians admit to using copy-and-paste functions in the EHR. While this behavior saves time in the short run, it systematically degrades note quality: outdated medication lists persist, resolved problems remain active, and contradictory information accumulates across encounters. Patient safety researchers at the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality have documented that copy-forward errors contribute directly to diagnostic mistakes and adverse events, including hospitalizations that might have been prevented had the clinical record been accurate.

Alert fatigue is another root cause that compounds the burden of fragmented data. Clinical decision support (CDS) systems embedded in EHRs are designed to catch dangerous drug interactions, flag abnormal values, and remind clinicians of overdue preventive care. In theory, these alerts save lives. In practice, the volume has become overwhelming: some physicians and nurses report receiving between 100 and 200 CDS alerts per day. At Brigham and Women's Hospital — one of the most prestigious academic medical centers in the country — physicians override approximately 98 percent of medication order alerts. Research published in JMIR Medical Informatics found that in one medication-related CDS system, only 7.3 percent of generated alerts were clinically appropriate. When physicians learn that the vast majority of alerts are irrelevant, they begin dismissing them reflexively — a conditioned response that creates exactly the kind of cognitive blind spot the alerts were designed to prevent. The result is a system that adds burden without proportional benefit, eroding trust in the very tools meant to support clinical judgment.

children.text: The Prior Authorization Crisis: When Interoperability Gaps Meet Insurance Bureaucracy

No single administrative burden in American medicine has generated more physician frustration — or caused more direct patient harm — than prior authorization. Prior authorization is the process by which insurers require physicians to obtain approval before prescribing certain medications, ordering specific imaging studies, or proceeding with recommended procedures. In principle, it is a cost-management tool. In practice, it has become a bureaucratic labyrinth that consumes an extraordinary share of physician and staff time. The AMA's 2024 nationwide survey of 1,000 practicing physicians found that practices complete an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, consuming approximately 13 hours of physician and staff time — roughly one and a half business days — every single week. Two in five physician practices employ staff dedicated exclusively to prior authorization tasks.

The connection to EHR interoperability is direct and underappreciated. Prior authorization processes are slow largely because clinical data does not flow automatically between provider EHR systems and insurer systems. Physicians must manually extract clinical information from the EHR, re-enter it into insurer portals or fax it via paper forms, and then wait — sometimes for days — for a decision. If interoperable APIs existed to transmit structured clinical data directly, the information exchange could happen in minutes rather than days. The status quo is expensive in human terms: 94 percent of physicians in the 2024 AMA survey reported that prior authorization contributes to physician burnout. That near-universal figure makes prior authorization one of the most universally agreed-upon sources of professional dissatisfaction in medicine today.

The patient consequences are equally alarming. According to the 2024 AMA survey, 93 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization causes care delays, with more than half saying delays occur "always" or "often." Seventy-eight percent of physicians reported that prior authorization often or sometimes results in patients abandoning a recommended course of treatment entirely — unable or unwilling to wait for approval, they simply go without care. Most seriously, nearly one in four physicians (24 percent) reported that prior authorization has led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care, including hospitalization, permanent impairment, or death. Of those reporting adverse events, 19 percent cited delays leading to hospitalization, 13 percent identified life-threatening events, and 7 percent reported disability, birth defects, or patient death as downstream consequences of authorization delays.

body.content: A primary care physician prescribes a biologic medication for a patient with severe rheumatoid arthritis. The insurer requires prior authorization. The physician's staff submits a paper form. Nine days pass. The insurer requests additional clinical documentation. The staff re-submits. Five more days pass. The patient, unable to manage pain and unable to take time off work for repeated calls to the insurer, abandons the prescription and returns to lower-efficacy over-the-counter options. Three months later, the patient presents to the emergency department with advanced joint damage. The total cost of the ED visit and specialist follow-up exceeds the annual cost of the biologic — and the patient has suffered irreversible harm. This scenario plays out thousands of times each day across the United States.

children.text: What Regulation Is Doing About EHR Burden

Federal policymakers have recognized for years that EHR burden and poor interoperability are not merely nuisances — they are structural failures of the health information technology ecosystem that cause measurable patient harm. The legislative response began in earnest with the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, which included sweeping provisions designed to promote the free flow of electronic health information and prohibit "information blocking" — practices by EHR vendors, health systems, or health information networks that impede access to or exchange of patient data. Penalties for information blocking violations can reach up to $1 million per violation for health IT developers and health information networks. Enforcement against healthcare providers became effective July 1, 2024, marking a turning point in the federal government's willingness to hold the ecosystem accountable.

On the interoperability infrastructure side, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) has advanced the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA), a nationwide framework designed to enable any HIPAA-covered entity to connect to a single network and exchange data with any provider connected to any participating Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN). The ONC's HTI-1 Final Rule, which took effect March 11, 2024, further implements the EHR Reporting Program from the Cures Act, requiring transparent reporting on certified health IT metrics. Together, these initiatives aim to shift the EHR ecosystem from fragmentation toward genuine clinical interoperability — a shift that, if successful, would directly reduce the manual data re-entry burden that consumes so much physician time.

The most targeted federal intervention on prior authorization specifically is the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule, known as CMS-0057-F. Finalized in early 2024, the rule requires impacted payers — including Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and qualified health plan issuers on federal exchanges — to implement FHIR-based Prior Authorization APIs, establish turnaround time limits of 72 hours for expedited requests and 7 calendar days for standard requests, and provide specific reasons for denial decisions. The operational provisions took effect January 1, 2026, with full API requirements due January 1, 2027. The rule also requires payers to implement a Provider Access API, enabling in-network providers to retrieve patient claims and encounter data directly — a foundational step toward the kind of data pre-population that could eliminate much of today's manual re-entry burden.

children.text: The U.S. Surgeon General and the AMA have both issued formal calls for systemic action on EHR burden. In 2022, Surgeon General Vivek Murthy's advisory on health worker burnout explicitly identified EHR and administrative burden as a primary structural driver of the crisis, and called on health systems, payers, and technology vendors to redesign workflows that prioritize clinician well-being alongside patient safety.
Interventions That Actually Work: From Ambient AI to FHIR Pre-Population

Amid the grim statistics on EHR burden, a set of interventions has emerged with genuine evidence of efficacy. The most discussed — and arguably the most promising — is ambient artificial intelligence documentation, often called the "ambient AI scribe." These systems use natural language processing to listen to physician-patient conversations and automatically generate structured clinical notes inside the EHR, dramatically reducing the manual typing and clicking that consumes so much of a physician's cognitive bandwidth. A quality improvement study of 263 physicians and advanced practice practitioners across six health care systems — published in JAMA Network Open — found that after 30 days of using an ambient AI scribe, burnout rates dropped significantly from 51.9 percent to 38.8 percent. The odds of burnout fell by 74 percent. Eighty-four percent of physicians reported a positive effect on patient communication, and 82 percent said their overall work satisfaction improved.

Health systems deploying ambient AI at scale are reporting similarly encouraging results. Between October 2023 and December 2024, 7,260 Permanente physicians used ambient AI tools across more than 2.5 million patient encounters, saving an estimated 15,791 hours of documentation time — equivalent to approximately 1,800 eight-hour workdays. Platforms such as Nuance DAX Copilot (integrated with Epic and other major EHRs), Abridge, and Suki are now deployed across hundreds of health systems. Studies consistently report reductions in after-hours charting, decreased cognitive load, and improved patient-physician eye contact and conversation quality. A 2026 real-world prospective observational time-motion study published in JMIR Medical Informatics documented significant time savings per clinical encounter using ambient AI tools in outpatient settings. Fifty-six percent of patients reported that ambient AI scribes had a positive impact on the quality of their visit, suggesting that the benefits extend beyond the clinician experience to the patient relationship itself.

Beyond ambient AI, several other high-impact interventions have evidence behind them. FHIR-enabled data pre-population — where a patient's prior labs, medications, and diagnoses flow automatically into the new encounter note from external health systems — directly attacks the manual re-entry burden that fragmented interoperability creates. Team-based inbox management, in which clinical staff handle prescription refill requests, routine test result communications, and referral coordination, can reduce physician inbox volume by 30 to 40 percent in well-designed implementations. Human medical scribes remain effective where ambient AI is not yet deployed: studies show they reduce physician documentation time by approximately 10 minutes per patient encounter and are associated with reduced after-hours EHR time. ONC's SAFER (Safety Assurance Factors for EHR Resilience) guides provide health systems with a structured self-assessment framework for identifying and mitigating EHR-related patient safety risks — including alert fatigue, poor workflow design, and inadequate usability testing — before they cause harm.

children.text: The EHR Market Today: Concentration and Scale

The U.S. electronic health records market is large, concentrated, and growing. Grand View Research estimated the U.S. EHR market at approximately $12.87 billion in 2024, with projections for sustained growth as adoption deepens and cloud-based platforms replace older on-premise installations. That dollar figure, however, obscures the most important structural fact: a small number of vendors command the overwhelming majority of the market, especially in the hospital sector where the highest-acuity and highest-cost care is delivered.

According to KLAS Research's 2024 acute care market analysis, four vendors — Epic, Oracle Health (formerly Cerner), MEDITECH, and TruBridge — together account for roughly 87% of acute care hospital EHR installations in the United States. Epic alone holds 42.3% of all acute care hospitals by count, but when the metric shifts from hospital count to hospital beds — a proxy for the volume of care actually delivered — Epic's share jumps to 54.9%. This distinction between counting hospitals and counting beds matters enormously: large academic medical centers and health systems serve exponentially more patients than small critical-access hospitals, so the vendor that dominates large institutions controls the data environment for a disproportionate share of American patients.

The ambulatory market — outpatient physician offices and clinics — tells a different story. Here the field is more fragmented, with eClinicalWorks capturing roughly 12–14% of the ambulatory market, Epic near 10–20% depending on methodology, and athenahealth around 7%. The ambulatory segment is far more price-sensitive than the inpatient segment, which explains why cloud-native vendors with subscription pricing models have found durable footholds even as Epic expands into large health system ambulatory practices. The U.S. ambulatory EHR market alone was estimated at $5.49 billion in 2024.

children.text: Epic's Dominance: A Private Company Running Half of America's Hospital Records

Epic Systems Corporation is headquartered in Verona, Wisconsin — a deliberate choice by its founder and CEO, Judy Faulkner, who started the company in a Madison, Wisconsin basement in 1979 with a $70,000 investment from friends and family. Faulkner has kept Epic entirely private, never taking venture capital or private equity money, and has stated publicly that Epic will never go public. This unusual corporate structure — a multi-billion-dollar private company with no outside investors — gives Epic extraordinary freedom to prioritize long-term strategic moves over quarterly earnings. By 2024, Epic reported $5.7 billion in annual revenue and held the medical records of more than 325 million people.

The scale of Epic's reach becomes concrete through MyChart, its patient-facing portal. As of early 2024, Epic reported 185 million active MyChart users — a number that rivals the active user base of many major consumer apps. When a patient logs into MyChart at a hospital in Boston, a clinic in rural Iowa, or a health system in California, they are interacting with the same underlying platform. This patient-portal ubiquity is both a convenience and a strategic lock-in mechanism: patients who are enrolled in MyChart have a strong implicit incentive to seek care within the Epic ecosystem, because their records, messaging threads, and appointment history are all resident there.

Epic's dominance at large academic medical centers is not accidental. The company historically pursued a strategy of landing flagship institutions — the University of Pennsylvania, Johns Hopkins, Kaiser Permanente, Cleveland Clinic — understanding that smaller community hospitals and physician practices would follow the referral patterns of the dominant regional health system. KLAS confirmed that in 2024, Epic added a net 176 acute care multispecialty hospitals, its largest-ever annual net gain, and won nearly 70% of all hospitals impacted by EHR decisions that year regardless of size. The competitive flywheel is self-reinforcing: more Epic installations mean more Epic-to-Epic data exchange, which is dramatically smoother than cross-vendor exchange, giving clinical staff at Epic sites a perceived interoperability advantage that further pressures non-Epic competitors.

body.analogy: Think of Epic's network effect like an operating system that everyone in an office already runs: sharing files is frictionless within the system, but the moment you need to exchange data with someone on a different platform, compatibility issues multiply. The more people adopt the dominant platform, the more the others face pressure to convert.
body.concept: Epic's Care Everywhere network makes data exchange nearly seamless between Epic sites, creating a powerful network effect that disadvantages hospitals still on competing EHRs.

body.content: When a patient cared for at a Mayo Clinic facility (Epic) is transferred to a Mass General Brigham hospital (also Epic), clinicians can pull that patient's full longitudinal record — allergies, medications, prior diagnoses, imaging reports — almost instantly via Epic's Care Everywhere framework. Performing the same query across a vendor boundary, say from an Epic site to an Oracle Health site, requires the hospitals to rely on external interoperability frameworks like Carequality, introducing additional query steps, potential data mapping inconsistencies, and latency. The technical gap is narrowing with FHIR APIs, but the lived experience for clinicians remains meaningfully different.
body.title: Care Everywhere: Epic-to-Epic Seamlessness

children.text: Oracle Health (Formerly Cerner) and the Troubled VA Contract

Cerner was Epic's primary rival for decades, particularly at mid-size community hospitals and large integrated delivery networks. That competitive landscape shifted in June 2022, when Oracle Corporation completed its acquisition of Cerner for $28.3 billion, rebranding the company as Oracle Health. Oracle's ambition was to layer its cloud infrastructure and database technology underneath Cerner's clinical software, creating a unified platform that could compete with Epic at scale. The reality of the post-acquisition integration has proven considerably messier. According to KLAS 2024 data, Oracle Health saw a net loss of 74 acute care hospitals during the year, with its market share declining from 23.4% to 22.9% — a continuation of a multi-year erosion.

The most high-profile test of Oracle Health's capabilities is the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs EHR modernization contract. The VA signed a deal with Cerner in May 2018, originally valued at $10 billion, to replace its legacy VistA system with the Cerner Millennium platform — later branded MHS GENESIS after the Department of Defense adopted the same system for its military health system. The DoD implementation has been comparatively successful: MHS GENESIS is now live at roughly 3,890 garrison facilities with over 197,200 end-users serving more than 9.5 million beneficiaries across the United States, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific. The VA implementation, however, has faced repeated delays, safety incidents, and congressional scrutiny, with lawmakers at various points demanding the contract be restructured or cancelled.

The VA contract's estimated lifetime cost has ballooned — some estimates project it could exceed $50 billion over 28 years — and as of recent reporting, the VA had spent roughly $5 billion to implement the system at only six of its 171 medical centers. The VA renegotiated the contract with Oracle Health to introduce stronger performance metrics and larger monetary penalties for non-compliance. The saga illustrates how even the best-resourced government healthcare agencies can struggle when a dominant EHR transition encounters the full complexity of a legacy clinical environment. For the broader interoperability agenda, the VA case demonstrates that vendor selection is only the starting point — implementation fidelity, change management, and sustained governance are equally determinative of whether new systems deliver value.

body.message: The Oracle Health VA contract is a live case study in the risks of large-scale EHR transitions. As of 2024–2025, the VA had spent approximately $5 billion implementing the system at only 6 of 171 medical centers, with costs projected to eventually exceed $50 billion over the full contract lifetime. Patient safety concerns, clinician dissatisfaction, and congressional pressure have accompanied the rollout. Policymakers and health systems alike cite this project as evidence that technical interoperability alone cannot compensate for poor implementation planning and insufficient workflow integration.
body.title: VA EHR Modernization: A Cautionary Tale

children.text: The Ambulatory and Community Health Market: A More Competitive Landscape

The outpatient physician office market operates under different economic logic than the hospital sector. A 10-physician internal medicine practice does not have a multi-million-dollar IT budget, a dedicated implementation team, or the negotiating leverage of a large health system. This price sensitivity has made the ambulatory market fertile ground for cloud-native, subscription-priced vendors. eClinicalWorks — a privately held company based in Westborough, Massachusetts — has built a substantial ambulatory presence serving roughly 12–14% of the U.S. ambulatory EHR market. The company's success is built on aggressive pricing, a broad feature set, and deep penetration into independent physician practices and specialty clinics.

athenahealth, now owned by Veritas Capital and Bain Capital after a 2019 buyout from Optum/UnitedHealth, holds approximately 7% of the ambulatory EHR market and distinguishes itself through a network-based model that provides revenue cycle management alongside clinical documentation. NextGen Healthcare and Modernizing Medicine serve specific specialty niches — NextGen has historically been strong in large specialty practices, while Modernizing Medicine's EMA platform dominates in dermatology, ophthalmology, and orthopedics. The ambulatory market's fragmentation means interoperability is harder to achieve: a patient's records may be split across a hospital Epic instance, a primary care eClinicalWorks installation, and a specialty Modernizing Medicine environment, with no single platform holding the complete picture.

Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) — the safety-net clinics that serve uninsured and low-income communities — face even sharper cost constraints and have developed a distinct ecosystem. OCHIN, a nonprofit health IT cooperative, has emerged as a critical infrastructure provider for FQHCs, enabling them to access the Epic platform through a shared instance model that dramatically reduces per-site cost. In 2024 alone, 33 rural and community health organizations implemented OCHIN's Epic model, with OCHIN Epic now supporting more than 1,900 care delivery sites in 37 states and reaching over 7 million patients. eClinicalWorks also serves a significant FQHC population, and multiple FQHCs selected its AI-enhanced EHR solutions in 2024. The FQHC market underscores a recurring theme: the economics of EHR adoption are inseparable from the economics of care delivery, and vendor decisions made at the market's lowest-margin margin have outsized consequences for health equity.

children.text: Market Concentration and What It Means for Interoperability

The relationship between market concentration and interoperability is complex and contested. On one hand, a highly concentrated market dominated by a single vendor creates a de facto network: if most hospitals run the same platform, data can flow readily within that platform's native exchange mechanisms. Epic's Care Everywhere framework exemplifies this — Epic sites can query one another for patient records with minimal friction, and the 185 million MyChart users represent an enormous longitudinal dataset that is navigable within the Epic ecosystem. From a pure data-flow perspective, a world where everyone ran the same EHR would minimize many interoperability challenges at the point of care.

The problem is what happens at the boundaries. The 22.9% of hospitals on Oracle Health, the 14.8% on MEDITECH, the vast ambulatory market on eClinicalWorks and athenahealth, and the millions of patients receiving care at FQHCs on mixed platforms — all of these are outside Epic's native exchange universe. When care flows across that boundary, the friction increases. This is where federal interoperability policy becomes essential. The 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking provisions, finalized by ONC, prohibit EHR vendors from practices that unreasonably restrict access to, exchange of, or use of electronic health information. The FHIR R4 standard has reached near-universal EHR vendor adoption — 92% of EHR vendors support it, 90% of health systems have FHIR-enabled APIs, and 81% of hospitals have enabled patient access APIs — creating a common technical language that theoretically enables cross-vendor exchange regardless of underlying platform.

TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — represents the most ambitious federal attempt to operationalize nationwide interoperability atop this FHIR foundation. TEFCA designates Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) as the connecting hubs, and organizations that participate in TEFCA agree to share data under a common governance framework. Crucially, a final rule issued in December 2024 established a "TEFCA Manner Exception" — providing that limiting exchange to TEFCA channels will not constitute information blocking when both parties are TEFCA participants and other conditions are met. This regulatory move is designed to steer the entire ecosystem toward TEFCA participation by giving vendors a safe harbor for TEFCA-based exchange while maintaining anti-blocking obligations elsewhere. Whether TEFCA can override the gravitational pull of dominant vendor networks remains the central open question for health data policy in the coming decade.

children.text: The open API mandate is changing competitive dynamics in ways the market has not fully absorbed. When any developer can build on top of Epic, Oracle Health, or athenahealth using standardized FHIR APIs, the EHR vendor loses some of its ability to lock customers into proprietary workflows. Patients and providers can increasingly choose best-of-breed applications — scheduling tools, remote monitoring platforms, AI-assisted documentation — that connect to any certified EHR via API. This "unbundling" of EHR functionality is one of the most significant structural shifts in the market.

children.text: Why FHIR Exists: The Problem It Solves

For most of the past four decades, healthcare data exchange ran on a standard called HL7 version 2, first released in 1987. HL7 v2 is a pipe-delimited text format — essentially a structured text file where each field is separated by a vertical bar character. Hospitals still send tens of millions of these messages every day for lab results, admission notifications, and discharge summaries. The problem is that HL7 v2 was never truly standardized: each hospital, lab, and payer customized the format to their own needs. The result was that two organizations could each claim HL7 v2 compliance yet be completely unable to exchange data without expensive custom interface engines sitting between them.

HL7 attempted to solve this chaos with version 3 and its companion standard, the Clinical Document Architecture (CDA). Released in 2005, CDA introduced XML-based documents like the Continuity of Care Document (CCD) and brought more rigorous modeling using a formal Reference Information Model (RIM). On paper, CDA was a major step forward. In practice, it proved so complex to implement that adoption required months of training, and the resulting documents were sprawling XML files sometimes hundreds of kilobytes long for a single patient encounter. Ambiguous specifications meant different vendors interpreted the standard differently, recreating the same fragmentation problem at a higher level of sophistication.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected direction. In 2011, Grahame Grieve — an Australian health informaticist running a small consulting firm called Health Intersections — published a proposal on the HL7 listserv under the name "Resources for Healthcare." He argued that instead of modeling the entire healthcare universe in a single monolithic schema, the industry should define discrete, self-contained data objects — resources — that could be exchanged individually over the web using the same RESTful HTTP conventions already powering every modern web application. HL7 adopted the proposal, renamed the project Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), and Grieve has served as FHIR Product Director at HL7 International ever since. FHIR's foundational insight was simple and radical: make healthcare data exchange feel like using the internet, not like implementing a mainframe EDI system.

body.analogy: HL7 v2 and CDA are like sending a fax — the technology works, but every machine has its own quirks, and you need a human on both ends to interpret the smudged output. FHIR is like sending a JSON API response — any developer with a browser and twenty lines of code can read it immediately.

children.text: Core Concepts: Resources, RESTful APIs, and Profiles

The fundamental unit of FHIR is the resource. A resource is a discrete, self-contained piece of healthcare information: a Patient, a Condition, a Medication, an Observation, an Encounter. Each resource has a defined structure — a set of typed fields, cardinality constraints, and a standard identifier — and can be serialized as either JSON or XML. FHIR R4 defines 145 resource types spanning clinical data, administrative data, financial records, and the specification infrastructure itself. Because each resource is independently addressable via a URL, any developer who can make an HTTP GET request can retrieve a patient's medication list without needing to parse thousands of lines of XML or understand a complex proprietary schema.

FHIR uses standard RESTful HTTP verbs to operate on resources. GET retrieves a resource or a collection of resources. POST creates a new resource. PUT updates an existing resource by replacing it in full. PATCH applies a partial update. DELETE removes a resource. This means that a FHIR server is, at its core, a web API — and developers already experienced building or consuming REST APIs can begin working with FHIR data without a steep learning curve. The specification also defines a $search operation with a rich query syntax, allowing applications to retrieve, for example, all Observations for a given patient with a specific LOINC code within a date range — expressed as a URL query string any web developer would recognize.

Because a generic resource like Observation must serve everything from a blood pressure reading to a pregnancy test result, FHIR introduces the concept of profiles to constrain and extend base resources for specific use cases. A profile is a StructureDefinition that narrows the allowable values in certain fields, makes optional elements required, and adds extensions for data elements not present in the base resource. Collections of profiles, terminology bindings, and example instances are packaged into Implementation Guides (IGs). The US Core Implementation Guide, developed by HL7 and referenced by U.S. federal regulation, defines the minimum data set that certified EHR systems must expose — ensuring that a patient's medications, allergies, and problem list are available in a predictable, consistent format regardless of the underlying vendor.

children.text: FHIR R4 vs R4B vs R5: Understanding the Version Landscape

FHIR R4, published on January 2, 2019, was a landmark release for one specific reason: for the first time, core components of the FHIR specification — the RESTful API framework, the XML and JSON serialization formats, and a set of foundational data types — passed HL7's normative ballot process. "Normative" in HL7 terminology means the specification has been formally reviewed, balloted, and approved as a stable standard that will not undergo breaking changes without a full new normative ballot cycle. This stability was what regulators and health systems needed to mandate FHIR in law: you cannot require vendors to implement a standard that might break next year. R4 became the regulatory baseline for U.S. federal interoperability rules and remains so today.

FHIR R4B (version 4.3.0) was published on May 28, 2022. Rather than a full new release, R4B was a limited, targeted update designed to bring selected new clinical features — particularly around subscriptions, citations, and evidence-based medicine resources — to maturity without breaking R4 compatibility. R4B maintained full backward compatibility with R4 for the vast majority of resources, meaning an R4 server could largely interoperate with an R4B client. For most implementers, especially those building systems to meet U.S. regulatory requirements, R4B represented a refinement rather than a migration target.

FHIR R5 was published on March 26, 2023. R5 expanded the normative core, refined the subscription framework, improved support for clinical reasoning and evidence-based medicine, and introduced a number of new resource types and cross-version analysis tools. However, because U.S. regulation explicitly cites FHIR R4 as the required standard, and because certification bodies and major EHR vendors have invested years building R4 implementations, R4 remains the de facto deployment standard for regulated healthcare in the United States. R5 adoption will grow over time — particularly as new Implementation Guides are written against it — but implementers in 2025 still encounter R4 as the universal baseline in production systems.

children.text: FHIR in U.S. Regulation: Federal Mandates Driving Adoption

The single most consequential event in FHIR's adoption history was the publication of two companion federal rules on May 1, 2020. The ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule — formally titled "21st Century Cures Act: Interoperability, Information Blocking, and the ONC Health IT Certification Program" — required certified EHR developers to implement a new standardized API criterion (§ 170.315(g)(10)) based specifically on HL7 FHIR Release 4. EHR developers were given 24 months from the publication date to update their technology, placing the compliance deadline in May 2022. This rule also codified information blocking prohibitions — making it illegal for EHR vendors, health systems, and health information networks to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information.

On the same day, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services published the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F). This rule required Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid programs, CHIP programs, and Qualified Health Plan issuers on the federal marketplace to implement FHIR-based Patient Access APIs — giving patients the right to request their claims data and clinical information through any third-party app of their choosing. Payers were required to make this API available by July 1, 2021. Together, these two rules created an unprecedented regulatory pull: the entire U.S. healthcare ecosystem — hospitals, clinics, payers, and health IT vendors — faced federal mandates to deploy FHIR R4 APIs within a defined timeline.

These rules operate alongside the U.S. Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI), ONC's standardized set of data elements that certified health IT must be capable of exchanging. USCDI defines the "what" — the clinical data classes and elements — while FHIR and the US Core Implementation Guide define the "how": the technical format and API by which that data is made accessible. TEFCA, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement, extends this further by establishing a national framework for health information network interoperability through designated Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs). The FHIR Roadmap for TEFCA, published by the Sequoia Project in December 2023, laid out a phased four-stage plan requiring all QHINs to progressively implement FHIR API exchange — with Stages 1 and 2 completing in 2024.

body.message: The ONC Cures Act Final Rule prohibits EHR vendors, health systems, and health information networks from taking any action that interferes with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information. Violations can result in civil monetary penalties. Withholding data from patients or restricting API access without a defined exception is a federal violation, not merely a best-practice failure.
body.title: Information Blocking Is Now Illegal

children.text: SMART on FHIR and Real-World Adoption

A FHIR API alone tells you what data is available and how to retrieve it. SMART on FHIR answers a different question: how should a third-party application authenticate, identify which patient context it's operating in, and receive the scoped access token it needs to retrieve only the data it's authorized to see? SMART — which stands for Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies — originated in 2010 as a project at Harvard Medical School and Boston Children's Hospital, funded by a four-year, $15 million grant from the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology. The project's goal was radical: write a medical application once and run it, unmodified, across different EHR systems. In the second half of 2013, the SMART team updated their framework to use FHIR as the underlying data model, and SMART on FHIR was publicly demonstrated at HIMSS in February 2014.

SMART on FHIR works by layering OAuth 2.0 authorization flows on top of FHIR APIs. When a clinician opens a SMART app from within their EHR, the EHR launches the app with a launch context — communicating which patient is currently in view and which practitioner is logged in. The app exchanges this context for an access token scoped to specific FHIR resources and operations (for example, patient/Observation.read or patient/MedicationRequest.read). The app then uses this token to make authenticated FHIR API calls. The entire flow uses industry-standard OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect protocols, meaning healthcare apps can leverage the same security infrastructure as consumer and enterprise software. SMART on FHIR 2.0 added backend services authorization for server-to-server use cases — enabling population health analytics, quality reporting, and payer data exchange without a human in the loop.

The major EHR vendors have fully embraced FHIR R4 and SMART on FHIR, in large part because federal regulation left them no choice — but adoption has also created genuine market opportunity. Epic operates fhir.epic.com, a developer portal through which thousands of third-party applications have registered. The Epic App Showroom (formerly App Orchard) hosts over 340 SMART on FHIR applications. Oracle Health's Ignite APIs — the FHIR platform for the former Cerner EHR — operate entirely on R4 and support SMART on FHIR launches from within the clinical workflow. A single SMART on FHIR application can, in principle, be registered with Epic, Oracle Health, and other EHRs separately, but the core application code — the JavaScript, Python, or mobile app logic — remains identical across platforms. This write-once, run-anywhere vision, first articulated in 2010, is now a practical reality across the majority of U.S. hospital beds.

SMART on FHIR real-world examples include: patient-facing apps that pull medication lists and vaccination records directly from hospital EHRs into a personal health record; clinical decision support tools that launch inside the EHR workflow and query live patient data to generate recommendations; payer-facing apps that retrieve prior authorization data and claims history; and research cohort tools that use backend SMART services to query populations across multiple institutions without requiring a human login session.

result.title: FHIR Fundamentals: The Modern Standard for Healthcare Data Exchange

children.text: What Is Health Information Exchange?

Health information exchange (HIE) is the electronic mobilization of health care information across organizations within a region, community, or hospital system. The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) defines HIE as the "electronic movement of health-related information among organizations according to nationally recognized standards." The purpose of HIE is simple but profound: when a patient is seen by any provider in a connected network, the relevant clinical history — diagnoses, medications, lab results, imaging, and care plans — should be available at the point of care, regardless of where it was originally created. Without HIE, clinicians too often make decisions without complete information, leading to duplicated tests, drug interactions, and preventable errors.

ONC recognizes three distinct forms of health information exchange. Directed exchange is the secure, point-to-point transmission of patient data from one known provider to another — the digital equivalent of a referral packet or discharge summary, transmitted via encrypted Direct Messaging rather than fax. Query-based exchange allows providers to search for and retrieve patient records from other providers on demand, which is especially valuable for unplanned or emergency care when the patient cannot provide a complete history. Consumer-mediated exchange gives patients themselves the ability to aggregate, control, and share their health information — for example, through a personal health record or a patient-facing app connected to their providers via FHIR APIs. Each mode addresses a different coordination scenario, and mature HIE ecosystems support all three simultaneously.

The scope of HIE in the United States is substantial. California alone has 15 HIEs, Texas has 12, and states like New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania each operate 8, reflecting a largely decentralized, market-driven pattern of exchange organization. Nationally, health information exchanges serve approximately 92 percent of the U.S. population, though coverage does not always translate to meaningful clinical use. HIE is foundational to population health management — enabling public health surveillance, care gap identification, and chronic disease registries — and to value-based care contracts that require providers to demonstrate coordinated, outcome-driven care. The shift from fee-for-service payment to value-based models has made HIE not merely convenient but economically essential for providers and payers alike.

children.text: Centralized HIE Architecture

In a centralized HIE architecture, participating organizations transmit copies of clinical documents to a shared, centrally managed repository — a Clinical Data Repository (CDR) — maintained by the HIE authority. Queries against this store are resolved locally within the repository, which means response times are fast and predictable. The HIE operator maintains a Master Patient Index (MPI) — a comprehensive registry that links every patient's demographic record across all contributing organizations to a single enterprise identifier. When a clinician queries the network, the MPI resolves the patient identity and the CDR returns the consolidated record. This architecture is particularly well-suited to regional networks where participants agree to cede data custody in exchange for a richer, continuously updated longitudinal record.

Vermont Information Technology Leaders (VITL), Vermont's designated statewide HIE, illustrates the real-world evolution of a centralized approach. Founded in 2005 as a public-private collaboration between the Vermont Association of Hospitals and Health Systems and state government, VITL has operated a central data infrastructure for Vermont's small but clinically complex population. Its strategic plan anticipates a hybrid data model blending a federated approach with a centralized repository for population health analytics. As of 2025, VITL is implementing a new, FHIR-native data repository as part of the state's broader vision for a Unified Health Data Space — a modern evolution that retains centralized analytical power while embracing open standards. Vermont's model demonstrates how small states can leverage centralization to build clinically rich, analytics-ready data assets that a purely federated network would struggle to assemble.

The governance complexity of centralized models is real and often underestimated. When patient data lives in a repository operated by a third-party HIE, critical questions arise: Who owns the data? Who can access it for secondary purposes such as research or quality reporting? What liability does the HIE bear if there is a breach? Centralized repositories also present a single point of failure — a successful cyberattack or catastrophic infrastructure failure could simultaneously disrupt access to records across every participating organization. These risks demand robust security controls, redundant infrastructure, and explicit legal agreements (often called data use and reciprocal support agreements, or DURSA) that define data rights, breach notification obligations, and permitted uses. Governance boards typically include representatives from member hospitals, payers, and patient advocates to balance competing interests over the shared repository.

body.title: Centralized vs. Federated: Core Trade-offs

children.text: Federated HIE Architecture

The federated model inverts the custody logic of centralization: clinical data remains within each participating organization's own systems, and the HIE provides only the connective tissue needed to locate and retrieve it on demand. The key infrastructure component is a Record Locator Service (RLS), sometimes called a patient index, which maintains a directory of where patient records exist — not the records themselves. When a clinician initiates a query, the RLS identifies which member organizations hold data for that patient, routes the query to those endpoints, and assembles the results into a coherent response. Because no copy of clinical content is stored centrally, participating organizations retain physical and legal control of their own data, making this model politically attractive in competitive markets where hospitals are reluctant to share data with a central authority that their rivals can also access.

CommonWell Health Alliance exemplifies the federated approach at national scale. Founded in 2013 by leading health IT vendors, CommonWell operates a vendor-neutral network in which data remains within the provider health IT systems where it was collected. CommonWell's core services include patient enrollment and identity management, record location (creating a virtual table of contents of where information about a patient exists across the network), and a query-and-retrieve capability that allows caregivers to pull needed data across trusted network members. The network covers more than 261 million unique individuals and has facilitated the exchange of more than 11 billion health care records since its founding. In February 2024, CommonWell was officially designated as a Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN) under TEFCA, validating its federated architecture as a backbone for the emerging national interoperability framework.

Federated architectures face two structural challenges that centralized designs avoid. First, query latency: because each query must be routed to multiple source systems, resolved, and assembled, response times depend on the slowest participating endpoint. A clinician in an emergency department waiting for records from three different health systems may find that one is temporarily offline, returning an incomplete picture. Second, data currency: federated queries retrieve records as they exist at the moment of the query, but there is no mechanism to proactively notify a care team when a patient's condition changes at another organization. This "pull only" model misses the event-driven use cases — such as an alert when a patient is admitted to an ED — that are increasingly important for care coordination and population health management. Emerging FHIR subscription mechanisms, discussed in Section 5, are beginning to address this gap within federated architectures.

body.analogy: A federated HIE works like a library catalog system: the catalog (the Record Locator Service) tells you which branch holds the book you need, but the book itself stays on the shelf at that branch until you request it. A centralized HIE is more like a single main library that collects copies of every book from every branch — faster to retrieve, but requiring trust that the main library will safeguard and return what was deposited.
body.concept: Federated vs. Centralized HIE data custody

children.text: Hybrid Architecture and the Network-of-Networks Era

Most real-world HIEs today do not fit neatly into either the centralized or federated category. Instead, they combine elements of both: a central directory or MPI for identity resolution, a centralized repository for high-value analytical data sets (e.g., ADT alerts, lab results, and medication histories), and federated query for detailed clinical documents held at source systems. This hybrid approach attempts to capture the query speed and analytical richness of centralization without requiring every participating organization to surrender custody of its entire record set. Vermont's VITL, for instance, explicitly describes its architecture as a hybrid blending centralized repository capabilities with federated exchange for certain data types. As FHIR APIs proliferate, the boundary between centralized and federated is increasingly blurred: an organization can expose FHIR endpoints that make its data queryable in near-real-time while also contributing certain data sets to a shared analytical environment.

At the national level, the United States has embraced a network-of-networks model through two complementary frameworks: Carequality and TEFCA. Carequality, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit and the nation's most widely adopted interoperability framework, provides a common package of legal terms, policy requirements, technical specifications, and governance processes that any health information network can adopt. Once two networks both subscribe to Carequality's rules, they can exchange data without negotiating separate bilateral agreements — the framework acts as a mutual recognition treaty for clinical data. As of 2024, Carequality enables the flow of more than 1.2 billion clinical documents every month. The eHealth Exchange — originally launched as the federal Nationwide Health Information Network (NHIN) and rebranded in 2012 — is one of Carequality's largest members, facilitating secure exchange of records for more than 300 million patients and processing roughly 25 billion data exchanges annually. Its network reaches all 50 states, 75 percent of U.S. hospitals, and four federal agencies including the Department of Defense, Veterans Affairs, CMS, and the Social Security Administration.

TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — represents ONC's most ambitious attempt to establish a nationwide, government-backed exchange floor. Under TEFCA, networks apply to become Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs), entities that agree to meet a common set of technical and policy requirements and to exchange data with every other QHIN without additional negotiation. The first QHINs were designated in December 2023. By late 2025, eleven networks had achieved QHIN status: eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, Health Gorilla, Konza, MedAllies, Kno2, CommonWell Health Alliance, eClinicalWorks (designated January 2025), Oracle Health Information Network (designated November 2025), Surescripts, and Netsmart. The QHIN model is explicitly federated at the network level — no single QHIN stores all the data — but each QHIN may itself be centralized, federated, or hybrid internally. FHIR-based exchange within TEFCA was piloted in 2025, and beginning January 1, 2026, QHINs must adopt HL7 FAST security procedures for all FHIR transactions.
