children.text: Sustainability, Governance, and the FHIR Transformation

Financial sustainability has been the Achilles' heel of health information exchange since the earliest community HIE experiments of the 1990s. Research consistently shows that only about 46 percent of operational HIEs can cover their operating costs with revenue from participants; among HIEs still in the planning stage, that figure drops to 36 percent. The core economic problem is a misalignment between who bears the cost of enabling exchange and who captures the benefit. A hospital that invests in HIE connectivity incurs real infrastructure and staffing costs, but many of the savings — avoided duplicate imaging, reduced readmissions, better-coordinated post-acute care — accrue to payers and to the health system as a whole rather than to the investing provider. Assessment fees have historically been the largest single revenue source for HIEs, followed by membership or subscription fees and state or federal grants. Continued dependence on grant funding, however, is widely recognized as a marker of poor long-term sustainability potential.

Governance structures shape both HIE sustainability and the quality of the data they produce. The dominant model is the private nonprofit, governed by a board representing member organizations — hospitals, physician groups, payers, and sometimes consumer advocates. Some scholars and policymakers have argued for treating HIE infrastructure as a public utility — regulated, mandated, and funded through a combination of government appropriations and assessed fees, much like the electrical grid or the public water system. Vermont's VITL approaches this model: it was created by legislative action, receives state funding, and operates as a designated statewide HIE with explicit public responsibilities. The public-utility framing aligns incentives better than a purely voluntary market model, but it requires sustained political will and a state government willing to backstop the HIE's operating costs through economic downturns and leadership transitions.

FHIR — HL7's Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources standard — is fundamentally reshaping HIE architecture. Mandated as the baseline requirement under the 21st Century Cures Act and ONC's interoperability regulations, FHIR R4 exposes clinical data via RESTful APIs that any application can query using standard web technologies. This democratizes access to health data, allowing new entrants — patient-facing apps, analytics platforms, care coordination tools — to participate in HIE without traditional integration engines or point-to-point interfaces. More significantly, FHIR R5 introduced topic-based subscriptions that enable event-driven exchange: rather than pulling records on demand, a care team can subscribe to receive a notification the moment a patient is admitted to another facility, discharged, or has a critical lab result. This event-driven capability bridges the most important gap in federated architectures and points toward a future where HIE is less about routing documents and more about delivering timely, actionable signals to the right person at the right moment. A 2025 global FHIR adoption survey found that 71 percent of respondents reported FHIR actively used in their country, up from 66 percent in 2024, and 78 percent of countries with electronic health data exchange regulations now mandate or advise FHIR.

body.message: HIEs that rely primarily on grant funding rather than participant-generated revenue are at elevated risk of closure when grant cycles end. When evaluating an HIE's long-term viability, look for diversified revenue (membership fees, transaction fees, analytics services) and evidence that participating organizations view the HIE as operationally essential rather than optionally convenient.

children.text: HIPAA Security Rule: What It Is and Who It Covers

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) established foundational privacy and security protections for health information. While the broader statute passed in 1996, the Security Rule that specifically governs electronic protected health information (ePHI) was published as a final rule in February 2003 and took effect on April 21, 2005 — giving the industry two years to build compliance programs before enforcement began. For over two decades, this single regulatory framework has governed how hospitals, insurers, clinics, and their vendors protect the most sensitive data Americans share with anyone: their medical records.

The Security Rule applies exclusively to ePHI — health information that is created, received, maintained, or transmitted in electronic form and that can be used to identify an individual. This is a critical distinction: paper records and purely verbal communications fall under the Privacy Rule, not the Security Rule. Every piece of digitally stored patient data, from an EHR record to a lab result sent by secure message, is ePHI and therefore subject to the Security Rule's three categories of safeguards: administrative, physical, and technical. Understanding which data qualifies as ePHI is the first step in building a defensible compliance posture, because scope errors — assuming a system is out of scope when it is not — are among the most common gaps auditors and regulators find.

Two categories of organizations must comply with the Security Rule: covered entities and business associates. Covered entities are health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, and healthcare providers who transmit health information electronically. Business associates are any vendors or contractors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit ePHI on a covered entity's behalf — from cloud storage providers to billing companies to telehealth platforms. The HITECH Act of 2009 extended direct Security Rule liability to business associates, meaning regulators can sanction a vendor directly, not merely through the covered entity that hired them. Business associate agreements (BAAs) — contracts specifying how ePHI may be used and protected — are the contractual mechanism that operationalizes this shared responsibility.

children.text: A persistent misconception is that "addressable" means "optional." Under the 2003 rule, an addressable specification still requires implementation unless the organization formally documents why it is not reasonable and appropriate and adopts an equivalent alternative. body.message: Any system that touches ePHI — even indirectly, such as a log aggregation tool that ingests audit trails from an EHR — may be considered in-scope for the Security Rule. Conduct a thorough data flow mapping exercise to identify every system that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits ePHI before scoping your compliance program.
body.title: Scope Creep Is a Compliance Risk

children.text: Administrative Safeguards: The Compliance Foundation That Most Organizations Get Wrong

Administrative safeguards are the policies, procedures, and training programs that govern how an organization manages the security of ePHI. They are the largest category in the Security Rule and, by OCR's own enforcement data, the most consistently deficient. Among all administrative requirements, the security risk analysis stands out as the single most commonly cited deficiency in OCR enforcement actions year after year. A 2016–2017 OCR compliance audit found that only 14 percent of covered entities were substantially fulfilling their regulatory responsibilities for risk analysis — meaning roughly 86 percent had meaningful gaps at the time of audit. That figure has improved since but risk analysis failures remain the dominant enforcement trigger.

What does a compliant risk analysis actually require? The Security Rule mandates an accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all ePHI the organization creates, receives, maintains, or transmits. OCR has been explicit that a risk analysis must cover all ePHI across all systems — not just the primary EHR. Organizations that base their risk analysis on a template form, or that scope it only to one system without mapping all data flows, are producing a non-compliant document. Following a risk analysis, the organization must implement a risk management plan that reduces identified risks to a reasonable and appropriate level — and that plan must be reviewed and updated on a regular basis, not filed and forgotten.

Other administrative safeguards include designation of a security official responsible for developing and implementing security policies, a workforce security program that grants access only to employees who need it, an information access management process, security awareness training for all workforce members (including phishing simulations and periodic refreshers), security incident procedures, and a contingency plan covering data backup, disaster recovery, and emergency mode operations. Each of these must be documented in written policies. In the fall of 2024, OCR launched a dedicated "Risk Analysis Initiative" and within six months had announced seven enforcement actions — all citing failure to conduct an adequate risk analysis as a foundational violation that enabled or worsened subsequent breaches.

The penalty illustrates that even smaller business associates face direct financial consequences for administrative safeguard failures — OCR does not reserve enforcement solely for large health systems.

children.text: Physical Safeguards: Protecting the Hardware That Holds Health Data

Physical safeguards govern the physical access to facilities, workstations, and devices that store or process ePHI. The Security Rule organizes physical safeguards into four standards: facility access controls, workstation use, workstation security, and device and media controls. While technical controls like encryption and firewalls receive more attention, physical safeguards address an equally important attack surface — the reality that an attacker who can walk into a server room, pick up an unencrypted laptop, or photograph a monitor displaying patient records has bypassed every technical control in place. Physical breaches also include less dramatic but highly common failures such as leaving a workstation unlocked, disposing of a hard drive without secure erasure, or allowing unauthorized visitors into restricted areas.

Facility access controls require covered entities to implement policies that limit physical access to electronic information systems and the facilities where they are housed to authorized personnel. Implementation specifications under this standard include contingency operations (ensuring authorized personnel can access facilities during an emergency), a facility security plan, access establishment and modification procedures, and validation procedures for personnel requesting access. Workstation use and security standards require that every workstation handling ePHI has a documented policy describing its expected use and physical surroundings, and that physical safeguards restrict access to authorized users — including locked screen policies, privacy screens in public-facing areas, and physical positioning of monitors away from foot traffic in reception areas.

Device and media controls address the movement of hardware and electronic media containing ePHI. Required specifications include disposal procedures (ensuring ePHI is destroyed before a device is retired), and media re-use policies (ensuring ePHI is cleared before a device is reassigned). Addressable specifications include accountability (tracking the movement of devices and media) and data backup and storage before movement. The rise of bring-your-own-device (BYOD) policies has significantly complicated physical safeguard compliance: HIPAA does not distinguish between corporate-owned and personal devices — if a personal smartphone stores or transmits ePHI, it falls within the Security Rule's scope and must be subject to the same device controls, including the ability to remotely wipe ePHI if the device is lost or the employee departs. Mobile Device Management (MDM) platforms have become a near-mandatory operational tool for organizations with any BYOD exposure.

body.message: Organizations that allow employees to access ePHI on personal devices without a formal BYOD policy and MDM enrollment face compounding risks: no remote wipe capability, no audit trail, no configuration enforcement. When a device is lost or stolen, the inability to confirm whether ePHI was present — let alone protected — may trigger breach notification obligations.

children.text: Technical Safeguards and the 2025 Security Rule Overhaul

Technical safeguards are the technology controls and related policies that protect ePHI and control access to it. The Security Rule identifies four technical safeguard standards: access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, and transmission security. Access controls require covered entities to implement technical policies that allow only authorized persons to access ePHI — implemented through required specifications for unique user identification (every user gets their own login, no shared credentials) and emergency access procedures, plus addressable specifications for automatic logoff and encryption and decryption. Audit controls require hardware, software, and procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems that contain or use ePHI — the logs that let you answer "who accessed this patient's record and when?" after an incident.

Transmission security — the requirement that covered entities guard against unauthorized access to ePHI being transmitted over electronic communications networks — is where the 2003 rule's age shows most clearly. Encryption of data in transit was listed as an addressable specification in 2003, meaning organizations could technically document a rationale for not encrypting. In practice, the industry has converged on Transport Layer Security (TLS) as the baseline for any network transmission of ePHI, and OCR has made clear through enforcement guidance that failure to encrypt transmissions is difficult to justify as reasonable and appropriate. Encryption of data at rest — stored on servers, databases, and portable devices — was also addressable under the 2003 rule and has similarly become a de facto requirement through enforcement pressure even before the proposed 2025 update.

On January 6, 2025, HHS published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) representing the most significant overhaul of the HIPAA Security Rule since its original publication — the first substantive update in over two decades. The proposed rule makes five structural changes that healthcare organizations must prepare for: First, the required/addressable distinction is eliminated — every implementation specification becomes mandatory, with only narrowly defined exceptions. Second, encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit is explicitly required, not merely addressable. Third, multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required, not optional. Fourth, regulated entities must conduct biannual vulnerability scans and annual penetration testing. Fifth, network segmentation to isolate systems that contain ePHI from other networks is required. The comment period closed March 7, 2025, and the final rule is expected to publish in 2026, with a 240-day compliance window after publication.

body.analogy: Think of the 2003 Security Rule as a building code that said walls "should generally" be fireproof — individual builders could document why drywall was sufficient for their situation. The 2025 proposed rule tears out that flexibility and says: every wall must meet the same fire-rating standard, period. The discretion that once allowed cost-based trade-offs is replaced by specific, measurable, auditable technical requirements.

children.text: Breach Statistics, Enforcement, and the Change Healthcare Wake-Up Call

The scale of healthcare data breaches has grown dramatically since OCR began publishing its breach portal in 2009. Between 2009 and 2025, OCR received reports of 7,357 healthcare data breaches affecting 500 or more individuals, collectively exposing the protected health information of more than 935 million Americans — nearly three times the U.S. population, reflecting the reality that many individuals have been breached multiple times. In 2023, OCR logged 746 large breaches affecting an average of 154,609 individuals each. The single largest breach that year — HCA Healthcare — affected 11.27 million individuals. Hacking and IT incidents accounted for 81% of 2023 breaches and 96% of breached records, with ransomware emerging as the dominant attack vector. OCR reported that large breaches involving ransomware increased 264% between 2018 and 2023.

In 2024, the Change Healthcare ransomware attack rewrote the scale of what a single healthcare data breach could look like. On February 21, 2024, ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware operators gained access to Change Healthcare — a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group and the largest healthcare payment processing network in the United States. The attack disrupted the ability of pharmacies to process prescription claims and of providers to submit bills for weeks. UnitedHealth Group ultimately disclosed that approximately 190 million Americans had their personal and healthcare data compromised — making it the largest healthcare data breach in U.S. history by a wide margin. The stolen data included health insurance information, medical records, billing data, and in many cases Social Security numbers. The company estimated the financial cost at $2.45 billion for the nine months ending September 30, 2024, and that figure continued to rise.

Total 2024 breach numbers reflected the Change Healthcare effect: while fewer large breaches were reported than in 2023 (663 vs. 746, a 9% decrease), the total number of individuals affected reached 242.9 million — the vast majority attributable to a single incident. Hacking and IT incidents accounted for 99.45% of all breached records in 2024. OCR's enforcement activity ran in parallel: the agency imposed 22 financial penalties in calendar year 2024, collecting $9.94 million in settlements. Fourteen of those actions cited Security Rule violations, and the Risk Analysis Initiative that launched in late 2024 added seven more enforcement actions in its first six months alone. The message from regulators is unambiguous: the cybersecurity crisis in healthcare has made HIPAA Security Rule compliance an urgent operational priority, not a check-the-box exercise.

children.text: HL7 v2 Origins and Dominance

In March 1987, a group of hospital CIOs, software vendors, and healthcare informaticists convened at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, convened by Dr. Sam Schultz, to solve a problem that was quietly strangling the modernization of American hospitals. Each clinical system — laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, admissions — had been built in isolation, and connecting any two of them required a bespoke, hand-crafted interface. With N systems in a hospital, you needed as many as N-squared custom integrations. The first version of HL7 (Health Level Seven) emerged from that 1987 meeting, and Version 2 was published the following year in 1988, adding billing and lab results workflows. HL7 v2 was not the most elegant technical design ever produced, but it was pragmatic, vendor-agnostic, and — crucially — it shipped at exactly the moment hospitals needed it.

Nearly four decades later, HL7 Version 2 remains the dominant messaging standard in global healthcare. HL7 International reports that 95% of U.S. healthcare organizations use HL7 v2, and the standard has been adopted across more than 35 countries. Estimates place HL7 v2 at handling roughly 85% of all healthcare data exchanges in the United States, with American hospitals collectively processing over 15 billion HL7 v2 messages annually. Every major EHR, laboratory information system, radiology information system, and pharmacy system supports HL7 v2. This is not simply legacy inertia — it is a reflection of how deeply the format is woven into clinical operations that cannot afford downtime, data loss, or ambiguity.

The enduring dominance of HL7 v2 is a case study in how standards succeed in high-stakes industries. The format works. It is human-readable enough that a trained analyst can eyeball a raw message and diagnose a problem. It is compact enough to perform well over slow network connections. And it arrived before the internet era, meaning it was designed for point-to-point TCP connections — the network topology that hospital infrastructure was built around. Newer standards like HL7 FHIR offer dramatically better design and web-native interoperability, but replacing HL7 v2 requires replacing thousands of carefully tuned, mission-critical interfaces. Most health systems will run HL7 v2 well into the 2040s alongside FHIR, not instead of it.

children.text: Message Structure: Segments, Fields, and the Pipe-Delimited Format

HL7 v2 messages are plain text, structured hierarchically using delimiter characters rather than XML tags or JSON keys. The vertical bar (pipe, "|") separates fields within a segment. The caret ("^") separates components within a field. The tilde ("~") separates repetitions of a field. And the ampersand ("&") separates sub-components. This means a raw HL7 v2 message looks, to the uninitiated, like line noise — but to integration engineers, each position carries precise clinical meaning. Every message begins with an MSH (Message Header) segment, which encodes the sending application, receiving application, message type, timestamp, and a unique message control ID. If any segment is the "shipping label" of the HL7 envelope, it is MSH.

After MSH, a patient-level message will typically contain a PID (Patient Identification) segment carrying demographics: medical record number, name, date of birth, sex, address, and contact information. The PID segment is the foundation for patient matching across disparate systems — a notoriously difficult problem given that the same patient may have different identifiers in the EHR, the lab system, and the insurance system. For clinical orders and results, the OBR (Observation Request) segment describes what was ordered — the test, the ordering provider, the specimen collection time — while one or more OBX (Observation Result) segments carry the actual result values, reference ranges, and abnormal flags. A single lab panel can generate dozens of OBX segments, one per analyte.

A realistic HL7 v2 lab result message (ORU^R01) might look like this: "MSH|^~\&|LAB_SYS|MAIN_HOSPITAL|EHR|MAIN_HOSPITAL|20240315143022||ORU^R01|MSG00123|P|2.5" on the first line, followed by "PID|1||MRN123456^^^MAIN_HOSPITAL||JOHNSON^SARAH^M||19820714|F" identifying the patient, then "OBR|1|ORD987654|LAB987654|85025^COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT^CPT" describing the CBC order, and finally a series of OBX lines such as "OBX|1|NM|718-7^HEMOGLOBIN^LN||13.8|g/dL|12.0-16.0|N|||F" carrying the hemoglobin result with value, units, reference range, and a normal flag. Parsing that string correctly requires knowing not just the delimiters but the HL7 data type and table definitions for every field position. This is why integration engines and parser libraries exist.

children.text: Common Message Types and Clinical Workflows

The ADT (Admit, Discharge, Transfer) family of messages is the heartbeat of hospital operations. When a patient arrives and is admitted, the registration system fires an ADT^A01 message to every downstream system — the pharmacy, the dietary system, the billing engine, the clinical documentation platform — so that each knows a new patient encounter has begun. When that patient moves from the emergency department to the ICU, an ADT^A02 transfer message propagates the location change. When they go home, ADT^A03 closes the encounter. And whenever patient demographics are corrected — a misspelled name, an updated insurance ID — ADT^A08 broadcasts the update. These four event types (A01, A02, A03, A08) alone account for the majority of ADT message volume in most health systems, and their reliable delivery is a prerequisite for accurate care coordination, billing, and quality reporting.

The ORM (Order Message) and ORU (Observation Result Unsolicited) pair forms the backbone of the diagnostic cycle. When a clinician places a lab or radiology order, the EHR sends an ORM^O01 to the laboratory or radiology information system. The receiving system acknowledges with an ACK (acknowledgment) message, then begins processing. When results are available, the lab system returns an ORU^R01 carrying OBX segments for each result. This bidirectional ORM-to-ORU loop happens millions of times per day across U.S. hospitals. For scheduling, SIU (Scheduling Information Unsolicited) messages — ranging from SIU^S12 (notification of new appointment) to SIU^S15 (notification of appointment cancellation) — synchronize scheduling modules across EHR, radiology, and referral management platforms. MDM (Medical Document Management) messages, particularly MDM^T02, carry transcribed clinical notes, operative reports, and discharge summaries from dictation and transcription platforms back into the EHR.

Understanding these message types is essential for anyone troubleshooting an integration failure or designing a new interface. When a provider complains that lab results are not appearing in the EHR, the problem is almost certainly in the ORU pipeline — perhaps a malformed OBX segment, an unrecognized LOINC code in OBX-3, or a mismatch in the patient identifier that prevents the result from attaching to the correct encounter. When the pharmacy does not know a patient has been admitted, the ADT^A01 message likely failed delivery or was silently dropped due to a message profile mismatch. Tracing the HL7 message type immediately narrows the diagnostic search space from the entire hospital IT ecosystem to a specific interface and segment.

children.text: The HL7 v2 Interoperability Problem: Standards That Do Not Standardize

HL7 v2's greatest strength — flexibility — is also its deepest flaw. The standard defines message structures but does not enforce vocabulary, implementation choices, or local customizations. Two systems that both claim compliance with HL7 v2.3 can be entirely incompatible in practice. One laboratory might encode hemoglobin results using a local code "HGB" in OBX-3, while another uses the LOINC code "718-7^HEMOGLOBIN^LN". Both are technically valid under HL7 v2.3. The receiving EHR, however, may only be configured to recognize LOINC codes — meaning the first lab's results will be received but silently fail to map, leaving clinicians staring at an empty result field while the data sits orphaned in an integration engine queue. This kind of silent failure is more dangerous than an outright error.

The Z-segment mechanism exemplifies this tension between flexibility and interoperability. Every HL7 v2 segment beginning with the letter "Z" is a locally defined, proprietary extension. Vendors use Z-segments to transmit data that either does not fit in standard segments or that they prefer to keep in custom structures — patient consent flags, scheduling metadata, insurance authorization codes. A ZIN segment from one vendor and a ZIN segment from a different vendor may share a name but carry completely different fields. Receiving systems that encounter an unknown Z-segment are typically configured to ignore it silently. This means critical data encoded in Z-segments by the sending system may simply vanish at the receiving end unless both parties have explicitly agreed on the custom structure, documented it, and implemented it — which requires ongoing bilateral coordination that rarely scales across a health system with hundreds of interfaces.

The practical consequence of HL7 v2's implementation flexibility is a phenomenon called "interface engine proliferation." Because each connection between two systems requires custom translation logic to reconcile differences in field usage, code sets, and Z-segments, health systems have accumulated integration engines — Mirth Connect, Rhapsody, InterSystems HealthShare, Cloverleaf — running thousands of individual channel configurations. A large academic medical center may operate 800 to 1,200 active HL7 interfaces, each one a small bespoke software artifact. This creates a massive, hidden infrastructure burden: every upgrade to an EHR or lab system can break dozens of interfaces, each of which must be individually tested and repaired. The interfaces collectively represent years of engineering effort and institutional knowledge that is rarely documented adequately.

body.message: HL7 v2 interfaces frequently accept and acknowledge messages (sending back an ACK) that they then fail to process correctly due to code mapping errors or unrecognized Z-segments. This means clinical data — lab results, medication orders — can appear to have been delivered successfully while actually being lost or misfiled. Integration monitoring tools that check beyond ACK status are essential for detecting these silent failures.
body.title: The Silent Failure Risk

body.analogy: Imagine if the United States had a national standard for electrical outlets that specified the shape of the plug but not the voltage, frequency, or current rating — and allowed any manufacturer to add extra pins labeled with whatever letters they chose. Every device would technically use the "standard" outlet, but you would need a custom adapter for every device-outlet combination. That is HL7 v2 interoperability in practice.
body.concept: HL7 v2 defines message structure (the plug shape) but leaves vocabulary, coding systems, and local extensions (the voltage and custom pins) to each implementer — creating the illusion of standardization while preserving the reality of point-to-point incompatibility.

children.text: HL7 v2 and FHIR Coexistence: The Long Transition

HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), published in 2014 and now at Release 4 and beyond, was designed to address almost every limitation of HL7 v2: it uses RESTful APIs and JSON/XML, enforces structure through defined resource types, mandates standard terminologies, and is natively web-compatible. The question is not whether FHIR is technically superior to HL7 v2 — it clearly is. The question is how to get from here to there without disrupting the billions of clinical transactions that depend on HL7 v2 every day. The answer, increasingly, is that they will coexist for decades. HL7 International has explicitly recognized this reality by publishing the official HL7 Version 2 to FHIR Implementation Guide, a project maintained by the Orders and Observations working group that provides standardized mappings from HL7 v2 messages, segments, and data types to their FHIR R4 equivalents.

The transport layer for HL7 v2 — MLLP, the Minimal Lower Layer Protocol — is another dimension of the legacy that will persist. MLLP wraps HL7 v2 messages in a simple envelope using start-of-block (ASCII 0x0B) and end-of-block (ASCII 0x1C) characters, then transmits the wrapped message over a persistent TCP connection. MLLP has no inherent security or encryption; it relies on TLS or IPsec at the network layer for protection of PHI in transit. It has no standard port — port 6660 is commonly used by convention — and it requires a persistent, stateful TCP connection between sender and receiver. Every major integration engine — Mirth Connect, Rhapsody, InterSystems, Cloverleaf — maintains MLLP listener and sender components as core capabilities. As long as legacy systems speak only MLLP, the integration engine's job is to receive MLLP HL7 v2, transform it to FHIR, and deliver it to modern API endpoints — acting as a universal translator at the boundary between eras.

The v2-to-FHIR mapping project (available at build.fhir.org/ig/HL7/v2-to-fhir) defines, for example, how the fields of an HL7 v2 PID segment map to FHIR Patient resource attributes: PID-3 (Patient Identifier List) maps to Patient.identifier, PID-5 (Patient Name) maps to Patient.name, PID-7 (Date of Birth) maps to Patient.birthDate, and so on. Similarly, an ADT^A01 message maps to a FHIR Bundle containing a MessageHeader, Patient, Encounter, and related resources. These mappings allow integration engines to serve as automated translators — converting the legacy pipe-delimited messages arriving from a 20-year-old laboratory system into standards-conformant FHIR resources that can be consumed by a modern clinical decision support platform or a patient-facing app operating under 21st Century Cures Act API mandates. The coexistence of v2 and FHIR is not a failure of modernization; it is the realistic, pragmatic path forward for an industry where patient safety cannot tolerate a big-bang replacement of working infrastructure.

A mismatch between the laboratory's local observation code in OBX-3 and the EHR's expected coding system (e.g., LOINC) is the most common cause of this "ghost delivery" failure pattern — the message arrives, is acknowledged, and is then silently discarded or queued as unmapped. children.text: What Is Information Blocking?

In 2016 Congress passed the 21st Century Cures Act with a deceptively simple goal: make health data flow freely. Section 4004 of that law created a legal prohibition against "information blocking" — defined in regulation at 45 CFR 171.103 as any practice by an "actor" that is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI), unless required by law or covered by one of the enumerated regulatory exceptions. The definition is intentionally broad. Congress wanted to capture the full spectrum of behaviors — technical, contractual, and cultural — that had historically kept data siloed inside individual systems.

Three categories of entities qualify as "actors" under the rule: (1) health IT developers of certified health IT, (2) health information exchanges and health information networks (HIEs/HINs), and (3) healthcare providers. The law applies a slightly different knowledge standard to each group. For health IT developers and HIEs/HINs, information blocking occurs when the actor knows, or should know, that a practice is likely to interfere with EHI access. For healthcare providers, the standard is higher — the provider must actually know that the practice is unreasonable and likely to interfere. This asymmetry reflects Congress's view that technology vendors are more sophisticated market actors who should be held to a more demanding standard.

The scope of electronic health information covered by the rule has expanded since the regulation first took effect. From April 5, 2021 through October 5, 2022, EHI was limited to the data classes and elements defined in the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) Version 1 — a relatively narrow set of clinical data including demographics, vital signs, laboratory results, and medications. Starting October 6, 2022, the definition expanded dramatically to encompass all information in a patient's HIPAA Designated Record Set (DRS) — every medical record, billing record, and other documentation used to make decisions about a patient, including images, wave files, and any other form of ePHI. This full-EHI expansion dramatically broadened the universe of data that actors must make available on request.

body.analogy: Think of information blocking like a toll bridge that was built with public funds but operated by a private company that then charges prohibitive tolls, only lets certain cars cross, and keeps the roadway in disrepair to discourage use. The 21st Century Cures Act is the law that says: the bridge must be open, the tolls must be reasonable, and the road must actually be drivable.
body.concept: Information blocking uses technical, contractual, or operational barriers to prevent the free flow of patient health data that patients and clinicians have a legal right to access.

children.text: The Eight Exceptions

The prohibition on information blocking is not absolute. ONC finalized eight regulatory exceptions — codified at 45 CFR Part 171, Subpart B — that describe the circumstances under which an actor's practice of limiting EHI access does NOT constitute information blocking. These exceptions are divided into two categories: five exceptions describing reasons an actor might not fulfill a request for EHI, and three exceptions describing procedures actors may use when they do fulfill such requests. Critically, meeting an exception is voluntary — an actor is never required to invoke one. And satisfying an exception requires meeting all of the conditions specified in the regulation; partial compliance does not shield an actor from liability.

The five "not fulfilling" exceptions are: (1) the Preventing Harm Exception, which allows actors to limit EHI access when there is a reasonable belief that doing so would prevent substantial harm to a patient or another person; (2) the Privacy Exception, which covers situations where applicable state or federal privacy law prohibits the disclosure — this exception has multiple sub-conditions tied to specific HIPAA and state law scenarios; (3) the Security Exception, which permits actors to take reasonable, temporary measures to protect the security of EHI during an identified security threat; (4) the Infeasibility Exception, which acknowledges that there are genuine technical, operational, or legal constraints that can make it infeasible to fulfill a particular request; and (5) the Health IT Performance Exception, which permits health IT systems to be taken offline or have performance temporarily degraded for maintenance, upgrades, and other routine operational activities.

The three "fulfilling requests" exceptions govern the manner in which actors respond to legitimate EHI requests: (6) the Content and Manner Exception allows actors to negotiate and maintain reasonable terms for the access, exchange, and use of EHI — but importantly, this exception requires that the actor first attempt to reach agreement using content and manner that meets the requestor's needs; (7) the Fees Exception permits actors to charge fees for providing EHI access, but those fees must be based on objective and verifiable cost-based criteria uniformly applied to all similarly situated requestors — a $50,000 fee for a connection that costs $500 to maintain would fall well outside this exception; and (8) the Licensing Exception allows health IT developers to require licensees to obtain licenses for interoperability elements, so long as the licensing terms are non-discriminatory and commercially reasonable.

children.text: Penalties and Enforcement

The enforcement architecture for information blocking is divided between two HHS agencies with distinct authorities over distinct actor categories. The HHS Office of Inspector General (OIG) holds primary enforcement authority over health IT developers, HIEs, and HINs. OIG finalized its civil monetary penalty (CMP) rule on June 27, 2023, with enforcement becoming effective September 1, 2023. Under this rule, OIG may impose penalties of up to $1 million per violation against covered health IT actors. OIG will consider the nature and extent of the practice, the harm or potential harm caused, the duration of the conduct, the actor's history of compliance, and whether financial loss to federal health care programs resulted.

Healthcare providers face a different enforcement mechanism — "disincentives" administered through existing Medicare payment programs rather than standalone fines. On June 24, 2024, HHS finalized the provider disincentives rule (published in the Federal Register at 89 FR 55496, effective July 1, 2024). Under this rule, eligible hospitals found to have committed information blocking lose the ability to earn three-quarters of their annual market basket increase under the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS). Critical Access Hospitals see their Medicare reimbursement drop from 101% of reasonable costs to 100%. Individual clinicians in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) face estimated median losses of $686, while group practices of six clinicians could lose over $4,100. Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) and ACO participants may be barred from the Medicare Shared Savings Program for at least one year — potentially worth millions in forgone shared savings payments.

The complaint and referral process runs through ONC (now rebranded as ASTP — the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy). Any person or entity may submit a complaint through the ONC Information Blocking Complaint Portal. Since the portal opened in April 2021 through early 2026, nearly 1,600 complaints have been submitted, with approximately 85 percent filed by or on behalf of patients, and more than 90 percent targeting healthcare providers rather than health IT developers or HIEs. ONC reviews complaints and refers those with potential violations to OIG (for health IT developers and HIEs) or to CMS and the relevant Medicare program administrators (for healthcare providers). Enforcement escalated significantly in September 2025 when HHS Secretary Kennedy directed agency resources toward active information blocking enforcement — marking the most aggressive federal posture since the law took effect.

children.text: Common Scenarios: What Counts as Information Blocking

ONC has published extensive sub-regulatory guidance illustrating the types of practices that are likely — or unlikely — to constitute information blocking. One of the clearest categories involves unreasonable fees. The Fees Exception permits cost-based charges, but ONC guidance makes clear that fees must be objectively verifiable, uniformly applied, and proportionate to the actual cost of providing access. Charging a third-party app developer or competing health system dramatically inflated fees — while offering no-cost or nominal-cost connections to affiliated or non-competing partners — is a paradigmatic information blocking violation. The disparate treatment itself is the red flag, independent of the absolute dollar amount.

Requiring proprietary data formats when standardized FHIR APIs are available is another common scenario. The 21st Century Cures Act requires certified health IT to offer a standardized API "without special effort" for any individual patient or population of patients. An actor that makes data technically available only through a legacy HL7 v2 feed, a proprietary export format, or a cumbersome portal download — while refusing to enable the certified FHIR API — may be engaging in information blocking even if the data is theoretically accessible. Similarly, conditioning access on proprietary software licenses, requiring patients or clinicians to use specific applications, or building technical obstacles into the API workflow (such as excessive authentication steps applied only to competitors' apps) can all constitute information blocking.

Refusing to connect with competing health systems or vendor-neutral platforms is one of the most commercially significant patterns ONC has identified. A hospital system that shares discharge summaries, referral records, and care plans freely within its own affiliated network — but systematically delays, degrades, or refuses data exchange with providers at competing health systems — is likely engaging in information blocking, even if each individual refusal has a stated operational justification. ONC has specifically flagged "excessive delays" as a concern: a weeks-long processing time for a records request that could be fulfilled in minutes through existing technology is not a technical limitation; it is a practice that discourages access and may constitute information blocking absent a valid exception.

body.content: A regional HIE offers FHIR API connections to health system members at no charge. When a digital health startup applies for a connection to access de-identified population data for a public health analytics project, the HIE quotes $50,000 in upfront fees plus $10,000 per month in maintenance — terms offered to no other connection partner. The startup files a complaint with ONC. The HIE cannot satisfy the Fees Exception because the fees are not based on objective, verifiable, uniformly applied cost criteria. OIG would likely find this to be information blocking.
body.title: Scenario: The $50,000 API Connection Fee

body.content: A large EHR vendor's app marketplace approves hundreds of third-party applications. When a competing EHR vendor submits an app designed to help patients migrate their records to the new platform, the app is denied approval. The reason given is vague "security concerns" — but no security review was conducted and similar apps from non-competing developers were approved without review. This is a textbook Licensing Exception failure: the terms are discriminatory based on competitive status, not objective security criteria.

children.text: Real Enforcement Cases and Industry Impact

As of early 2026, no entity has been publicly named as the subject of a completed enforcement action with a final penalty imposed — a reality that reflects both the complexity of information blocking investigations and the deliberate sequencing of the federal enforcement ramp-up. The enforcement machinery has been built in visible stages. OIG finalized its CMP rule in June 2023. Provider disincentives were finalized in June 2024. HHS Secretary Kennedy issued a high-profile enforcement directive in September 2025. In February 2026, ASTP/ONC announced it had begun issuing letters of nonconformity to certain certified EHR developers related to API performance and potential information blocking, with formal notices of investigation to follow. The industry has been operating in an enforcement environment that was fully assembled only within the prior eighteen months.

The industry response to the information blocking framework has been substantial even in the absence of completed enforcement cases. Epic, the largest EHR vendor by U.S. market share, launched its App Orchard marketplace and has supported SMART on FHIR app authorization across its installed base. Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) upgraded its APIs to HL7 FHIR R4, the standard mandated by the ONC certification program. In real-world performance studies published in peer-reviewed literature, Oracle Cerner sites achieved bulk FHIR data export speeds of over 8,000 resources per minute for datasets of 5 to 16 million resources, while Epic sites exported at 1,555 to 2,500 resources per minute. These numbers reflect genuine technical investment in interoperability infrastructure — investment directly incentivized by the information blocking framework and the threat of CMP liability.

The population-level impact on data liquidity has been meaningful. The requirement that all certified health IT support standardized FHIR APIs has created the technical substrate for a new generation of interoperability use cases — from payer-to-provider data exchange under the CMS Interoperability Rule to patient-directed data aggregation through apps like Apple Health and CommonHealth. The ONC complaint portal data offers a revealing window into where friction remains: the fact that 90 percent of complaints name healthcare providers, not health IT developers, suggests that the cultural and organizational barriers to data sharing — not just the technical ones — remain the primary obstacle. Hospitals and clinician practices that have long treated patient data as an institutional asset are now being told, by federal law, that the patient's right to that data supersedes institutional convenience.

Industry Watch: In September 2025, the HHS-OIG and ASTP jointly issued an Enforcement Alert — a formal agency communication signaling that investigations are underway and that completed enforcement actions will be made public. Compliance officers at health IT companies and health systems should treat this alert as a direct warning that the years-long ramp-up period is ending.

children.text: Every time a patient is admitted to a hospital, an invisible machine swings into motion. The registration clerk's keystrokes in the admissions system must instantly reach the lab, the pharmacy, the radiology scheduling software, the billing engine, and the nursing floor's electronic whiteboard — all of which may be built by different vendors, running different software versions, and speaking subtly different dialects of the same messaging standard. The device that makes this happen is the interface engine, sometimes called an integration engine. It is among the least glamorous and most mission-critical pieces of infrastructure in healthcare IT.

Interface engines sit at the heart of hospital interoperability, acting as simultaneous translators, traffic directors, and circuit breakers for the flood of clinical data generated every second in a modern health system. Understanding how they work, who the major vendors are, and where the technology is heading is essential for anyone involved in health IT strategy, clinical informatics, or digital health product development.
What Interface Engines Do: The Translator and Router Function

At their core, interface engines perform three functions: they receive a message from a source system, transform it into the format the destination system expects, and route it to the right place at the right time. In a hospital without an interface engine, every system that needs to talk to every other system requires its own custom, hand-coded connection — what the industry calls a point-to-point interface. With ten systems, that means potentially 90 individual connections. Add a twentieth system and the number explodes to 380. This combinatorial nightmare is why the hub-and-spoke architecture that interface engines enable was such a transformative idea: each system connects once to the central engine, and the engine handles the rest.

The dominant message format flowing through these engines is HL7 version 2 (HL7 v2), a standard developed in the late 1980s that never quite standardized in practice. Each EHR vendor implements HL7 v2 slightly differently — different segment orderings, custom Z-segments carrying proprietary data, and varying interpretations of optional fields. An ADT (Admit-Discharge-Transfer) A01 message from Epic looks meaningfully different from one produced by Cerner or MEDITECH, even though all three claim compliance with the same specification. The interface engine's transformation layer — typically expressed as mapping logic written in a proprietary scripting language or JavaScript — handles these differences, reshaping the incoming message into exactly what the downstream system needs.

These messages travel between systems and engines using MLLP — the Minimal Lower Layer Protocol. MLLP is a lightweight TCP/IP wrapping protocol that solves a fundamental problem: TCP/IP delivers a continuous stream of bytes with no natural message boundaries. MLLP wraps each HL7 message in a start-block character (ASCII 0x0B) and an end-block character (ASCII 0x1C followed by a carriage return), allowing the receiving application to know precisely where one message ends and the next begins. Despite being technically simple, MLLP remains the backbone of clinical messaging in 2025 — it is reliable, low-overhead, and baked into decades of installed software that no one is eager to touch.

body.analogy: An interface engine is like an international airport hub. Passengers (messages) arrive from dozens of origin cities (source systems), speaking different languages and holding tickets in different formats. The hub translates their documents, routes them to the correct departure gate, and ensures they make their connecting flight — even when the rules change seasonally and new airlines keep arriving.

children.text: The Major Platforms: Rhapsody, Mirth Connect, Cloverleaf, and InterSystems

The commercial interface engine market is dominated by a handful of platforms that have each been battle-tested across thousands of hospital deployments. Rhapsody, now a standalone company after spinning out of Orion Health, is the most recognized name in the space. It has earned the Best in KLAS Integration Engine award for fifteen consecutive years as of 2024, a track record that reflects both its technical depth and its support quality. Rhapsody supports all major healthcare message standards — HL7 v2, HL7 v3, FHIR, DICOM, X12 — and is used by more than 1,900 healthcare teams across 31 countries. An independent Forrester study found that health systems using Rhapsody achieved a 193% return on investment over three years, driven primarily by reduced integration engineering time and improved data reliability.

Infor Cloverleaf, which has been in the healthcare integration market for over 20 years, occupies a similar enterprise tier. More than 500,000 applications are connected through Cloverleaf globally, with over one billion messages passing through the platform daily. Its strengths lie in its mature HL7 v2 processing capabilities and its long track record in large academic medical centers and integrated delivery networks. InterSystems Health Connect (part of the HealthShare family) takes a different architectural approach, embedding the integration engine within a broader data platform built on the InterSystems IRIS data platform. One documented large health system deployment runs 1,000 interfaces, processes 104 million messages per weekday, and connects 136 systems — all through a single InterSystems installation built in under a year.

Mirth Connect, historically the go-to open-source option, powered roughly one-third of all public Health Information Exchanges in the U.S. and was deployed in over 40 countries. Owned and maintained by NextGen Healthcare, it offered a free community edition alongside a commercial support tier. However, with the release of version 4.6, NextGen has transitioned Mirth Connect from its dual open-source/commercial licensing model to a single proprietary license — meaning the source code for new versions is no longer publicly available. This shift prompted the community to fork the codebase into a project called Open Integration Engine, which aims to preserve the open-source option for organizations that built workflows around the free tier. The Mirth transition is a cautionary tale about the risks of building critical infrastructure on vendor-controlled open-source projects.

children.text: Modern iPaaS and API Management: The Cloud Era of Integration

Traditional interface engines were designed for an era of on-premises data centers, persistent TCP connections, and relatively stable message volumes. The shift to cloud computing, mobile applications, and consumer-facing health platforms has created demand for a different kind of integration tool: the Integration Platform as a Service, or iPaaS. These cloud-native platforms are built around RESTful APIs, event-driven architectures, and elastic scalability — properties that legacy MLLP-based engines were never designed to deliver. The healthcare iPaaS market is growing at nearly 30% annually, driven by EHR interoperability mandates and the expansion of telehealth infrastructure.

MuleSoft, now part of Salesforce, is among the most widely deployed iPaaS platforms in healthcare. Its API-led connectivity model organizes integrations into three layers: System APIs that expose raw data from source systems (like an EHR), Process APIs that orchestrate business logic across multiple systems, and Experience APIs that deliver tailored data to specific consumers like mobile apps or patient portals. MuleSoft's healthcare accelerator includes pre-built assets for converting HL7 v2 messages, C-CDA documents, and X12 transactions into FHIR R4 resources, then ingesting them into data stores like AWS HealthLake. This FHIR facade pattern — where an API layer presents a modern FHIR interface over a legacy backend — is one of the most common architectural patterns in current healthcare integration projects.

Cloud providers have also entered the integration space with native healthcare services. AWS HealthLake provides a FHIR R4-compliant data store with built-in natural language processing for unstructured clinical data. Azure Health Data Services combines a FHIR server, DICOM service, and analytics capabilities into a single managed platform. Google Cloud's Healthcare API supports FHIR, HL7 v2, and DICOM natively. These services are not interface engines in the traditional sense — they do not perform the complex message transformation and routing that Rhapsody or Cloverleaf handle — but they serve as the destination and normalization layer that modern integration architectures route data toward. The practical result is a hybrid architecture: legacy interface engines handling v2 traffic on the hospital side, feeding cloud-native FHIR platforms that serve the analytics and application layers.

children.text: Building and Managing Interfaces: The Full Lifecycle

Building a new interface is rarely as simple as connecting two systems and pressing go. The lifecycle of a single interface — from initial requirements gathering to production monitoring — typically spans four to twelve weeks for a straightforward feed, and can stretch to three to four months for complex multi-system integrations involving custom segment mapping, error handling logic, and compliance with specific data governance rules. For a full enterprise implementation involving dozens of interfaces, the timeline often extends to six to eighteen months. The cost of a single custom point-to-point interface can reach $8,000 or more when labor is factored in, which helps explain why large health systems with hundreds of interfaces face annual integration budgets in the millions.

Interface management does not end at go-live. Every time a source system undergoes a version upgrade — a new EHR release, a lab analyzer software update, a billing system migration — every interface connected to that system must be reviewed, potentially retested, and possibly rewritten. This change management burden is one of the most underestimated costs in healthcare IT. A large hospital system might execute dozens of EHR upgrades and vendor changes per year, each touching multiple interfaces. Interface inventory management — maintaining an accurate, up-to-date catalog of every active interface including its business owner, message types, volume baseline, and dependencies — is considered a best practice but is poorly implemented at many organizations.

Modern interface engines provide monitoring dashboards that track message queue depth, throughput rates, error rates, and acknowledgment latency in real time. A sudden drop in message volume on an ADT feed can indicate that the sending system has crashed or lost network connectivity — catching this through monitoring is far preferable to discovering it when a nurse notices the patient board has stopped updating. Sophisticated engines support dead-letter queues, where messages that cannot be processed are held for human review rather than silently dropped, and reprocessing capabilities that allow a backlog of held messages to be replayed once an issue is resolved. These operational features are often the deciding factor when health systems choose between competing platforms.

When a source system is decommissioned or upgraded, discovering what depends on it becomes an emergency archaeology project. Maintaining a living interface inventory — including business owners, downstream dependencies, and message volume baselines — is not glamorous work, but it dramatically reduces the cost and risk of every future system change.

children.text: The Transition to FHIR: Will Interface Engines Disappear?

FHIR has generated enormous enthusiasm in the interoperability world, and for good reason: it replaces the opaque, pipe-delimited structure of HL7 v2 with clean JSON resources accessible via standard RESTful APIs. ONC and CMS rules now require certified EHRs and payers to expose FHIR US Core APIs, and the UK's NHS, Australia's My Health Record, and health systems in dozens of other countries are embedding FHIR into national interoperability strategies. Organizations implementing FHIR-based integrations report up to 60% reductions in the time required to build new application connections, compared to traditional HL7 v2 interface development.

Despite this momentum, HL7 v2 is not going away on any near-term horizon. In 2024, 95% of U.S. healthcare organizations were still using HL7 v2, and the standard handles an estimated 85% of all healthcare data exchanges. The reason is embedded infrastructure: laboratory instruments, medical devices, legacy pharmacy systems, and decades-old departmental applications speak HL7 v2 natively and will not be replaced simply because a superior standard exists. Replacing every HL7 v2 feed in a large health system would require years of parallel operation, enormous capital investment, and careful change management — resources most health systems are not in a position to commit simultaneously.

The realistic ten-year outlook is a hybrid architecture in which interface engines play a transformed but persistent role. Rather than disappearing, they evolve into v2-to-FHIR translation layers: receiving legacy HL7 v2 messages from clinical systems, converting them to FHIR R4 resources, and handing them off to cloud-based FHIR servers for storage and downstream consumption. Major vendors are already investing in exactly this capability — Rhapsody, InterSystems, and Cloverleaf all support FHIR natively alongside v2. The interface engine of 2030 will look less like a message broker and more like a universal translator standing between a legacy clinical world and a modern API ecosystem. The organizations that navigate this transition most successfully will be those that treat integration as a strategic competency rather than a back-office function.

FHIR is not replacing interface engines — it is giving them a new job. The engine of the future translates HL7 v2 messages from legacy systems into FHIR resources for cloud platforms, serving as the essential bridge between the clinical world that exists and the interoperability world we are building toward.

children.text: Your health data tells a story that spans decades — every diagnosis, every medication, every lab value, every surgery. Yet for most of American healthcare history, patients have been passive observers of that story, unable to read it, let alone share it. Physicians held records in file cabinets. Hospitals locked data inside proprietary systems. Insurers sat on years of claims that patients never saw. The 21st century brought electronic health records, but digitizing a locked file cabinet does not make information free.

That reality is now changing — not because the industry chose transparency voluntarily, but because federal law now mandates it. A converging set of regulations — the 21st Century Cures Act, the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F), and the ONC Cures Act Final Rule — have created enforceable patient rights to electronic health data. APIs are the pipes. FHIR is the language. SMART on FHIR is the security handshake. Together, they are building the infrastructure for true health data portability. This lesson examines the legal foundations of those rights, the technical systems built to fulfill them, the real-world barriers that still limit access, and the road ahead.

children.text: The Original Foundation: HIPAA's Right of Access

Long before FHIR or APIs existed, patients already had a federal right to their health information. The HIPAA Privacy Rule, codified at 45 CFR §164.524, grants every patient the right to inspect and obtain a copy of their protected health information (PHI) maintained in a designated record set. This right covers medical records, billing records, and any other records used to make decisions about the individual.

The mechanics are straightforward on paper. A patient submits a written request to a covered entity — a hospital, physician practice, insurer, or their business associates — and the covered entity must act on that request within 30 calendar days of receipt. A single 30-day extension is permitted if the entity notifies the patient in writing of the reason for delay and provides a date by which it will complete the action. Covered entities may charge a reasonable, cost-based fee — but that fee can only cover labor for copying, supplies, and postage. They cannot charge for retrieving or reviewing the records, a distinction the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) at HHS has repeatedly emphasized in enforcement actions. When a patient uses a patient portal's View, Download, and Transmit functionality, no fee may be charged at all.

Despite this longstanding right, compliance was historically poor. Providers routinely imposed excessive fees, demanded notarized requests, required patients to appear in person, or simply failed to respond within the legally required window. OCR launched a Right of Access Initiative in 2019, specifically targeting providers who delayed, denied, or overcharged patients for their records. The initiative has resulted in dozens of settlements and civil monetary penalties. As recently as December 2024, OCR finalized a $200,000 penalty against OHSU for Right of Access violations, and reached a $60,000 settlement with South Broward Hospital District. These enforcement actions signal that HHS treats patient access as a genuine legal obligation — not a courtesy.

Under HIPAA 45 CFR §164.524, patients have the right to direct their PHI to a third party of their choosing — including a health app, a caregiver, or another provider. Covered entities cannot refuse on the grounds that they do not trust the receiving app or question the patient's reason for sharing.

body.message: HIPAA's Right of Access applies to 'designated record sets' — not necessarily every record a clinician ever created. Psychotherapy notes, certain quality assurance records, and information compiled for legal proceedings may be excluded. The 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking rules extend further, covering all electronic health information (EHI) — a broader category than HIPAA's designated record set.

children.text: 21st Century Cures Act: The Information Blocking Prohibition

The 21st Century Cures Act, signed into law in December 2016, took the concept of patient access and reframed it as a prohibition framework. Rather than simply granting rights to patients, it made it illegal for 'actors' in the healthcare ecosystem — health IT developers, health information networks, and healthcare providers — to engage in practices that interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI). This prohibition, codified in the ONC Cures Act Final Rule at 45 CFR Part 171, took effect April 5, 2021.

The statute defines information blocking broadly: any practice that a provider, health IT developer, or health information network knows is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage access, exchange, or use of EHI — unless the practice falls within a defined exception. ONC codified eight categories of permissible exceptions, including practices necessary to prevent harm, protect privacy, maintain security, comply with other laws, or address infeasibility. If an actor cannot fit their practice within one of these eight exceptions, the practice is presumed to be information blocking. The scope of EHI covered by the prohibition expanded in October 2022 from a subset of structured data to nearly all information in a patient's designated record set — including clinical notes, imaging reports, and behavioral health records.

Enforcement unfolded in stages. ONC began enforcing against health IT developers and health information exchanges on September 1, 2023, with civil monetary penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation. Disincentives for healthcare providers became effective July 1, 2024 — making the prohibition fully operational across all actor types. Providers found to have committed information blocking may lose Meaningful Use status, receive a zero score in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, or be excluded from the Medicare Shared Savings Program for at least one year. A February 2026 HHS announcement of a formal crackdown on health data blocking signals continued and intensifying enforcement.

body.content: A regional hospital system charges patients $1 per page plus a $25 administrative fee to retrieve records requested for care coordination with another provider. Under HIPAA, the $25 fee is impermissible — it covers retrieval, not copying. Under the Cures Act information blocking rules, any policy that systematically discourages patients from exercising their access rights, without a valid exception, could constitute information blocking — even if the fee would survive HIPAA scrutiny. The two frameworks overlap but are not identical; compliance with one does not guarantee compliance with the other.

children.text: CMS-9115-F: The Patient Access API Mandate for Payers

While the 21st Century Cures Act and the ONC Cures Act Final Rule primarily regulate providers and health IT developers, CMS took parallel action on the payer side with the Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F), finalized in May 2020. This rule targets a data trove that patients had almost never been able to access: their insurance claims and clinical data held by Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid managed care organizations, CHIP plans, and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges.

CMS-9115-F requires affected payers to implement a Patient Access API — a FHIR R4-based interface that patients can use to retrieve their own data. The API must expose adjudicated claims and encounter data, clinical data (including laboratory results), prior authorization decisions, and formulary and coverage information. Critically, the rule requires that payers make data available going back to January 1, 2016 — giving patients a multi-year view of their own insurance history, not just recent claims. CMS enforced compliance beginning July 1, 2021 after exercising enforcement discretion through the first half of that year.

The Patient Access API uses SMART on FHIR for authorization. When a patient wants to connect a third-party app to their insurance data, the app redirects the patient to the payer's authorization server. The patient logs in with their insurer credentials and grants the app specific permissions using OAuth 2.0 scopes. The payer's server then issues a time-limited access token — the patient's credentials are never shared with the third-party app. The app presents this token to the FHIR API and retrieves the patient's data. The patient can revoke access at any time through the payer's portal. This architecture brings health insurance data access into alignment with how consumers already authorize apps to access their bank accounts or email.

Subsequent rulemakings have layered additional requirements on top of CMS-9115-F. The 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) added requirements for Prior Authorization APIs, mandating that payers expose prior authorization decisions and timelines via FHIR and publicly report prior authorization metrics beginning in 2026. Each new mandate extends the scope of payer data that patients can access programmatically, steadily dismantling the information asymmetry that has defined the payer-patient relationship for decades.
What Data Does the Patient Access API Expose?
