children.text: Blue Button 2.0, Apple Health Records, and the Patient App Ecosystem

CMS's own implementation of the Patient Access API concept predates CMS-9115-F. Blue Button 2.0 — launched as a production API in 2018 — gives Medicare beneficiaries the ability to authorize third-party apps to access their Medicare Part A (hospital), Part B (outpatient), and Part D (prescription drug) claims and encounter data. The API serves FHIR-formatted data for over 60 million Medicare beneficiaries — one of the largest repositories of longitudinal health claims data in the world. Beneficiaries authorize apps through Medicare.gov, retaining full control over which applications can access their information and for how long.

Blue Button 2.0 demonstrated both the promise and the persistent challenge of patient-facing health data APIs. On the promise side, the program proved that a FHIR API could operate at Medicare's scale — hundreds of millions of claims records served to authorized apps on demand. It attracted dozens of registered production applications spanning personal health management, care coordination, research platforms, and benefits navigation services. On the challenge side, actual beneficiary uptake remained modest: despite the size of the eligible population, the fraction of Medicare's 60 million beneficiaries who connected an app to Blue Button 2.0 was small. Access rights and technical capability do not automatically translate into patient engagement.

Apple Health Records represents perhaps the most visible consumer-facing implementation of FHIR-based patient access. Launched with 12 hospital partners in 2018, the feature uses the FHIR R4 standard and the SMART on FHIR authorization framework to pull clinical records directly into the iPhone Health app. By 2024, more than 500 hospitals and health systems were connected to Apple Health Records. ONC data from 2024 found that 70% of U.S. hospitals enabled patient access via FHIR-configured apps — up from 49% in 2021 — and that 57% of patients used app-based access to medical records, compared to 38% in 2020. The program demonstrates that patients will adopt health data apps when the user experience is genuinely frictionless.

The SMART on FHIR standard, developed originally at Boston Children's Hospital and HL7, provides the authorization layer that makes the app ecosystem interoperable. SMART App Launch version 2.2.0 layers OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect on top of FHIR, providing a standardized way for apps to request specific scopes of patient data, confirm patient identity via OpenID Connect claims, and receive time-limited access tokens. This framework is now required by the ONC Cures Act Final Rule for certified health IT — meaning any EHR vendor seeking ONC certification must support it. The result is a genuine ecosystem: any SMART-compatible patient app can, in principle, connect to any certified EHR, without custom integration work.

body.analogy: Think of SMART on FHIR like the 'Sign in with Google' button that thousands of apps use. You never give the third-party app your Google password — Google's servers verify your identity and issue a limited permission token. SMART on FHIR does the same thing for health data: your EHR or payer verifies who you are and hands the app a time-limited key to specific parts of your record — nothing more, nothing less. The result is consent-based, scoped, revocable access that puts the patient in control.

children.text: The Gap Between Rights and Reality: Persistent Barriers

Despite a robust legal framework and steadily improving technical infrastructure, patient access to health data remains far from universal in practice. ONC's 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) data found that while 77% of individuals nationally were offered online access to their health information, only 65% of those offered access actually used it. Among portal users, only 32% had used the download feature to save a copy of their records, and only 21% had transmitted their records to a third party. The majority of patients with portal access were using it passively — viewing, but not moving, their data.

The barriers are both structural and sociodemographic. On the structural side, patients with care scattered across multiple health systems face fragmentation: a portal from each provider, each requiring separate login credentials, each showing only that system's data. Patients who have seen five specialists in three health systems may need five portals to assemble a complete picture of their care. CommonWell Health Alliance and Carequality — the two major nationwide health information exchange frameworks, both now connected to TEFCA — enable provider-to-provider data sharing across organizations. But patient-initiated cross-provider exchange, where a patient directs their records from one system to another without involving a clinician, remains technically complex and poorly supported in most consumer-facing applications.

On the sociodemographic side, ONC data consistently documents disparities in portal access and use by race, ethnicity, income, education, and geography. Patients with lower health literacy may struggle to interpret clinical notes and lab values even when they can access them. Non-English speakers face language barriers in portal interfaces designed primarily for English-language users. Rural patients may lack reliable broadband for app-based access. Lower-resourced hospitals — small, rural, and Critical Access facilities — lag significantly behind large academic medical centers in deploying FHIR-enabled app APIs, meaning patients at those facilities may not yet have the same technical access as patients at well-resourced systems.

There is also the question of what patients can do once they have their data. A FHIR bundle of clinical data is rich and machine-readable, but it was not designed for lay audiences. Allergy codes, procedure codes, SNOMED-coded diagnoses, and LOINC-coded lab values are meaningful to clinicians and software systems — but a patient staring at a raw FHIR JSON file is not meaningfully informed. The real frontier of patient access is not just getting data out of systems — it is translating that data into actionable insight for the person it belongs to.

In 2024, 70% of U.S. hospitals enabled patient access via FHIR app APIs — up from 49% in 2021. Progress is real, but 30% of hospitals still do not provide this mandated capability, disproportionately affecting patients at small, rural, and Critical Access facilities.
The Road to True Portability: What Comes Next

The regulatory infrastructure built between 2016 and 2024 has established that patients have enforceable rights to their electronic health information. The technical infrastructure — FHIR R4, SMART on FHIR, Patient Access APIs, Blue Button 2.0, TEFCA — has created standardized pipes through which that data can flow. What the ecosystem now needs is the final layer: applications, data intermediaries, and user experiences that make portable health data genuinely useful to patients in the moments that matter.

TEFCA, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement finalized by ONC in January 2022 and operationalized through Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) beginning in 2023, is building the nationwide backbone for patient-directed exchange at scale. CommonWell and Carequality have both committed to TEFCA connectivity, potentially unifying the major nationwide exchange frameworks under a single governance structure. Under TEFCA's Individual Access Services, patients will be able to direct the movement of their records from any TEFCA-connected organization to any other — regardless of which EHR or payer system those organizations use.

The longer-term vision — a single, patient-controlled longitudinal health record — aggregates data from every provider, payer, pharmacy, lab, and device the patient has ever interacted with. Several companies are building toward this model, pulling FHIR data from multiple sources simultaneously using SMART on FHIR and assembling it into a unified timeline. As AI-powered interpretation layers mature, patients may eventually receive not just a copy of their records, but a personalized, plain-language explanation of what those records mean — closing the loop between access and understanding.

Two risks deserve attention as patient access expands. First, privacy: when patients share data with apps via SMART on FHIR, those apps are not necessarily covered entities under HIPAA — they may be regulated only by the FTC, which applies a weaker standard. A patient who shares their Medicare claims with a wellness app may have significantly less protection than they realize. Second, equity: if the apps and platforms that make portable data useful are designed for the already-connected and already-literate patient, the information blocking prohibition will have succeeded technically while failing the patients who most need to benefit from it. True portability is not just a legal right — it is an equity imperative.
Patients should not have to fight for their own health information. Data blocking is a patient safety issue — when records do not follow the patient, care suffers.

points: HIPAA's Right of Access (45 CFR §164.524) gives patients the right to their records within 30 days; fees can only cover copying costs — not retrieval, search, or review.

The 21st Century Cures Act prohibits information blocking by providers, health IT developers, and health information networks under 45 CFR Part 171; full enforcement across all actor types has been active since July 2024.
CMS-9115-F requires Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and QHP payers to expose adjudicated claims and clinical data via FHIR Patient Access APIs, with data going back to January 1, 2016.

Blue Button 2.0 delivers FHIR-formatted Medicare claims data for over 60 million beneficiaries; Apple Health Records connects to 500+ facilities — both use SMART on FHIR for patient-authorized app access.

SMART on FHIR (OAuth 2.0 + OpenID Connect) is the standard authorization layer for patient-facing health apps, required for ONC-certified health IT; it enables consent-based, scoped, revocable access.

As of 2024, 77% of patients were offered portal access but only 65% used it, and only 32% downloaded records — legal access rights and technical availability do not automatically produce patient engagement.
CommonWell, Carequality, and TEFCA are building nationwide exchange infrastructure; patient-directed exchange across system boundaries remains the hardest problem to solve at scale.
The equity frontier: low-resourced hospitals lag in FHIR API deployment; apps that make portable data useful must be designed for patients with low digital literacy and limited connectivity.

result.title: Patient Access to Health Data: Rights, APIs, and the Road to True Portability

children.text: Americans move between jobs, between states, and between life stages. When they do, their health coverage often moves with them or, more precisely, it disappears and reappears in a different form. A factory worker switches from employer-sponsored Medicaid managed care to a Marketplace plan after a layoff. A retiree transitions from commercial insurance to Medicare Advantage. A young adult ages off a parent's plan and enrolls in a state Medicaid program. Each of these transitions is not just an administrative event. It is a potential rupture in the continuity of care. The new payer inherits a member but not a record. The patient's diagnosis history, prior authorization approvals, chronic medication regimen, and recent specialist consultations exist somewhere on a server operated by the previous plan but are invisible to the clinicians and care managers now responsible for that person's health.

This invisibility has real consequences. A care manager at the new plan who does not know about a patient's recent hospitalization cannot schedule appropriate follow-up. A prior authorization reviewer who cannot see a previously approved six-month course of specialty medication may deny continuation, creating an abrupt gap in treatment. A disease management program that does not know a member has diabetes cannot enroll them in population health outreach. Every one of these failures costs money in duplicated diagnostic tests, avoidable hospitalizations, and adverse drug events, and most importantly it costs health. The problem is structural: the health insurance system has historically treated membership data as proprietary, not portable.

Payer-to-payer data exchange is the regulatory and technical effort to fix this structural failure. The concept is straightforward: when a member changes health plans, the new payer should be able to request and receive relevant clinical and administrative data from the previous payer, so that care continues without interruption. The execution has proved far more complex. This lesson traces the regulatory journey from CMS-9115-F's original 2022 mandate through its supersession by CMS-0057-F's January 2027 deadline, explains the technical architecture built on HL7's Da Vinci PDex Implementation Guide, and examines the real-world challenges of member identity matching, consent management, and data operationalization that stand between the regulatory vision and clinical impact.
The Coverage Gap Problem: Who Actually Switches Plans and Why It Matters

The scale of health plan switching in the United States is large enough to constitute a persistent public health challenge in its own right. The problem is most acute in Medicaid, where administrative-driven disenrollment and re-enrollment, a phenomenon researchers call churning, affects tens of millions of people each year. Before the COVID-19 public health emergency froze Medicaid eligibility redeterminations, studies found that among full-benefit Medicaid beneficiaries enrolled at any point in a given year, roughly 10% experienced a gap in coverage of less than one year. Approximately 4% were disenrolled and re-enrolled within three months, and nearly 7% within six months. These are not people who became ineligible for coverage. They are people who lost coverage due to paperwork failures, outdated addresses, or administrative processing errors, and then regained it shortly after.

The Medicaid unwinding that followed the end of pandemic-era continuous enrollment protections in April 2023 provided a stark illustration of this dynamic at extreme scale. States resumed eligibility redeterminations after a pause of more than three years, and over the following two years, more than 25 million people were disenrolled from Medicaid. Studies found that 69% of disenrollments were procedural rather than eligibility-based, meaning the vast majority of people who lost coverage were likely still eligible. Many re-enrolled within weeks or months, but each gap represented a period during which the re-enrolling member was invisible to their plan. Any care coordination, disease management, or prior authorization history accumulated during years of prior enrollment was gone from the new plan's view.

In Medicare Advantage, approximately 10% of the 11.3 million enrollees studied in 2019, roughly 1.2 million people, voluntarily switched plans during the open enrollment period. In the Affordable Care Act Marketplace, switching rates are substantially higher: 43% of enrollees switched plans between 2015 and 2016, driven by premium volatility, insurer exits, and annual re-evaluation of cost-sharing structures. Each of these transitions creates a potential data gap. And unlike Medicaid churning where the member may return to the same plan, Marketplace switching typically involves entirely different payers who have no established data-sharing relationship.

children.text: The root problem: when a member moves from one health plan to another, the new plan has their enrollment demographics but none of their clinical history. Diagnoses, prior authorizations, chronic condition status, and care plans must be rebuilt from scratch at cost to both the member's health and the system's efficiency.
The Regulatory Journey: From CMS-9115-F to CMS-0057-F

The regulatory effort to mandate payer-to-payer data exchange begins with the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule, published May 1, 2020 and commonly cited as CMS-9115-F. This landmark rule required Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plans on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges to implement not only a Patient Access API for members but also a payer-to-payer data exchange process. Specifically, payers were required to, upon member request, send clinical and administrative data to another payer when the member changed plans. The original compliance deadline for the payer-to-payer provisions was January 1, 2022.

That deadline proved aspirational. On December 8, 2021, weeks before the deadline, CMS announced that it would exercise enforcement discretion and not take action to enforce the payer-to-payer provisions of CMS-9115-F. The agency's rationale was candid: the FHIR-based technical standards needed for payer-to-payer exchange had not yet matured to the point where standardized, reliable exchange was feasible at scale. CMS wanted to avoid a situation where payers exchanged data in inconsistent, non-standard formats that would undermine interoperability rather than advance it. The agency committed to addressing the challenges through future rulemaking and delivered on that commitment through CMS-0057-F.

The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule, known as CMS-0057-F, was released on January 17, 2024 and represents the definitive federal framework for payer-to-payer data exchange. The rule establishes that the same categories of impacted payers must implement and maintain a FHIR R4-based Payer-to-Payer API. The compliance deadline is January 1, 2027. The rule explicitly recommends the Da Vinci Payer Data Exchange PDex Implementation Guide as the technical standard for this API, building on the HL7 infrastructure that payers were already deploying for the Patient Access API.

The scope of data that must be exchanged under CMS-0057-F is substantial and specific. Payers must make available adjudicated claims and encounter data excluding provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing details, data classes and elements from the content standards adopted by ONC under USCDI, and prior authorization information excluding drugs. Critically, the rule requires payers to exchange data with a date of service within five years of the exchange request, and for data originating before January 1, 2016, the requirement is limited to data with a service date on or after that date. This means a newly enrolled member can trigger a request for up to five years of claims, clinical data, and prior authorization history from their previous plan.

children.text: How Payer-to-Payer Exchange Works: The PDex Technical Architecture

The technical foundation for payer-to-payer exchange is the Da Vinci Payer Data Exchange Implementation Guide, version 2.2.0, developed by the Da Vinci Project, a collaboration of HL7 and health industry members including payers, providers, and health IT vendors. The PDex IG defines how FHIR R4 resources should be packaged, queried, and exchanged specifically for payer use cases. It establishes the data model covering which FHIR profiles apply to claims, diagnoses, medications, and prior authorizations in a payer context, the access pattern using FHIR RESTful APIs with SMART on FHIR authorization, and the identity-matching operation called $member-match that allows a requesting payer to establish that the member they are asking about is the same person the previous payer has records for.

The $member-match operation is the linchpin of the entire exchange. When a member enrolls with a new payer and consents to data exchange, the new payer does not have the previous plan's internal member ID. What it has is the member's enrollment demographics: name, date of birth, gender, and potentially a subscriber ID from the previous plan if the member can provide it. The $member-match operation allows the new payer acting as the requesting payer to send these demographics to the previous payer's FHIR endpoint and receive back a confirmed patient identifier, specifically a FHIR UMB Unique Member Business identifier, that can then be used to query clinical and administrative data. The operation uses mTLS mutual Transport Layer Security for the connection and OAuth 2.0 dynamic client registration for authorization, ensuring that only verified, credentialed payers can initiate data requests.

The PDex IG supports two exchange patterns: single-member exchange and bulk exchange. Single-member exchange handles individual member data requests, the primary use case when a specific member enrolls and requests their history. Bulk exchange, introduced in PDex v2.2.0, allows a new payer to perform member matching and data requests for large populations simultaneously, for example at the end of an open enrollment period when thousands of new members join at once. Bulk exchange uses the FHIR Asynchronous Request Pattern with an HTTP POST kick-off that returns a 202 Accepted response with a Content-Location status endpoint, followed by polling until a completion manifest referencing NDJSON output files is available. This mirrors the bulk data export pattern already used for provider access and analytics.

body.analogy: Think of payer-to-payer exchange like porting your phone number when you switch carriers. When you leave one carrier, you do not lose your number. You authorize the transfer, your new carrier sends a request to your old carrier using a standardized protocol, and your number follows you. Payer-to-payer exchange works the same way: when you switch health plans, you give consent, your new payer sends a $member-match request to your old payer using FHIR APIs, and your five years of claims history and clinical records follow you to your new plan instead of disappearing when you sign up.

body.title: The Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange Workflow

children.text: The previous payer must respond to data requests within one business day under CMS-0057-F. This tight turnaround is designed to ensure that clinical continuity information is available to the new plan before the first care interaction, not weeks later when the member may have already faced a prior authorization denial or a duplicated diagnostic workup.
What Data Must Flow: Claims, Clinical Records, and Prior Authorizations

The data scope defined by CMS-0057-F for payer-to-payer exchange is deliberately broad. The goal is not merely to transmit a summary. It is to give the new plan enough context to meaningfully continue care. The three primary categories of required data are adjudicated claims and encounter data, USCDI-standard clinical information, and prior authorization history. Each category serves a distinct clinical and administrative purpose, and together they constitute something close to a portable health record from the payer's perspective.

Adjudicated claims and encounter data forms the backbone of the exchange. In FHIR terms, claims are represented primarily through the ExplanationOfBenefit resource, which encodes the provider who rendered care, the date of service, the diagnosis and procedure codes, the amount billed, and the amount paid. Five years of this data gives the receiving plan a longitudinal picture of a member's care utilization: how many times they have been hospitalized, what specialists they regularly see, what chronic conditions drive most of their claims, and what their total cost of care looks like. This information is invaluable for risk stratification, care gap identification, and accurate actuarial modeling. CMS-0057-F explicitly excludes provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing information from the required exchange, focusing the mandate on clinically relevant data rather than financial settlement details.

The USCDI clinical data requirement builds on the United States Core Data for Interoperability standard, which ONC updates annually to define the minimum clinical data set that health IT systems must be able to exchange. In the payer context, USCDI data includes patient demographics, active problems and diagnoses, medications, allergies, immunizations, laboratory results, vital signs, and clinical notes where the payer holds them. Not every payer holds rich clinical data, as some hold only claims. But where clinical data exists, for example from value-based care arrangements that include clinical data feeds from provider networks, it must be included in the exchange. This requirement ensures that exchange is not limited to administrative claims codes but includes the richer clinical context that claims alone cannot convey.

Prior authorization history may be the most operationally critical component of the exchange. A member with a complex condition such as metastatic cancer, multiple sclerosis, or severe rheumatoid arthritis may have an active prior authorization for a specialty medication or an ongoing approval for a home health service. If the new plan does not know about this authorization, its clinical reviewers may treat the member as a new case, requiring them to re-submit clinical documentation, go through a fresh review process, and potentially experience a gap in treatment during the review period. CMS-0057-F requires the previous payer to include prior authorization data in the exchange package, including the service authorized, the authorization number, the dates, and the clinical rationale. For members with active authorizations, this single requirement may be the highest-value element in the entire exchange.

body.content: A 52-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis switches from a Medicaid managed care plan to a Marketplace plan during open enrollment. Her previous plan had an active prior authorization for natalizumab, a high-cost specialty infusion administered monthly. Without payer-to-payer exchange, her new plan's prior authorization team would receive a fresh PA request from her neurologist with no context and might require a step therapy protocol starting with lower-cost alternatives, even though she has already demonstrated failure on multiple prior agents. With payer-to-payer exchange, the new plan receives the prior authorization history including the clinical rationale, the active approval status, and the treatment duration. The care manager can onboard her into the specialty pharmacy program on day one, avoiding a treatment gap that could trigger a relapse.
body.title: Real-World Scenario: Prior Authorization Continuity for a Complex Patient

children.text: The Hard Problems: Identity Matching, Consent, and Data Operationalization

If payer-to-payer data exchange were purely a regulatory and technical standards problem, the January 2027 deadline would be straightforward to meet. The real difficulty lies in three operational challenges that no regulation or implementation guide can fully solve: member identity matching, consent management, and post-ingestion data operationalization. These challenges sit at the intersection of incomplete data, legal complexity, and organizational capability, and industry experience with early implementations suggests they are where most exchange attempts break down in practice.

Member identity matching is the foundational challenge. The $member-match operation in the PDex IG provides a standardized protocol for matching demographics, but it cannot compensate for demographic data quality problems that are endemic to the health insurance industry. Names are recorded inconsistently, with William at one plan and Bill at another. Dates of birth contain transcription errors. Women who have changed their name after marriage may appear under different names at different plans. Addresses are outdated. Social Security Numbers, which would provide a reliable matching key, are not universally collected for privacy reasons and are not included in the FHIR $member-match operation's standard input. The United States has no national patient identifier, a persistent gap in the country's health IT infrastructure, meaning that matching must rely on probabilistic algorithms applied to imperfect demographic data. A match that fails produces no data transfer. A false match could result in the wrong patient's records being disclosed.

Consent management presents its own complexity. CMS-0057-F requires member opt-in consent before a payer can initiate a data request to a previous plan. This sounds straightforward but raises several operational questions. How does the new plan verify that the consent it has obtained is legally sufficient to authorize the previous plan to disclose data? Will one covered entity accept a consent record gathered by another covered entity as sufficient authorization for disclosure under HIPAA? The PDex IG includes consent resource handling within the $member-match workflow, but payers must implement internal processes for capturing, storing, and transmitting consent documentation in a way that both the requesting plan and the disclosing plan trust. For members who have behavioral health or substance use disorder treatment history, categories of data that carry heightened legal protections under 42 CFR Part 2, consent requirements are even more stringent, and the current PDex framework does not yet have a fully standardized solution for segmenting these sensitive records from a bulk exchange.

Post-ingestion operationalization may be the least-discussed but most consequential challenge. A payer can successfully receive a FHIR bundle of ExplanationOfBenefit resources from a previous plan and still fail to use them effectively. This happens when the internal systems receiving the data lack the workflow integration to surface prior authorization history to reviewers at the moment of decision, or when member identity confidence scores from the matching process are not propagated through the data pipeline, leaving care managers uncertain whether they are looking at the right patient's records. A 2025 industry report found that payer-to-payer interoperability most often fails in the post-ingestion layer where member identity confidence, provenance clarity, completeness signaling, workflow routing, and exception handling remain too immature to translate received data into clinical action. Receiving the data and using the data are not the same thing.

body.message: CMS-0057-F establishes a compliance deadline for implementing and maintaining the Payer-to-Payer FHIR API, meaning the technical capability must be in place and functional. But regulatory compliance does not guarantee clinical impact. A payer can pass an API audit and still fail to route prior authorization history to reviewers in time to prevent a treatment gap, or fail to surface a member's chronic condition profile to care managers during onboarding. The measure of true success in payer-to-payer exchange is not whether the API endpoint responds. It is whether the data received improves outcomes for the member who switched plans.

body.title: Payer-to-Payer Exchange: Technical Compliance vs. Clinical Impact

children.text: The Road to 2027 and Beyond: Adoption Landscape and Future Trajectory

With the January 2027 deadline approaching, the health insurance industry faces a substantial implementation sprint. Unlike the Patient Access API where payers had years of experience building FHIR infrastructure and SMART on FHIR authorization before the compliance date arrived, the Payer-to-Payer API introduces genuinely new complexity: payer-to-payer trust frameworks, mTLS endpoint management, bulk member matching, and the operational workflows described above. Early industry assessments suggest that while most large national payers have PDex development programs underway, regional plans and smaller Medicaid managed care organizations face significant resource and technical capability gaps.

The Sequoia Project, a non-profit health IT policy organization, has identified payer-to-payer exchange as a priority for its TEFCA framework expansion. While TEFCA currently focuses primarily on provider-to-provider and provider-to-payer exchange, the Sequoia Project has noted that January 2027 creates an opportunity to connect payer-to-payer exchange into the TEFCA trust fabric, providing participating payers with pre-built trust agreements, endpoint directories, and identity assurance frameworks that individual bilateral agreements cannot efficiently provide. If this integration succeeds, it would address one of the most persistent operational barriers to payer-to-payer exchange: the need for each requesting payer to negotiate individual trust agreements with each potential responding payer, creating an exponential scaling problem in a market with hundreds of health plans.

The longer-term regulatory trajectory points toward increasingly granular and comprehensive data exchange. CMS-0057-F is not the final word on payer-to-payer exchange. It is the framework on which subsequent requirements will be built. Likely areas for future rulemaking include real-time exchange rather than the one-week initiation window currently permitted, expanded data scope to include more structured clinical data as payers acquire it through value-based arrangements, and integration with national patient identity initiatives. The Da Vinci Project continues to evolve the PDex IG, with version 2.2.0 having introduced bulk exchange patterns and improved consent handling, and future versions expected to address behavioral health data segmentation and enhanced provenance requirements.

For members, the potential impact is substantial but conditional on execution quality. A Medicaid member who churns and loses coverage for three months due to a paperwork failure before re-enrolling should, under a fully implemented payer-to-payer exchange regime, have their chronic condition history, active care plans, and prior authorization approvals available to the re-enrolling plan within days rather than requiring months of manual record reconstruction. A Medicare Advantage enrollee who switches plans during open enrollment should not have to re-document their medical history to a new care manager. An ACA Marketplace member who changes plans because their previous insurer exits the market should not lose their oncologist's prior authorization for chemotherapy continuation. These are the outcomes that the regulatory framework is designed to produce, and they will only materialize if payers invest not just in API compliance, but in the operational infrastructure that turns received data into clinical action.

Payer-to-payer exchange is the missing link in health data continuity. The Patient Access API gave members the right to retrieve their own data. Provider access APIs gave clinicians direct access to payer data. Payer-to-payer exchange closes the loop by ensuring that when a member changes plans, their history follows them automatically without requiring the member to personally gather and transport their own records between insurers.

points: CMS-9115-F (2020) originally required payer-to-payer data exchange by January 1, 2022, but CMS exercised enforcement discretion in December 2021 because FHIR standards had not yet matured sufficiently for reliable standardized exchange at scale.

CMS-0057-F (January 2024) supersedes the earlier framework with a definitive mandate: impacted payers must implement a FHIR R4 Payer-to-Payer API by January 1, 2027, exchanging up to 5 years of claims, USCDI clinical data, and prior authorization history.

The technical backbone is the Da Vinci PDex Implementation Guide v2.2.0, which defines the $member-match operation for identity resolution, mTLS and OAuth 2.0 for security, and both single-member and bulk asynchronous exchange patterns.

The $member-match operation resolves the identity problem: the requesting payer submits enrollment demographics and the previous payer returns a confirmed FHIR patient identifier that unlocks the clinical data query, without relying on a national patient identifier that the U.S. does not yet have.

The previous payer must respond to data requests within one business day, and the new payer must initiate the request within one week of member consent and enrollment, ensuring clinically relevant data arrives before the first care interaction.

Three operational challenges dominate real-world implementation: member identity matching failures from demographic data quality problems, consent management complexity especially for sensitive behavioral health records under 42 CFR Part 2, and post-ingestion operationalization failures where received data never reaches clinical workflows.

More than 25 million Medicaid disenrollments occurred during the 2023-2025 unwinding with 69% attributable to administrative rather than eligibility reasons, illustrating the massive scale of the coverage continuity problem that payer-to-payer exchange is designed to address.

Regulatory compliance with the January 2027 API mandate is necessary but not sufficient: the measure of success is whether prior authorization history, chronic condition profiles, and care plans are surfaced to the right people at the right moment to prevent treatment gaps for members who switch plans.

children.text: The Two Fundamental Patterns of Health Data Exchange

Every interoperability transaction in U.S. healthcare ultimately reduces to one of two architectural patterns: a system asks for data it needs right now (query-based, or pull), or a system automatically sends data when something clinically significant happens (event-based, or push). These are not competing standards — they are complementary strategies, each built for a different workflow need. Understanding when to reach for each pattern is one of the most important practical skills in health IT.

Query-based exchange assumes that the receiver knows they need data and knows roughly when to ask for it. A primary care physician opening a patient chart before an annual wellness visit might query a health information network to retrieve recent specialist notes, lab results, or medication lists from other institutions. The request is deliberate, human-initiated, and tied to a moment of care. The network responds with whatever it can locate, and the clinician reviews the results. This model works well for planned encounters and scheduled workflows.

Event-based exchange, by contrast, assumes that something has already happened — a patient was admitted to the emergency department, a lab value crossed a critical threshold, a prescription was filled — and that the receiving party needs to know about it immediately, without waiting to be asked. The originating system pushes a notification or full message to one or more recipients who have subscribed to that type of event. The receiver does not need to poll or remember to check; the information arrives in their workflow automatically. This model is essential for care transitions, population health monitoring, and time-sensitive clinical alerts.

body.analogy: Think of query-based exchange like a library: you walk in when you need a book and search the catalog yourself. Event-based exchange is like a subscription service: the moment the next issue is published, it lands in your mailbox — you never had to ask.
body.concept: Library vs. subscription service as a metaphor for pull vs. push data exchange

body.title: Query-Based vs. Event-Based Exchange at a Glance

children.text: Query-Based Exchange: FHIR, CommonWell, and Carequality

Query-based exchange is the backbone of the two largest U.S. health information networks: CommonWell Health Alliance and Carequality. Both networks enable participating providers to locate and retrieve patient records from other members, regardless of which EHR vendor they use. CommonWell leverages IHE standards — including PIX for patient identity matching, XCA for cross-community document retrieval, and XDS.b for document registration — as well as modern FHIR-based interfaces such as the IHE MHD profile. Carequality overlays governance and legal reciprocity on top of the same technical substrate, enabling providers on CommonWell to exchange with providers on other frameworks such as Epic's CareEverywhere and eHealth Exchange.

The FHIR RESTful model has transformed query-based exchange by making individual clinical data elements — not just documents — retrievable on demand. A FHIR R4 server exposes standardized endpoints such as GET /Patient, GET /Condition, GET /MedicationRequest, and GET /Observation. A requesting system authenticates via SMART on FHIR, presents a patient identifier, and the server returns a JSON bundle containing only the data elements requested. This granularity is a significant upgrade from CDA-based document exchange, where a 200-page continuity of care document might be returned when all a clinician needed was the current medication list.

CommonWell has been investing in transitioning its network toward discrete FHIR resource exchange. Its Record Locator Service (RLS) enables a querying system to discover where a given patient's records reside across member organizations, then retrieve specific FHIR resources such as labs, medications, and allergies — in addition to traditional documents. This combination of a centralized patient identity index and distributed FHIR data retrieval is the emerging architecture for national-scale query-based exchange.

steps.description: The querying system submits patient demographics to a Master Patient Index or Record Locator Service to find matching identifiers at other organizations. CommonWell uses IHE PIX; TEFCA-aligned networks use the TEFCA Common Agreement patient matching requirements.

body.title: How a FHIR Query-Based Exchange Works

children.text: TEFCA, which became fully operational in 2024 with eight designated Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs), is built primarily around query-based document exchange. FHIR-based QHIN-to-QHIN exchange was piloted in 2025, representing the next phase of network evolution from document retrieval toward discrete resource query.
Event-Based Exchange: HL7 v2 ADT, FHIR Subscriptions, and Direct

Event-based exchange has been part of health IT since the earliest days of HL7. HL7 version 2 (v2), first published in 1987 and still running on the majority of hospital interfaces worldwide, is fundamentally an event-driven messaging standard. When something happens in a clinical system — a patient is registered, transferred, or discharged — the system generates a v2 message and pushes it to every downstream system that needs to know. The most common v2 message type for this purpose is the ADT (Admit, Discharge, Transfer) message. ADT A01 signals an admission; ADT A02 signals an intra-facility transfer; ADT A03 signals a discharge. These three message types, along with ADT A04 (registration) and ADT A08 (patient information update), handle the vast majority of care transition notifications in U.S. hospitals today.

The CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (85 FR 25510), finalized in May 2020 and effective April 30, 2021, codified event-based exchange as a federal Condition of Participation. Under 42 CFR 482.24(d), Medicare and Medicaid participating hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, and critical access hospitals (CAHs) that use an EHR must send electronic patient event notifications upon admission, discharge, and transfer to the patient's established primary care practitioner, the patient's established care team, and post-acute care providers with whom the patient has an established relationship. The rule permits hospitals to transmit notifications using HL7 v2 ADT messages, C-CDA summary care records, or FHIR-based APIs, giving flexibility while mandating the workflow.

CMS required hospitals to send ADT event notifications by April 30, 2021. This mandate made event-based exchange a federal compliance requirement for every Medicare- and Medicaid-participating inpatient facility in the country — not just a best practice.

On the modern FHIR side, the R4 Subscription resource introduced a mechanism for clients to register interest in data changes on a FHIR server. However, the original R4 Subscription model — based on criteria strings evaluated against the server's data set — proved difficult to implement consistently across vendors. The FHIR community responded with a significant redesign in R5, introducing SubscriptionTopic resources that define specific event types (such as "patient admitted" or "lab result critical") as canonical, versioned artifacts. Because FHIR R4 remains the dominant version in production systems, HL7 published the Subscriptions R5 Backport Implementation Guide (version 1.2.0-ballot) to extend topic-based subscription semantics to R4 and R4B servers through extensions and profiles, without requiring a full upgrade.

The HL7 Da Vinci Project's Unsolicited Notifications Implementation Guide (version 1.1.0, published April 2025) builds directly on the R5 backport to define a standardized FHIR messaging framework for Admit, Discharge, and Transfer notifications. The Da Vinci Alerts IG specifies FHIR MessageBundle structures for each event type, defines required profiles such as the ADT Notification Condition and ADT Notification Coverage, and describes the roles of Sender, Intermediary (such as an HIE), and Recipient. An intermediary can receive a notification from a hospital and forward it to multiple downstream recipients — PCPs, care managers, post-acute facilities — using a single standardized pipeline.

body.content: A 72-year-old Medicare patient with congestive heart failure presents to an emergency department not affiliated with her primary care practice. The hospital's EHR fires an HL7 v2 ADT A04 (registration) message to its HIE interface engine within seconds of registration. The HIE translates the message to a FHIR MessageBundle conformant with the Da Vinci Alerts IG and routes it to the patient's PCP practice via the practice's care management platform. The care manager sees the alert within three minutes of the patient's arrival, reaches out to the ER care team to share the patient's active medication list and recent echocardiogram, and schedules a transitional care management visit before the patient is discharged. The PCP practice bills a TCM code 99496 — a reimbursable workflow that would not have been triggered without the real-time notification.

children.text: Direct Messaging: Secure Push for Care Coordination

Direct Secure Messaging — often called simply "Direct" — is a push-based interoperability standard built on S/MIME-encrypted email over SMTP, governed by the DirectTrust network of accredited Health Information Service Providers (HISPs). Every certified EHR in the United States must support Direct as a condition of ONC certification. Unlike HL7 ADT, which sends structured event messages to known endpoints registered in an interface engine, Direct allows any credentialed provider to push a C-CDA summary document to any other credentialed provider using a Direct address that looks like a standard email address (provider@hospital.directaddress.net).

Direct is most commonly used for care transition summaries — the transition of care (ToC) and referral documents sent when a patient moves from a hospital to a skilled nursing facility, from a specialist back to a primary care physician, or from one care setting to another. The meaningful use program explicitly required that a C-CDA ToC summary be sent via Direct to the next provider of care upon discharge, making Direct the first federally-mandated push-based exchange mechanism in U.S. healthcare.

Direct has real limitations: it carries documents, not discrete data elements; it has no built-in acknowledgment or delivery confirmation standard; and its query-based counterpart (XCDR, or Direct Query) never achieved wide adoption. Nevertheless, Direct remains widely deployed and relevant, particularly for referral workflows, transition of care summaries, and secure communication between clinicians at different organizations. In many markets, a single patient discharge triggers both a Direct C-CDA push to the receiving facility's Direct address and an HL7 ADT push to the PCP's care management platform — both event-based mechanisms, but serving different receivers and different purposes.

body.message: Direct Messaging is frequently confused with FHIR-based exchange. Direct is an encrypted email protocol that carries C-CDA XML documents. FHIR is a RESTful API standard for structured data resources. They address different problems: Direct delivers a complete clinical summary to a known recipient; FHIR APIs expose queryable, structured data to authorized applications. Modern interoperability strategies often deploy both.
body.title: Common Misconception: Direct Is Not FHIR

children.text: Choosing the Right Pattern: A Decision Framework

Selecting between query-based and event-based exchange is not an either/or decision — most mature interoperability architectures deploy both. The choice of which pattern to use for a given workflow depends on four key variables: the urgency of the information, whether a care event has already occurred, whether the receiver knows to look for data, and the technical capabilities of both the sending and receiving systems.

When urgency is high and a care transition has just occurred — an admission, a discharge, a transfer, a critical lab result — event-based push is almost always the right answer. Waiting for a clinician to manually query for a record that may not yet be associated with the patient in a network index introduces exactly the delay that causes preventable readmissions and medication errors. The receiver needs to know something happened before they know to ask.

When the receiver is initiating a scheduled care encounter and wants to assemble the most complete picture of a patient's history before the visit — annual wellness, specialist consultation, post-acute admission assessment — query-based exchange is more appropriate. The clinician can pull records from multiple institutions, reconcile them against the local record, and use the consolidated view to inform care planning. FHIR RESTful queries through networks like CommonWell/Carequality or TEFCA are well-suited to this use case.

A growing class of workflows benefits from combining both patterns. Payers and care management organizations, for example, may subscribe to ADT event notifications to learn when a member is admitted to any facility in the network. Upon receiving that event, they automatically trigger a FHIR query against the admitting hospital to retrieve the patient's current problem list, active medications, and recent labs — enabling a care manager to contact the patient within hours of admission with a complete clinical picture. This event-triggered query pattern is increasingly common in value-based care programs and is explicitly supported by the Da Vinci Project's broader suite of implementation guides.

Time to notification is measured in minutes, not hours
The receiver doesn't know to look for the data

Regulatory compliance (CMS ADT CoP) is required

body.title: When to Use Each Pattern

children.text: TEFCA and the Evolving Landscape

TEFCA's Common Agreement governs both query-based document exchange and message-based (push) exchange across QHINs. The initial TEFCA launch in 2024 focused on query-based document retrieval — enabling providers to locate and retrieve C-CDA documents across all participating QHINs through a single governance framework. FHIR-based QHIN-to-QHIN exchange, enabling discrete resource queries at national scale, was piloted in 2025 as Stage 3 of the TEFCA implementation roadmap. As TEFCA matures, both query and event-based exchange are expected to be available as first-class exchange modalities within the national network.

body.content: An accountable care organization (ACO) managing 15,000 Medicare beneficiaries subscribes to ADT feeds from every hospital within a 50-mile radius. When an attributed patient is admitted, the ACO's care management platform receives an ADT A01 notification within minutes. The platform automatically fires a series of FHIR GET requests — Condition, MedicationRequest, AllergyIntolerance, Observation (recent labs) — against the hospital's FHIR R4 endpoint. The care manager reviewing the case sees a consolidated view of the admission diagnosis, current medications, and active conditions in a single screen, without any manual chart pulling. The ACO's analytics layer simultaneously flags whether the admission was potentially avoidable, feeding quality improvement workflows.
body.title: Event-Triggered Query in Value-Based Care

children.text: Implementation Considerations and Common Pitfalls

Organizations implementing event-based exchange must solve three technical problems that do not arise in query-based workflows: endpoint management, duplicate notification handling, and patient matching at speed. In a query model, the querying system controls the request and has time to resolve patient identity before retrieving data. In an event-based model, notifications arrive asynchronously and may reference patients using identifiers unfamiliar to the receiving system. A robust ADT notification receiver must be able to match incoming notifications to local patients in near-real time, handle duplicate ADTs for the same event (common in production environments), and route notifications to the correct care team member without manual intervention.

On the sending side, hospitals deploying ADT notifications under the CMS Conditions of Participation must maintain accurate, current lists of the patients' established care providers and their electronic endpoints. A notification sent to an outdated Direct address or decommissioned HL7 endpoint meets the letter of the rule but fails to achieve its clinical purpose. Several intermediary vendors — including Rhapsody, Nuvolo, and CarePort Health (now Altera) — provide ADT notification routing services that maintain endpoint directories and handle delivery confirmation on behalf of hospitals.

FHIR Subscription implementations face their own challenges. The original R4 Subscription model required servers to evaluate arbitrary criteria strings — essentially running live queries — for every data change across the entire resource set, creating significant performance burdens. The topic-based model in R5 and the backport IG shifts this burden from runtime query evaluation to compile-time topic definition: a SubscriptionTopic is a canonical resource that defines exactly which events trigger notifications, reducing server overhead and enabling vendors to optimize notification pipelines. Implementers adopting the Da Vinci Alerts IG should verify that their FHIR server vendor supports the R5 backport SubscriptionTopic extensions before committing to this pattern.

body.message: Event-based exchange, if poorly scoped, can overwhelm care teams with notifications. ADT alerts for every patient encounter — regardless of attribution, care relationship, or clinical urgency — rapidly become noise that clinicians learn to ignore. Effective implementations filter notifications by panel membership, risk score, or care program enrollment, and route alerts to the appropriate team member rather than broadcasting to everyone.
body.title: Alert Fatigue Is a Real Risk

points: Query-based exchange (pull) is initiated by the receiver and best suited for planned encounters, pre-visit chart prep, and longitudinal record assembly; FHIR RESTful APIs and networks like CommonWell/Carequality are the primary mechanisms.

Event-based exchange (push) is initiated by the sender when a clinical event occurs and is essential for care transitions, real-time alerts, and population health monitoring — the receiver does not need to know to ask.
HL7 v2 ADT messages remain the dominant event-based mechanism in U.S. hospitals; ADT A01, A02, A03, and A04 cover the vast majority of care transition notifications.

The CMS Interoperability Final Rule (effective April 30, 2021) mandated that Medicare/Medicaid hospitals send electronic ADT notifications to PCPs and post-acute providers upon admission, discharge, and transfer.

FHIR Subscriptions, and specifically the Da Vinci Unsolicited Notifications IG (v1.1.0), provide a modern, standardized FHIR messaging framework for ADT-type events that integrates with the R5 Subscriptions Backport IG.

Direct Secure Messaging is a widely deployed push mechanism for care transition summary documents (C-CDA) but carries documents — not discrete FHIR resources — and is complementary to, not a replacement for, ADT notifications.
Event-triggered query — subscribing to ADT events and then automatically firing FHIR GET requests for discrete data — is the emerging pattern for value-based care and ACO care management workflows.
Alert fatigue is a real implementation risk; effective event-based exchange requires filtering by panel membership, risk stratification, and intelligent routing to prevent notification overload.

body.explanation: Event-based ADT notification is the correct answer because the practice needs to be informed of the admission event in real time — without having to proactively query or wait until discharge. Query-based exchange requires the practice to know when and where to ask; Direct messaging occurs at discharge, too late for proactive transitional care management outreach. The ADT push model is exactly what the CMS ADT Conditions of Participation was designed to mandate and support.

Event-based ADT notification, where the hospital pushes an admission notification to the practice's care management platform in real time upon patient registration.

body.question: A primary care practice wants to be notified within minutes whenever one of their attributed patients is admitted to any hospital in the region, so they can proactively reach out and schedule a transitional care management visit. Which interoperability pattern is best suited for this workflow?

children.text: The Problem SMART Solves: Vendor Lock-In and the Closed EHR

Before SMART on FHIR, integrating a third-party application with an EHR was an expensive, bespoke engineering project. Every major EHR vendor — Epic, Cerner, Allscripts — had its own proprietary API, its own authentication scheme, and its own data model. A clinical decision support tool built for Epic needed to be almost entirely rewritten to run in Cerner, and then rewritten again for Meditech. The result was that innovation happened slowly, mostly inside large vendors, while smaller companies with genuinely useful ideas could not afford the integration tax required to reach clinicians at scale.

The conceptual breakthrough came in 2010 when researchers at Harvard Medical School and Boston Children's Hospital launched a project called Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies — SMART. Led by physician-informaticist Josh Mandel, the project's explicit goal was to create an "app store for healthcare": a standard platform layer so that a developer could write an application once and run it, unmodified, on any EHR that supported the standard. Early SMART used its own clinical data models (now called SMART Classic). In the second half of 2013, the team updated the platform to use the emerging HL7 FHIR standard for data exchange, giving birth to SMART on FHIR. The new platform debuted publicly at the HIMSS conference in February 2014, with prototype demonstrations from several commercial EHR vendors and app developers.

The fundamental promise of SMART on FHIR is separation of concerns. The EHR remains responsible for storing and managing clinical data. The SMART framework provides a standardized mechanism for a third-party application to request access to that data, receive permission from the user, and launch inside the clinical workflow — all without the EHR vendor having to build the feature themselves. For the first time, the EHR could become an extensible platform rather than a monolithic silo.

children.text: How SMART on FHIR Works: OAuth 2.0 Meets the Clinical Workflow

At its core, SMART on FHIR is a profile on top of two well-established internet standards: OAuth 2.0 for authorization and HL7 FHIR for clinical data. OAuth 2.0 is the same protocol that powers "Sign in with Google" and "Connect with Facebook" across the web — a battle-tested framework for letting a user grant a third-party application limited access to their data without sharing their password. SMART on FHIR adapts this framework specifically for the healthcare context, adding the concept of clinical launch context (which patient is currently on the screen?), healthcare-specific scopes, and EHR-embedded app launching.

body.analogy: Imagine the EHR is a secured apartment building. OAuth 2.0 is the intercom system. When a SMART app wants in, it rings the intercom (authorization request). The resident — the clinician or patient — decides whether to buzz the app in (grant consent). The building then issues a temporary keycard (access token) that only opens the specific doors the resident approved. The app never learns the master key.
body.concept: SMART on FHIR uses OAuth 2.0 to grant apps time-limited, scoped access to EHR data — never the master credentials.

children.text: SMART defines two primary launch patterns. In the EHR Launch flow, the EHR initiates the sequence: a clinician clicks an app icon inside the EHR interface, and the EHR passes a launch token and the FHIR server base URL to the app. The app uses these to request an authorization code, which it exchanges for an access token along with the current patient context (patient ID, encounter ID, practitioner ID). The app then uses the access token to call FHIR APIs and retrieve the data it needs — all without the clinician needing to log in again or manually identify the patient. In the Standalone Launch flow, the app starts independently (e.g., from a mobile phone or patient portal) and prompts the user to select a patient or log in directly. Both flows use the same underlying OAuth 2.0 authorization code exchange mechanism.

children.text: SMART scopes are the permission language of the framework. They follow the pattern context/ResourceType.action. The context is patient (data limited to the in-context patient), user (data the logged-in user can see), or system (machine-to-machine, no user in the loop). The ResourceType is any FHIR resource name such as Observation, MedicationRequest, or Condition. The action is read (r), search (s), or write (c, u, d). So patient/Observation.rs means "read and search Observations for the current patient." Scopes give EHR administrators fine-grained control over what any given app is permitted to access, and users can review exactly what permissions they are granting before approving.
The SMART App Gallery and Real-World Clinical Use Cases

SMART Health IT maintains a publicly accessible App Gallery at apps.smarthealthit.org where developers can list applications built on the SMART standard. The gallery is organized by audience (clinicians, patients, researchers) and serves as a discovery mechanism for healthcare organizations evaluating third-party tools. Dozens of clinical applications are listed, spanning cardiovascular risk, pain management, oncology, mental health, and population analytics — demonstrating that the platform has moved well beyond proof-of-concept into active clinical use at institutions including Boston Children's Hospital and Duke Medicine.

Several production SMART apps illustrate the breadth of what the platform enables. The ASCVD Risk Calculator, embedded in EHRs at multiple institutions, pulls a patient's lab results, demographics, and medication list via FHIR and computes a 10-year cardiovascular risk score in real time — without the clinician copying any data. The Pain Management Summary dashboard aggregates opioid prescription history, pain assessments, and PDMP data into a single view, supporting safer prescribing decisions. COSRI (Clinical Opioid Summary with Rx Integration) connects directly to state Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs via SMART. Each of these apps runs inside the EHR workflow, launched with a single click, and presents information in the context of the patient already on screen.

CDS Hooks is the complementary standard that extends SMART's reach into proactive clinical decision support. Where SMART apps are user-launched, CDS Hooks allows external services to automatically fire decision support suggestions at defined moments in the clinical workflow — when a medication is ordered, when a patient's chart is opened, or when a diagnosis code is entered. The SMART project team at Harvard Medical School has led the development of CDS Hooks as part of the broader FHIR-based interoperability ecosystem, and the two standards are designed to work together: a CDS Hook suggestion can launch a SMART app for deeper investigation or action. Together they represent a complete architecture for embedded clinical intelligence.

children.text: SMART Backend Services: Machine-to-Machine Authorization

Not every FHIR integration involves a human sitting at a keyboard. Population health analytics platforms, payer data pipelines, automated quality reporting systems, and Bulk FHIR export jobs all need to authenticate against a FHIR server without a user present. The SMART Backend Services specification, published by HL7 International as part of the SMART App Launch Implementation Guide, defines exactly how to handle this scenario. It uses the OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials grant flow, adapted for healthcare, with JSON Web Token (JWT) assertions for client authentication.

The SMART Backend Services flow works as follows. The client system is pre-registered with the FHIR authorization server and is assigned a set of pre-authorized scopes — for example, system/Patient.rs and system/Observation.rs, which grant read and search access to those resources for all patients the client has been authorized to access. At runtime, the client generates a short-lived, one-time-use authentication JWT signed with its private key. It posts this JWT to the authorization server's token endpoint using a standard OAuth 2.0 client credentials request. The server validates the JWT signature against the client's registered public key, confirms the pre-authorized scopes, and issues an access token. The client then uses this token to call FHIR APIs — including the $export operation for Bulk FHIR — without any human interaction. The specification requires TLS 1.2 or higher for all exchanges.

SMART Backend Services is the authorization backbone for the Bulk FHIR ecosystem. When a hospital system needs to export a million patient records to a population health vendor for annual quality reporting, or when a payer needs to automatically retrieve claims-linked clinical data, Backend Services provides the secure, auditable, machine-to-machine credential exchange that makes it possible. Unlike the EHR Launch flow, there is no consent screen — the data access has been negotiated and pre-authorized at the system administration level, with appropriate Business Associate Agreements in place. This makes Backend Services powerful but also requires careful governance: the scopes granted to a backend client should follow the principle of least privilege, requesting only the resource types and actions the pipeline genuinely needs.

body.message: SMART Backend Services does not involve a real-time consent screen. Access is granted based on prior administrative agreements between the client system and the FHIR server. Organizations deploying backend clients must ensure appropriate data use agreements, audit logging, and scope minimization policies are in place before go-live.
body.title: Backend Services Requires Pre-Authorization

children.text: Regulatory Mandate: How SMART on FHIR Became Required Law

SMART on FHIR moved from an academic research project to a federal legal requirement through the 21st Century Cures Act and the ONC's Health IT Certification Program. The 2015 Edition Certified EHR Technology (CEHRT) rules first introduced FHIR-based API requirements. The 2015 Edition Cures Update — implementing the Cures Act final rule — went significantly further. It replaced the earlier SMART v1 App Launch Framework with the SMART App Launch Implementation Guide Release 2.0.0 (SMART v2) as the required standard. Any EHR seeking ONC certification must now support SMART on FHIR compliant application access, including verifying SMART authorization flows, refresh tokens, and token revocation as part of the certification testing process.

The three largest EHR vendors have built developer ecosystems around SMART on FHIR. Epic's App Orchard (now called the Epic Showroom) is a vetted marketplace where third-party developers list SMART-compatible applications. Developers register their apps, receive sandbox credentials, and go through a validation process before their apps can be deployed at Epic customer sites. Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) operates the Code Console developer portal, where developers register SMART applications, configure redirect URIs, and access Cerner Millennium sandbox environments. Validated integrations can be listed on the Oracle Healthcare Marketplace. These marketplaces collectively represent hundreds of commercially available SMART applications across clinical decision support, patient engagement, revenue cycle, and population health.

The SMART brand has also extended beyond EHR integration into patient-held credentials through SMART Health Cards. Developed in response to COVID-19 by the Vaccination Credential Initiative — a coalition that included Epic, Cerner, Microsoft, Salesforce, and dozens of health systems — SMART Health Cards use a combination of W3C Verifiable Credentials and HL7 FHIR to encode vaccination records as cryptographically signed QR codes. By January 2022, approximately 80% of Americans who had received a COVID-19 vaccine had access to a SMART Health Card through state health departments, healthcare systems, pharmacies, and employer portals. The same technical framework is now being extended to other health documents including lab results, insurance cards, and referral authorizations — demonstrating that the SMART ecosystem has grown far beyond its original EHR launch use case.
