children.text: Every day, billions of clinical observations, diagnoses, prescriptions, and lab results move between hospitals, pharmacies, payers, and public health agencies. But data moving between systems is not the same as data being understood by those systems. A lab result labeled 'Glucose' in one EHR might arrive at a receiving system as a free-text string with no machine-readable meaning. A diagnosis coded 'Type 2 DM' in one notation may be opaque to a clinical decision support engine expecting a different code. Without a shared vocabulary — a universal clinical language — every data exchange risks producing noise instead of knowledge.

Three terminologies sit at the heart of clinical data interoperability in the United States: SNOMED CT for clinical concepts (diseases, findings, procedures), LOINC for observations and measurements (lab tests, vital signs, assessments), and RxNorm for medications and drugs. Together, these standards form the computable foundation that allows software to reason about patient data rather than merely store it. Federal regulators — ONC, CMS, and the HHS Office of the National Coordinator — mandate their use in certified EHR systems and FHIR-based APIs, making fluency in these vocabularies non-negotiable for any healthcare interoperability professional.

body.analogy: Think of SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm as three different dictionaries in a single clinical language. SNOMED CT is the medical encyclopedia — it defines what conditions, procedures, and findings are. LOINC is the measurement handbook — it defines what was tested or observed and how. RxNorm is the pharmacy formulary — it defines what was prescribed and in what form. A complete clinical picture requires all three.

children.text: SNOMED CT: The Clinical Concept Backbone

SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine — Clinical Terms) is the world's most comprehensive multilingual clinical healthcare terminology. Governed by SNOMED International, a nonprofit standards development organization founded in 2007, SNOMED CT is licensed in more than 40 countries and serves as the preferred vocabulary for encoding clinical findings, diagnoses, symptoms, procedures, body structures, organisms, and substances within electronic health records.

The January 2020 International Edition already surpassed 350,000 active concepts, and the terminology continues to grow with each biannual release. In the US, NLM distributes the US Edition of SNOMED CT — which extends the International Edition with US-specific content — through the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) Terminology Services. Users must accept the UMLS Metathesaurus License Agreement and hold a UMLS account; for US-based healthcare organizations, access is free of charge as part of a national arrangement managed through the NLM.
Structure: More Than a Code List

Unlike ICD-10-CM — which is a flat classification system built primarily for billing and epidemiology — SNOMED CT is a poly-hierarchical, description logic-based terminology. Each concept has a unique numeric identifier (ConceptID), one or more human-readable descriptions (Fully Specified Name, Preferred Term, synonyms), and a set of relationships to other concepts that define its meaning formally. A concept like 'Type 2 diabetes mellitus' carries relationships expressing that it is a subtype of diabetes mellitus, involves the pancreas, and is associated with insulin resistance — information that a classification code alone cannot convey.

The two systems are complementary, not competing. The NLM publishes and maintains an official SNOMED CT-to-ICD-10-CM map that enables semi-automated billing code generation from SNOMED CT-encoded clinical data. This means a clinician can document in SNOMED CT for clinical precision, and the EHR can automatically suggest the correct ICD-10-CM billing code — reducing administrative burden while preserving clinical fidelity.

USCDI and ONC Mandate: The ONC HTI-1 Final Rule requires certified health IT to use SNOMED CT US Edition for clinical conditions and problems. USCDI v3 — mandatory for certified EHRs by January 2026 — specifies SNOMED CT as the required terminology for the Problems data class. The March and September US Edition releases ensure providers have access to the latest concepts for compliance.
LOINC: Naming What Was Tested or Observed

LOINC (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes) provides the universal standard for identifying medical laboratory observations, clinical measurements, and health assessments. Developed and maintained by the Regenstrief Institute — a health informatics research organization at Indiana University — LOINC was created in 1994 and has grown into one of the most widely adopted health data standards in the world. As of 2023, LOINC contains approximately 101,632 terms covering everything from a routine serum albumin level to a zygomatic arch X-ray report, with thousands of new concepts added in each semiannual release.
What LOINC Names

LOINC's primary focus is answering the question: 'What was measured or observed, and how?' Every LOINC code represents a unique combination of up to six defining attributes — the component (analyte), the property being measured (e.g., mass concentration), the time aspect (point in time vs. 24-hour collection), the system (specimen type — serum, urine, blood), the scale of measurement (quantitative, ordinal, narrative), and optionally the method used. This six-part axis structure means that a serum sodium measured on a point-in-time specimen with a quantitative result gets a different LOINC code than a 24-hour urine sodium — even though both measure 'sodium.'

body.content: LOINC 2951-2: Sodium [Moles/volume] in Serum or Plasma. This code specifies: Component = Sodium; Property = Substance Concentration (SCnc); Time = Point; System = Serum/Plasma; Scale = Quantitative. A receiving laboratory information system can parse this code and know exactly what to render, what units to expect, and how to alert on abnormal values — without any free-text parsing.

children.text: LOINC's reach extends well beyond the clinical laboratory. Survey instruments and functional assessments — including the PHQ-9 depression screen, the GAD-7 anxiety scale, and dozens of social determinants of health (SDOH) screenings — are encoded in LOINC. Vital signs such as blood pressure, heart rate, body weight, and oxygen saturation have standardized LOINC codes used in FHIR Observation resources. Document types (discharge summaries, progress notes, operative reports) also carry LOINC codes, enabling document-level indexing and retrieval across health systems.

LOINC is the mandated standard for laboratory tests in USCDI v3 and for the Observations data class in US Core FHIR profiles. CMS and ONC require LOINC codes on all structured lab result data exchanged via FHIR APIs as part of the 21st Century Cures Act regulations.
LOINC and the Lab Ecosystem

The Regenstrief Institute collaborates extensively with the FDA, CDC, and the Association of Public Health Laboratories (APHL) to create LOINC codes for emerging needs. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Regenstrief team rapidly created dedicated LOINC codes for SARS-CoV-2 diagnostic tests — enabling consistent surveillance reporting across all 50 states within weeks of the first tests becoming available. This agility illustrates why LOINC is indispensable for public health response: without standardized observation codes, surveillance data from thousands of labs would have been irreconcilable.
RxNorm: Making Drug Data Interoperable

RxNorm is the National Library of Medicine's standardized nomenclature for clinical drugs. First introduced as a full monthly release in 2005, RxNorm celebrated its 20th anniversary in 2025. Its core purpose is deceptively simple but enormously powerful: assign a single normalized name and unique identifier (called an RxCUI — RxNorm Concept Unique Identifier) to each distinct combination of active ingredient, strength, and dose form, regardless of which manufacturer made it or what brand name it carries.
The Problem RxNorm Solves

Drug naming in the United States is a labyrinth. A single active ingredient may appear under dozens of brand names across hundreds of National Drug Code (NDC) entries — each representing a specific manufacturer, package size, and labeler. Metformin hydrochloride 500 mg oral tablet, for instance, might have hundreds of distinct NDC codes from different generic manufacturers. Without normalization, a clinical decision support rule written against one NDC would miss all the others. A pharmacist's allergy alert system would fail to recognize a therapeutic duplicate if the incoming order used a different brand name than the one in its database.

RxNorm resolves this fragmentation by mapping all NDC codes for equivalent drug products to a single RxCUI representing the normalized clinical drug concept. The December 2025 RxNorm full release contains 14,592 base ingredients, 17,544 clinical drug entries, and 9,721 branded drug entries. NLM normalizes NDCs to the 11-digit HIPAA format without dashes, ensuring consistent identification. RxNorm also models relationships between concepts: an ingredient links to all its dose forms, which link to all their strengths, which link to all NDC packages — creating a navigable drug knowledge graph.

body.content: A patient is prescribed 'Metformin HCl 500 mg oral tablet' (RxCUI: 860975). This single RxCUI represents the normalized concept regardless of whether the dispensed product is from Teva, Mylan, or any other manufacturer. An EHR sending a FHIR MedicationRequest with this RxCUI allows any receiving system — a pharmacy, a care management platform, a payer — to unambiguously identify what was prescribed without needing to know the specific NDC.

body.message: NDC codes are NOT suitable for clinical interoperability on their own. They encode manufacturer, package size, and labeler — not the clinical drug concept. A clinical decision support rule built on NDC codes must be updated every time a manufacturer changes packaging or enters the market. RxNorm abstracts above this variability to support durable, maintainable clinical logic.

children.text: RxNorm is designated as the required standard for medication information in USCDI, and the HTI-1 Final Rule mandates the July 2022 RxNorm Full Monthly Release (or later) as the minimum standard for certified health IT systems as of December 31, 2025. FHIR MedicationRequest, MedicationDispense, and MedicationAdministration resources in US Core all require RxNorm codes for medication representation.
How SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm Work Together

In a modern EHR or FHIR-based health information exchange, these three terminologies operate as complementary layers of a unified clinical data model. SNOMED CT encodes the clinical context — the patient's conditions, findings, and procedures. LOINC encodes the observations that inform that context — the lab test that confirmed a diagnosis, the vital sign that prompted an intervention. RxNorm encodes the therapeutic response — the medication prescribed as a result. Together, they make a complete clinical record computable.

steps.title: A patient presents with fatigue and polyuria. The clinician's EHR problem list captures 'Suspected Type 2 diabetes mellitus' using SNOMED CT concept 73211009.
The clinician orders a fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c. The orders carry LOINC codes 1558-6 (Fasting glucose in serum/plasma) and 4548-4 (Hemoglobin A1c/Hemoglobin.total in Blood).
Results return from the laboratory with LOINC-coded observation codes and UCUM-coded units, enabling automated interpretation and alert generation.
Diagnosis confirmed: the problem list is updated to 'Type 2 diabetes mellitus' (SNOMED CT 44054006). The ICD-10-CM map automatically suggests E11.9 for billing.
Metformin 500 mg oral tablet is prescribed. The MedicationRequest carries RxCUI 860975 alongside the NDC for the specific dispensed package.
The complete, coded record — conditions in SNOMED CT, labs in LOINC, medications in RxNorm — flows to the payer, care manager, and public health registry without loss of meaning.

children.text: Value Sets: Curating Subsets for Specific Purposes

Raw terminologies contain hundreds of thousands of concepts, but most clinical applications need only relevant subsets. A quality measure for diabetes management needs only the SNOMED CT codes for type 2 diabetes mellitus — not all 350,000 concepts. A FHIR-based allergy list needs only the RxNorm codes for common allergens. These curated subsets are called value sets, and the Value Set Authority Center (VSAC) — maintained by the NLM — is the authoritative repository for value sets used in US clinical quality measures and regulatory requirements.

VSAC serves as the official source for value sets used in CMS electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) and digital quality measures (dQMs). Each value set consists of carefully selected codes drawn from SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, ICD-10-CM, and other standard vocabularies, with explicit versioning tied to specific terminology releases. As CMS transitions its eCQMs to FHIR-based dQMs — with FHIR-formatted value sets available for the 2027 reporting period — VSAC becomes an even more critical infrastructure component, linking regulatory requirements directly to computable clinical terminology.

VSAC Integration: Any certified EHR or quality reporting system participating in CMS quality programs must implement value sets from VSAC. These value sets reference specific versions of SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm — meaning a terminology update in one vocabulary can cascade into required value set updates across the entire quality measurement ecosystem.
Cross-Terminology Mapping

The SNOMED CT-to-ICD-10-CM map is the most widely used cross-terminology map in US healthcare, enabling automated generation of billing codes from clinical documentation. Similarly, the SNOMED CT-to-LOINC collaboration — formalized as the SNOMED-LOINC ontology — defines formal relationships between SNOMED CT clinical concepts and LOINC observation codes, enabling richer semantic queries. For example, the SNOMED CT concept for 'Measurement of serum creatinine' can be formally linked to LOINC 2160-0 (Creatinine [Mass/volume] in Serum or Plasma), allowing a FHIR server to answer queries that span both terminologies seamlessly.
Real-World Impact: When Vocabularies Fail — and When They Succeed

The stakes of clinical terminology interoperability are not abstract. When terminologies are absent, inconsistent, or incorrectly mapped, the consequences range from administrative inefficiency to direct patient harm. The U.S. healthcare system loses an estimated $30 billion annually in avoidable inefficiencies — including unnecessary repeat diagnostics, delayed treatment decisions, and administrative overhead — that can be traced in part to poor data interoperability at the semantic level.
Terminology Failures in Practice

Consider a patient with a documented penicillin allergy in one hospital's EHR system. When that patient transfers to a different hospital or visits an urgent care clinic, their record arrives as a PDF or a raw HL7 v2 message with a free-text allergy field reading 'PCN allergy.' The receiving EHR's clinical decision support engine, which checks for SNOMED CT-coded allergy concepts, does not recognize 'PCN allergy' as a coded entry. The alert does not fire. Without the proper SNOMED CT allergy concept code (e.g., 372687004 — Allergy to penicillin), the safety net disappears at the exact moment the patient crosses organizational boundaries.

Medication errors are another critical failure mode. A clinician attempting to prescribe 3.125 mg of carvedilol (a common heart failure dose) may find the EHR's medication picker lists only 6.25 mg tablets — because the EHR was not mapped to the correct RxNorm concepts for the 3.125 mg strength (RxCUI 200256). The clinician must manually override, creating both cognitive burden and documentation ambiguity. When RxNorm normalization is incomplete or out of date, these gaps propagate across e-prescribing, pharmacy dispensing, and medication reconciliation workflows.

body.content: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the rapid creation of LOINC codes for SARS-CoV-2 tests (e.g., LOINC 94500-6 for the SARS-CoV-2 RNA PCR test) enabled the CDC to aggregate standardized lab results from thousands of testing sites across the country within a unified surveillance framework. States that had already implemented LOINC-coded lab reporting could contribute data within days. Those relying on free-text or non-standard codes required manual curation, introducing delays of days to weeks into public health surveillance — a real-world demonstration of what standardized terminology makes possible at scale.

children.text: ONC and CMS Enforcement

Federal regulations have progressively tightened terminology requirements to address these failure modes. The 21st Century Cures Act established information blocking prohibitions and required ONC-certified health IT to support USCDI data elements with required terminologies. The HTI-1 Final Rule (effective 2025) mandates specific minimum releases of SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm in certified systems. By July 4, 2026, networks participating in TEFCA (Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement) must expose data via FHIR APIs aligned with US Core IG and USCDI v3 — with labs coded in LOINC, medications in RxNorm, and conditions in SNOMED CT. Non-compliance carries information blocking penalties of up to $1 million per violation under ONC enforcement authority.
The goal is not just data exchange — it is data understanding. A lab result that cannot be interpreted by the receiving system is not interoperability; it is just file transfer.

The convergence of regulatory pressure, FHIR adoption, and value-based care incentives is accelerating the transition from free-text and proprietary coding to standardized, computable vocabularies. Health systems that invest in clean SNOMED CT problem lists, LOINC-coded lab results, and RxNorm-normalized medication records today are building the data foundation for AI-driven clinical decision support, population health analytics, and seamless patient data portability that will define the next decade of healthcare.

points: SNOMED CT (350,000+ concepts) is the world's most comprehensive clinical terminology, governed by SNOMED International and distributed in the US by NLM via UMLS with a free UMLS license.

LOINC (~101,600 terms) is the universal standard for naming lab tests, vital signs, and clinical observations, maintained by the Regenstrief Institute and required by USCDI for the Observations data class.

RxNorm, managed by NLM, normalizes drug names to ingredient + strength + dose form (RxCUI), solving the NDC fragmentation problem and enabling durable clinical decision support across all medications.
SNOMED CT and ICD-10-CM serve different purposes: SNOMED CT captures clinical meaning at the point of care; ICD-10-CM classifies for billing. The NLM SNOMED-to-ICD map bridges them automatically.

VSAC (Value Set Authority Center) is the NLM-maintained authoritative repository for curated terminology subsets used in CMS quality measures and regulatory reporting, now transitioning to FHIR-based dQMs.
ONC's HTI-1 Final Rule and USCDI v3 (mandatory for certified EHRs by January 2026) legally require SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm for specific FHIR data elements across all certified health IT systems.

Terminology failures — free-text drug names, uncoded allergy entries, non-standard lab identifiers — contribute to $30+ billion in annual US healthcare inefficiency and create direct patient safety risks.
FHIR US Core Implementation Guide binds these three terminologies to specific resource types: Condition → SNOMED CT, Observation/DiagnosticReport → LOINC, MedicationRequest → RxNorm.

body.explanation: LOINC is the standard for laboratory observations, including serum sodium (LOINC 2951-2). Without a LOINC code, the receiving system has no machine-readable way to identify the analyte, units, specimen type, or scale — making automated interpretation, clinical decision support, and duplicate detection impossible. The result exists as data but cannot be acted upon as information.

options.text: RxNorm — the receiving pharmacy will not be able to dispense the correct electrolyte supplement.
SNOMED CT — the receiving EHR cannot classify the finding under the correct diagnosis hierarchy.
LOINC — the receiving system cannot reliably interpret what was measured, risking misinterpretation or duplicate testing.
ICD-10-CM — the claim for the lab test cannot be submitted without the correct procedure code.

children.text: What Is USCDI?

The United States Core Data for Interoperability — universally abbreviated as USCDI — is a standardized set of health data classes and constituent data elements that ONC (the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology) has designated as the minimum dataset required for nationwide, interoperable health information exchange. Think of USCDI as the federal government's official answer to a fundamental question: when any two health IT systems in the United States share patient data, which fields must both sides be capable of sending and receiving?

USCDI was first published in July 2020 as part of the ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule. Before USCDI existed, its predecessor — the Common Clinical Data Set (CCDS) — served a similar purpose, but lacked the structured versioning and annual update cycle that USCDI introduced. USCDI is not a FHIR implementation guide, a claims format, or a coding system. It sits one level above all of those: it defines *what* data must be interoperable, leaving the technical *how* to implementation guides like HL7 FHIR US Core.

USCDI defines the minimum dataset for interoperability — it tells the healthcare ecosystem which data elements every certified health IT system must be able to exchange, regardless of vendor or care setting.

The standard is managed entirely by ONC, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). ONC maintains USCDI through an open, publicly participatory process: any stakeholder — a hospital, a health IT developer, a patient advocacy group, or an individual clinician — can submit new data element proposals via the ONC New Data Element and Class (ONDEC) Submission System. Submissions go through a maturity-level review. Elements that reach Level 2 maturity by October of a given year are eligible for inclusion in the following year's draft USCDI, which is published in January. After public comment and review by the Health IT Advisory Committee (HITAC), the final version is published each July.

children.text: USCDI Version History: From v1 to v6

ONC has published new USCDI versions every year since 2020, each one expanding the required dataset to reflect evolving clinical practice, public health priorities, and equity goals. Understanding the version history helps explain why compliance timelines vary across programs and why EHR vendors may support different versions simultaneously.
Version 1 — July 2020

USCDI v1 was the first published version and became the regulatory baseline for Certified EHR Technology (CEHRT) under the 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule. It encompassed 52 data elements across 16 data classes. Key additions over the predecessor CCDS included Clinical Notes, Provenance, Pediatric Vital Signs, and patient Address. USCDI v1 set the floor for what any ONC-certified EHR must be capable of exchanging.
Version 2 — July 2021

USCDI v2 added three new data classes and 22 new data elements, with an explicit focus on advancing health equity. The most significant additions were Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (SOGI) data elements — long requested by LGBTQ+ health advocates — and Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) data elements that allow clinicians to document housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers.
Version 3 — July 2022 (Now the Regulatory Baseline)

USCDI v3 is the most consequential version to date from a regulatory standpoint. The HTI-1 Final Rule, effective February 2024, adopted USCDI v3 as the new baseline standard for certified health IT. Importantly, ONC mandated that all health IT modules certified to criteria referencing USCDI must upgrade to v3 by January 1, 2026 — a hard compliance deadline that is reshaping EHR upgrade cycles across the industry. USCDI v3 expanded to 19 data classes and 94 data elements.

The 19 data classes in USCDI v3 cover: Allergies and Intolerances, Assessment and Plan of Treatment, Care Team Members, Clinical Notes, Clinical Tests, Diagnostic Imaging, Encounter Information, Goals, Health Insurance Information (new in v3), Health Status/Assessments (new in v3, absorbing Health Concerns), Immunizations, Laboratory, Medications, Patient Demographics/Information, Problems, Procedures, Provenance, Referral Notes, and Vital Signs. New equity-focused data elements include Disability Status, Mental/Cognitive Status, Functional Status, and Pregnancy Status.
USCDI v3 is the current mandatory baseline. All ONC-certified EHRs must support v3 by January 1, 2026 under the HTI-1 Final Rule.
Versions 4, 5, and 6 — Continued Annual Expansion

USCDI v4 added 20 data elements and one new data class to v3, including Alcohol Use, Substance Use, Physical Activity Assessments, Treatment Intervention preferences, Care Experience Preferences, and Medication Adherence data elements. USCDI v5, published July 2024, added 16 new data elements and two new data classes. USCDI v6 was published July 2025 with 6 additional data elements. Draft USCDI v7, released January 2026 for public comment, proposes 30 new data elements — the largest single-version expansion in the standard's history.

children.text: USCDI and the ONC Certification Program

USCDI does not exist in a vacuum — its power comes from its direct linkage to the ONC Health IT Certification Program. To participate in federal programs like the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS), the Medicare and Medicaid Promoting Interoperability programs, and several value-based care models, providers must use Certified EHR Technology (CEHRT). Certification, in turn, requires EHR products to demonstrate they can exchange the specific data classes and elements defined in the current regulatory baseline version of USCDI.

This creates a powerful compliance chain: federal payment programs require CEHRT → CEHRT certification requires USCDI support → USCDI defines which data elements must be interoperable. The result is that every major EHR vendor selling to hospitals, physician groups, or ambulatory clinics that accept Medicare or Medicaid must build USCDI compliance into their core product.

body.content: A regional hospital system using Epic or Oracle Health must ensure its EHR can receive and send all 94 data elements in USCDI v3 — including the new Health Insurance Information class and the equity-focused Disability Status elements — before its next CEHRT certification renewal. Failure to meet the January 1, 2026 deadline risks losing certification, which would disqualify the system from participating in MIPS and could result in Medicare payment penalties.

children.text: The 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (2020) was the original legislative trigger that made USCDI certification mandatory. The subsequent HTI-1 Final Rule (effective February 8, 2024) updated the regulatory baseline from USCDI v1 to USCDI v3 and introduced the January 1, 2026 transition deadline. Notably, after January 1, 2026, ONC will no longer allow new certifications to reference USCDI v1 — v3 becomes the only valid baseline. This is not a soft guideline but a hard regulatory requirement.

children.text: USCDI+: Domain-Specific Extensions Beyond the Core

USCDI defines the national minimum dataset — but minimum is often not enough for specialized programs. ONC created USCDI+ (pronounced 'USCDI plus') to address exactly this gap. USCDI+ is an extension mechanism that allows federal agencies and programs to define domain-specific datasets that go beyond the core USCDI standard without fragmenting the broader interoperability ecosystem.

Under the USCDI+ framework, a program identifies additional data elements it needs beyond USCDI — elements that are too specialized or too nascent to be appropriate for the universal baseline but that the program's participants must be able to exchange. These elements are documented, published, and harmonized using the same structured USCDI methodology, creating a consistent, machine-readable specification for developers.

USCDI+ is not a replacement for USCDI — it is a structured extension layer. Every USCDI+ dataset builds on top of the core USCDI standard. Programs using USCDI+ still require full USCDI compliance as the foundation.

The first and most prominent USCDI+ domain is USCDI+ Quality, developed jointly by ONC and CMS to support digital quality measurement. USCDI+ Quality establishes a harmonized baseline of data elements needed for a wide range of quality measurement use cases — including CMS electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs), CMS's Data Element Library, AHRQ Common Formats, and NCQA HEDIS measures. By creating a consistent USCDI+ Quality data element list, ONC and CMS aim to reduce the fragmentation that currently exists when different quality programs require the same underlying clinical data but specify it in incompatible ways.

CDC has also engaged with the USCDI+ framework for public health reporting extensions. The model reflects a broader philosophy: rather than allow each federal program to independently define and require its own proprietary dataset — which would force EHR vendors to build dozens of separate integrations — USCDI+ creates a managed, centrally coordinated extension layer where new program needs are documented and harmonized against each other and against the core standard.

children.text: How USCDI Maps to the US Core FHIR Implementation Guide

USCDI tells you *what* data must be interoperable. The US Core FHIR Implementation Guide (IG) — published by HL7 and maintained in close coordination with ONC — tells you *how* to represent and exchange that data using FHIR resources and profiles. Understanding the relationship between these two standards is essential for any health IT developer building interoperability solutions.

The US Core IG defines FHIR profiles — constrained versions of base FHIR resources — that implement each USCDI data class and element with Must Support constraints, terminology bindings, and search parameters. For example, the USCDI Allergies and Intolerances data class maps to the US Core AllergyIntolerance profile; the USCDI Clinical Notes data class maps to the US Core DocumentReference and DiagnosticReport profiles; the USCDI Patient Demographics class maps to the US Core Patient profile.

Each new version of US Core is designed to align with a corresponding version of USCDI. US Core v6 aligns with USCDI v3; US Core v7 and later versions align with subsequent USCDI releases. However, the mapping is not always one-to-one. A single USCDI data class may map to multiple FHIR profiles, and many US Core profile elements have no direct USCDI counterpart — because US Core's scope is broader than certification. US Core also includes elements needed to make FHIR technically functional that USCDI does not explicitly require.

body.message: USCDI data class names and FHIR resource names often differ. 'Health Status/Assessments' in USCDI does not map cleanly to a single FHIR resource — it spans Observation, Condition, and other resources depending on the specific data element. Always consult the US Core USCDI mapping table when implementing FHIR APIs for USCDI compliance.
body.title: FHIR Naming vs. USCDI Naming

children.text: For ONC certification, EHRs must demonstrate they support the FHIR-based APIs specified in the certification criteria — which reference US Core profiles as the implementation specification for USCDI-required data. In practice, this means demonstrating that a FHIR server can return Patient, AllergyIntolerance, Condition, MedicationRequest, DiagnosticReport, Observation, DocumentReference, and other US Core-profiled resources for the data elements required by the certified USCDI version.

USCDI and FHIR US Core are complementary initiatives, with USCDI defining high-level data requirements and FHIR US Core providing detailed FHIR-based profiles for meeting those requirements. Mapping between them is necessary for achieving interoperability and consistency in healthcare data exchange.
Real-World Implementation Challenges

Despite USCDI's clear regulatory mandate and structured versioning process, real-world implementation remains far from uniform. Multiple categories of challenges have emerged as the standard has expanded from 52 data elements in v1 to 94 in v3 — and continues to grow with each annual release.
Data Class Ambiguity

One of the most persistent criticisms of USCDI — raised prominently by the Electronic Health Record Association (EHRA) — is the ambiguity in data class definitions. When a data class definition is broad or imprecise, EHR vendors may implement it in materially different ways while both claiming compliance. This ambiguity creates friction at exactly the point where standardization is supposed to reduce it: when two certified systems try to exchange the 'same' data element and find it encoded differently.
Legacy Systems and Upgrade Costs

Many hospitals — particularly critical access hospitals, rural facilities, psychiatric hospitals, and safety-net providers — run older EHR infrastructure that was certified to USCDI v1 or earlier CCDS standards. Upgrading to USCDI v3 compliance is not a configuration change; it often requires significant software development, data migration, and staff retraining. ONC data shows that while 86% of non-federal acute care hospitals have adopted a certified EHR, only 67% of psychiatric hospitals have done so — a gap that reflects real structural barriers in the certification upgrade pathway.
Coded vs. Unstructured Data

USCDI compliance assumes data exists in structured, coded form. But in clinical practice, a substantial portion of medically significant information lives in unstructured clinical notes, scanned documents, and free-text fields. Oncology is a stark example: many pathology results remain uncoded in EHRs because clinicians manually transcribe pathology reports without applying standardized terminologies like SNOMED CT or LOINC. An EHR may be technically certified to send the Laboratory data class, but if the underlying data is unstructured, the API call returns incomplete or absent records.
Version Lag Between Certification and Clinical Reality

Because USCDI is updated annually but regulatory baselines are set through formal rulemaking — a process that takes 18-24 months — there is always a gap between the most current USCDI version and the version required for certification. As of 2026, the regulatory baseline is USCDI v3 (published 2022), while ONC has already published v5 and v6 and is drafting v7. Programs that want to use elements from v4 or v5 for quality measurement must rely on USCDI+ or non-regulatory mechanisms — adding complexity for developers who must support multiple versions simultaneously.

body.content: A care coordination vendor building a post-discharge follow-up platform wants to capture Medication Adherence data — an element added in USCDI v4. If the EHRs they integrate with are only certified to USCDI v3, they have no standardized way to request that data element via the FHIR API. They must either negotiate custom extensions with each EHR vendor, use an HL7 FHIR Questionnaire workaround, or wait until the regulatory baseline advances to v4 — which may be years away.

children.text: Vermont is a small state — fewer than 650,000 residents spread across rugged, rural terrain. Yet Vermont has built one of the most mature statewide health information exchange ecosystems in the United States, connecting nearly every hospital, most health centers, and hundreds of independent practices into a single, governed data network. At the center of that network sits Vermont Information Technology Leaders (VITL), a nonprofit designated by state law to operate the Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE). Alongside it, the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB) administers VHCURES — Vermont's All-Payer Claims Database — providing a complementary financial lens on how care is delivered and paid for across the state. Together, VITL and VHCURES form the twin pillars of Vermont's interoperability architecture, demonstrating both the promise and the hard-won lessons of state-led health IT.

This lesson traces Vermont's journey: the legislative mandate that created VITL, the clinical and administrative services the VHIE provides, the population-level power of claims data, the integrations that tie it all together through the Blueprint for Health, and the challenges that remain — from rural connectivity gaps to questions of long-term funding sustainability.
VITL: A Legislative Mandate for Statewide Connectivity

VITL was founded in 2005 as a private, nonprofit organization charged with advancing health care delivery and reform in Vermont through the aggregation and exchange of health information. Vermont's legislature subsequently codified VITL's role through Act 107 of 2006, formally designating it as the exclusive operator of the statewide health information exchange network. This legislative backstop was critical: unlike many states where HIE efforts fragmented into competing regional networks, Vermont's approach created a single, authoritative exchange from the start.

Under Vermont statute (18 V.S.A. Chapter 219), VITL is required to be named in the state's Health Information Technology Plan as the operator of the statewide HIE network. The statute also mandates that privacy standards applied on the network be no less stringent than those required under HIPAA. This statutory foundation gave VITL both legitimacy and accountability — participating organizations knew they were connecting to a legally recognized, regulated infrastructure rather than a voluntary pilot project.

Key framing: VITL's mission is to securely aggregate, standardize, and share the data needed to improve the effectiveness of healthcare for Vermonters. Its vision is to be a leader in collaboratively delivering actionable data that leads to better health.

For its first decade, VITL focused primarily on building connectivity — signing up hospitals, health centers, and physician practices, and standing up the core technical infrastructure. The Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB), established by Act 48 of 2011, was later given oversight authority over VITL's budget and strategic plan, ensuring that VITL's priorities remained aligned with Vermont's broader health care reform goals. However, as of July 1, 2025 — through Act 62 of 2025 — responsibility for the Health IT Plan and VITL oversight was formally moved away from the GMCB as Vermont reorganized its health system governance.

children.text: What the Vermont Health Information Exchange Actually Does

The Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE) is a secure, statewide data network that enables health care providers, ACOs, and other approved users to electronically exchange and access medical records. Far from a passive data warehouse, the VHIE delivers a suite of active services that change how care is coordinated across Vermont.
VITLAccess: The Clinical Portal

VITLAccess is VITL's web-based clinical portal — the primary interface through which authorized clinicians and care coordinators access patient data. Rebuilt in spring 2022 with a significantly improved user interface, VITLAccess provides a longitudinal, consolidated health record drawing from all contributing organizations. A clinician seeing a patient in a rural emergency department at 2 a.m. can pull up that patient's medication list, allergy history, recent lab results, imaging reports, and care plans — all from a single screen, even if the data originated from a hospital on the other side of the state.

The 2022 redesign added several critical capabilities: immunization data drawn from the Vermont Immunization Registry and hospital systems, improved patient-matching algorithms to reduce duplicate records and ensure comprehensive record assembly, and the ability to print or download multiple results or documents simultaneously. These improvements reflected lessons from clinician feedback about the original portal and represent the iterative, user-centered design approach VITL has pursued.
Core Data Services

Beyond the portal itself, the VHIE supports several distinct data service categories. Clinical document exchange allows participating organizations to push and pull structured clinical documents such as Continuity of Care Documents (CCDs) generated at the point of care. Medication history aggregation draws from pharmacies connected to the network, giving prescribers visibility into what a patient has actually filled — not just what was prescribed in their own system. Lab results delivery routes results from connected laboratories back to ordering providers. And care alerts notify care coordinators when patients experience significant clinical events such as emergency department visits or hospitalizations, enabling timely follow-up.

body.content: A patient with diabetes managed by a primary care practice in Rutland is admitted to a hospital in Burlington following a hypoglycemic episode. The VHIE immediately gives the Burlington ED clinicians access to the patient's full medication list — including insulin dosing — their most recent HbA1c, and the care plan from their endocrinologist. When the patient is discharged, a care alert flows back to the Rutland practice, triggering a follow-up call within 48 hours. No fax machine, no phone tag — just connected systems.
body.title: Example

children.text: VITL has also progressively expanded the scope of data flowing through the VHIE. Under Beth Anderson's leadership as CEO (2020-2025), the exchange broadened participation to include pharmacies, clinical laboratories, behavioral health providers, and ambulance services. This expansion was not merely additive — it addressed longstanding gaps where patients' behavioral health and substance use treatment records were invisible to the acute care system, creating dangerous information asymmetries at critical moments.

children.text: VHCURES: Vermont's All-Payer Claims Database

Where the VHIE captures the clinical story of a patient's care, VHCURES — Vermont's Health Care Uniform Reporting and Evaluation System — captures the financial story. VHCURES is Vermont's All-Payer Claims Database (APCD), maintained and managed by the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB). It is one of the most comprehensive claims datasets in the country, and it plays a central role in Vermont's ability to understand, evaluate, and regulate its health care system.

VHCURES receives medical and pharmacy claims data from three payer categories: commercial health insurers (including third-party administrators and pharmacy benefit managers), Vermont Medicaid, and Medicare. Any insurer serving 200 or more Vermont resident members is required to submit data to VHCURES. The database contains eligibility information — whether a patient is covered — as well as the full claims record of services delivered and payments made.

children.text: VHCURES is a powerful analytical tool precisely because it crosses payer boundaries. A researcher studying opioid prescribing patterns, a policymaker evaluating hospital pricing, or a health plan benchmarking its network performance can all draw on VHCURES to understand Vermont's health care system in ways that no single payer's data could support. The GMCB uses VHCURES as a core input for its hospital budget review process, its analysis of health care spending growth, and its assessment of the All-Payer ACO Model's impact on Vermont's cost trajectory.

Data from VHCURES is released in two formats: a Public Use File, which is de-identified and available for broad research use, and a Limited Use Dataset, which contains more granular information and is available to qualified researchers under data use agreements with privacy protections. The GMCB's APCD Snapshot tool provides publicly accessible metadata about what is in VHCURES — which health plans are contributing, the highest-volume procedures in the state, and how the dataset has evolved over time — giving policymakers and the public a window into the data without requiring full data access.

Critical distinction: VHCURES (claims data) and the VHIE (clinical data) are complementary but separate systems. Claims data tells you what was billed and paid. Clinical data tells you what actually happened at the point of care. Vermont is one of a handful of states actively working to link these two data streams to build a more complete picture of health and care delivery.
The Blueprint for Health: Where VITL Data Drives Reform

Vermont's Blueprint for Health is a statewide quality improvement program that has, since its expansion in the late 2000s, worked to transform primary care delivery across the state. It is one of the most long-running and closely studied multi-payer primary care reform efforts in the United States. And it could not function at scale without VITL.

Practices participating in the Blueprint for Health are required to sign agreements with VITL and connect their EHR systems to the VHIE. This connectivity serves two core purposes: care coordination at the individual patient level (through VITLAccess), and population-level outcomes measurement through the state's clinical data registry. The registry aggregates clinical data from participating practices and makes it available for quality reporting — allowing the state to track metrics like diabetes control rates, blood pressure management, and preventive care delivery across its entire primary care network.

VITL also shares data with other key reform initiatives. OneCare Vermont — the state's All-Payer ACO — uses VHIE data to support care management for its attributed population. The Vermont Department of Health connects to VITL for public health reporting, including immunization registries, disease surveillance, and population health monitoring. This web of data-sharing agreements, each governed by formal legal agreements and privacy protections, is what transforms a simple health information exchange into a reform infrastructure.

body.analogy: Think of Vermont's health data ecosystem as a utility grid: VITL is the transmission network that moves power (data) from generators (EHRs, pharmacies, labs) to consumers (clinicians, care coordinators, public health agencies). VHCURES is the billing meter that tracks how much power was consumed and what it cost. The Blueprint for Health is the efficiency program that uses both the transmission data and the billing data to reduce waste and improve outcomes. None of these pieces works as well without the others.

children.text: Persistent Challenges: Rural Connectivity, Small Practices, and Sustainability

Vermont's health information exchange achievements are real and significant, but so are the headwinds VITL and its partners face. Three challenges stand out as particularly structural: rural broadband limitations, the burden on small practices, and long-term funding sustainability.
Rural Broadband: Infrastructure Before Interoperability

Vermont is one of the most rural states in the country — approximately 93% of its land area is classified as rural, and thousands of residents live in areas with no reliable broadband access. Vermont's own 2021 telecommunications planning documents identified 51,000 homes and businesses as unserved or underserved, with limited private-market incentive to extend service to those locations. For health IT, this is a foundational barrier: an EHR cannot connect to the VHIE if the practice does not have reliable internet. Telehealth cannot substitute for in-person care if patients cannot maintain a stable video connection.

Vermont has pursued state and federal funding to address this gap. However, in 2025, federal cancellation of Vermont's $5.3 million Digital Equity Grant — funding intended to support broadband expansion and digital literacy — underscored the fragility of relying on federal dollars for infrastructure that is foundational to the state's health reform strategy.

body.message: Small rural practices — often a single physician or a small group — face the steepest interoperability challenges. They may lack the IT staff to manage an EHR, the bandwidth to use the VHIE reliably, or the financial resources to absorb interface build costs. Vermont's HIE is comprehensive in coverage, but coverage statistics must be read with an eye toward which practices are connected versus which remain on the margins.
body.title: Watch Out

children.text: Funding Sustainability

VITL's funding has historically depended on a combination of state appropriations, federal grants, and fees from participating organizations. Research into VITL's early development identified funding sustainability as a persistent challenge: stakeholders recognized the need for a sustainable business model but had not yet resolved it, with interviewees concluding that some form of ongoing public-private partnership would be the only viable long-term approach. That tension has not fully resolved. Federal health IT funding has fluctuated, and the political environment around health IT investment continues to shift.
TEFCA and National Connectivity: Protective Trade-offs

As TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — has grown into a national interoperability framework, with over 9,200 organizations signed up across 10 Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) as of early 2026, Vermont has moved carefully. Vermont enacted shield laws protecting reproductive health data and gender-affirming care data, and state officials have noted that participating in national data-sharing at the TEFCA level makes it difficult to guarantee those protections will be honored when data crosses state lines. Vermont is actively exploring what TEFCA participation might look like while maintaining its protective legal framework — a real tension between connectivity and privacy that other states with similar laws will increasingly face.

The 2025 VITL Annual Report (submitted to the Vermont Legislature in January 2026) noted that the VITL team spent the end of 2025 mapping a new strategic future — exploring new technologies and interoperability approaches to meet the health system's evolving needs in 2026 and beyond. With a new CEO in place following Beth Anderson's departure in July 2025, VITL stands at a pivotal inflection point between its foundational work connecting Vermont's providers and the next phase of contributing to national interoperability.
Lessons for the Broader Interoperability Field

Vermont's approach offers several lessons that have influenced thinking about HIE design nationally. First, legislative designation matters. By naming VITL as the exclusive statewide network operator in statute, Vermont avoided the fragmentation that plagued many states that allowed multiple competing HIEs to develop in parallel. A single, authoritative, governed network is structurally more efficient for building participation than a competitive marketplace where providers must choose which network to join.

Second, the combination of clinical data (VHIE) and claims data (VHCURES) under coordinated state oversight creates analytical power that neither dataset alone provides. Vermont policymakers can examine not just what care was delivered but whether that care aligned with clinical guidelines, whether it was delivered efficiently, and whether it produced outcomes that justify its cost. This dual-lens approach is increasingly recognized as the gold standard for health system evaluation.

Third, embedding HIE participation as a requirement — rather than an option — for participating in reform programs like the Blueprint for Health creates a natural on-ramp that ties financial incentives to connectivity. Practices that want the enhanced payments that come with Blueprint participation must connect to VITL. This approach produced broad participation in a small, rural state that might otherwise have struggled to achieve critical mass.

Vermont is a proof point that a small state with the right legislative framework, a nonprofit operator with a clear mandate, and persistent integration with reform programs can build health information exchange infrastructure that serves nearly an entire state's population.

At the same time, Vermont's experience underscores the limits of what an HIE alone can accomplish. Data flows through VITL only because organizations have connected — and connecting requires broadband, EHR systems, staff capacity, and funding. The hardest-to-reach patients and providers are also the hardest to connect to the network. Vermont's next chapter in interoperability will likely depend as much on solving broadband access and small-practice IT support as it does on any technical advances in data standards or exchange protocols.

children.text: Vermont's Health Data Infrastructure

Vermont is a national model for statewide health information exchange. The Vermont Information Technology Leaders (VITL), a non-profit organization established in 2005, operates the Vermont Health Information Network (VHIN) — the statewide HIE that connects providers, hospitals, labs, and payers across Vermont and provides real-time clinical data exchange. Vermont's small population (approximately 650,000), strong legislative support, and cooperative health system culture have enabled VITL to achieve participation levels and data completeness that elude most state HIEs.

children.text: The Vermont All-Payer Claims Database

Vermont operates one of the most comprehensive All-Payer Claims Databases (APCD) in the country — the Vermont Healthcare Claims Uniform Reporting and Evaluation System (VHCURES). The APCD collects claims data from all payers (commercial, Medicaid, Medicare Advantage, workers' compensation) operating in Vermont. VITL provides analytics services on top of VHCURES data, enabling the state to track statewide utilization patterns, identify high-cost areas, monitor value-based contract performance, and evaluate policy interventions. The combination of APCD (administrative claims) and VHIN (clinical data) gives Vermont a level of analytic capability that few states match.

body.content: A patient arrives at Central Vermont Medical Center's emergency department unconscious after a motor vehicle accident. The ED nurse queries VITL through the EHR: within seconds, VITL returns: active medications (including warfarin — critical for trauma management), known allergies (penicillin), recent labs (INR drawn three days ago at the patient's primary care office), and a recent hospital admission at UVM Medical Center two weeks prior. Without VITL, the ED team would need to call the PCP and UVM (both likely unreachable at 2am), risk dosing a patient on anticoagulation without knowing their INR level, and potentially miss the prior hospitalization's clinical context. VITL's real-time query delivered the clinical history needed for immediate, safe care decisions.
body.title: VITL in Clinical Practice — Emergency Department Use Case

children.text: VITL and the Blueprint for Health

VITL is tightly integrated with Vermont's Blueprint for Health — the state's primary care transformation and all-payer model. Blueprint practice facilitators use VITL data to provide practices with population health reports showing care gaps, high-risk patients, and quality measure performance. Community Health Teams (CHTs) — the social determinants and care coordination teams embedded in Blueprint practices — use VITL ADT alerts to identify patients who are frequent ED visitors and proactively engage them in care management. VITL is not just infrastructure; it is the data backbone of Vermont's value-based care system.
VITL Governance and Funding

VITL is governed by a board that includes representatives from hospitals, primary care practices, payers, and the State of Vermont (Agency of Human Services). This multi-stakeholder governance structure ensures that VITL serves all participants rather than being captured by any single interest group. Funding comes from three sources: participating organization assessment fees (hospitals and payers pay based on size and use), state budget appropriations through the Agency of Human Services, and federal Medicaid enhanced match funds for qualifying HIE infrastructure. Vermont's relatively small and cooperative health system landscape has made this funding model more stable than in larger, more competitive states.

VITL and TEFCA: VITL participates in the eHealth Exchange QHIN, providing Vermont providers access to patient records from across the country. A Vermonter who summers in Maine and winters in Florida can have clinical records retrieved from both states when presenting at a Vermont ED — via the eHealth Exchange network that VITL connects to as a participant. This national reach, layered on top of VITL's statewide foundation, creates genuinely comprehensive cross-organizational data access for Vermont providers.
Lessons From Vermont for Other States

Vermont's HIE success reflects several features that are not universal: a small, geographically coherent population; strong legislative support and statutory mandate for HIE participation; a relatively cooperative (rather than fiercely competitive) hospital market; a single statewide Medicaid agency; and a culture of public-private collaboration in healthcare reform. Replicating Vermont's model in a large, fragmented, competitive health system market (like California or Texas) would require different approaches — more federated architecture, stronger regulatory mandates, and more complex governance structures.

body.message: Vermont's HIE success is partly a function of Vermont being Vermont: small, progressive, cooperative, and willing to use government as a platform for collective action in healthcare. The lessons from VITL — invest in governance as much as technology, align funding to value delivered, integrate with care delivery models — transfer broadly. The specific model (centralized, state-funded, mandate-supported) does not transfer directly to states with different political economies.
body.title: Vermont's Model Is Not Exportable Without Adaptation

body.analogy: VITL is to Vermont's health system what a town library is to a small town: a shared public good, collectively funded, that benefits every resident regardless of which private institution they interact with. The library does not compete with bookstores — it complements them. VITL does not compete with health systems — it connects them.

body.explanation: VITL's success reflects Vermont's particular combination of factors: small population making statewide coverage achievable, cooperative (not fiercely competitive) health system dynamics, strong legislative support, state budget investment, and integration with the Blueprint for Health giving providers immediate value from participation. These contextual factors, not just technology choices, explain VITL's success — and why the model does not directly transfer to larger, more competitive states.

children.text: A System That Forgets: The Reality of Healthcare Data Silos

Imagine that every time you moved to a new city, your entire life history — your relationships, your job experience, your education — was wiped from memory, and you had to start over as a stranger. In American healthcare, this happens to patients every single day. When a patient walks into an emergency department after a car accident, the physicians treating them often have no idea what medications they take, what allergies they have, or what chronic conditions they manage. When a specialist receives a referral, they may have no access to the primary care notes that explain why the patient was referred. When a patient is discharged from a hospital and transferred to a skilled nursing facility, the complete discharge summary may arrive days later — by fax.

This is the problem of healthcare interoperability, or more precisely, the lack of it. Healthcare interoperability is the ability of different health information systems, devices, and applications to access, exchange, integrate, and cooperatively use data in a coordinated way across organizational, regional, and national boundaries. The word is awkward and technical, but the stakes could not be more human. When health data cannot follow the patient, the patient becomes the most error-prone link in their own care chain — forced to recall complex medication regimens from memory, repeat procedures they have already undergone, and navigate a system that treats every encounter as if it were the first.

The U.S. healthcare system has spent decades and hundreds of billions of dollars building electronic health records, imaging archives, laboratory systems, pharmacy networks, and insurance platforms — yet these systems are largely isolated from one another, unable to communicate seamlessly. Each island of data is technically sophisticated in isolation; together, they form a fragmented archipelago that fails patients at precisely the moments when continuity of information matters most: during emergencies, care transitions, and the management of complex chronic conditions.

body.analogy: Think of the U.S. healthcare data landscape as a country where every city speaks a different language and uses a different currency. Within each city, commerce works fine. But the moment you try to travel from one city to another, the system breaks down. A prescription written in Boston is illegible in Phoenix. A lab result from a community clinic is unreadable by the hospital two miles away. No single traveler — or patient — can be fully served.

children.text: The Financial Toll: Billions Lost to Administrative Friction and Duplication

The financial cost of poor interoperability is staggering, even by the standards of a system that routinely deals in trillions of dollars. CAQH, which tracks administrative efficiency across the healthcare industry, reported in its 2025 Index that the U.S. healthcare system still has a remaining $21 billion annual savings opportunity from fully automating manual and partially manual administrative transactions — tasks like eligibility verification, prior authorization, claims, and referrals — that are currently slowed or blocked by data systems that cannot talk to each other. Notably, the same research showed that over the past decade, the industry has avoided an estimated $258 billion in administrative costs through increased electronic automation — a remarkable achievement that also illustrates how much had been wasted before.

Prior authorization alone consumes an extraordinary share of clinical and administrative resources. Because payers and providers use different data systems that do not share information automatically, staff at physician offices must manually retrieve patient history, compile supporting clinical documentation, and submit requests through proprietary payer portals — often by phone or fax. The CAQH research found that the average time saved per patient visit when providers use fully automated administrative workflows is 70 minutes. Multiply that by hundreds of millions of patient visits annually, and the scale of reclaimed clinical capacity becomes vivid. That is time physicians and nurses could spend with patients rather than navigating bureaucratic systems designed for a pre-digital era.

Duplicate testing is another enormous and well-documented cost driver directly tied to interoperability failure. When a patient's prior laboratory results are inaccessible to a new treating physician, the physician has no choice but to reorder tests already performed. A landmark study published in BMC Medical Informatics found that duplication of testing — defined as a repeat within 12 hours — occurred in 32% of cases examined, with 20% of cases having at least one test that was clinically unindicated. Across the system, redundant testing alone is estimated to waste up to $5 billion annually in the United States. These are not abstractions. They are real resources — physician time, technician effort, reagents, imaging machine capacity, and patient inconvenience — consumed repeatedly by the same system failure.

Duplicate and redundant medical testing — driven largely by inaccessible prior records — wastes an estimated $5 billion per year in the United States, according to research published in BMC Medical Informatics and affiliated studies.

children.text: The Human Cost: Patient Safety Failures When Data Cannot Follow the Patient

The financial costs of poor interoperability, as significant as they are, pale in comparison to the human costs. The most consequential failures happen not to spreadsheets, but to people. When health data does not flow with the patient, clinicians are forced to make decisions under conditions of preventable ignorance — and preventable ignorance causes preventable harm.

Medication safety is one of the clearest casualties. The World Health Organization estimates that medication errors cost approximately $42 billion annually worldwide and account for 1% of total global health expenditure. In the United States, approximately six percent of hospitalizations are attributable to medication allergies known to cause adverse drug reactions. Many of these are not mysterious or unforeseeable events; they are cases where the allergy was documented somewhere in the healthcare system, but the system treating the patient at that moment had no access to that documentation. AHRQ's PSNet has published case studies of medication-induced hemolytic reactions in patients with clearly documented allergies that were simply invisible to the treating facility because the information lived in a different, non-interoperable EHR.

Incomplete records create a broader pattern of harm that researchers have documented across care settings. Studies of primary care incident reports find that nearly half of all patient safety incidents related to information flow involved inadequate, missing, or incorrect information. One analysis found 18 documented cases of serious patient harm directly attributable to patient data management and documentation failures in a single study period. Nearly all adverse events in one major study were classified as preventable — meaning the harm would not have occurred if the right information had been available to the right clinician at the right time.

body.content: A patient is stabilized at a rural emergency department after a cardiac event and transferred to a regional hospital for catheterization. The transfer arrives with a paper summary; the detailed EHR record, including a recent echocardiogram and a complex medication reconciliation from an outpatient cardiologist, is unavailable because the originating and receiving hospitals use different EHR systems with no active health information exchange. The receiving team must repeat several diagnostic steps, delay the procedure, and administer a medication that interacts with the patient's existing regimen — all because the data did not travel with the patient. This is not a hypothetical; it is the daily operational reality for a majority of U.S. hospitals.

That means roughly 30% of American hospitals still cannot reliably perform one or more of these basic data exchange functions — leaving millions of patients at risk when they move across care settings.

children.text: The Revolving Door: How Data Gaps Drive Preventable Hospital Readmissions

Care transitions — the handoffs between care settings when patients move from hospital to home, from primary care to specialist, from emergency department to observation unit — are the most dangerous moments in a patient's healthcare journey. They are dangerous precisely because they require seamless data flow, and that seamless data flow frequently does not exist.

Hospital readmissions are the most measurable symptom of care transition failure. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) operates the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), which penalizes hospitals financially for excess readmissions within 30 days of discharge for conditions including heart failure, pneumonia, and hip/knee replacement. In 2024, 70% of U.S. hospitals faced financial penalties under this program — a figure that underscores how pervasive care transition failures remain. These are not isolated failures at poorly managed institutions; they are system-wide indicators of what happens when discharge information, medication reconciliation, and follow-up care instructions do not reliably reach the next provider in the chain.

Research has directly linked health information exchange participation to reduced readmission rates. A study published in Health Affairs found that HIE participation was associated with a 1.3 percentage point greater reduction in the probability of unplanned 30-day readmissions for acute myocardial infarction compared to non-participating hospitals. Systematic reviews of HIE outcomes have consistently found that when clinical data can travel across organizational boundaries, hospitals admit fewer patients unnecessarily, emergency departments are used more appropriately, and the overall cost of care declines.

The mechanism is straightforward: when a discharging hospital can electronically notify a primary care physician of a patient's discharge, share the complete medication list, flag pending follow-up tests, and transmit the discharge summary in a structured format the receiving system can read — the likelihood of a patient falling through the cracks drops substantially. When that information arrives by fax three days later, or not at all, the patient is left to navigate the transition alone, often with incomplete understanding of their own treatment plan.

children.text: COVID-19: When Interoperability Failures Become a National Emergency

The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020-2021 provided an unprecedented stress test of the U.S. healthcare data infrastructure — and the results were sobering. The pandemic revealed with stark clarity what public health officials and health informaticists had been warning about for years: that fragmented, non-interoperable health data systems were not merely inefficient but genuinely dangerous at the population scale.

Case reporting — the foundational public health function of knowing where a disease is spreading and how fast — was crippled by data fragmentation. Across federal, state, and local jurisdictions, data platforms used different definitions, different formats, and different transmission mechanisms. A case reported to a state health department in one format could not automatically flow to a CDC system expecting a different format. The result was that public health officials were making containment and resource allocation decisions based on data that was days or weeks out of date, incomplete in geographic coverage, and systematically missing demographic information on race and ethnicity that was critical for identifying and addressing disparate community impacts.

Vaccination record management proved equally problematic. Many primary care practices were unable to reliably capture vaccination status or receive vaccination data from the immunization information systems operated by states — systems that were themselves fragmented and often unable to exchange data across state lines. Patients who received their first vaccine dose in one state and their second dose in another created records that often could not be reconciled. Healthcare workers administering vaccines frequently had no electronic visibility into a patient's prior vaccination history.

A subsequent analysis published in Health Affairs Scholar documented that hospitals faced significant challenges in COVID-19 public health reporting due to interoperability gaps in their data exchange infrastructure. Research published in PMC identified that the fundamental problem was not a lack of data, but a lack of data infrastructure capable of aggregating, standardizing, and sharing that data in real time. The pandemic did not create these fragmentation problems; it revealed them — at a cost measured not in dollars, but in lives.

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed a hard truth: a healthcare system that cannot share data seamlessly in routine times will fail catastrophically under stress. Interoperability is not a technical nicety — it is a foundational requirement of public health resilience.
The Policy Response: How ONC and CMS Are Mandating a Better Future

Recognizing the scale of the problem, the federal government has made healthcare interoperability a central policy priority over the past decade. The legislative foundation is the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, which directed both the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to take concrete regulatory action to advance interoperability and prohibit practices that block the flow of health information.

ONC's Cures Act Final Rule, finalized in 2020, established several landmark requirements. It mandated that EHR vendors adopt standardized application programming interfaces (APIs) based on the HL7 FHIR standard, enabling patients and authorized third-party applications to access structured electronic health information at no cost. It prohibited "information blocking" — practices by health IT developers, health networks, or providers that unreasonably prevent or interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information. Penalties for information blocking can reach up to $1 million per violation for certified health IT developers, with provider-facing disincentives tied to federal payment programs.

CMS reinforced these requirements through its Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule, which required Medicare and Medicaid payers to implement FHIR-based APIs giving patients electronic access to their claims and clinical data. The Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange rule extended this further, requiring health plans to share patient clinical information with new plans when patients change coverage — addressing a long-standing gap where years of clinical history would simply disappear when a patient switched insurers.

These policy mandates reflect a recognition that market forces alone have proven insufficient to drive interoperability. Individual health systems and EHR vendors have historically had financial incentives to retain patient data within their networks rather than share it with competitors. Regulation has been necessary to override those incentives and establish a floor of data-sharing behavior that the entire system must meet. ONC's stated goal is a future in which any patient can securely access, share, and use all of their electronic health information, regardless of where that information was created or by whom.
