children.text: What the Evidence Shows: The Proven Benefits of Interoperability

Beyond documenting the costs of fragmentation, a growing body of research demonstrates the concrete benefits that emerge when health information can actually flow across organizational boundaries. These studies provide the evidence base for the policy investments and regulatory mandates that have defined the past decade of health IT policy.

The Health Affairs study on HIE and acute myocardial infarction readmissions is representative of a consistent research finding: when clinical information travels with the patient, outcomes improve and costs fall. Systematic reviews of HIE outcomes published in JMIR Medical Informatics and the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association have found that HIE participation is associated with fewer duplicate procedures, reduced imaging orders, lower emergency department costs, and improved ambulatory quality of care. Studies with more rigorous research designs consistently report benefits across these domains.

The 2025 CAQH Index provides perhaps the most comprehensive quantitative picture of what improved data exchange has already achieved administratively: an estimated $258 billion in administrative costs avoided through electronic transactions over the measurement period, with a documented 70-minute time savings per patient visit when fully automated administrative workflows are in place. This is time returned to clinical care — to the patient-physician relationship — rather than to administrative overhead.

Population health management is another domain where interoperability pays measurable dividends. When a health system can aggregate clinical data across all of its patients — including data from outside its own walls — it can identify high-risk patients before they deteriorate, coordinate proactive outreach, and target care management resources where they will have the greatest impact. These capabilities depend entirely on the ability to access and integrate data from multiple sources: EHRs, labs, pharmacies, social determinants screening tools, and payer claims feeds. Interoperability is the infrastructure on which population health rests.

When clinical information travels with the patient, outcomes improve, costs fall, and clinicians can focus on care rather than the search for missing data. Interoperability is not a technology project — it is the prerequisite for a functioning healthcare system.
Key Takeaways

points: Poor healthcare interoperability imposes an estimated $21 billion in remaining annual administrative waste, with redundant testing alone costing up to $5 billion per year in the United States.
Nearly half of all patient safety incidents related to information flow involve missing, inadequate, or incorrect information — and the vast majority of adverse events are considered preventable.
Medication errors tied to missing allergy and medication history cost an estimated $42 billion annually worldwide and drive approximately 6% of U.S. hospitalizations.

In 2024, 70% of U.S. hospitals faced financial penalties under CMS's readmissions reduction program — a direct measure of how frequently care transitions fail when data does not travel with the patient.

Research in Health Affairs found that HIE participation reduces 30-day readmission rates for heart attack patients by 1.3 percentage points — demonstrating that better data exchange produces measurable clinical improvements.

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed systemic interoperability failures in case reporting, vaccination records, and demographic data collection, revealing that fragmented data infrastructure is a public health risk, not merely an administrative inconvenience.

The 21st Century Cures Act, ONC's Cures Act Final Rule, and CMS's Interoperability and Patient Access Rule represent the largest federal regulatory push in history to mandate FHIR-based data sharing and prohibit information blocking.

Interoperability is not a technical end goal in itself — it is the infrastructure prerequisite for safe care transitions, effective population health management, clinical decision support, and a patient experience that respects continuity across a lifetime of care.

children.text: The Members Who Need the Most — and Cost the Most

Most of Medicaid managed care concerns medical care — doctor visits, hospital stays, prescriptions. But a distinct and enormously important category of need falls outside acute medical care entirely: help with the basic activities of daily living for people who cannot manage them alone. An elderly person who can no longer bathe or dress safely, an adult with a disability who needs daily support, a person with a serious chronic condition who requires ongoing assistance — these people need long-term services and supports (LTSS). They are among Medicaid’s most complex and most expensive members, and how managed care serves them is the subject of this lesson.

LTSS refers to the hands-on services that help people live safely when they need assistance with daily life because of age, disability, or chronic conditions. It spans two settings: institutional care (nursing facilities) and home- and community-based services (HCBS) that let a person receive the same support while remaining in their own home or community. When a state delivers these services through capitated managed care, the result is Managed Long-Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) — and it represents one of the most consequential and challenging frontiers of Medicaid managed care.

This matters because LTSS is where managed care’s stakes are highest. The members are vulnerable, the services are intensely personal, the costs are large, and the central policy goal — helping people live in the community rather than in institutions — depends heavily on how well the plan coordinates care. Done well, MLTSS can integrate fragmented services and keep people at home; done poorly, it can fail the people least able to advocate for themselves.

Key Concept: Long-term services and supports (LTSS) help people with daily living due to age, disability, or chronic conditions, spanning institutional care and home- and community-based services (HCBS). Managed LTSS (MLTSS) delivers these through capitated managed care, with the plan coordinating all approved supports for each participant.

children.text: What LTSS Covers

LTSS encompasses the supports a person needs to manage activities of daily living (ADLs) — bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, mobility — and related needs, when age, disability, or chronic illness makes them unable to do so independently. In an institutional setting, both fee-for-service and MLTSS programs provide room and board, nursing care, personal care, and therapy services for low-income individuals who need this level of assistance. The nursing facility has historically been the default setting for people who cannot live safely on their own.

But institutions are not the only option, and increasingly not the preferred one. States may choose to provide home- and community-based services (HCBS) — the same kinds of personal care, assistance, and supports, delivered in a person’s own home or community rather than in a facility. HCBS lets a beneficiary receive help with daily living while continuing to live at home, preserving independence and community connection. The choice between institutional and community-based LTSS is at the heart of LTSS policy, and as we will see, shifting the balance toward HCBS is a central goal of MLTSS.

LTSS is distinct from acute medical care in ways that shape how it must be managed. It is ongoing rather than episodic, deeply personal, often delivered in the home by aides rather than in clinics by physicians, and intertwined with a person’s housing, family, and community. Managing it well requires skills and infrastructure quite different from managing medical care — which is exactly why bringing LTSS into managed care is both promising and difficult.
MLTSS and Care Coordination

Under MLTSS, a state contracts with capitated managed care plans to deliver and, crucially, coordinate long-term services and supports. Under a MLTSS system, the managed care plan coordinates the delivery of all approved supports and services for each program participant — acting as the single entity responsible for assembling a coherent package of care around a person with complex, often multiple needs. This coordination role is the heart of MLTSS’s promise.

The appeal of capitated MLTSS is that it can integrate what fee-for-service fragments. A capitated managed care plan can offer more flexible benefit packages and opportunities for integrating acute and long-term services and supports — bringing a member’s medical care and their daily-living supports under one coordinated roof. For a person with both serious medical conditions and functional needs, this integration can mean the difference between disjointed services and a single care plan that addresses the whole person. The capitation also gives the plan flexibility to fund non-traditional supports that keep someone safely at home.

body.message: For acute care, a plan’s main task is paying for and managing discrete medical services. For MLTSS, coordination IS the service — assembling personal care, medical care, housing supports, and family involvement into a workable daily-living plan for a vulnerable person. A plan that pays claims but fails to coordinate has failed at the core purpose of MLTSS.
body.title: Coordination Is the Whole Job

children.text: Rebalancing: Moving Care Into the Community

The dominant policy goal driving MLTSS is rebalancing — shifting the LTSS system away from costly, less-integrated institutional settings toward more cost-effective, more integrated community settings. Nursing facility care is expensive and, for most people, far less desirable than living at home. States see MLTSS as a useful tool to rebalance their LTSS systems toward HCBS, simultaneously honoring members’ strong preference to remain in the community and reducing the cost of institutional care.

States use specific mechanisms to drive rebalancing through MLTSS. These include paying plans a blended per-member-per-month capitation rate (blending the cost of institutional and community members so the plan is not penalized for moving someone home), implementing financial incentives to transition enrollees from institutional facilities to community settings, and requiring plans to report on rebalancing-related quality metrics to measure progress. The capitation structure is what makes this work: because the plan bears the full cost, it benefits financially when it can safely support someone in lower-cost community care rather than an expensive nursing facility — aligning the financial incentive with the member’s preference.

Beyond rebalancing, states increasingly use MLTSS as a platform to integrate Medicare and Medicaid for dual-eligible individuals — the people enrolled in both programs, who are often the highest-need and highest-cost population in all of health care. Because dual eligibles get acute care through Medicare and LTSS through Medicaid, their care is notoriously fragmented across two programs that rarely coordinate. MLTSS programs can serve as the vehicle to integrate Medicare and Medicaid services in one health plan responsible for delivering all covered services — a powerful (if complex) opportunity to unify the care of those who need coordination most.

children.text: The Promise and the Difficulty

MLTSS sits at the frontier of Medicaid managed care precisely because it is the hardest thing managed care attempts. The members are the most vulnerable, the services the most personal, the coordination the most demanding, and the consequences of failure the most severe. The promise is real: an integrated, capitated plan can coordinate fragmented services, fund flexible community supports, align incentives with keeping people at home, and unify Medicare and Medicaid for dual eligibles. Increasing numbers of states are pursuing MLTSS for exactly these reasons — expanding HCBS, promoting community inclusion, ensuring quality, and increasing efficiency.

body.analogy: Managing acute care is like a plan paying for occasional repairs on a house — discrete jobs, billed and managed one at a time. MLTSS is more like being responsible for helping an aging person stay in their home: it means coordinating the aide who helps them dress, the doctor who manages their conditions, the ramp that lets them reach the door, and the family who checks in — all woven into one daily plan. The capitated plan profits not by doing more procedures, but by keeping the person safe and at home, which is cheaper than a nursing facility and what the person wanted anyway.
body.concept: How MLTSS coordinates care for complex members

children.text: But the difficulty is equally real, and it amplifies every concern raised earlier in the course. The under-provision incentive is especially dangerous when the member cannot easily advocate for themselves and the "service" is hands-on personal care. Network adequacy is harder when the providers are home-care aides facing chronic workforce shortages. Quality measurement is harder for personal supports than for clinical procedures. And the capitation incentive to move people into the community, while generally aligned with member preference, must be carefully overseen to ensure no one is pushed out of needed institutional care prematurely. MLTSS magnifies both the benefits and the risks of managed care.

This lesson closes the care-management-and-quality module by showing managed care applied to its most demanding population. It draws together threads from across the course: the capitation and rate-setting that make blended rates possible, the network adequacy that must extend to home-care providers, the quality measurement that must capture rebalancing, and the oversight that must protect members who cannot protect themselves. MLTSS is where the abstract machinery of Medicaid managed care meets the most human stakes — and where doing it well, or badly, most directly shapes whether vulnerable people live with dignity in their own homes or not.

points: Long-term services and supports (LTSS) are the hands-on services that help people manage daily living due to age, disability, or chronic conditions, spanning institutional care (nursing facilities) and home- and community-based services (HCBS).

Managed LTSS (MLTSS) delivers these services through capitated managed care, with the plan responsible for coordinating all approved supports for each participant; 24 states used MLTSS as of December 2023.
LTSS differs from acute care — it is ongoing, deeply personal, often home-based, and intertwined with housing and family — so coordination, not claims payment, is the core job of an MLTSS plan.
Capitated MLTSS can integrate acute and long-term services under one coordinated plan and fund flexible community supports, addressing the whole person rather than fragmented services.

The dominant goal is rebalancing — shifting LTSS from costly institutional settings toward community-based HCBS — driven by blended capitation rates, transition incentives, and rebalancing quality metrics that align the plan’s financial interest with members’ preference to stay home.

States increasingly use MLTSS as a platform to integrate Medicare (acute) and Medicaid (LTSS) for dual-eligible members, the highest-need population whose care is otherwise fragmented across two programs.

MLTSS magnifies managed care’s risks: the under-provision incentive is most dangerous for members who cannot self-advocate, home-care network adequacy is strained by workforce shortages, and quality is harder to measure for personal supports.

MLTSS is the frontier of Medicaid managed care, drawing together capitation, network adequacy, quality measurement, and oversight, where doing the job well or badly most directly determines whether vulnerable people can live with dignity at home.

children.text: A joint CMS-HRSA regulatory action finalized in December 2025 establishes, for the first time, mandatory minimum obstetric emergency capabilities for all Medicare-participating hospitals with emergency departments—regardless of whether they maintain a labor and delivery unit. The rule directly targets the 89-county maternal care desert problem identified in the 2025 March of Dimes Access Index.
What the Mandate Requires

By July 1, 2026, every participating hospital ED must demonstrate three core capabilities: (1) a stocked obstetric emergency cart compliant with the ACOG Hemorrhage Bundle specifications, including uterotonic medications, compression sutures, and Level I resuscitation equipment for neonates; (2) at least one registered nurse per shift with current ALSO (Advanced Life Support in Obstetrics) or NRP (Neonatal Resuscitation Program) certification; and (3) a documented transfer agreement with a facility providing comprehensive obstetric care within 60 minutes transport time.

The United States loses more women to obstetric hemorrhage in rural emergency departments than in labor and delivery units. This mandate addresses the silent front door of the maternal mortality crisis.

children.text: The Strategic Opportunity Inside the Compliance Burden

The transfer agreement requirement—often viewed as purely administrative—represents a leverage point for rural hospitals to negotiate formal clinical partnerships with regional referral centers. Several RHT program states, including Georgia (Obstetric Carts initiative) and North Carolina (ROOTS Hub model), have pre-positioned grant funding specifically to offset the cost of ALSO certification and cart procurement for CAHs.

Hospital CFOs should run a net-revenue analysis before assuming the mandate is purely a cost center. Rural EDs that achieve ALSO certification frequently see increased volumes of prenatal visits and early labor presentations that were previously being bypassed in favor of distant delivery centers.

children.text: Who Owns a Quality Measure?

A quality measure is not a casual statistic. Behind every measure — say, "percentage of adults with diabetes whose blood sugar is controlled" — sits an organization responsible for defining it precisely, keeping it current with the evidence, and deciding when to retire it. That organization is called the measure steward.

Measure stewardship is a formal, ongoing responsibility. Stewards approve a measure's content, update the diagnostic and procedure codes tied to its technical specifications, adjust the measure as clinical evidence changes, and can withdraw it from use when it becomes obsolete. A related role, the measure developer, does the technical work of building and maintaining measures, often under a steward's direction; a single organization can play both roles.

Understanding who stewards which measures matters because it tells you where a measure's authority and accountability live. The U.S. measurement ecosystem is dominated by a handful of organizations, each with a distinct role — and the landscape shifted notably in 2023.

A measure steward is the organization responsible for defining a quality measure, keeping its specifications current with clinical evidence, and retiring it when obsolete. Measure developers build and maintain measures, often under a steward's direction.
NCQA: Steward of HEDIS

The National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) is a private nonprofit and the steward of HEDIS — the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — one of the most widely used performance-measurement tools in health care. When a health plan reports a "HEDIS measure," NCQA wrote and maintains the specification.

NCQA's influence comes from both its measures and its accreditation programs. Health plans seek NCQA accreditation, and HEDIS results feed directly into plan ratings and into many state Medicaid and Medicare Advantage oversight processes. Because NCQA controls the specifications, it effectively defines what "good" looks like for a huge swath of preventive and chronic-care quality.

NCQA is also driving the transition from manual chart-based HEDIS reporting toward fully digital quality measures — a shift covered later in this course — which positions it at the center of the field's technical future as well as its present.
In short, NCQA is the steward most associated with ambulatory, preventive, and chronic-disease measurement across commercial, Medicaid, and Medicare Advantage plans.
CMS and The Joint Commission

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is the single largest force in U.S. quality measurement. CMS stewards most measures developed under its contracts, and its measure inventory houses over 500 measures used across dozens of federal programs — from hospital reporting to physician payment. Because CMS measures are tied to payment and public reporting for Medicare and Medicaid, they carry enormous weight.

The Joint Commission (TJC) plays a different but complementary role. TJC accredits hospitals and other facilities, and its accredited organizations must meet performance-measurement requirements by submitting data through TJC's ORYX program — including electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) and chart-abstracted measures. For hospitals, TJC accreditation is often a practical prerequisite for participating in Medicare.

The division of labor is roughly this: NCQA dominates health-plan and ambulatory measurement, CMS dominates federal payment and public-reporting programs, and TJC ties measurement to facility accreditation. Many measures flow between them — a single eCQM might be developed for CMS, reported through TJC's ORYX, and overlap with HEDIS.

body.title: Major Quality Measurement Organizations

children.text: Endorsement and the NQF Transition

Stewards develop and maintain measures, but a separate function determines whether a measure is considered scientifically sound and worthy of national use: endorsement. Section 1890 of the Social Security Act requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to contract with a "consensus-based entity" (CBE) to run a transparent, multi-stakeholder process for endorsing quality and cost measures and keeping them updated.

For most of the field's history, that consensus-based entity was the National Quality Forum (NQF) — a nonprofit whose "NQF-endorsed" stamp became the gold standard signaling a measure had passed rigorous scientific review. The CBE also convenes the Measure Applications Partnership (MAP), a multi-stakeholder group that recommends to HHS which measures to use in CMS programs, as part of an annual "pre-rulemaking" process.

This changed in 2023. Effective March 27, 2023, NQF was no longer the contracted CBE for CMS; CMS instead awarded the contract to the Battelle Memorial Institute, which now runs the consensus-based functions under the banner of the Partnership for Quality Measurement (PQM). Notably, PQM charges no membership dues, opening participation to the public for free. Separately, in August 2023 The Joint Commission acquired NQF, which continues some endorsement activities within TJC.

body.message: A common outdated belief is that "NQF endorses measures for CMS." Since March 2023, the contracted consensus-based entity is Battelle, operating as the Partnership for Quality Measurement (PQM). NQF itself was acquired by The Joint Commission later in 2023.
body.title: NQF Is No Longer the CMS Consensus-Based Entity

children.text: How the Pieces Fit Together

Put together, the lifecycle of a measure crosses several of these organizations. A developer builds a measure; a steward (NCQA, CMS, or another) maintains it; the consensus-based entity endorses it through a transparent process; the Measure Applications Partnership recommends whether it should be used in federal programs; and CMS or accreditors like TJC then put it into payment and reporting.

This layered structure exists to balance two things: rigor and accountability. No single organization should be able to declare a measure "good" and force it into payment unilaterally. By separating stewardship, endorsement, and program selection, the system builds in scientific review and public input before a measure can affect how providers are paid or rated.

For anyone working in quality, the practical lesson is to always know a measure's provenance: who stewards it, whether it is endorsed, and which programs use it. Those facts determine how authoritative the measure is, how stable its specifications are, and how seriously providers must take it.

children.text: How States Bend the Rules

Medicaid is governed by a detailed set of federal requirements in the Social Security Act. But the law also contains a powerful escape hatch: Section 1115. This provision lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services approve experimental, pilot, or demonstration projects that depart from the normal rules, as long as the Secretary finds they are likely to promote the objectives of the Medicaid program.

In practice, Section 1115 lets a state ask the federal government for permission to run its Medicaid program differently than the statute would otherwise allow — covering populations or services that are not normally eligible, testing new payment models, or restructuring delivery. It is the single most flexible tool in Medicaid, and it has made the program a genuine laboratory for policy experimentation.

The breadth of the authority is striking: under Section 1115, the Secretary can waive almost any of the state plan requirements in Section 1902 of the Act to the extent necessary to carry out the demonstration. That is why 1115 waivers can reshape a state's program in ways that look very different from "textbook" Medicaid.

A Section 1115 demonstration waiver lets the HHS Secretary approve state Medicaid projects that depart from normal federal rules, as long as they are found likely to promote the objectives of Medicaid. It is the program's most flexible authority.
The Budget Neutrality Guardrail

The flexibility of Section 1115 is not unlimited. The central guardrail is "budget neutrality": over the life of the demonstration, federal Medicaid spending under the waiver may not exceed what federal spending would have been without it. In other words, a state can rearrange how federal dollars are used, but it generally cannot use a waiver to draw down more federal money than it otherwise would have.

Budget neutrality is a longstanding policy and practice rather than an explicit statutory command, and it is typically calculated on a per-enrollee basis. This lets a state reinvest projected savings from one part of its program into new services elsewhere — funding innovations without increasing net federal cost.

This requirement is why waiver negotiations are so technical. Much of the back-and-forth between a state and CMS is about how to project the "without-waiver" baseline and demonstrate that the proposed demonstration will stay within it over the approval period.
Budget neutrality is the core guardrail of Section 1115: federal spending under the waiver cannot exceed what it would have been without the waiver, usually measured on a per-enrollee basis.
How a Waiver Gets Approved

Getting an 1115 waiver is a deliberate, transparent process. Before a state even submits its application to CMS, federal rules require it to provide public notice and hold a state-level public comment period of at least 30 days, publishing the application, objectives, and estimated impact on enrollment and spending.

Once the state submits a complete application, CMS opens its own 30-day federal public comment period, posting the application and collecting comments online. CMS then reviews each proposed policy case by case to judge whether it aligns with Medicaid's objectives, and negotiates terms with the state — a process that can stretch from several months to a couple of years.

Because 1115 authority is meant for research and demonstration, states must also commit to evaluation. They are required to have an approved, publicly available evaluation strategy and to submit interim and final ("summative") evaluation reports, so that the lessons of each experiment are documented.

children.text: What States Use Waivers For

Section 1115 waivers have been used for an enormous range of purposes, and the dominant uses shift with each administration's priorities. Some states have used waivers to expand coverage to new populations; others to restructure financing; others to test conditions on eligibility. The same tool can be pointed in very different policy directions.

Three recurring categories illustrate the range. Some administrations approved work and community-engagement requirements, conditioning coverage for some adults on employment or related activities. Many states have used Delivery System Reform Incentive Payment (DSRIP) waivers to fund provider-led delivery system transformation. And more recently, states have used waivers to address health-related social needs (HRSN) such as housing and nutrition.

This flexibility is why people call 1115 waivers "laboratories of democracy" — they let individual states test approaches that, if successful, can inform national policy, and if unsuccessful, are contained to the demonstration rather than imposed everywhere.

children.text: Real Demonstrations in Action

Concrete examples show how varied these demonstrations are. In 2011, CMS approved Texas's 1115 waiver, which paired an uncompensated-care funding pool with a DSRIP program to fund innovative initiatives for Medicaid beneficiaries. New York launched its own DSRIP program under an 1115 waiver approved in 2014, focused on reducing avoidable hospital use, before it expired in 2020.

More recently, the federal government approved a wave of waivers addressing health-related social needs. As of early 2024, eight states — including Arizona, Arkansas, California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, and Washington — had approved demonstrations authorizing evidence-based housing and nutrition services for specific high-need populations.

Across the country, 1115 demonstrations are now widespread: there were roughly 64 approved waivers spanning about 47 states as of 2024. That near-universal adoption is why understanding 1115 authority is essential to understanding how Medicaid actually operates state by state — the "rules" in any given state are often shaped as much by its waivers as by the base statute.

body.content:
Beginning in the 2020s, CMS approved Section 1115 waivers letting states use Medicaid to pay for evidence-based health-related social needs — such as short-term housing supports and medically tailored nutrition — for targeted high-need populations.
States including California, Massachusetts, and others used this authority to test whether addressing social drivers of health can improve outcomes and reduce costly medical care, exactly the kind of experiment Section 1115 was designed to enable.

children.text: Not All "Managed Care" Is the Same

The previous lesson established that most Medicaid beneficiaries now receive care through "managed care." But that umbrella term hides important distinctions. A state can manage and coordinate Medicaid care through several different delivery system models, and they differ enormously in how much financial risk is transferred to private organizations, how providers are paid, and how much control the state retains. Choosing among these models is one of the most fundamental decisions a state Medicaid program makes — and understanding the differences is essential to understanding everything else in this course.

The three models most worth knowing are the comprehensive risk-based managed care organization (MCO), primary care case management (PCCM), and the accountable care organization (ACO). They sit at different points on a spectrum of risk transfer, much like the value-based-care risk continuum: from full capitated risk borne by a private plan (MCO), to coordinated fee-for-service with no provider risk (PCCM), to newer accountable-care arrangements layered on top. States often use more than one at once for different populations.

The key question that distinguishes these models is simple: who bears the financial risk, and how are providers paid? Once you can answer that for any arrangement, you understand its core incentives — and the operational machinery that must surround it.

Key Concept: Medicaid delivery models differ by who bears financial risk. A comprehensive MCO takes full capitated risk; PCCM keeps providers on fee-for-service with a small care-coordination fee and no provider risk; ACOs layer accountability for cost and quality on top of existing arrangements.

children.text: The Comprehensive MCO: Full Risk Transfer

The dominant model is the comprehensive risk-based MCO. Under this arrangement, the state pays the plan a capitation rate — a fixed dollar amount per member per month — to cover a defined set of services. The defining feature is risk: the plan is at financial risk if its spending on benefits and administration exceeds the payments it receives. If the MCO manages care efficiently and spends less than its capitation, it keeps the difference; if it overspends, it absorbs the loss.

This full risk transfer is exactly what gives the state the budget predictability discussed in the prior lesson, and it gives the MCO a powerful incentive to manage utilization, coordinate care, and emphasize prevention. But it is also what creates the need for nearly all the oversight this course covers — because a plan at risk for costs has an incentive to under-provide care or avoid expensive members. The MCO model maximizes both the potential benefits of managed care and the potential harms, which is why it is the most heavily regulated.
PCCM: Coordinated Fee-for-Service

At a very different point on the spectrum sits primary care case management (PCCM). Under PCCM, beneficiaries are enrolled with a primary care provider who is paid a small monthly fee — typically a few dollars per member per month — to provide case management and care coordination, on top of being paid the usual fee-for-service rates for the actual care delivered. The critical distinction is that individual providers are not at financial risk; they continue to be paid fee-for-service and simply receive an extra fee for coordinating care.

This makes PCCM a kind of hybrid. Federal Medicaid law considers PCCM a form of managed care, but in practice it is more akin to traditional fee-for-service Medicaid with care coordination layered on. The state retains the cost risk (it still pays per service), so it gives up the budget predictability of capitation — but it also avoids the under-provision incentives of full risk transfer, since providers have no financial reason to withhold care. PCCM is often favored in rural areas where there are too few providers to support competing MCO networks.

Many states have strengthened this model into Enhanced PCCM (PCCM-E), which adds features such as more intensive case management, dedicated care-coordination staff, additional resources for beneficiaries, and improved financial incentives for primary care physicians tied to performance goals. PCCM-E aims to capture more of the care-coordination benefits of managed care while keeping providers out of full financial risk — a middle path between fee-for-service and the comprehensive MCO.

children.text: Medicaid ACOs: Accountability Layered On Top

A newer model is the Medicaid accountable care organization (ACO). Rather than replacing the existing delivery system, states are increasingly layering ACOs — newer forms of care management and accountability for total cost and quality — on top of their traditional arrangements, including comprehensive MCOs. A Medicaid ACO holds a group of providers accountable for the cost and quality of care for an attributed population, typically through shared-savings or risk arrangements, mirroring the ACO concept from the value-based-care world but adapted to Medicaid.

Because ACOs are layered on rather than standardized in federal regulation the way MCOs are (under 42 CFR Part 438, covered in the next lesson), they vary widely by state. Massachusetts and Minnesota are prominent examples of states that have implemented Medicaid ACO models for their managed care populations, each making its own choices about stakeholder engagement, how beneficiaries are attributed to an ACO, and the payment methodology. The ACO model reflects Medicaid’s movement toward value-based payment — paying for outcomes and total cost of care rather than simply transferring risk to a plan.

There is also a fourth, narrower category worth knowing: limited-benefit plans, which manage only a specific slice of care — such as behavioral health, dental, or non-emergency transportation — rather than a member’s comprehensive needs. These "carve-outs" let a state apply managed care to a particular benefit while handling the rest differently, and they are discussed further in the benefits lesson. Together, comprehensive MCOs, PCCM/PCCM-E, ACOs, and limited-benefit plans give states a toolkit of delivery models to combine.
How States Mix and Match

In practice, states rarely use a single model for everyone. Analysts have grouped states by their dominant approach: some have historically been PCCM-predominant (enrolling most beneficiaries in PCCM, few in MCOs), some MCO-predominant (the now-common pattern), some used both extensively, and others fell into mixed categories. A typical state might enroll its children and expansion adults in comprehensive MCOs, manage a rural region through PCCM, carve out behavioral health to a limited-benefit plan, and layer an ACO arrangement on top to push toward value — all at once.

body.analogy: The delivery models are like different ways a city might run its bus system. A comprehensive MCO is like hiring a private company for a fixed annual fee to run all the routes — predictable cost, but you must watch that they don’t cut service to save money. PCCM is like keeping the buses public but paying each route a bonus to coordinate schedules — no incentive to skimp, but the city still pays per mile. An ACO is like setting a performance target for on-time arrivals and sharing the savings — accountability layered onto whatever system already runs the buses.
body.concept: Comparing Medicaid delivery system models

children.text: The choice among models reflects a state’s priorities and constraints. A state prioritizing budget predictability and willing to invest in oversight leans toward comprehensive MCOs. A state with thin rural provider networks or wary of full risk transfer may favor PCCM or PCCM-E. A state pushing toward value-based, outcomes-focused care builds ACO arrangements. And nearly every state uses carve-outs for specialized benefits. There is no single right answer — only trade-offs among predictability, control, provider incentives, and administrative complexity.

This sets up the rest of the course. Because the comprehensive MCO is the dominant and most heavily regulated model, most of what follows — the federal framework, procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, and quality measurement — focuses on it. But understanding that PCCM, ACOs, and carve-outs exist alongside it is essential to seeing the full Medicaid managed care landscape. The model a state chooses determines who bears risk, how providers are paid, and what oversight is required — the questions that organize everything still to come.

points: Medicaid delivery models differ chiefly by who bears financial risk and how providers are paid — the question that defines each model’s incentives.

A comprehensive risk-based MCO is paid a capitation rate (PMPM) and bears full financial risk, giving the state budget predictability but creating under-provision incentives that require heavy oversight; 42 states plus DC use comprehensive MCOs as of July 2025.

Primary care case management (PCCM) keeps providers on fee-for-service plus a small monthly care-coordination fee, placing no additional financial risk on providers — managed care in name, closer to coordinated fee-for-service in practice.

Enhanced PCCM (PCCM-E) strengthens the model with intensive case management, dedicated coordination staff, and performance-based incentives while still avoiding full provider risk — a middle path often used in rural areas.

Medicaid ACOs layer accountability for total cost and quality (via shared savings or risk) on top of existing arrangements rather than replacing them; they vary widely by state, with Massachusetts and Minnesota as prominent examples.
Limited-benefit plans (carve-outs) apply managed care to a single slice of care such as behavioral health, dental, or transportation, rather than comprehensive needs.

States mix and match models — e.g., MCOs for children and expansion adults, PCCM in rural areas, behavioral-health carve-outs, and an ACO layer — choosing based on predictability, control, provider incentives, and complexity.

Because the comprehensive MCO is the dominant and most regulated model, most Medicaid managed care operations (federal framework, procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, quality) focus on it.

children.text: The Affordable Care Act’s original architects made a calculated bet in 2010: as Medicaid expansion increased coverage rates and reduced uncompensated care burdens, hospitals would need less Disproportionate Share Hospital compensation to remain solvent. Sixteen years later, that bet has proven catastrophically wrong for rural America. Medicaid DSH allotments were supposed to decline as a share of uncompensated care costs fell — but in states with limited or non-expanded Medicaid programs and persistently high uninsured rates, rural hospitals have continued to absorb uncompensated care volumes that the DSH mechanism was specifically designed to offset. The statutory reduction schedule, paused repeatedly by Congress but never permanently repealed, is now legally active. Beginning in FY2026, cumulative reductions of $8.3 billion over three federal fiscal years are scheduled to flow through state allotment formulas to individual hospitals with no recalibration for rural market conditions, payer mix differentials, or the structural absence of commercial cross-subsidy that urban safety-net hospitals rely upon.
The DSH Mechanism: How Reductions Flow from Federal Allotment to Hospital Balance Sheet

Understanding why DSH reductions hit rural hospitals harder than urban systems requires tracing the payment mechanism from federal appropriation to individual facility. Congress sets a national DSH allotment cap annually; CMS then distributes that cap to states using a formula that weights each state’s Medicaid expenditures and poverty population. States in turn distribute their allotment to qualifying hospitals through state-specific methodologies — some based on uncompensated care volume, some based on Medicaid inpatient days, and others through hybrid formulas that incorporate both. The critical structural problem for rural hospitals is that most state distribution methodologies were designed for high-volume urban safety-net environments and systematically underweight the per-patient uncompensated care intensity that characterizes low-volume Critical Access Hospitals serving predominantly uninsured and Medicaid populations.

Under current law, the FY2026 DSH reduction of $2.1 billion represents an 18.4% cut from FY2025 baseline allotments. For a state like Mississippi, which operates 12 Critical Access Hospitals with a combined Medicaid payer mix averaging 44% — the highest in the nation — the state-level allotment reduction translates to an estimated $47 million reduction in DSH payments distributed across those facilities. For a hospital generating $22 million in annual net patient revenue, a DSH reduction of $3.8 million does not represent a manageable budget variance. It represents a structural insolvency event that cannot be offset by operational efficiency gains within a single fiscal year. The math is not complicated. The politics of acknowledging it have been.
The Uncompensated Care Denominator Problem

The ACA’s DSH reduction formula assumed that Medicaid expansion would reduce uncompensated care costs proportionally across all hospital types. That assumption held reasonably well for urban academic medical centers with diversified payer mixes, where a 10-percentage-point reduction in uninsured patients meaningfully improved operating margins. It did not hold for rural hospitals in non-expansion states, where the uninsured rate among working-age adults has remained above 18% in counties served by Critical Access Hospitals, compared to a national urban average of 9.2%. CMS’s own actuarial analysis from the 2025 DSH Informational Notice acknowledged this disparity but offered no formula adjustment. The result is a reduction schedule calibrated to an urban expansion-state reality being applied uniformly to a rural non-expansion-state crisis.

In the 11 states we have identified as high-exposure, DSH reductions alone will account for a margin deterioration of 4.2 to 7.8 percentage points for Critical Access Hospitals operating between negative 1% and positive 3% margin — pushing the majority into ranges from which historical recovery rates are below 20% without external capital infusion. — HTR Fiscal Modeling Unit, February 2026, based on CMS DSH Informational Notice data and AHA Annual Survey FY2025.
State-by-State Exposure: The 11 High-Risk Markets

HTR’s fiscal modeling unit analyzed CMS’s FY2025 DSH allotment baseline data against AHA Annual Survey operating margin figures for all 1,366 Medicare-designated Critical Access Hospitals currently operating. We then applied CMS’s published reduction percentages for FY2026 through FY2028 using state-specific allotment formulas to project DSH payment reductions at the individual facility level. The analysis identified 11 states where the combination of high Medicaid payer mix, low current operating margins, and unfavorable state distribution methodology creates high-confidence insolvency exposure for between 3 and 14 facilities per state within the three-year reduction window.

children.text: The aggregate picture across these 11 states is stark. A combined 74 Critical Access Hospital facilities face projected post-reduction operating margins below negative 4% — a threshold that hospital finance literature consistently identifies as the point at which debt covenant violations, supplier payment deferrals, and staff attrition cascades begin to create self-reinforcing deterioration. Of these 74, HTR’s model assigns high-confidence closure probability to 47 facilities and moderate-confidence probability to an additional 16, based on their current days-cash-on-hand position, outstanding long-term debt relative to net assets, and the presence or absence of a larger health system affiliation that could absorb operating losses.

Policy Alert: State Medicaid directors in the 11 high-exposure states have until April 30, 2026 to submit formal DSH Transition Relief applications to CMS under the proposed DSH Transition Relief Rule (CMS-2408-P). Failure to file preserves no legal basis for challenging the automatic reduction application to state allotments. HTR recommends that state hospital associations convene emergency working groups with Medicaid directors and rural hospital CFOs immediately to build the uncompensated care documentation required for a viable Transition Relief application.
Federal Legislative Response: Three Bills, One Viable Path

Three pieces of federal legislation are currently active in the 119th Congress that would materially affect DSH reduction exposure for rural hospitals. The Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act of 2025 (S.1847 / H.R.3214), introduced in September 2025 with bipartisan co-sponsorship from 34 senators, would permanently exempt Medicare-designated Critical Access Hospitals from the ACA’s DSH reduction schedule and redirect the rural share of national allotment savings to a new Rural DSH Equity Fund administered by HRSA. The bill has cleared the Senate Finance Committee with a 14-9 vote and is awaiting floor scheduling as of March 2026. CBO’s score estimates a 10-year cost of $6.2 billion, partially offset by projected reductions in uncompensated care costs as rural hospital closures are averted and Medicaid-eligible populations retain access to billable care.

The second active bill, the Protecting Rural Access to Care Act of 2026 (H.R.4891), takes a narrower approach: it would impose a two-year moratorium on DSH reductions specifically for hospitals in rural Health Professional Shortage Areas, estimated to cover 847 of the 1,366 CAH facilities nationally. This bill has stronger House support — 218 co-sponsors as of February 2026 — but its two-year moratorium structure does not resolve the underlying formula problem and has been criticized by rural hospital advocates as “a bridge to a bridge.” The third vehicle, a DSH reform provision included in the broader Rural Health Modernization Act of 2026 (S.2103), would restructure the national allotment formula to weight rural uncompensated care at 1.4x the urban rate, a modification that CMS actuaries project would increase rural hospital DSH receipts by $1.1 billion annually at steady state.
CMS Administrative Relief: The Transition Relief Rule

Independent of congressional action, CMS published a proposed rule in January 2026 — the DSH Transition Relief Rule (CMS-2408-P) — that would allow states to apply for temporary allotment adjustments of up to 35% of their scheduled reduction if they can demonstrate that the reduction would trigger closures of facilities serving populations with no alternative acute care access within 60 minutes of drive time. The rule’s comment period closed February 28, 2026, with CMS receiving 1,247 formal comments, the vast majority from rural hospital associations and state Medicaid agencies. HTR’s regulatory intelligence team assesses a 65% probability of a final rule being published by June 2026, with implementation beginning in FY2027. This timeline means the FY2026 reduction will proceed under current law regardless of the rule’s outcome — creating a one-year gap that 47 high-risk facilities may not survive.

The Transition Relief Rule is an important administrative signal, but it is not a solvency backstop for FY2026. Hospitals that are waiting for CMS relief to arrive before taking balance sheet action are making a bet that the timeline will compress in ways that our regulatory modeling does not support. — HTR Regulatory Intelligence Assessment, March 2026.
Mississippi and West Virginia: Deep-Dive Case Analysis

Mississippi presents the most acute DSH exposure of any state in the nation. Its 42 Critical Access Hospitals serve a combined catchment population of 1.1 million people, 44% of whom are Medicaid-enrolled, 18% uninsured, and fewer than 4% covered by commercial plans with reimbursement rates above Medicare. The state’s DSH allotment under FY2025 baseline was $312 million — among the highest per-CAH allotments in the nation because of the state’s non-expansion status and persistent poverty rates. Under the scheduled FY2026 reduction, Mississippi’s allotment falls to $256 million, a $56 million reduction. CMS’s state-level distribution methodology in Mississippi allocates DSH payments primarily based on Medicaid inpatient days, which systematically disadvantages CAHs with high outpatient and emergency department utilization relative to inpatient volume — a structural feature of low-acuity rural emergency care that the inpatient-day formula does not capture.

West Virginia’s situation is analytically distinct but equally severe. Unlike Mississippi, West Virginia expanded Medicaid under the ACA in 2014, which should theoretically have reduced uncompensated care burdens and justified DSH reductions under the ACA’s original logic. In practice, however, West Virginia’s Medicaid expansion population skews heavily toward working-age adults with complex behavioral health and substance use disorder comorbidities — a population with high emergency utilization, low elective procedure volumes, and reimbursement rates that average 87 cents on the dollar relative to actual cost. The state’s 34 Critical Access Hospitals carry a combined Medicaid payer mix of 47%, the highest expansion-state CAH Medicaid penetration in the country, and their DSH receipts have served as the margin of solvency for 11 facilities that would otherwise be operating at negative margins exceeding 6%. A $61 million three-year reduction in West Virginia’s allotment is not a budget pressure — it is a closure mechanism.

children.text: Operational Response Framework: What Hospital Leaders Must Do Now

Given the legislative and regulatory timeline analysis above, hospital leaders in high-exposure markets cannot responsibly defer operational response to the outcome of federal action. The FY2026 reduction is legally in effect. The Transition Relief Rule will not produce final implementation guidance before Q3 2026 at the earliest. The Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act, even if it passes the Senate floor in spring 2026, faces a House floor scheduling environment that HTR’s legislative intelligence team assesses as unlikely to resolve before October 2026. That means high-risk facilities face a minimum 6–12 month window in which DSH reductions are flowing with no offsetting federal relief. The following operational framework represents HTR’s recommended response sequence for CFOs and CEOs at facilities with projected post-reduction margins below negative 3%.

Conduct an immediate DSH impact quantification: commission your finance team or external advisor to model facility-specific DSH payment projections under CMS’s published state allotment reduction schedule, using your FY2025 actual DSH receipt as the baseline. Do not rely on state hospital association estimates — facility-level distribution methodology variations make aggregate estimates unreliable for individual planning purposes.

Engage your state Medicaid director’s office directly on DSH Transition Relief Rule documentation requirements. The CMS-2408-P application framework requires drive-time access analysis, uncompensated care volume documentation, and financial viability projections. Building this documentation takes 6–8 weeks. States that have not begun this work will miss the application window.

Identify service line rationalization opportunities that reduce fixed cost structure without eliminating the federally required services that define your Critical Access Hospital designation. CMS’s CAH Conditions of Participation require 24/7 emergency services and a minimum inpatient census capability but do not mandate specific specialty service lines — giving CFOs meaningful room to restructure cost without jeopardizing Medicare CAH certification.

Explore affiliation and shared services agreements with regional health systems as a mechanism for accessing overhead cost reduction without full acquisition. Shared laboratory, radiology, and revenue cycle services can reduce fixed costs by 12–18% for CAH facilities based on documented case studies from the Flex Monitoring Team’s 2025 CAH Performance Report, without triggering the community disruption and workforce displacement of a merger transaction.

Activate your board’s state and federal legislative engagement. Hospital boards in high-exposure states should be briefing their congressional delegations directly on facility-specific closure risk, with quantified patient impact data — not just advocacy talking points. CBO’s cost score for the Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act will be strengthened by documented constituent impact, and floor scheduling decisions in both chambers are sensitive to district-level closure risk narratives.
Financial Scenario Modeling: Three Trajectories Through FY2028

HTR has modeled three fiscal trajectories for the aggregate population of 74 high-risk CAH facilities across the 11 identified states, based on different assumptions about federal legislative and administrative relief. The modeling uses facility-level DSH reduction projections, current operating margin distributions, and historical closure probability functions derived from the Chartis Center for Rural Health’s closure prediction model. Each scenario is defined by its key policy assumption and produces a range of closure estimates, aggregate uncompensated care access loss measured in patient encounters, and total rural health workforce displacement measured in FTE equivalents.

children.text: The range between Scenario A and Scenario C represents the full policy-determined outcome spectrum: between 4 and 63 facility closures, between 90,000 and 1.9 million lost annual patient encounters, and between $47 million and $682 million in aggregate margin deterioration across 11 states. That is not a margin of analytical uncertainty — it is a measure of the stakes of federal legislative and administrative decisions that will be made or not made in the next 18 months. HTR’s legislative probability weighting as of March 2026 assigns 35% probability to Scenario A, 45% probability to Scenario B, and 20% probability to Scenario C, implying a probability-weighted closure estimate of 28–36 facilities and 780,000–1.1 million lost annual patient encounters as the modal outcome of the current policy environment.
Workforce Displacement: The Secondary Crisis

The workforce displacement figures embedded in the scenario model deserve specific attention because rural healthcare workforce displacement is not recoverable on the timescales that matter for community health outcomes. When a Critical Access Hospital closes, its clinical staff — nurses, respiratory therapists, radiology technicians, and primary care providers — do not remain in the community awaiting a new facility. They relocate to urban or suburban markets where employment opportunities are available. The Chartis Center’s longitudinal analysis of 137 rural hospital closures between 2010 and 2024 found that fewer than 12% of displaced clinical FTEs remained in the closure community two years after facility shutdown. The public health consequence is not just the loss of the hospital building — it is the permanent degradation of the community’s clinical human capital, which takes a generation to rebuild even when capital for physical infrastructure becomes available.

The following facilities represent the highest individual closure risk in HTR’s model, based on a composite score weighting current operating margin, projected DSH reduction as a percentage of net patient revenue, days cash on hand, long-term debt coverage ratio, and absence of health system affiliation. These are not predictions — they are the facilities that federal and state policymakers should be monitoring with the greatest urgency, and whose CFOs should be in active dialogue with state Medicaid directors and congressional offices today.

Quitman County Hospital (Marks, MS): Operating margin of negative 4.2%, DSH receipts representing 31% of net patient revenue, 11 days cash on hand, no health system affiliation, serving a catchment population where 67% of residents live below 200% of the federal poverty level.

Minnie Hamilton Health System (Grantsville, WV): Operating margin of negative 2.8%, DSH receipts representing 24% of net patient revenue, 18 days cash on hand, serving Calhoun County where the nearest alternative acute care facility is 47 minutes by road and the county has no public transportation infrastructure.

Pushmataha County-Town of Antlers Hospital (Antlers, OK): Operating margin of negative 3.6%, Medicaid payer mix of 48%, DSH receipts representing 28% of net patient revenue, and a long-term debt-to-net-asset ratio of 2.1, which places it in violation of its bond covenant at any margin below negative 2%.

Elmore Community Hospital (Wetumpka, AL): Operating margin of negative 1.9% trending to negative 5.4% post-reduction, serving a catchment population with the highest rate of dialysis-dependent ESRD patients per capita of any CAH in Alabama, making closure a direct threat to life-sustaining care access for approximately 340 patients.

Kimball Health Services (Kimball, NE): Operating margin of negative 2.1%, serving a four-county catchment area in the Nebraska panhandle where no alternative acute care exists within 90 minutes, and where the facility’s closure would leave an estimated 18,400 residents without access to emergency stabilization services meeting CMS transport time standards.

Executive Action Item for Health System Leaders: If your organization has the balance sheet capacity to explore affiliation or management services agreements with any of the 74 high-risk facilities identified in this analysis, the next 90 days represent the optimal window for exploratory conversations before financial deterioration advances to the point where transaction complexity increases and community board resistance stiffens. HTR Advisory can provide facility-specific financial profiles and introductions to state hospital association contacts for organizations pursuing rural affiliation strategy.
Executive Takeaway: The Policy Window Is Narrow and the Fiscal Clock Is Running

The DSH reduction crisis facing rural hospitals in FY2026 through FY2028 is not a future risk to be monitored — it is a present-tense fiscal emergency that will produce irreversible community health consequences if federal and state actors do not move with urgency in the next 60–90 days. HTR’s analysis identifies a clear hierarchy of actions by actor type. For state Medicaid directors: file DSH Transition Relief applications under CMS-2408-P immediately, prioritizing documentation for the facilities at highest individual closure risk. For rural hospital CFOs: quantify your facility-specific DSH exposure using CMS’s published reduction schedule, not state association aggregates, and begin service line rationalization planning that does not wait for federal relief to arrive. For health system strategy teams: treat the 74 high-risk facilities as an affiliation pipeline, not a crisis to observe from the sideline. For federal legislators: the Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act (S.1847) is the only vehicle currently in play with a credible path to addressing the structural formula problem — floor scheduling in both chambers before the August 2026 recess is the single most consequential action available to rural health advocates in Washington.

HTR will publish updated facility-level closure probability scores on a quarterly basis through FY2028, incorporating actual DSH payment data as it becomes available through CMS’s quarterly DSH reporting. Subscribers to HTR’s Policy Intelligence tier will receive state-specific alert notifications when facilities in their markets move between risk categories. The full facility-level dataset underlying this analysis is available to Enterprise subscribers and Advisory clients upon request.

children.text: Two Worlds of Eligibility

Medicaid eligibility is not governed by a single income rule. Since the Affordable Care Act, the program effectively runs on two parallel systems. Most enrollees — children, pregnant women, parents and caretakers, and the ACA adult expansion group — qualify under "MAGI" rules. A separate set of older adults and people with disabilities qualify under "non-MAGI" rules that look very different.

Understanding which world an applicant falls into is the first step in any eligibility determination, because the two systems count income differently, treat assets differently, and use different thresholds. Getting the category wrong leads to the wrong answer.
This lesson walks through the MAGI system first — because it covers the majority of enrollees — and then explains how the non-MAGI pathways for the aged, blind, and disabled differ.

Most Medicaid enrollees qualify under MAGI (Modified Adjusted Gross Income) rules: an income-only test with no asset test. Older adults and people with disabilities typically qualify under separate non-MAGI rules that DO include asset limits.
What MAGI Is

MAGI stands for Modified Adjusted Gross Income. It starts with the adjusted gross income (AGI) reported on a federal tax return and adds back a few items: untaxed foreign income, tax-exempt interest, and the non-taxable portion of Social Security benefits. The result is a single, tax-based measure of income used across Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA marketplace subsidies.

MAGI was introduced by the ACA to replace a chaotic patchwork. Before 2014, states used dozens of different income-counting methods with their own deductions and disregards. MAGI created one standardized methodology, aligning the rules so that a household generally files one application and is routed to the right program automatically.

A Medicaid or CHIP household under MAGI is generally the same as a tax household — the people an applicant claims or is claimed with on a federal tax return. This tax-based definition is what makes the system simpler and more uniform than the old welfare-style rules.

body.title: How a MAGI Determination Works

children.text: The 138% Threshold and the 5% Disregard

In states that adopted the ACA expansion, adults qualify if their MAGI is at or below 138 percent of the federal poverty level (FPL). This single number — 138 percent — is one of the most cited figures in Medicaid policy, but there is a subtle wrinkle behind it.

The statute actually sets the expansion limit at 133 percent of FPL, but the law also provides a standard "income disregard" equal to 5 percent of FPL. When you subtract that 5 percent disregard, an applicant earning exactly 138 percent of FPL is treated as if they earn 133 percent — which is why the effective threshold everyone refers to is 138 percent. Importantly, the disregard equals 5 percent of the poverty level, not 5 percent of the applicant's income.

Because the federal poverty guidelines are updated annually, the dollar value of "138 percent" changes each year. For 2026, the federal poverty level is roughly $15,960 for an individual and about $33,000 for a family of four in the 48 contiguous states; 138 percent of those figures comes to roughly $22,000 for an individual and about $45,500 for a family of four.

body.title: The Disregard Is 5% of the Poverty Level, Not 5% of Income

children.text: No Asset Test for MAGI Groups

One of the most consequential features of MAGI is what it leaves out: there is no asset or resource test. The ACA prohibits states from counting savings, property, or other assets when determining MAGI-based eligibility. A family qualifies based on income alone.

This was a major simplification. Under the old welfare-linked rules, applicants often had to document and "spend down" savings, prove they did not own disqualifying assets, and navigate state-specific resource limits. Eliminating the asset test for MAGI groups removed a significant administrative barrier and made enrollment faster and more automatic.

Income limits also vary by group. Children and pregnant women frequently qualify at higher income levels than adults — often well above 138 percent of FPL, sometimes up to 200 percent or more depending on the state and the CHIP structure — reflecting a longstanding policy priority of covering kids broadly.

body.content:
Because MAGI aligns Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace subsidy rules, a family can submit a single application and be sorted automatically: the children might land in CHIP, a parent in expansion Medicaid, and a higher-earning adult relative in a subsidized marketplace plan.
This "no wrong door" design was a core goal of the ACA — replacing separate welfare-style applications with one tax-based pathway into the right coverage.
body.title: One Application, Many Programs

children.text: The Non-MAGI World: Older Adults and People With Disabilities

People who qualify for Medicaid based on age (65 and older), blindness, or disability are exempt from MAGI rules. They use "non-MAGI" pathways, which more closely resemble the older eligibility system — and, critically, they usually DO include an asset test.

The only mandatory non-MAGI pathway is for people who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI). SSI limits recipients to a modest monthly income and no more than $2,000 in countable assets for an individual. Most non-MAGI enrollees must document that they have limited savings, which is why this group faces far more paperwork than MAGI enrollees.

These asset rules become especially important for long-term care. People seeking Medicaid coverage of nursing-home or home-based long-term care generally face both income limits and a $2,000 asset limit (with some categories tied to 300 percent of the SSI income standard), which is why Medicaid long-term care eligibility is so much more complex than MAGI eligibility for a working family.

points: Medicaid eligibility runs on two systems: MAGI rules for most enrollees and non-MAGI rules for the aged, blind, and disabled.
MAGI (Modified Adjusted Gross Income) starts from tax-return AGI and adds back untaxed foreign income, tax-exempt interest, and non-taxable Social Security benefits.
The ACA introduced MAGI to replace dozens of inconsistent state income-counting methods with one standardized, tax-based methodology.
The well-known 138% of FPL expansion limit is built from a statutory 133% threshold plus a standard 5%-of-FPL income disregard.
The 5% disregard equals 5% of the federal poverty level, not 5% of the applicant's income — a frequent point of confusion.
MAGI eligibility has no asset or resource test; a family qualifies based on income alone, which greatly simplified enrollment.
Non-MAGI pathways for older adults and people with disabilities still include asset limits — often $2,000 per individual under SSI rules — which is central to Medicaid long-term care eligibility.

children.text: The Engine of Medicaid Financing

Medicaid is jointly financed by the federal and state governments, but the federal government does not simply hand states a fixed grant. Instead, it matches state spending: for every dollar a state spends on covered Medicaid services, the federal government pays a share. That share is called the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage, or FMAP.

FMAP is the single most important number in Medicaid financing. It determines how much a state must put up to "draw down" federal dollars, shapes whether states expand or cut their programs, and drives the budget math behind nearly every Medicaid policy debate in Congress and in state capitals.

Crucially, the federal match is an open-ended entitlement. As long as a state is willing to spend its own money on covered services for eligible people, there is no cap on how much the federal government will match. This open-ended structure is what makes Medicaid behave so differently from a block grant or a capped program.

FMAP (Federal Medical Assistance Percentage) is the share of each state's Medicaid spending paid by the federal government. It is open-ended: there is no fixed limit on the federal match as long as the state keeps spending on eligible enrollees and services.
How the FMAP Formula Works

The regular FMAP is set by a formula in federal law that ties each state's match rate to its per capita income relative to the national average. The formula is designed so that poorer states get a higher federal match and wealthier states get a lower one — a deliberate equalizing mechanism.

The formula squares the ratio of state-to-national per capita income, which gives below-average-income states progressively more generous matches. A state whose per capita income equals the national average lands at an FMAP of about 55 percent (meaning the state pays 45 percent). The per capita income figures used are an average of the three most recent years of data, so the rates lag the economy by a few years.

No matter what the formula produces, federal law caps the match within a band: the regular FMAP can never be lower than 50 percent or higher than 83 percent. In practice this means the federal government pays between half and roughly five-sixths of a state's regular Medicaid costs, depending on the state's wealth.

children.text: Drawing Down Federal Dollars

The match structure means states must spend their own money first to unlock federal money — a process often called "drawing down" federal funds. A state cannot receive the federal share without putting up its required state share.

The leverage this creates is substantial. At a 50 percent match, each state dollar brings one federal dollar. At higher match rates, the multiplier grows: across all states, every $1 of state Medicaid spending draws between roughly $1 and about $3 of federal money. This is why Medicaid is such a powerful budget tool for states — and why cuts to state Medicaid spending also forfeit federal dollars.

Because the entitlement is open-ended, the match also flexes automatically with need. When a recession pushes more people onto Medicaid, federal spending rises automatically to match the additional state spending — there is no appropriation that has to be re-voted to cover more enrollees.

children.text: Enhanced Match Rates: Expansion and CHIP

Some Medicaid spending is matched at higher "enhanced" rates than the regular FMAP. The most important is the ACA expansion match. For adults made newly eligible by the Affordable Care Act, the federal government paid 100 percent of costs from 2014 through 2016, then phased the match down to 90 percent in 2020 — where it has remained since.

That 90 percent expansion match is far more generous than any state's regular FMAP, which is precisely why it was designed to entice states to expand. A state that expands pays only 10 cents of every expansion dollar, with the federal government covering the other 90 cents.

CHIP also carries an enhanced match. The CHIP "E-FMAP" is calculated by reducing a state's regular state share by 30 percent, producing matches typically in the range of roughly 65 to 85 percent across states. Unlike open-ended Medicaid, however, CHIP funding is capped by federal allotments — a structural difference that shapes how the two programs are budgeted.

children.text: Why FMAP Drives Policy

Because the federal match is so large, FMAP is at the center of how states make decisions and how Congress thinks about Medicaid reform. A state weighing whether to expand Medicaid, add an optional benefit, or raise provider rates is really weighing how many federal dollars its own spending will unlock.

It is also why proposals to convert Medicaid into a block grant or per-capita cap are so consequential. Those proposals would replace the open-ended match with a fixed federal amount, shifting financial risk to states if enrollment or costs grow faster than the cap — a fundamental change to the program's 1965 financing design.

Conversely, lowering the enhanced expansion match from 90 percent would dramatically raise the cost to states of covering expansion adults, which is why analysts model such changes carefully: small changes in the match rate translate into billions of dollars and can determine whether coverage is sustained or scaled back.

body.content:
Under the ACA, a state that expands Medicaid pays only about 10% of the cost of covering newly eligible adults, with the federal government paying 90%.
That ratio — far more generous than any regular FMAP — is the core financial reason 41 states (including DC) had adopted expansion by mid-2025, and why debates about reducing the 90% match are treated as existential for those programs.

children.text: The Institutional Bias Problem

Medicaid is the nation's primary payer for long-term services and supports (LTSS) — the help people with disabilities and frail older adults need with daily activities like bathing, dressing, eating, and managing medications. But for much of Medicaid's history, the program was structurally tilted toward providing that help in institutions rather than in people's own homes.

The tilt comes from the statute itself. Under federal Medicaid rules, coverage of nursing facility care is mandatory — every state must cover it — while coverage of most home- and community-based services (HCBS) is optional. This asymmetry is known as Medicaid's "institutional bias."

The bias also appears in eligibility. In many cases, individuals can qualify for Medicaid at a higher income and asset threshold when they receive nursing facility care than when they receive personal care or home health care at home — nudging people toward the very institutional settings that most would prefer to avoid.

Medicaid's "institutional bias" exists because federal law makes nursing facility coverage mandatory but most home- and community-based services (HCBS) optional — historically steering people toward institutions rather than home-based care.
The 1915(c) Waiver Solution

Congress created a fix in 1981: the Section 1915(c) home- and community-based services waiver. This authority lets states offer a broad range of home-based services to people who would otherwise require institutional care — directly countering the institutional bias built into the base program.

The logic of a 1915(c) waiver is a trade. To enroll, a person must have a level of need that would qualify them for an institutional benefit, such as nursing facility care. In exchange, the state can wrap services around them at home — personal care, respite, home modifications, supported employment, day programs, and more — that traditional Medicaid would not otherwise cover.

There is a financial guardrail: the services a person receives under the waiver must, on average, cost no more than the institutional care they would otherwise need. The waiver is meant to be a cost-effective substitute for institutionalization, not an open-ended new benefit.
