children.text: Olmstead: When the Supreme Court Stepped In

The push toward community-based care got a powerful boost from the courts. In Olmstead v. L.C., decided June 22, 1999, the Supreme Court held that the unjustified institutional segregation of people with disabilities is a form of discrimination prohibited by Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

The case involved two women in Georgia, Lois Curtis and Elaine Wilson, who had been kept confined in a state psychiatric hospital for years after clinicians agreed they were ready for community placement. The Court established a three-part test: community placement is required when treatment professionals deem it appropriate, the individual does not oppose it, and it can be reasonably accommodated given the state's resources and the needs of others.

This principle, known as the ADA's "integration mandate," reframed home- and community-based care as a civil right rather than merely a policy option. It created sustained legal pressure on states to expand HCBS and reduce unnecessary institutionalization.
Unjustified institutional segregation of people with disabilities is a form of discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act — the core holding of Olmstead v. L.C. (1999).
The Rebalancing of Long-Term Care

Together, the 1915(c) waiver authority and the Olmstead decision drove a dramatic "rebalancing" of Medicaid long-term care away from institutions and toward the community. The shift over two decades was profound.

In 1999, when Olmstead was decided, about 27 percent of Medicaid LTSS spending went to home- and community-based services and roughly 73 percent went to institutional care. By 2020, those proportions had essentially flipped: around 63 percent of LTSS spending went to HCBS and only about 38 percent to institutions.

This reversal represents one of the most significant structural changes in the history of American long-term care — moving from a system that assumed institutional placement to one in which most Medicaid long-term care dollars now support people living in their own homes and communities.

children.text: Waiting Lists: The Catch

There is a major catch to HCBS waivers. Because most HCBS are optional, states are allowed to cap the number of people they serve under a waiver — limiting the number of "slots." When demand for home-based services exceeds the available slots, the result is a waiting list.

These waiting lists are large and persistent. Roughly 700,000 people were on HCBS waiver waiting lists in 2016, and about 710,000 in 2023 — meaning hundreds of thousands of people who qualify for home-based care must wait, sometimes for years, for a slot to open. People with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD) make up about two-thirds of those waiting.

Waiting lists expose the central tension of the HCBS waiver model: institutional care is a mandatory entitlement that no one waits for, while community-based care — the option most people prefer — can be capped and rationed. This is why advocates continue to push for stronger HCBS guarantees, and why waiting-list size is a closely watched measure of how well a state is meeting the spirit of Olmstead.

body.message: Because nursing facility care is a mandatory Medicaid benefit but HCBS is optional and can be capped, a person can be entitled to institutional care immediately while waiting years for a home-based waiver slot — the opposite of what most people want.

children.text: Born in 1965: A Great Society Program

Medicaid was created on July 30, 1965, when President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965 (Public Law 89-97). The same law created Medicare. Medicaid was added as Title XIX of the Social Security Act, and Johnson signed the bill in Independence, Missouri, with former President Harry Truman — who had championed national health insurance two decades earlier — at his side.

Both programs were part of Johnson's "Great Society" agenda, a sweeping set of domestic reforms aimed at reducing poverty and racial injustice. But the two programs were built very differently. Medicare was designed as a uniform federal program for people 65 and older. Medicaid, by contrast, was designed as a federal-state partnership: the federal government would pay a share of the cost, but each state would run its own program within federal rules.

This design choice is the single most important thing to understand about Medicaid. Because states administer their own programs, "Medicaid" is really 56 different programs — one for each state, the District of Columbia, and the territories — each with different eligibility rules, covered benefits, and provider payment rates. Two people with identical incomes can qualify in one state and be turned away in another.

Medicaid is authorized by Title XIX of the Social Security Act. It is jointly financed by the federal and state governments but administered by the states within federal guidelines — which is why eligibility and benefits vary widely from state to state.
From Welfare Add-On to Health Insurer

In its early decades, Medicaid was tightly tied to cash welfare. Eligibility was generally linked to receipt of welfare benefits, meaning that to get Medicaid you usually had to qualify for a cash-assistance program first. This linked health coverage to welfare status rather than treating it as health insurance in its own right.

A key early expansion came in 1972, when Congress created the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program. SSI consolidated cash assistance for low-income aged, blind, and disabled people, and in most states it led to automatic Medicaid eligibility for SSI recipients. This permanently expanded Medicaid's role as a payer for people with disabilities and the low-income elderly — populations that remain among the program's most expensive enrollees today.

Over the following decades, Congress gradually decoupled Medicaid from welfare. A series of laws in the 1980s extended coverage to low-income pregnant women and children regardless of welfare status, transforming Medicaid into a broad health-financing program rather than a welfare appendage.

children.text: CHIP and the Coverage of Children

The next major milestone came in 1997, when the Balanced Budget Act created the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), originally known as SCHIP. CHIP was designed to cover children in families that earned too much to qualify for Medicaid but could not afford private insurance — generally children in families below roughly 200 percent of the federal poverty level.

CHIP gave states a new, capped pot of federal money and substantial flexibility: states could run CHIP as an expansion of Medicaid, as a separate program, or as a combination of both. Together, Medicaid and CHIP became the backbone of children's health coverage in the United States, and the two programs are now reported and tracked together in most federal enrollment data.

CHIP was enacted as part of the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which provided roughly $40 billion in federal funding through fiscal year 2007 to cover low-income, uninsured children not eligible for Medicaid.
Unlike Medicaid, which is an open-ended entitlement, CHIP funding is capped — states receive a set federal allotment each year. This structural difference still shapes how the two programs are financed and renewed by Congress today.

children.text: The ACA and the Biggest Expansion in 50 Years

The Affordable Care Act (ACA), signed in 2010, called for the single largest expansion in Medicaid's history. Starting January 1, 2014, the ACA extended Medicaid eligibility to nearly all non-elderly adults with incomes up to 138 percent of the federal poverty level — including, for the first time, low-income adults without dependent children, who had historically been excluded in most states.

The ACA also created a single, income-based eligibility standard called Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI), replacing a patchwork of welfare-linked rules with one application and one set of rules aligned with the insurance marketplaces. The federal government agreed to pay an unusually generous share of the cost for the newly eligible adults to encourage states to expand.

But in 2012, the Supreme Court changed the plan. In National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius, decided June 28, 2012, the Court ruled that the federal government could not force states to expand Medicaid by threatening to withhold all of their existing Medicaid funding. The practical effect was to make the ACA Medicaid expansion optional for each state.

children.text: Medicaid Today: Scale and Significance

Six decades after its creation, Medicaid is one of the largest sources of health coverage in the United States. In fiscal year 2023, Medicaid provided coverage to roughly 96 million individuals over the course of the year at a total cost of about $894 billion. The federal government paid approximately 69 percent of that total and states paid the rest.

Medicaid represented about 18 percent of all national health spending in 2023, making it comparable in scale to Medicare and one of the dominant payers in the entire health system. It is also the nation's primary payer for long-term care and a major financer of births, behavioral health, and care for people with disabilities.

Enrollment fluctuates with the economy and with policy. It surged during the COVID-19 pandemic when states were temporarily barred from disenrolling people, then fell sharply during the post-pandemic "unwinding." As of February 2026, about 74.9 million people were enrolled in Medicaid and CHIP combined — still slightly above pre-pandemic levels but well below the pandemic peak.

result.title: Medicaid's Origins: 1965 to Today

children.text: How Most People Actually Get Medicaid

When people imagine Medicaid, they often picture the state directly paying a doctor each time an enrollee gets care. But that fee-for-service model is no longer how most Medicaid works. Today the majority of enrollees get their care through private health plans under contract with the state, known as Medicaid managed care organizations, or MCOs.

Under managed care, the state pays an MCO a fixed monthly amount for each enrolled member, and the MCO takes on the responsibility — and the financial risk — of arranging and paying for that member's covered care. This shifts day-to-day operations from the state to private plans and fundamentally changes the incentives in the program.

The scale of this shift is enormous. In 2024, more than 73 million people — about 85 percent of Medicaid enrollees — received some or all of their care through a Medicaid managed care plan, and comprehensive risk-based managed care is now the primary delivery system in nearly three-quarters of states.

A Medicaid managed care organization (MCO) is a private health plan paid a fixed monthly amount per enrollee by the state to arrange and pay for that enrollee's covered care. Most Medicaid enrollees are now in managed care rather than fee-for-service.
Capitation: Paying Per Member, Per Month

The defining feature of MCOs is capitation. Instead of paying for each service after it happens, the state pays the MCO a predetermined, per-member-per-month (PMPM) amount to cover and coordinate all of an enrollee's Medicaid services. The plan keeps the difference if it spends less than the capitation payment and absorbs the loss if it spends more.

This is what makes managed care "risk-based." The financial risk of an enrollee's care moves from the state to the plan. In theory this gives MCOs an incentive to keep members healthy and coordinate care efficiently; in practice it also creates a tension — a plan can profit by spending less, so strong oversight is needed to ensure it does not skimp on necessary care.

Federal rules require that capitation rates be "actuarially sound" — projected to cover all reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs under the plan's contract. Rates are set in advance by actuaries based on expected enrollment, the health profile (or "acuity") of members, and projected utilization.

children.text: The Main Types of Managed Care

Not all "managed care" is the same. State Medicaid programs use three main types of arrangements. The dominant model is comprehensive risk-based managed care, in which an MCO is fully at risk for a broad set of benefits in exchange for capitation — this is what most people mean by "Medicaid managed care."

A second model is primary care case management (PCCM). PCCM is really a managed fee-for-service system: enrollees are linked to a primary care provider who is paid a small monthly fee to coordinate care, but services are still billed fee-for-service. The state, not a plan, keeps the financial risk.

A third category is limited-benefit plans, which manage only a specific slice of care — such as behavioral health, dental, or non-emergency transportation — rather than the full benefit package. A single enrollee might be in a comprehensive MCO for most care and a limited-benefit plan for one carved-out service.

children.text: Networks and Access

Because an MCO is responsible for arranging care, it builds a network of contracted providers — primary care doctors, specialists, hospitals, behavioral health clinicians — that its members use. The composition of that network directly determines whether members can actually get the care they are entitled to.

This is why states impose network adequacy standards on MCOs, requiring them to maintain enough providers, within reasonable distances and wait times, to serve their enrollees. A capitation payment is meaningless if members cannot find a doctor who participates, so access standards are a core part of holding plans accountable.

Network adequacy is a recurring challenge in Medicaid because provider payment rates are often lower than commercial or Medicare rates, which can limit how many providers are willing to participate. Ensuring adequate networks is therefore one of the central oversight responsibilities states take on when they contract with MCOs.

body.content:
Medicaid managed care has grown into one of the largest privatized public programs in the country: a small number of large insurers operate Medicaid plans across many states, collectively covering tens of millions of enrollees.
This scale is why CMS and state Medicaid agencies devote so much attention to contract requirements, network standards, and financial oversight — the day-to-day Medicaid experience of most enrollees now runs through these private plans.
body.title: A Large, Privatized Delivery System

children.text: Accountability: The Medical Loss Ratio

A key tool for holding MCOs accountable is the medical loss ratio (MLR). The MLR measures how much of the capitation revenue a plan actually spends on health care for members, as opposed to administration and profit. A higher MLR means more of each dollar went to care.

Since 2019, federal rules have required states to set capitation rates so that each MCO can reasonably be expected to achieve an MLR of at least 85 percent. In other words, at least 85 cents of every capitation dollar should go to medical care and quality improvement, leaving no more than 15 cents for administration and profit.

The MLR is a direct response to the central risk of capitation: that a plan paid a fixed amount might pad its margins by underspending on care. By setting a floor on medical spending, the MLR — alongside network adequacy rules, quality reporting, and contract oversight — forms the accountability backbone of Medicaid managed care.

body.message: Capitation gives MCOs an incentive to coordinate care efficiently, but also a financial incentive to spend less — which could mean denying or delaying needed care. The 85% medical loss ratio floor, network adequacy standards, and quality reporting exist precisely to counter that risk.
body.title: Capitation Cuts Both Ways

children.text: Why Measure Medicaid Quality?

Covering people is only half of Medicaid's job; the other half is making sure the care they receive is actually good. Because most Medicaid enrollees now get care through private managed care plans paid a fixed amount per member, there is a built-in risk that a plan could cut corners to save money. Quality measurement is how states and the federal government keep watch.

Quality measurement turns vague questions — "Are kids getting their vaccines?" "Can adults get appointments when they need them?" — into standardized numbers that can be compared across plans, across states, and over time. Those numbers feed oversight, public reporting, and increasingly, payment.

Three pillars dominate Medicaid quality measurement: HEDIS (clinical process and outcome measures), CAHPS (patient experience surveys), and the federal Adult and Child Core Sets (a standardized national reporting set). This lesson walks through each and how they fit together.

Medicaid quality measurement converts care into standardized, comparable numbers. The three pillars are HEDIS (clinical measures), CAHPS (patient experience), and the federal Adult and Child Core Sets (national reporting).
HEDIS: The Clinical Yardstick

HEDIS — the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — is the most widely used set of health plan performance measures in the United States. It is developed and maintained by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), a private nonprofit, and used by commercial, Medicare, and Medicaid plans alike.

HEDIS consists of more than 70 measures spanning the full spectrum of care — prevention, acute care, and chronic care. It captures structure, process, and outcomes: things like childhood immunization status, follow-up after a hospitalization for mental illness, controlling high blood pressure, and screening for cancer. Because the specifications are standardized, one plan's diabetes-control rate can be compared directly with another's.

Standardization is the whole point. Without common definitions, every plan could define "well-child visit" or "blood pressure control" differently, making comparison meaningless. HEDIS provides the shared yardstick that lets states benchmark plans against each other and against national norms.

children.text: CAHPS: Asking Patients Directly

HEDIS tells you what was done clinically, but it cannot tell you what care felt like to the person receiving it. That is the job of CAHPS — the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems. CAHPS is a family of standardized patient-experience surveys originally developed under the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ).

The CAHPS Health Plan Survey asks members directly about their experiences. It produces four global ratings — overall health care, the health plan, the personal doctor, and the specialist seen most often — plus composite scores in areas like getting care quickly, getting needed care, customer service, and how well doctors communicate.

CAHPS is tightly integrated with HEDIS: NCQA asks plans to submit results from a modified version of the CAHPS Health Plan Survey as part of HEDIS reporting. Together, the two give a fuller picture — HEDIS for clinical performance, CAHPS for the patient's lived experience.

children.text: The Adult and Child Core Sets

To make quality comparable across all 50 states, CMS maintains standardized national measure sets specifically for Medicaid and CHIP: the Core Set of Adult Health Care Quality Measures and the Core Set of Children's Health Care Quality Measures. Many of these draw on HEDIS and CAHPS specifications.

For years, state reporting on these Core Sets was voluntary, which meant patchy and inconsistent national data. That changed in 2024: reporting of the Child Core Set and of the behavioral health measures within the Adult Core Set became mandatory for all states, the District of Columbia, and the territories. The first round of mandatory reporting had to be submitted and certified by states by December 31, 2024.

Mandatory reporting is a significant step. It gives CMS and the public a consistent, nationwide view of how Medicaid and CHIP are performing on priorities like children's preventive care and behavioral health — and creates accountability that voluntary reporting never could.

body.content:
The 2024 mandatory behavioral health measure set drew 7 measures from the Child Core Set and 11 from the Adult Core Set, covering areas such as follow-up after mental health hospitalization and monitoring for people on certain medications.
CMS uses these measures to track and push progress on behavioral health across state Medicaid and CHIP programs — an area of intense need that consistent national reporting can finally illuminate.
body.title: Behavioral Health in the Core Sets

children.text: Turning Measures Into Accountability: The EQRO

Measures are only useful if the underlying data is trustworthy and someone acts on it. In Medicaid managed care, that role falls to the External Quality Review Organization (EQRO). Federal rules require every state that contracts with managed care plans to hire at least one independent EQRO to conduct an annual external quality review of each plan.

The EQRO evaluates each plan on quality, timeliness, and access to care, and produces an annual technical report. Two of its core activities are validating the performance-measure data plans report and conducting HEDIS Compliance Audits — the industry's gold-standard check that a plan can produce valid, reliable measure data. Up to 40 states use the HEDIS Audit for exactly this purpose.

This is the loop that ties the whole system together: plans report HEDIS and CAHPS results, states fold many of those into the federal Core Sets, and independent EQROs validate the data and hold plans accountable. Quality measurement is not paperwork for its own sake — it is the mechanism that protects enrollees in a program where most care is delivered by private plans paid a fixed amount.

children.text: A Three-Year Pause on Disenrollment

In normal times, Medicaid enrollees must renew their eligibility periodically — typically once a year — and states disenroll people who no longer qualify or who fail to complete the paperwork. The COVID-19 pandemic suspended that machinery for three years, creating the conditions for what became the largest coverage disruption in the program's history.

At the start of the pandemic in 2020, Congress passed the Families First Coronavirus Response Act (FFCRA). It offered states enhanced federal Medicaid funding in exchange for a condition: states had to keep nearly everyone continuously enrolled, regardless of whether their circumstances changed. This "continuous enrollment provision" meant that for three years, almost no one was disenrolled from Medicaid.

The result was an unprecedented surge in enrollment. Medicaid and CHIP rolls grew by more than 23 million people, reaching nearly 95 million by the time the provision ended — a historic high driven not by a sudden spike in poverty but by the simple fact that the normal "exit door" had been bolted shut.

The "continuous enrollment provision" of the 2020 Families First Coronavirus Response Act barred states from disenrolling most Medicaid members for three years in exchange for extra federal funding. Enrollment swelled to nearly 95 million.
When and How the Pause Ended

The continuous enrollment provision was originally tied to the COVID-19 public health emergency. But in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, signed December 29, 2022, Congress "delinked" the two — setting a fixed end date of March 31, 2023, rather than letting it ride on the emergency declaration. This gave states a predictable date to plan around.

Starting April 1, 2023, states resumed normal eligibility reviews. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) gave states an "unwinding period" of up to 12 months to initiate renewals for their entire caseload — meaning every enrollee's eligibility had to be re-checked over the following year, a massive administrative undertaking after three years of paused renewals.

The enhanced federal funding that came with continuous enrollment was phased down on a schedule rather than cut off at once: a 6.2 percentage-point boost ran through March 2023, then 5 points through June, 2.5 points through September, and 1.5 points through December 2023. States had to meet certain reporting and procedural requirements to keep the phased-down funding.

children.text: The Scale of the Disenrollment

As states worked through their backlogs, the numbers were staggering. By the time the unwinding concluded in most states, KFF found that about 25 million people had lost Medicaid coverage through the process. Roughly 56 million renewals were completed with coverage retained — meaning about 31 percent of completed renewals ended in disenrollment.

Yet the program did not shrink below where it started. Because of the pandemic-era growth, total Medicaid/CHIP enrollment after the unwinding remained roughly 10 million higher than pre-pandemic levels — the rolls came down sharply from their peak but settled above February 2020.

Outcomes varied enormously by state, reflecting differences in renewal policies and systems. Disenrollment rates ranged from highs around 57 percent in some states to lows around 12 percent in others — a reminder that, as always in Medicaid, where you live shapes what happens to you.

children.text: Procedural Terminations: Losing Coverage Over Paperwork

The most important policy lesson of the unwinding is hidden in why people lost coverage. Among those disenrolled, nearly seven in ten — about 69 percent — were dropped for "procedural" reasons: missing paperwork, an outdated mailing address, an unreturned form. Only about 31 percent were actually determined to be ineligible.

This distinction matters enormously. A procedural termination does not mean a person no longer qualifies for Medicaid — it means the state could not confirm their eligibility through the renewal process. Many of those disenrolled were almost certainly still eligible and simply got caught in administrative churn, losing coverage they were entitled to keep.

States can reduce procedural terminations through "ex parte" (automatic) renewals, in which the state confirms eligibility using data it already has — such as tax and wage records — without requiring the enrollee to fill out anything. States with strong ex parte systems had far lower procedural disenrollment rates.

body.message: About 69% of unwinding disenrollments were for paperwork or procedural reasons, not because the person was found ineligible. A "procedural termination" means the state could not verify eligibility — many of those people still qualified and lost coverage they were entitled to.
body.title: Procedural Termination Is Not the Same as Ineligibility

children.text: Children and the Ex Parte Problem

Children were hit especially hard, and one specific system flaw made it worse. In August 2023, CMS determined that 29 states were running their automatic (ex parte) renewals at the household level instead of the individual level. Because children typically qualify for Medicaid or CHIP at higher income thresholds than adults, this flaw improperly dropped many children who should have kept coverage.

Federal officials sounded the alarm, estimating that potentially millions of children across many states had been improperly disenrolled. CMS directed states to fix their systems and to reinstate affected children — including providing retroactive coverage — illustrating how a technical configuration error can ripple into a large-scale coverage loss for the program's most vulnerable enrollees.

The episode reinforced a broader theme: in a program as large and decentralized as Medicaid, administrative design choices — how renewals are processed, whether data is used automatically, how a household is defined — can matter as much as the underlying eligibility rules in determining who actually stays covered.

body.content:
In August 2023, CMS found that 29 states were processing automatic renewals at the household level rather than per individual. Because kids qualify at higher income limits than adults, eligible children were dropped when the whole household was evaluated together.
CMS ordered states to correct the error and reinstate improperly disenrolled children with retroactive coverage — a real example of how a single processing rule affected the coverage of large numbers of children.

children.text: Four Major Populations

Medicaid does not cover everyone who is poor. It covers specific groups of low-income people defined by federal law and state choices. The program organizes its enrollees into four major populations: children, non-disabled (often called "non-elderly") adults, people who qualify on the basis of a disability, and adults age 65 and older.

Historically, eligibility was "categorical" — you had to fit into a recognized category (such as a child, a pregnant woman, a parent, an aged person, or a person with a disability) and also have a low income. The 2010 Affordable Care Act added a fifth pathway for low-income adults generally, but the categorical structure still shapes how the program works, how benefits are set, and how spending is distributed.

Understanding these four groups is the key to understanding Medicaid's finances, because the populations that make up most of the enrollment are not the populations that drive most of the spending — a tension that runs through nearly every Medicaid policy debate.

Medicaid enrollees fall into four major groups: children, non-disabled adults, people eligible due to disability, and adults 65 and older. Children are the largest group by enrollment, but older adults and people with disabilities drive the majority of spending.
Children: The Largest Group

Children are the single largest group of Medicaid enrollees. Together with the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), Medicaid covers a large share of all American children, financing a substantial fraction of all births and serving as the backbone of pediatric coverage for low-income families.

Children also receive Medicaid's most comprehensive benefit guarantee: Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment, known as EPSDT. EPSDT requires states to cover periodic and as-needed medical, vision, hearing, and dental screening for children under 21 — and, crucially, to cover any service needed to "correct or ameliorate" a child's physical or mental condition, even if that service is otherwise optional for adults.

Despite being the largest enrollment group, children are relatively inexpensive to cover because most are healthy. In fiscal year 2023, children represented roughly 35 percent of full-benefit enrollment but only about 15 to 16 percent of Medicaid spending.

EPSDT is the most comprehensive pediatric benefit in American health coverage: states must cover any medically necessary service for an eligible child, even services that are optional for adult enrollees.
The Elderly and People With Disabilities: Where the Money Goes

The populations that drive Medicaid spending are adults 65 and older and people who qualify on the basis of a disability. Together these two groups make up a minority of enrollment but the majority of spending, because they tend to have chronic conditions, complex needs, and high rates of long-term care use.

The per-enrollee numbers make the gap vivid. Spending per enrollee is highest for people with disabilities (around $20,950) and older adults (around $20,194) — roughly six times the per-enrollee spending for children (around $3,321), according to KFF analysis of federal data.

This is also why Medicaid is the nation's primary payer for long-term services and supports (LTSS). Medicare generally does not pay for extended nursing-home stays or ongoing personal care, so Medicaid fills that gap — covering nursing facility care and home-based care for people who have exhausted their resources.

children.text: Dual Eligibles: Covered by Both Medicare and Medicaid

A particularly important subgroup is "dual eligibles" — people enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid. These are typically low-income older adults or people with disabilities who qualify for Medicare but also meet Medicaid's income and asset limits. For them, Medicare is the primary payer and Medicaid wraps around it, covering premiums, cost-sharing, and benefits Medicare does not, such as long-term care.

Dual eligibles are a small share of enrollees but a hugely disproportionate share of cost. As of 2024, roughly 13.7 million Americans were enrolled in both programs. This high-need population accounts for a disproportionate share — about a third — of combined Medicare and Medicaid spending, which is why aligning and coordinating their care is a major policy priority.

Medicaid and Medicare are the first- and second-largest public payers for long-term services and supports, together accounting for roughly 63.6 percent of all LTSS spending nationwide in 2023.
Because Medicare generally does not cover extended nursing-home or personal-care needs, Medicaid is the de facto national long-term care program — a role most enrollees and families do not anticipate until they need it.

children.text: Mandatory vs. Optional Benefits

Just as eligibility groups are split into mandatory and optional, so are benefits. Federal law requires every state Medicaid program to cover a core set of mandatory benefits. These include inpatient and outpatient hospital services, physician services, laboratory and x-ray services, nursing facility services, family planning, federally qualified health center and rural health clinic services, and EPSDT for children.

Beyond that floor, states may choose to cover a wide range of optional benefits — such as prescription drugs (covered by every state in practice), dental care for adults, physical therapy, and home and community-based services. Because these are optional, the exact benefit package an adult receives depends heavily on which state they live in.

This mandatory-versus-optional structure, layered on top of the mandatory-versus-optional eligibility groups, is what makes Medicaid so variable. Two adults with the same income and the same diagnosis can receive very different coverage simply because they live in different states.

children.text: Special Needs Plans: Targeting the Highest-Need Beneficiaries

Not every Medicare Advantage plan is open to everyone. Special Needs Plans (SNPs) are a category of MA plan restricted to beneficiaries with specific characteristics, designed to tailor benefits, provider networks, and care management to populations with concentrated needs. They are one of the fastest-growing parts of the entire Medicare program.

There are three types. Chronic Condition SNPs (C-SNPs) serve people with specific severe or disabling chronic conditions, such as diabetes or heart failure. Institutional SNPs (I-SNPs) serve people who live in institutions like skilled nursing facilities (or who need that level of care). Dual Eligible SNPs (D-SNPs) serve people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid.

SNPs have grown dramatically. They now account for about 21 percent of all Medicare Advantage enrollees, up from just 13 percent in 2018, and between 2024 and 2025 they made up nearly half of the total growth in MA enrollment. SNPs are no longer a niche — they are a major engine of MA expansion.

There are three SNP types: C-SNP (chronic conditions), I-SNP (institutional), and D-SNP (dual eligible). All are Medicare Advantage plans, but enrollment is limited to beneficiaries who meet the plan’s specific eligibility criteria.

children.text: Dual Eligibles and the Rise of D-SNPs

Dual eligibles — people enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid — are among the most complex and expensive beneficiaries in the entire health system. They tend to be poorer, sicker, and more likely to need long-term services and supports, and historically they have had to navigate two completely separate programs with separate rules, cards, and benefits.

D-SNPs are designed to bring those two programs together. They are by far the largest SNP category: over 80 percent of all SNP enrollees are in D-SNPs, and D-SNP enrollment grew from about 2.2 million in 2018 to roughly 5.8 million in 2024. As more duals enroll, D-SNPs increasingly define how this high-need population experiences coverage.

The core challenge is integration. A D-SNP can be loosely or tightly coordinated with the enrollee’s Medicaid coverage, and CMS classifies the more integrated forms as Highly Integrated Dual Eligible (HIDE) SNPs and Fully Integrated Dual Eligible (FIDE) SNPs. FIDE SNPs go furthest — covering nearly all Medicaid services, including long-term services and supports, under one coordinated umbrella.

children.text: The 2025 Push Toward Integration

CMS has made integrating Medicare and Medicaid for dual eligibles a top priority, and a set of rules taking effect in 2025 sharply accelerates that push. The central change is a new integrated-care Special Enrollment Period (SEP): starting January 1, 2025, full-benefit dual eligibles can switch into an integrated D-SNP (FIDE, HIDE, or an applicable integrated plan) once per month to align their Medicare and Medicaid coverage.

At the same time, FIDE SNPs are now required to operate with "exclusively aligned enrollment," meaning their members must also be in the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan — so the two halves of coverage finally move together. Additional requirements phase in over the following years to further consolidate and align dual coverage.

The goal is to end the fragmentation that has long plagued dual eligibles: a single, coordinated plan responsible for both Medicare and Medicaid benefits, with unified care management and appeals. For the dual-eligible population, these rules represent one of the most significant structural changes in years.

body.content: A Fully Integrated Dual Eligible (FIDE) SNP is the most tightly integrated D-SNP. It must provide nearly all Medicaid services — including long-term services and supports (LTSS), Medicaid behavioral health, home health, and durable medical equipment — under one plan with exclusively aligned enrollment. For a dual eligible needing nursing-home-level care, that means a single entity coordinating both their Medicare medical care and their Medicaid long-term care, rather than two disconnected programs.
body.title: FIDE SNPs and Long-Term Services

children.text: A Concentrated Market

As Medicare Advantage has grown, it has also consolidated. A handful of large insurers now dominate. In 2024, UnitedHealthcare and Humana together accounted for nearly half — about 47 percent — of all Medicare Advantage enrollment nationwide.

At the local level the concentration is even starker. As of 2024, about 90 percent of Medicare beneficiaries lived in a county where MA enrollees had plans from just one or two insurers, and the great majority of counties were classified as highly or very highly concentrated. Rural counties were the most concentrated of all.

This concentration matters for policy. Limited competition can mean less pressure on plans to improve benefits or restrain costs, and it gives a few firms enormous influence over how most Medicare beneficiaries receive care. Market structure, not just payment formulas, shapes what Medicare Advantage actually delivers.

body.message: Beneficiaries often see dozens of MA plan options, but most of those plans are offered by the same few insurers. With UnitedHealthcare and Humana alone holding ~47% of national enrollment and most counties dominated by one or two firms, the MA "marketplace" is far less competitive than the plan count suggests.
body.title: Choice on paper, concentration in practice

children.text: Why MA Market Dynamics Matter

The growth of SNPs and the consolidation of the MA market are reshaping who controls high-need care. D-SNPs in particular are becoming the dominant vehicle for the dual-eligible population — the very people whose care is most expensive and most fragmented — putting private plans at the center of one of health policy’s hardest problems.

These dynamics also intersect with the overpayment concerns from the previous lesson. SNPs enroll sicker patients with higher risk scores, and concentrated markets reduce competitive pressure, both of which influence how much Medicare ultimately pays and what beneficiaries receive in return.

For anyone working in Medicare, the lesson is that Medicare Advantage is not a single uniform product. It is a fast-evolving market of specialized plans and dominant insurers, and the 2025 integration rules show that policymakers are actively trying to steer that market toward better-coordinated care for the people who need it most.
Medicare Advantage is no longer one product but a consolidating market of specialized plans — and D-SNPs are quietly becoming the front door to care for America’s sickest, poorest beneficiaries.

children.text: The Private Option Inside Medicare

Medicare Advantage (Part C) lets beneficiaries receive their Medicare benefits through a private health plan instead of directly from the government. An MA plan must cover everything Original Medicare Parts A and B cover, and the great majority also bundle in Part D drug coverage. In exchange for taking on this role, the plan receives a fixed monthly payment from CMS for each enrollee.

The trade-off for beneficiaries is real. In return for using a plan’s provider network and following its rules — including prior authorization for many services — enrollees often get extra benefits Original Medicare lacks, like dental, vision, hearing, and an annual out-of-pocket maximum that traditional Medicare does not have.

Medicare Advantage grew from the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 (originally "Medicare+Choice") and was renamed and expanded by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003. Over the following two decades it went from a niche option to the way most beneficiaries now get their Medicare.

Medicare Advantage plans are paid a risk-adjusted, capitated (per-member-per-month) amount by CMS to cover all Part A and B benefits — a fundamentally different payment model from the fee-for-service of Original Medicare.
From Niche to Majority

The headline fact about Medicare Advantage is its explosive growth. In 2024, more than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries — about 32.8 million people, or 54 percent — were enrolled in MA plans, up from roughly 38 percent of Part A and B spending share not long before.

This shift has profound consequences. As MA crosses the majority threshold, a growing share of all Medicare dollars flows through private insurers rather than directly to providers, and the largest insurers (such as UnitedHealthcare and Humana) have become dominant players in Medicare. Provider networks, prior authorization, and plan marketing now shape the experience of most beneficiaries.

Growth has been fueled by generous extra benefits, heavy marketing, and a payment structure that — as later sections explain — has tended to pay plans well. For the health system, MA is no longer an alternative to Medicare; for most beneficiaries, it is Medicare.

children.text: How Medicare Pays MA Plans: Benchmarks, Bids, and Rebates

Medicare pays MA plans through a benchmark-and-bid system. The benchmark is the maximum CMS will pay for an enrollee in a given county, set as a percentage of estimated traditional-Medicare spending in that county — ranging from 95 percent in high-cost counties to 115 percent in low-cost counties. Each plan then submits a bid: its estimated cost to provide Part A and B benefits.

If a plan bids below its benchmark — which nearly all plans do — it receives a rebate equal to a share of the difference between the benchmark and its bid. That share depends on the plan’s star rating: 70 percent for plans with at least 4.5 stars, 65 percent for 3.5–4 stars, and 50 percent for lower-rated plans. Plans must return rebates to enrollees as lower premiums, reduced cost-sharing, or supplemental benefits.

This is why MA plans can offer "$0 premium" coverage with dental and vision: the rebate funds those extras. It also ties plan revenue directly to quality ratings, since higher stars mean both a larger rebate share and quality-bonus increases to the benchmark itself.

children.text: Risk Adjustment and Star Ratings

Capitated payment creates an obvious risk: a plan could profit by enrolling only healthy people. Medicare counters this with risk adjustment. The CMS-HCC (Hierarchical Condition Categories) model raises a plan’s per-enrollee payment for sicker members based on their documented diagnoses, so plans are paid more to care for higher-need patients.

Quality is governed by the Star Ratings system, which rates plans from 1 to 5 stars on dozens of measures spanning clinical quality, patient experience, and customer service. Stars do double duty: they determine quality-bonus payments and they set the rebate share a plan keeps. In 2025, about 75 percent of MA enrollees were in plans receiving bonus payments, at an estimated federal cost of at least $12.7 billion.

Together, risk adjustment and star ratings are the levers that make capitation workable — paying more for sicker patients and rewarding measured quality — but, as the next section shows, they are also where the program’s biggest controversies live.

body.content: In 2025, federal spending on Medicare Advantage quality-bonus payments totaled at least $12.7 billion, with roughly 75% of MA enrollees in plans that earned bonuses. Bonuses raise a plan’s benchmark (most by 5 percentage points, and "double bonus" counties by 10), which is why plans invest heavily in their star ratings — even small movements across a star threshold can mean large revenue swings.
body.title: The $12.7 Billion Quality Bonus

children.text: The Overpayment Controversy

For all its popularity, Medicare Advantage faces a serious and well-documented critique: it costs taxpayers more than traditional Medicare would for similar enrollees. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) estimated that 2024 MA spending was about 23 percent higher than fee-for-service — roughly $88 billion in a single year.

MedPAC attributes this to two forces. "Coding intensity" — plans documenting more diagnoses to raise risk scores — made MA risk scores about 20 percent higher than they would be in traditional Medicare, worth roughly $54 billion. "Favorable selection" — MA tending to enroll healthier-than-average beneficiaries relative to their risk scores — added roughly $36 billion more.

These findings drive ongoing policy fights over how to reform risk adjustment, audit coding, and recalibrate benchmarks. They are essential context: Medicare Advantage delivers real benefits to enrollees, but its payment design has produced systematic overpayments that strain the very trust funds discussed earlier in this course.

body.message: Medicare Advantage often gives enrollees richer benefits and an out-of-pocket cap — but MedPAC estimates it cost taxpayers about $88 billion more than traditional Medicare in 2024, mostly from coding intensity and favorable selection. Both can be true at once.
body.title: Popular with enrollees, costly to taxpayers

children.text: A Safety Net, Not Comprehensive Insurance

A common misconception is that Medicare pays for everything once you turn 65. It does not. Traditional Medicare was designed in 1965 as a safety net against catastrophic costs, not as a comprehensive benefit, and it still carries substantial cost-sharing and significant coverage exclusions. Understanding these gaps is the single best way to understand why the Medigap and Medicare Advantage markets exist.

Cost-sharing in traditional Medicare comes in three forms: deductibles you pay before coverage kicks in, coinsurance (a share of each cost), and premiums for ongoing coverage. The dollar figures change every year; the structure does not.

The most consequential design feature is what traditional Medicare lacks: an out-of-pocket maximum. Unlike employer plans and Medicare Advantage, Original Medicare Parts A and B set no annual cap on what a beneficiary can owe — a single catastrophic illness can generate unlimited 20 percent coinsurance.

Original Medicare (Parts A + B) has no annual out-of-pocket maximum. This is the central financial risk of traditional Medicare and the main reason most beneficiaries add Medigap or choose Medicare Advantage.
Part A Cost-Sharing (Hospital)

Part A cost-sharing is organized around the "benefit period," a concept that surprises many beneficiaries. A benefit period begins when you are admitted as an inpatient and ends only after you have been out of a hospital or skilled nursing facility for 60 consecutive days. The deductible is charged per benefit period, not per year — so two separate hospitalizations months apart can each trigger the full deductible.

In 2025, the inpatient hospital deductible is $1,676 per benefit period. Days 1–60 carry no additional coinsurance after the deductible. Days 61–90 cost $419 per day. Beyond 90 days, you tap into 60 "lifetime reserve days" at $838 per day — and once used, those reserve days are gone forever.

Skilled nursing facility (SNF) coverage follows a separate schedule and has a critical precondition: Medicare only pays for SNF care after a qualifying inpatient hospital stay of at least three days. SNF days 1–20 carry no coinsurance; days 21–100 cost $209.50 per day in 2025; and after day 100, the beneficiary pays the full cost.

children.text: Part B Cost-Sharing (Medical)

Part B covers physician visits, outpatient care, preventive services, and durable medical equipment. In 2025, the standard Part B premium is $185.00 per month and the annual deductible is $257. After the deductible, beneficiaries typically pay 20 percent coinsurance of the Medicare-approved amount for most services.

That 20 percent has no ceiling. For a routine office visit it is trivial; for an expensive course of chemotherapy, dialysis, or specialty infusions billed under Part B, the 20 percent share can run into the tens of thousands of dollars in a single year — with no out-of-pocket maximum to stop it.

Higher-income beneficiaries pay more than the standard premium through IRMAA, the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount, which adds surcharges to both Part B and Part D premiums above set income thresholds.

children.text: What Medicare Does NOT Cover

Beyond cost-sharing, traditional Medicare simply excludes whole categories of care that older adults frequently need. Routine dental, vision, and hearing care — including most dentures, eyeglasses, and hearing aids — are not covered by Original Medicare.

The largest gap is long-term care. Medicare does not pay for custodial long-term care — help with bathing, dressing, eating, and other daily activities in a nursing home or at home over the long run. Medicare covers only short-term, skilled care for recovery. Long-term custodial care is paid out of pocket, by long-term care insurance, or by Medicaid once a person spends down their assets.

These exclusions are not minor. They are precisely the benefits that Medicare Advantage plans advertise — many MA plans add dental, vision, and hearing benefits — and they are a major reason beneficiaries weigh MA against Original Medicare plus a supplement.

children.text: How Medigap Fills the Gaps

Because Original Medicare has no out-of-pocket maximum and substantial cost-sharing, most traditional-Medicare beneficiaries buy a Medicare Supplement policy, known as Medigap. Sold by private insurers, Medigap plans are standardized into lettered plans (such as Plan G and Plan N) so that the same letter offers the same benefits no matter which company sells it.

Medigap covers cost-sharing in Original Medicare — Part A and Part B coinsurance and copayments, and depending on the plan, deductibles. By capping the beneficiary’s exposure, Medigap effectively creates the out-of-pocket protection that Original Medicare itself lacks.

But Medigap does not fill the benefit gaps. Medigap plans generally do not cover dental, vision, hearing, or long-term care. For those, beneficiaries must buy separate standalone policies — or choose a Medicare Advantage plan that bundles such benefits in. This trade-off, cost protection versus added benefits, is the core choice every new beneficiary faces.

body.content: Consider a Part B patient on an expensive specialty infusion drug billed at $300,000 a year. Under Original Medicare alone, the 20% coinsurance — about $60,000 — would fall on the patient with no cap to stop it. A Medigap Plan G would cover that Part B coinsurance after the small Part B deductible, turning a potentially ruinous bill into a predictable, modest cost. This is exactly the financial risk Medigap was built to address.

children.text: Two Trust Funds, Two Very Different Designs

Medicare does not run on a single pot of money. It runs on two separate trust funds with fundamentally different financing rules, and understanding the split is the key to understanding every Medicare solvency headline you will ever read. The Hospital Insurance (HI) Trust Fund pays for Part A. The Supplementary Medical Insurance (SMI) Trust Fund pays for Part B and Part D.

The HI Trust Fund works like Social Security: dedicated payroll taxes flow in while workers are employed, and benefits flow out in retirement. When payroll-tax revenue exceeds Part A spending, the surplus accumulates in the trust fund; when spending exceeds revenue, the fund is drawn down. Because its income is capped by what the tax brings in, the HI fund can actually run dry.

The SMI Trust Fund is the opposite. No payroll taxes are dedicated to it. Instead it is filled each year by general federal revenue plus beneficiary premiums, and the federal contribution is set prospectively to cover projected costs. Because Congress simply appropriates whatever is needed, the SMI fund is, by design, always solvent — it cannot "go broke."

HI (Part A) is funded by dedicated payroll taxes and can be exhausted. SMI (Parts B and D) is funded by general revenue and premiums set to cover costs, so it is automatically solvent. Almost every "Medicare is going bankrupt" story is really about the HI Trust Fund only.

children.text: Part A: The Medicare Payroll Tax

Part A is financed primarily by the Medicare payroll tax. Employees pay 1.45 percent of their earnings and employers pay a matching 1.45 percent, for a combined 2.9 percent. Self-employed workers pay the full 2.9 percent themselves. Unlike the Social Security tax, the Medicare payroll tax has no wage cap — it applies to every dollar of earnings.

Since 2013, an Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9 percent applies to high earners — on wages above $200,000 for individual filers and above $250,000 for joint filers. This extra tax is paid only by the employee, not matched by the employer, and was added by the Affordable Care Act to shore up HI financing.

This pay-as-you-go design means today’s workers are largely funding today’s retirees. That works well when there are many workers per beneficiary and strains badly when there are few — which is exactly the demographic squeeze Medicare now faces.

children.text: Parts B and D: General Revenue and Premiums

Part B and Part D are paid out of the SMI Trust Fund. For Part B, the law sets standard beneficiary premiums to cover about 25 percent of projected per-enrollee costs, with the remaining roughly 75 percent coming from general federal revenue — that is, from the broad federal budget funded by income taxes and borrowing.

Higher-income beneficiaries pay more through the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA), a surcharge added to both Part B and Part D premiums above certain income thresholds. Part D is financed similarly: enrollee premiums plus a large federal subsidy, with additional support for low-income beneficiaries.

The trade-off is important. Because SMI leans so heavily on general revenue, it never faces insolvency — but every dollar of growth in Part B and Part D spending directly enlarges the federal deficit. So SMI’s fiscal pressure shows up not as a trust-fund crisis but as a rising claim on the overall federal budget.

body.content: Medicare Advantage (Part C) does not have its own trust fund. CMS pays MA plans a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month capitation rate drawn from both the HI and SMI trust funds, in proportion to the Part A and Part B services those plans cover. So as MA enrollment grows past half of all beneficiaries, a growing share of both trust funds flows through private plans rather than directly to providers.
body.title: Medicare Advantage and Both Trust Funds

children.text: The HI Trust Fund Solvency Problem

Each year the Medicare Trustees publish projections of when the HI Trust Fund will run short. The 2025 Trustees Report projects HI depletion in 2033 — three years earlier than the prior report’s 2036 estimate, a change driven mainly by higher projected health care costs.

Crucially, depletion does not mean Medicare ends or that Part A stops. It means incoming payroll-tax revenue would cover only about 89 percent of Part A costs in 2033 — leaving an 11 percent shortfall that Congress would have to close through higher taxes, lower payments, or other policy changes.

The underlying driver is demographic. The worker-to-beneficiary ratio has fallen from about 4.6 workers per beneficiary at Medicare’s founding to roughly 2.9 today, and is projected to drop to about 2.5 by 2030 as baby boomers retire. Fewer workers supporting more retirees is the core arithmetic behind every solvency warning.

body.message: If the HI Trust Fund is depleted in 2033, Part A would still pay roughly 89 cents on the dollar from ongoing payroll taxes — it would not shut down. The depletion date is a policy deadline, not the end of the program.
body.title: "Trust fund depletion" is not bankruptcy

children.text: Why Financing Drives Payment Reform

Medicare’s financing structure is the engine behind decades of payment reform. Because the HI Trust Fund cannot simply print money and SMI growth widens the deficit, CMS has a powerful incentive to slow the rate of spending growth rather than just cut benefits.

That is why CMS has invested so heavily in delivery-system reform — accountable care organizations, bundled payments, value-based purchasing, and the work of the CMS Innovation Center. Each is an attempt to get the same or better care for less money, extending trust-fund solvency without slashing eligibility or coverage.

For anyone working in health care, the lesson is direct: Medicare’s payment changes are not arbitrary. They are downstream of a financing system under demographic strain, and they will keep coming as long as the worker-to-beneficiary ratio keeps falling.
Medicare’s solvency math — fewer workers funding more retirees — is the quiet force pushing American health care from paying for volume toward paying for value.

children.text: Why Medicare Was Created

Before 1965, growing old in America often meant losing health coverage exactly when you needed it most. Private insurers either refused to cover older adults or charged premiums most retirees could not afford, and roughly half of Americans over 65 had no health insurance at all. Aging was, in effect, a pre-existing condition that the private market would not insure.

President Lyndon B. Johnson signed Medicare into law on July 30, 1965, as part of the Social Security Amendments of 1965. The same statute created Medicaid. Medicare became Title XVIII of the Social Security Act and Medicaid became Title XIX — the legal "titles" you still hear referenced today.

Johnson held the signing ceremony at the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri, to honor former President Harry Truman, who had proposed national health insurance back in 1945 only to be blocked by Congress. Truman was enrolled as Medicare’s very first beneficiary and received the first Medicare card.

Medicare is a social insurance program: workers pay into it through payroll taxes during their careers and draw benefits in retirement, regardless of income. This is fundamentally different from Medicaid, which is means-tested and targets low-income people.

body.content: When Johnson signed Medicare into law at the Truman Library on July 30, 1965, he enrolled 81-year-old former President Harry Truman as the program’s first beneficiary. Truman and his wife Bess received the first two Medicare cards. Johnson chose the venue deliberately to credit Truman, who had first proposed national health insurance two decades earlier.
body.title: Harry Truman, Medicare Card #1

children.text: The Four Parts of Medicare

Medicare grew from a two-part program into a four-part program over four decades. Parts A and B existed from the start in 1965 and together are called "Original" or "Traditional" Medicare. Part C (Medicare Advantage) was created by the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 — originally called Medicare+Choice — letting beneficiaries get their benefits through private plans. Part D, the outpatient prescription drug benefit, was created by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 and took effect on January 1, 2006.

Part A is Hospital Insurance. It covers inpatient hospital stays, skilled nursing facility care following a qualifying hospital stay, hospice, and some home health. Most beneficiaries pay no Part A premium because they (or a spouse) paid Medicare payroll taxes for at least 40 quarters — ten years — of work.

Part B is Medical Insurance. It covers physician visits, outpatient care, preventive services, durable medical equipment, and drugs administered in a clinical setting. Part B requires a monthly premium. Part C, Medicare Advantage, is a private-plan alternative that must cover everything A and B cover and usually bundles in Part D drug coverage. Part D is the standalone voluntary prescription drug benefit delivered by private plans.

children.text: Who Is Eligible

Medicare eligibility is not purely about turning 65. The program has four distinct pathways to coverage, and understanding them is essential because they carry different rules about premiums and waiting periods.

The main pathway is age. U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents who have worked 40 quarters (ten years) in Medicare-covered employment are entitled to premium-free Part A at 65 and can enroll in Part B for a monthly premium. People who reach 65 without enough work quarters can still buy into Part A by paying a premium.

The disability pathway covers people under 65 who have received Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) for 24 months; they are then automatically enrolled in Parts A and B. Two conditions bypass the standard 24-month wait: people with End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) generally qualify about three months after starting regular dialysis or after a kidney transplant, and people with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) qualify immediately upon receiving SSDI.

children.text: How Big Medicare Is

Medicare is one of the largest payers in the world. As of 2025, about 68.9 million Americans are enrolled, and roughly 90 percent of them are age 65 or older; the rest qualify through disability, ESRD, or ALS. In 2024, about 61.2 million beneficiaries had both Part A and Part B.

The program is also a massive share of public finances. Medicare made up roughly 13.5 percent of the federal budget in 2024, and in 2024 Medicare spending reached about $1.1 trillion — around 21 percent of all national health expenditures. In short, more than one in five U.S. health care dollars flows through Medicare.

The pressure is demographic. The United States hit "Peak 65" in 2025, with a record 4.18 million people turning 65 in a single year — an average of about 11,400 every day. This wave of aging baby boomers is why Medicare financing, payment reform, and the shift toward value-based care dominate health policy debates.

children.text: Why Medicare’s Structure Matters

Medicare’s four-part design shapes nearly everything about how American health care is paid for. Because Part A is funded by a dedicated payroll-tax trust fund while Part B and Part D draw heavily on general revenue and premiums, the parts face very different fiscal pressures — a distinction explored in the next lesson on financing.

Medicare also sets the pace for the entire system. Private insurers frequently benchmark their payment rates to Medicare, and Medicare’s policy experiments — prospective payment, accountable care organizations, bundled payments — ripple outward to Medicaid and commercial payers. When Medicare changes how it pays, the whole market tends to follow.

Finally, the rapid growth of Medicare Advantage has shifted the program toward private administration. More than half of eligible beneficiaries are now in Part C plans, which changes how care is managed, how providers are reimbursed, and where federal dollars actually go.
Medicare did not just insure older Americans — it became the single most powerful force shaping how the entire U.S. health care system is financed and delivered.

children.text: Why Star Ratings Exist

Medicare Advantage is a consumer marketplace. Unlike traditional Medicare — which is run by the federal government and is largely standardized — Medicare Advantage is delivered by private insurance companies that must compete for enrollees. From the beginning, policymakers recognized that consumers needed a standardized, publicly available signal of plan quality to make informed choices. The Star Ratings system, formally established under the Medicare Modernization Act and expanded significantly by the ACA, provides that signal on a scale of 1 to 5 stars.

The Star Ratings system serves two distinct purposes that are sometimes in tension. First, it is a consumer information tool: the ratings are published on Medicare Plan Finder, and research shows that beneficiaries use star ratings when selecting plans — higher-rated plans attract more enrollees. Second, it is a financial incentive mechanism: plans with 4 or more stars receive quality bonus payments that can total hundreds of millions of dollars annually for large insurers. Both functions are served by the same set of measures, which creates pressure to optimize for measured metrics at the expense of unmeasured aspects of care.

The Star Ratings program has evolved substantially since its inception. CMS has progressively raised performance thresholds, added new measures, introduced methodological improvements like outlier deletion, and incorporated new domains such as health equity. Each annual cycle of measure updates and cut-point changes produces winners and losers among the nation's more than 700 Medicare Advantage contracts — and the financial consequences can run into the hundreds of millions of dollars per percentage point of star rating change.

Medicare Advantage Star Ratings simultaneously function as a consumer choice signal published on Medicare Plan Finder and as a financial incentive mechanism that awards billions of dollars in quality bonus payments to plans achieving 4 or more stars.
The Nine Domains and Forty-Plus Measures

The overall star rating for a Medicare Advantage Prescription Drug (MA-PD) plan is computed from performance across nine domains, with a maximum of 42 individual measures (40 unique measures, with 2 duplicated across Part C and Part D calculations). The nine domains span both clinical quality and member experience: Staying Healthy (screenings and vaccines), Managing Chronic Conditions (disease-specific clinical outcomes), Plan Responsiveness and Care (access and appeals), Member Complaints and Changes (grievances and disenrollment), and Drug Pricing and Patient Safety (Part D-specific).

Not all measures carry equal weight in the final star rating calculation. CMS applies a triple-weight to measures it considers highest-priority: patient experience surveys (Health Outcomes Survey and Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems, known as CAHPS), care coordination measures, and medication adherence measures. Double-weighted measures include preventive care screenings and chronic disease management. Single-weighted measures include administrative outcomes like complaint rates. This weighting structure means that member experience and care coordination dominate the overall rating in a way that the raw count of measures does not suggest.

Cut points — the thresholds separating 1-star from 2-star, 2-star from 3-star, and so on — are recalculated each year based on the distribution of plan performance during the measurement period. This means that achieving a 4-star rating requires hitting a different absolute performance threshold each year, depending on how the industry as a whole performed. In a year when most plans improved, cut points shift upward, and a plan that maintained the same absolute score might drop from 4 to 3 stars. This relative performance architecture creates both competitive pressure and financial instability.

children.text: The Quality Bonus Payment Formula

The financial stakes of star ratings are substantial. Plans that achieve at least 4 stars receive a quality bonus payment (QBP) that increases their county-level benchmark rate by 5 percentage points. This benchmark increase translates directly into higher capitated payments per enrollee. For a large Medicare Advantage plan enrolling hundreds of thousands of beneficiaries, a 5-percentage-point benchmark increase can mean hundreds of millions of dollars in additional annual revenue — the difference between profitability and loss in many markets.

The QBP formula also affects how plans share their rebate — the amount by which their bid falls below the quality-adjusted benchmark. Plans with 3 stars or below retain 50 percent of the rebate to fund additional benefits. Plans with 3.5 to 4 stars retain 65 percent. Plans with 4.5 or 5 stars retain 70 percent. The retained rebate is used to fund supplemental benefits (dental, vision, hearing, transportation, meals) that differentiate plans in the consumer market. Higher-rated plans therefore have both higher benchmarks and higher rebate retention — a compounding financial advantage that makes the 4-star threshold the most consequential boundary in Medicare Advantage finance.

Medicare Advantage quality bonus payments reached at least $11.8 billion in 2024 and are projected to total at least $12.7 billion in 2025, according to KFF analysis. These amounts represent a substantial subsidy embedded within the Medicare Advantage program. Critics argue that the bonus program pays out regardless of whether quality improvements are clinically meaningful or whether they produce better health outcomes — inflating spending without proportionate benefit to beneficiaries.

children.text: The 2025 Ratings Shock and the Tukey Method

The 2025 Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, released in October 2024, produced a striking decline across the industry. The average plan star rating fell from 4.07 in 2024 to 3.92 in 2025 — the first time the average had fallen below 4.0 since the early years of the program. More dramatically, only 7 plans achieved a 5-star rating in 2025, compared with 38 in 2024. The share of MA prescription drug plans achieving 4 or more stars dropped from 43 percent to 40 percent.

The primary driver of this decline was CMS's introduction of the Tukey Outlier Deletion Method for calculating cut points. This statistical technique removes extreme outliers from the performance distribution before calculating the thresholds between star levels. When outliers at the low end of performance are removed, the distribution shifts upward — and so do the cut points. The result is that a plan must now achieve higher absolute performance to earn the same star rating. CMS argued that the Tukey method produces more accurate cut points that better represent the typical range of plan performance.

The industry reacted with significant alarm. Plans that had maintained 4-star status for multiple years suddenly found themselves at 3.5 or 3 stars — with all the financial consequences that implies. Several large insurers, including UnitedHealth Group and Humana, disclosed that the rating declines would cost them hundreds of millions of dollars in reduced bonus payments. CMS received significant industry pushback and litigation, arguing that the methodology changes were insufficiently explained and implemented too abruptly.

body.message: Plan strategies to improve star ratings can include genuine quality improvements — better care coordination, more effective disease management — or gaming behaviors that improve measured scores without improving underlying care. Examples of the latter include aggressive outreach to complete HEDIS chart reviews without changing clinical processes, or narrowing supplemental benefits to lower the denominator of certain denominators. CMS periodically audits for gaming and adjusts measure specifications to reduce these opportunities.
body.title: Gaming vs. Genuine Improvement

children.text: Strategic Implications for Health Plans

Achieving and maintaining 4-star status has become one of the highest-priority strategic objectives for Medicare Advantage plans. Plans invest heavily in star ratings improvement programs: dedicated care management teams focused on HEDIS measure gaps, CAHPS survey outreach to improve member experience scores, pharmacy programs to improve medication adherence measures, and data analytics platforms that identify at-risk members before they miss screenings or fall out of compliance on chronic disease measures.

The CAHPS survey — which asks members to rate their experience with the plan, providers, and customer service — is particularly important given its triple weighting. Plans invest in member engagement programs, simplified appeals processes, and provider network management specifically to drive up CAHPS scores. The challenge is that CAHPS measures member perceptions, which are influenced by factors ranging from genuine care quality to marketing messaging and member demographics — making them both important outcome signals and susceptible to perception management.

Plans also monitor their performance within the Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI) — a CMS mechanism that adjusts star ratings upward for plans with high shares of dual-eligible and low-income subsidy beneficiaries. The CAI is discussed in detail in the next lesson on equity and the LIS problem, but for strategic purposes, it means that plans enrolling high shares of low-income beneficiaries receive partially offsetting adjustments to their star rating that help account for the expected performance challenges associated with serving socially disadvantaged populations.

body.analogy: Think of the Medicare Advantage Star Ratings system as a restaurant inspection score that directly determines how much your supplier will charge you for ingredients. A restaurant that falls from an A to a B doesn't just lose some customers — it also faces higher wholesale prices for everything it buys. The inspection criteria change every year, and a new scoring method might drop dozens of A-rated restaurants to B overnight. That is essentially what happened to Medicare Advantage plans in 2025.

children.text: How Mental Health Conditions Are Classified

Mental health conditions are diagnosed using standardized criteria, most commonly the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, currently in its fifth, text-revised edition (DSM-5-TR). The DSM groups conditions into broad families — mood disorders, anxiety disorders, trauma-related disorders, psychotic disorders, and others — each defined by specific symptoms, duration, and degree of functional impairment.

Two distinctions matter throughout this course. First, a diagnosis requires that symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment — feeling sad or worried is not, by itself, a disorder. Second, conditions exist on a spectrum of severity. The same diagnosis can be mild and manageable in one person and disabling in another, which is why the same condition can appear in both "any mental illness" and "serious mental illness" prevalence figures.

This lesson surveys the most common and most consequential conditions a non-clinician working in health care should recognize: depression, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. The goal is fluency with what these conditions are and how common they are — not the ability to diagnose them.

A mental health condition is diagnosed when specific symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment over a defined period — using standardized criteria from the DSM-5-TR. Severity ranges from mild to disabling within the same diagnosis.
Mood Disorders: Depression and Bipolar Disorder

Mood disorders involve disturbances in a person’s emotional state. Major depressive disorder is the most common: in a recent year, an estimated 21.0 million U.S. adults (8.3%) had at least one major depressive episode, with prevalence higher among women (10.3%) than men (6.2%). A major depressive episode is far more than ordinary sadness — it involves persistent low mood or loss of interest lasting at least two weeks, plus changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, and sometimes thoughts of death or suicide.

Depression’s impact is global and enormous. The World Health Organization identified depression as the single leading cause of disability worldwide, with more than 300 million people living with it. It is a leading driver of the lost productivity that makes behavioral health so costly economically.

Bipolar disorder is a distinct mood disorder marked by episodes of both depression and mania (or hypomania) — periods of abnormally elevated mood, energy, and activity. An estimated 2.8% of U.S. adults had bipolar disorder in the past year. Distinguishing bipolar disorder from unipolar depression is clinically critical, because antidepressants alone can trigger manic episodes; the two conditions require different treatment.

children.text: Anxiety Disorders

Anxiety disorders are the most prevalent class of mental health conditions overall. They involve excessive, persistent fear or worry that is out of proportion to the situation and interferes with daily life. The family includes generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and specific phobias.

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterized by chronic, hard-to-control worry about many things, accompanied by restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and physical tension. An estimated 2.7% of U.S. adults had GAD in the past year, with women affected more often (3.4%) than men (1.9%). Anxiety disorders often begin earlier in life than mood disorders and frequently co-occur with depression.

Anxiety disorders are highly treatable — psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy) and medication are both effective — yet many people never seek care, in part because symptoms are normalized or attributed to stress. Recognizing anxiety as a treatable medical condition rather than a personality trait is a key step in closing the treatment gap.
