children.text: Trauma-Related Conditions: PTSD

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) can develop after exposure to a traumatic event such as combat, assault, a serious accident, or disaster. Its hallmark symptoms include intrusive memories or flashbacks, avoidance of reminders, negative changes in mood and thinking, and heightened arousal such as being easily startled or hypervigilant.

An estimated 3.6% of U.S. adults had PTSD in the past year, and like several other conditions it is more common in women (5.2%) than men (1.8%). PTSD frequently co-occurs with depression and substance use disorders, and it illustrates an important principle: many behavioral health conditions are responses to life experience, not simply chemical imbalances.

PTSD is treatable with trauma-focused psychotherapies and, in some cases, medication. Its prevalence and its strong links to trauma exposure are reasons that "trauma-informed care" — designing services so they do not re-traumatize people — has become a guiding principle across behavioral health and increasingly across general health care.

children.text: Psychotic Disorders: Schizophrenia

Schizophrenia is among the most serious and disabling mental health conditions, even though it is far less common than mood or anxiety disorders. NIMH estimates the prevalence of schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders in U.S. adults at less than 1% — commonly cited in the range of about 0.25% to 0.64%. Despite its rarity, schizophrenia accounts for a disproportionate share of disability, homelessness, and contact with the criminal justice system.

Schizophrenia involves psychosis — a loss of contact with reality that can include hallucinations (such as hearing voices) and delusions (fixed false beliefs) — along with "negative" symptoms like reduced motivation and emotional expression, and cognitive difficulties. Onset typically occurs in late adolescence or early adulthood.

Because schizophrenia so often qualifies as a serious mental illness, it sits at the center of the premature-mortality problem discussed earlier in this course: people with schizophrenia die many years earlier than average, largely from preventable physical illness. This makes integrated medical and behavioral care especially urgent for this population.

body.message: Schizophrenia affects well under 1% of adults, yet drives a large share of disability and early death. People with schizophrenia are far more likely to be victims of violence than perpetrators — a fact often distorted by media coverage. Stigma itself is a barrier to care.
body.title: Rare but Severe — and Often Misunderstood

children.text: What "Parity" Means

Mental health parity is the principle that health insurance should cover behavioral health care — mental health and substance use treatment — no more restrictively than it covers physical health care. For most of the history of American health insurance, this was not the case: plans routinely imposed tighter visit limits, higher copays, and harder approval requirements on mental health benefits than on medical or surgical ones, treating the mind as somehow less deserving of coverage than the body.

Parity is not the same as a coverage mandate. A parity law says, in effect, "if you cover behavioral health, you must do so on equal terms" — it governs how generously a covered benefit is administered, not whether the benefit must exist. As we will see, this distinction shaped decades of legislation, because early parity laws left a giant loophole: a plan could comply by simply not covering behavioral health at all.

Understanding parity is essential to understanding the treatment gap from the first track of this course. Even when effective treatments exist and a person has insurance, restrictive coverage and administrative barriers can put care out of reach. Parity law is the main policy tool aimed at this barrier.

Mental health parity requires that insurers cover behavioral health no more restrictively than physical health. Parity governs how a benefit is administered — not, by itself, whether the benefit must be offered at all.
The Legislative Arc: 1996 to the ACA

Federal parity developed in three major steps. The Mental Health Parity Act of 1996 was the first, but it was narrow: it only required that lifetime and annual dollar limits on mental health benefits match those for medical benefits. It did not require plans to cover mental health at all, and it left untouched visit limits, cost-sharing, and other restrictions — so plans easily worked around it.

The landmark step was the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act of 2008 (MHPAEA). It dramatically broadened parity to cover financial requirements (copays, deductibles) and treatment limitations, and crucially added substance use disorders alongside mental health. But MHPAEA still did not require plans to offer behavioral health benefits — it governed plans that chose to.

The Affordable Care Act (ACA) closed the remaining loophole for many people. Beginning in 2014, the ACA made mental health and substance use disorder services one of ten "essential health benefits" that individual and small-group market plans must cover — and must cover at parity. Together, MHPAEA and the ACA both required coverage and required it to be equal, extending federal parity protections to tens of millions of Americans.

children.text: The Two Kinds of Limits: QTLs and NQTLs

MHPAEA regulates two categories of limits. Quantitative treatment limitations (QTLs) are numerical: visit limits, day limits, copays, deductibles, and other measurable restrictions. Because they are easy to compare, QTLs were the easy win — after MHPAEA, virtually all plans dropped behavioral-health-specific numerical limits that exceeded their medical limits.

Nonquantitative treatment limitations (NQTLs) are where parity gets hard. These are non-numerical management practices — prior authorization requirements, medical-necessity criteria, step therapy, provider network composition, and how reimbursement rates are set. NQTLs are not banned, but they may not be applied more stringently to behavioral health than to comparable medical care. Because they are subjective and hard to measure, NQTLs are the frontier of parity enforcement.

A 2021 law (the Consolidated Appropriations Act) and a 2024 final rule pushed plans to prove NQTL compliance by performing and documenting "comparative analyses" — formal demonstrations that, for example, their prior-authorization rules for therapy are no tougher than those for physical-therapy. This is the central battleground of modern parity enforcement.

children.text: Why Parity on Paper Is Not Parity in Practice

Despite decades of law, real-world parity remains elusive — and the gaps are well documented. One major problem is "ghost networks": insurer provider directories listing in-network behavioral health clinicians who are, in reality, unreachable, no longer practicing, or not accepting new patients. Investigations have found that a large majority of listed providers in some networks could not actually deliver care, making the on-paper network meaningless.

A second gap is reimbursement. MHPAEA prohibits unequal financial treatment of patients but does not directly regulate how much insurers pay providers. Research has found that reimbursement for office visits with medical and surgical clinicians was on average about 22% higher than for behavioral health clinicians — and that patients went out of network to see a behavioral health professional roughly 3.5 times more often than for medical or surgical care. Low pay drives clinicians out of networks, and narrow networks force patients to pay out of pocket.

These gaps explain a frustrating paradox: a person can have "parity-compliant" insurance and still be unable to find an in-network therapist who can see them. The law has eliminated the crude numerical disparities but struggled with the subtler structural ones — networks, reimbursement, and administrative friction — that determine whether care is actually accessible.

children.text: Enforcement Today

Parity enforcement is shared among federal agencies — the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and the Treasury — and state insurance regulators. The 2024 final rule strengthened requirements for the NQTL comparative analyses, including objective data on network adequacy and reimbursement, in an effort to close the loopholes that allow ghost networks and arbitrary prior authorization to persist.

Enforcement, however, remains contested. In May 2025, the federal departments announced they would not enforce the new provisions of the 2024 final rule while related litigation (an industry lawsuit) plays out, plus an additional period afterward. This pause left uncertainty about exactly which 2024 requirements are in force and underscored how politically and legally fraught parity enforcement continues to be.

The takeaway is that parity is a decades-long, still-unfinished project. The legal principle is settled and broad coverage exists, but turning "equal coverage on paper" into "equal access in practice" depends on enforcing the harder NQTL standards — and that effort is ongoing, uneven, and subject to political and legal headwinds.

children.text: Why MIPS Was Created: The Death of the SGR and the Birth of MACRA

For nearly two decades, Medicare physician payment operated under the shadow of the Sustainable Growth Rate (SGR) formula — a mechanism Congress invented in 1997 to prevent physician spending from exceeding GDP growth. The SGR failed in its purpose almost immediately. Whenever physician spending exceeded the SGR target, the formula required automatic fee cuts that Congress consistently reversed through emergency "doc fix" legislation, rather than allow payment rates to collapse. By 2015, the accumulated deficit had grown to the point where the pending automatic cut was 21.2% — an amount no one considered politically or practically possible to implement.

On April 16, 2015, President Obama signed the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA) into law, with rare bipartisan support. MACRA permanently repealed the SGR and replaced the patchwork of overlapping quality reporting programs — the Physician Quality Reporting System (PQRS), the Value Modifier, and the Meaningful Use program for electronic health records — with a single unified framework: the Quality Payment Program (QPP). The QPP offered physicians two paths: the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) and participation in Advanced Alternative Payment Models (Advanced APMs).

MIPS launched January 1, 2017, as the default track for most Medicare-participating clinicians. It was designed to consolidate performance measurement into a single composite score, reduce administrative duplication, and begin moving physician payment toward a value orientation by adjusting fees up or down based on quality, cost, and technology adoption. For the first time, physician payment adjustments under Medicare would be explicitly tied to measured performance — not just volume.

Key Concept: MIPS (Merit-Based Incentive Payment System) is the primary track of the CMS Quality Payment Program, established by MACRA in 2015. It scores eligible clinicians on four performance categories — Quality, Cost, Promoting Interoperability, and Improvement Activities — and adjusts Medicare Part B payment rates up or down by up to ±9% based on their composite score.

children.text: The Four Performance Categories: What MIPS Actually Measures

MIPS organizes performance measurement into four weighted categories, each contributing a share of the 100-point composite score used to determine a clinician's payment adjustment. For 2024, the category weights are: Quality (30%), Cost (30%), Promoting Interoperability (25%), and Improvement Activities (15%). These weights represent a significant evolution from the program's early years, when Quality carried 60% of the score and Cost was minimal. The increasing weight of Cost reflects CMS's intent to hold clinicians more accountable for the total expense of the care they deliver.

The Quality category requires clinicians to report on at least six quality measures from a list of hundreds, including one outcome measure or one high-priority measure. Measures span clinical domains such as diabetes management, cancer screening, cardiovascular risk reduction, and behavioral health. Performance is benchmarked against historical rates, so a clinician who outperforms their peers on a measure earns more points in that measure's category. The Cost category, by contrast, does not require any reporting — CMS calculates it directly from Medicare claims, attributing episode and total cost of care metrics to the responsible clinician.

The Promoting Interoperability (PI) category, worth 25% of the composite score, evaluates the use of certified electronic health record technology, with measures focused on patient access to records, electronic prescribing, health information exchange, and public health reporting. The Improvement Activities category, at 15%, allows clinicians to earn points by attesting to participation in one of approximately 95 defined activities — such as care coordination, patient engagement, clinical practice improvement, or population health management — each weighted as medium or high impact.

children.text: Performance Thresholds, Payment Adjustments, and the 2026 Outlook

The MIPS payment adjustment applies to Medicare Part B payments in the year two years after the performance year — so 2024 performance determines 2026 payment rates. For 2024, the performance threshold is 75 points on the 100-point composite scale. Clinicians who score at or above 75 points receive a neutral or positive payment adjustment; those who score below 75 receive a negative adjustment; those below 18.75 points (the exceptional negative threshold) receive the maximum penalty of -9%.

The statutory maximum positive adjustment is also ±9%, but the actual positive adjustment is constrained by the program's budget-neutrality requirement: the total positive adjustments paid must be funded by the total negative adjustments collected. In practice, because the vast majority of MIPS-eligible clinicians score above the performance threshold, the positive adjustment pool is spread thinly across a large number of clinicians. For 2026 payments (based on 2024 performance), CMS estimated the maximum positive adjustment at only approximately +1.05% — the lowest in program history — despite the statutory maximum of +9%.

This dynamic reveals a fundamental tension in MIPS design. The program was built to create meaningful financial incentives for improvement, but budget-neutrality has compressed the actual positive adjustment to the point where it provides a weak incentive for the additional administrative burden required to optimize performance. The threat of the -9% penalty has been more behaviorally significant than the promise of a +1.05% bonus — a pattern that raises questions about whether MIPS is actually changing clinical behavior or primarily ensuring compliance.

children.text: Who Must Participate and Who Is Exempt

Not every Medicare-participating clinician is subject to MIPS. CMS defines eligibility through a low-volume threshold: clinicians must exceed all three of the following criteria to be required to participate — billing more than $90,000 for Medicare Part B-covered services, seeing more than 200 Medicare patients, and providing more than 200 covered professional services to Part B patients in a year. Clinicians who fall below any one of these thresholds are exempt from MIPS requirements, though they may choose to voluntarily report.

Clinicians who qualify to participate in an Advanced Alternative Payment Model (Advanced APM) — such as a qualifying ACO under the Medicare Shared Savings Program, or certain CMS Innovation Center models — are exempt from MIPS and instead receive the Advanced APM incentive. Through 2022, this incentive included a 5% lump-sum bonus on Medicare Part B payments. That bonus expired at the end of 2022, creating a significant policy debate about whether the financial case for joining an Advanced APM had been sufficiently weakened to slow the transition to value-based care.

Certain other clinicians are excluded: those in their first year of Medicare participation, those enrolled in Medicare Advantage, and certain facility-based clinicians who may be scored under a facility-based scoring option. Additionally, small practices and solo practitioners — particularly those in rural or underserved areas — have historically faced disproportionate MIPS penalties, in part because they lack the administrative infrastructure to optimize reporting across four performance categories simultaneously.

body.message: MIPS adjustments apply only to Medicare Part B allowed charges — not to total revenue from all payers. A physician who earns the maximum +9% MIPS bonus still receives only a 9% increase on their Medicare-specific claims, which may represent a fraction of their overall practice revenue. The financial impact of MIPS is often smaller than it appears from the headline adjustment percentages.
body.title: Common Misconception

children.text: Administrative Burden: MIPS's Most Persistent Criticism

Since its launch, MIPS has been criticized by physician organizations, small practices, and health policy researchers for imposing substantial administrative costs that are disproportionate to the financial incentives on offer. Participating in MIPS requires clinicians to understand hundreds of quality measures, select appropriate reporting mechanisms (claims, registry, EHR, or QCDR), maintain certified EHR technology meeting PI requirements, attest to improvement activities, and monitor their performance relative to benchmarks that shift annually. For a small or solo practice, this work often requires either significant staff time or the engagement of a third-party reporting vendor.

The disproportionate impact on small practices is well-documented. According to American Medical Association data, 49% of solo physicians received MIPS payment penalties in recent performance years, compared to 29% of small practices and 18% of rural practices. Larger health systems and multispecialty group practices, with dedicated quality reporting teams and sophisticated EHR implementations, consistently outperform solo and small group practitioners on MIPS scores — not necessarily because they deliver better care, but because they have more administrative capacity to optimize the reporting process.

This critique reflects a deeper concern about MIPS as a policy instrument: it measures and rewards the ability to navigate a complex reporting system as much as it measures or rewards actual quality of care. CMS has attempted to address administrative burden through the development of MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs) — streamlined reporting pathways organized around specific specialties or clinical conditions — but adoption has been slow and the program structure remains complex for most participating clinicians.

body.content:
The American Medical Association has consistently documented the administrative cost of MIPS participation. In surveys of physician practices, the AMA found that MIPS-related administrative work can consume 15 or more hours per physician per week when preparing for reporting periods, diverting clinical staff to documentation and data-entry tasks rather than patient care.
The AMA has called for fundamental MIPS reform, arguing that the program's administrative overhead exceeds its clinical benefit for the majority of participating clinicians — particularly those in independent and small-group practice settings that lack the infrastructure of large health systems.
body.title: AMA MIPS Burden Research

children.text: MIPS vs. Advanced APMs: The Two Paths of the Quality Payment Program

MACRA was designed to offer two fundamentally different paths toward value-based payment. MIPS is an incremental path — it preserves the fee-for-service payment architecture while layering on quality-and-cost measurement and a modest payment adjustment. It asks clinicians to report and be measured, but does not fundamentally change how their revenue is generated. Advanced APMs, by contrast, require clinicians to take on significant financial risk — or at minimum, meaningful quality accountability — in exchange for relief from MIPS reporting and an additional financial incentive.

Advanced APMs include the Medicare Shared Savings Program at its highest risk tracks, the ACO REACH model, certain bundled payment models, and designated CMMI Innovation models. Qualifying for the Advanced APM bonus requires that a threshold percentage of a clinician's Medicare payments or patients be tied to the qualifying Advanced APM, and that the model involve more-than-nominal financial risk or a medical home model meeting CMS criteria. For 2026, the Advanced APM incentive is now subject to policy review following the expiration of the 5% bonus at end of 2022.

The design tension between MIPS and Advanced APMs reflects a broader policy debate: should the transition to value-based care be gradual and voluntary, preserving FFS while adding quality signals, or should it require providers to take on actual financial accountability for outcomes and cost? MIPS has been criticized as a "value-based care on training wheels" approach that generates compliance activity without fundamentally realigning incentives. Advanced APMs represent the deeper structural shift, but they require data infrastructure, care redesign capabilities, and risk tolerance that many smaller practices simply do not have.

body.analogy: MIPS is like a performance review at work — your score affects your raise by a few percent, but your underlying job and pay structure remain the same. Advanced APMs are more like moving from a salaried role to a performance-based partnership: the risk is higher, but so is the potential reward, and the nature of your work fundamentally changes.

children.text: When Quality Scores Become Paychecks

So far this course has treated quality measurement mostly as information — scores that inform improvement and public comparison. The Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) is where measurement turns directly into money. Under MIPS, a clinician's measured performance adjusts their Medicare payments up or down.

MIPS was created by the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA), the law that repealed Medicare's old physician-payment formula. MACRA established the Quality Payment Program (QPP), which gives clinicians two tracks: MIPS, and Advanced Alternative Payment Models (APMs) such as certain ACOs that take on financial risk.

MIPS is the default track for most clinicians billing Medicare Part B who are not in an Advanced APM. It consolidated several older, separate programs into one scoring system — making it the largest pay-for-performance program for physicians in the country.

MIPS (Merit-based Incentive Payment System), created by MACRA in 2015, is the track of Medicare's Quality Payment Program that ties a clinician's Medicare Part B payments directly to their measured performance.
The Four Performance Categories

A MIPS score is built from four performance categories, each capturing a different dimension of practice. The first is Quality — clinical quality measures the clinician selects and reports, the direct descendant of the older quality-reporting programs.

The second is Cost, which measures the total cost of care attributed to the clinician and is calculated by CMS from Medicare claims, requiring no separate data submission. The third is Improvement Activities, which credits activities that improve care processes, patient engagement, and access. The fourth is Promoting Interoperability (formerly "Meaningful Use"), which requires using certified EHR technology (CEHRT) to share information and engage patients.

For 2024, the category weights are Quality 30 percent, Cost 30 percent, Promoting Interoperability 25 percent, and Improvement Activities 15 percent. Notably, Quality and Cost are now weighted equally — a deliberate shift reflecting the program's push to hold clinicians accountable not just for doing the right things but for doing them efficiently.

children.text: From Categories to a Final Score

The four weighted categories combine into a single MIPS final score on a 0-to-100 scale. That number is then compared against a national "performance threshold" to determine whether a clinician's payment goes up, down, or stays flat.

For recent performance years the threshold is 75 points. A final score above 75 earns a positive adjustment, a score below 75 earns a negative adjustment, and a score exactly at 75 is neutral. Clinicians scoring very low (below a separate floor) face the steepest penalties.

Crucially, the categories are not independent silos — a strong showing in Quality and Promoting Interoperability can offset a weaker Cost score, and vice versa. This is why MIPS strategy is about optimizing the weighted total, not maxing out any single category.

children.text: The Payment Adjustment: Stakes and Mechanics

The financial consequences are significant. MIPS applies a Medicare Part B payment adjustment of up to plus or minus 9 percent based on the final score. For a practice with substantial Medicare volume, a 9 percent swing is a major revenue event.

Two design features shape how this plays out. First, MIPS is budget-neutral: the penalties collected from low performers fund the bonuses paid to high performers, and adjustments are distributed on a sliding scale. That means a high score does not guarantee the full 9 percent bonus — the actual upside depends on how everyone else performed.

Second, there is a two-year lag. Performance in one year determines the payment adjustment two years later — for example, 2023 performance affects 2025 Medicare payments. Clinicians must therefore manage MIPS prospectively, because by the time the adjustment hits, the performance period is long closed.

children.text: Why MIPS Matters — and Its Critics

MIPS matters because it operationalizes everything earlier in this course at national scale: the measure stewards, the measure types, and the quality measures themselves all feed into a program that moves real Medicare dollars for hundreds of thousands of clinicians. It is the clearest example of "what gets measured gets paid for."

It is also heavily criticized. Clinicians cite administrative burden, complexity, and frequent rule changes; researchers question whether MIPS scores correlate well with actual patient outcomes, and whether the program meaningfully improves care relative to its reporting cost. The equally-weighted Cost category in particular is contentious because attribution of cost to an individual clinician is difficult.

CMS has acknowledged these concerns and is steering toward "MIPS Value Pathways" (MVPs) — more focused, specialty-relevant measure sets meant to reduce burden and improve relevance. The direction of travel is toward the Advanced APM track and value-based models, but for most clinicians today, MIPS remains the program that connects quality measurement to their Medicare paycheck.

body.content:
Under MACRA's Quality Payment Program, clinicians fall into one of two tracks. Most report through MIPS and receive a performance-based Part B adjustment. Others participate in Advanced Alternative Payment Models — such as certain ACOs that bear financial risk — which can exempt them from MIPS and offer separate incentives.
The long-term policy goal is to move more clinicians out of MIPS and into risk-bearing Advanced APMs.

result.title: MIPS and Quality Payment Program Measures

children.text: The Rule That Limits How Much a Plan Can Keep

The previous two lessons explained how a state sets a capitation rate and adjusts it for the health of each plan’s members. But once the money is paid, a new question arises: how much of it must actually be spent on care, versus kept by the plan as administration and profit? Without an answer, a capitated plan could pocket a large share of public dollars while delivering minimal care — the worst version of the under-provision incentive that runs through this entire course. The medical loss ratio (MLR) is the rule that answers this question and sets a floor on how much of each capitation dollar must go to members.

The medical loss ratio is the share of premium (capitation) revenue that a plan spends on medical care and quality improvement, rather than on administration, marketing, and profit. An 85% MLR means at least 85 cents of every dollar goes to care and quality, leaving at most 15 cents for everything else. The MLR is, in effect, a profit-and-overhead limit expressed from the other direction: by requiring most of the money to be spent on care, it caps how much can be retained.

For Medicaid, the MLR is both a financial-integrity safeguard and a complement to rate-setting. Recall from the rate-setting lesson that certified rates must target an MLR of at least 85%; the MLR requirement then measures whether actual spending lived up to that target. Together, they ensure rates are built to fund care and that the money paid actually reaches care. This lesson explains how the MLR is calculated, enforced, and where it differs from its better-known commercial cousin.

Key Concept: The medical loss ratio (MLR) is the share of capitation revenue a plan spends on medical care and quality improvement rather than administration and profit. Under 42 CFR 438.8, any state-mandated minimum MLR must be at least 85%, functioning as a floor on care spending and a cap on overhead and profit.

children.text: How the MLR Is Calculated

The MLR is a fraction: care-and-quality spending divided by adjusted revenue. Federal rules (42 CFR 438.8) define each part precisely. The numerator is the sum of the plan’s incurred claims (the direct cost of covered services, including payments to network providers and amounts for claims still being processed or incurred but not yet reported), plus expenditures for activities that improve health care quality, plus fraud prevention activities. In other words, the numerator captures money spent on actual care and on legitimate quality and integrity work — the things the MLR is meant to reward.

The denominator is adjusted premium revenue: the plan’s premium (capitation) revenue minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing and regulatory fees. Subtracting those taxes and fees is important — it ensures the plan is not penalized for money it never really had to spend on care, because that money went to the government, not to overhead or profit. Dividing the care-and-quality numerator by the adjusted-revenue denominator yields the MLR percentage.

One technical refinement matters: the credibility adjustment. Small plans with few enrollees have MLRs that swing widely due to random statistical variation — a single catastrophic case can distort a small plan’s ratio. The credibility adjustment accounts for this random variation related to the number of enrollees, giving smaller plans some allowance so they are not unfairly penalized (or rewarded) for what is essentially statistical noise rather than how they actually managed care. Larger plans, whose numbers are statistically stable, receive little or no adjustment.

children.text: Remittance: What Happens When a Plan Falls Short

Setting a minimum MLR is meaningless without a consequence for missing it, and that consequence is the remittance — a payment a plan must make when its MLR falls below the minimum. If a plan’s MLR comes in below 85% (meaning it spent less than 85% on care and kept more than 15%), the state can require the plan to remit the shortfall. This is what gives the MLR teeth: a plan cannot simply under-spend on care and pocket the difference, because the difference must be paid back.

Some states have built creative alternatives to a straight cash remittance. In North Carolina, plans that miss the MLR may contribute to health-related resources in lieu of all or part of the remittance, submitting proposals that align with the state’s quality strategy for approval. Tennessee similarly lets a plan below 85% either remit funds or propose a community reinvestment plan for state approval. These approaches turn the penalty into reinvestment — redirecting underspent dollars back into community health rather than simply clawing them to the treasury.

body.message: Because the numerator includes quality-improvement and provider-incentive spending, plans can be tempted to inflate those categories to artificially raise their MLR and avoid remittances. The 2024 final rule specifically targets this, noting that disconnecting provider incentive payments from actual measurable quality standards creates a risk of artificially inflated qualifying costs and manipulated MLR percentages.
body.title: Watch for MLR Manipulation

children.text: How Medicaid MLR Differs From Commercial

The MLR concept is most famous from the Affordable Care Act, which applies it to commercial insurance — but the Medicaid version differs in two crucial ways. First, enforcement and where the money goes. In the ACA Marketplaces, plans that miss the MLR target must return the excess to enrollees as rebates — totaling $1.1 billion in 2023. In Medicaid, by contrast, any remittance goes to the state (and ultimately back to federal and state taxpayers who funded the capitation), not to individual enrollees, because Medicaid enrollees did not pay premiums in the first place.

Second, and more striking, is that the Medicaid MLR is largely optional for states. Under federal law, states that contract with MCOs have the flexibility to decide whether to impose a minimum MLR requirement at all, and if so, whether to collect remittances from plans that fall short. Federal rules require that all plans calculate and report their MLR, and that any state-set minimum be at least 85% — but they do not force a state to set a minimum or to collect a remittance. CMS considers a minimum MLR with a remittance to be a reasonable program-integrity approach, but it is the state’s choice.

This flexibility is consequential and controversial. It means a state could require plans to report MLRs that reveal low care spending and high retention, yet collect nothing back — a gap critics have noted, observing that Congress and CMS have stopped short of a uniform, mandatory Medicaid MLR with required rebates. The reporting requirement still creates transparency and pressure, but the actual financial bite depends on whether each state chooses to wield it.
Why the MLR Completes the Financial Spine

The MLR is the final piece of the rate-setting module’s financial spine, and it interlocks with the other two. Rate-setting determines how much a plan is paid; risk adjustment ensures that payment matches the health of the members enrolled; and the MLR ensures that, whatever the plan is paid, most of it is actually spent on care. Remove any one and the system fails: a sound, risk-adjusted rate could still be largely pocketed without an MLR floor, and an MLR floor on an unsound rate would just enforce inadequate spending. The three work only together.

body.analogy: The MLR is like a rule that a charity must spend at least 85 cents of every donated dollar on its mission, keeping no more than 15 cents for overhead and salaries. Donors (here, taxpayers) get assurance their money reaches the cause rather than the office. And if the charity spends too little on the mission, it must give the surplus back. The Medicaid twist is that whether the "give it back" rule is enforced — and how strictly — is left to each state to decide.
body.concept: How the medical loss ratio works

children.text: The MLR also reframes how to think about a managed care plan’s profit. A plan does not profit by being paid more — the capitation is fixed and risk-adjusted — nor simply by spending less on care, because the MLR floor limits that. In principle, a plan profits by managing care efficiently: reducing avoidable utilization and administrative waste while still meeting the MLR and quality requirements. The MLR is designed to channel the plan’s drive for profit away from skimping on care and toward genuine efficiency, which is the behavior managed care is supposed to reward.

For the student, the MLR is the clearest expression of how Medicaid managed care tries to reconcile private profit with public purpose. By requiring most of every public dollar to reach care, it limits the harm a profit motive can do; by leaving plans room for efficiency gains, it preserves the incentive that makes managed care work. Its optional, state-by-state enforcement also illustrates the federal-state tension that runs through Medicaid — a federal floor on the percentage, but state discretion on whether to enforce it. Master the MLR, and you understand the rule that keeps capitation honest about where the money goes.

points: The medical loss ratio (MLR) is the share of capitation revenue a plan spends on medical care and quality improvement rather than administration and profit; an 85% MLR means at least 85 cents of every dollar goes to care.
Under 42 CFR 438.8, any state-mandated minimum MLR must be at least 85%, functioning simultaneously as a floor on care spending and a cap on overhead and profit.

The MLR numerator is incurred claims plus quality-improvement and fraud-prevention spending; the denominator is adjusted premium revenue (premium minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing/regulatory fees).
A credibility adjustment accounts for random statistical variation in small plans, so a few catastrophic cases do not unfairly distort a small plan’s MLR.

When a plan’s MLR falls below the minimum, the state can require a remittance (paying back the shortfall); some states (e.g., North Carolina, Tennessee) allow community reinvestment plans in lieu of cash remittance.

Medicaid MLR differs from commercial/ACA MLR in two ways: remittances go to the state (not rebated to enrollees as in the ACA’s $1.1 billion in 2023 rebates), and setting a minimum MLR and collecting remittances is largely optional for states.

Because the numerator includes quality and provider-incentive spending, plans can attempt to inflate it to avoid remittances — a manipulation the 2024 final rule specifically targets by tightening the link between incentive payments and measurable quality.
The MLR completes the financial spine with rate-setting and risk adjustment, channeling a plan’s profit motive away from skimping on care and toward genuine efficiency.

children.text: Trust, but Verify — Independently

A state can write a strong contract with detailed network, quality, and reporting requirements, but a contract is only as good as the oversight behind it. How does a state actually know whether its MCOs are delivering quality care, maintaining adequate networks, and treating enrollees fairly — rather than simply claiming to? The answer combines two layers: the state’s own ongoing monitoring, and an independent, expert review conducted by a third party called an External Quality Review Organization (EQRO). This lesson is about how Medicaid managed care is actually watched.

The need for independent review flows directly from the central tension of managed care. A capitated plan has both the incentive to under-provide care and control over much of the data used to judge it. Relying solely on the plan’s self-reporting would be like grading students on tests they score themselves. The EQRO exists to break that conflict — to provide the state and CMS an objective, expert assessment of each plan’s quality, timeliness, and access, based on validated data rather than the plan’s word.

Understanding monitoring and oversight completes the procurement-and-contracting story. The procurement chose the plans; the contract defined their obligations; and oversight — anchored by the EQRO — is how the state verifies those obligations are met and acts when they are not.

Key Concept: States oversee MCOs through ongoing monitoring plus an annual External Quality Review (EQR) conducted by an independent External Quality Review Organization (EQRO), which assesses each plan’s quality, timeliness, and access and reports findings the state uses to hold plans accountable.
What External Quality Review Is

External Quality Review (EQR) is the analysis and evaluation, by an independent EQRO, of aggregated information on the quality, timeliness, and access to health care services that a managed care plan furnishes to Medicaid or CHIP enrollees. Those three dimensions — quality, timeliness, and access — are the lens through which every EQR assesses a plan. The federal parameters that states must follow when conducting EQR are set out at 42 CFR §§ 438.350, 438.354, 438.358, 438.360, and 438.364, making EQR a federally required, structured process rather than an ad hoc review.

The EQRO must be genuinely independent and qualified. Federal rules require the EQRO to have staff with demonstrated experience and knowledge of Medicaid beneficiaries, managed care delivery systems, and quality assessment methods; sufficient physical, technological, and financial resources; and the clinical and nonclinical skills to carry out the work. This independence and expertise are what give the EQRO’s findings credibility — it is not the plan grading itself, and it is not a generalist auditor, but a specialized organization equipped to evaluate managed care quality.
The Mandatory EQR Activities

EQR is built from a defined set of EQR-related activities — the work, set out at 42 CFR § 438.358, that produces the data the EQRO analyzes. Several activities are mandatory, performed on each plan. One is a compliance review, which states must conduct on each plan once within a three-year period, assessing the plan’s compliance with structural and operational standards. Another is the validation of performance measures — independently confirming that the quality measures a plan reports (such as HEDIS measures, covered later) are accurate rather than self-flattering. A third is the validation of performance improvement projects (PIPs) that are part of the plan’s QAPI program.

The crucial word in those activities is "validation." The EQRO does not simply accept the numbers a plan reports; it validates them — checking the methodology and data so that a plan cannot inflate its measured performance. This is the heart of breaking the self-reporting conflict. Beyond the mandatory activities, federal rules also define optional activities states may add, and the 2024 final rule and updated EQR protocols expanded the toolkit, including validation related to network adequacy. The mandatory core ensures every state’s EQR covers the essentials, while options let states tailor deeper scrutiny.

children.text: The EQR Technical Report — and What States Do With It

The product of all this work is the annual EQR technical report, which the EQRO must provide to the state and CMS for each plan. The report describes how the data was aggregated and analyzed for each EQR activity and draws conclusions about the quality, timeliness, and access to care the plan furnishes. Critically, it assesses each plan’s strengths and weaknesses on those dimensions and offers recommendations for improving services and for how the state can target the goals and objectives in its quality strategy. The technical report is the authoritative, independent scorecard on each plan.

But a report only matters if the state acts on it, and here states vary considerably. They range from simply noting plan performance to taking real consequences — using EQR findings to inform contract changes, require corrective action plans (CAPs), impose financial penalties, and reduce or freeze the auto-assignment of new enrollees to a poor-performing plan. That last tool is particularly powerful: auto-assignment (how the state distributes enrollees who do not choose a plan) is a major source of membership, so freezing it directly hits a plan’s growth and revenue. The strongest oversight ties EQR findings to tangible consequences.

body.message: The EQR technical report is only as effective as the state’s willingness to act on it. States that merely "note" poor performance exert little pressure; states that link EQR findings to corrective action plans, financial penalties, and frozen auto-assignment turn independent review into real accountability. Oversight is a choice, not just a process.
body.title: A Report Without Consequences Changes Nothing

children.text: The State’s Broader Monitoring Role

The EQRO is the centerpiece, but the state retains a broad, ongoing monitoring role that surrounds it. As the contract lesson described, federal rules require states to maintain a monitoring system spanning administration, appeals and grievances, claims, finance and MLR, encounter data, medical and utilization management, program integrity, network management, quality improvement, and LTSS. CMS reinforces this with required reports — the Annual Program Oversight Report under 42 CFR § 438.66(e), the Medical Loss Ratio Summary Report, and the Access Standards Report — that compel states to compile and submit evidence of their oversight to the federal government.

body.analogy: State oversight of MCOs works like the oversight of a restaurant. The state’s ongoing monitoring is the manager checking the books, the complaints, and the daily operations. The EQRO is the independent health inspector who arrives annually, validates that the kitchen really meets standards rather than taking the owner’s word, and files a detailed report on what is clean and what is not. And the enforcement tools — corrective action plans, fines, freezing new business — are what give the inspection teeth. Without the independent inspector, the owner grades their own kitchen; without enforcement, even a damning inspection changes nothing.
body.concept: The layers of Medicaid managed care oversight

children.text: This layered structure — independent expert review (EQRO) plus continuous state monitoring plus federal reporting — exists because the stakes are so high and the conflict of interest so real. Billions in public dollars flow to private plans serving vulnerable populations, and those plans profit by spending less. Oversight is the mechanism that lets a state capture managed care’s benefits (predictability, coordination) while guarding against its risks (under-provision, cherry-picking, poor quality). It is the practical answer to the question that opened the course: how do you trust private plans with public care?

This lesson closes the procurement-and-contracting arc and opens onto the rest of the course. Oversight depends on the data and standards established elsewhere: the quality measures validated by the EQRO are detailed in the HEDIS and quality lessons; the financial oversight connects to the rate-setting and MLR module; the network reviews connect to the network-adequacy lesson. Monitoring is not a separate silo but the verification layer that makes every other requirement real. A state that selects good plans, writes a strong contract, and oversees rigorously has built the full machinery of accountable Medicaid managed care.

points: States oversee MCOs through two layers: their own ongoing monitoring and an annual External Quality Review (EQR) conducted by an independent External Quality Review Organization (EQRO).
EQR is the independent analysis of aggregated information on the quality, timeliness, and access to care a plan furnishes, governed by federal parameters at 42 CFR §§ 438.350–438.364.

The EQRO must be independent and qualified, with demonstrated expertise in Medicaid beneficiaries, managed care delivery, and quality assessment — so findings come from a specialized third party, not the plan grading itself.

Mandatory EQR activities (438.358) include a compliance review once every three years, validation of reported performance measures, and validation of performance improvement projects (PIPs); states may add optional activities such as network-adequacy validation.
The key word is "validation" — the EQRO verifies the accuracy of what plans report rather than accepting it, breaking the self-reporting conflict of interest.

The annual EQR technical report assesses each plan’s strengths, weaknesses, and recommendations on quality, timeliness, and access, and is provided to the state and CMS as the authoritative independent scorecard.

States vary in acting on findings — from merely noting performance to imposing corrective action plans, financial penalties, and reducing or freezing auto-assignment of enrollees (a powerful lever on a plan’s revenue).

Surrounding the EQRO, states maintain a broad monitoring system and submit federally required reports (Annual Program Oversight Report under 438.66(e), MLR Summary Report, Access Standards Report), creating a layered structure that lets states capture managed care’s benefits while guarding against its risks.

children.text: Accountability for the Whole Patient

Every payment system covered so far pays for a piece of care — a hospital stay, a physician visit, a post-acute episode. The Accountable Care Organization (ACO) model takes a different angle entirely: it holds a group of providers accountable for the total cost and quality of care for a defined population of patients, no matter where that care happens.

An ACO is a group of doctors, hospitals, and other providers who voluntarily join together to coordinate care for a population of Medicare beneficiaries. If they keep total spending below a target while meeting quality standards, they share in the savings. The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) is Medicare’s largest and permanent ACO program, created by the Affordable Care Act of 2010.

Crucially, MSSP is built on top of traditional fee-for-service, not instead of it. Providers in an ACO keep billing and getting paid the normal Part A and B way. The shared-savings (or shared-loss) settlement happens afterward, based on how total spending for their attributed patients compared to a benchmark.

An ACO is held accountable for the total cost and quality of care for a population of patients. Under MSSP, providers keep receiving normal fee-for-service payments, then settle up against a spending benchmark at year-end — sharing savings if they beat it, and (in two-sided models) losses if they exceed it.
How the Shared Savings Program Works

MSSP works through three core mechanics: attribution, benchmarking, and settlement. First, Medicare beneficiaries are attributed (assigned) to an ACO based on where they get most of their primary care. An ACO must have at least 5,000 attributed fee-for-service beneficiaries to participate.

Second, CMS sets a spending benchmark — an expected total cost of care for those attributed patients, based on history and regional spending. Third, at the end of the performance year, CMS compares actual spending to the benchmark. If the ACO spent less and met quality standards, it shares in the savings; if it spent more, it may owe a share of the losses, depending on its track.

Quality is a gate, not an afterthought. An ACO that generates savings but fails to meet CMS quality standards does not get to keep the money. This pairing — savings only if quality holds — is what distinguishes shared savings from simple cost-cutting.

children.text: One-Sided vs. Two-Sided Risk

The single most important variable in an ACO arrangement is how much financial risk it bears. In one-sided (upside-only) models, the ACO shares in savings if it beats the benchmark but owes nothing if it overspends — a gentle on-ramp that protects new ACOs from losses while they build capabilities.

In two-sided (downside) risk models, the ACO shares in savings but also must repay a share of losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. In exchange for that risk, two-sided ACOs keep a larger share of any savings they generate. MSSP organizes these options into the BASIC track (which glides from upside-only Level A up to risk-bearing Level E) and the ENHANCED track (the highest level of risk and reward).

CMS has steadily pushed ACOs toward downside risk because that is where the savings are. In 2024, roughly two-thirds of ACOs were in the higher-risk Level E or ENHANCED arrangements, and those risk-bearing ACOs generated the large majority of the program’s total savings. Skin in the game changes behavior.

children.text: Does It Work? The Evidence

After a slow start, MSSP has become the largest accountable-care program in the country and is now producing record results. For performance year 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs generated about $2.4 billion in net savings to Medicare — the highest in the program’s history — while nearly every ACO met CMS quality standards.

Participation keeps growing. For 2025, 476 ACOs participated, and the program serves millions of traditional-Medicare beneficiaries through hundreds of thousands of providers. The data consistently show that two-sided, risk-bearing ACOs deliver most of the savings, which is why the program’s design keeps nudging organizations toward downside risk.

Alongside the permanent MSSP, the CMS Innovation Center runs ACO models that test more aggressive designs — most notably ACO REACH, which uses full or partial capitation and a strong health-equity focus, serving millions of beneficiaries through participating ACOs. MSSP is the durable backbone; the Innovation Center models are the laboratory.

children.text: Why ACOs Matter

ACOs represent a fundamentally different theory of payment reform than the per-case programs that came before. Instead of fine-tuning the price of each service, they make providers accountable for the whole — the total spending and quality of a population — and let the providers figure out how to deliver better care for less.

This shifts incentives toward exactly the activities fee-for-service neglects: care coordination, prevention, managing chronic disease, reducing avoidable hospitalizations, and steering patients to high-value post-acute care. An ACO profits by keeping people healthy and out of the hospital, not by doing more to them.

For Medicare, ACOs are central to the long-term strategy of moving traditional fee-for-service toward value. CMS has set goals to have all traditional-Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship — making the ACO model not a side experiment but the intended future of the program.
The ACO flips the core question of payment: not "how do we price each service?" but "who is accountable for the whole patient?"

The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), created by the ACA in 2010, is Medicare’s largest, permanent ACO program.
MSSP runs on attribution (minimum 5,000 beneficiaries), a spending benchmark, and a year-end settlement — built on top of normal fee-for-service payments.
Quality is a gate: an ACO must meet CMS quality standards to keep any shared savings.
One-sided models share savings with no downside; two-sided models share savings and losses but let ACOs keep a larger share — organized as the BASIC and ENHANCED tracks.
In 2024, MSSP generated a record ~$2.4 billion in net savings, with risk-bearing (Level E/ENHANCED) ACOs producing most of the savings.
ACOs reward coordination, prevention, and avoiding unnecessary care, and are central to CMS’s goal of moving all traditional-Medicare beneficiaries into accountable care relationships.

children.text: Beyond the Genome

Throughout this course, the genome has been the central object — the DNA sequence that drives diagnosis, risk, and drug response. But the genome is only the blueprint. It tells you what could happen, not what is actually happening in a person's cells right now. The frontier of genomic medicine is moving beyond DNA alone to capture the dynamic, real-time biology that the genome only sets the stage for. Two forces are driving this frontier: multi-omics and artificial intelligence.

These are not yet routine clinical tools the way sequencing has become, but they represent where the field is heading and are already transforming research and parts of practice. Understanding them is understanding the trajectory of genomic medicine — what the next decade is likely to deliver, and why the interpretation and equity challenges from earlier lessons will both be reshaped by these technologies.

This lesson covers two distinct but related advances: multi-omics, which broadens the view from DNA to the full molecular state of the body, and AI, which is increasingly the engine for making sense of the vast data genomics produces. Together they define the emerging shape of precision medicine.

The genome is the blueprint, not the live picture. The frontier of genomic medicine moves beyond DNA to capture the body's dynamic molecular state (multi-omics) and uses AI to make sense of the resulting data — together defining where precision medicine is heading.
Multi-Omics: The Full Molecular Picture

Genomics reads DNA, but DNA is just the first layer of biology. The "-omics" are the comprehensive measurement of each biological layer, and multi-omics is the integration of several of them to build a far richer picture of health and disease than any single layer provides. The key layers are genomics (the DNA blueprint), transcriptomics (which genes are actually switched on, measured via RNA), proteomics (the proteins that do the cell's work, measured by mass spectrometry), metabolomics (the small molecules of metabolism, a real-time snapshot of cellular activity), and epigenomics (the chemical marks that regulate gene activity).

The power of multi-omics comes from integration. The genome tells you what genes a person has; the transcriptome tells you which are active; the proteome tells you what proteins are actually present; the metabolome tells you the downstream consequences. Layered together — with their interactions — they reveal disease mechanisms, biomarkers, and drug targets that no single layer could show. Multi-omics has become a central pillar of precision medicine, drug discovery, and translational research precisely because biology is multilayered, and reading only the DNA misses most of the story.

The clinical promise is more precise, mechanism-level understanding of an individual's disease — for example, in oncology, integrating a tumor's genome, gene-expression profile, and protein activity to choose therapy more accurately than genome alone allows. The challenge is integration: combining these massive, heterogeneous datasets into something interpretable and clinically actionable is genuinely hard, and is one of the central problems the field is working on — which is exactly where AI enters.

children.text: AI: Making Sense of Genomic Data

Genomics generates staggering amounts of data — a single genome is billions of base pairs, and multi-omics multiplies that across layers and across populations of millions (the biobanks of an earlier lesson). The fundamental bottleneck has never been generating the data; it has been interpreting it. Artificial intelligence, and specifically deep learning, has emerged as the most powerful tool for finding the patterns in this data that humans cannot, and it is rapidly becoming essential infrastructure for genomic medicine.

The most celebrated example is protein structure prediction. AlphaFold, developed by Google DeepMind, used deep learning to predict the three-dimensional structures of proteins from their sequences — a problem that had stumped biology for fifty years. Its database now contains predicted structures for over 200 million proteins, and the work was recognized with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper). AlphaFold 3 (2024) extended this to predict how proteins interact with DNA, RNA, and drug molecules, with major implications for drug discovery.

AI is also tackling the interpretation bottleneck from the variant-interpretation lesson — the problem of variants of uncertain significance. Tools such as AlphaMissense use AlphaFold-derived structural understanding to predict whether missense variants are likely to be harmful, helping triage the flood of variants of uncertain significance. More broadly, AI is being applied to variant calling, disease-risk prediction, image analysis, and integrating multi-omics data. The pattern is consistent: as data outgrows human capacity to interpret it, AI becomes the means of extracting clinical meaning.

body.content:
Recall the variant-interpretation lesson's central challenge: most genetic variants are "variants of uncertain significance" (VUS) — we find them but cannot say whether they cause disease, partly because we don't know how they affect the resulting protein.
AlphaFold can predict a protein's 3D structure from its sequence, and tools like AlphaMissense use that structural understanding to predict whether a given missense variant is likely damaging. This doesn't eliminate the VUS problem, but it gives interpreters a powerful new line of evidence — AI directly attacking the bottleneck that limits clinical genomics.
body.title: AlphaFold and the Interpretation Problem

children.text: Promise, Hype, and Hard Limits

Multi-omics and AI are genuinely transformative, but it is essential to distinguish real capability from hype. AI in genomics is a powerful tool, not magic. AI models are only as good as the data they are trained on — which means they inherit, and can amplify, the diversity deficit from the equity lesson. An AI trained mainly on European-ancestry genomic data will perform worse for everyone else, potentially widening rather than narrowing disparities. The equity problems of genomics do not disappear with AI; they can get worse if not deliberately addressed.

There are other hard limits. AI predictions (like AlphaMissense scores) are powerful evidence but not proof — a predicted-damaging variant still requires careful clinical interpretation, not automatic reclassification. Multi-omics integration remains technically difficult and largely confined to research and specialized settings rather than routine care. And both raise the data-governance, privacy, and consent questions from earlier lessons at even greater scale. The frontier is real, but it is a frontier — promising and rapidly advancing, not finished or universally available.

The responsible posture is informed enthusiasm tempered by realism. These technologies will reshape genomic medicine, and clinicians should understand their trajectory. But they amplify existing challenges (especially equity) as much as they create new capabilities, and they do not replace the fundamentals this course has emphasized: careful interpretation, genetic counseling, informed consent, and attention to who benefits. The best use of AI and multi-omics is as powerful tools wielded within that disciplined framework.

body.message: AI models are only as good as their training data. Because genomic data is ~86% European-ancestry (the diversity deficit), AI tools trained on it perform worse for underrepresented populations — potentially widening health disparities rather than closing them. AI predictions are also evidence, not proof; a predicted-damaging variant still needs clinical interpretation. The frontier is powerful but does not erase — and can worsen — the equity and interpretation challenges from earlier lessons.

children.text: Where Genomic Medicine Is Heading

Multi-omics and AI together sketch the trajectory of precision medicine: from reading the static genome toward capturing the dynamic, multilayered molecular state of each patient, and from human interpretation toward AI-assisted analysis of data at a scale no human could process. The vision is a far more complete, mechanism-level, individualized picture of health and disease — and faster, more accurate translation of that picture into clinical action.

But this future will be built on the foundations the rest of the course laid. The interpretation challenge (now AI-assisted), the equity challenge (now potentially amplified by AI), the consent and privacy challenges (now at even greater scale), and the need for counseling and human judgment all persist and in some ways intensify. The frontier does not make the fundamentals obsolete; it raises the stakes on getting them right. Better technology with worse equity is not progress.

For clinicians and program leaders, the practical takeaway is to understand the trajectory without being captured by the hype: multi-omics and AI are coming and will be powerful, but they are tools to be integrated thoughtfully into a practice that already does the fundamentals well. A precision-medicine program that masters careful genomic interpretation, robust consent, strong counseling, and attention to equity will be ready to absorb these advances responsibly. That is exactly what the final lesson addresses: how to build a precision-medicine program in practice.

children.text: A Network Is Only Real If You Can Reach It

A managed care plan’s most basic promise is access: that its enrollees can actually get the care they need from the providers in its network. But "having a network" on paper means nothing if the listed doctors are too far away, booked for months, no longer practicing, or not accepting Medicaid patients. Network adequacy is the set of standards and oversight that turns the promise of a network into a reality enrollees can use. It is where the abstract idea of "access to care" becomes measurable — in miles, minutes, ratios, and days.

The stakes are not theoretical. Medicaid serves people who often face transportation barriers, limited time off work, disabilities, and language barriers. For them, a provider 90 minutes away or with a three-month wait is effectively no provider at all. Network adequacy standards exist precisely because a capitated plan has a financial incentive to keep its network lean — and because a thin network is one of the quietest ways a plan can under-deliver care while still technically covering the benefit.

This lesson goes deeper into the network adequacy requirements introduced in the federal-framework lesson, focusing on how adequacy is actually defined and measured — and confronting the persistent gap between networks as reported and networks as experienced, the problem of "ghost networks."

Key Concept: Network adequacy standards require a plan to maintain enough accessible providers to serve its enrollees, measured through time-and-distance limits, provider-to-enrollee ratios, and appointment wait-time standards (42 CFR 438.68). The challenge is ensuring the network is real in practice, not just on paper.

children.text: How Network Adequacy Is Measured

States use several complementary types of standards to measure network adequacy, and most use more than one. Time-and-distance standards limit how far or how long an enrollee should have to travel to reach a provider of a given type — for example, a primary care physician within 30 minutes or 15 miles. Provider-to-enrollee ratios require a minimum number of providers relative to the enrolled population, ensuring there are enough providers to go around. And appointment wait-time standards, added by the 2024 final rule, limit how long an enrollee must wait to be seen.

Under 42 CFR 438.68, states must develop quantitative network adequacy standards (other than wait times) for specified provider types if covered under the contract — primary care (adult and pediatric), OB/GYN, behavioral health, specialists, hospitals, pharmacy, and pediatric dental, among others. In setting time-and-distance standards, states must consider the geographic location of providers and enrollees, the distance and travel time involved, and the means of transportation Medicaid enrollees ordinarily use — a recognition that a car-owning suburbanite and a bus-dependent rural enrollee face very different "distances" to the same provider.

The 2024 final rule added the appointment wait-time standards covered in the federal-framework lesson: routine appointments within 15 business days for primary care and OB/GYN, and within 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use care. These standards phase in over time — the rule’s key provisions apply to contracts beginning roughly three to four years after the rule’s July 9, 2024 effective date — giving states and plans time to build the monitoring infrastructure. Wait-time standards matter because they capture a dimension that geography misses: a provider can be close by and still inaccessible if they cannot see the patient for months.

body.title: The Tools for Measuring Network Adequacy

children.text: The Ghost Network Problem

For decades, network adequacy was judged largely on the provider lists plans submitted — and that created a gaping vulnerability. Plans can report large networks that bear little relation to the care enrollees can actually obtain, a phenomenon known as "ghost networks" or "phantom networks." The numbers are alarming: research found that more than one-third of doctors listed in Medicaid networks did not provide care to Medicaid patients in 2023, and in one study of Oregon Medicaid behavioral health, 58.2% of network directory listings were phantom providers who did not see Medicaid patients.

Ghost networks arise in several ways. A listed provider may have moved, retired, or died; may not actually accept the plan’s Medicaid product; or may not be taking new patients. Sometimes the directory information is simply wrong. The effect is the same regardless of cause: the network looks adequate on paper while enrollees, especially those seeking behavioral health care, call provider after provider and cannot get an appointment. The problem is most severe precisely where access is most critical — behavioral health, where directories are notoriously inaccurate and HHS oversight has repeatedly found limited networks padded with inactive providers.

body.message: A plan can fully satisfy a count-based or distance-based standard while delivering little actual access, because the listed providers are inactive, mislisted, or closed to new Medicaid patients. This is why modern oversight tests directories against reality rather than trusting the plan’s submitted lists.
body.title: A Paper Network Is Not a Real Network

children.text: Testing the Network Against Reality

Closing the gap between reported and real networks requires verification, and the 2024 rule’s central tool is the secret shopper survey. States must use annual secret shopper surveys to test plan compliance with appointment wait-time standards and to assess the accuracy of provider directories. A third party — independent of both the state and the plans — poses as an enrollee and tries to schedule an appointment with a directory-listed provider. This directly tests what a real member experiences, exposing the ghost providers that paper reviews miss.

Network adequacy verification is also built into the oversight system covered earlier: validation of plan network adequacy is a mandatory External Quality Review activity, with states and EQROs required to use a network adequacy validation protocol. This layers independent EQRO validation on top of secret-shopper testing and the plans’ own Network Adequacy and Access Assurances Reports — multiple checks designed to catch the discrepancy between what plans claim and what enrollees can actually access.

Yet verification means little without enforcement, and here the record has been weak. Enforcement of network adequacy standards has been notably limited: from 2016 to 2022, CMS sent letters to only five insurers whose plans failed network adequacy requirements, and had imposed no sanctions for network adequacy failures as of 2024. Penalties, when assessed, often fail to produce sustained change. The 2024 rule’s stronger measurement tools are a meaningful step, but the persistent gap between detecting inadequacy and penalizing it remains the field’s central unsolved problem.
Why Network Adequacy Is the Truest Test of Access

Network adequacy is where managed care’s promise is most directly tested, because it concerns the single thing enrollees care about most: can I actually see a doctor when I need one? Every other element — the capitation rate, the quality measures, the contract terms — is ultimately in service of this. A program can be financially sound and well-governed and still fail its members if they cannot get appointments. This is why network adequacy has become a focal point of regulation, and why the 2024 rule invested so heavily in measuring it more honestly.

body.analogy: A provider directory without verification is like a restaurant guide that lists hundreds of places without checking which are still open. The guide looks impressive and the "network" seems vast — until you drive across town to three listings that turned out to be closed, moved, or not taking reservations. The secret shopper survey is the guide’s editor actually calling each restaurant to confirm it exists and can seat you. A directory is only as good as the verification behind it; the same is true of a provider network.
body.concept: Reported networks vs. verified access

children.text: The flexibility states have in defining standards is both a strength and a weakness. It lets a state tailor standards to its geography — a rural state needs different time-and-distance limits than a dense urban one, and telehealth can legitimately extend access where in-person providers are scarce. But that same flexibility means standards vary widely in rigor, and a state can set standards loose enough that almost any network passes. Combined with weak enforcement, this is how inadequate networks persist despite a framework designed to prevent them. Stronger measurement helps only if states are willing to set meaningful standards and act on violations.

This lesson connects the benefits-and-network module to the access goals at the heart of the federal framework. The carve-in/carve-out decision set the scope of what a plan covers; network adequacy ensures the plan has real providers for those covered services; and the next lesson, on provider credentialing, concerns how plans actually bring providers into the network. Network adequacy is the bridge between a covered benefit and a delivered service — and the place where the difference between a network that exists on paper and one that works in practice is decided.

points: Network adequacy standards require a plan to maintain enough accessible providers to serve its enrollees, turning the abstract promise of "access" into measurable limits — and they counter a capitated plan’s incentive to keep networks lean.

States measure adequacy with multiple complementary tools: time-and-distance standards, provider-to-enrollee ratios, and (from the 2024 rule) appointment wait-time standards, often supplemented by telehealth.

Under 42 CFR 438.68, states set quantitative standards for specified provider types and, for time-and-distance, must consider providers’ and enrollees’ locations, travel time, and the transportation enrollees ordinarily use.

The 2024 final rule added wait-time standards (15 business days for primary care/OB-GYN, 10 for outpatient behavioral health) that phase in roughly three to four years after the July 9, 2024 effective date.

"Ghost networks" are a pervasive problem: more than one-third of Medicaid network doctors did not see Medicaid patients in 2023, and 58.2% of listings were phantom in one Oregon behavioral health study — networks that look adequate on paper but fail in practice.
Verification tools test directories against reality: annual secret shopper surveys by independent third parties, plus network adequacy validation as a mandatory External Quality Review activity.

Enforcement has been weak — CMS sent only five network-adequacy letters from 2016–2022 and had imposed no sanctions as of 2024 — leaving a persistent gap between detecting inadequacy and penalizing it.

Network adequacy is the truest test of access (can a member actually see a doctor?), and state flexibility in setting standards is both a strength (tailoring to geography and telehealth) and a weakness (loose standards plus weak enforcement let inadequate networks persist).

children.text: The Most Successful Genetic Program You've Never Thought About

Almost every person born in the United States has already been screened for genetic disease — at birth, usually before they left the hospital, and almost certainly without remembering it. Newborn screening is the largest and one of the most successful applications of genetics in public health, quietly preventing death and disability in thousands of children every year. It is genomic medicine operating at population scale, and it has been doing so for decades.

Newborn screening is a public-health program that tests every baby shortly after birth for a panel of serious, treatable conditions — many of them genetic or metabolic — so that treatment can begin before irreversible harm occurs. The defining logic is early detection: for these conditions, a baby looks completely healthy at birth, but without prompt treatment will suffer severe, permanent damage. Screening catches them in the narrow window when intervention still works.

This lesson explains how newborn screening works, why it is a model of effective public-health genomics, and how genome sequencing may transform it. It is a concrete example of nearly everything the course has covered — testing, treatable conditions, consent, equity — operating in the real world at the scale of an entire population of newborns.

Newborn screening tests nearly every baby shortly after birth for serious, treatable conditions — so treatment can start before irreversible harm. It is the largest, most successful application of genetics in public health, operating at population scale for decades.
How Newborn Screening Works

Newborn screening has three parts, performed within roughly 24 to 48 hours after birth. The best known is the blood test, or "heel stick," in which a few drops of blood from the baby's heel are placed on a special card and analyzed for dozens of conditions. The other two parts are a hearing screen (for hearing loss) and a pulse-oximetry test (for critical congenital heart defects). Together they screen for the major treatable conditions detectable at birth.

Which conditions are screened is guided by the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) — a list maintained at the federal level (HHS) that recommends conditions for every state to screen. The RUSP includes 35 core conditions plus 26 secondary conditions. Conditions are added based on evidence that screening produces net benefit: the condition must be serious, detectable, and — crucially — treatable, so that early detection actually changes the outcome.

A key feature is that newborn screening is administered by the states, not nationally, so the exact panel varies somewhat by state even though the RUSP provides a common recommended baseline. This is why a baby in one state may be screened for slightly different conditions than a baby in another — a federalism quirk with real consequences. Newborn screening is also unusual in being typically mandatory or opt-out (rather than opt-in), reflecting its public-health framing: the benefit to children is judged great enough to justify near-universal participation.
