body.title: The Newborn Screening Process

children.text: Why It Works: The Public-Health Logic

Newborn screening is a textbook case of effective screening because it satisfies the classic criteria. The conditions are serious (causing death or severe disability if untreated). They are detectable before symptoms appear (the baby looks healthy at birth). There is a treatment that works if started early (special diet, medication, or other intervention). And the screening test is accurate enough to use at population scale. When all of these hold, screening saves lives — and for these conditions, they do.

The classic example is phenylketonuria (PKU), a metabolic condition where the body cannot process the amino acid phenylalanine. Undetected, PKU causes severe intellectual disability. Detected at birth, it is managed with a special diet, and the child develops normally. PKU screening — one of the original newborn-screening tests — demonstrated the entire paradigm: a simple test at birth turning a devastating disease into a manageable condition. Many RUSP conditions follow the same logic.

This is why newborn screening is held up as a model: it shows genetics delivering enormous, measurable public-health benefit through early detection and treatment of conditions that are individually rare but collectively meaningful. It embodies the prevention-and-actionability principle that runs through this course — testing matters most when knowing the result lets you do something about it. Newborn screening is that principle at its most successful.

body.content:
A newborn appears perfectly healthy. The heel-stick blood spot reveals elevated phenylalanine — phenylketonuria (PKU). Untreated, PKU would cause severe, irreversible intellectual disability over the following months.
Because it was caught at birth, the baby is started on a special low-phenylalanine diet, and develops normally. The same baby, born before newborn screening existed, would likely have been disabled for life. PKU is why newborn screening exists — proof that a simple test at birth can turn a devastating genetic disease into a manageable one.
body.title: PKU: The Paradigm Case

children.text: The Genomic Frontier of Newborn Screening

Today's newborn screening relies mainly on biochemical tests (measuring metabolites and analytes), not DNA sequencing. But a major question facing the field is whether to add — or eventually replace it with — genome sequencing. Genomic newborn screening (NBSeq) would read a baby's DNA directly and could, in principle, screen for hundreds or thousands of conditions rather than dozens, including many not detectable by current biochemical methods.

This is being actively studied in large pilot programs. The BabySeq Project (begun in 2013 by Dr. Robert Green) was the first to sequence healthy newborns and study the effects of returning results. The GUARDIAN study, launched in 2022 in New York City with a goal of sequencing 100,000 newborns, analyzes a curated set of conditions (around 255 genes, of which roughly 156 have an established treatment). Major international programs — Generation (UK), FirstSteps (Greece), and Rady's BeginNGS — are pursuing the same question, with more than 30 initiatives worldwide.

Genomic newborn screening is genuinely promising but raises every hard issue from this course's ethics lessons, amplified. Which conditions should be reported — only treatable ones, or also untreatable and adult-onset conditions? How is consent handled for an infant who cannot consent (the pediatric-autonomy problem)? What about variants of uncertain significance and false positives at massive scale? And the diversity deficit means sequencing-based screening could be less accurate for underrepresented populations. The promise is real, but so are the unresolved ethical and equity questions, which is why it remains in carefully studied pilots rather than universal practice.

body.message: Adding genome sequencing to newborn screening could detect far more conditions — but it raises the consent, secondary-findings, VUS, and equity issues from earlier lessons at enormous scale, and for infants who cannot consent. Which conditions to report (treatable only? adult-onset?), false positives, and the ancestry diversity deficit are all unresolved. This is why NBSeq is in studied pilots (BabySeq, GUARDIAN, Generation), not universal practice.
body.title: Genomic Newborn Screening Amplifies Every Ethical Question

children.text: Lessons from Newborn Screening

Newborn screening teaches several things about genomic medicine done well. First, the actionability principle is everything: the program works because it screens for conditions where early detection changes outcomes, and the RUSP's inclusion criteria are built around treatability. Second, scale is achievable: genetics can be delivered to an entire population reliably and affordably when the program is well-designed. Third, public-health framing changes the ethics: the near-universal, opt-out model is justified by the magnitude of benefit to children.

It also previews the central tension of genomics' future. Newborn screening is so successful precisely because it is narrow and disciplined — it screens only for serious, treatable conditions. Genome sequencing could vastly expand it, but expansion means confronting the trade-offs the field has so far avoided in this domain: more findings of uncertain value, harder consent, and the risk of generating anxiety or harm rather than benefit. The future of newborn screening is, in miniature, the future of genomic medicine: how to expand capability without losing the discipline that made it valuable.

For clinicians and program leaders, newborn screening is both a model and a cautionary lesson. It shows what genomic medicine can achieve when focused on actionable conditions at scale — and it shows that the hard part of expansion is not the technology but the judgment about what to look for, what to report, and how to do so responsibly. The next lessons turn to other population-scale screening (carrier screening) and to the emerging multi-omics-and-AI frontier, before the course concludes with how to build a precision-medicine program in practice.

children.text: Why Cancer Care Needed Its Own Value-Based Model

Cancer care sits at the intersection of several cost crises in American healthcare. Chemotherapy drug prices have risen dramatically — targeted therapies can cost $100,000 or more per patient per year — and utilization is intensive, with patients receiving not just drugs but frequent lab work, imaging, supportive care, and hospitalizations for complications. Yet the fee-for-service system that governed oncology for decades provided no mechanism to reward coordination, reduce emergency visits, or guide patients toward evidence-based regimens. Oncologists were paid for administering drugs (via the buy-and-bill system), not for managing the comprehensive trajectory of a patient's cancer care.

The fragmentation problem in oncology is acute. A Medicare beneficiary receiving chemotherapy may interact with a medical oncologist, a radiation oncologist, a surgeon, a hospitalist, a palliative care team, social workers, and home health aides — often in separate organizations with no shared data, no common care plan, and no financial incentive to reduce unnecessary emergency department visits or duplicative imaging. When a patient calls at 2 a.m. with fever and chills during neutropenia, the default in a fragmented system is to send them to the ER, where the cost of a workup can exceed $5,000, even when a phone triage protocol with a nurse practitioner might safely manage the situation.

CMS recognized this problem and launched the Oncology Care Model (OCM) in 2016 as the first cancer-focused alternative payment model in the federal portfolio. OCM ran through June 30, 2022, involving 122 oncology practices and five commercial payer partners. It was succeeded by the Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM), which launched July 1, 2023, with a refined episode structure and narrower scope focused on seven high-cost cancer types. Both models used a common architecture: a six-month chemotherapy episode triggered by the start of systemic treatment, a monthly enhanced payment to fund care coordination, and a performance-based payment tied to end-of-episode cost and quality.

The Oncology Care Model was the first alternative payment model specifically designed for cancer care. It ran from 2016 to 2022, covering chemotherapy episodes for any cancer type treated at participating practices, and served as the proof-of-concept for the successor Enhancing Oncology Model launched in 2023.

children.text: The OCM Episode: Structure and Payment Architecture

An OCM episode is triggered when a Medicare beneficiary begins a course of systemic chemotherapy at a participating practice. The episode lasts six months from the date of the first chemotherapy claim. Unlike a surgical bundle anchored to a single procedure, a six-month oncology episode encompasses a dynamic, evolving clinical situation: cycles of chemotherapy, supportive care, scans to assess treatment response, management of side effects, and potentially a treatment switch if the first regimen fails. The breadth of included services reflects both the comprehensiveness of cancer care and the challenge of attributing costs to any single responsible clinician.

The OCM payment structure had two components. First, the monthly enhanced oncology services (MEOS) payment: $160 per beneficiary per month for each month of the six-month episode, regardless of outcomes. The MEOS was explicitly designed as an upfront investment — an infrastructure subsidy to pay for the care coordination staff, extended hours access, and data reporting requirements that CMS required all participating practices to implement. Over a full six-month episode, a single patient generated $960 in MEOS payments to the practice.

The second component was performance-based payments (PBPs): additional payments made retrospectively if a practice's actual episode spending fell below a risk-adjusted benchmark price and the practice met quality thresholds. PBPs were available only to practices that achieved both cost and quality targets, ensuring that cost reductions did not come at the expense of care quality. Practices that generated excess costs above the benchmark owed a repayment in the model's two-sided risk phase — a key distinction from programs that offer upside-only participation.

children.text: What OCM Required Practices to Do

Participation in OCM was not simply a financial arrangement — it required oncology practices to undergo substantive operational transformation. CMS specified six care delivery functions that all participating practices had to implement: (1) 24/7 patient access to an oncologist or advanced practice clinician with access to the patient's medical record; (2) care coordination, including a designated care team for each patient; (3) patient navigation — assigning a navigator to help patients understand their diagnoses, manage treatment side effects, and navigate the healthcare system; (4) evidence-based treatment — documenting adherence to clinical guidelines from ASCO, NCCN, or comparable bodies; (5) comprehensive care plans developed within three months of treatment initiation; and (6) electronic quality reporting to CMS.

The 24/7 access requirement was among the most impactful changes. Oncology practices accustomed to referring after-hours patients to the emergency department had to establish structured telephone triage protocols staffed by oncology-trained nurses. The data on after-hours triage are compelling: patients who can reach an oncology nurse at night are far less likely to end up in the emergency department for manageable symptoms — fever, nausea, pain — that do not require hospital-level intervention. The MEOS payment was intended to cover the staffing cost of this function.

Patient navigation deserves special attention as a care delivery innovation. An oncology navigator — typically a nurse or social worker — acts as the patient's guide and advocate throughout the treatment course. Navigators schedule and track appointments, coordinate transportation, connect patients with financial assistance programs, manage prescription adherence, and serve as the first point of contact when something goes wrong. Research consistently shows that navigation programs reduce treatment delays, improve adherence, and decrease emergency utilization, particularly for patients from low-income or underserved communities who face the greatest structural barriers.

body.content:
UNC Lineberger's OCM participation centered on expanding its nurse navigation program as the care coordination backbone for the model. Navigators worked with patients on treatment adherence, side-effect management, and after-hours triage, using structured telephone protocols to avoid unnecessary ER visits.
The program demonstrated reductions in unplanned hospitalizations and ED visits among navigated patients, consistent with the national OCM evidence on practices that invested heavily in navigation infrastructure. The experience reinforced the lesson that OCM's care quality requirements were not just compliance checkboxes — they were the actual mechanisms of cost and quality improvement.
body.title: University of North Carolina Lineberger Comprehensive Cancer Center — OCM Navigation

children.text: What the OCM Evaluation Found: Savings, Losses, and Quality

The final OCM evaluation, covering all nine performance periods through the model's June 2022 conclusion, revealed a complex picture of modest relative savings overwhelmed by MEOS payments. The evaluation found a $499 relative reduction per episode in OCM vs. comparison episodes — meaning practices that participated in OCM spent about $499 less per episode than comparable non-participating practices, after risk adjustment. This looks like success on its face, but the evaluation found that the average MEOS payments received by participating practices totaled approximately $720 per episode.

When MEOS payments and performance-based payments were included in the net calculation, the OCM program resulted in an estimated net loss to Medicare of $639 million over its six years of operation. The program reduced FFS claims but paid out more in MEOS and PBP payments than it recovered in savings. This is the core tension in oncology value-based care: the coordination infrastructure needed to improve care is expensive, and the savings it generates — mostly from avoided emergency visits and hospitalizations — may not be large enough to offset the infrastructure investment at scale.

Quality results were mixed. The evaluation found no significant changes, either positive or negative, in hospitalizations, emergency department visits, or measured quality outcomes for the overall OCM patient population. However, one positive finding emerged in equity: adherence to high-cost drugs improved for patients who were Black, Hispanic, or low-income — populations that historically received less aggressive or guideline-concordant treatment. This represents a meaningful equity improvement and aligns with one of the model's explicit goals of reducing treatment disparities.

children.text: The Enhancing Oncology Model: Lessons Applied

CMS launched the Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM) on July 1, 2023, incorporating lessons from the OCM evaluation. The most consequential design change was the shift from a universal chemotherapy trigger to a narrow focus on seven high-cost, high-volume cancer types: high-risk breast cancer, lung cancer, chronic leukemia (CLL), small intestine/colorectal cancer, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, and high-risk prostate cancer. These conditions were selected because OCM data showed they had the highest episode costs, the highest variation in spending, and therefore the greatest potential for achievable savings.

EOM retained the six-month episode structure and the monthly care management payment (now called the monthly care management payment or MCMP, paid at $70 per beneficiary per month — reduced from OCM's $160 to improve net savings potential). EOM also requires practices to take on two-sided financial risk from the start of the model — unlike OCM, which phased practices into downside risk gradually. This faster risk exposure is intended to sharpen the financial incentives for cost management and distinguish practices willing to commit to the model from those testing the waters for upside-only payments.

EOM also strengthened the health equity requirements built into the model. Participating practices must collect and report patient-level race, ethnicity, and social determinants of health data; develop a health equity plan; and demonstrate measurable efforts to reduce disparities in treatment and outcomes. This reflects a deliberate evolution from OCM, where equity was a secondary goal, to EOM, where it is a first-order accountability measure. A second cohort of EOM participants launched July 1, 2025, indicating continued CMS commitment to the oncology VBC program.

body.analogy: Running an OCM practice is like running a restaurant that charges a fixed price for a full meal, no matter what courses the diner orders. The $160 MEOS payment per month is the fixed cover charge — it pays for the kitchen staff and service setup. The performance-based payment is like a tip only given if the diner leaves satisfied and the total cost to the house stays under budget. If the kitchen spends more on ingredients than the cover charge brings in, the restaurant loses money — which is exactly what happened to Medicare net of MEOS payments in the OCM.
body.concept: Oncology Care Model Payment Architecture

children.text: Implications for the Future of Specialty Value-Based Care

The OCM and EOM experience holds lessons that extend well beyond oncology. They demonstrate that applying VBC principles to specialty care is structurally harder than applying them to surgical episodes, because the episode cost structure is more complex, the patient population is more fragile, and the care coordination demands are higher. The oncology experience has also highlighted the fundamental tension in alternative payment model design: the coordination infrastructure needed to improve care requires upfront investment, and those investments must generate sufficient downstream savings to justify their cost to the payer.

The models have also demonstrated the importance of data infrastructure. Oncology practices that succeeded in OCM were those that invested in real-time dashboard tools to track their episode spending, identify high-cost patients early in the episode, and monitor care plan adherence. Practices that tried to manage OCM performance using quarterly claims reports — too delayed to guide clinical interventions — consistently underperformed those with live analytics tools. The lesson generalizes: VBC success is a data analytics challenge as much as a clinical care challenge.

Finally, the oncology VBC experience raises profound questions about the appropriate boundary of value-based accountability in end-of-life care. Patients with metastatic disease receiving chemotherapy near the end of life generate very high episode costs, and those costs are largely driven by clinical and patient preferences about aggressive versus palliative treatment rather than by efficiency failures. Any model that holds practices financially accountable for total episode cost must grapple with the risk that financial incentives inadvertently discourage appropriate aggressive treatment for patients who want it, or conversely, encourage premature transitions to hospice for financial reasons. This ethical dimension requires ongoing vigilance in model design and evaluation.

body.message: The OCM's estimated $639 million net loss to Medicare reflects a payment design issue — the $160 MEOS was set too high relative to achievable savings — not a failure of the care coordination concept. The equity improvements and coordination infrastructure built by participating practices have lasting value beyond the financial reconciliation. EOM's reduced monthly payment and narrower episode focus are direct responses to this design lesson.
body.title: Net Loss Does Not Mean the Model Failed

children.text: Cancer Is a Disease of the Genome

Of all the clinical applications of genomics, oncology is where it has transformed practice most profoundly. The reason is fundamental: cancer is, at its root, a disease of the genome. Tumors arise and grow because of acquired (somatic) genetic changes in their cells — the same somatic variants distinguished from germline in the foundations lesson. Reading a tumor's genome is increasingly the way we understand and treat it.

This reframes cancer classification itself. Traditionally, cancer was defined by where it started and what it looked like under the microscope — "lung cancer," "breast cancer." Precision oncology adds (and sometimes supersedes) this with molecular classification: what genetic alterations are driving this particular tumor? Two lung cancers that look identical may have completely different driver mutations and require completely different drugs.

The clinical payoff is targeted therapy: drugs designed to attack the specific molecular alteration driving a tumor, rather than the blunt instrument of traditional chemotherapy that poisons all dividing cells. For the right patient with the right mutation, targeted therapy can be dramatically more effective and less toxic. Somatic genomics is what identifies who that patient is.

Cancer is fundamentally a disease of the genome, driven by acquired (somatic) mutations. Reading a tumor's genome reveals the alterations driving it, enabling targeted therapies aimed at those specific drivers — the foundation of precision oncology.
Driver Mutations and Targeted Therapy

Within a tumor's many mutations, some are "drivers" — alterations that actively promote the cancer's growth — and these are the targets. When a driver is something a drug can block, identifying it transforms treatment. The classic examples are now standard of care: EGFR mutations in lung cancer (treated with EGFR inhibitors), ALK fusions (ALK inhibitors), BRAF mutations (BRAF inhibitors in melanoma and others), and HER2 amplification in breast cancer (HER2-targeted drugs).

The list of actionable drivers keeps growing — EGFR, ALK, BRAF, ROS1, RET, MET, NTRK, HER2 and more — each potentially matched to a specific inhibitor. A lung adenocarcinoma is no longer treated as a single disease; it is tested for a panel of driver alterations, and the result determines which targeted drug (if any) the patient receives. The mutation, not just the organ, drives the prescription.

To find these drivers, oncology uses comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) — next-generation sequencing panels that simultaneously test a tumor for dozens or hundreds of cancer-related genes. Rather than testing one gene at a time, CGP reads the tumor's relevant genome at once, identifying drivers, fusions, and other alterations. CGP has become standard of care for many advanced solid tumors precisely because it efficiently surfaces the actionable targets that determine therapy.

body.title: Example Actionable Driver Alterations

children.text: Tumor-Agnostic Therapy: A Paradigm Shift

The molecular view of cancer led to a genuinely new idea: tumor-agnostic (or tissue-agnostic) therapy — treating a cancer based purely on its molecular alteration, regardless of where in the body it arose. This inverts a century of oncology, which organized everything around the organ of origin.

The first example was pembrolizumab, an immunotherapy the FDA approved in 2017 for any solid tumor that is microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) or mismatch-repair deficient — the first drug approved for a molecular feature rather than a cancer type. In 2018, larotrectinib was approved for any solid tumor carrying an NTRK gene fusion; across 17 different tumor types, it produced an overall response rate around 75 percent. A single drug, effective across wildly different cancers, because they share one molecular driver.

Tumor-agnostic approvals are profound for precision oncology because they fully decouple treatment from anatomy: a colon cancer, a sarcoma, and a thyroid cancer that all carry an NTRK fusion can all receive the same targeted drug. This is only possible because comprehensive genomic profiling identifies the shared molecular target. It is the clearest expression of cancer as a disease of the genome — treated by its genetics, not its location.

body.content:
NTRK gene fusions are rare but occur across many different cancer types. Larotrectinib, a selective TRK inhibitor, was approved in 2018 as a tumor-agnostic therapy for any solid tumor with an NTRK fusion.
In an integrated analysis spanning 17 tumor types, it achieved an overall response rate of about 75% (with complete responses in ~13%). The same drug worked dramatically across cancers that look nothing alike under the microscope — because they share one molecular driver. This is precision oncology decoupling treatment from tumor location.
body.title: Larotrectinib and NTRK Fusions

children.text: Liquid Biopsy and Companion Diagnostics

Getting tumor DNA traditionally required a tissue biopsy — invasive, sometimes risky, and not always feasible. A major advance is the liquid biopsy: detecting circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) shed by the tumor into the bloodstream, from a simple blood draw. This lets clinicians profile a tumor's genetics without a needle in the tumor, and to re-sample over time to track how the cancer evolves.

FDA-approved ctDNA liquid biopsy tests like Guardant360 and FoundationOne Liquid CDx use next-generation sequencing of blood-borne tumor DNA to identify actionable alterations across many genes. Liquid biopsy is especially valuable when tissue is insufficient, when serial monitoring is needed, or to detect emerging resistance mutations as a tumor adapts to treatment.

These tests are often "companion diagnostics" — tests formally linked to a specific drug, used to identify the patients who should (or should not) receive it. A companion diagnostic is the gatekeeper for a targeted therapy: it confirms the tumor carries the driver the drug targets. This pairing of a diagnostic test with a therapy is central to how precision oncology is regulated and delivered — the drug and the test are approved and used together.

A note connecting to the foundations lesson: tumor profiling sometimes incidentally reveals germline findings (an inherited cancer-predisposition variant present in the tumor sample too). This is why oncology genomics and hereditary-cancer genetics (the next lesson) overlap — a somatic test can surface a germline result with implications for the patient's family.
The Realities and Limits

Precision oncology is transformative but not universal. Not every tumor has an actionable driver — many patients are profiled and found to have no targetable alteration, and still need conventional chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. Comprehensive genomic profiling expands options but does not guarantee a targeted treatment exists for a given patient.

Resistance is another reality: tumors evolve, and a cancer that responds beautifully to a targeted drug often develops new mutations that escape it — which is part of why serial liquid biopsy and switching therapies matter. And targeted therapies and genomic profiling are expensive, raising the cost and access questions that run through this curriculum, with the same equity concern that genomic databases underrepresent some populations (a later lesson).

Still, the trajectory is clear and powerful: oncology has moved decisively from treating cancers by where they start to treating them by what is driving them molecularly. Comprehensive genomic profiling, targeted therapy, tumor-agnostic drugs, and liquid biopsy together represent genomics' most mature and impactful clinical application. Cancer is a disease of the genome, and reading that genome is now central to fighting it. The next lesson turns from these acquired, somatic changes to the inherited, germline side of cancer and other hereditary conditions.

body.message: Comprehensive genomic profiling is powerful but not a guarantee — many tumors have no actionable driver, and those patients still need conventional treatment. Tumors also evolve resistance to targeted drugs over time. Precision oncology expands the options dramatically but does not replace the rest of cancer care; it is a high-value addition, not a universal cure.
body.title: Not Every Tumor Has a Target

children.text: Two Budgets, Two Fundamentally Different Questions

Every hospital builds two distinct budgets each year, and confusing them is a recipe for financial trouble. The operating budget answers the question: "What will it cost to run the hospital day to day this year, and what revenue will those operations bring in?" The capital budget answers a different question entirely: "What major, long-lived assets should we invest in to keep the hospital functioning and competitive for years to come?" One is about keeping the lights on this year; the other is about buying the building the lights hang in.

The distinction tracks the difference between operating expenses (OpEx) and capital expenditures (CapEx). An operating budget covers personnel salaries, supplies and materials, drugs, and administrative overhead — the recurring costs consumed within the year. A capital budget covers durable goods and long-term assets: imaging machines, surgical robots, beds, building renovations, and new facilities — items that deliver value over many years. The accounting, the approval process, and the strategic stakes differ for each.

Though separate, the two budgets are deeply intertwined. A capital decision made this year — buying a new surgical robot — drives operating costs for years afterward through maintenance, supplies, staffing, and the depreciation that flows back onto the income statement. Understanding how the two budgets relate is essential to grasping how hospitals actually plan and fund their futures.

Key Concept: The operating budget plans recurring annual revenue and expenses (salaries, supplies, overhead). The capital budget plans investments in long-lived assets (equipment, buildings) that provide value beyond one year. They are separate documents but each shapes the other.

children.text: The Operating Budget: Running the Hospital This Year

The operating budget is the financial plan for the hospital’s ongoing operations over the coming fiscal year. On the expense side it includes personnel salaries and benefits (the largest component, as the cost-accounting lessons established), medical and surgical supplies, pharmaceuticals, utilities, and administrative overhead. On the revenue side it projects net patient revenue based on expected volumes and payer mix, plus other operating revenue. The difference between projected operating revenue and operating expense is the budgeted operating margin.

Building the operating budget is fundamentally an exercise in forecasting: how many patients will the hospital treat, in what mix of services, paid by which payers, at what cost? Hospitals approach this in different ways. Incremental budgeting starts from last year’s budget and adjusts for expected changes — simpler but prone to perpetuating old inefficiencies. Zero-based budgeting builds the budget from scratch each year, justifying every expense — more rigorous and more revealing, but far more labor-intensive. Most hospitals land somewhere in between.

Because the operating budget governs the recurring money that keeps care flowing, it is the document most departments interact with daily. Variances — the gaps between budgeted and actual results — are tracked monthly, and managers are held accountable for explaining and correcting them. The operating budget is, in effect, the hospital’s financial steering wheel for the year.
The Capital Budget: Investing in the Long Term

The capital budget allocates funding to the purchase of durable, long-lived assets — and the stakes per decision are far higher. A single capital request might be a robotic surgical system, a CT or MRI machine, a building renovation, or an entirely new off-site clinic. What makes something "capital" rather than "operating" is defined by the organization’s written capitalization policy, which sets a minimum dollar threshold and an expected service life (more than one year) for an item to be treated as a capital asset. There is no universal dollar figure; each hospital sets its own threshold.

Capital assets are accounted for differently from operating expenses, and this is where the two budgets connect on the financial statements. Rather than being expensed all at once, a capital asset’s cost is spread across its useful life through depreciation — the periodic charge reflecting the gradual consumption of the asset, most commonly spread evenly (straight-line) over its estimated life. So the MRI machine bought from the capital budget shows up year after year as depreciation in the operating budget, quietly linking a one-time capital decision to ongoing operating costs.

body.message: Whether a purchase hits the capital budget or the operating budget depends on the hospital’s capitalization threshold. A $400 piece of equipment is an operating expense; a $400,000 imaging system is a capital asset depreciated over years. Misclassifying items distorts both budgets and the financial statements — which is why a clear written capitalization policy matters.
body.title: Capitalize or Expense? The Threshold Decides

children.text: Hospitals also plan how to fund capital. One important mechanism is funded depreciation — a designated financial account a hospital builds up specifically to fund future debt service and capital expenditures. Setting aside funds as assets depreciate helps ensure money is available to replace them when they wear out, rather than scrambling for financing at the moment of need.
How Capital Decisions Actually Get Made

The defining reality of capital budgeting is scarcity: hospitals operate with a fixed annual capital budget, so every approved request competes with every other department’s needs. Radiology’s new scanner competes with cardiology’s catheterization lab, with the roof that needs replacing, with the electronic health record upgrade. Unlike operating costs that recur predictably, capital requests are discrete, large, and mutually exclusive — approving one often means denying another.

The process typically begins when a clinical department identifies a need and submits a capital request that includes the clinical justification, estimated cost, and expected return. Decision-makers then weigh these requests against one another using criteria such as essential service needs, regulatory and safety requirements, alignment with strategic priorities, historical budgets, and the organization’s overall financial position. The strategic planning process serves to assess and prioritize future capital goals against the hard limits of financial reality.

body.title: The Capital Budgeting Process

children.text: Why the Two Budgets Must Be Read Together

The deepest insight of this lesson is that the operating and capital budgets cannot be managed in isolation, because each shapes the other. Capital investments drive future operating costs: a new facility requires staff, supplies, utilities, and maintenance; a new technology requires trained operators and service contracts. A hospital that approves a gleaming new surgical wing without budgeting for the operating costs to run it has set a trap for its future self. Conversely, funding for capital purchases may need to come from operating surplus, so a thin operating margin directly constrains the capital a hospital can afford.

body.analogy: The two budgets are like a household’s monthly budget versus its decision to buy a house. The monthly budget covers groceries, utilities, and gas — recurring and adjustable. Buying a house is a capital decision: a large, long-lived asset paid for over time, which then locks in years of mortgage payments, property taxes, and upkeep that reappear in every future monthly budget. Smart families plan both together; so do smart hospitals.
body.concept: Operating budget vs. capital budget

children.text: Recent trends make capital planning especially pressing. Fitch reported that hospital capital expenditures rose to a median of 123.4% of depreciation expense in FY24 — up from 109.1% the prior year and the highest level since 2013. Spending above 100% of depreciation means hospitals are reinvesting faster than their assets are wearing out, a healthy sign after years of deferred investment, but one that depends on operating margins strong enough to fund it. The average-age-of-plant ratio from the financial-ratios lesson is the warning gauge here: aging facilities eventually force capital spending whether or not the operating budget can comfortably support it.

For anyone learning hospital finance, the takeaway is to always ask which budget a decision lives in and how it ripples into the other. A supply cost is operating; a building is capital; but the building generates operating costs forever after. The most consequential financial decisions a hospital makes — whether to build, what technology to buy, how to fund it — happen in the capital budget, while the operating budget determines whether the hospital can keep those promises year after year. Mastering the relationship between the two is mastering how a hospital plans to survive both this year and the next decade.

points: Hospitals build two distinct budgets: the operating budget for recurring annual revenue and expenses (salaries, supplies, overhead), and the capital budget for long-lived asset investments (equipment, buildings) that deliver value beyond one year.
The operating budget is a forecasting exercise built incrementally (adjusting last year’s) or zero-based (justifying every expense from scratch), and managers track monthly variances against it.
Whether a purchase is "capital" or "operating" is set by the hospital’s written capitalization policy, which defines a minimum dollar threshold and a useful life of more than one year.

Capital assets are not expensed at once but spread across their useful life via depreciation (commonly straight-line), which links one-time capital decisions to ongoing operating costs on the financial statements.
Funded depreciation is a designated account hospitals build up to finance future debt service and capital replacement as assets wear out.

Capital budgeting is governed by scarcity: a fixed annual capital pool forces departments’ large, discrete requests to compete, prioritized by clinical need, safety, strategy, ROI, and financial capacity.
The two budgets must be read together because capital investments drive future operating costs, and capital funding often depends on operating surplus — so each constrains the other.

Capital spending is rising (Fitch: capex at a median 123.4% of depreciation in FY24, highest since 2013), reflecting reinvestment in aging facilities that depends on operating margins strong enough to fund it.

children.text: Medications for Opioid Use Disorder (MOUD)

The single most important advance in treating opioid use disorder is medication. Three medications are approved by the FDA: methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone. Collectively they are called medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) — the term that has largely replaced the older phrase "medication-assisted treatment." These are not a crutch or a substitute addiction; they are evidence-based treatment that saves lives.

The evidence is unambiguous. People with opioid use disorder taking prescribed methadone or buprenorphine are roughly 50% less likely to die of overdose than those receiving no medication. Because the opioid crisis is, above all, a crisis of death, this mortality benefit is the central reason MOUD is considered the gold standard of care.

Yet despite this, the majority of people with opioid use disorder never receive these medications — blocked by stigma (including the false belief that MOUD just "replaces one drug with another"), regulatory hurdles, and a shortage of prescribers. Understanding how MOUD works and where it is delivered is essential to understanding the response to the overdose crisis.

Three FDA-approved medications treat opioid use disorder — methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone (collectively MOUD). Methadone and buprenorphine cut the risk of overdose death by roughly half compared with no medication.

children.text: How the Three Medications Work

The three medications all act on the brain’s mu-opioid receptor, but in different ways. Methadone is a long-acting full opioid agonist: it fully activates the receptor, which suppresses cravings and withdrawal without producing the highs and crashes of short-acting opioids like heroin or fentanyl. It has been used to treat opioid use disorder for more than 50 years.

Buprenorphine is a partial agonist: it activates the receptor only partially, relieving withdrawal and cravings while producing a "ceiling effect" that lowers the risk of respiratory depression and overdose. Naltrexone is the opposite — a full antagonist that blocks the receptor entirely, so opioids produce no effect; it is non-addictive but requires the patient to be fully detoxed before starting, which makes initiation harder.

These mechanisms explain the different delivery rules. Methadone’s full-agonist potency and diversion risk are why it is tightly regulated; buprenorphine’s ceiling effect makes it safer to prescribe in ordinary office settings; and naltrexone, having no abuse potential, faces the fewest restrictions of all.

body.title: The Three Medications for Opioid Use Disorder

body.message: A persistent and harmful myth holds that methadone or buprenorphine merely substitute one addiction for another. The science is clear: these medications stabilize brain chemistry, reduce illicit use, and cut overdose deaths roughly in half. Stigma against MOUD is itself a barrier to lifesaving care.
body.title: MOUD Is Treatment, Not "Another Addiction"

children.text: Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs): The Methadone Setting

Methadone for opioid use disorder can only be dispensed through an Opioid Treatment Program (OTP) — a specially certified clinic, by federal law. OTPs must be certified by SAMHSA and accredited, and they operate under detailed federal regulations. This is a uniquely restrictive arrangement: methadone for addiction cannot simply be prescribed at a pharmacy the way most medications are.

OTPs provide a highly structured environment. Historically, patients had to come to the clinic daily to take their methadone under observation, with "take-home" doses earned over time as they stabilized — a model designed to minimize diversion but one that imposes a significant burden on patients’ work and family life. SAMHSA has updated OTP regulations (with changes finalized in 2024) to make some pandemic-era flexibilities, such as expanded take-home doses and telehealth, permanent.

OTPs typically offer more than medication — counseling, case management, and other services on-site — which can be valuable, but the daily-visit structure and the stigma of attending a "methadone clinic" are real barriers. OTPs are the only legal home for methadone, but they are not the only setting for treating opioid use disorder.

body.content:
Because methadone is a full opioid agonist with real overdose and diversion risk, federal law restricts its dispensing for addiction to SAMHSA-certified, accredited Opioid Treatment Programs operating under strict rules — including, traditionally, observed daily dosing.
This makes OTPs lifesaving but also explains why access is geographically uneven: many rural areas have no OTP within a reasonable distance.
body.title: Why Methadone Is Confined to OTPs

children.text: Office-Based Treatment (OBOT): Buprenorphine in Mainstream Care

Buprenorphine changed the geography of treatment. Unlike methadone, buprenorphine can be prescribed in ordinary medical offices — known as office-based opioid treatment (OBOT) — and filled at a regular pharmacy. This makes it possible to treat opioid use disorder in primary care, the very integration the rest of this course champions.

For years, however, prescribing buprenorphine required a special federal "X-waiver," with mandatory training and caps on the number of patients a provider could treat. The X-waiver was widely blamed for limiting access. The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (through the MAT Act) eliminated the X-waiver entirely: now any practitioner with a standard DEA registration that includes Schedule III authority can prescribe buprenorphine for opioid use disorder, subject to state law, with no patient cap.

The same legislation, via the related MATE Act, introduced a new one-time eight-hour training requirement on treating substance use disorders for most DEA-registered prescribers. The net effect was to remove a major bottleneck: in principle, the entire prescribing workforce can now treat opioid use disorder with buprenorphine, helping push treatment into mainstream and primary care settings.

children.text: Bringing Opioid Treatment Into Mainstream Care

The arc of opioid use disorder treatment has been a slow movement from segregation toward integration. Methadone remains confined to specialized OTPs, but buprenorphine — especially after the X-waiver’s removal — can now be woven into primary care, where most patients already have a relationship with a clinician. This is exactly the kind of integration the SAMHSA-HRSA continuum envisions, applied to addiction.

The remaining barriers are no longer mainly legal but practical and cultural: prescriber comfort and willingness, stigma, counseling capacity, and ensuring rural communities have access. Vermont’s Hub-and-Spoke model, covered later in this course, is one of the most influential attempts to solve exactly this problem — connecting specialized "hub" programs with primary-care "spokes" so that buprenorphine treatment can reach patients close to home.

The bottom line for this lesson: opioid use disorder is treatable with medications that cut deaths roughly in half, delivered either through highly structured OTPs (methadone) or, increasingly, through office-based buprenorphine in mainstream care. Expanding access to MOUD is the core clinical strategy of the response to the overdose crisis.

Medications for opioid use disorder cut the risk of overdose death roughly in half — yet most people with the disorder never receive them. Closing that gap is the central task of the overdose response.

children.text: Our Vision: A System Without Ceilings

The current landscape of healthcare is often defined by its limitations—budgetary constraints, fragmented data, and reactive care models. At Health Transformation Review, we envision a future where these ceilings are dismantled. Our vision is a global ecosystem where every technological advancement and policy shift is calibrated to a single, uncompromising metric: the maximization of human vitality.
Transformation is not an incremental adjustment to the status quo; it is the purposeful redesign of the engine itself.
The Mission: The Two Pillars of Transformation
To move the needle on value-based care, we must operate with clinical precision across two distinct yet inseparable domains:

1. Optimizing Care: We dissect the mechanics of delivery. This means leveraging Health Information Exchanges (HIE), integrating AI-driven diagnostics, and refining policy to eliminate the 'noise' of administrative friction. Optimization is about making the machine lean, fast, and unerringly accurate.

2. Maximizing Health: While care is the process, health is the product. Maximizing health goes beyond the absence of disease; it is the proactive pursuit of peak human performance and systemic resilience. We focus on the innovations that allow individuals to stay outside the clinical environment, thriving in their own lives.
We are moving from a world of volume-based intervention to a world of value-based wellness. The bridge between the two is built with data, policy, and unyielding innovation.

children.text: Pulling the Course Together

This course has moved from awareness to action — from defining health equity, through the social determinants and disparity data, to algorithmic bias, CMS requirements, language access, community health workers, and cross-sector partnership. Each of those is a piece. This final lesson is about the whole: how an organization actually becomes equitable, weaving these pieces into its strategy, structure, and culture rather than treating them as a scattered collection of initiatives.

The central failure mode is the equity initiative that exists in isolation — a committee here, a dashboard there, a screening pilot somewhere else — none of it connected to how the organization sets strategy, allocates resources, or evaluates leaders. Such efforts produce activity without transformation. They are visible enough to claim credit and disconnected enough to change nothing fundamental, and they tend to evaporate when budgets tighten or attention shifts.

Genuine organizational equity transformation is different. It treats equity as a core dimension of quality and mission, embeds it in governance and accountability, builds the infrastructure to act on it, and sustains it as a cultural commitment rather than a campaign. This lesson covers the frameworks and requirements that describe what that transformation looks like — and why culture, not policy alone, is what ultimately determines whether it sticks.

Scattered equity initiatives produce activity without transformation. Real change comes from embedding equity into strategy, governance, infrastructure, and culture — treating it as core to quality and mission, not a side campaign.
The IHI Framework for Organizational Equity

The most influential roadmap for organizational transformation is the Institute for Healthcare Improvement's 2016 white paper, "Achieving Health Equity: A Guide for Health Care Organizations." It lays out a framework of five interdependent components, and its core argument is that meaningful progress requires work across all five — not cherry-picking the comfortable ones.

The five components are: make health equity a strategic priority (embed it in the organization's mission, strategy, and goals at the highest level); develop structure and processes to support health equity work (governance, dedicated leadership, and infrastructure); deploy specific strategies to address the multiple determinants of health on which the organization can have direct impact; decrease institutional racism within the organization; and develop partnerships with community organizations to improve health and equity in the community.

Two of these components are the ones organizations most often skip, and they are the ones that distinguish transformation from theater. Making equity a genuine strategic priority — with board and C-suite ownership, not a side office — is what gives the work resources and durability. And explicitly addressing institutional racism within the organization, rather than only treating disparities as external phenomena, requires examining the organization's own policies, practices, and culture. Avoiding these two is how organizations stay busy without changing.

children.text: When Equity Becomes a Requirement: The Joint Commission

Organizational equity is no longer purely voluntary for accredited hospitals. The Joint Commission — the body that accredits most US hospitals — issued new Leadership standards on health equity effective January 1, 2023, and then elevated health equity to a National Patient Safety Goal effective July 1, 2023. That elevation is significant: a National Patient Safety Goal places health equity alongside core safety priorities, signaling that inequitable care is a safety failure.

The standard (LD.04.03.08) was deliberately placed in the Leadership chapter, with the Joint Commission explaining that "success demands leadership" and that achieving equity requires commitment from the C-suite and the board. Its elements of performance are concrete and map almost exactly onto this course: designate an individual to lead equity work, assess patients' health-related social needs, analyze quality and safety data to identify disparities, develop an action plan to address them, act when the organization falls short of its goals, and inform stakeholders about progress.

Read as a checklist, those requirements are a compact summary of organizational equity: leadership ownership, SDOH screening, stratified data analysis, a data-to-action plan, accountability for results, and transparency. The Joint Commission essentially codified the operational core of this course into accreditation. As with CMS, the strength and persistence of such requirements depends on the accreditor's ongoing priorities — but the elevation to a National Patient Safety Goal marked a real shift from equity as aspiration to equity as a measured standard of practice.

Effective January 1, 2023, the Joint Commission introduced a Leadership standard requiring accredited hospitals to treat health care disparities as a quality and safety priority; effective July 1, 2023, it elevated this to a National Patient Safety Goal.
Its elements of performance require designating an equity leader, assessing patients' health-related social needs, analyzing data to identify disparities, creating and acting on an improvement action plan, and informing stakeholders of progress — placing equity in the Leadership chapter because, in the Joint Commission's words, "success demands leadership."

children.text: Governance, Accountability, and Infrastructure

Both the IHI framework and the Joint Commission standard converge on the same insight from the data-to-action lesson: equity work succeeds or fails on governance and accountability. The organizations that transform have senior, named ownership of equity — often a chief health equity officer or equivalent reporting at the executive level — and board-level attention, not a junior coordinator buried in an org chart. Leadership ownership is what converts equity from a values statement into a resourced priority.

Accountability is the mechanism, and it echoes the strongest finding of this course: tying leadership performance and compensation to measurable equity outcomes is what most distinguishes organizations that make progress. A board that reviews stratified equity metrics with the same seriousness as financial metrics, and a C-suite whose evaluations include equity targets, will produce sustained attention. Without that, equity competes against everything that is actually measured and rewarded — and loses.

Infrastructure makes the accountability real. That means the REaL data systems to measure disparities, the disparity dashboards to make them visible, the screening and referral workflows to act on social needs, and the staff capacity — including community health workers — to do the relational work. The pieces from earlier lessons are not separate projects; they are the infrastructure that an equity-committed organization assembles into a coherent capability. Transformation is, in large part, the work of connecting them.

body.title: Equity Theater vs. Equity Transformation

children.text: From Policy to Culture

The final and hardest step is cultural. Policies, standards, and dashboards are necessary, but an organization can have all of them and still deliver inequitable care if equity is not woven into how people actually think and behave day to day. Culture is what determines whether a clinician pauses at a borderline pulse-oximeter reading in a darker-skinned patient, whether a registration clerk asks the REaL data question well, whether a team treats a disparity on the dashboard as a real problem or a number to explain away.

Cultural transformation is slower and less tidy than policy change, and it cannot be mandated into existence. It is built through sustained leadership messaging, through training that connects to real clinical situations, through hiring and promotion that value equity competence, and through repeatedly demonstrating that the organization acts on disparities rather than merely measuring them. It is reinforced every time leadership funds an equity intervention over a competing priority, and undermined every time equity is the first thing cut under pressure.

The throughline of this entire course has been the move from awareness to action — and organizational transformation is where that move is completed. An organization that has internalized equity does not need a campaign to remember it; it shows up in strategy, governance, infrastructure, daily practice, and the assumptions people no longer have to be reminded of. That is the destination: not a set of programs, but an organization for which equitable care is simply how it does its work. Getting there is difficult, ongoing, and — given the disparities documented throughout this course — among the most important work in health care.
Equity that lives only in policy can be revoked with a memo. Equity that lives in culture is how an organization behaves when no one is checking.

children.text: The Newest Pillar of Medicare

For its first four decades, Medicare had a glaring gap: it generally did not cover outpatient prescription drugs. A senior could have a heart attack covered under Part A, but the medications to prevent the next one were largely on their own dime. Part D, created by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 and effective January 1, 2006, finally closed that gap.

Part D is unusual in its structure. Rather than the government providing the benefit directly, it is delivered entirely by private plans — either standalone Prescription Drug Plans (PDPs) that attach to Original Medicare, or drug coverage built into Medicare Advantage plans (MA-PDs). Beneficiaries pay premiums, and the federal government heavily subsidizes the cost.

Enrollment is voluntary, but there is a catch: beneficiaries who go without creditable drug coverage and sign up late face a permanent late-enrollment penalty added to their premium. This nudge is designed to keep healthy beneficiaries in the risk pool rather than waiting until they get sick.

Part D is the Medicare outpatient prescription drug benefit, created by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 (effective 2006). It is delivered entirely through private plans — standalone PDPs or Medicare Advantage drug plans — and subsidized by the federal government.
Formularies and Tiers

Every Part D plan has a formulary — its list of covered drugs. Plans are not required to cover every drug, but they must cover a wide range across therapeutic categories and include certain protected classes. Two plans can cover very different drugs at very different prices, which is why drug coverage, not just premium, should drive plan choice.

Within a formulary, drugs are sorted into tiers. Lower tiers (preferred generics, generics) carry low copays; higher tiers (preferred brand, non-preferred, and specialty) carry higher copays or coinsurance. Plans use tiering to steer patients toward lower-cost drugs and to negotiate with manufacturers.

Plans also use utilization management tools: prior authorization (requiring approval before a drug is covered), step therapy (try a cheaper drug first), and quantity limits. These tools control costs but can create access barriers, making formulary design one of the most consequential — and contested — features of any Part D plan.

children.text: The Benefit Structure — and the End of the Donut Hole

The standard Part D benefit has long moved through phases. A beneficiary first pays a deductible (up to $590 in 2025), then enters an initial coverage phase sharing costs with the plan. Historically, beneficiaries then hit the infamous "donut hole" — a coverage gap where they paid a much larger share — before reaching catastrophic coverage.

That donut hole is now gone. As of 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act restructured Part D into a simpler three-phase benefit — deductible, initial coverage, and catastrophic — with no coverage gap in between. The change makes drug costs far more predictable for beneficiaries.

The headline reform is a hard out-of-pocket cap. Beginning in 2025, beneficiary out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs is capped at $2,000 per year (indexed thereafter; the cap is $2,100 in 2026). Once a beneficiary hits the cap, the plan covers the rest of their covered drug costs for the year — a profound change for people on expensive medications.

children.text: The Inflation Reduction Act Transformation

The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) is the most significant change to Medicare drug coverage since Part D itself. Beyond the out-of-pocket cap and donut-hole elimination, it capped insulin cost-sharing at $35 per month (effective 2023 for Part D insulin), making a life-sustaining drug affordable for millions.

The IRA also requires drug manufacturers to pay rebates to Medicare if they raise prices faster than inflation — an inflation-rebate provision designed to restrain price growth. And it created the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan, effective January 1, 2025, which lets any Part D enrollee spread their out-of-pocket costs into capped, interest-free monthly installments instead of paying a large bill all at once at the pharmacy.

Most historically, the IRA gave Medicare the power to negotiate prices for certain high-spend drugs — something the original 2003 law had explicitly forbidden. CMS selected the first 10 drugs, and the negotiated prices (ranging from a 38 percent to a 79 percent discount off 2023 list prices) take effect in 2026, with more drugs added in later years.

Effective in 2026, these prices are estimated to save Medicare beneficiaries about $1.5 billion in out-of-pocket costs and the Medicare program roughly $6 billion per year. It is the first time in Part D’s history that Medicare has directly negotiated drug prices.

children.text: Why Part D Matters Now

Part D sits at the intersection of Medicare’s biggest tensions: access, cost, and the role of private plans. It made drugs vastly more accessible to seniors, but it also embodied the original political bargain of relying on private plans and barring price negotiation — a bargain the IRA has now substantially rewritten.

The IRA reforms ripple far beyond beneficiaries’ wallets. The out-of-pocket cap shifts more cost onto plans and manufacturers, reshaping plan bids and premiums. Price negotiation challenges the pharmaceutical industry’s pricing model and has prompted litigation. And inflation rebates change manufacturers’ incentives to raise prices.

For anyone working in Medicare, Part D is now one of the most dynamic areas of the program. Understanding formularies, the new three-phase benefit, the $2,000 cap, and drug price negotiation is essential to understanding where Medicare — and American drug policy — is heading.
With the Inflation Reduction Act, Medicare crossed a line it had refused to cross for two decades: it began negotiating what it pays for drugs.

children.text: The Hardest Money to Collect

After the payer has paid its share, a balance often remains that the patient owes — the deductible, coinsurance, copay, or the full amount for uninsured care. Collecting that patient portion is the final step of the revenue cycle, and it is the hardest. Patient balances are slower, more expensive, and less likely to be collected than payer balances.

This challenge has grown with the rise of high-deductible plans, which shifted thousands of dollars of responsibility onto patients (the theme from the financial-counseling lesson). The result is a national medical-debt problem: medical debt has climbed, and roughly 15 million Americans carry medical collections on their credit reports, per a 2024 CFPB report.

Patient collections sits at the uncomfortable intersection of revenue and human hardship. The same balance is simultaneously money the provider needs to stay viable and a potential source of financial distress for a patient. Handling it well requires both effective collection practice and genuine compassion and compliance — a balance this lesson works to strike.

Patient collections — recovering the portion the patient owes after insurance — is the final and hardest step of the revenue cycle. Patient balances are slower, costlier, and less collectible than payer balances, especially as high-deductible plans grow.
Best Practices for Patient Collections

The most effective patient collections happen early, not late. The single biggest lever is to collect at or before the point of service (the POS collections from the counseling lesson), because the odds of collecting fall sharply once the patient leaves. Clear upfront estimates and financial conversations prevent the surprise bills that drive non-payment.

When a balance does remain, proven practices include: clear, timely, easy-to-understand statements; multiple convenient payment channels (online, mobile, autopay); and flexible options like payment plans or negotiated settlements that recover the debt while preserving the patient relationship. Engaging patients early and often about their responsibility prevents misunderstandings and overdue balances.

Increasingly, organizations use "propensity-to-pay" models — machine-learning models that estimate a patient's likelihood and ability to pay — to focus collection effort where it will actually work and to tailor the approach (payment plan vs. financial assistance vs. standard billing). This makes collections both more efficient and more humane, directing assistance to those who need it and gentle reminders to those who can simply pay.

children.text: Bad Debt vs. Charity Care

When a patient balance is not collected, it is written off — but how it is classified matters enormously, both financially and ethically. There are two categories. Bad debt is care for which the provider expected payment but ultimately did not receive it — typically from patients who could pay but did not, or who were ineligible for assistance. Charity care is care for which the provider did not expect payment, provided to patients who are uninsured or experiencing poverty.

The distinction is not just accounting semantics. Charity care reflects a deliberate decision not to pursue payment from someone who cannot afford it; bad debt reflects a failure (or refusal) to collect from someone who could. Crucially, hospitals generally are not supposed to pursue collections for bills that qualify for financial assistance or charity care — so a balance that should be charity care must not be treated as bad debt and chased.

Getting this classification right is both a compliance obligation and a matter of integrity. Misclassifying charity-care-eligible patients as bad debt and sending them to collections harms vulnerable people and can violate the rules described in the next section. The screening that distinguishes the two — checking whether a patient qualifies for assistance — is therefore a required step, not an optional courtesy.

children.text: Section 501(r): Rules for Nonprofit Hospitals

Nonprofit hospitals — the majority of U.S. hospitals — operate under specific federal rules in Section 501(r) of the tax code, added by the Affordable Care Act, that constrain how they handle patient collections. These rules exist to ensure that tax-exempt hospitals genuinely serve their communities, including those who cannot pay.

Section 501(r)(4) requires a hospital to establish a written Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) covering emergency and medically necessary care. Section 501(r)(6) requires the hospital to make reasonable efforts to determine whether a patient is eligible for assistance under that FAP before engaging in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) — aggressive steps like selling the debt, suing, or reporting it to credit bureaus.

The practical effect is a required sequence: before a nonprofit hospital can pursue aggressive collection against a patient, it must first screen the patient for financial assistance. This bakes the bad-debt-versus-charity-care distinction into law for nonprofits — you cannot treat a balance as bad debt to be aggressively collected until you have confirmed the patient does not qualify for charity care.

body.message: Under Section 501(r), nonprofit hospitals must make reasonable efforts to determine whether a patient qualifies for financial assistance BEFORE taking "extraordinary collection actions" (suing, selling the debt, credit reporting). Pursuing aggressive collection without that screening violates the rule — and may target someone who actually qualified for charity care.
body.title: Screen for Assistance Before Aggressive Collection

children.text: The Shifting Rules on Medical Debt

The regulatory environment around patient collections is in flux, and practitioners must track it. A high-profile example: in January 2025, the federal Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) finalized a rule to remove most medical bills from consumer credit reports. However, in July 2025 a federal court vacated that rule, finding it exceeded the Bureau's authority under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. The federal ban, in other words, did not ultimately take effect.

Meanwhile, a number of states (such as California, New York, and Connecticut) have enacted their own laws restricting or prohibiting medical debt from being reported to credit bureaus, though the interaction between these state laws and federal law has itself become contested. The net result is a patchwork that varies by state and continues to change.

For the revenue cycle, the lesson is that patient collections is not just an operational discipline but a compliance-sensitive, ethically charged, and evolving area. The durable best practices — collect early, communicate clearly, offer flexibility, screen for assistance, and classify write-offs honestly — hold regardless of which way specific regulations swing. Patient collections is where the entire revenue cycle ends, and doing it well means collecting what is genuinely owed while protecting patients who cannot pay. With this, the seven-step cycle is complete; the final module turns to the technology and analytics that run across all of it.

children.text: The Patient Became a Major Payer

For most of the history of health insurance, the patient owed relatively little out of pocket — a small copay, perhaps. That has changed dramatically. The rise of high-deductible health plans means patients now shoulder a large and growing share of the bill, often thousands of dollars before insurance pays anything. The patient has become, in effect, one of the provider's major payers.

This shift created a new front-end discipline: patient financial counseling. Its job is to help patients understand what they will owe, set up how they will pay, and ideally collect some of it up front — before the patient leaves and the balance becomes much harder to collect. It is the front-end's answer to the reality that patient balances are now a serious revenue stream and a serious collection risk.

Financial counseling also serves the patient. Surprise medical bills are a leading cause of financial distress and medical debt. Clear, upfront estimates and conversations about payment options and assistance are both good revenue-cycle practice and good patient care — one of the places where the financial and ethical interests genuinely align.

Patient financial counseling helps patients understand their out-of-pocket responsibility, arrange payment, and pay up front where possible — a front-end discipline that grew as high-deductible plans made patients a major payer.
Calculating What the Patient Owes

A good estimate starts with the eligibility data from verification (the earlier lesson). To calculate a patient's estimated out-of-pocket responsibility, the provider combines the negotiated price for the service with the patient's specific benefit details: copay, coinsurance percentage, how much of the deductible remains, and progress toward the out-of-pocket maximum.

This is genuinely hard to get right. The provider may not know in real time exactly how much of a patient's deductible has already been spent elsewhere, and some charges (pathology, anesthesia, an affiliated physician's services) come from separate billers the hospital does not control. Facility fees and unforeseen charges from complications or longer stays add further uncertainty.

Because of this, an estimate is exactly that — an estimate, not a guarantee. Patients should be told clearly that the final bill may differ. Managing that expectation honestly is part of good counseling; an estimate presented as a promise sets up a dispute later when the real bill arrives.

body.title: Building a Patient Cost Estimate

children.text: The Legal Framework: Price Transparency

Two federal rules now require much of this estimation rather than leaving it optional. The Hospital Price Transparency rule, effective January 1, 2021, requires every U.S. hospital to post its standard charges online in two ways: a comprehensive machine-readable file covering all items and services, and a consumer-friendly display of at least 300 "shoppable" services (or a compliant price-estimator tool).

The machine-readable file must include gross charges, the discounted cash price, payer-specific negotiated charges, and the de-identified minimum and maximum negotiated charges. The intent is to let patients shop and compare prices — though in practice the data has been criticized as inconsistent and hard for ordinary patients to use.

For the revenue cycle, price transparency is both a compliance obligation and an opportunity. Organizations that build accurate, usable estimator tools satisfy the rule and simultaneously give their financial counselors the data to produce reliable estimates — turning a regulatory burden into a collections advantage.

Note the distinction: price transparency applies broadly to hospital charges, while the No Surprises Act's Good Faith Estimate (next section) targets the uninsured and self-pay specifically. Both push in the same direction — patients should know costs before care.
The No Surprises Act and Good Faith Estimates

The No Surprises Act, effective January 1, 2022, added specific protections — including the Good Faith Estimate (GFE) requirement for uninsured and self-pay patients. When such a patient schedules a service (or asks), the provider must give a good faith estimate of the expected charges within defined timeframes (generally one to three business days depending on how far out the service is scheduled).

The GFE has real teeth. If the final billed charges exceed the estimate by $400 or more, the patient can use a Patient-Provider Dispute Resolution (PPDR) process — within 120 days of the bill — to challenge the charge. Crucially, while a dispute is underway, the provider may not move the bill to collections, threaten collections, or must pause collections if already started.

For the revenue cycle, this raises the stakes on estimate accuracy for self-pay patients: a lowball estimate is not just bad service, it creates a legal dispute right and a collections freeze. Done well, though, the GFE process can actually support collections — a clear, accurate estimate given upfront makes patients more willing to pay at or near the time of service.

body.message: Under the No Surprises Act, if an uninsured/self-pay patient's final charges exceed their Good Faith Estimate by $400 or more, they can invoke dispute resolution within 120 days — and the provider must not pursue collections while the dispute is pending. Accurate self-pay estimates are both a service and a compliance necessity.
body.title: A Good Faith Estimate Off by $400+ Triggers Dispute Rights

children.text: Point-of-Service Collections and Compassion

The payoff of good estimation is point-of-service (POS) collections — collecting the patient's expected responsibility at or before the time of care. POS collection is a tracked RCM metric because money collected upfront dramatically improves cash flow and reduces bad debt: once a patient leaves with a balance, the odds of collecting fall sharply, and half of patient balances can go unpaid.

But POS collections must be balanced with compassion and compliance. Counseling should surface options for patients who cannot pay in full: payment plans, sliding-scale discounts, and — critically — screening for charity care and financial assistance, which nonprofit hospitals are obligated to offer. Aggressively demanding payment from a patient who qualifies for charity care is both unethical and, increasingly, legally risky.

The mature view is that financial counseling sits exactly where revenue and patient welfare meet. Done poorly, it produces surprise bills, disputes, and medical debt. Done well, it gives patients clarity and options while improving collections — converting the front-end's financial conversation from an adversarial one into a transparent, manageable part of care. This completes the front-end; the next module turns to the mid-cycle, where care becomes a coded bill.

When a provider gives a patient a clear, accurate out-of-pocket estimate before a procedure, the patient can plan — and is far more likely to pay at or near the time of service.
This is why estimation and POS collections go together: the same data that satisfies price-transparency and Good Faith Estimate rules also gives financial counselors the basis to collect upfront, improving cash flow and reducing the bad debt that piles up once a patient leaves with an unpaid balance.
