body.title: Responding to Pulse Oximeter Bias

points: Pulse oximeters estimate oxygen using light, and skin pigmentation interferes — causing the device to overestimate true oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin.
Sjoding et al. (NEJM 2020) found occult hypoxemia in 17.0% of Black vs 6.2% of white patients — nearly three times more missed dangerous hypoxia.
A falsely reassuring reading can delay admission, oxygen therapy, ICU transfer, and treatment eligibility — turning a device error into a clinical one.
During COVID-19, when SpO2 drove triage and treatment thresholds, this bias likely contributed to the already severe racial mortality gap.
The bias arose because oximeters were historically validated on mostly light-skinned participants — unrepresentative development data, not malicious design.
The fix is better devices validated across all skin tones, not a race-based correction (which would repeat the eGFR mistake); pigmentation is the real variable.
FDA issued draft guidance (early 2025) for larger, more diverse validation studies, and clinicians should confirm suspected hypoxia with arterial blood gas.

body.explanation: Occult hypoxemia is dangerously low true oxygen (arterial saturation <88%) that the pulse oximeter misses, showing a reassuring 92-96% reading instead. Sjoding et al. found it in 17.0% of Black patients versus 6.2% of white patients — nearly three times more often — because greater skin pigmentation causes the device to overestimate oxygen saturation. This means hypoxia in darker-skinned patients can go undetected and untreated.

options.text: Pulse oximeters underestimated oxygen in Black patients, causing unnecessary oxygen therapy
Occult hypoxemia (true arterial saturation <88% despite a 92-96% oximeter reading) occurred nearly three times as often in Black patients — 17.0% vs 6.2%
There was no measurable difference in accuracy once disease severity was controlled
The device was equally inaccurate for all patients, so race was not a factor

children.text: Where It All Comes Together

This is the capstone of the course, and it brings everything together. You now understand what quality measures are, how they are built and stewarded, how they tie to payment, how to surface disparities, and how to test and verify improvement. The quality dashboard is where all of that becomes a living, daily instrument — and the reporting culture is what determines whether the dashboard actually drives better care or just decorates a wall.

A quality dashboard is a curated, visual display of an organization's key quality measures, designed so the right people can see how care is performing and act on it. Done well, it makes quality visible and continuous rather than an annual reporting chore. Done poorly, it becomes a graveyard of charts no one reads.

But a dashboard is only half the story. The most beautiful dashboard fails if the organization's culture punishes the people who surface bad numbers. So this final lesson covers both the technical artifact (the dashboard) and the human system around it (the reporting culture) — because quality improvement needs both.

A quality dashboard is a curated visual display of key measures that makes quality visible and actionable day to day. But it only works inside a reporting culture where people can surface bad results without fear.
Choosing What Goes on the Dashboard

The single most important dashboard decision is which measures to include. The temptation is to show everything; the discipline is to show what matters. A dashboard crammed with dozens of metrics overwhelms users and hides the signal — the same usability-vs-detail trade we saw with star ratings, now at the organizational level.

Good dashboards select KPIs tied to the organization's specific goals and present a balanced view across the dimensions this course has covered: structure, process, and outcome measures, plus balancing measures to catch unintended consequences. They map naturally onto the IOM aims — safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, equitable — so leaders see quality as a whole, not a pile of disconnected numbers.

Crucially, an equity-ready dashboard does not stop at the aggregate. It includes stratified views so disparities are visible at a glance, applying Lesson 13's principle that the average hides the inequity. A dashboard that only shows blended averages will systematically conceal the gaps an organization most needs to act on.

children.text: Designing a Dashboard That Gets Used

Beyond what is shown, how it is shown determines whether a dashboard drives action. Several design practices recur across effective healthcare dashboards. First, it should be interactive with drill-down: a leader sees an organization-level number and can click into a department, unit, or clinician to find where a problem lives.

Second, it should be timely, ideally near-real-time, with automated alerts when a measure crosses a threshold — turning the dashboard from a rear-view mirror into an early-warning system. This is exactly where the digital-measures and data-quality lessons pay off: dashboards are only as current and trustworthy as the underlying data pipeline.

Third, and most important for this course, dashboards should display measures over time using run charts and control charts, not just single numbers or simple red/green indicators. Embedding SPC (Lesson 17) into the dashboard is what lets viewers tell signal from noise at a glance — so the organization reacts to real change and avoids tampering with random variation.

body.message: Dashboards that reduce a measure to a single number or a red/green status — with no trend, no control limits — make it impossible to tell signal from noise. Embed run charts and control charts so users react to genuine special-cause change, not random common-cause variation.
body.title: A Red/Green Light Without SPC Invites Tampering

children.text: From Board to Bedside

A mature quality dashboard is not one screen for one audience. The same underlying data is presented differently at different levels — what is sometimes called "board to bedside." A hospital board sees a high-level strategic view of organizational quality; a department manager sees unit-level detail; a frontline clinician sees their own panel of patients and care gaps.

This layered visibility matters because action happens at every level. Boards set priorities and hold leadership accountable; managers run improvement; clinicians close individual care gaps. When each level can see the data relevant to its decisions — and trace how its piece connects to the whole — the dashboard aligns the entire organization around quality.

Increasingly, organizations also push selected measures to public-facing dashboards. Public transparency — the same principle behind Care Compare from Lesson 7 — adds external accountability and signals confidence. Internally and externally, the throughline is that quality data must reach the people positioned to act on it, in a form they can use.

body.content:
A single quality program might surface the same readmission data three ways: a board dashboard showing the system-wide rate and trend against strategic targets; a manager view showing rates by unit with drill-down; and a clinician view listing that clinician's recently discharged patients at risk.
Each audience sees the level of detail it can act on, all drawn from one trusted data source.
body.title: Board-to-Bedside Visibility

children.text: The Reporting Culture: Where Dashboards Live or Die

The hardest part of quality measurement is not technical — it is cultural. A dashboard surfaces problems by design. If an organization responds to bad numbers by blaming and punishing the people who reported them, staff learn to hide problems, game the metrics, or quietly stop reporting. The dashboard then shows only flattering data and becomes useless or worse.

The antidote is a "just culture": an environment that balances accountability with learning, recognizing that most errors stem from system failures rather than bad individuals. Its foundation is psychological safety — the shared belief that people can report mistakes, near-misses, and bad results without fear of humiliation or punishment. Research consistently links non-punitive reporting to higher reporting rates, more organizational learning, and fewer adverse events.

Two practices make this real. First, non-punitive reporting systems so people surface problems instead of hiding them. Second, closed feedback loops: staff must see that their reports lead to actual change, or they stop reporting. A quality dashboard embedded in a just culture becomes a shared tool for learning; the same dashboard in a culture of blame becomes a weapon, and the data goes dark. This is the final, essential lesson of the course: measurement only improves care when the culture around it is safe enough to tell the truth.

You can build the perfect dashboard, but if people are punished for what it shows, they will make sure it never shows anything real. Culture decides whether measurement improves care or hides its failures.

points: A quality dashboard is a curated visual display of key measures that makes quality visible and actionable, turning measurement from an annual chore into a daily instrument.
The most important decision is which measures to show — select goal-tied KPIs and balance structure, process, outcome, and balancing measures across the IOM aims.
An equity-ready dashboard includes stratified views so disparities are visible rather than hidden inside aggregate averages.
Effective dashboards are interactive with drill-down, near-real-time with threshold alerts, and display SPC run/control charts so users can tell signal from noise.
Reducing measures to a single number or red/green status without SPC invites tampering with random variation.
"Board to bedside" design presents the same data at the right level of detail for boards, managers, and frontline clinicians, plus public transparency for external accountability.
Dashboards only improve care inside a "just culture" with psychological safety, non-punitive reporting, and closed feedback loops — without it, people hide or game the data.

body.explanation: A dashboard surfaces problems by design, so a punitive response teaches staff to hide or game the data — and the dashboard goes dark. Improvement requires a "just culture" with psychological safety, non-punitive reporting, and closed feedback loops, so people surface real problems and trust that reporting leads to change. The best dashboard cannot overcome a culture of blame.

children.text: How You Know the Revenue Cycle Is Healthy

A revenue cycle has many moving parts and a lot of money flowing through it, which means you cannot manage it by intuition. You need numbers — key performance indicators (KPIs) — that tell you, objectively, whether claims are going out clean, whether cash is coming in fast, and whether revenue is leaking. KPIs are the dashboard of the revenue cycle.

The challenge is that everyone calculates metrics slightly differently, which makes benchmarking against peers meaningless. To solve this, the Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) created the MAP Keys — a standardized set of revenue-cycle KPIs with consistent, objective calculations. There are about 29 MAP Keys organized into five groups: Patient Access, Pre-Billing, Claims, Account Resolution, and Financial Management.

Standardization is what makes a KPI trustworthy. When a "denial rate" or "days in AR" is computed the same way everywhere, an organization can compare itself to national benchmarks and know whether it is leading or lagging. This lesson covers the handful of KPIs that matter most and the benchmarks that define good performance.

RCM KPIs are standardized metrics that reveal revenue-cycle health. HFMA's MAP Keys (~29 KPIs across five groups) provide consistent calculations so organizations can benchmark against national peers rather than guess.
Speed: Days in Accounts Receivable

The most watched RCM metric is "Days in Accounts Receivable" (Days in AR) — the average number of days it takes to collect payment after a service is delivered. It is a measure of speed: lower is better, because money owed but not yet collected is money the organization cannot use.

The widely cited benchmark is 30 to 40 days, with the MGMA benchmark at under 40 days and leading organizations achieving under 30. A companion metric, "AR over 90 days," tracks the share of receivables that have aged past 90 days; the benchmark is to keep this under 10 percent, because older receivables are progressively harder to collect.

Days in AR is powerful because it integrates the health of the whole cycle into one number. If claims are denied, delayed, or poorly followed up, the money sits in AR longer and the metric rises. A creeping Days in AR is often the first sign that something upstream is broken.

children.text: Cleanliness: Clean Claim Rate and First-Pass Resolution

Two closely related KPIs measure how often claims are done right the first time. The clean claim rate is the percentage of claims submitted without errors that are accepted by the payer on first submission. The benchmark is 95 percent or higher, with high performers aiming for around 98 percent.

The first-pass resolution rate (sometimes called first-pass yield) measures the percentage of claims that are paid without any resubmission or appeal — "claims paid right the first time." The industry standard here is also 95 percent or higher. The two metrics are related but distinct: a claim can pass the clearinghouse clean yet still be denied by the payer, so first-pass resolution is the stricter, more outcome-focused measure.

These cleanliness metrics matter enormously because rework is expensive. Every claim that is rejected or denied must be corrected and resubmitted, costing staff time and delaying cash. A high clean claim rate directly shortens Days in AR — the cleaner the claim, the faster the payment — which is why these are among the most actionable KPIs in the cycle.

children.text: Yield: Denial Rate and Net Collection Rate

Two KPIs measure how much of what is owed actually gets collected. The denial rate is the percentage of claims denied by payers. The optimal benchmark is under 5 percent, with the best performers near 2 percent; an industry average tends to run between 5 and 10 percent. A rising denial rate is a direct hit to revenue and a signal of upstream problems.

The net collection rate (NCR) measures the percentage of collectible revenue an organization actually captures — that is, of the money it was contractually entitled to (after legitimate contractual adjustments), how much did it collect. Strong performers exceed 95 percent. A net collection rate well below 95 percent means real, earned money is being lost to write-offs, missed follow-up, and unworked denials.

Net collection rate is especially important because it strips out the contractual discounts that make "gross" numbers misleading. It answers the bottom-line question: of the dollars we should have collected, how many did we actually get? That is the truest measure of whether the revenue cycle is doing its job.

children.text: Efficiency and Using KPIs Well

A final essential KPI is cost to collect — total revenue-cycle expenses divided by total collections. It answers how much it costs the organization to collect each dollar. A lower cost to collect means a more efficient revenue cycle, and it is the metric that keeps efficiency honest: you can improve collections by throwing endless staff at the problem, but cost to collect reveals whether that effort is worth it.

No single KPI tells the whole story, and they interact. A practice can post a high net collection rate while its Days in AR balloons (it collects everything, but slowly), or a low denial rate while leaving easy money uncollected. The discipline is to watch a balanced set — speed (Days in AR), cleanliness (clean claim / first-pass), yield (denial rate / net collection), and efficiency (cost to collect) — together.

Used well, these KPIs turn the revenue cycle into a managed system: trends are tracked over time, benchmarked against HFMA MAP Keys and specialty norms, and used to target improvement where the numbers say it is needed. Every later lesson in this course ultimately moves one of these KPIs — fewer denials, cleaner claims, faster AR, higher net collections. They are the scoreboard for everything that follows.

body.message: A single KPI can mislead — high net collection with ballooning Days in AR, or a low denial rate while easy revenue goes uncollected. Track speed, cleanliness, yield, and efficiency together, and compare them to standardized benchmarks (HFMA MAP Keys) rather than judging any one metric alone.
body.title: Watch KPIs as a Balanced Set, Not in Isolation

children.text: The Systems That Run the Cycle

Every step covered so far — verification, coding, charge capture, claims, posting, AR, collections — runs on software. Modern revenue cycle management is impossible to do at scale by hand, so this module turns to the technology that powers it. The starting point is understanding the core systems and, critically, how they connect to the electronic health record (EHR).

Two systems sit at the center. The EHR is the clinical system of record — where care is documented, orders are placed, and the data that drives coding and charges originates. The practice management system (PMS) — or its hospital equivalent, the patient accounting system — handles the financial side: scheduling, registration, billing, claims, payments, and AR. RCM software is the family of tools that manages the revenue functions, whether built into these systems or layered on top.

The single most important fact about this technology is the relationship between the clinical and financial systems. Because what is documented clinically determines what can be billed financially, the EHR and the billing system must share data cleanly. How well they integrate largely determines how well the whole revenue cycle works.

RCM runs on software: the EHR (clinical system of record) and the practice management / patient accounting system (financial side). Because clinical documentation drives billing, how well these systems integrate largely determines revenue-cycle performance.
Why EHR Integration Matters

When the EHR and billing systems are integrated, patient and clinical data flows continuously from documentation into billing without re-keying. A registration entered once populates the claim; a documented and coded service flows into charge capture automatically; a posted payment updates the patient's account everywhere at once. Integration eliminates the silos that traditionally separated clinical and financial workflows.

The payoff is concrete: less manual data entry, fewer transcription errors, more accurate CPT and charge capture, and faster claims. Recall that administrative complexity wastes an estimated $266 billion a year — much of it the friction of disconnected systems and manual re-entry. Integration attacks that waste directly by letting data move once and be used everywhere.

Technically, this integration is built on the interoperability standards from elsewhere in the HTR curriculum — HL7 and FHIR APIs, plus direct database connections — to create the continuous data flow between clinical documentation and billing. The same standards that move data between organizations also move it between the clinical and financial systems within one organization.

children.text: The Big Platforms

In the hospital and large-health-system world, two integrated platforms dominate. Epic's revenue cycle module (Resolute, alongside its registration and scheduling tools) ties billing and coding workflows directly to the patient record, offering automated claim generation, coding assistance, denial management, and revenue reporting inside the same system clinicians use.

Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) offers comparable integrated revenue-cycle capabilities (its newer platform branded RevElate), spanning registration through claim submission and reimbursement, with the goal of improving coding accuracy, reducing denials, and improving revenue capture by keeping clinical and financial functions on one system.

For smaller practices, integrated EHR-plus-practice-management products from many vendors serve the same role on a smaller scale. The common thread is that these are enterprise systems designed so registration, clinical documentation, coding, billing, and AR all live in one connected platform — the "single system of record" model.

It is worth knowing these names because the platform an organization runs shapes its entire RCM operation — its workflows, its reporting, its integration burden, and even which third-party tools it can bolt on.
Integrated vs. Best-of-Breed

A fundamental strategic choice underlies all RCM technology: the integrated (enterprise) approach versus the best-of-breed approach. An integrated system is a single-vendor platform handling clinical and financial functions together. A best-of-breed strategy selects the leading specialized product for each function — a top EHR, a top RCM tool, a top denial-analytics platform — and integrates them.

Each has clear trade-offs. Integrated systems offer seamless internal data flow, one vendor for support and updates, and minimal integration points — everything is designed to work together. But they typically offer less depth in any single function than a specialized standalone product. Best-of-breed offers superior depth in each area but introduces the significant challenge of interoperability: the specialized systems must be connected with robust HL7/FHIR interfaces, or the benefits dissolve into data silos.

The right choice depends on the organization. A large system with complex payer contracts and high claim volume may need the denial-analytics depth that a dedicated RCM platform provides, accepting the integration work. A smaller practice may be far better served by one integrated system that "does most of this" and connects cleanly to a few outside tools, avoiding the integration burden entirely.

children.text: Choosing and Living With RCM Technology

The practical reality is that most organizations land somewhere on a spectrum between fully integrated and fully best-of-breed — typically a core integrated platform supplemented by a few specialized tools where the platform falls short (often denial management, contract management, or patient-payment tools). The integration question becomes "how do I get a system that does most of this, then connects cleanly to the few outside tools I really need?"

Whatever the architecture, the success criterion is the same: clean, continuous data flow from registration through collection, with minimal manual re-entry and minimal silos. A beautiful denial-analytics tool that does not receive timely, accurate data from the EHR is useless; a perfectly integrated platform with weak denial logic still loses revenue. Technology serves the cycle, not the other way around.

This sets up the rest of the module. With the core systems and their integration understood, the next lessons examine the more advanced technology layered on top: predictive analytics and AI that mine this integrated data to prevent denials and predict payment, and the dashboards that turn all of it into the KPIs and benchmarks that manage the revenue cycle.

body.message: A best-of-breed tool with cutting-edge features is worthless if it cannot get clean, timely data from the EHR — and a slick integrated platform with weak denial logic still loses revenue. When evaluating RCM technology, the quality of data flow between clinical and financial systems matters more than any single feature list.

children.text: Three Documents That Tell the Whole Story

Every hospital, whether a rural critical-access facility or a multibillion-dollar academic system, tells its financial story through the same three core documents: the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement. Together with the footnotes to the audited financials, these reports answer three different but related questions: Did the hospital make money this year? What does it own and owe right now? And where did its cash actually come from and go? Learning to read them is the single most transferable skill in hospital finance.

A crucial wrinkle is that the names change depending on who owns the hospital. Because most U.S. hospitals are nonprofit, their statements often carry nonprofit terminology: the income statement becomes the "statement of operations" or "statement of activities," and what a for-profit calls "equity" a nonprofit calls "net assets." The concepts underneath are nearly identical — only the labels differ. This lesson uses both names so you can read either kind of statement with confidence.

The goal is not to become an accountant. It is to be able to pick up a hospital’s financials and quickly form a judgment: Is this organization profitable, liquid, and solvent — or is it heading for trouble? Each of the three statements illuminates one of those three dimensions, and together they reveal far more than any single number like "revenue" or "margin" ever could.

Key Concept: The income statement shows profitability (a flow over time), the balance sheet shows financial position (a snapshot at a moment), and the cash flow statement shows liquidity (where cash actually moved). Reading all three together prevents the mistakes that come from looking at any one alone.
The Income Statement: Did the Hospital Make Money?

The income statement — the statement of operations for a nonprofit — measures financial performance over a period, usually a fiscal year. It starts with revenue and subtracts expenses to arrive at the bottom line. At the top sits the hospital’s lifeblood: net patient service revenue (NPSR), the revenue a hospital expects to collect for services provided after subtracting contractual allowances (the negotiated discounts off its list prices). NPSR is the primary source of revenue for nearly every hospital.

The most important structural feature of a hospital income statement is the split between operating and non-operating items. Transactions that management deems ongoing, major, or central to providing health care — patient revenue and the expenses to deliver care — are reported as operating revenue and expenses. Everything else, most notably investment income from the hospital’s reserves and endowment, is reported as non-operating. This distinction is why a hospital can post a positive bottom line while losing money on actual patient care: strong investment returns can mask a negative operating margin.

body.title: Operating Income Is the Number That Matters Most

children.text: The Balance Sheet: What Does the Hospital Own and Owe?

The balance sheet — the statement of financial position — is a snapshot at a single moment in time, built on one unbreakable equation: assets equal liabilities plus net assets (equity). Assets are what the hospital owns; liabilities are what it owes; net assets are what would be left over if it paid off everything. The two sides always balance, which is the origin of the name.

Assets divide into current assets — cash, short-term investments, and accounts receivable (money owed by payers for care already delivered) — and non-current assets, dominated by property, plant, and equipment (PP&E): the buildings, MRI machines, and infrastructure that make a hospital so capital-intensive. Liabilities divide the same way: current liabilities like accounts payable and short-term debt, and long-term liabilities like bonds payable and pension obligations. The gap between what a hospital owns and owes — its net assets — reflects its accumulated financial strength and its capacity to reinvest and to borrow.

For nonprofit hospitals, the equity section uses distinctive language. Following FASB ASU 2016-14 (effective 2018), net assets are reported in two categories: net assets without donor restrictions (formerly "unrestricted") and net assets with donor restrictions (formerly "restricted"). Net assets without donor restrictions can be used for any purpose advancing the mission, while restricted net assets carry conditions set by the donor. When analysts assess a nonprofit hospital’s financial cushion, they focus on the unrestricted portion, because that is the money truly available to absorb shocks.

body.content:
Imagine two hospitals that both report a 3% operating margin this year — identical on the income statement.

Hospital A has months of cash in reserve, modest debt, and strong unrestricted net assets. Hospital B has nearly drained its cash, carries heavy bond debt, and has thin net assets. The income statement says they are equally healthy; the balance sheet reveals that Hospital B is one bad quarter from a crisis. This is why no one judges a hospital on profitability alone.
body.title: Why the Balance Sheet Catches What the Income Statement Misses

children.text: The Cash Flow Statement: Where Did the Cash Go?

Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. The income statement is built on accrual accounting, recording revenue when care is delivered — even if the payer takes months to pay. A hospital can report healthy "profit" while its bank account drains, because reported revenue is not the same as collected cash. The cash flow statement closes this gap by tracking the actual movement of money, organized into three activities: operating, investing, and financing.

Cash from operating activities shows whether day-to-day care generates real cash — the most important section for judging sustainability. Cash from investing activities captures purchases and sales of long-term assets, such as buying a new surgical robot or building a wing (large negative numbers here are normal and often healthy, signaling reinvestment). Cash from financing activities reflects borrowing and repaying debt and changes in long-term financing. Reading the three together shows not just whether a hospital made money, but whether that money is real and where it is being deployed.

body.analogy: The three statements are like a fitness assessment. The income statement is your weight change over the year (did you gain or lose?). The balance sheet is a snapshot of your body composition today (muscle vs. fat, strength vs. fragility). The cash flow statement is your actual heartbeat — the real-time circulation that keeps you alive regardless of what the scale says. A good doctor looks at all three; so does a good analyst.
body.concept: How the three financial statements work together

children.text: The First Numbers an Analyst Looks For

Once you can navigate the three statements, a handful of figures give a fast read on a hospital’s health. The most famous is days cash on hand (DCOH) — how many days the hospital could keep operating using only its available cash if all revenue stopped. It is calculated as cash plus cash equivalents plus short-term investments, divided by average daily operating expenses (total expenses minus depreciation and amortization, divided by the days in the period). DCOH draws on both the balance sheet (cash) and the income statement (expenses), which is why it requires reading the statements together.

Benchmarks give the number meaning. Strong liquidity is generally considered to be roughly 150–205 days of cash on hand, with the exact target varying by hospital size, location, and ownership. A hospital with 200 days of cash has a deep cushion; one with 30 days is in danger. Alongside DCOH, analysts check the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities; 1.0 or higher means short-term obligations are covered) and days in accounts receivable (how long, on average, it takes to collect payment — where a rising number means cash is stuck in unpaid claims).

These metrics are the bridge to the next lesson on financial ratios, but the point here is structural: each ratio pulls data from one or more of the three core statements. You cannot compute days cash on hand without the balance sheet and income statement; you cannot judge collection efficiency without net patient revenue and accounts receivable. Mastering the statements is the prerequisite for every ratio, dashboard, and bond rating that follows — and for forming an honest judgment about whether a hospital is built to last.

Nonprofit hospitals use different labels: the income statement is the "statement of operations/activities" and "equity" is called "net assets," but the underlying concepts are essentially the same.
Net patient service revenue (NPSR) — revenue expected after contractual allowances — sits at the top of the income statement and is the primary revenue source for nearly every hospital.
Always separate operating income from the bottom line: a hospital can show overall "profit" while losing money on patient care, propped up by non-operating investment income.

The balance sheet rests on assets = liabilities + net assets; for nonprofits, FASB ASU 2016-14 splits net assets into "without donor restrictions" (formerly unrestricted) and "with donor restrictions" (formerly restricted).
The cash flow statement reconciles accrual "profit" with real cash, separating operating, investing, and financing activities — and cash from operations is the truest test of sustainability.

Every financial ratio pulls from one or more of the three statements, so mastering the statements is the prerequisite for ratios, dashboards, and bond ratings.

children.text: You Cannot Improve What You Cannot See

Every previous lesson in this course points to the same operational prerequisite: to act on a disparity, you first have to be able to see it. That requires data on who your patients are — their race, ethnicity, and language — collected accurately and at sufficient detail to stratify outcomes. This is "REaL" data: Race, Ethnicity, and Language. Without it, a health system is effectively colorblind to its own inequities, unable to tell whether its diabetes control, cancer screening, or maternal outcomes differ across the populations it serves.

The single most common reason health systems cannot identify disparities in their own care is poor REaL data quality. Race and ethnicity fields are frequently missing, guessed at by staff rather than self-reported, collapsed into a handful of coarse categories, or recorded inconsistently across registration, the EHR, and claims. When the underlying data is unreliable, every downstream analysis inherits that unreliability.

This makes REaL data collection foundational rather than clerical. It is the substrate on which stratified quality measurement, targeted intervention, and progress tracking all depend. A health system that wants to do equity work but has not invested in high-quality, self-reported, granular REaL data is building on sand.

REaL data — Race, Ethnicity, and Language — is the foundation of all equity measurement. If it is missing, guessed at, or too coarse, a health system cannot see its own disparities, let alone act on them.
How REaL Data Goes Wrong

REaL data quality fails in a handful of predictable ways, and each has a known remedy. The most damaging is collecting race by staff observation rather than patient self-report. A registration clerk guessing a patient's race produces data that is both inaccurate and biased — and it denies patients the basic dignity of defining their own identity. The fix is straightforward: ask patients to self-identify, at registration or through the patient portal.

A second common failure is conflating race and ethnicity — for example, treating "Hispanic" as a race rather than collecting Hispanic/Latino ethnicity separately from race. Federal standards keep these distinct (a person can be Hispanic and any race), and collapsing them destroys analytic value. A third failure is excessive coarseness: lumping everyone into five or six broad buckets hides enormous within-group variation. A "Asian" category that combines Hmong, Korean, Filipino, and South Asian patients can mask disparities that only appear when the data is disaggregated.

Language is often the most neglected element. Preferred spoken language and preferred written language are frequently not collected at all, or are conflated with ethnicity. Yet language access is directly tied to safety and quality — and, as a later lesson covers, to legal requirements. Finally, missing data is often simply coded "Unknown" or "Declined" and abandoned, rather than triggering a protocol to ask again at the next encounter.

children.text: The Standards: OMB Categories and the IOM Framework

REaL data is not collected ad hoc; there are national standards that make data comparable across organizations. The baseline comes from the Office of Management and Budget's Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 (SPD 15), which sets the minimum race and ethnicity categories used across federal data. In March 2024, OMB issued the first major revision to SPD 15 since 1997 — a significant change worth knowing.

The 2024 revision made two notable changes. It moved to a combined race-and-ethnicity question (rather than asking Hispanic ethnicity separately from race), allowing respondents to select one or multiple categories. And it added "Middle Eastern or North African" (MENA) as a distinct minimum category; previously, MENA respondents were tabulated as White. The updated minimum categories are American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, Middle Eastern or North African, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and White. The revision also encourages collecting more detailed data beyond these minimums.

For health care specifically, the influential framework is the 2009 Institute of Medicine report "Race, Ethnicity, and Language Data: Standardization for Health Care Quality Improvement." It recommended collecting the OMB categories plus more granular ethnicity and preferred-language data drawn from national standard sets — precisely so that quality metrics can be stratified, disparity-reduction initiatives organized, and progress reported in consistent, comparable ways. The IOM framework is why "granular ethnicity" and "language need" are now standard concepts in health-system data design.

body.content:
OMB's Statistical Policy Directive No. 15 sets the federal minimum race/ethnicity categories. The March 28, 2024 revision — the first since 1997 — combined race and ethnicity into one multi-select question and added a Middle Eastern or North African (MENA) category, which had previously been folded into "White."
The 2009 IOM report "Race, Ethnicity, and Language Data" built the health-care framework: collect OMB categories plus locally selected granular ethnicity and preferred-language data, so quality performance can be stratified and disparities tracked consistently across organizations.
body.title: OMB SPD 15 (2024 Revision) and the IOM REaL Framework

children.text: The Aggregate Trap: Why Stratification Matters

The entire point of collecting REaL data is to stratify outcomes — to break a performance measure down by group rather than reporting a single average. The reason this matters so much is what we can call the aggregate trap: a perfectly respectable overall number can conceal a severe disparity underneath it.

Consider a hospital reporting a 72% colorectal cancer screening rate — at or above the national benchmark, apparently fine. But stratified by race, the same data might show white patients at 79%, Black patients at 61%, and Hispanic patients at 54%. The aggregate hides a 25-percentage-point gap. The hospital looks like a strong performer while systematically underserving entire groups of patients. Only stratification reveals the problem, and only revealing it makes action possible.

This is why "we treat everyone the same" is not a defense — and is often the very mechanism that lets disparities persist unexamined. A health system committed to equity reports its key measures stratified by race, ethnicity, language, and ideally payer and geography, and it treats a wide gap between groups as a quality defect demanding a response, not as a statistic to file away.

body.message: The aggregate trap is the most important reason to collect and use REaL data. A clinic can sit at or above a national benchmark in aggregate while one subgroup lags far behind. Reporting only the overall number is not neutral — it actively conceals the inequity. Always stratify key measures by race, ethnicity, and language.
body.title: A good average can hide a serious disparity

children.text: Building the Data Infrastructure

Turning these principles into reliable data requires deliberate operational work. It starts at the front lines: registration and intake staff need training and scripting to ask self-identification questions respectfully and to explain why the information is collected, which improves both completeness and accuracy. EHR configuration matters too — the system must support separate race, ethnicity, granular-ethnicity, and language fields, and ideally let patients self-report through a portal.

Trust is a real and legitimate barrier. Some patients are wary of providing demographic data, often for understandable historical reasons. The remedy is transparency: explaining that the data is used to ensure all groups receive equitable care and to identify and close gaps — not to discriminate — measurably increases willingness to self-identify. How the question is asked matters as much as whether it is asked.

Finally, REaL data quality has to be measured and managed like any other data quality problem. That means tracking the share of records with complete, self-reported race, ethnicity, and language; auditing for the failure modes above; and building protocols to re-request missing data at subsequent encounters. A health system that monitors its REaL data completeness the way it monitors clinical metrics will steadily improve the foundation everything else rests on.

children.text: From Customary Charges to a Standardized Scale: The RBRVS Origin Story

Before 1992, Medicare paid physicians based on "customary, prevailing, and reasonable" (CPR) charges — essentially whatever a doctor had historically billed, benchmarked against regional and specialty norms. This system was both inflationary and opaque. Surgeons and proceduralists, who had established high historical charges, received payments that bore little relationship to the actual time, skill, or effort their work required. Primary care physicians, whose cognitive work left a smaller billing footprint, were systematically underpaid by comparison.

In the late 1980s, Harvard economist William Hsiao led a landmark study commissioned by the Health Care Financing Administration (now CMS) to develop a more rational basis for physician payment. The resulting system — the Resource-Based Relative Value Scale (RBRVS) — assigned each physician service a relative value unit (RVU) intended to reflect the actual resources required: physician time and effort, practice overhead, and malpractice insurance. The Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989 authorized the creation of the Medicare Fee Schedule based on RBRVS, which took effect on January 1, 1992.

The introduction of RBRVS was a genuine improvement over CPR. It replaced an arbitrary, charge-history-based system with one grounded in explicit resource measurement. However, as decades of subsequent evidence would show, the RBRVS contained structural biases — particularly in how it valued procedural work relative to cognitive work — that would persist and intensify over time.

Key Concept: The Resource-Based Relative Value Scale (RBRVS) is the payment system used by Medicare and most other payers to set physician fees. Each service is assigned relative value units (RVUs) that reflect the estimated resource cost — physician work, practice expense, and malpractice — and then multiplied by a dollar conversion factor to produce the actual payment.

children.text: Anatomy of an RVU: Three Components, One Payment

Every Medicare-covered physician service is assigned a total RVU that is the sum of three distinct components. The first is the physician work RVU (wRVU) — intended to capture the time, technical skill, physical effort, mental effort and judgment, and stress associated with the service. The second is the practice expense RVU (PE RVU) — reflecting the overhead costs of running a medical practice: staff, equipment, supplies, and facilities. The third is the malpractice RVU (PLI RVU) — representing the professional liability insurance costs attributable to the service.

To produce a payment amount, each RVU component is first adjusted by a geographic practice cost index (GPCI) — a locality-based multiplier that reflects cost differences across regions. The adjusted RVUs are then summed and multiplied by the national conversion factor. For example, in 2025 the conversion factor is $32.35. A service assigned 2.0 work RVUs in a locality with a GPCI of 1.0, combined with practice expense and malpractice components, might yield a total payment in the range of $80–$120 depending on the specific service. The formula is: Payment = (wRVU × work GPCI + PE RVU × PE GPCI + PLI RVU × PLI GPCI) × Conversion Factor.

The conversion factor is set annually by CMS through the Physician Fee Schedule rulemaking process. Critically, the conversion factor has largely stagnated or declined in real (inflation-adjusted) terms over the past two decades, even as practice costs have risen. For CY 2025, CMS finalized a conversion factor of $32.3465 — a decrease of $0.94 (approximately 2.83%) from the CY 2024 rate of $33.29. This persistent downward pressure on the conversion factor, combined with rising overhead costs, has squeezed physician practice margins — particularly in primary care specialties that cannot offset revenue declines with high procedure volume.

children.text: The RUC: The Committee That Sets the Scale

RVU values are not set unilaterally by CMS. They are developed and recommended primarily through the AMA/Specialty Society Relative Value Scale Update Committee — universally known as the RUC. The RUC is a private advisory body convened by the American Medical Association whose 32 voting members represent physician specialty societies. CMS accepts the vast majority of RUC recommendations, historically in excess of 90% of submitted values.

The composition of the RUC has been a persistent source of criticism. Primary care physicians — family physicians, general internists, general pediatricians — represent only about 19% of RUC seats, despite accounting for nearly a quarter of the physician workforce and handling approximately 35% of all patient visits. Procedural and surgical specialties, by contrast, hold the majority of seats and have historically proposed RVU values that favor their own services. Since CMS adopted most of those recommendations, the result has been a payment schedule that systematically overvalues procedures relative to the cognitive work of primary care.

The RUC process has also been criticized for its opacity. RUC deliberations are not public, and the specialty society survey instruments used to estimate physician time and effort have been questioned for their reliability. When the Government Accountability Office (GAO) examined the RUC process in 2012, it found that CMS lacked the independent data it needed to validate RUC recommendations and recommended that CMS develop additional mechanisms to review values. Despite these critiques, the RUC remains the central institution through which RBRVS values are set.

body.content:
In 2021, CMS substantially revised the work RVU values for office-based evaluation and management (E/M) codes — the CPT codes used for primary care and specialist office visits. The revision increased wRVUs for complex visits (99214, 99215) by roughly 30–40%, representing the most significant effort in RBRVS history to correct the documented undervaluation of cognitive, relationship-based care.
However, because the Medicare fee schedule is budget-neutral by law, the increases for E/M codes required offsetting reductions in other services. Procedural specialties — including surgery, radiology, and others — saw payment reductions as a consequence. The revaluation also had limited impact on total physician compensation because commercial insurers, which cover the majority of patient visits for most physicians, did not uniformly follow Medicare's revised relativities.
body.title: The 2021 Evaluation and Management Code Revaluation

children.text: Why RVUs Favor Procedures Over Primary Care

The structural bias toward procedures in the RBRVS system is not a subtle phenomenon — it is the defining driver of the specialty income gap in American medicine. A 30-minute surgical procedure routinely generates more wRVUs than an hour of complex cognitive work with a patient managing multiple chronic conditions. This is partly a historical artifact of how the original RVU values were set — based on physician surveys of time and effort conducted in the early 1990s, when procedural work was more clearly demarcated and more easily quantified than the diffuse cognitive labor of primary care.

The consequence is a compensation structure that sends powerful signals to medical students choosing specialties. When primary care physicians can earn $250,000–$280,000 annually while surgical subspecialists routinely earn $400,000–$700,000 or more, the RBRVS payment differential is a major factor driving specialty selection. The United States has a well-documented shortage of primary care physicians — a shortage that worsens as each cohort of medical graduates makes rational economic choices in response to the signals embedded in the payment system.

The problem is compounded by the fact that primary care is where prevention, early detection, and chronic disease management happen — the services that could most efficiently reduce downstream high-cost utilization. A payment system that chronically under-reimburses primary care is, in effect, a system that chronically underinvests in the part of the healthcare pipeline most capable of reducing total spending and improving population health.

children.text: wRVUs as a Productivity Metric: How Employers Use RVUs

Beyond Medicare payment, wRVUs have become the dominant productivity benchmark in physician employment contracts. Hospitals, health systems, and large group practices routinely compensate employed physicians based on wRVU production — a physician who generates more wRVUs earns a higher base or bonus. This adoption of the Medicare payment unit as an internal incentive metric has propagated the procedural bias of the RBRVS system into the employment structures of academic medical centers, community hospitals, and private practices across the country.

The wRVU-based compensation model was widely adopted because it seemed to solve the problem of measuring physician productivity in a consistent, specialty-comparable way. A wRVU is a wRVU whether earned by a cardiologist, a hospitalist, or a family physician. However, using wRVUs as the compensation metric imports all the valuation biases of the RBRVS directly into compensation design. A physician whose work consists of managing complex elderly patients with multiple chronic conditions — the kind of patient for whom cognitive coordination is the primary clinical need — will produce fewer wRVUs per hour than a physician who performs high-volume, lower-complexity procedures.

The shift toward value-based care is creating pressure on wRVU-based compensation models because many of the activities that generate value under population health contracts — care gap closure, panel management, preventive outreach, care coordination — do not correspond to any billable CPT code and generate no wRVUs. Forward-thinking health systems are beginning to supplement or replace wRVU compensation with models that include panel quality metrics, total cost of care performance, and population health outcomes. This transition, however, requires significant investment in data infrastructure and a willingness to bear transition risk.

The wRVU is now used in two ways: (1) as the unit for Medicare physician fee calculation, and (2) as the dominant internal productivity metric in physician employment contracts. Both uses carry the same procedural bias — and both will need to evolve as healthcare moves toward value-based payment.
The Conversion Factor Problem: Stagnant Pay in an Inflationary World

The conversion factor translates RVU relativities into actual dollar payments. Its trajectory over the past two decades has been a consistent source of concern for physician organizations. The conversion factor has not kept pace with the Medicare Economic Index (MEI) — CMS's own measure of the inflation in physician practice costs — for most of the post-2002 period. The result is that even as the nominal conversion factor has fluctuated, its real purchasing power has declined. Physicians who relied on Medicare payment for a substantial share of their revenue faced compounding economic pressure.

The CY 2025 conversion factor of $32.3465 represents a 2.83% decrease from the 2024 rate of $33.29. This reduction followed the expiration of a temporary 2.93% increase Congress enacted for 2024. Without periodic congressional action to boost the conversion factor above its statutory baseline, it will continue to decline as the budget-neutrality requirement and the absence of an inflation adjustment built into the fee schedule law compound over time.

This dynamic has important implications for the transition to value-based care. If FFS payment is declining in real terms but value-based payment models remain in development and carry financial risk, the intermediate period — when providers are partially in FFS and partially in value-based contracts — is economically dangerous for practices. CMS and Congress have repeatedly acknowledged this "valley of death" between FFS and value-based payment without fully resolving it. Physician organizations have argued that stabilizing the conversion factor is a precondition for the kind of patient investment in value-based infrastructure that the transition requires.

body.message: RVUs and CPT codes are related but distinct. A CPT code identifies what service was rendered; an RVU is the assigned value of that service. The same CPT code can have different payment amounts in different payers' fee schedules — commercial insurers negotiate their own conversion factors and may apply different relative values. Medicare's RBRVS is the anchor, but it is not the only fee schedule in use.
body.title: Important Distinction

children.text: Choosing Who Will Manage Billions in Public Care

When a state decides to run its Medicaid program through managed care, it must choose which private organizations will receive billions of dollars to care for its most vulnerable residents. This choice is made through a procurement — a formal, competitive process built around a Request for Proposals (RFP). The stakes could hardly be higher: a single state’s Medicaid managed care contracts can be worth tens of billions of dollars over their life and determine the care of millions of people. Getting the procurement right is one of the most consequential things a state Medicaid agency does.

The procurement is also where the abstract requirements of the federal framework become concrete commitments. The RFP translates Part 438’s rules and the state’s own priorities into specific demands that bidding plans must meet, and the evaluation determines which plans best satisfy them. Increasingly, procurement is also how states drive innovation — using the competition to push plans toward value-based payment, health equity, and better member experience. The RFP is not just a purchasing document; it is a policy instrument.

This lesson walks through how the process works, from RFP development to contract award, and confronts a reality that has come to dominate Medicaid procurement in recent years: the explosion of bid protests and litigation that can delay or undo even a carefully run selection.

Key Concept: States select Medicaid MCOs through a competitive procurement built around a Request for Proposals (RFP). Plans submit bids that are scored against predetermined criteria; the highest-scoring bidders are awarded contracts, subject to negotiation, readiness review, and an increasingly common gauntlet of protests.

children.text: The Procurement Process, Step by Step

A Medicaid managed care procurement follows a structured sequence. It begins with the state developing the RFP, which includes a scope of work or model contract specifying what plans must do, and a set of predetermined questions and criteria. The state publicly advertises the procurement and accepts bids. It then evaluates the proposals — typically using a formal scoring system — announces its intent to award contracts to the winning bidders, negotiates final contracts, conducts "readiness reviews" to verify the new plans can actually operate, and finally implements. The whole process typically takes 18 to 24 months.

A key structural choice is how many plans to admit. Some states use an "any willing and qualified bidder" approach, contracting with every plan that meets the requirements. But most states limit the number of MCOs through a competitive procurement, awarding contracts only to the highest-scoring bidders. Limiting the field gives the state more leverage and concentrates enrollment (helping plans achieve scale), but it also raises the stakes of each award — and the incentive for losing bidders to challenge it.

body.title: The MCO Procurement Sequence

children.text: The readiness review deserves emphasis. Winning a contract on paper is not the same as being able to deliver care on day one. Before implementation, the state verifies that each selected plan has an adequate provider network, functioning claims systems, member services, and the operational infrastructure to serve enrollees. A plan that cannot pass readiness review can delay an entire program’s launch, which is why the period between award and go-live is intensely operational.
How Bids Are Scored

The heart of the procurement is the evaluation, and most Medicaid agencies use formal scoring rubrics to ensure a fair and standardized process. The state typically releases the scoring rubric along with the RFP, so bidders know in advance how their answers will be judged. Each question carries a point value, and evaluators rate responses against a defined scale. In Hawaii’s 2021 procurement, for example, answers were rated on a zero-to-five scale — zero being "Very Poor" and five "Excellent" — with each RFP question worth a set number of points.

What states ask for in those questions has been evolving. States are increasingly asking bidders to demonstrate actual results rather than make promises — to respond to case scenarios showing how the plan would handle needs unique to the Medicaid population, and to provide evidence of past performance. A rubric can be deliberately designed to reward innovation, steering the competition toward the state’s policy goals. This is how a procurement becomes a policy lever: by attaching points to value-based payment commitments, health-equity strategies, or member-experience improvements, the state pulls the whole market in that direction.

The discipline of releasing a clear rubric in advance serves a second purpose beyond fairness: defensibility. As the next section shows, procurements are now routinely challenged, and a transparent, well-documented scoring process is a state’s best protection against having its award overturned. States are responding by strengthening evaluation frameworks, clarifying scoring criteria, and emphasizing transparency precisely so their decisions can withstand scrutiny.
The Protest Problem

In recent years, bid protests and litigation have become a structural feature of Medicaid procurement rather than an occasional exception. Because a single award can be worth billions and losing bidders may be shut out of a state’s market for years, the incentive to challenge an unfavorable decision is enormous. Protests are now an increasingly anticipated component of competitive procurements, frequently delaying implementation by six months or more — and sometimes far longer.

The 2024–2025 period offered vivid examples across the country. In Florida, a losing bidder sued to block new contracts while protests continued. In Rhode Island, bidders protested a roughly $15 billion award — pointing out, among other things, that the review team was composed entirely of agency employees in violation of state procurement rules — prompting the state to reevaluate proposals, cancel the solicitation, extend incumbent contracts, and prepare a revised RFP. In Texas, the STAR and CHIP procurement was tied up in litigation for nearly two years, with courts pausing the process over deficiencies in the state’s evaluation methodology, including the premature disclosure of competitors’ proposals to one bidder. In Georgia, incumbent protests pushed an anticipated July 2025 go-live to late 2026 or early 2027.

body.message: While some protests are simply losing bidders fighting to stay in the market, others expose legitimate procedural gaps — flawed scoring, insufficient documentation, conflicts of interest, or unclear criteria. Either way, the delay is real: members keep their current plans, new innovations wait, and the state’s timeline can slip by months or years.
body.title: Protests Expose Real Flaws — and Cause Real Delays

children.text: Why Procurement Defensibility Now Drives the Process

The rise of protests has fundamentally changed how states approach procurement. Escalating protest activity and judicial scrutiny have raised the bar for procurement defensibility — meaning a state must be able to prove, in detail, that its process was fair, well-documented, free of conflicts, and faithful to its own published rules. This has slowed procurements down, but the slowdown does not mean states are abandoning managed care. It reflects a recalibration toward more durable, defensible procurement structures built to withstand litigation, policy volatility, and operational complexity.

body.analogy: A Medicaid procurement is like a high-stakes talent competition where the prize is a multibillion-dollar contract. The judges must publish their scorecard in advance, score every contestant the same way, document their reasoning, and avoid any appearance of favoritism — because every losing contestant has a lawyer ready to challenge the result. A sloppy or biased judging process doesn’t just produce a bad winner; it can get the whole competition thrown out and restarted, leaving everyone in limbo for a year.
body.concept: Why procurement fairness and documentation matter

children.text: For the state, the practical lesson is that the quality of the process matters as much as the quality of the choice. A perfectly reasonable selection can be undone by a flawed procedure — an evaluator with an undisclosed conflict, a scoring inconsistency, a leaked document. The defensibility imperative pushes states toward independent evaluators, meticulous documentation, clear criteria, and transparency, all of which also tend to produce better, fairer selections. Good process and good outcomes increasingly go together.

This lesson connects directly to what follows. The RFP and resulting contract are where the state codifies everything it will require of its plans — the network adequacy standards, quality requirements, and reporting obligations covered in the next lesson; the capitation rates and MLR rules covered in the rate-setting module; and the value-based purchasing goals covered later. The procurement is the moment the state exercises its leverage, because once the contract is signed, the state must work within its terms. Choosing the right plans through a defensible process is the foundation on which all subsequent oversight rests.

points: States select Medicaid MCOs through a competitive procurement built around a Request for Proposals (RFP) that translates federal rules and state priorities into specific, scored requirements.

The process follows a sequence — RFP development, advertising and bid receipt, scored evaluation, intent to award, contract negotiation, readiness review, and implementation — typically lasting 18 to 24 months.

Most states limit the number of MCOs by awarding contracts only to the highest-scoring bidders (rather than accepting any willing qualified bidder), which raises the leverage and the stakes of each award.
Readiness review verifies that a selected plan can actually operate — adequate network, claims systems, member services — before go-live, and a plan that fails it can delay an entire program launch.

Bids are scored with formal rubrics released alongside the RFP (e.g., Hawaii’s 0–5 scale), and states increasingly require evidence of results and case-scenario responses, using point allocations to reward innovation and steer the market.

Bid protests and litigation have become a structural feature of procurement, frequently delaying implementation by six months or more, with 2024–2025 examples in Florida, Rhode Island, Texas, and Georgia.

Protests can expose real procedural flaws — biased or all-internal review teams, flawed scoring, leaked competitor proposals, conflicts of interest — and can force reevaluation, cancellation, or multi-year delays.

Escalating scrutiny has made procurement defensibility paramount, pushing states toward independent evaluators, meticulous documentation, clear criteria, and transparency — which also produce fairer, better selections.

children.text: A Genuine Dilemma, Not a Settled Answer

Earlier in this course, risk adjustment appeared as a technical fix: to compare hospitals fairly on outcomes, you statistically adjust for how sick their patients were, so a hospital treating sicker people is not unfairly penalized. That logic is sound for clinical risk. But when the "risk" in question is a social factor — poverty, housing instability, race — risk adjustment becomes one of the most contested questions in all of quality measurement.

The dilemma is real and unresolved: should quality measures be adjusted for the social risk of a provider's patients? Reasonable experts come down on opposite sides, and the answer has large consequences for which hospitals get penalized and whether disparities are revealed or concealed. This lesson lays out both sides honestly rather than pretending there is a clean answer.

The stakes are concrete. Get it wrong one way and you unfairly punish safety-net hospitals for serving disadvantaged patients. Get it wrong the other way and you statistically erase the very disparities the last lesson worked to reveal.

Adjusting quality measures for social risk factors (like poverty) is genuinely contested: it can make provider comparisons fairer, but it can also mask real disparities in the quality of care those patients receive.
The Case For Social Risk Adjustment

The argument for adjustment starts with fairness to providers. A patient's outcome — say, whether they are readmitted within 30 days — depends heavily on factors outside the hospital's control: whether they can afford medications, have stable housing, can get to follow-up appointments, or have social support at home.

A safety-net hospital serving many low-income patients will tend to have worse raw outcomes than a hospital serving an affluent population, even if its actual care is just as good or better. Without social risk adjustment, that hospital looks worse and gets penalized — which can drain resources from exactly the institutions caring for the most vulnerable, worsening inequity.

There is real evidence for this. In the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), social risk adjustment via "peer grouping" — comparing hospitals to others with similar shares of disadvantaged patients — substantially changed performance assessments and reduced penalties among safety-net hospitals. Proponents argue this makes comparisons more equitable and protects the providers the system most needs.

body.content:
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program adopted "peer grouping" as its approach to social risk: hospitals are compared to others serving a similar proportion of dual-eligible (low-income) patients, rather than to all hospitals.
Systematic review evidence shows this narrowed the penalty gap between hospitals serving more versus fewer socially disadvantaged patients — concrete proof that social risk adjustment materially shifts who gets penalized.
body.title: Peer Grouping in the HRRP

children.text: The Case Against: Masking Disparities

The opposing argument is just as serious. If you adjust a quality measure for social risk, you are effectively building lower expectations for disadvantaged patients into the math. You are telling the measure: "do not count it against this hospital that its poor patients did worse." But what if the poor patients did worse partly because the hospital actually delivered them worse care?

In that case, social risk adjustment masks a real disparity. It statistically absorbs the gap between what advantaged and disadvantaged patients received and makes it disappear from the score — the exact opposite of the stratification work in the previous lesson, which aimed to expose that gap. Critics warn this can entrench a two-tier system by making unequal care invisible and unaccountable.

This concern carries real institutional weight. A 2020 report to Congress from HHS's Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE) recommended against using social risk adjustment for performance measures that reflect a provider's quality of care — precisely because doing so could obscure quality differences that ought to be surfaced and fixed.

body.title: The Social Risk Adjustment Debate

children.text: A Way Through: Separate the Purposes

The most influential resolution recognizes that the answer depends on what the measure is for. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) recommended using two different approaches depending on purpose: keep public-reporting measures unadjusted for socioeconomic factors so disparities stay visible, but use peer comparison for financial penalties so hospitals are judged against similar institutions.

This split is elegant. For transparency and accountability — telling the public and the hospital itself where the gaps are — you do NOT adjust, so the disparity shows. For deciding penalties — where unfairly punishing safety-net hospitals does real harm — you compare like with like via peer grouping. The same data serves equity in both directions, depending on the use.

A complementary move, central to the previous lesson, is to favor stratification over adjustment for understanding disparities. Stratifying reveals the gap by group; adjusting hides it inside one number. Many equity experts therefore argue: stratify to see and target disparities, and reserve risk adjustment (especially social risk) for fair payment comparisons — not for the measures meant to expose inequity.

body.title: Matching the Method to the Purpose

children.text: The Deeper Question: Adjusting for Race

The thorniest version of this debate is whether to use race itself in risk adjustment or clinical algorithms. Historically, many clinical algorithms embedded race as a variable, and a major reform movement has worked to remove race where it functioned as a crude, biologically unjustified proxy that worsened disparities.

Yet even here the picture is not simple. Some researchers note that the data quality of key predictors can differ by race group — for example, family history may be less reliably documented for Black patients — and argue that in narrow, carefully justified cases, accounting for race can actually improve predictive fairness rather than harm it. The lesson is not "race adjustment is always wrong" but that every use must be scrutinized for whether it corrects a data problem or encodes a biased assumption.

The throughline of this lesson is intellectual honesty. Risk adjustment is a powerful, necessary tool, and also a potential instrument for hiding inequity. The mature stance is to ask, every time: what is being adjusted for, why, for what purpose, and does this adjustment reveal injustice or conceal it? Anyone working in quality measurement must be able to hold that tension rather than reach for a slogan.

body.message: Deciding what to risk-adjust for is a value judgment, not just a statistical choice. The same adjustment can promote fairness (judging hospitals on what they control) or mask injustice (erasing a real quality gap). Always ask what is being adjusted, why, and for what purpose.
body.title: Adjustment Is Never Neutral

points: Risk adjustment is sound for clinical risk, but adjusting quality measures for social risk factors (poverty, housing, race) is genuinely contested.
The case for adjustment: outcomes depend on factors outside a provider's control, and without adjustment, safety-net hospitals are unfairly penalized — draining resources from the vulnerable.
In the HRRP, social risk adjustment via peer grouping reduced penalties for safety-net hospitals, showing it materially changes who is penalized.
The case against: adjusting for social risk can mask real disparities in quality of care, building lower expectations for disadvantaged patients into the measure.
A 2020 ASPE report to Congress recommended against social risk adjustment for measures that reflect a provider's quality of care.
MedPAC's resolution separates purposes: leave public-reporting measures unadjusted so disparities stay visible, but use peer comparison for financial penalties.

Many experts favor stratification (to reveal disparities) over adjustment (which hides them), and insist every adjustment — especially for race — be scrutinized for whether it reveals or conceals injustice.

result.title: The Problem with Risk Adjustment and Health Equity

children.text: What Is Risk Adjustment and Why Does It Exist?

When Medicare pays a private health plan to cover a beneficiary, it faces a fundamental problem: sicker patients cost more. Without correction, plans would compete by cherry-picking healthy enrollees — a practice called "favorable selection" — leaving the sickest patients with fewer options and worse care. Risk adjustment is the statistical mechanism that corrects this distortion by modifying per-member payments to reflect the expected health costs of each enrollee.

The core logic is straightforward. A Medicare Advantage plan enrolling a 70-year-old with diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease should receive substantially more per month than a plan enrolling a healthy 65-year-old. Without that adjustment, the plan covering the sicker patient would face a financial loss — creating pressure to cut services, narrow networks, or exit the market. Risk adjustment removes that incentive by making the financial playing field level regardless of who enrolls.

CMS has used risk adjustment in Medicare Advantage since 2004. The model inputs demographic characteristics (age, sex, Medicaid dual-eligibility status, disability status) and diagnosed health conditions into a predictive formula. The output is a risk score — a number expressing how expensive a patient is expected to be relative to the average Medicare beneficiary, who has a risk score of 1.0. A score of 1.4 means the plan receives 40 percent more per month than average; a score of 0.7 means 30 percent less.

Risk adjustment transforms capitated payments from flat per-member amounts into condition-adjusted amounts, ensuring that plans covering sicker populations are adequately compensated and have no financial motive to avoid high-need patients.

children.text: How Hierarchical Condition Categories Work

The CMS-HCC (Hierarchical Condition Category) model is the actuarial engine behind Medicare Advantage risk adjustment. It assigns ICD-10 diagnosis codes to condition categories that have been grouped by clinical and cost similarity. Each category carries an additive risk score coefficient — a number calibrated from fee-for-service Medicare claims data showing how much that condition, on average, raises expected annual costs above baseline.

The word "hierarchical" reflects an important design choice: when multiple conditions in the same disease family are present, only the most severe applies. A patient diagnosed with both "Type 2 diabetes without complications" and "Type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease" counts only in the more severe CKD category, not in both. This prevents double-counting within a clinical hierarchy while still allowing additive scoring across unrelated disease categories. A patient with diabetes, heart failure, and cancer would receive coefficients for all three separate disease groups.

Demographic factors are also built into the model. Age and sex interact with conditions — the same diabetes diagnosis carries different coefficients for a 68-year-old versus a 78-year-old, reflecting different baseline risk levels. Dual-eligibility status (being enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid) and disability status add further adjustments, because low-income and disabled beneficiaries tend to have higher healthcare utilization even controlling for diagnosed conditions.
