children.text: Model V28: The 2024 Overhaul

CMS substantially revised the HCC model beginning in 2024 with the introduction of Version 28 (V28), which replaced the longstanding Version 24 (V24). The transition was phased over three years: V28 applied to 33 percent of payment in 2024, 67 percent in 2025, and 100 percent beginning January 1, 2026. V28 expanded the number of condition categories from 86 to 115, reflecting advances in clinical knowledge and updated cost data from more recent Medicare claims.

One major change was the removal of several diagnosis codes that had been subject to widespread manipulation. V28 reduced the number of valid ICD-10 codes that map to HCCs from 9,797 under V24 to 7,770 under V28 — a reduction of over 2,000 mappable codes. CMS determined that many of these removed codes lacked strong predictive power for future costs or were being entered on risk-adjustment-specific encounters rather than as genuine clinical findings. The net effect of V28 is projected to reduce average Medicare Advantage risk scores by approximately 3.12 percent.

The model recalibration matters enormously for plan finances. A 3 percent reduction in average risk scores across the entire Medicare Advantage program — which covers over 33 million beneficiaries — translates to billions of dollars in reduced annual payments. Plans with the highest concentrations of previously-manipulated diagnoses face the steepest payment reductions, creating strong financial pressure to improve the integrity of their coding practices.

body.content:
Under the old V24 model, certain conditions like "vascular claudication" and "morbid obesity due to excess calories" mapped to HCCs that contributed meaningfully to risk scores. Under V28, these and hundreds of similar codes were removed or recategorized because they showed weak predictive validity in claims data analysis.
Plans that had been aggressively coding these conditions through in-home health risk assessments saw the largest payment reductions. CMS structured the 3-year phase-in specifically to allow time for plans to adjust their clinical documentation workflows rather than face an immediate financial cliff.

body.message: Under the risk adjustment rules, diagnoses must come from a physician, nonphysician practitioner, or facility encounter — and must be documented in the medical record. Diagnoses captured only on health risk assessments without supporting clinical documentation do not qualify under RADV audit standards, even if they were accepted for payment.

children.text: The Upcoding Problem and Federal Oversight

Risk adjustment creates a perverse financial incentive: the more diagnoses a plan documents, the more money it receives. Plans discovered that aggressive diagnosis capture — particularly through in-home health risk assessments (HRAs) conducted by plan-employed vendors — could substantially boost risk scores without corresponding increases in actual care delivered. The OIG and MedPAC have documented this "coding intensity" problem for over a decade.

In October 2024, HHS OIG published a report estimating that diagnoses reported only on HRAs and HRA-linked chart reviews — and not on any other service records — resulted in approximately $7.5 billion in risk-adjusted payments for 2023 that lacked adequate clinical documentation support. The top 13 health conditions accounted for $5.6 billion of that total, with nearly half ($2.7 billion) generated from in-home HRAs. OIG recommended CMS exclude HRA-only diagnoses from risk adjustment calculations.

CMS conducts Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV) audits to verify that submitted diagnoses are supported by medical record documentation. In 2023, CMS finalized updated RADV audit methodology that significantly strengthened the extrapolation approach — meaning that if an audit finds a certain percentage of diagnoses are unsupported, CMS can recover overpayments estimated across the plan's entire enrolled population, not just the audited sample. The industry challenged the rule in court, but CMS has proceeded with enforcement.

children.text: Risk Adjustment in Other Value-Based Programs

HCC-based risk adjustment is not limited to capitated Medicare Advantage payments. Risk scores are used across a wide range of value-based programs to ensure that providers caring for sicker patient panels are not unfairly penalized in quality and cost comparisons. In the Medicare Shared Savings Program, ACO benchmark calculations are risk-adjusted to reflect the clinical complexity of assigned beneficiaries. Without this adjustment, ACOs serving rural or low-income populations with higher burdens of chronic disease would systematically appear to perform worse than those serving healthy suburban populations.

The ACA's individual market also uses a separate risk adjustment program (not HCC-based) administered by CMS to redistribute funds among insurers on the exchanges, compensating plans that enroll sicker populations at the expense of those that enroll healthier ones. This prevents the "death spiral" dynamic in which sick individuals cluster in high-premium plans while healthy individuals opt out, destabilizing the market.

Despite these protections, risk adjustment remains an imperfect science. The model predicts expected costs from prior-year diagnoses, but health status can change rapidly. Newly diagnosed conditions mid-year are not captured until the next payment cycle. The model also underpredicts costs for some high-cost outlier patients and overpredicts for others. These limitations mean that even a well-designed risk adjustment system will produce some payment inaccuracies — the goal is minimizing systematic bias, not achieving perfection.

result.title: Risk Adjustment & HCC Scores: Leveling the Playing Field

children.text: The Problem That Risk Adjustment Solves

The previous lesson showed how states set capitation rates and organize them into rate cells by age, gender, eligibility, and region. But those broad cells leave a dangerous gap. Within the same cell — say, adult expansion enrollees in one region — one plan might enroll relatively healthy members while another enrolls people with diabetes, serious mental illness, and disabilities. If both plans receive the same capitation, the plan with sicker members is badly underpaid and the plan with healthier members is overpaid. Worse, every plan now has a powerful incentive to attract the healthy and avoid the sick. This is the cherry-picking problem, and risk adjustment is the tool built to solve it.

Risk adjustment modifies the capitation payment to each plan based on the measured health status of the members it actually enrolls. A plan that enrolls sicker, more expensive members receives more; a plan that enrolls healthier, cheaper members receives less. The goal, in the words of the field, is to align expected revenues with expected costs so that both high- and low-cost enrollees are attractive to plans. When risk adjustment works, a plan no longer profits by avoiding sick people — it is paid fairly to care for them.

This makes risk adjustment one of the most important safeguards in all of Medicaid managed care. It directly attacks the central risk of capitation — that plans will select healthy members and shun expensive ones — by changing the economics so that caring for the sick is financially viable. Understanding how it works is essential to understanding how managed care can serve vulnerable, high-need populations at all.

Key Concept: Risk adjustment modifies capitation payments based on the measured health status of each plan’s enrolled members — paying more for sicker members and less for healthier ones — to align expected revenue with expected cost and remove the incentive to cherry-pick healthy enrollees.

children.text: How Risk Adjustment Works

At its core, risk adjustment assigns each member a risk score reflecting their predicted health care costs relative to the average. A member with no significant conditions might have a risk score near 1.0 (average); a member with multiple chronic illnesses might score 3.0 or higher, signaling expected costs three times the average. The plan’s overall risk score is the average across its members, and its capitation is adjusted up or down accordingly. A plan with a population risk score of 1.2 enrolls members who are 20% costlier than average and is paid more to reflect that.

These risk scores are built from data the program already collects. Risk-adjustment models typically use diagnosis or pharmaceutical codes from claims or encounter data to measure illness burden among enrolled members. This is another reason the encounter data emphasized in the contract and oversight lessons matters so much: it is the raw material from which risk scores — and therefore payments — are calculated. Inaccurate or incomplete encounter data produces inaccurate risk scores and unfair payments.

Risk adjustment can be applied prospectively (using a member’s diagnoses from a prior period to set payment for the coming period) or concurrently/retrospectively (adjusting for conditions in the same period being paid). Prospective adjustment is more common and predictable, but retrospective adjustment can better reduce a plan’s worry about unexpectedly sick enrollees. Either way, the model translates clinical reality into a payment signal that follows the patient to whichever plan enrolls them.
CDPS: The Workhorse Model

The dominant risk-adjustment model in Medicaid is the Chronic Illness and Disability Payment System (CDPS), developed at the University of California, San Diego. CDPS is a diagnosis-based model: it uses ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes, grouped into categories for different diseases and conditions (such as psychiatric or cancer categories), to measure each member’s illness burden. Its adoption is striking — of the 38 Medicaid programs that risk-adjust MCO payments, 33 use CDPS or a related model, making it the de facto standard for Medicaid.

CDPS was designed specifically for the Medicaid population, which is exactly why it dominates. Unlike models built for commercial or Medicare populations, CDPS accounts for the chronic illnesses, disabilities, and complex conditions disproportionately present among Medicaid enrollees, helping ensure more accurate funding for complex care needs. This Medicaid-specific calibration matters: a risk model that underweighted the conditions common in Medicaid would systematically underpay the plans serving the neediest members.

The model has enhanced variants that add pharmacy data. Medicaid Rx (MRx) is a pharmacy-based system that uses National Drug Code (NDC) data to infer conditions from the drugs a member takes, and CDPS+Rx combines diagnosis-based CDPS with pharmacy-based MRx for a fuller picture. Pharmacy data can capture conditions that diagnosis codes miss and can be timelier. The model is also periodically updated — the Institute for Medicaid Innovation partnered with UC San Diego to refresh the weights using national Medicaid managed care data, producing CDPS+Rx version 7 — so the payment signal stays calibrated to current clinical and cost patterns.

children.text: Reallocation, Budget Neutrality, and Limits

Risk adjustment is typically applied in a budget-neutral way: it does not change the total amount the state spends, but reallocates it among plans. The mechanism effectively shifts capitation payments away from plans with healthier-than-average members toward plans with sicker-than-average members, bringing each plan’s payment closer to the expected cost of the members it actually enrolls. The total pie stays the same; risk adjustment just slices it according to who is caring for whom. This is what makes it a fairness mechanism rather than a spending increase.

The better the model predicts cost, the better it works. The stronger a risk-adjustment tool’s predictive capacity, the less incentive plans have to cherry-pick healthy enrollees, because plans can trust that the system will adequately compensate them if they end up with relatively expensive members. A precise model makes sick members no less attractive than healthy ones, which is the entire point. A crude model leaves residual incentives to select, undermining the goal.

body.message: No risk model predicts cost perfectly. Research from Medicare Advantage shows that even after risk adjustment, plans can enroll members with high risk scores but lower-than-predicted actual costs — "overpriced" enrollees. Risk adjustment dramatically reduces the incentive to cherry-pick, but it does not eliminate selection entirely, which is why oversight of enrollment and quality remains necessary.
body.title: Risk Adjustment Is Powerful but Imperfect

children.text: Why Risk Adjustment Holds the System Together

Risk adjustment is the quiet linchpin that makes Medicaid managed care viable for vulnerable populations. Without it, the financial logic of capitation would steadily push plans to compete for the healthy and shun the sick, leaving the most expensive and most needy members — people with disabilities, serious mental illness, and complex chronic conditions — as financial liabilities no plan wants. Risk adjustment flips that logic: by paying more for sicker members, it makes those members financially viable to enroll and care for, which is a precondition for serving them at all.

body.analogy: Risk adjustment is like adjusting a potluck contribution by what each guest will actually eat. If everyone paid the same flat amount, hosts would compete to invite light eaters and shun anyone with a big appetite. Instead, the organizer estimates each guest’s appetite (risk score) and pays the host accordingly, so a host who welcomes the hungriest guests is funded to feed them — and no host has a reason to turn anyone away. The total budget is the same; it is just shared out to match who is actually being fed.
body.concept: How risk adjustment reallocates capitation

children.text: This lesson sits at the center of the rate-setting module for a reason. The previous lesson built the base capitation rate; this one refines it to match the actual health of enrolled members; and the next lesson, on medical loss ratios, ensures that whatever a plan is paid, enough of it goes to care. Together they form the financial spine of managed care: a sound rate, adjusted for risk, with a floor on how much must be spent on members. Risk adjustment is the part that makes the system fair across plans serving different populations.

For the student, the essential takeaway is that risk adjustment is what allows a capitated system to serve the sick. It is imperfect — no model captures cost perfectly, and residual selection incentives remain — but it transforms the economics enough that plans can compete on managing care well rather than on avoiding expensive people. When you see a Medicaid program risk-adjust its payments with CDPS, you are watching the mechanism that keeps the promise of managed care honest for the members who need care the most.

points: Risk adjustment modifies capitation payments based on the measured health status of each plan’s enrolled members — more for sicker members, less for healthier ones — to align expected revenue with expected cost.
Its central purpose is to remove the cherry-picking incentive: by paying fairly for sick members, it makes both high- and low-cost enrollees attractive to plans.

Each member gets a risk score relative to the average (1.0); a plan’s payment is adjusted by the average risk score of its members, calculated from diagnosis and pharmacy codes in claims/encounter data.

Risk adjustment can be prospective (prior-period diagnoses set future payment) or concurrent/retrospective; prospective is more common, while retrospective can better reduce plans’ fear of unexpectedly sick enrollees.

The dominant model is the diagnosis-based Chronic Illness and Disability Payment System (CDPS) from UC San Diego — used by 33 of the 38 Medicaid programs that risk-adjust — designed specifically for the Medicaid population’s chronic and disabling conditions.

Enhanced variants add pharmacy data: MRx uses NDC drug codes, and CDPS+Rx combines diagnosis- and pharmacy-based measurement; the model is periodically updated (e.g., CDPS+Rx version 7) to stay calibrated.
Risk adjustment is typically budget-neutral, reallocating the same total spending away from healthier plans toward sicker plans rather than increasing overall cost.

It is powerful but imperfect — even after risk adjustment, plans can enroll high-scoring but lower-cost "overpriced" members — so it greatly reduces but does not eliminate selection, and oversight remains necessary.

result.title: Risk Adjustment in Medicaid Managed Care

children.text: Not All Patients Need the Same Thing

A defined population is not uniform. A few members are gravely ill and need intensive, hands-on management; some are at rising risk and need a nudge before they get worse; most are relatively healthy and mainly need routine preventive care. Treating everyone the same wastes resources on the well and under-serves the sick. Risk stratification is the discipline of sorting a population by risk so that effort and resources go where they will do the most good.

This matters because population health resources — care managers, outreach, programs — are finite. You cannot intensively manage everyone. Risk stratification answers the essential operational question: of my whole panel, who needs what level of attention? It is the targeting engine of population health management.

The economic case is overwhelming, because healthcare spending is extraordinarily concentrated. Identifying and managing the small group driving most of the cost is where population health earns its return — and risk stratification is how you find them.

Risk stratification sorts a defined population into tiers of risk so finite resources (care managers, outreach, programs) target the patients who need them most. It is the targeting engine of population health management.
The Concentration of Cost

The single fact that justifies risk stratification is the staggering concentration of healthcare spending. In the United States, roughly 5 percent of the population accounts for nearly half of all health expenditures, and about 20 percent accounts for 80 percent of total spending. A tiny slice of patients drives an enormous share of cost.

The driver is chronic illness and complexity. Spending for people with five or more chronic conditions is roughly 17 times higher than for people with no chronic conditions. The sickest, most complex patients — those with multiple interacting conditions, often compounded by social needs — are both the highest-cost and the highest-need.

This concentration is good news for population health, because it means a focused effort can have outsized impact. You do not have to fix everyone's cost; if you can keep the highest-risk 5 percent healthier and out of the hospital, you move the majority of the spending. Risk stratification is what lets you find that 5 percent — and the "rising risk" patients who are about to join them.

children.text: The Risk Pyramid

Risk stratification is classically visualized as a pyramid (often associated with Kaiser Permanente). The population is divided into tiers, each needing a different intensity of intervention. Understanding the tiers is understanding the whole model.

At the broad base are low-risk patients — the majority, mostly healthy, who need wellness and primary prevention (screenings, vaccines, healthy-behavior support). In the middle is the "rising risk" tier: patients with emerging issues (early or single chronic conditions) who need secondary prevention to keep them from progressing. Near the top are high-risk patients with established chronic conditions requiring active disease management. At the small apex are the complex, highest-risk patients who need intensive, coordinated case management.

The "rising risk" tier deserves special attention because it is where population health can change the trajectory. High-risk patients are already expensive and partly locked in; low-risk patients are fine. But rising-risk patients are at the tipping point — a well-timed intervention can keep them from becoming high-risk, which is both clinically better and far cheaper. Smart programs invest heavily here, not just at the apex.

children.text: How Risk Is Actually Calculated

Sorting patients into the pyramid requires a method to score risk, and several established tools exist — most built on the data infrastructure from the previous lesson. The most prominent in U.S. value-based care is the Hierarchical Condition Categories (HCC) model, which calculates a Risk Adjustment Factor (RAF) score from a patient's documented diagnoses; a higher RAF means a more complex, higher-cost patient. HCC/RAF is central to Medicare Advantage and ACO payment.

Other validated tools include the Adjusted Clinical Groups (ACG) system (which often shows the strongest statistical performance for predicting utilization), the Charlson Comorbidity Index (a weighted count of conditions predicting mortality and future use), and condition-specific tools like the LACE score for post-discharge readmission risk (Length of stay, Acuity, Comorbidities, ED visits; a score of 10 or higher flags high readmission risk).

These data-driven models are powerful but imperfect, which is why most programs combine them with clinical judgment. An algorithm scores the whole panel quickly and consistently, but a primary care team often knows things the data misses — a patient's fragile housing, a recent loss, a worrying trajectory not yet in the codes. The best stratification blends algorithmic scoring with human knowledge of the patient.

body.title: Common Risk Stratification Tools

children.text: From Score to Action

A risk score is useless until it drives a different action. The entire point of stratification is to match intervention intensity to risk tier: low-risk patients get automated preventive reminders; rising-risk patients get targeted outreach and lighter-touch programs; high-risk patients get enrolled in disease management; the complex apex gets a dedicated care manager and intensive coordination.

This tiering is what makes finite resources go far. A care-management team that tried to call every patient would accomplish little; the same team focused on the stratified high-risk and rising-risk tiers can meaningfully change outcomes and cost. Stratification turns "manage the population" from an impossible slogan into a concrete, prioritized worklist.

Stratification is also not a one-time exercise. Patients move between tiers as their health changes, so risk scores must be refreshed regularly and the worklists updated. A patient who was low-risk last year may be rising-risk now; catching that movement early is exactly the proactive, whole-population behavior that defines population health. The next lessons build directly on this: predictive analytics sharpens who is rising, and care-gap analysis turns the tiers into specific to-dos.

body.message: Stratification only creates value when each tier triggers a different intensity of intervention. Computing risk scores but treating everyone the same defeats the purpose. And because patients move between tiers over time, scores must be refreshed regularly and worklists updated — stratification is continuous, not one-time.
body.title: A Risk Score That Doesn't Change the Action Is Wasted

points: Risk stratification sorts a defined population into risk tiers so finite resources target the patients who need them most — the targeting engine of population health.
Healthcare spending is extremely concentrated: ~5% of people drive nearly half of spending, ~20% drive 80%, and those with 5+ chronic conditions cost ~17x those with none.
The risk pyramid has tiers: low risk (prevention), rising risk (the tipping point for secondary prevention), high risk (disease management), and complex/highest risk (intensive case management).
The "rising risk" tier offers the biggest opportunity to change trajectory and avoid costly progression, so smart programs invest there, not only at the apex.
Risk is scored with tools like HCC/RAF (diagnosis-based, central to MA/ACO payment), ACG, the Charlson Comorbidity Index, and LACE (readmission risk).
Data-driven models should be combined with clinical judgment, which captures factors (social, recent events) the codes miss.
A risk score must drive a different action per tier, and because patients move between tiers, stratification must be refreshed continuously.

body.explanation: High-risk patients are already expensive and partly locked in; low-risk patients are fine. Rising-risk patients are at the tipping point, where a well-timed intervention (secondary prevention) can keep them from progressing into the high-risk, high-cost tier. Catching and acting on this group early is where population health most changes both outcomes and cost trajectory.

options.text: Because rising-risk patients are the cheapest to ignore
Because they are at a tipping point — a timely intervention can prevent them from becoming high-risk, which is both clinically better and far cheaper than managing them once they deteriorate
Because they account for nearly all healthcare spending already
Because they require no intervention at all

children.text: In 2024, the CMS Hospital Price Transparency rule transitioned from a bureaucratic suggestion to an operational mandate. With maximum penalties rising to over
$2 million per year
for large health systems, CFOs are recalculating the cost of non-compliance. However, the decision is rarely about the fine; it is about the strategic risk of data exposure.
1. The 2024 Enforcement Shift

The initial rollout saw fewer than 20% of hospitals fully compliant. CMS responded by standardizing machine-readable file (MRF) formats and automating audits. The 'Good Faith' defense is no longer viable. Systems must now weigh the certainty of the penalty against the uncertainty of market reaction.
2. The Calculus: Penalties vs. Rate Leakage
For a $2B revenue health system, a $2M fine is a rounding error (0.1% of revenue). The real threat is
Rate Leakage
. If payers see that a competitor negotiated a rate 15% lower for the same DRG, they will aggressively leverage that data in the next contract cycle to compress margins.
Actuarial Risk: While the penalty is capped at $2M, the downside risk of rate compression from exposed negotiated rates can exceed $15M annually for a mid-sized system.
3. The CDHP Opportunity
The defensive posture ignores the rise of
Consumer-Driven Health Plans (CDHPs)

. With 30% of commercial lives now in high-deductible plans, price has become a primary selection factor for elective procedures. Hospitals that obfuscate pricing are losing volume to ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) that present clear, bundled rates.
Strategic Verdict

Stop viewing transparency as a compliance check-box. Systems with competitive unit costs should weaponize transparency to capture CDHP market share, while high-cost systems must accelerate value-based contract adoption to hide unit-price variances.

children.text: Population health management—the discipline of identifying and proactively managing patients with chronic disease risk before they require acute care—has been practiced at urban academic medical centers and large integrated delivery networks for over a decade. Its penetration into rural health systems has been far slower, constrained by the same fragmented EHR infrastructure and limited care coordination staffing that limits every other quality initiative in rural settings.
The Registry Infrastructure: What You Actually Need

The foundational technology for population health management in rural settings does not require a population health platform costing $500,000. Eighty-three percent of the rural health systems with documented outcomes in the published evidence base are running their registries on their existing EHR’s built-in panel management or registry tools. The technology gap is almost never the binding constraint. The binding constraints are data completeness (SDOH data is rarely in the EHR) and care coordinator capacity.

body.title: Rural Chronic Disease Registry: Minimum Data Elements for Effective Risk Stratification

children.text: Risk Stratification Methodologies That Work in Rural Populations

Rural populations present risk stratification challenges that urban-calibrated models handle poorly. The most widely used commercial risk stratification algorithm—the Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) model—significantly underpredicts risk for rural populations because it underweights transportation barriers and SDOH factors that are highly predictive of rural acute care utilization. Rural systems that have achieved the best outcomes are using augmented HCC models that add SDOH scores and ED utilization history as independent predictors.

The specific SDOH factors with the highest predictive value for rural acute care utilization, based on a 2025 JAMA Internal Medicine analysis of 87,000 rural patients, are: (1) food insecurity (OR 2.8 for 30-day readmission), (2) transportation barrier (OR 2.4), and (3) lack of regular social contact (OR 1.9 for 90-day acute care utilization). These factors are not captured in the HCC model and must be added as data elements.

The HCC model sees a diabetic patient with an HbA1c of 9.2. The augmented rural model sees that same patient—plus the fact that she lives 34 miles from the nearest pharmacy, has no reliable transportation, and eats alone. Those three facts predict her next hospitalization better than the HbA1c.

DATA COLLECTION PRIORITY: Implement a standardized SDOH screening protocol (AHC HRSN screener or PRAPARE) at every primary care encounter. SDOH data is the highest-value addition to a rural risk stratification model and the most commonly missing element in rural EHR infrastructure.

children.text: Rural health’s investment narrative shifted fundamentally in 2024–2025. For most of the past decade, health technology venture capital treated rural markets as a distribution problem—a secondary consideration after urban market penetration. The combination of federal RHT program funding, AHEAD model financial incentives, and demonstrably large total addressable markets in rural chronic disease has inverted that assumption.
Where the $4.8 Billion Is Going

Rock Health’s Q4 2025 report identifies three categories absorbing the majority of rural-focused health tech investment: AI-enabled diagnostic tools for rural primary care (42% of deal flow by dollar volume), remote patient monitoring and chronic disease management platforms (31%), and rural telehealth specialty access networks (19%). The remaining 8% is distributed across pharmacy technology, workforce platforms, and behavioral health.

body.title: 2025 Rural Health Tech Venture Capital: Category Breakdown

children.text: The Three Categories With Highest Deployment Probability

Remote patient monitoring is the investment category most likely to reach meaningful rural deployment in the next 24 months. The evidence base is mature, reimbursement codes (CPT 99453–99458) are established, and the FDA clearance pathway for most RPM devices is well-understood. The primary deployment barrier—broadband access—is being addressed by parallel federal investment. Fifteen rural health systems in RHT program states have already piloted RPM programs with results showing 34% reduction in 30-day readmissions.

AI diagnostic tools present the highest long-term value but the most complex deployment path. Regulatory clearance timelines for FDA De Novo and 510(k) pathways average 18–28 months for AI/ML-based diagnostics. The rural systems best positioned to benefit are those that have already invested in EHR data quality—AI tools that require clean, structured data will fail in organizations with fragmented medical records.

The rural health investment wave will create winners and losers among health systems. The winners will be those that did the data hygiene work before the tools arrived. The losers will discover their data is not AI-ready at the worst possible time.

STRATEGIC OPPORTUNITY: RHT program states including Virginia (CareIQ initiative), South Carolina (Tech Catalyst Fund), and Nevada (Outcomes Accelerator) have dedicated capital and technical assistance specifically to connect rural health systems with vetted health tech companies. These programs offer a lower-risk pathway than direct venture partnership for health system leaders evaluating new technology.

children.text: The HHS Office for Civil Rights reported 168 ransomware attacks on U.S. hospitals in 2025, a record high and an 87% increase over 2024. Rural hospitals accounted for 61% of successful breaches despite representing only 31% of the total hospital count. The disparity reflects structural vulnerabilities—understaffed IT departments, legacy EHR systems with known unpatched vulnerabilities, and flat network architectures—that have made rural facilities the preferred target for ransomware threat actors.
Why Rural Hospitals Are the Preferred Target

Three factors make rural hospitals disproportionately attractive targets. First, limited IT staffing: the average rural hospital has 1.8 FTE IT staff for a facility that may have 200–400 network endpoints. Urban health systems average 1 IT FTE per 15–20 endpoints. Second, legacy infrastructure: 68% of rural hospitals are running at least one clinical system on an operating system that is out of mainstream support—typically Windows Server 2012 or earlier—creating known and widely exploited attack surfaces. Third, willingness to pay: rural hospitals have demonstrated higher ransom payment rates because they cannot sustain EHR downtime without patient safety consequences and often lack the data backup architecture to restore from backups.

Ransomware groups explicitly target rural hospitals because they know the facility will pay. The combination of critical systems, minimal IT staff, and limited backup capability creates a near-perfect coercion environment.

body.title: 2025 Rural Hospital Ransomware: Attack Vector and Impact Data

children.text: The Five Controls CMS Will Codify in 2026

Based on the HHS Healthcare Cybersecurity Performance Goals published in December 2024 and CMS rulemaking signals, five controls are widely expected to be codified as Conditions of Participation in a 2026 Interim Final Rule: (1) mandatory multi-factor authentication on all remote access systems, (2) network segmentation isolating clinical systems from administrative networks, (3) immutable offline backup tested quarterly, (4) annual mandatory cybersecurity training for all staff with access to clinical systems, and (5) a documented incident response plan with a defined RTO/RPO for EHR restoration.

HHS has paired the anticipated CoP requirements with a $50M rural cybersecurity grant program through HRSA, specifically designed to fund the infrastructure upgrades required for compliance. Grant applications are expected to open in Q2 2026 with priority scoring for CAHs and rural PPS hospitals with fewer than 100 beds.

FUNDING AVAILABLE: HRSA Rural Hospital Cybersecurity Grant Program (expected Q2 2026 opening): $50M available, priority scoring for CAHs and rural PPS <100 beds. Prepare pre-application materials now: current incident response plan, IT asset inventory, and backup architecture documentation.

children.text: The Kaufman Hall National Hospital Flash Report for January 2026 confirms what rural health system analysts have been tracking since mid-2024: the rural hospital financial crisis has entered a new, more acute phase. Forty-three percent of rural hospitals reported negative operating margins in FY 2025, the highest share since the measure was first tracked in 2012 and a 7-point deterioration from FY 2024’s already alarming 36%.
The Three Structural Drivers

The deterioration is driven by three converging pressures. First, labor cost inflation: median rural hospital RN hourly wage increased 18% between 2023 and 2025, while Medicaid rates in most states increased less than 4% over the same period. The gap between input cost inflation and reimbursement growth is the single largest contributor to negative margin expansion.

Second, payer mix erosion: rural counties have experienced disproportionate commercial insurance coverage loss as employers reduce benefit generosity. The share of rural hospital revenue from commercial payers—which subsidize Medicare and Medicaid shortfalls—fell from 31% in 2022 to 27% in 2025. For a $50M rural hospital, this shift represents approximately $2M in lost contribution margin.

Third, volume fragmentation: telehealth expansion and improved transportation have enabled some rural patients to self-select to urban specialty centers for procedures that previously generated revenue for local facilities. Rural hospitals are losing profitable procedural volumes while retaining unprofitable complex and behavioral health volumes.

body.title: Rural Hospital Financial Metrics: FY 2023 vs FY 2025

children.text: The Four Operating Models Generating Positive Margins

Despite the aggregate deterioration, 57% of rural hospitals maintained positive operating margins in FY 2025. Analysis of this cohort reveals four distinct operating models that are outperforming: (1) regional referral network anchors that have formalized upstream referral relationships with smaller CAHs; (2) vertically integrated primary care systems that capture both primary and specialist revenue within a single entity; (3) CAHs that have moved aggressively into swing-bed skilled nursing, generating a 3–8% margin premium; and (4) FQHC look-alike hybrids that blend grant revenue with Medicaid cost-based reimbursement.

The rural hospitals that will survive 2026 have already decided what business they are in. The ones that will not have been trying to be everything to everyone with a cost structure built for a different era.

STRATEGIC ALERT: Rural hospital boards should commission a full service-line contribution margin analysis before Q3 2026. Facilities carrying negative-margin service lines without a strategic rationale are consuming reserves that will be needed for AHEAD or RHT program co-investments.

children.text: The Rural Hospital Regulatory Relief Act of 2026 represents a structural inflection point for the 1,366 Critical Access Hospitals operating across 45 states. After years of incremental waivers and temporary pandemic-era flexibilities, Congress has codified three permanent regulatory changes that, in aggregate, CMS projects will return an estimated $2.1 billion annually to rural hospital operating budgets.
The Three Core Provisions

Provision One eliminates the 96-hour physician certification requirement for CAH inpatient admissions—a rule that has historically functioned as a de facto discharge mandate, forcing early patient transfers and undermining the case-mix complexity that sustains CAH revenue. The repeal takes effect January 1, 2027, giving facilities a 12-month runway to renegotiate payer contracts that depended on short-stay averages.

Provision Two expands the CAH swing-bed program to include observation status patients, closing a longstanding gap that excluded a growing share of rural admissions from swing-bed cost-based reimbursement. The American Hospital Association estimates this single change will add an average of $680,000 in annual revenue to eligible facilities.
Eliminating the 96-hour rule is not a minor administrative fix. It is the single most consequential reimbursement change for rural hospitals since the Balanced Budget Act of 1997.

children.text: The Compliance Window Executives Must Not Miss

Provision Three establishes a voluntary ‘Safe Harbor Compliance Pathway’ that allows CAHs to self-certify compliance with updated quality reporting requirements without undergoing a full CMS validation survey for three years. The window to enroll opens July 1, 2026, and closes December 31, 2026. Facilities that miss this window default to the standard survey cycle, which carries an average 14-month wait time.
Health system executives should prioritize three immediate actions:
(1) audit current payer contracts for 96-hour-linked length-of-stay incentives

children.text: HRSA’s January 2026 National Center for Health Workforce Analysis report projects that rural hospitals face a cumulative nursing shortage cost of $1.2 trillion between 2026 and 2035—a figure that aggregates vacancy-driven agency staffing premiums, turnover replacement costs, and lost revenue from service line contraction. For individual rural hospitals, this translates to an average annual workforce cost premium of $1.8M to $3.2M above their 2019 baseline.
Why Retention Economics Matter More Than Recruitment

The dominant rural workforce strategy has historically focused on recruitment: loan repayment, signing bonuses, and rural training pipelines. The emerging evidence, however, is that the economic return on retention investments is substantially higher. A 2025 Robert Wood Johnson Foundation study found that the average all-in cost of replacing a rural RN—including recruitment advertising, agency coverage, orientation, and productivity ramp-up—is $62,000 per departure. Against this figure, retention investments that reduce turnover by even 5 percentage points generate a 4:1 to 6:1 ROI.
Every rural RN who walks out the door costs $62,000 to replace. A $15,000 retention investment that prevents that departure has a 4:1 return. The math is not complicated. The execution is.

body.title: Rural RN Retention Interventions: Cost, Effect Size, and ROI Comparison

children.text: The Three Highest-ROI Strategies in Detail

Flexible self-scheduling generates the highest ROI of any single retention intervention. Research from the ANA and AONL consistently shows that schedule control is the top-ranked factor in rural RN job satisfaction surveys—outranking compensation in most age cohorts. The implementation cost is primarily administrative software ($15–25K annually for a 100-bed facility) and the management culture shift to trust-based scheduling.

Clinical ladder programs with tuition reimbursement address a specific retention vulnerability: the RN who leaves not because of dissatisfaction but because of perceived career ceiling. Rural hospitals that implemented ANCC Pathway to Excellence® programs saw 24–28% reductions in turnover in the first 36 months, with the highest retention effect among the 26–35 age cohort.

Housing subsidies are the retention intervention with the fastest-growing evidence base. Five RHT program states—Vermont, West Virginia, Kentucky, Montana, and New Mexico—have allocated RHT funds specifically for rural clinician housing, reflecting a recognition that the rural workforce crisis is, in part, a real estate crisis in communities where workforce housing has simply not been built.

BUDGET PLANNING: Rural hospital CFOs should model the break-even point between agency traveler reliance and a direct retention investment portfolio. At $62K average replacement cost, a single RN retention intervention that prevents 5 departures per year funds itself with $250K–$300K in savings against the typical $40–60K total investment.

children.text: The narrative of Vermont's healthcare crisis has long focused on funding models and reimbursement rates, but the underlying mathematical reality is far more brutal: we are running out of people. The state is currently caught in a 'Demographic Pincer' movement. On one side, the demand for high-acuity care is accelerating as the population over 65 is projected to exceed 30% of the total state census by 2040. On the other side, the labor pool capable of delivering that care is evaporating.

This is not merely a recruitment challenge; it is a labor solvency crisis. Data from the Vermont Legislative Research Service and recent workforce assessments indicate a structural deficit that cannot be filled by traditional educational pipelines alone. With a forecasted 13% decline in the working-age population between 2020 and 2030, the state faces a scenario where the ratio of caregivers to patients becomes mathematically unsustainable for rural critical access hospitals.
The Math of Attrition: 1,200 vs. 400

The disparity between supply and demand is stark. The 2024-2026 Vermont Nursing Needs Assessment revealed that the state requires approximately 1,200 new Registered Nurses (RNs) annually to maintain current service levels and replace retiring staff. However, Vermont's educational institutions currently graduate only about 400 RNs per year. This structural gap of 800 nurses annually creates a compounding deficit that disproportionately impacts rural facilities, which lack the brand equity and salary leverage of the UVM Health Network.

We are attempting to fill a leaking bucket with a thimble. When the local educational pipeline supplies only 33% of the necessary replacement rate, rural hospitals are forced to cannibalize each other's staff or turn to the predatory economics of contract labor.

The consequences of this deficit are visible in the operational contraction of rural healthcare. We are witnessing the slow-motion closure of service lines—birthing units, dialysis centers, and psychiatric beds—not because the physical infrastructure is lacking, but because the human infrastructure has eroded. The closure of these units forces patients to travel further for care, increasing the burden on the remaining centralized hubs and further straining their capacity.
The Travel Nurse Dependency Loop

To plug these gaps, Vermont hospitals have become addicted to travel nursing agencies, creating a destructive feedback loop. The economics of travel nursing are essentially a transfer of wealth from non-profit hospital operating margins to private staffing equity. While a staff RN in Vermont might earn an average of $41.38 per hour, travel nurses can command rates upwards of $102 per hour—often working alongside the very staff nurses they out-earn by a factor of 2.5.

body.title: The Cost of Dependency: Staff vs. Travel Labor (2024 Est.)

children.text: This wage disparity shatters morale and incentivizes local nurses to leave their permanent positions to become travelers themselves, further depleting the core staff. For rural hospitals already operating on razor-thin margins (with 9 out of 14 Vermont hospitals reporting operating losses in 2023), this premium labor cost is catastrophic. It accelerates the depletion of reserves and effectively subsidizes a transient workforce at the expense of long-term community resilience.
Housing as Health Policy

Even if recruitment efforts were perfectly funded, Vermont faces a physical barrier to entry: housing. The acute shortage of affordable housing in rural Vermont acts as a hard cap on workforce expansion. Hospital recruiters frequently report candidates accepting offers, only to withdraw them weeks later after failing to find a place to live within a reasonable commuting distance.

This intersection of housing and health policy is critical. Without a coordinated strategy to develop workforce housing specifically for healthcare professionals, salary incentives are rendered ineffective. The '13% workforce decline' is not just about age; it is about the inability of younger families to physically enter the Vermont economic ecosystem. Until housing is treated as a component of the healthcare infrastructure, the vacancy rates in rural nursing will remain stubbornly high.

children.text: The CDC’s December 2025 Rural-Urban Health Disparities Surveillance Report presents a picture that defies simple characterization. Aggregate rural-urban health outcome gaps—measured by age-adjusted mortality, preventable hospitalization rates, and chronic disease control—have improved modestly since 2020 in some categories and deteriorated sharply in others. Understanding the divergence is essential for allocating the limited clinical and financial resources available for rural health equity investment.
Where Gaps Are Narrowing

Cardiovascular disease mortality is the clearest positive trend. The rural-urban age-adjusted cardiovascular mortality gap has narrowed from 37% in 2019 to 28% in 2024, driven by three parallel forces: improved telehealth access for cardiac monitoring and medication management, the expansion of CAH cardiac rehabilitation programs supported by RHT infrastructure funding, and improved statin and antihypertensive medication adherence enabled by community pharmacy expansion in rural markets.

Cancer screening rates show improvement in colorectal and cervical cancer, with the rural-urban gap narrowing 8–12 percentage points since 2020. Mobile screening unit deployment—a strategy adopted by 14 state RHT programs—is the primary driver, with each additional mobile unit estimated to close approximately 3–4% of the rural-urban screening gap in its service area over 24 months.

body.title: Rural-Urban Health Outcome Gap Trends: 2019–2024

children.text: Where Gaps Are Widening: The Three Crisis Categories

Maternal mortality is the most alarming widening disparity. The rural maternal mortality rate reached 61% above the urban rate in 2024—up from 48% in 2019—driven by a combination of obstetric unit closures (86 rural hospitals lost their OB units between 2020 and 2024), worsening hemorrhage management capability at rural EDs receiving transferred patients, and deteriorating postpartum follow-up rates as rural primary care capacity has shrunk.

The rural mental health and suicide mortality gap has widened from 74% to 89% above urban rates over the same period, reflecting both the absolute shortage of rural mental health providers and the failure of telehealth expansion to fully compensate for the loss of community mental health center capacity in rural markets. Rural counties with no licensed mental health provider within 30 miles—now numbering 1,242—show the steepest deterioration.

The maternal mortality data is not a slow-moving trend we can plan around. A 61% rural premium means that a woman giving birth in rural Georgia faces dramatically higher mortality risk than her urban counterpart. This is a measurable, preventable, ongoing harm.

INVESTMENT PRIORITY: The evidence base is clear that the three widening disparity categories—maternal mortality, mental health, and SUD—require targeted direct investment, not general rural health system improvement. Programs that improve average rural health outcomes without specifically targeting these categories will not bend the mortality curve on the indicators that matter most.

body.caption: Multi-panel trend chart showing rural-urban health outcome gap trajectories from 2019–2024 for six health categories, with narrowing trends shown in green lines (cardiovascular, cancer screening) and widening trends shown in red lines (maternal mortality, suicide, opioid overdose), annotated with key policy interventions at their implementation dates.

children.text: Investment Priorities Based on the Evidence
Maternal mortality: fund obstetric emergency capability in EDs, not just new labor units—the emergency presentation gap is where deaths are occurring
Mental health: target the 1,242 counties with no licensed mental health provider within 30 miles for telepsychiatry partnership funding
SUD: expand MAT access points—the evidence for buprenorphine/naltrexone in rural settings is stronger than for any other SUD intervention
Cardiovascular: sustain cardiac rehabilitation and medication adherence programs—these are working and are at risk from telehealth reimbursement expiration

result.summary: The CDC’s 2025 Rural-Urban Health Disparities Surveillance Report reveals a bifurcated trend: cardiovascular disease mortality disparities are narrowing modestly, while maternal mortality, mental health, and substance use disorder outcome gaps are widening at an accelerating rate. This analysis disaggregates the drivers, identifies the intervention categories with demonstrated effectiveness, and maps the current policy landscape against the evidence base.
result.title: The Rural-Urban Health Outcome Gap in 2026: A Data-Driven Analysis of Where Disparities Are Widening, Where They Are Closing, and Why

children.text: The debate over full-practice authority (FPA) for nurse practitioners and, increasingly, physician assistants, has moved from professional turf to empirical policy evaluation. With 27 states and D.C. now granting NPs FPA, a decade of implementation evidence allows researchers to distinguish the conditions under which scope expansion actually closes access gaps from those in which it produces minimal change.
The Access Improvement Evidence Base

A 2025 Health Affairs meta-analysis of 14 studies across FPA and non-FPA states found a statistically significant but geographically concentrated access improvement: the average FPA state saw a 12% increase in NP-provided primary care visits in rural Health Professional Shortage Areas in the first three years post-enactment. However, two-thirds of that improvement was concentrated in states that paired FPA with Medicaid reimbursement parity—states that granted FPA without parity showed no statistically significant access change.
Full-practice authority without Medicaid reimbursement parity is a permission slip without a paycheck. The access gains only materialize when NPs can build financially viable independent practices.
Feasibility Conditions That Drive or Suppress Impact

body.title: FPA Impact Conditions: Factors That Amplify or Suppress Rural Access Gains

children.text: The Political Feasibility Landscape in 2026

Twelve states have active FPA legislation in the 2026 session, including three—Indiana, Kansas, and South Carolina—where rural hospital associations have formally endorsed the bills following years of opposition. The shift reflects the financial reality that physician recruitment in rural markets has become prohibitively expensive, with average rural primary care physician salary premiums now exceeding $85,000 above urban equivalents.

The remaining political opposition is concentrated in state medical associations and some specialty societies. The most effective legislative strategy observed in successful FPA states has been data-sharing agreements between NP associations and rural hospital coalitions that document specific unfilled positions that NP FPA would address—converting an abstract policy debate into a concrete vacancy count.

FEASIBILITY VERDICT: FPA legislation is a high-probability access intervention only when packaged with Medicaid reimbursement parity and NP-owned practice authorization. Standalone FPA without these co-conditions has insufficient evidence to justify the political capital required for passage.

body.caption: Heat map of the United States showing states with full-practice authority (dark blue), restricted practice (medium blue), and reduced practice (light blue) for nurse practitioners, overlaid with rural primary care HPSA designations in red.

children.text: Recommendations for State Health Policy Teams
Bundle FPA legislation with explicit Medicaid reimbursement parity provisions
Conduct rural vacancy audit before legislative introduction to build stakeholder coalition
Include hospital privileging reform in the legislative package to prevent post-FPA access suppression
Model 3-year access impact projections using Health Affairs FPA evidence base for fiscal notes

result.summary: Twenty-seven states now grant full independent practice authority to nurse practitioners, yet rural patient access improvements have been uneven. This feasibility study examines the fiscal, workforce, and political conditions under which scope-of-practice expansion produces measurable access gains in rural primary care deserts versus conditions where the policy produces minimal effect.

children.text: What "Social Determinants of Health" Means

Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age — and the wider forces and systems that shape those conditions. They include income, education, housing, neighborhood safety, access to nutritious food, transportation, social support, and exposure to discrimination. The World Health Organization and US health agencies use slightly different wording, but the core idea is identical: most of what determines health happens outside the clinic.

This is not a claim that medical care is unimportant. When you have a heart attack, an appendicitis, or a treatable cancer, clinical care is decisive. The point is about populations rather than individual emergencies: across a whole community, the distribution of who gets sick and who dies early is shaped far more by social and economic conditions than by the quality of the hospitals.

For health systems, this reframing has enormous practical consequences. A system that optimizes only clinical quality — better protocols, newer equipment, higher adherence to guidelines — while ignoring where its patients live, what they eat, and whether they can pay rent is improving a variable that explains a minority of outcomes. The SDOH evidence is the argument for looking upstream.

SDOH are the non-medical conditions that shape health — income, housing, education, food, neighborhood, social connection. Across populations, they explain far more of health outcomes than clinical care does.
The Evidence: How Much Does Clinical Care Actually Explain?

The most influential framework for quantifying this comes from the County Health Rankings & Roadmaps model, developed by the University of Wisconsin Population Health Institute with the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. It groups the modifiable determinants of health into four categories and assigns each a weight based on its contribution to health outcomes.

In that model, social and economic factors carry the largest weight at 40%, followed by health behaviors at 30%, clinical care at 20%, and the physical environment at 10%. In other words, clinical care — the entire apparatus of doctors, hospitals, medications, and procedures — accounts for roughly one-fifth of what drives health outcomes. The other 80% lies in behaviors and the social and physical conditions that heavily shape those behaviors.

These weights are estimates, not precise constants, and researchers debate them at the margins. But the central message is robust and repeatedly validated: empirical analyses of the model find social and economic factors are the strongest predictor of health outcomes, ahead of behaviors, clinical care, and physical environment. A health system serious about outcomes cannot treat the 80% as someone else's problem.

children.text: The Five Healthy People 2030 SDOH Domains

The US federal framework for organizing SDOH comes from Healthy People 2030, the decade-long set of national health objectives published by the Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion. Social determinants of health is one of its three overarching priority areas, alongside health equity and health literacy. Healthy People 2030 organizes SDOH into five domains, which have become the standard vocabulary for screening, measurement, and intervention.

The five domains are economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context. Each captures a cluster of conditions with strong, independent links to health — and each maps to specific, actionable interventions a health system or community organization can deploy.

Using a shared taxonomy matters more than it might seem. When a clinic, a payer, a community-based organization, and a public health department all describe social needs in the same five-domain language, they can screen consistently, share data, and coordinate referrals. The Healthy People 2030 framework is the connective tissue that lets those handoffs happen.

children.text: How Strong Are the Links? Two Well-Studied Examples

It is one thing to assert that social conditions matter; it is another to show the magnitude. Two of the most rigorously studied SDOH-to-health links — social connection and education — illustrate how large these effects are when measured carefully.

Social isolation is a striking case. A 2010 meta-analysis by Julianne Holt-Lunstad and colleagues benchmarked the mortality risk of weak social connection against established risk factors and found it comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day — a comparison the US Surgeon General later cited in a formal advisory on loneliness. A follow-up 2015 meta-analysis covering over 3 million participants found social isolation associated with a 29% increase in mortality risk and living alone with a 32% increase. (Researchers caution the cigarette analogy can oversimplify, but the underlying mortality signal is robust.)

Education shows a similarly powerful gradient. People with more education live longer and healthier lives, and the relationship is graded — each additional level of attainment is associated with better outcomes. Education works through multiple channels: higher income, safer jobs, greater health literacy, and more control over one's circumstances, echoing the social-gradient findings of the Whitehall studies.

body.content:
Brigham Young University researcher Julianne Holt-Lunstad led meta-analyses establishing social connection as a major determinant of survival. The 2010 analysis benchmarked weak social ties against smoking, obesity, and physical inactivity, finding the mortality effect of social isolation comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes per day.
The 2015 follow-up, pooling over 3 million participants, found social isolation raised mortality risk by 29% and living alone by 32%. The work directly informed the 2023 US Surgeon General's Advisory on the epidemic of loneliness and isolation — moving social connection from a soft concern to a measured public health priority.
body.title: Social Connection as a Mortality Risk Factor (Holt-Lunstad)

children.text: Why This Reframes the Health System's Job

If 80% of health outcomes are driven by factors outside clinical care, then a health system that wants to improve outcomes — especially under value-based contracts that pay for results rather than visits — has to engage the social conditions of its population. This does not mean hospitals must become housing agencies or food banks. It means they must screen for social needs, connect patients to resources, and partner with the organizations that address those needs.

There is also an equity dimension. Social and economic disadvantage is not randomly distributed; it tracks race, income, and place because of the structural factors covered earlier in this course. That means SDOH burdens fall hardest on exactly the populations with the worst health outcomes. Addressing social needs is therefore not a separate agenda from equity — it is one of the most direct levers for reducing disparities.

The remaining lessons in this part of the course turn from evidence to practice: how clinical teams screen for social needs with validated tools, how they document them, and how specific interventions in housing and food security are showing measurable health and cost effects. The evidence in this lesson is the foundation; the next lessons are about acting on it.

body.message: The SDOH evidence justifies screening patients for social needs — but asking someone whether they are food insecure or about to be evicted, and then having nothing to offer, can erode trust and cause harm. Effective SDOH work pairs screening with a real referral pathway. The next lesson covers how to do this responsibly.
body.title: Screening without action can backfire

children.text: CMS’s 2024 Quality Payment Program updates added SDOH screening rates to the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) measure set, creating a financial incentive for rural practices to document social needs screening. The predictable result has been a surge in screening rates accompanied by minimal change in patient outcomes: rural practices are asking the PRAPARE or AHC HRSN questions, documenting the responses, and then doing nothing with the data because no referral infrastructure exists.
The Closed-Loop Referral Network: What Separates Effective From Performative SDOH Programs

The defining characteristic of SDOH programs that generate clinical outcomes is the closed-loop referral: a workflow in which a positive SDOH screen automatically generates a referral to a community resource, and the referral system tracks completion and feeds resolution data back to the clinical team. Without the feedback loop, a positive food insecurity screen that generates a referral to a food pantry the patient never contacts is indistinguishable—in the clinical record—from a referral that resulted in three months of regular food access.

body.title: SDOH Screening Program Maturity Levels: Rural Health System Archetypes

children.text: Four Rural Health Systems That Built It

Carilion Clinic (Virginia) partnered with Unite Us to build a closed-loop referral network across seven rural counties. In the first 18 months, 62% of referred patients received a community service within 30 days, and the cohort showed a 16% reduction in ED utilization compared to matched controls. The investment was $280,000 in the first year (Unite Us licensing, care coordinator training, community organization onboarding).

CHAP’s rural network in Appalachian Kentucky embedded community health workers—rather than software platforms—as the referral mechanism. CHWs with deep community relationships achieved 71% referral completion rates and generated an average $3,400 reduction in 12-month care costs per enrolled patient with multiple SDOH needs. The labor model (CHW salary: $38,000–48,000) is accessible to rural systems that cannot afford enterprise SDOH platforms.

The technology is the easy part. A food pantry that does not have capacity to absorb 200 new patients does not become more capable because you build an elegant referral interface. The network is the hard part.

NETWORK BUILDING PRIORITY: Before selecting an SDOH technology platform, conduct a community resource capacity audit. Map the actual service capacity of every organization in your referral network. A closed-loop system that routes patients to over-capacity organizations will generate lower completion rates than a manual system with a well-resourced CHW.

body.caption: Closed-loop SDOH referral workflow diagram showing the patient screening, positive needs identification, digital referral generation, community organization receipt and service delivery, resolution confirmation, and EHR feedback documentation steps with completion rate annotations at each stage.

Conduct community resource capacity audit before platform selection—technology cannot substitute for community capacity
Evaluate Unite Us, FindHelp, and CHW-based models against your specific community resource landscape
Set 60% referral completion rate as the minimum threshold for a viable closed-loop program
Build resolution tracking feedback into any technology contract as a non-negotiable requirement

children.text: From Knowing to Asking

The previous lesson established that social conditions drive most health outcomes. But a health system cannot act on a patient's housing instability or food insecurity if it does not know about it — and these needs are usually invisible in a standard clinical encounter. SDOH screening is the structured practice of asking patients directly about their social needs so that those needs can be documented and addressed.

A consistent finding across the literature is that patients are generally willing to answer these questions when they are asked respectfully, confidentially, and with a clear purpose. Screening surfaces needs clinicians would otherwise never learn about — a patient skipping medications to pay rent, a parent rationing food, an older adult who cannot get to appointments. None of these is visible on a lab panel.

But screening is only the first step, and doing it badly can cause harm. Asking someone whether they are food insecure and then offering nothing in response signals that the system sees the problem and does not care — eroding the trust screening was meant to build. Responsible SDOH screening is always designed as the front end of a pathway that ends in a referral and, ideally, a confirmed connection to help.

SDOH screening structures the question "what do you need outside the clinic?" Patients will generally answer when asked respectfully — but screening must be paired with a real response, or it erodes trust rather than building it.
The Major Validated Screening Tools

Several validated screening instruments are in wide use. They differ in length, setting, and the domains they emphasize, but they share the goal of standardizing how social needs are captured so that data can be aggregated, compared, and acted on. Two tools dominate US practice: PRAPARE and the CMS Accountable Health Communities tool.

PRAPARE — the Protocol for Responding to and Assessing Patients' Assets, Risks, and Experiences — was developed by the National Association of Community Health Centers (NACHC) together with AAPCHO and the Oregon Primary Care Association. It comprises 21 questions, including 16 core measures, covering housing, food, employment, education, transportation, and social support. PRAPARE is the most widely used tool in Federally Qualified Health Centers and is designed to map to ICD-10 Z-codes for documentation.

The CMS Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Health-Related Social Needs (HRSN) Screening Tool is a shorter, 10-item instrument published by CMS in 2017. Its core covers five domains — housing instability, food insecurity, transportation problems, utility needs, and interpersonal safety — with optional supplemental questions on financial strain, employment, mental health, and more. It was built for the AHC model and has become a federal reference standard for health-related social needs.

children.text: Z-Codes: Documenting Social Needs in the Record

Identifying a social need is only useful if it is recorded in a way the system can use. ICD-10-CM Z-codes in the Z55-Z65 range are the standardized diagnosis codes for documenting social determinants of health. They let a clinician capture a social need as structured data that can be counted across a panel, reported for quality programs, and increasingly used by payers to understand and address population needs.

The categories map cleanly to the screening domains: Z55 covers education and literacy problems; Z56 employment and unemployment; Z57 occupational exposures; Z58 physical environment; Z59 housing and economic circumstances (Z59.0 is homelessness); Z60 the social environment; and Z62-Z65 various psychosocial circumstances. Per ICD-10 guidance, these are reported as secondary diagnoses, and notably they may be documented based on information from any clinician involved in the patient's care — not only the billing provider — which means social workers, nurses, and case managers can supply the documentation.

The central problem with Z-codes is not the codes themselves but how rarely they are used. CMS reported that Z-codes were documented for only about 1.6% of Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries in 2019, despite social needs being far more prevalent than that. The barriers are practical: many clinicians do not know the codes exist, lack a workflow for capturing them, or are unsure who is permitted to document them. Improving Z-code capture is a recurring target of health-system equity initiatives.

children.text: Closing the Loop: From Referral to Confirmed Help

Screening identifies a need and Z-codes document it, but neither solves anything on its own. The decisive step is the referral — connecting the patient to a community resource that can actually address the need — and, ideally, confirming the connection happened. The quality of this handoff is what separates SDOH programs that improve outcomes from those that simply generate data.

Referrals exist on a spectrum. A paper pamphlet listing food banks is the weakest form — the patient is left to navigate alone. A "warm" referral, where a staff member helps make the connection during the visit, is stronger. The strongest is a closed-loop referral: the receiving organization confirms the patient connected with services and reports that outcome back to the care team, so the loop is closed and the system knows whether the need was met.

A set of community resource and referral platforms has emerged to enable closed-loop referrals at scale, building shared directories and digital handoffs between health care and community-based organizations. The best known are findhelp (formerly Aunt Bertha) and Unite Us. These platforms let a clinic send an electronic referral, track its status, and receive confirmation — turning a vague suggestion into an accountable transaction.

body.content:
findhelp (formerly Aunt Bertha) operates a searchable national directory of social-service programs that lets clinical teams and patients find and connect to local resources, with referral tracking.
Unite Us builds coordinated-care networks that link health care organizations with community-based organizations and provide closed-loop referral tracking — the referring team is notified when a patient is served. Both are used by health systems, payers, and Medicaid programs to make social-needs referrals accountable rather than aspirational.
body.title: Unite Us and findhelp — Closed-Loop Referral Networks

children.text: Designing Screening That Helps Rather Than Harms

Putting the pieces together, an effective SDOH screening program has four linked components: a validated tool appropriate to the setting, a respectful workflow for asking, structured documentation (including Z-codes), and a referral pathway capable of closing the loop. Missing any one of these undermines the others. A great tool with no referral pathway just catalogs suffering; a great referral network with no screening never finds the patients who need it.

Workflow and trust matter as much as instrument choice. Who asks the questions, how they are framed, whether the patient understands why, and whether the encounter feels safe all shape whether screening yields honest answers. Embedding community health workers or trained staff to conduct screening and follow up on referrals consistently produces better engagement than handing patients a form in a waiting room.

Finally, screening should be designed with the populations it serves, not just for them. Tools and workflows that are language-concordant, culturally appropriate, and sensitive to the stigma around needs like food insecurity or interpersonal safety will capture far more than a generic checklist. The goal is not a completed questionnaire — it is a patient whose unmet need was identified and actually addressed.

body.message: Requiring clinicians to screen without giving them time, training, documentation tools, or a referral network sets the program up to fail — and can damage patient trust. Before scaling screening, ensure the downstream referral pathway and the staff capacity to act on findings are genuinely in place.
body.title: Do not let screening become an unfunded mandate

children.text: The Authority That Lets States Reinvent Medicaid

Medicaid is governed by detailed federal rules — who must be covered, what services must be offered, how programs must operate. These rules create consistency, but they also constrain experimentation. So how do states test bold new approaches, like covering housing as a health benefit or running an all-payer global budget, when the standard rules would not allow it? The answer is the Section 1115 demonstration waiver — the single most powerful tool states have to reinvent their Medicaid programs, and the engine behind most major Medicaid managed care innovation.

Section 1115 of the Social Security Act gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to approve experimental, pilot, or demonstration projects likely to promote the objectives of the Medicaid program. What makes Section 1115 uniquely powerful is its breadth: it combines extensive waiver authority with a broadly defined purpose. The Secretary can waive almost any Medicaid state plan requirement and can permit federal matching funds for costs not otherwise matchable — letting states cover services and populations Medicaid normally would not. In effect, Section 1115 is a license to experiment with the program’s core rules.

For Medicaid managed care, 1115 waivers are foundational. Many states’ entire managed care programs operate under 1115 authority, and the boldest delivery and payment innovations — from value-based reforms to addressing social needs — are tested through these demonstrations. Understanding Section 1115 is understanding how Medicaid changes and how the most ambitious managed care experiments become possible.

Key Concept: A Section 1115 demonstration waiver lets the HHS Secretary waive most Medicaid rules and authorize federal funding for normally non-matchable costs, so states can test experimental approaches. Demonstrations must be "budget neutral" to the federal government and are generally approved for five years, then renewable.

children.text: How Section 1115 Works

A Section 1115 demonstration is, formally, a research and demonstration project: states must have an approved, publicly available evaluation strategy, because the authority is meant to test and evaluate new policy approaches, not simply to expand programs. The breadth is remarkable — under Section 1115, the Secretary can waive almost any state plan requirement under §1902 (with narrow exceptions like citizenship rules), to the extent necessary to carry out the demonstration. This lets states restructure eligibility, benefits, delivery systems, and payment in ways the standard rules would forbid.

Equally important is the "expenditure authority" that comes with 1115: the Secretary can permit federal financial participation for costs not otherwise matchable (CNOM) — federal dollars for services and populations not included in the regular Medicaid state plan. CNOM authority is how a state can use Medicaid funds for things like housing supports or services for populations Medicaid does not normally cover. Without it, the boldest innovations would have no funding mechanism; with it, states can finance genuinely new approaches with federal matching dollars.

The approval process is rigorous and often slow. A state submits a detailed application — describing the demonstration, enrollment estimates, requested authorities, research hypotheses, and documentation of public comment — and CMS reviews it case by case to determine whether the objectives align with Medicaid’s. There is a federal 30-day public comment period, and CMS must consider all comments. Negotiation typically takes anywhere from six months to two years, longer for comprehensive waivers that may encompass most of a state’s Medicaid spending, because each program element must be separately negotiated.
