children.text: Budget Neutrality: The Central Constraint

The most important limit on Section 1115 is budget neutrality: a demonstration must not cost the federal government more than it would have spent without the waiver. Federal Medicaid expenditures under the demonstration cannot exceed what federal spending would have been without it, over the course of the project. This single rule shapes nearly every 1115 design, because it means a state cannot simply ask the federal government to pay for new things — it must show that, on net, the demonstration stays within the federal spending it would have incurred anyway.

Budget neutrality is typically calculated on a per-enrollee basis: per-enrollee spending under the demonstration cannot exceed the projected per-enrollee spending in the "without-waiver baseline." This creates a powerful dynamic. If a state spends below that baseline, the difference counts as savings — and the state can use accumulated savings to finance the costs-not-otherwise-matchable spending on populations or services Medicaid does not normally cover. In other words, a state that manages care efficiently enough to come in under its baseline can reinvest the savings into innovative services. Budget neutrality is both a constraint and, paradoxically, the funding source for innovation.

body.message: Budget neutrality means an 1115 demonstration cannot simply add federal cost — new services and populations must generally be financed from savings the demonstration itself generates against the without-waiver baseline. This is why 1115 innovations are framed as investments expected to reduce other spending, not as straightforward expansions.
body.title: Innovation Must Pay for Itself

children.text: What States Are Testing

Section 1115 has become the primary vehicle for the most ambitious Medicaid innovations, and recent years have seen a wave of demonstrations addressing health-related social needs (HRSN) — the social factors like housing and food that drive health outcomes. In 2022 CMS announced a demonstration opportunity to expand states’ tools to address enrollees’ health-related social needs, and by February 2024 had approved eight states under the HRSN framework — Arizona, Arkansas, California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, and Washington. These waivers authorize evidence-based housing and nutrition services for high-need populations, including coverage of rent or temporary housing and utilities for up to six months and meal support for up to six months.

The specific demonstrations are striking in scope. New York’s January 2024 waiver amendment included up to $3.673 billion to build HRSN infrastructure, including new "Social Care Networks," and to reimburse for HRSN services through Medicaid. Massachusetts’s MassHealth waiver supports housing (security deposits, rent, relocation, home modifications, housing case management), food security, and transportation. Arkansas’s supports housing deposits, moving costs, and tenancy-sustaining services. A separate 1115 opportunity addressed reentry for justice-involved individuals — partially waiving the Medicaid "inmate exclusion" so states can provide pre-release services — with the Biden administration approving 19 state reentry waivers.

These innovations are politically contingent, which is itself a defining feature of 1115. Because demonstrations are approved at the Secretary’s discretion, their direction shifts with administrations. In March 2025, the Trump administration rescinded the Biden administration’s HRSN guidance; CMS indicated this does not nullify existing HRSN approvals, but that it will consider HRSN and social-determinant requests on a case-by-case basis going forward. This illustrates a core truth about 1115: it is a powerful tool for innovation precisely because it is discretionary, which also means the innovations it enables can be expanded or curtailed as federal priorities change.
Why 1115 Is the Engine of Medicaid Innovation

Section 1115 occupies a unique place in Medicaid: it is the mechanism through which the program evolves. Almost every major delivery and payment innovation — including the all-payer and global-budget models discussed in the value-based-care course, comprehensive managed care expansions, and the social-needs demonstrations above — runs through 1115 authority. When a state wants to do something genuinely new with Medicaid, the path almost always leads to a Section 1115 waiver. It is, in a real sense, where the future of Medicaid is tested before it becomes standard.

body.analogy: Section 1115 is like a sanctioned "sandbox" or pilot program within a heavily regulated system. The standard Medicaid rules are the building code everyone must follow; an 1115 waiver is special permission to construct an experimental building that breaks some of those rules — but only if you can prove it won’t cost the city more than a normal building (budget neutrality), you document what you’re testing (evaluation), and you get the regulator’s sign-off (case-by-case approval). The sandbox is where new designs get proven before, sometimes, becoming the new code.
body.concept: How Section 1115 enables Medicaid innovation

children.text: The tension at the heart of 1115 is between flexibility and accountability. Its flexibility is what makes innovation possible — without it, Medicaid would be frozen in its statutory form. But that same discretionary flexibility means demonstrations can advance one administration’s priorities and be unwound by the next, that budget-neutrality calculations can be contested, and that "demonstrations" sometimes operate for decades without ever conclusively demonstrating anything. The required evaluations are meant to provide accountability, but the political nature of approval means 1115 is as much a policy instrument as a research tool.

This lesson sets up the course’s conclusion. The next and final lesson looks at where Medicaid managed care is heading — toward social determinants of health and whole-person care — and Section 1115 is precisely the authority making that direction possible. The HRSN demonstrations covered here are the leading edge of that future. Understanding 1115 means understanding not just a regulatory mechanism, but the very channel through which Medicaid managed care reaches beyond medical care toward the social factors that shape health, and through which the program will continue to transform in the years ahead.

points: A Section 1115 demonstration waiver lets the HHS Secretary waive almost any Medicaid state plan requirement (§1902) and authorize federal funding for normally non-matchable costs, so states can test experimental approaches — the most powerful tool for Medicaid innovation.
Section 1115 is uniquely broad, combining extensive waiver authority with a broadly defined purpose, and many states run their entire managed care programs and boldest reforms under 1115 authority.

1115 demonstrations are formally research projects requiring a public evaluation strategy, and expenditure authority (costs not otherwise matchable, CNOM) is what lets states fund services and populations outside the regular state plan.

The approval process is rigorous and slow — a detailed application, a 30-day federal comment period, and case-by-case CMS review — typically taking six months to two years, longer for comprehensive waivers.

Budget neutrality is the central constraint: federal spending under the demonstration cannot exceed without-waiver spending (usually per-enrollee), and savings below the baseline can finance innovative CNOM services — making innovation largely self-funded.

A wave of recent 1115s address health-related social needs (HRSN): eight states (AZ, AR, CA, MA, NJ, NY, OR, WA) approved by February 2024 for housing and nutrition services, including New York’s $3.673 billion Social Care Networks; a separate opportunity approved 19 state reentry waivers partially waiving the inmate-exclusion policy.

1115 innovations are politically contingent — in March 2025 the Trump administration rescinded the Biden HRSN guidance (without nullifying existing approvals), shifting to case-by-case review — reflecting that discretionary approval enables both expansion and curtailment.

Section 1115 is the engine through which Medicaid evolves, including the all-payer/global-budget and social-needs innovations, balancing flexibility (enabling innovation) against accountability (evaluation requirements amid political discretion).

children.text: A Spectrum, Not a Switch

The previous lesson described the painful straddle between fee-for-service and value-based care. This lesson maps the destination side of that straddle in detail, because "value-based payment" is not one thing — it is a continuum of arrangements that transfer progressively more financial risk from the payer to the provider. At one end, a provider can earn a bonus for good performance while bearing no real downside. At the other, a provider receives a fixed payment to cover all of a population’s care and bears the full financial consequence if costs run high. Understanding where a contract sits on this continuum is the single most important thing to know about it.

The reason the continuum matters so much is that risk and reward move together. Arrangements with little downside risk are safe but offer modest upside; arrangements with full risk offer the largest rewards but can bankrupt a provider that miscalculates. Hospitals and physician groups generally move along this continuum over time — starting cautiously and taking on more risk as they build the capabilities to manage it. This lesson walks the spectrum from the gentlest to the most aggressive forms of risk-bearing.

Key Concept: Value-based payment is a continuum of risk transfer: from upside-only shared savings (bonus, no penalty), to two-sided risk (share savings and losses), to risk corridors (capped sharing), to capitation (a fixed payment covering all care, full provider risk). More risk means more potential reward — and more potential loss.

children.text: Upside-Only: The Gentle On-Ramp

The first step onto the risk continuum is upside risk, also called one-sided risk or shared savings. The provider is measured against a predetermined financial benchmark — typically the expected total cost of care for its attributed population. If the provider keeps actual costs below that target while meeting quality standards, it shares in the savings, earning a portion of the difference. Crucially, if costs exceed the target, the provider is not penalized: there is upside but no downside.

This asymmetry makes upside-only the natural starting point. It lets a provider learn to manage cost and quality, build the necessary data and care-coordination infrastructure, and earn rewards — all without risking a loss. The Medicare Shared Savings Program’s entry-level tracks work this way. The trade-off is that the rewards are modest precisely because the risk is low; payers do not pay large bonuses to providers who share none of the downside. Upside-only is a training ground, not a permanent home.

Indeed, the entire system is designed to push providers off the on-ramp over time. Because organizations typically grow into downside risk after starting upside-only — either pulled by larger financial incentives or pushed by contract mandates and program rules — two-sided arrangements are described as the more mature or advanced form of risk sharing. The gentle on-ramp exists to get providers ready for the road ahead.
Two-Sided Risk and Risk Corridors

The next step is two-sided risk, where the provider shares both savings and losses. If total cost of care comes in under the benchmark, the provider shares the savings as before; but if costs exceed the benchmark, the provider must share the loss — facing reimbursement cuts or owing money back to the payer. This is a fundamentally different proposition: the provider now has real money at stake in both directions, which sharpens the incentive to control costs but also exposes it to genuine financial danger.

To make two-sided risk survivable, contracts use risk corridors. A risk corridor caps the shared savings or losses using "risk bands": as actual results deviate further from the benchmark, the provider moves into bands where it shares a smaller percentage of the gains or losses. The effect is to limit how much a provider can win or lose in any period, protecting both sides from catastrophic swings. Risk corridors are the shock absorbers that let providers take on downside risk without betting the entire organization on a single bad year.

No penalty if costs exceed the benchmark
Lower reward, minimal danger

right.label: Two-Sided Risk

children.text: Capitation: Taking on the Full Risk

At the far end of the continuum sits capitation — the most complete transfer of financial risk to the provider. Under capitation, a provider receives a fixed payment per attributed patient, paid per member per month (PMPM), to cover a defined scope of care regardless of how many services that patient actually uses. The PMPM amount represents the expected cost of providing those services. If the provider’s actual costs for its patient panel come in below the capitation budget, it keeps the difference as surplus; if costs exceed the budget, the provider absorbs the loss.

Capitation comes in degrees of breadth. Primary care capitation pays a fixed PMPM for routine primary care and care coordination — a relatively contained risk. Specialty capitation pays specialists a fixed amount for a defined service area like oncology or behavioral health. Global capitation is the most sweeping: a provider or group takes full financial responsibility for all of a population’s care — hospital, specialist, and ancillary services alike. Global capitation makes the provider function almost like an insurer, which is why it represents one of the highest degrees of risk transfer short of starting an insurance plan.

body.title: The Risk Continuum, From Lowest to Highest

children.text: Because capitation transfers so much risk, it requires sophisticated protective machinery. Risk adjustment is essential: PMPM rates must be adjusted upward for sicker patients, or providers would be paid too little to care for high-need populations (and would be tempted to avoid them). Risk pools — a portion of the capitation withheld and paid out only if costs stay controlled — align incentives within physician groups. And stop-loss or reinsurance protects the provider against catastrophic individual cases, capping the loss any single very-sick patient can impose. Without these mechanisms, capitation would be a reckless bet rather than a managed risk.
Choosing Where to Stand on the Continuum

The central strategic question for any provider is not whether to take risk, but how much, how fast, and with what protections. Moving up the continuum increases both the potential reward and the required capability. Upside-only demands basic cost and quality reporting. Two-sided risk demands genuine ability to manage total cost of care. Capitation demands actuarial sophistication, robust data, deep care-management infrastructure, and enough scale to spread risk across a population — capabilities a small or unprepared provider simply will not have.

body.analogy: The risk continuum is like levels of investing. Upside-only shared savings is a savings account with a bonus — safe, modest returns, no chance of loss. Two-sided risk is a diversified portfolio with stop-loss orders — real gains and losses, but bounded. Capitation is running your own fund where you keep all the profit but cover all the losses. You move to higher-risk levels only as your knowledge, reserves, and tools grow — and you use protections (risk corridors, reinsurance) the same way an investor uses hedges.
body.concept: The value-based risk continuum

children.text: The mismatch between risk and capability is where providers get hurt. A group that jumps to capitation without the infrastructure to manage utilization, or without adequate risk adjustment for a sick population, can be financially destroyed by costs it cannot control. Conversely, a sophisticated, well-capitalized system that stays in upside-only leaves substantial reward on the table and signals it is not serious about value. Matching the level of risk to the organization’s real capabilities — and building those capabilities deliberately before advancing — is the essence of value-based financial strategy.

This continuum connects directly to the models covered in the value-based-care course: accountable care organizations typically operate in the shared-savings-to-two-sided-risk range, while Medicare Advantage and advanced primary care models push toward capitation. The same logic governs all of them. As payers and federal policy increasingly favor downside risk and full accountability, providers across the country are being pushed steadily rightward along this continuum. Knowing exactly what each arrangement transfers — and what capabilities and protections each demands — is what separates organizations that thrive under value-based payment from those that merely survive it.

points: Value-based payment is a continuum of increasing risk transfer from payer to provider: upside-only shared savings, two-sided risk, risk corridors, and capitation — with reward and danger rising together.
Upside-only (one-sided) risk lets providers share savings if they beat a cost benchmark with no penalty for overspending; it is the low-reward training ground for building value-based capabilities.
Two-sided risk requires providers to share both savings and losses, exposing them to real financial danger and marking the more mature, advanced stage of risk sharing.
Risk corridors cap shared savings and losses using risk bands, acting as shock absorbers that make two-sided risk survivable by limiting how much a provider can win or lose.

Capitation pays a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) amount to cover a defined scope of care regardless of utilization; it ranges from primary care to specialty to global capitation, the broadest and riskiest.
Global capitation transfers full financial risk for all of a population’s care, making the provider function almost like an insurer — one of the highest degrees of risk transfer possible.
Capitation requires protective machinery: risk adjustment (higher PMPM for sicker patients), risk pools (withheld payments tied to performance), and stop-loss/reinsurance against catastrophic cases.

The strategic key is matching the level of risk to the organization’s real capabilities and building those capabilities before advancing; ACOs sit in the shared-savings-to-two-sided range while Medicare Advantage and advanced primary care push toward capitation.

children.text: The Question at the Heart of the Debate

Should a hospital be held to the same quality standard if half its patients live in poverty as a hospital whose patients are predominantly middle-class? Should a primary care practice treating a community with high rates of food insecurity, unstable housing, and limited transportation be judged on the same readmission rate curve as a practice in a wealthy suburb? These are not rhetorical questions. They are policy choices embedded in every value-based payment program — and the answer determines whether those programs help or harm the safety-net providers that serve America's most vulnerable patients.

Social risk adjustment refers to the practice of modifying quality and cost benchmarks — or risk scores — to account for patients' social and economic circumstances that are unrelated to the quality of clinical care. When a patient is readmitted to the hospital partly because she has no transportation to her follow-up appointment, no refrigerator for her medications, and no one at home to monitor her condition, that readmission reflects her social circumstances — not her provider's clinical competence. The debate is whether the payment system should account for that reality.

The stakes are enormous. The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing Program, the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System, and the Shared Savings Program all use outcome and quality metrics that are sensitive to patients' socioeconomic status. Safety-net hospitals and practices that disproportionately serve low-income and disabled populations have argued for years that these programs systematically penalize them — not for delivering poor care, but for serving poor patients.

Social risk factors — including income level, housing stability, food security, education, transportation access, and social support — are estimated to influence up to 80 percent of health outcomes. Yet most value-based payment programs historically adjusted only for clinical diagnoses, not for these upstream determinants.
The NQF and the Evidence Base

The National Quality Forum (NQF) established an expert panel in 2014 to examine whether quality measures should be adjusted for social risk factors. The panel's report called for adjustment "under a defined set of circumstances," concluding that failing to adjust might worsen health disparities by creating systematic financial pressure on providers who serve disadvantaged populations. This finding sparked a multi-year policy debate involving CMS, MedPAC, the National Academy of Medicine, and Congress.

In 2017, the NQF completed a multi-stakeholder trial that tested social risk adjustment across multiple quality measures. The trial found that incorporating social risk factors into performance measurement was feasible — though challenging — and that social risk factors were statistically significant predictors of outcomes on many measures. The study documented clear performance disparities between providers serving high-social-risk versus low-social-risk populations, validating concerns that unadjusted comparisons were systematically misleading.

Research has consistently shown that dual-eligible beneficiaries (those who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid) and low-income subsidy recipients in Medicare Advantage perform worse on clinical quality measures, have higher readmission rates, and score lower on patient experience surveys — even when controlling for clinical diagnoses. These patterns persist across different geographic regions, health systems, and care settings, suggesting that the disparity is driven by social circumstances rather than differences in clinical care quality.

body.content:
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), established by the ACA in 2012, penalizes hospitals with higher-than-expected 30-day readmissions for conditions including heart failure, pneumonia, and hip/knee replacement. Safety-net hospitals — which serve disproportionately high shares of low-income and uninsured patients — have consistently received higher penalties under HRRP.
A 2016 Health Affairs analysis found that safety-net hospitals were three times more likely to receive the maximum readmission penalty than non-safety-net hospitals, despite evidence that their readmission rates were largely driven by patients' social circumstances rather than poor hospital care. Congress partially addressed this in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021, which created a peer-grouping system that compares hospitals to others with similar shares of low-income patients — a form of social risk adjustment for HRRP.
body.title: Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program and Safety-Net Hospitals

children.text: The Two Sides of the Policy Debate

The case for social risk adjustment rests on fairness and access. If safety-net providers are systematically penalized in value-based programs because of who their patients are rather than how well they perform clinically, the programs create a perverse incentive to avoid serving vulnerable populations. Over time, financial penalties can reduce resources available for quality improvement, drive providers to exit the market, or create pressure to limit services to high-risk patients. The ultimate losers are the patients who most depend on those providers.

The case against social risk adjustment is also grounded in legitimate policy concerns. Critics argue that adjusting outcome measures for patients' social circumstances could mask genuine disparities in the quality of care delivered to low-income patients. If a hospital serving mostly poor patients actually does deliver inferior care, adjusting the benchmark to account for poverty could obscure that reality and remove the accountability pressure that drives improvement. From this perspective, social risk adjustment could become a tool for excusing poor performance rather than addressing its root causes.

A third position — increasingly adopted by CMS — attempts to split the difference. Rather than adjusting outcome benchmarks for social risk, this approach focuses on measuring and rewarding active interventions to address social needs: screening patients for SDOH, connecting them to community resources, reducing disparities in performance within a provider's own patient population. This "stratification and accountability" approach holds that providers should not be rewarded merely for serving a disadvantaged population, but should be rewarded for actively reducing disparities within that population.

left.label: Arguments For Adjustment
points: Prevents systematic financial penalties on safety-net providers
Removes incentive to avoid enrolling or treating vulnerable patients
Reflects reality that social factors drive outcomes beyond providers' control
Supported by NQF, National Academy of Medicine, and safety-net advocates

right.label: Arguments Against Adjustment
points: Could mask genuine disparities in care quality for low-income patients
Removes accountability pressure to improve outcomes for disadvantaged populations
May create perverse incentive to label patients as socially disadvantaged
Difficult to implement consistently without reliable standardized SDOH data

body.title: Social Risk Adjustment: The Core Policy Debate

children.text: What CMS Has Actually Done

CMS has moved incrementally toward incorporating social risk into payment programs, though it has not adopted comprehensive social risk adjustment for most quality measures. The most significant step was the peer-grouping adjustment for HRRP, enacted in 2021, which compares hospitals' readmission rates to peers with similar socioeconomic patient mixes rather than to the national average. This approach acknowledges that different hospitals operate in structurally different environments without fully excusing poor performance.

In 2024, CMS issued regulations requiring hospitals participating in federal payment programs to screen all patients for five social determinants: food insecurity, housing instability, transportation needs, utility difficulties, and interpersonal safety. These screening requirements create a standardized data foundation that could eventually support more rigorous social risk adjustment. CMS also established billing codes for Social Determinants of Health Risk Assessments, Community Health Integration services, and Principal Illness Navigation — creating reimbursement pathways for directly addressing social needs.

For Medicare Advantage, CMS introduced the Health Equity Index (HEI) as part of the Star Ratings system, taking effect for 2027 star ratings based on 2024–2025 performance data. The HEI rewards plans that achieve high performance specifically among enrollees with social risk factors — dual-eligible beneficiaries, low-income subsidy recipients, and disability-status enrollees. Rather than adjusting benchmarks downward, the HEI adds bonus points for demonstrating equitable outcomes across all enrolled populations.

children.text: The Data Problem and the Path Forward

The most practical obstacle to comprehensive social risk adjustment is data. Unlike clinical diagnoses, which are captured through standardized ICD-10 codes in medical claims, social risk factors are inconsistently documented across health systems, insurers, and geographic regions. Poverty is not an ICD-10 code. Housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers are documented in some EHR systems but not others, and the definitions and screening tools vary widely.

The 2024 SDOH screening mandates represent an attempt to solve this data problem at the population level by requiring consistent, standardized screening across all Medicare- and Medicaid-participating hospitals. Over time, if these requirements are enforced and data is aggregated at the CMS level, it becomes possible to construct reliable patient-level social risk profiles that could support more refined payment adjustments. Several states — including Massachusetts, New York, and California — have moved faster than federal policy by requiring SDOH documentation in Medicaid managed care contracts.

The Vermont Blueprint for Health offers an instructive model. Vermont has integrated social risk data collection into its community health team model, using standardized SDOH screening across all primary care practices. This data informs both population health interventions and, increasingly, payment arrangements that account for the social complexity of a practice's attributed population. Vermont's approach suggests that social risk adjustment is not just technically feasible but operationally achievable when built systematically into care delivery infrastructure from the ground up.

The emerging CMS framework distinguishes between "adjusting for" social risk (lowering benchmarks for disadvantaged populations) and "rewarding action on" social risk (paying for SDOH screening, community health integration, and demonstrated disparity reduction). Both approaches are moving forward simultaneously in different programs.

points: Social risk adjustment modifies quality and cost benchmarks to account for patients' social and economic circumstances — income, housing, food security — that drive outcomes beyond providers' clinical control.

The NQF's 2014 expert panel endorsed social risk adjustment under defined circumstances, and a 2017 multi-stakeholder trial confirmed it is feasible and that social factors are significant predictors of outcomes.

The core policy debate pits fairness concerns (safety-net providers are unfairly penalized) against accountability concerns (adjustment could mask genuine care quality disparities for low-income patients).

Congress partially adopted social risk adjustment for the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program in 2021 by creating socioeconomic peer groups rather than comparing all hospitals to a single national benchmark.
CMS's 2024 SDOH screening mandate requires hospitals to screen patients for five social domains, building the data infrastructure needed for more systematic social risk adjustment in the future.

The CMS Health Equity Index, effective for 2027 Star Ratings, rewards Medicare Advantage plans for achieving equitable outcomes across social risk subgroups — an "accountability for equity" approach rather than benchmark adjustment.
The absence of standardized, reliable social risk data remains the primary technical barrier to comprehensive social risk adjustment in federal value-based payment programs.

children.text: The Low-Income Subsidy and Who It Represents

Within Medicare Advantage, no group of beneficiaries is more politically and programmatically complex than those who receive the Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) — also called Extra Help. The LIS program subsidizes Part D prescription drug costs for Medicare beneficiaries with limited income and resources, reducing or eliminating premiums, deductibles, and copayments for eligible enrollees. In 2024, over 14 million Medicare beneficiaries received some form of the low-income subsidy, representing roughly 40 percent of all Part D enrollees.

LIS beneficiaries are disproportionately represented in certain Medicare Advantage plans — particularly dual-eligible special needs plans (D-SNPs) that specialize in serving people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. These beneficiaries carry significant social complexity: they are more likely to have multiple chronic conditions, unstable housing, food insecurity, limited health literacy, and barriers to transportation. They are also more likely to miss appointments, have lower medication adherence rates, and score lower on patient experience surveys — through no fault of the plans that serve them.

The Star Ratings system was designed when Medicare Advantage enrollment was dominated by relatively affluent, healthy seniors. As D-SNPs and LIS-serving plans have grown — driven by CMS policy and market dynamics — the system has had to grapple with a fundamental design tension: should plans serving the most complex, socially disadvantaged populations be held to identical performance standards as plans serving predominantly healthy, high-income beneficiaries?

Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries — also called Extra Help recipients — are Medicare Part D enrollees with limited income and resources who receive federal subsidies for prescription drug costs. Plans serving high LIS concentrations consistently face structural performance disadvantages in the Star Ratings system that are only partially offset by existing adjustments.
How the Star Ratings System Disadvantages LIS-Heavy Plans

The Star Ratings system measures performance on approximately 42 metrics, and LIS status correlates negatively with performance on a wide range of them. Medication adherence measures — which are triple-weighted in the Part D domain — show consistent LIS gaps. Research across multiple years of CMS data shows that LIS beneficiaries are significantly less likely to adhere to statins, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and oral diabetic medications, even when controlling for demographics and clinical diagnoses. The reasons are structural: cost-sharing (even if subsidized), transportation barriers, social instability, and limited pharmacy access in low-income neighborhoods.

CAHPS patient experience scores — triple-weighted measures in the Part C domain — also show systematic LIS disadvantages. LIS beneficiaries report lower satisfaction with their health plan and care experience across multiple CAHPS domains, including communication with providers, coordination of care, and plan responsiveness. Research has found that these lower CAHPS scores reflect real experience differences driven by factors including neighborhood poverty, language barriers, and concentration of LIS beneficiaries in plans with less administrative capacity — but they are partially attributable to social circumstances rather than plan performance.

The cumulative effect is that plans serving high concentrations of LIS beneficiaries face a structural performance headwind on multiple high-weight measures simultaneously. A plan serving 60 percent LIS beneficiaries competing against a plan serving 15 percent LIS beneficiaries for the same star rating faces a mathematically different challenge. This creates an equity paradox: the plans most committed to serving America's most vulnerable Medicare beneficiaries are the plans most financially penalized by the quality measurement system.

body.content:
Dual Eligible Special Needs Plans (D-SNPs) enroll beneficiaries who are simultaneously eligible for Medicare and Medicaid — the highest-complexity, most socially disadvantaged subset of Medicare beneficiaries. D-SNPs typically report substantially lower star ratings than non-SNP Medicare Advantage plans, with many D-SNPs concentrated at 3 to 3.5 stars even when delivering care that health equity advocates consider high quality.
A 2024 analysis found that D-SNPs disproportionately serve beneficiaries with mental illness, substance use disorders, housing instability, and multiple chronic conditions — all characteristics associated with lower measured performance on star rating metrics. Despite serving arguably the most important population in Medicare, D-SNPs are persistently disadvantaged in the quality bonus payment system.
body.title: D-SNPs and the LIS Performance Gap

children.text: The Categorical Adjustment Index: A Partial Solution

CMS has been aware of the LIS performance gap for years and has responded with the Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI). The CAI adds points to a contract's overall star rating to adjust for the mean within-contract performance disparity associated with its percentage of enrollees receiving the Part D low-income subsidy or dual eligibility and those who are disabled. The adjustment is applied at the contract level, not the measure level, and it primarily benefits contracts with high LIS/dual-eligible enrollment.

The CAI works by examining the gap between LIS/dual-eligible beneficiaries and non-LIS beneficiaries within the same plan on each measure. If a plan's LIS beneficiaries score significantly lower than its non-LIS beneficiaries on the same measures, the CAI provides an upward adjustment to partially offset the penalty. The goal is to ensure that such contracts' performance is not understated solely because of the composition of their enrolled population.

The CAI has limitations, however. Critics argue that it is insufficiently generous to fully offset the performance disadvantage facing heavily LIS-concentrated plans, and that the within-contract comparison methodology misses much of the structural disadvantage these plans face. Plans serving 80 percent LIS beneficiaries cannot simply be compared to themselves — they need comparison against the very different standard that applies to plans serving mostly healthy, wealthy seniors. The CAI represents an incremental accommodation rather than a fundamental redesign of the measurement framework.

children.text: The Health Equity Index: A New Framework

CMS introduced a new mechanism — the Health Equity Index (HEI) — as part of a broader effort to align Medicare Advantage incentives with health equity goals. Unlike the CAI, which adjusts for the penalty associated with having many LIS beneficiaries, the HEI is designed to reward plans that actively improve outcomes specifically for their most disadvantaged enrollees. The HEI takes effect for 2027 Star Ratings, measuring performance in 2024 and 2025.

The HEI replaces the existing reward factor in the star ratings program. Plans earn HEI points based on their performance on specific quality measures among their Social Risk Factor (SRF) population — defined as enrollees receiving Extra Help/LIS, dual-eligible beneficiaries, and disability-status enrollees. Plans whose social risk factor members make up at least the contract-level median SRF enrollment can earn up to 0.4 points added to their unrounded star rating. Plans with at least 50 percent of the median SRF enrollment can earn up to 0.2 points.

The HEI represents a philosophical shift from the CAI. Rather than simply adjusting for the negative performance effect of having many LIS beneficiaries, the HEI creates a positive incentive for achieving high quality specifically among LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries. A plan that serves many LIS enrollees but does not improve their outcomes receives no HEI reward. A plan that actively closes care gaps, improves medication adherence, and achieves high CAHPS scores among its LIS population earns a meaningful star rating bonus. This shifts the frame from "compensation for disadvantage" to "reward for demonstrated equity."

children.text: What These Changes Mean for Policy and Practice

The combination of the CAI and the emerging HEI represents genuine progress toward a more equitable Medicare Advantage quality measurement system — but substantial structural problems remain. The core measurement framework still compares all plans on the same absolute performance thresholds using annually-shifted cut points that do not distinguish between plans serving 10 percent LIS beneficiaries and plans serving 80 percent LIS beneficiaries. Until CMS adopts either separate rating tracks for D-SNPs or individual measure-level social risk adjustment, the most vulnerable beneficiaries will continue to be served by plans that are disproportionately penalized in the quality bonus payment system.

For plans strategically, the HEI creates new data requirements and care management priorities. Plans need to identify their SRF population, track measure performance specifically within that subgroup, and build targeted interventions to close equity gaps — not just overall performance gaps. This requires more granular data infrastructure than most plans have historically maintained, and it requires care management programs that are designed specifically for the social complexity of LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries rather than programs designed for the general MA population and then applied to SRF members by default.

The broader policy implication is that health equity and Medicare Advantage financial performance are increasingly linked. A plan that ignores equity — that achieves high average star ratings by serving predominantly healthy, wealthy seniors while its LIS minority underperforms — will no longer be rewarded by the same program mechanics as a plan that achieves equitable outcomes across its full enrolled population. Whether the HEI is sufficiently generous to overcome the structural disadvantages faced by the most LIS-concentrated plans remains to be seen after the 2027 ratings are released.

The Health Equity Index takes effect for 2027 Star Ratings and measures performance in 2024–2025. Plans need to start now building care management programs specifically designed for their Social Risk Factor population — LIS recipients, dual-eligible beneficiaries, and disabled enrollees — to position for the HEI reward.

children.text: Did It Actually Change, or Is That Just Noise?

You run a PDSA cycle to improve a measure. The next month, the number goes up. Did your change work — or did the number just wiggle the way it always does? This is the central question of improvement, and answering it wrong is one of the most common and costly mistakes in quality work. Statistical Process Control (SPC) exists to answer it rigorously.

The temptation is to compare two data points — this month versus last — and declare victory or defeat. But every process varies naturally from moment to moment. A single up-or-down move tells you almost nothing. SPC replaces this "two-point trap" with charts that plot data over time and use statistical rules to separate real signals from random noise.

SPC was invented by the physicist Walter Shewhart in the 1920s for manufacturing and later championed in health care through the Deming lineage that also gave us the Model for Improvement. Its two workhorse tools — the run chart and the control chart — are the standard way QI teams know whether their changes are working.

Statistical Process Control (SPC), invented by Walter Shewhart, plots data over time and uses statistical rules to distinguish real change (signal) from natural variation (noise) — replacing the unreliable habit of comparing just two data points.
The Big Idea: Two Kinds of Variation

SPC rests on one foundational distinction: all variation is either "common cause" or "special cause," and the two demand opposite responses. Getting this wrong leads to exactly the kind of meddling that makes processes worse.

Common cause variation is the natural, inherent jitter of a stable process — the random ups and downs you would expect even when nothing has changed. A process showing only common cause variation is "in statistical control": predictable, even if not necessarily good. Reducing common cause variation requires changing the process itself.

Special cause variation is different in kind — a signal that something outside the usual process happened. It is what your improvement is trying to create (a good special cause) or what a problem introduces (a bad one). The whole purpose of SPC is to reliably tell these apart, so you act on real signals and leave random noise alone.

children.text: The Run Chart: The First-Step Tool

The simplest SPC tool is the run chart: a plot of your measure over time with a horizontal line at the median. It needs no complex statistics and works with relatively little data, which makes it the perfect first step when baselining a process or starting a new improvement project.

Even without control limits, a run chart detects non-random patterns through a few well-defined rules. A "shift" is an unusually long run of consecutive points all above or all below the median (for example, with about 20 points, a run longer than 7 signals a shift). A "trend" is a long run of points all going up or all going down. A "crossings" signal looks at how often the line crosses the median — too few crossings indicates non-random variation.

These rules are deliberately simple but statistically grounded: each is calibrated so that a random process would rarely trigger it by chance. When a run chart shows a shift after your intervention, that is real evidence your change moved the process — far stronger than eyeballing two points.

children.text: The Control Chart: Adding the Limits

The control chart — Shewhart's original invention — is the more powerful sibling of the run chart. It adds two things: the center line is the mean (not the median), and it includes statistically calculated Upper and Lower Control Limits (the UCL and LCL).

Those control limits are typically set at ±3 standard deviations from the mean — which is why they are called "3-sigma limits." They represent the boundaries of expected common cause variation. A point falling outside the control limits is a strong special-cause signal: something genuinely unusual happened, because a stable process would essentially never produce a point that far out by chance.

This is the key capability a run chart lacks: because it has control limits, a control chart can detect "out-of-control" conditions and assess whether a process is stable and predictable. Run charts reveal shifts and trends; control charts also tell you whether the process is in statistical control. There is a trade-off, though — the 3-sigma rule is actually less sensitive to small shifts (up to about 2 standard deviations) than the run chart's shift and crossings rules, so the tools are complementary, not strictly ranked.

children.text: Why This Matters for Quality Improvement

SPC is the analytic engine that makes the rest of this course honest. Stratified disparity data, HEDIS rates, eCQM results, PDSA tests — all of them produce numbers that move over time, and SPC is how you tell whether a move is real. Without it, teams chase noise: celebrating random upticks, panicking over random dips, and "fixing" processes that never actually changed.

Deming's warning is the heart of it: treating common cause variation as if it were special cause (tampering) makes a stable process worse, while ignoring a true special cause misses a real problem or a real win. SPC charts give teams a disciplined, shared way to avoid both errors — and to know when a PDSA change has genuinely shifted the process.

Practically, the workflow is: start with a run chart to baseline and catch early signals, move to a control chart as you accumulate data and need to judge stability, and annotate the chart with when interventions happened so you can see their effect. This connects measurement to action — and it sets up the final lesson, where these charts live inside the dashboards that make quality visible day to day.

Use SPC charts and their rules, not single-point comparisons, to decide whether to act.

children.text: For the past six years, the Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE) has operated on a modular 'best-of-breed' architecture, integrating disparate components for MPI, FHIR repositories, and terminology services. While this served the initial phase of data liquidity, the market has matured. Technology is now a commodity, and the state's imperative must shift from infrastructure maintenance to solving the nation's highest cost of care per capita.
The Integration Trap

Maintaining individual contracts and integration points for vendors like Verato and Medicasoft creates significant overhead. This 'plumbing' distraction forces leadership to focus on API management and server uptime rather than clinical outcomes. Every upgrade risks breaking the ecosystem, requiring continuous, expensive engineering hours.
In the current mature market, building your own HIE infrastructure is akin to a hospital building its own MRI machines rather than buying them from Siemens or GE.
The Solution: CRISP Shared Services (CSS)

The recommended path is to adopt the CSS 'HIE in a Box' model, a non-profit support organization serving 9+ states. This shifts VHIE from a 'Builder' model to a 'Subscriber' model, leveraging massive economies of scale.

children.text: Equity Is Built Into Population Health

Recall the founding definition from the first lesson: population health is the health outcomes of a group AND the distribution of those outcomes within it. That word "distribution" makes equity intrinsic — a population health program that improves the average while leaving disparities intact has, by definition, failed at half its job. This module is about making that equity commitment operational.

The core tool is the same one from the Clinical Quality Measurement course: stratification — breaking apart an aggregate metric and reporting it separately for different groups. An overall diabetes-control rate of 70 percent can hide that one group is at 85 percent and another at 50 percent. Only by disaggregating do you see the gap; the average actively conceals it.

For population health specifically, stratification is not just a reporting exercise — it is a targeting tool. Once you can see which subgroups of your defined population are faring worse, you can direct your finite care-management, outreach, and program resources to close those gaps, the same way risk stratification directs resources by risk. Equity stratification is risk stratification with an equity lens.

Equity is intrinsic to population health's definition (outcomes AND their distribution). Stratification — reporting a metric separately by subgroup instead of as one average — is how you see disparities the average hides, and then target resources to close them.
The Prerequisite: REL Data

You cannot stratify by characteristics you do not record. The foundational requirement is REL data — race, ethnicity, and language — collected in a standardized, codable way. Without it, disparities in your population are real but invisible, and equity work cannot even begin. REL data is the bedrock of equity stratification.

Good REL data follows standards. The gold standard is self-reported data (patients identify their own race, ethnicity, and language), collected using categories aligned to federal Office of Management and Budget (OMB) standards and allowing people to select multiple races. Critically, standards encourage granular data that can be aggregated up — because broad categories hide disparities within them (the experiences of different Asian or Hispanic subgroups, for example, can differ enormously).

These standards are evolving. In 2024, OMB updated its race/ethnicity standards — moving to a combined race-and-ethnicity question, adding a new "Middle Eastern and North African" (MENA) category, and requiring collection of detailed responses. The trend is toward more granular, more self-determined, more complete REL data, precisely because better data reveals disparities that coarser data conceals. For a population health program, building robust self-reported REL collection is foundational equity infrastructure.

body.title: Collecting REL Data Well

children.text: When the Data Is Missing: Indirect Estimation

The hard reality is that most health plans and delivery systems lack complete REL data — large shares of patients have missing or unrecorded race and ethnicity. This is the equity version of the data-quality problem that runs through this curriculum: the information that would reveal disparities is simply not there, hampering efforts to monitor utilization, track quality by group, and target interventions.

When self-reported data is incomplete, organizations use indirect estimation. The standard method is BISG — Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding, developed by RAND — which combines the probability of race/ethnicity from a person's surname (using Census surname data) with the racial/ethnic composition of their neighborhood (Census geocoding) to estimate likely race/ethnicity. It is reasonably accurate at the group level, with C-statistics around 0.93 to 0.94 for major groups.

But BISG carries a crucial limitation that must be respected: it is designed to estimate disparities at the GROUP or population level, not to classify any specific individual's race. Its individual-level accuracy (sensitivity and predictive value) is far lower than its group-level performance. So BISG is appropriate for measuring population disparities and targeting community-level interventions — but using it to label an individual patient's race would be both inaccurate and ethically fraught. Indirect estimation is a stopgap for population analysis, never a substitute for asking the patient.

body.message: Indirect estimation methods like BISG estimate race/ethnicity well at the group level (for measuring population disparities) but are far less accurate for any single person. Using BISG to classify an individual patient's race is inaccurate and ethically problematic. It is a population-analysis stopgap when self-reported data is missing — not a replacement for asking patients directly.
body.title: BISG Is for Populations, Not Individuals

children.text: Beyond Race: Language, SDOH, and Intersections

Equity stratification is not limited to race and ethnicity. Language is a powerful and actionable axis — patients with limited English proficiency face real barriers, and stratifying by preferred language reveals gaps that language-access services (interpreters, translated materials) can directly close. This is why the "L" in REL matters as much as the R and E.

Social determinants and social risk factors (the SDOH and Z-code data from the determinants lesson) are equally important stratification axes — income, housing instability, food insecurity, disability, geography. And as the Clinical Quality Measurement course emphasized, disparities often live at the INTERSECTION of factors: stratifying by race alone, or income alone, can understate a gap that only appears when you cross them (e.g., race by dual-eligibility). The richer and more standardized the data, the more precisely a population health program can locate its inequities.

The practical upshot is that equity stratification draws on the whole data infrastructure built earlier in this course — REL data, language, SDOH/Z codes — and slices the population's metrics along all of them, looking especially at intersections, to find where care is falling short for whom.

body.content:
A population health program reports an overall hypertension-control rate of 68%, which meets its target. Stratified by race and preferred language, it discovers control is 78% among English-speaking White patients but only 52% among Spanish-speaking Hispanic patients.
The aggregate hid a 26-point gap. Now visible, it points to a concrete fix: Spanish-language self-measured-BP education and interpreter-supported care management for that subgroup — equity stratification turning an invisible disparity into a targeted intervention.
body.title: Finding a Hidden Disparity by Stratifying

children.text: From Seeing to Closing the Gap

Stratification only diagnoses; it does not treat. Seeing a disparity is the necessary first step, but the value comes from acting on it — directing population health resources to the lagging subgroups and tracking whether the gap narrows. The equity-focused quality improvement principles from the Clinical Quality Measurement course apply directly: put the disparity itself on the dashboard as a tracked metric, and judge success by whether it shrinks, not just whether the average rises.

This guards against a real failure mode: a program can improve its overall metrics while the gap widens, if its interventions reach the already-advantaged faster than the disadvantaged. Population health, with its proactive outreach and care management, is well-positioned to prevent this — by deliberately targeting the subgroups stratification flags as behind, rather than letting improvement flow to whoever is easiest to reach.

The throughline is that equity is not a separate program bolted onto population health — it is woven through every step. Risk stratification should consider equity; care management should be deployed to close disparities; chronic-disease and behavioral programs should be designed to reach the groups faring worst. Stratification is the lens that makes all of this visible and actionable. The next lesson covers community health workers — one of the most effective tools for actually reaching and closing gaps in underserved populations.

A practical equity-stratification routine for any population health program: collect standardized self-reported REL (supplemented by careful population-level indirect estimation where needed), stratify every key metric by race, ethnicity, language, and social risk — including intersections — put the gaps on the dashboard, target resources to the lagging groups, and re-measure to confirm the disparities are actually closing.

children.text: The Average Hides the Inequity

Every measure so far in this course produces a single number for an organization — one breast-cancer-screening rate, one blood-pressure-control rate. That single number is an average across everyone the measure covers. And an average, by design, hides variation. A hospital with an excellent overall score can still be delivering very different care to different groups of patients.

This is the core insight of equity-focused measurement: an aggregate measure can look fine while masking serious disparities underneath. If care is excellent for one population and poor for another, the blended average may land in a perfectly acceptable range — and the inequity stays invisible precisely because no one disaggregated the number.

The remedy is stratification: breaking a measure apart and reporting it separately for different groups — by race, ethnicity, language, and social risk factors. Stratification is how a hidden disparity becomes a visible, addressable problem. It connects directly to "equity," the sixth IOM aim from the first lesson of this course.

Stratification means reporting a quality measure separately for different patient groups (by race, ethnicity, language, social risk) instead of as one average — revealing disparities that an aggregate score hides.
Why the Aggregate Fails — A Concrete Example

The power of stratification is easiest to see in real data. CMS's Office of Minority Health publishes stratified reports of Medicare performance, and they repeatedly show gaps that the overall numbers conceal.

In one CMS analysis, stratifying a measure by both race and dual-eligibility (a marker of low income) at the same time revealed a 24 percentage-point gap between subgroups: White non-dual enrollees had the highest rate (about 70.6 percent) while Black dual-eligible enrollees had the lowest (about 46.8 percent). A single average would have buried that entire 24-point spread inside one unremarkable-looking number.

Crucially, that gap only appeared when race and dual status were crossed together. Stratifying by race alone, or income alone, understated it. This is the intersectionality point: disparities often live at the intersection of factors, so the way you slice the data determines what you can see.

children.text: You Cannot Stratify Without the Data

Stratification has a hard prerequisite: you must have data on the characteristics you want to stratify by. The foundational requirement is race, ethnicity, and language (REL) data, ideally collected directly from patients in a standardized way. Without REL data, the disparity is real but unmeasurable.

In practice, REL data is often incomplete or missing — the same data-quality problem from the previous lesson, now with equity stakes. When self-reported data is unavailable, organizations sometimes estimate race and ethnicity indirectly; for HEDIS, for example, CMS has estimated group membership by combining administrative data, surname analysis, and residential location (geocoding).

Indirect estimation is a stopgap, not a substitute — it introduces error and can misclassify individuals. The durable solution is collecting accurate self-reported REL and social-risk data directly, which is why this is a major focus of equity work and why CMS and Medicaid are increasingly moving to require standardized collection of race, ethnicity, language, disability status, and related factors.

body.message: You can only stratify by characteristics you actually record. Missing or low-quality race/ethnicity/language data means disparities exist but stay invisible. Indirect estimation (surname, geocoding) is a stopgap that introduces error — self-reported standardized data is the real fix.
body.title: No REL Data, No Disparity Measurement

children.text: Beyond Race: Social Risk and SDOH

Equity stratification is not limited to race and ethnicity. Social determinants of health (SDOH) and social risk factors — income, housing instability, food insecurity, disability status, geography, dual-eligibility — are powerful axes for revealing disparities, and often interact with race.

The CMS example above used dual-eligibility as a proxy for low income, and it was the combination with race that exposed the largest gap. Increasingly, quality programs stratify by social risk factors and compare subgroup performance to benchmarks, because where a disparity is driven by social conditions, the improvement strategy differs from one driven by, say, clinical access.

This is also why SDOH data collection (screening for housing, food, transportation needs) and standardized coding of those needs matter for measurement, not just for care. The richer and more standardized the social-risk data, the more precisely an organization can locate and target the inequities in its care.

children.text: From Visibility to Accountability

Stratification is moving from optional analysis to required practice. CMS has built health-equity stratified reporting into its programs, and Medicaid and CHIP have moved toward making standardized, stratifiable quality measures mandatory — including collecting a core set of demographic and social-risk metrics specifically to identify and address disparities.

This shift matters because what is required gets done. As long as stratification was voluntary, many organizations reported only the aggregate and never saw their internal gaps. Mandating disaggregated reporting forces the inequities into view, which is the necessary first step toward closing them.

But stratification only diagnoses; it does not treat. Seeing a 24-point gap tells you a problem exists, not how to fix it — and, as the next lesson explores, it raises a thorny technical question about whether and how to risk-adjust for social factors. Stratification is the indispensable first move of equity-focused quality measurement: you cannot close a gap you refuse to look at.
An aggregate quality score can be entirely acceptable and still conceal a population receiving far worse care. Stratification is how the field stops hiding behind the average.

children.text: Beyond Individual Prejudice

When most people hear the word "racism," they picture individual bigotry — a specific person holding and acting on explicit prejudice. That is interpersonal racism, and it is real. But it is not the main engine of health disparities. Structural racism refers to the totality of ways in which societies foster discrimination through mutually reinforcing systems — housing, education, employment, criminal justice, credit, and health care — that systematically advantage some groups and disadvantage others, often with no individual intending harm.

The distinction is not academic. If health disparities were caused mainly by a handful of prejudiced individuals, the solution would be to identify and remove those individuals. But structural racism operates through ordinary, "race-neutral" rules and the accumulated weight of historical policy. A mortgage map drawn in 1937, a school funded by local property taxes, a highway routed through a particular neighborhood — none of these requires a bigot in the room to produce racially patterned harm decades later.

For the health workforce, this reframing changes what counts as the problem and what counts as a solution. Good intentions and personal fairness are necessary but nowhere near sufficient. Reducing disparities requires examining the systems — admission criteria, algorithms, referral patterns, neighborhood investment — that produce unequal outcomes regardless of anyone's intent.

Structural racism is produced by interlocking systems and historical policy, not primarily by individual prejudice. That is why personal good intentions, while necessary, cannot by themselves close health gaps.
Redlining: A Policy Whose Maps Still Predict Health

In 1933, during the Great Depression, Congress created the Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) to refinance mortgages and stem foreclosures. Beginning in 1935, as part of its City Survey project (which ran through 1940), the HOLC produced color-coded "residential security maps" of more than 200 cities, grading neighborhoods for lending risk: A ("Best," outlined green), B ("Still Desirable," blue), C ("Declining," yellow), and D ("Hazardous," outlined red).

The grading was explicitly racial. Neighborhoods with Black residents — and often any non-white or immigrant population — were routinely marked red and deemed hazardous for lending, regardless of housing quality. Being "redlined" meant residents could not obtain the mortgages that built intergenerational wealth for white families in the green and blue zones. The maps codified and accelerated residential segregation and disinvestment.

The remarkable and disturbing finding of modern research is how well those 1930s maps still predict health today, more than 80 years later. Studies overlaying HOLC grades on current health data find that formerly redlined neighborhoods have lower life expectancy and higher rates of asthma, diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, and poor mental health. The mechanism runs through concentrated poverty, environmental hazard siting, lack of green space, and chronic stress — the durable physical legacy of a discriminatory credit policy.

body.content:
Researchers have linked HOLC grades to modern outcomes across many US cities. One national analysis found life expectancy roughly 3.6 years lower on average in historically redlined (grade D) communities versus the highest-graded (grade A) communities, with one study measuring an average drop from about 80.5 years in grade-A tracts to 75.7 years in grade-D tracts.
Asthma is a striking marker: prevalence rose from about 8.6% in grade-A tracts to 10.7% in grade-D tracts, and redlined neighborhoods show elevated rates of asthma-related emergency department visits. The maps were drawn for credit, but they ended up describing who breathes clean air and who lives longest.
body.title: HOLC Redlining and Present-Day Health

children.text: How Structure Becomes Biology

A reasonable question is how a policy from the 1930s, long since formally abolished, can still register in someone's blood pressure or birth weight today. The answer is that structural disadvantage operates through concrete, measurable pathways — it does not require ongoing intentional discrimination to keep producing harm.

Wealth is the clearest channel. Home equity is the primary way American families build and pass on wealth; denying mortgages to Black families for decades produced a racial wealth gap that persists today and shapes everything downstream — the quality of schools a family can access, the neighborhood they can afford, the financial cushion they have for a health emergency. Environmental exposure is another: redlined and disinvested neighborhoods were disproportionately chosen as sites for highways, industrial facilities, and waste — concentrating air pollution that drives asthma and cardiovascular disease.

Chronic stress is the third pathway, and it connects structural racism back to the social gradient. The physiological wear of living with discrimination, economic precarity, and unsafe environments — sometimes described as "weathering" — accelerates biological aging and contributes to hypertension, preterm birth, and other outcomes. The structure, in other words, gets under the skin.

children.text: Bias Inside the Clinic: The Evidence

Structural racism does not stop at the hospital door. A large body of research documents racial disparities in clinical care — in pain management, diagnostic workups, and treatment recommendations — that persist after controlling for clinical variables, insurance, and disease severity. These are not usually the product of conscious prejudice. They reflect unconscious associations and, in some cases, outright false beliefs that clinicians absorb from the same culture as everyone else.

The most cited evidence is a 2016 study by Hoffman and colleagues, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers surveyed white medical students and residents about false beliefs regarding biological differences between Black and white people — for example, the false claim that Black people's skin is thicker or their nerve endings less sensitive. Half of the sample endorsed at least one such false belief. Those who did rated a Black patient's pain as lower than an identical white patient's and made less accurate treatment recommendations.

The finding is sobering precisely because the participants were trainees in good standing at US medical schools, not extremists. It demonstrates that the inputs to clinical decisions — pain ratings, perceived credibility, presumed risk — can be racially skewed by beliefs the clinician may not even know they hold. This is why individual goodwill is not enough, and why system-level safeguards (standardized protocols, decision support, bias training, and stratified outcome monitoring) matter.

children.text: What This Means for the Health Workforce

Recognizing structural racism reframes the job of reducing disparities. It is not enough to ask clinicians to be kind and fair, though they should be. The leverage points are systemic: where a health system invests, which neighborhoods it serves and how, which algorithms it deploys, how it collects and stratifies data, and whether it audits its own care for racially patterned gaps.

At the individual level, the evidence on implicit bias points toward humility and structure rather than self-congratulation. No clinician is immune to the unconscious associations documented in the research, so the protective measures are procedural: standardized pain protocols that reduce discretion in skewed directions, second looks on referral decisions, and decision support that surfaces guideline-concordant care regardless of who the patient is.

At the organizational level, the redlining evidence argues for treating place as a clinical variable. A patient's ZIP code carries the accumulated history of housing policy and environmental exposure; a system serious about equity uses that information to target outreach, screening, and community investment where structural disadvantage is concentrated — rather than treating every patient as if they started from the same line.

body.message: Awareness of unconscious bias is a starting point, not a solution. Studies show one-off implicit bias trainings rarely change behavior on their own. Durable change comes from pairing awareness with structural safeguards — standardized protocols, decision support, accountability for stratified outcomes — that constrain how much individual discretion can drift in a biased direction.
body.title: Implicit bias training alone is not a fix

children.text: The United States healthcare system stands at a critical juncture. Despite spending significantly more per capita than any other developed nation, outcomes in chronic disease management and life expectancy often lag behind peer countries. To resolve this, we must examine the structural pillars that support the delivery of care: Economics, Policy, and Technology.
I. Economics: Moving Beyond Fee-for-Service

The persistent reliance on Fee-for-Service (FFS) models remains the primary driver of systemic waste. By rewarding volume over value, the system incentivizes acute interventions rather than preventive health. Transitioning to Value-Based Care (VBC) is no longer a choice—it is a fiscal necessity for national solvency.
The challenge is not just that we spend too much, but that the incentives within our economic frameworks are misaligned with the goals of health and longevity.
**STRATEGIC IMPERATIVE:** We must decouple provider revenue from the number of procedures performed and align it with longitudinal patient wellness and population health metrics.

children.text: II. Policy: From Access to Affordability

Policy serves as the architect of the market. While recent years have focused on expanding insurance access, policy must now shift toward controlling the underlying costs of delivery. Fragmentation between federal and state mandates continues to create 'care deserts' and deep inequities.
**STRATEGIC IMPERATIVE:** Legislators must mandate radical price transparency and interoperability standards to shift policy from passive oversight to active market-shaping.

children.text: III. Technology: The Great Efficiency Catalyst

In 2026, AI-driven workflows are finally addressing the administrative tax on clinicians. However, technology without data liquidity is merely an expensive silo. True transformation requires that tools serve the doctor-patient relationship, not further complicate it.
Technology is the lever, but policy and economics are the fulcrum. One cannot lift the burden of the healthcare crisis without the others being perfectly placed.

**STRATEGIC IMPERATIVE:** Technology implementation must prioritize the reduction of clinician burnout by automating back-office functions and enabling real-time, precision diagnostics at the point of care.

children.text: Conclusion

Transformation occurs at the intersection of these three pillars. By legislating economic models that prioritize health and leveraging technology to scale those models, the US can move toward a sustainable and equitable healthcare future.

children.text: A Framework for Thinking About Quality

If you want to measure the quality of care, you first need a way to organize what you are measuring. The dominant framework for doing this was created by one physician-scholar, Avedis Donabedian, and it has shaped quality measurement for more than half a century.

Donabedian first laid out his model in a 1966 article, "Evaluating the Quality of Medical Care," which became one of the most-cited public health articles of the 20th century. His insight was deceptively simple: information about quality can be drawn from three categories — structure, process, and outcome — and these three categories are causally linked.

The linkage is the heart of the model. As Donabedian put it, good structure increases the likelihood of good process, and good process increases the likelihood of good outcome. Understanding which kind of measure you are looking at — and how the three relate — is foundational to everything else in quality measurement.

The Donabedian model organizes quality measurement into three categories — structure, process, and outcome — linked by a chain: good structure makes good process more likely, and good process makes good outcomes more likely.
Structure: The Conditions of Care

Structure measures capture the relatively stable characteristics of the providers and the environment in which care is delivered — the context, not the care itself. Donabedian defined structure as the stable attributes of the settings where care happens.

Concrete examples include the physical plant (hospital buildings and equipment), human resources (staffing levels, nurse-to-patient ratios, clinician credentials), and organizational features (financing, governance, whether the hospital uses a certified electronic health record). These are things you can often verify without watching a single patient encounter.

Structure measures are easy to assess and relatively stable over time, which makes them attractive. Their weakness is that they are the furthest removed from the patient. A hospital can have excellent facilities and well-credentialed staff and still deliver poor care — good structure makes good care more likely, but does not guarantee it.

For this reason, structure measures are often treated as necessary preconditions rather than proof of quality. They answer the question "is the capacity for good care in place?" — not "did good care actually happen?"
Process: What Was Actually Done

Process measures capture the transactions between patients and providers — what clinicians actually do during care. They answer the question "are we doing the things we say we should do?" Process measures assess whether evidence-based care was properly applied.

Examples are everywhere in quality programs: the share of diabetic patients who received an eye exam, the percentage of heart-attack patients given aspirin on arrival, whether a patient was screened for depression, or the time between a discharge order and the patient actually leaving. Each captures a specific, controllable step in the care process.

Process measures have a major practical advantage: they are directly actionable and largely within the provider's control. If a process measure is low, the team usually knows exactly what to fix. They also require little or no risk adjustment, because they measure what clinicians did rather than how sick the patients were — which is why many quality programs lean heavily on process measures.
