body.title: Process vs. Outcome Measures

children.text: Outcome: The Result for the Patient

Outcome measures capture the effects of care on the health status of patients and populations — the results that ultimately matter. Examples include surgical-site infection rates, 30-day mortality, hospital readmissions, functional status, and patient-reported quality of life.

Donabedian called outcomes the "ultimate validators" of the quality of care, and intuitively they are what everyone cares about. But outcome measures carry two serious complications. First, outcomes have time lags and are often influenced by many factors beyond any single provider — a 30-day readmission depends not just on hospital care but on the patient's other conditions, medication adherence, and social circumstances.

Second, because they reflect patient mix, outcome measures usually require risk adjustment — statistical correction for how sick the patients were — to be compared fairly. Without it, a hospital that treats sicker patients looks worse even if its care is excellent. Risk adjustment promotes fair comparison, but it is technically difficult and, done poorly, can itself distort incentives.

body.message: Because outcomes are high-stakes, they are more vulnerable to gaming than process or structure measures. A classic example: a measure tracking patient falls led some facilities to confine patients to bed, reducing falls but harming recovery. Measuring the right outcome — and watching for perverse responses — is essential.
body.title: Outcome Measures Can Be Gamed

children.text: Balancing Measures and Using the Framework

Modern quality improvement adds a fourth practical category that does not fit neatly into Donabedian's triad: balancing measures. A balancing measure watches for unintended consequences — checking that improving one thing did not quietly worsen another.

For example, a team working to reduce hospital length of stay might track 30-day readmissions as a balancing measure, to make sure faster discharges are not simply sending patients home too soon. Balancing measures guard against the "whack-a-mole" risk that optimizing a single metric creates a new problem elsewhere.

In practice, robust quality programs use a mix of all these measure types. Structure confirms the foundation is in place, process shows whether the right care was delivered, outcomes validate whether patients actually benefited, and balancing measures catch side effects. No single type tells the whole story — the art of measurement is combining them into a coherent picture.

body.content:
Consider sepsis care. A structure measure might be whether the hospital has a 24/7 rapid-response team. A process measure is the share of septic patients who received antibiotics within the first hour. An outcome measure is sepsis mortality.
A balancing measure might track unnecessary antibiotic use, ensuring the drive for speed does not fuel antibiotic overuse. Together they show whether good structure led to good process and ultimately to good outcomes — exactly the chain Donabedian described.
body.title: The Donabedian Chain in Action

children.text: What Is a Substance Use Disorder?

A substance use disorder (SUD) is a medical condition in which the recurrent use of alcohol or drugs causes clinically significant impairment — including health problems, disability, and failure to meet responsibilities at work, school, or home. It is not a moral failing or a simple lack of willpower. The leading federal science agency, the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), defines addiction as a chronic, relapsing brain disease characterized by compulsive drug seeking and use despite harmful consequences.

The DSM-5-TR diagnoses substance use disorders using 11 criteria, spanning impaired control (using more than intended, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, craving), social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological signs (tolerance and withdrawal). Severity is graded by how many criteria a person meets: 2–3 indicates a mild disorder, 4–5 moderate, and 6 or more severe. A severe substance use disorder is what most people mean by "addiction."

Framing SUDs as chronic medical conditions — similar to diabetes or hypertension in that they involve relapse, require ongoing management, and respond to treatment — reshapes how the health system should respond. It points toward long-term, evidence-based treatment rather than short-term punishment or one-time detox.

A substance use disorder is a diagnosable medical condition graded mild (2–3 criteria), moderate (4–5), or severe (6+) on 11 DSM-5-TR criteria. NIDA classifies addiction as a chronic, relapsing brain disease — not a moral failing.

children.text: Alcohol: The Most Common Substance Use Disorder

Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is by far the most prevalent substance use disorder in the United States. In 2023, an estimated 28.9 million people aged 12 or older — about 10.2% of that population — had an alcohol use disorder. Because alcohol is legal, socially accepted, and widely available, AUD is frequently underestimated and underdiagnosed.

Alcohol’s health toll is broad: it contributes to liver disease, several cancers, cardiovascular disease, injuries, and tens of thousands of deaths each year, in addition to the direct harms of dependence. Yet because heavy drinking is normalized, many people with AUD never see it as a treatable medical problem.

Effective treatments exist, including FDA-approved medications (such as naltrexone and acamprosate) alongside behavioral therapies and mutual-support programs. As with mental illness, the central challenge is not the absence of effective treatment but the failure to connect people to it.
Alcohol use disorder is the single most common substance use disorder — about 28.9 million people aged 12+ in 2023 — yet because alcohol is legal and normalized, it is widely underdiagnosed.
Opioids and the Overdose Crisis

Opioids — a class that includes prescription painkillers, heroin, and illicitly manufactured fentanyl — are at the center of the deadliest drug crisis in U.S. history. About 5 million adults had an opioid use disorder in the past year in 2023. While that is far fewer than have alcohol use disorder, opioids account for a hugely disproportionate share of overdose deaths.

The crisis has unfolded in waves: first prescription opioids, then heroin, and since around 2013 a third wave driven by illicitly manufactured fentanyl — a synthetic opioid roughly 50–100 times more potent than morphine. In 2023, synthetic opioids (primarily fentanyl) were involved in the large majority of opioid overdose deaths, with nearly 73,000 deaths involving synthetic opioids other than methadone.

The total death toll is staggering but recently improving. There were an estimated 107,543 drug overdose deaths in the United States in 2023 — the first annual decline since 2018 — and provisional data show deaths fell sharply again in 2024, to roughly 80,000, a nearly 27% drop. The improvement is real but uneven, and fentanyl remains the dominant driver of overdose mortality.

children.text: Beyond Opioids and Alcohol

Substance use disorders also involve stimulants (methamphetamine and cocaine), cannabis, sedatives, and other drugs. Stimulant-related deaths have risen in recent years, often in combination with fentanyl — a pattern sometimes called "polysubstance" overdose, where more than one drug is involved.

Cannabis use disorder is increasingly recognized as legalization expands access; while cannabis is far less lethal than opioids, a meaningful share of regular users develop a disorder marked by impaired control and continued use despite problems. The key clinical point is that the same DSM-5-TR framework — impaired control, social impairment, risky use, tolerance and withdrawal — applies across substances.

Polysubstance use complicates both diagnosis and treatment and is a major reason that overdose deaths have been so hard to reduce: reversing one drug’s effects may not address the others involved. Treatment systems increasingly have to address whole patterns of use rather than a single substance.

body.content:
CDC data show that as the fentanyl wave grew, overdose deaths increasingly involved fentanyl combined with stimulants such as methamphetamine or cocaine.
This polysubstance pattern means harm-reduction and treatment can no longer assume a single drug is involved — a person may need treatment addressing both opioid and stimulant use at once.
body.title: The Rise of Polysubstance Overdose

children.text: Treatment Works — When People Can Reach It

Despite the grim death tolls, substance use disorders are treatable. For opioid use disorder in particular, medications for opioid use disorder (methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone) are the gold-standard, evidence-based treatment and substantially reduce overdose death and improve survival. Alcohol use disorder likewise has effective medications and therapies.

Yet the treatment gap is enormous. Of the 48.5 million people aged 12 or older with a substance use disorder in 2023, only about 15.6% received any treatment, leaving more than 41 million people untreated. Stigma, criminalization, cost, and a shortage of treatment capacity all contribute.

Understanding SUDs as chronic, treatable medical conditions — not crimes or character flaws — is the foundation for the treatment-system and integration topics in the rest of this course. The later tracks on the ASAM criteria, opioid treatment programs, and Vermont’s Hub-and-Spoke model are all responses to this same challenge: how to actually deliver effective treatment at scale.
Substance use disorders are chronic, treatable medical conditions — yet in 2023 fewer than one in six people with an SUD received any treatment.

children.text: The Cycle, Step by Step

The previous lesson described the revenue cycle in three broad phases — front-end, mid-cycle, and back-end. This lesson zooms in to the individual steps that make up those phases, giving you the end-to-end map of how a single patient encounter becomes collected revenue.

A note on numbering: different sources count the revenue cycle in anywhere from 7 to 13 steps, depending on how finely they slice the work. The exact count is not sacred — what matters is understanding the sequence and how each step depends on the one before it. This lesson uses a clean 10-step framework that captures the essential flow.

The single most important principle to carry through all ten steps is that they are a chain. Each step hands off to the next, and an error early in the chain (a wrong insurance ID at registration) silently propagates downstream and often surfaces only as a denied claim weeks later. Getting the early steps right is far cheaper than fixing the late ones.

The revenue cycle is a sequential chain from scheduling to collection. Sources count 7-13 steps; what matters is the flow and the dependencies — early errors propagate downstream and become expensive denials.
Steps 1-3: Getting the Patient in the Door (Front-End)

Step 1 is scheduling and pre-registration. Before the visit, the practice captures the patient's demographic and insurance information — ideally in real time while the patient is still on the phone — so problems can be caught early. Step 2 is registration, where that information is confirmed and completed at check-in.

Step 3 is eligibility verification and prior authorization. The provider confirms with the insurer that the patient's coverage is active and that the planned service is covered, and obtains prior authorization for services that require the payer's advance approval. This step is the front line of denial prevention: services delivered to an ineligible patient or without required authorization are frequently never paid.

These first three steps are deceptively important. They generate no clinical care and feel like paperwork, but they determine whether the eventual claim has any chance of being paid. The industry rule of thumb is that the cheapest denial to fix is the one prevented here, before the patient is ever seen.

children.text: Steps 4-6: Turning Care Into a Bill (Mid-Cycle)

Step 4 is clinical documentation: the provider records what was assessed and done during the visit. This is the raw material for everything financial that follows — if it is not documented, it cannot be coded or billed. Step 5 is medical coding, where certified coders translate the documented diagnoses and services into standardized codes (ICD-10 for diagnoses, CPT and HCPCS for procedures and services).

Step 6 is charge capture: the coded services are recorded as charges in the billing system, ensuring the provider bills for everything that was actually performed. Missed charge capture is pure lost revenue — care delivered but never billed — while incorrect charges drive denials.

This mid-cycle trio is where clinical care literally becomes money. It is also where accuracy is hardest and most consequential: the codes and charges generated here are exactly what the payer scrutinizes. Good documentation, accurate coding, and complete charge capture together determine both whether the claim is paid and whether it is paid the correct amount.

children.text: Steps 7-10: Getting Paid (Back-End)

Step 7 is claim submission. The charges are assembled into a claim, "scrubbed" (checked for errors before it goes out), and submitted to the payer — usually through a clearinghouse. A claim that arrives clean gets paid much faster than one that arrives with errors.

Step 8 is payment posting and remittance. When the payer adjudicates the claim, it sends back a remittance (an electronic remittance advice, or the patient-facing explanation of benefits) showing what it paid, adjusted, or denied; the provider posts those payments to the patient's account. Step 9 is denial management and appeals: analyzing why claims were denied, correcting and resubmitting them, and appealing when the denial is wrong.

Step 10 is accounts receivable follow-up and patient collections: chasing unpaid balances still sitting with insurers (third-party follow-up) and billing patients for whatever portion they owe. The cycle "closes" only when the full balance is collected or written off. Then, with the next encounter, it begins again — which is why it is called a cycle, not a line.

children.text: Why the Chain Matters

The power of viewing RCM as a 10-step chain is that it reveals where revenue actually leaks. A denial at step 9 is almost never really a step-9 problem — it usually traces back to a missed verification at step 3, weak documentation at step 4, or a coding error at step 5. The back-end is where problems become visible, but the front-end and mid-cycle are where they are created.

This is why high-performing organizations push effort "upstream." Preventing a denial at registration costs a fraction of reworking it after the fact, and a clean claim avoids the entire expensive cycle of denial, appeal, and follow-up. The whole discipline of RCM is largely about catching errors as early in the chain as possible.

Each remaining lesson in this course examines one or more of these steps in depth — verification, prior authorization, coding, clean claims, denials, appeals, payment posting, AR, collections, and the technology that ties them together. Keep this 10-step map in mind as the backbone; everything else hangs off it.

body.message: Denials surface at the back of the cycle but are typically created at the front — a wrong insurance ID, a missing authorization, a documentation gap, or a coding error. Fixing problems upstream is far cheaper than reworking them downstream, which is why RCM pushes effort toward the front of the chain.
body.title: A Back-End Denial Is Usually a Front-End Failure

children.text: The Number an ACO Lives or Dies By

The previous lesson showed that an ACO earns savings by keeping spending below a benchmark. This lesson is about the spending itself: total cost of care (TCOC), the single number that determines whether a value-based organization succeeds or fails financially. If population health is the method and the ACO is the contract, TCOC is the scoreboard.

Total cost of care is a holistic view of all healthcare spending for an entire population over a period — inpatient, outpatient, professional, pharmacy, and ancillary services, everything. It is typically expressed as a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month (PMPM) figure, so populations of different sizes and health profiles can be compared fairly. The HealthPartners TCOC framework is a widely used standard for measuring it.

The discipline of managing TCOC is different from managing a single disease or a single patient. It requires zooming out to the whole population's spending, finding where the money actually goes, and pulling the levers that reduce avoidable cost without harming care. This lesson covers where the cost concentrates and how to manage it down.

Total cost of care (TCOC) is all healthcare spending for a population over a period — inpatient, outpatient, professional, pharmacy, ancillary — usually expressed as a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month (PMPM) figure. It is the scoreboard for value-based success.
PMPM and Risk Adjustment

The standard unit of TCOC is per member per month (PMPM): total healthcare spending divided by the number of member-months in the population. PMPM normalizes cost to a comparable per-person, per-month figure, which is how value-based contracts, budgets, and benchmarks are expressed. A population's PMPM is the headline number leaders watch.

But raw PMPM is misleading without risk adjustment, because populations differ in how sick they are. A practice serving older, sicker patients will have a higher PMPM than one serving young, healthy patients — not because it is wasteful, but because its patients are genuinely more costly. Risk adjustment (the HCC/RAF methods from the risk-stratification lesson) corrects for this, so a risk-adjusted PMPM reflects efficiency rather than just patient mix.

This connects directly to the equity and risk-adjustment debates elsewhere in the curriculum: how you risk-adjust shapes whether comparisons are fair, and poorly done risk adjustment can either penalize those serving the sickest or mask real inefficiency. For TCOC management, the practical point is that you manage the risk-adjusted number — comparing your population's cost to what it "should" be given its risk, then attacking the gap.

children.text: Where the Money Actually Goes

Managing TCOC starts with knowing where cost concentrates — and it concentrates dramatically, echoing the risk-stratification lesson. High-cost claimants (HiCCs) are a tiny fraction of the population but a huge share of spend: patients with $100,000+ in annual claims are under 1 percent of claimants but nearly 30 percent of total medical and pharmacy expense, and the very highest-cost claimants (over $250,000/year) are around 0.16 percent of the insured population yet about 9 percent of all healthcare costs.

A second concentrated and fast-growing driver is specialty pharmacy. Specialty drugs are only about 2 percent of prescriptions but often drive 50 percent or more of total pharmacy spend. A small number of patients on high-cost specialty and infused medications can dominate a population's pharmacy budget, and this spend is growing rapidly — making pharmacy management a central TCOC concern, not an afterthought.

A third driver is avoidable acute utilization, especially emergency department visits. An estimated 18 million avoidable ED visits occur each year, and treating the same problem in the ED is roughly 3 to 10 times more expensive than in urgent care, primary care, or telehealth. Each prevented avoidable ED visit can save on the order of $1,500 to $3,000. Knowing this map — high-cost claimants, specialty pharmacy, avoidable acute care — tells you exactly where to aim TCOC management.

children.text: The Levers to Pull

With the cost map in hand, TCOC management deploys specific levers at each concentration. For high-cost claimants, the lever is intensive care management — the population health toolkit aimed at the highest tier of the pyramid, preventing the complications and acute events that drive their cost (often combined with case-by-case review of these expensive patients).

For specialty pharmacy, the levers are pharmacy-specific: prior authorization and step therapy to ensure appropriate use, biosimilar adoption (lower-cost versions of biologic drugs), rebate negotiation, and especially site-of-care steerage. Site-of-care steerage means directing where a patient receives an expensive infusion — a hospital outpatient setting can cost dramatically more than a physician's office or the patient's home for the identical drug. Eliminating site-of-care price differentials for specialty drugs can save in the range of 4 to 36 percent depending on the medication.

For avoidable acute utilization, the levers are the prevention and access strategies from across this course: strong primary care and same-day access so patients do not default to the ED, care management and chronic-disease programs to prevent the crises that lead to admissions, transitional care to prevent readmissions, and patient education on appropriate care settings. The throughline is that almost every TCOC lever is a population health activity from an earlier lesson, now aimed explicitly at the dollars.

body.content:
A patient needs a regular high-cost infused medication. Administered in a hospital outpatient department, it might cost several times more than the identical drug given in a physician's office or at home.
A TCOC program identifies these patients and works with the PBM/medical vendor to steer the infusions to the lower-cost site — saving anywhere from a few percent to a third of the cost per the EBRI estimate, with no change in the actual treatment the patient receives. Same drug, same dose, lower total cost of care.
body.title: Site-of-Care Steerage for an Infusion

children.text: Managing Cost Without Harming Care

The defining discipline of TCOC management is reducing cost without reducing necessary care — and the distinction is everything. The legitimate target is avoidable, low-value spending: the preventable admission, the duplicate test, the ED visit that should have been a primary care visit, the specialty drug given in a needlessly expensive setting. Cutting these improves value. Cutting necessary care to hit a number is both unethical and, in a value-based contract with a quality gate, financially self-defeating.

This is why TCOC is always managed alongside quality. An ACO that lowers its PMPM by skimping on care will fail its quality measures and forfeit savings (and harm patients). The right framing is efficiency: deliver the same or better outcomes at lower cost by eliminating waste, not by withholding value. Risk adjustment and quality gates are the guardrails that keep TCOC management honest.

TCOC ties the financial story of this course together. Population health's clinical activities — risk stratification, care management, chronic-disease programs, prevention — all ultimately express themselves in this one risk-adjusted PMPM number. Master where cost concentrates and which levers move it without harming care, and you have the financial discipline that makes value-based population health sustainable. The final module turns to ensuring all of this reaches everyone equitably, and to measuring whether it actually works.

body.message: The only legitimate way to reduce total cost of care is to eliminate avoidable, low-value spending — preventable admissions, duplicate tests, misplaced sites of care — never necessary care. In a value-based contract, skimping on care fails the quality gate and forfeits savings anyway. Risk adjustment and quality measures are the guardrails that keep TCOC management honest.
body.title: Lower Cost by Cutting Waste, Not Care

children.text: The United States healthcare system stands at a critical juncture. Despite spending significantly more per capita than any other developed nation, the outcomes—ranging from life expectancy to chronic disease management—often lag behind peer countries. To understand this paradox, we must look beyond the symptoms and examine the structural pillars that support, and sometimes undermine, the delivery of care: Economics, Policy, and Technology.
The challenge is not just that we spend too much, but that the incentives within our economic and policy frameworks are misaligned with the goals of health and longevity.
Section 1: The Economic Paradox of Fee-for-Service

For decades, the US healthcare economy has been dominated by the fee-for-service (FFS) model. In this environment, volume is rewarded over value. Health systems are economically incentivized to perform more procedures and fill more beds rather than keeping populations healthy. This 'sick-care' economy creates a massive administrative burden, as payers and providers engage in a constant tug-of-war over reimbursement and medical necessity.

children.text: Section 2: Policy as the Architect of Accessibility

Policy serves as the rulebook for the healthcare market. From the Affordable Care Act (ACA) to more recent shifts in Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement, legislative decisions dictate who gets care and at what cost. However, policy often lags behind market realities. Fragmentation between federal and state-level mandates creates 'care deserts' and significant disparities in health equity.

In 2025, we are seeing AI-driven clinical workflows and precision medicine move from theoretical to practical application. Yet, technology without interoperability is merely an expensive silo. The challenge remains integrating these tools so they reduce clinician burnout rather than adding to the data fatigue.

children.text: Two Questions: What and Why

Cheap sequencing made genetic testing feasible, but "a genetic test" is not one thing. To use genetics in medicine you must understand two distinct dimensions: WHAT the test looks at (how much of the genome, examined how) and WHY it is being done (the clinical purpose). Confusing these is a common source of error — the right test depends on both.

This lesson maps both dimensions: the technical methods (from a single gene up to the whole genome) and the clinical purposes (diagnostic, predictive, carrier, pharmacogenomic). And it addresses the increasingly important question of direct-to-consumer testing versus clinical-grade testing, which differ in ways that matter enormously for patients.

The practical goal is to be able to reason about which test fits a clinical situation, what it can and cannot tell you, and how to interpret what comes back. A genetic test ordered or interpreted incorrectly can mislead a patient about their health, their cancer treatment, or their family — so understanding the test landscape is foundational clinical knowledge.

A genetic test has two dimensions: WHAT it examines (single gene up to whole genome) and WHY (diagnostic, predictive, carrier, or pharmacogenomic). The right test depends on both, and clinical-grade testing differs importantly from direct-to-consumer tests.
How Much of the Genome: The Methods

Tests differ in how much DNA they examine, trading focus for breadth. Single-gene testing looks at one specific gene — ideal when a condition has distinctive features and a known causative gene (e.g., testing the HBB gene for sickle cell disease, or testing a relative for a known familial variant). It is precise and inexpensive but blind to everything else.

Gene panels examine a defined set of genes — from a few to many hundreds — chosen because they could all explain a particular presentation (e.g., a hereditary-cancer panel, or a cardiomyopathy panel). Panels are the workhorse for conditions that can be caused by many genes. Going broader, whole exome sequencing (WES) reads the exome — only about 1 to 2 percent of the genome, but the protein-coding portion that harbors roughly 85 percent of known disease-causing variants — making it an efficient catch-all when the causative gene is unknown.

Whole genome sequencing (WGS) reads essentially all the DNA, coding and non-coding, providing the most complete picture; it is used when a strong genetic suspicion remains unexplained by WES. Separately, chromosomal microarray (CMA) detects large deletions, duplications, and copy-number changes (with higher detection than the older karyotype), and karyotyping visualizes whole-chromosome abnormalities. CMA and karyotype are mainstays of prenatal and developmental diagnosis. The general principle: start as targeted as the clinical question allows, and broaden only as needed.

code.Best_For: Distinctive condition with known gene; testing relatives
Conditions caused by many possible genes

body.title: Genetic Test Methods by Breadth

children.text: Why the Test: The Clinical Purposes

The same sequencing technology serves very different clinical purposes, and the purpose shapes interpretation and counseling. Diagnostic testing seeks to confirm or rule out a suspected genetic condition in a symptomatic patient — answering "what does this person have?" Predictive (or presymptomatic) testing assesses future risk in a currently healthy person — for example, testing for a BRCA variant to gauge future cancer risk, or for a known familial condition.

Carrier testing identifies whether a healthy person carries a recessive variant they could pass to children even though they are unaffected themselves (relevant to cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, Tay-Sachs, and others) — central to reproductive planning. And pharmacogenomic testing examines genes affecting drug metabolism to guide medication choice and dosing (the subject of the next lesson).

These purposes carry different stakes and counseling needs. A diagnostic result explains current illness; a predictive result delivers risk information about a future that may never come, with profound psychological and family implications; a carrier result matters mainly for reproduction; a pharmacogenomic result guides prescribing. The same BRCA variant means different things tested diagnostically in a cancer patient versus predictively in their healthy sibling. Matching the purpose to the situation — and counseling appropriately — is as important as choosing the right method.

children.text: Clinical-Grade vs. Direct-to-Consumer

A patient may arrive with results from a direct-to-consumer (DTC) test like 23andMe, and understanding how these differ from clinical testing is essential. DTC tests are ordered by the consumer without a clinician, and report a mix of ancestry, traits, and FDA-authorized health information (some disease-risk variants, carrier status, and pharmacogenomic findings). In 2018, 23andMe became the first company to receive FDA marketing authorization for DTC health-related tests.

But DTC tests have critical limitations that patients often misunderstand. They do not diagnose conditions — they identify predispositions, not certainties. They examine only specific, pre-selected variants, so they miss rare or novel variants in the same genes (a DTC BRCA test checks only a few variants and can give false reassurance to someone who actually carries a different pathogenic BRCA variant). And their accuracy and relevance vary by ancestry, because the variants tested were studied largely in particular populations.

The practical guidance: DTC results should not be acted on clinically without confirmation by a clinical-grade test and professional interpretation. A reassuring DTC result does not rule out a condition, and a concerning one must be verified before any medical decision. Clinical-grade testing — ordered and interpreted by professionals, often with genetic counseling — is the standard for any result that will drive care.

body.message: DTC tests check only a few pre-selected variants, so a "negative" result can falsely reassure someone who carries a different pathogenic variant the test did not look for. DTC results identify predispositions, not diagnoses, and vary in accuracy by ancestry. Never act clinically on a DTC result without confirmation by clinical-grade testing and professional interpretation.

children.text: Choosing and Interpreting Tests Well

Putting the dimensions together, choosing a genetic test is a clinical reasoning exercise: define the question (diagnostic, predictive, carrier, pharmacogenomic), then pick the narrowest method that can answer it (single gene or panel if the candidates are known; WES or WGS if not). Broader is not always better — a whole genome generates far more variants of uncertain significance and incidental findings to interpret and counsel about.

Interpretation is where the difficulty lies, as the previous lessons established. Every test result must be read through the ACMG classification lens, and the broader the test, the more uncertain findings (VUS) and unexpected secondary findings it will surface — each requiring careful interpretation and, often, genetic counseling. The test is only the first step; making sense of the result, in the context of the patient and their family, is the harder work.

The throughline is that genetic testing is powerful but must be matched to purpose, chosen at the right breadth, distinguished from consumer testing, and interpreted carefully. With this map of the testing landscape established, the next lessons dive into the major clinical applications — pharmacogenomics, oncology, and hereditary conditions — where these tests are actually put to use to change care.

body.content:
A child presents with unexplained developmental delay and no clear diagnosis. A single-gene test would be a shot in the dark; a clinician might start with chromosomal microarray (to catch copy-number causes) and, if negative, proceed to whole exome sequencing to search broadly for a causative variant.
Contrast this with a healthy adult whose mother carries a known BRCA1 variant: here a targeted single-variant test for that specific familial variant is exactly right — precise, inexpensive, and definitive. Same toolkit, different question, different correct test.
body.title: Matching Test to Question

points: A genetic test has two dimensions: WHAT it examines (breadth) and WHY (clinical purpose); the right test depends on both.

By breadth: single-gene (one gene), panels (a defined set), whole exome (coding ~1-2% but ~85% of known pathogenic variants), whole genome (all DNA), and microarray/karyotype (copy-number/chromosomal).
The principle is to start as targeted as the question allows and broaden only as needed, since broader tests generate more uncertain and incidental findings.

By purpose: diagnostic (confirm illness), predictive (future risk in the healthy), carrier (recessive variants passable to children), and pharmacogenomic (drug response) — each with different stakes and counseling needs.
Direct-to-consumer tests (e.g., 23andMe, FDA-authorized for some health reports in 2018) identify predispositions, not diagnoses, and check only pre-selected variants.
A "negative" DTC result can falsely reassure, accuracy varies by ancestry, and DTC results must be confirmed by clinical-grade testing before driving care.
Interpretation through the ACMG lens is the hard part; broader tests surface more VUS and secondary findings, often requiring genetic counseling.

DTC results identify predispositions, not diagnoses, and should never be acted on (or used for reassurance) without clinical confirmation.

children.text: Pushing Value Down to the Provider

A subtle but important point runs through this entire course: capitating an MCO transfers risk to the plan, but it does not automatically change how that plan pays the doctors and hospitals delivering care. An MCO can receive a capitated, value-oriented payment from the state and then turn around and pay its providers on straight fee-for-service — recreating the very volume incentives managed care was supposed to escape, just one layer down. Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the effort to close that gap: to push value-based payment all the way down from the state, through the MCO, to the providers who actually deliver care.

This matters because the state’s ultimate goal is better care at sustainable cost, and that depends on the incentives facing the people at the bedside, not just the plan’s balance sheet. So states increasingly use their contracts with MCOs to require or encourage the plans to adopt value-based arrangements with their providers — shared savings, bundled payments, capitation, pay-for-performance, and the like. VBP in Medicaid is, in essence, the state using its leverage over MCOs to spread value-based payment throughout the delivery system.

This lesson examines how states drive provider-level value-based payment through their MCOs, the frameworks they use to define it, the targets they set, and the powerful financial mechanism — state directed payments — that increasingly carries these efforts. It connects the risk continuum from the hospital-finance course directly to the Medicaid managed care machinery built throughout this one.

Key Concept: Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the state’s use of its MCO contracts to require or encourage plans to pay their providers through value-based arrangements (shared savings, bundles, capitation, pay-for-performance) — pushing value-based payment from the state, through the plan, to the provider level.

children.text: How States Drive VBP Through MCOs

States generally use two approaches to drive value-based payment through their Medicaid MCOs. The first is setting value-based payment targets — requiring that a certain percentage of an MCO’s provider payments flow through value-based arrangements, without dictating exactly which models. The second is prescriptively directing MCOs to adopt specific payment models — telling plans precisely what kind of value-based arrangement to use. Many states blend the two: setting an overall target while specifying acceptable model types.

The trend is unmistakably toward more requirements. More states are requiring the use of VBP or alternative payment models in the contracts between their MCOs and providers, with roughly 26 states defining the types of VBP model that MCOs must use. This reflects a recognition that simply capitating the MCO is not enough — the state must affirmatively require the plan to transmit value-based incentives to providers, or the plan may default to paying providers in ways that perpetuate volume-driven care.

To make targets concrete, states set saturation targets — the share of MCO payments that must be value-based — and often ramp them up over time. About 19 states have set required minimum saturation targets, and a classic example is Arizona, where the required proportion of MCO revenues in value-based arrangements started at 5% in 2013, rose to 10% in 2014, and climbed to 20% in 2015 and 2016. This gradual ramp gives plans and providers time to build the capabilities value-based payment requires while steadily increasing the pressure to adopt it.

children.text: The HCP-LAN Framework: A Common Language

A challenge in requiring VBP is defining what actually counts as "value-based." Without a common standard, every state and plan might define it differently, making targets meaningless and comparison impossible. To solve this, many states adopt the Health Care Payment Learning & Action Network (HCP-LAN) framework, a widely used classification that sorts payment arrangements into categories by how much they tie payment to value and risk — from pure fee-for-service (Category 1), to fee-for-service linked to quality (Category 2), to alternative payment models built on fee-for-service architecture (Category 3), to population-based payment (Category 4).

The framework gives states a precise vocabulary for their requirements. About 17 states specifically reference the HCP-LAN framework in defining acceptable VBP arrangements, and of those, 10 specify the categories MCOs should use — usually HCP-LAN Category 2C or higher, meaning at least fee-for-service tied to quality and ideally more advanced models. Even states that do not explicitly cite HCP-LAN typically use definitions that align with or overlap its categories. The framework has become the de facto common language for Medicaid VBP, letting a state say exactly how far up the value ladder it expects its plans to push.

This connects directly to the risk continuum from earlier study. HCP-LAN’s categories essentially map the same spectrum — from no risk (fee-for-service) through pay-for-performance and shared savings up to full population-based capitation. When a state requires its MCOs to move providers to "Category 3 or higher," it is requiring them to move providers up the risk continuum into shared savings and beyond. The framework is how that abstract continuum becomes a concrete, measurable contract requirement.
State Directed Payments: The Growing Mechanism

The most consequential and fastest-growing tool for VBP in Medicaid managed care is the state directed payment (SDP). Created when CMS updated the managed care regulations in 2016, SDPs allow a state to direct how its MCOs pay providers — overriding the normal rule that plans set their own provider rates. Through SDPs, a state can require MCOs to use minimum or maximum fee schedules, make uniform rate increases for selected providers, require participation in multi-payer models, or require providers to participate in value-based purchasing arrangements. SDPs are how a state reaches through the MCO to shape provider payment directly.

SDPs have exploded in scale. Between February 2023 and August 2024, CMS approved 302 state directed payment arrangements across 40 states and Puerto Rico, and the arrangements approved as of August 2024 are projected to spend $110.2 billion a year — nearly a 60% increase over the $69.3 billion projected just eighteen months earlier. This staggering growth reflects how central SDPs have become to state Medicaid strategy, both for raising provider payment (often toward Medicare levels) and for advancing value-based and quality goals. The VBP-oriented SDPs tie payments to metrics like patient satisfaction, reduced readmissions, and improved chronic-disease management.

This rapid growth drew regulatory attention. In 2024, CMS released a managed care rule with additional updates intended to improve the oversight and transparency of directed payments — a response to concerns that SDPs were growing so fast, and channeling so much money, that they needed tighter guardrails. States now report a range of evaluation measures for their SDPs, such as hospitalization and readmission rates, utilization and timeliness of preventive and specialty care, and outcomes for common chronic conditions, so the billions flowing through SDPs can be tied to demonstrable results rather than simply raising payments.

body.message: State directed payments let states reach through MCOs to shape provider payment and advance value-based goals, but their explosive growth to $110+ billion a year prompted CMS to tighten oversight and transparency in 2024. The same mechanism that can drive value-based purchasing can also simply inflate payments, which is why CMS is demanding clearer evaluation of what SDPs actually achieve.
body.title: SDPs Are Powerful — and Under Scrutiny

children.text: Why VBP Ties the Course Together

Value-based purchasing is where Medicaid managed care reconnects with the broader value-based-care movement that this body of study began with. Everything earlier in this course built the machinery of managed care — selecting plans, setting rates, ensuring networks and quality, overseeing performance. VBP is the layer that aims that machinery at the ultimate goal: not just transferring risk to plans, but actually changing how care is paid for and delivered all the way to the provider, so that value, not volume, drives the system from top to bottom.

body.analogy: A state requiring VBP through its MCOs is like a parent company that pays its regional managers (the MCOs) a fixed budget and then insists those managers also pay their store employees (providers) based on customer satisfaction and results, not just hours worked. Without that insistence, a regional manager might pocket the efficiency and still pay employees the old way — so the incentive to improve never reaches the front line. VBP requirements, HCP-LAN categories, and state directed payments are the parent company’s way of making sure the new incentives flow all the way down to where the work actually happens.
body.concept: Pushing value-based payment to the provider level

children.text: The honest caveat is that requiring VBP does not guarantee it works. As the hospital-finance course showed, value-based payment’s benefits depend on execution — providers must have the data, scale, and capabilities to manage risk, and shared savings must actually offset lost volume. A state can mandate that 50% of MCO payments be "value-based" and still see little change if the underlying arrangements are weak (mere pay-for-performance bonuses rather than real risk) or if providers lack the infrastructure to respond. The targets and frameworks are necessary scaffolding, but the building still depends on genuine capability beneath them.

This lesson opens the final module by showing Medicaid managed care reaching toward value. The next lesson, on Section 1115 waivers, examines the federal authority that lets states innovate beyond standard rules — including many of the boldest VBP and delivery-reform experiments. And the closing lesson looks at where the whole field is heading, toward social determinants and whole-person care. Value-based purchasing is the bridge: it takes the managed care structure built across this course and points it at the same destination the entire value-based-care movement is pursuing — paying for health and outcomes rather than volume of services.

points: Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the state’s use of MCO contracts to require or encourage plans to pay their providers through value-based arrangements, pushing value-based payment from the state through the plan to the provider level.

It matters because capitating an MCO does not change how the MCO pays providers; without VBP requirements, plans may keep paying providers fee-for-service and recreate volume incentives one layer down.
States drive VBP two ways: setting value-based payment targets (a minimum share of payments that must be value-based) and prescriptively directing MCOs to adopt specific models, often combined.

About 26 states define required VBP model types and 19 set minimum saturation targets, frequently ramped over time — Arizona moved from 5% of MCO revenues in value-based arrangements in 2013 to 20% by 2015–2016.

Many states use the HCP-LAN framework to define "value-based," with ~17 referencing it and 10 specifying categories (usually Category 2C or higher); the framework maps the same risk continuum from fee-for-service to population-based payment.

State directed payments (SDPs), created by CMS in 2016, let states direct how MCOs pay providers — including requiring VBP participation — and have grown explosively to a projected $110.2 billion a year as of August 2024 (302 arrangements in 40 states), up ~60% in 18 months.

The rapid SDP growth prompted CMS to tighten oversight and transparency in 2024 and to require evaluation measures (readmissions, preventive care, chronic-disease outcomes), since SDPs can either advance value or simply inflate payments.

Requiring VBP does not guarantee results — benefits depend on execution, provider capability, and whether the arrangements involve real risk — so targets and frameworks are necessary scaffolding but not sufficient on their own.

children.text: The Equity Gap That Value-Based Care Must Confront

Value-based care was designed to improve quality while reducing costs — a goal that sounds universal but has been implemented in ways that systematically exclude or disadvantage the people who most need better care. The promise of VBC is that if we pay for outcomes rather than volume, the entire health system will orient toward keeping people healthy and intervening effectively when they get sick. But that promise breaks down when the populations most likely to get sick are also the populations whose providers are most financially penalized for serving them, and whose social circumstances make achieving measured outcomes hardest.

Health disparities in the United States are pervasive, well-documented, and stubbornly persistent. Black Americans have shorter life expectancies than white Americans, higher rates of preventable hospitalizations, worse outcomes for nearly every major chronic disease, and less access to high-quality specialty care. Hispanic Americans face systematic barriers to accessing care due to language, immigration status, and geographic concentration in underserved communities. Rural Americans — regardless of race — face provider shortages, longer travel distances to specialists, and hospital closures that have accelerated over the past decade. These are not statistical abstractions; they are the lived experiences of tens of millions of Americans who depend on a healthcare system that was not designed with them in mind.

Research consistently estimates that social determinants of health — factors like income, education, housing quality, food security, neighborhood safety, and transportation access — drive between 50 and 80 percent of health outcomes. Clinical care accounts for roughly 20 percent. This means that value-based programs focused exclusively on clinical quality metrics are, at best, optimizing a minority of the drivers of health. A VBC system that ignores social determinants is like a building code that focuses only on the foundation while ignoring whether the occupants have heat, water, and a safe neighborhood.

Social determinants of health — income, housing, education, food security, transportation, and neighborhood safety — account for an estimated 50–80% of health outcomes. A value-based care system that ignores these upstream factors cannot achieve equitable health improvement, regardless of how well it optimizes clinical delivery.

stats.context: Up to 80% of health outcomes are driven by social determinants rather than clinical care — CMS SDOH Framework 2025
stats.label: Health Outcomes from Social Factors

children.text: How Current VBC Design Can Worsen Disparities

The architecture of most value-based payment programs contains features that can actively worsen health disparities, even when the programs' intentions are positive. The clearest example is financial benchmarking based on historical costs. When ACOs or hospitals have their savings targets set relative to their own historical spending, providers who historically underserved low-income populations — spending less not because of efficiency but because patients couldn't afford care — will have lower baselines and therefore must improve more to earn bonuses. Conversely, providers who historically overspent may generate "savings" simply by stopping unnecessary high-cost care, even without improving outcomes.

Quality metrics in VBC programs are similarly biased by the populations they measure. Preventive care rates, disease management outcomes, and patient experience scores are all sensitive to social determinants that providers cannot control. A physician practicing in a food desert who consistently struggles to improve her patients' HbA1c levels despite excellent clinical care faces the same performance benchmark as a physician in an affluent community where patients can afford fresh food, have stable employment, and can take time off to manage their chronic conditions. Without social risk adjustment, the quality measurement system punishes the former and rewards the latter.

Provider network and geographic access issues compound these problems. VBC programs are most effective when patients have consistent, ongoing relationships with their primary care providers — the foundation of care coordination and preventive care. But underserved communities have higher rates of safety-net provider dependence, federally qualified health center (FQHC) utilization, and emergency department use as primary care. These non-standard care patterns make attribution difficult in ACO models and reduce the effectiveness of care coordination interventions designed around assumptions of regular primary care visits.

body.message: Value-based care programs that penalize providers for serving disadvantaged populations create incentives for "cream skimming" — the strategic avoidance of high-risk, high-complexity, socially disadvantaged patients in favor of healthier, wealthier ones. When financial models reward efficiency over equity, providers who serve the most vulnerable patients can face the steepest penalties, creating pressure to deprioritize or exclude these populations from VBC arrangements.
body.title: The "Cream Skimming" Risk

children.text: The Social Determinants Framework in Practice

Addressing social determinants within a VBC framework requires moving beyond clinical-only interventions. Several models have demonstrated that systematic SDOH screening and community-based intervention — when integrated with clinical care delivery — can improve both health outcomes and financial performance. The logic is compelling: a patient who loses her apartment will generate emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and uncontrolled chronic disease management costs that dwarf the cost of housing support. If the VBC arrangement captures the savings from those avoided costs, investing in housing support can be financially rational, not just compassionate.

The Camden Coalition of Healthcare Providers in Camden, New Jersey pioneered the concept of "hotspotting" — identifying the highest-cost, most frequently hospitalized patients and providing intensive community-based support to address both clinical and social needs. By targeting the top 1 percent of cost drivers with wraparound services including housing assistance, transportation, medication management, and care coordination, the Coalition demonstrated significant reductions in hospital utilization. The model has since been replicated in dozens of communities and influenced the design of complex care management programs in Medicare and Medicaid.

The Vermont Blueprint for Health, which has operated since 2008 and covers all payers in Vermont, integrates community health teams — social workers, care coordinators, community health workers — with primary care practices. These teams address SDOH needs alongside clinical needs, with a shared data system that allows providers across settings to track patients' social circumstances alongside their medical records. Vermont's model has been associated with reduced emergency department utilization, slower cost growth, and improved quality scores — providing one of the most comprehensive demonstrations that SDOH integration can work at a statewide population level.

body.content:
The Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Model, launched by CMMI in 2017, tested whether systematically identifying and addressing health-related social needs — through screening, referral, and community navigation — could reduce Medicare and Medicaid utilization and costs.
The model operated across over 30 bridge organizations that screened over 800,000 beneficiaries for five core social needs: housing instability, food insecurity, transportation difficulties, utility needs, and interpersonal safety. Participants were randomized to awareness (referral information only), assistance (community navigation), and alignment (coordinating community services). Results showed that community navigation significantly reduced inpatient admissions and emergency department visits for beneficiaries with at least one unmet social need, validating the clinical and financial case for integrating SDOH screening into Medicare care delivery.
body.title: CMS Accountable Health Communities Model

children.text: What an Equity-Centered VBC System Looks Like

Building a VBC system that works for everyone requires changes at multiple levels: the data infrastructure for measuring equity, the payment architecture that removes penalties for serving disadvantaged populations, the workforce that can address social and clinical needs together, and the community partnerships that connect healthcare systems to social services. None of these changes is simple, and all of them require sustained policy commitment across multiple administrations.

On measurement, equity-centered VBC requires stratifying all quality measures by race, ethnicity, income, disability status, and social risk factor status — and holding providers accountable for reducing within-panel disparities, not just improving average performance. CMS has moved in this direction with the Health Equity Index for Medicare Advantage and has proposed measure stratification requirements for the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing program starting in 2026. But the data infrastructure for consistent race and ethnicity reporting in healthcare claims remains incomplete, and many providers cannot accurately stratify their own quality data by social characteristics.

On workforce, community health workers (CHWs) have emerged as one of the highest-value tools for bridging clinical care and social needs. CHWs are trusted community members who provide health education, navigation, care coordination, and social support — often in patients' homes and in community settings rather than clinical offices. CMS created dedicated billing codes for CHW services in 2024, making it possible for the first time to reimburse CHW activities under Medicare and Medicaid. This represents a significant structural change that could enable systematic SDOH intervention at scale.

body.title: Components of an Equity-Centered VBC System

children.text: The Policy Landscape and What Remains Unresolved

CMS has articulated a health equity commitment across multiple programs and policy documents, but translating that commitment into payment design that meaningfully advances equity is a work in progress. The 2022 CMMI Strategic Refresh explicitly named health equity as a central goal of value-based care model design, committing that all future Innovation Center models would include health equity elements. The AHC model, Enhanced Primary Care Transformation model, and ACO REACH all included equity-specific requirements or bonuses. Yet CMMI also terminated several models early in 2025, raising uncertainty about the long-term trajectory of equity-focused innovation.

Medicaid is potentially a more powerful lever for health equity in VBC than Medicare, because Medicaid disproportionately serves the populations with the most pronounced health disparities — low-income adults, children, people with disabilities, and pregnant women. Several states have moved aggressively to incorporate SDOH into Medicaid managed care contracts: North Carolina's Healthy Opportunities Pilots funded social services through Medicaid for the first time, testing whether braiding healthcare and social service funding could improve outcomes for the most complex enrollees. Massachusetts, Oregon, and California have implemented similar Medicaid innovations.

The fundamental unresolved tension is between universalism and targeting. A truly equitable VBC system would require different standards, different investments, and different timelines for providers and populations at different starting points — a form of affirmative payment design that explicitly prioritizes closing gaps rather than maximizing average performance. American health policy has historically struggled with this kind of targeted approach, preferring universal standards that appear fair on paper but embed structural inequities in practice. Resolving that tension — acknowledging that equity sometimes requires differential treatment — is the defining political and policy challenge for the next generation of value-based care design.

body.analogy: A school system that grades every student on the same curve regardless of whether they had tutors, stable housing, and enough food is not measuring academic achievement — it is measuring socioeconomic advantage. Value-based care faces the same problem: measuring health outcomes on a single universal scale when the determinants of those outcomes are profoundly unequal.
body.concept: Health Equity and VBC Performance Measurement

points: Social determinants of health — income, housing, education, food security, and transportation — drive up to 80 percent of health outcomes, meaning VBC programs focused only on clinical quality metrics are optimizing a minority of what actually drives health.

Current VBC program design can worsen disparities through historical cost benchmarking, unadjusted quality metrics, and financial penalties that disproportionately fall on safety-net providers serving the most disadvantaged populations.

The "cream skimming" risk — providers strategically avoiding high-complexity, socially disadvantaged patients — is a real consequence of VBC financial models that penalize rather than reward serving vulnerable populations.

Community health workers, SDOH screening programs, and cross-sector partnerships between healthcare and social services represent proven operational strategies for addressing social determinants within VBC arrangements.

The Vermont Blueprint for Health and CMS Accountable Health Communities Model provide real-world evidence that integrating SDOH screening and community navigation into VBC can reduce hospitalizations and emergency department utilization.

CMS has committed to health equity as a central design principle for future Innovation Center models, and has created new billing codes for community health workers and SDOH risk assessments — but comprehensive equity-adjusted payment design remains incomplete.

Building a VBC system that works for everyone requires stratified quality measurement, social risk adjustment, universal SDOH screening, community health integration, and outcome accountability for demonstrated disparity reduction — not just average performance improvement.

The model demonstrated that community navigation significantly reduced inpatient admissions and emergency department visits for beneficiaries with at least one unmet social need, validating the premise that addressing SDOH can reduce healthcare utilization and cost.

result.title: Who Gets Left Behind: Health Equity, Social Determinants, and Building a VBC System That Works for Everyone

children.text: The Fundamental Problem: A System That Pays for Sickness, Not Health

The United States spends more on healthcare than any other nation in the world — $5.3 trillion in 2024, approximately $14,885 per person. And yet, by nearly every measure of population health, the country performs below its peer nations. Life expectancy in the U.S. was 78.4 years in 2023, nearly 4 years shorter than the average among comparable wealthy countries. Rates of chronic disease, preventable hospitalizations, and avoidable deaths are persistently higher in the U.S. than in nations that spend far less. The paradox is stark: more spending, worse outcomes.

This paradox is not the result of incompetent physicians, inferior technology, or inadequate hospitals. On most measures of technical medical capability — cancer survival rates, cardiac intervention outcomes, cutting-edge diagnostic tools — American medicine is among the best in the world. The problem is structural. The way the United States pays for healthcare systematically rewards the wrong things: it rewards treating illness rather than preventing it, rewards individual services rather than coordinated care, and rewards volume rather than value. The payment architecture shapes the behavior of every actor in the system, and the current architecture is pointing almost everyone in the wrong direction.

Value-based care (VBC) is the policy response to this misalignment. It is a broad umbrella term for payment and care delivery approaches that tie financial incentives to quality outcomes, patient experience, and cost-efficiency — rather than to the raw count of services delivered. Understanding value-based care requires first understanding the problem it is designed to solve: the incentive structure of fee-for-service medicine and the consequences that structure produces.

Key Concept: Value-based care is a healthcare payment and delivery model in which providers are compensated based on patient health outcomes and the efficiency of care delivery — rather than on the volume of services provided. The central idea is to align financial incentives with the goal of keeping patients healthy.

children.text: The Triple Aim: The Framework Behind Value-Based Care

The intellectual foundation of the value-based care movement is the Triple Aim, a framework articulated by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) in 2008. The Triple Aim holds that health system improvement requires simultaneously pursuing three goals: improving the patient experience of care (including quality and satisfaction), improving the health of populations, and reducing the per-capita cost of healthcare. These three dimensions are not naturally in tension — indeed, the Triple Aim's central insight is that addressing all three together is both possible and necessary.

Fee-for-service medicine is structurally incapable of pursuing the Triple Aim because it optimizes only for volume — which is a proxy for neither quality nor health. A system that pays for more services will generate more services, regardless of whether those services improve the patient experience, improve population health, or reduce cost. The Triple Aim requires payment mechanisms that can reward coordination, prevention, and efficiency rather than activity.

Over time, IHI and others have expanded the framework to a "Quadruple Aim" that adds a fourth dimension: improving the health and well-being of the healthcare workforce. This addition acknowledges that provider burnout — driven in part by the administrative burden of documentation-heavy FFS billing and compliance programs like MIPS — is itself a systemic problem that undermines care quality. A truly value-based system should improve the experience of care for clinicians, not just patients.

The problem is not that American medicine lacks quality. The problem is that the payment system rewards the wrong quality — the quality of filling out a claim, not the quality of keeping a patient well.
The Spectrum of Value-Based Payment Models

Value-based care is not a single payment model — it is a spectrum of approaches that shift incentives away from pure volume and toward quality, efficiency, and outcomes. These models vary in the degree of financial risk they impose on providers, the scope of services they cover, and the populations they address. Understanding the landscape of models is essential for anyone navigating healthcare finance and policy.

At one end of the spectrum are pay-for-performance (P4P) programs, which layer quality bonuses or penalties on top of existing FFS payments. MIPS is a prominent example: it preserves fee-for-service billing while adjusting final payments up or down based on a quality and cost score. P4P models represent the lowest-risk entry point into value-based care — they do not require providers to change their fundamental revenue model — but they also generate the least structural change in care delivery because the FFS volume incentive remains intact.

Moving up the risk spectrum, bundled payment models establish a single fixed payment for an entire episode of care — for example, a total knee replacement including surgery, inpatient stay, rehabilitation, and follow-up visits over a defined period. Providers who manage the episode below the target price retain the savings; those who exceed it share in the loss. Bundled payments create powerful incentives for care coordination across the inpatient and post-acute continuum, but they apply only to defined episodes and do not address population health or primary prevention.

children.text: Accountable Care Organizations: The Flagship VBC Model

Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are the most widely deployed model of value-based care in the United States. An ACO is a group of doctors, hospitals, and other healthcare providers who agree to share accountability for the quality and total cost of care for an assigned population of patients. Rather than being paid for each individual service, ACO participants receive their FFS payments as usual — but at year's end, if the ACO's total spending for its attributed beneficiaries is below a risk-adjusted benchmark, the ACO earns a share of those savings. If spending exceeds the benchmark, the ACO may owe losses back, depending on its risk track.

The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) is the largest ACO program in the United States. As of January 2024, 480 MSSP ACOs include more than 608,000 clinicians providing care to nearly 11 million Medicare beneficiaries. In 2023, MSSP ACOs generated $2.1 billion in net savings for Medicare — the largest in the program's more than ten-year history — while also demonstrating quality improvements in diabetes management, blood pressure control, cancer screening, and depression care.

The ACO REACH (Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health) model, administered by CMMI, tests a deeper form of accountable care with full global capitation risk. In 2023, the 132 ACO REACH participants managed care for more than 2 million Medicare beneficiaries, generating $695 million in net savings. The model explicitly incorporates health equity requirements — ACOs must develop health equity plans and report on disparities for high-need populations — marking a significant expansion of the VBC framework beyond cost and quality to address systemic disparities in care access and outcomes.

ACOs in the program earned shared savings payments totaling $3.1 billion — also a record. Performance also improved on quality measures related to diabetes care, blood pressure control, colorectal and breast cancer screening, statin therapy, and depression screening.
As of January 2024, 480 ACOs participated, covering nearly 11 million beneficiaries through the work of more than 608,000 clinicians. The program demonstrates that large-scale ACO participation can simultaneously reduce Medicare spending and improve measured quality — the core promise of the Triple Aim.

children.text: Capitation and Global Budgets: The Deepest Form of VBC

At the far end of the value-based care spectrum are capitation and global budget models, which represent the most complete structural departure from fee-for-service. Under full capitation, a provider organization receives a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment from a payer to cover all covered services for an assigned population — regardless of how many services are actually used. The provider keeps the margin if it delivers care efficiently; it absorbs the loss if it does not. Capitation fully inverts the FFS incentive: instead of more services = more revenue, the logic becomes appropriate care = retained margin.

Global budgets extend this logic to entire health systems or regions. Rather than paying on a per-patient basis, a global budget model sets an annual spending total for a defined population and gives a delivery system or state accountability for staying within that budget while meeting quality standards. Global budgets are common in other countries — the UK's NHS operates largely on a global budget basis — but they are rare in the United States, where Maryland's hospital global budget program and Vermont's All-Payer ACO model are the most prominent examples.

Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model, launched in 2018, is particularly noteworthy because it aligned Medicare, Medicaid, and major commercial insurers under a single, statewide value-based payment framework — the first attempt in the U.S. to create multi-payer payment alignment at the state level. The model has driven significant investment in primary care infrastructure and care coordination in Vermont, and it offers a potential blueprint for other states seeking to address both cost and health equity through payment reform.

children.text: Why the Transition Is Hard — and Why It Is Happening Anyway

The case for value-based care is compelling in theory, and the evidence from programs like MSSP and ACO REACH is increasingly convincing in practice. Yet the transition from fee-for-service to value-based payment has been slower and more contested than reformers hoped when the ACA established CMMI in 2010. The reasons are structural, financial, and cultural. Provider organizations that built their facilities, staffed their teams, and financed their operations around FFS revenue cannot rapidly restructure without risk. A hospital that derives 40% of its margin from high-volume elective procedures does not easily absorb the shift to a model that rewards reducing utilization.

There is also the challenge of measurement. Value-based payment requires robust quality metrics, reliable patient attribution, risk adjustment that does not penalize providers caring for sicker or more complex populations, and data infrastructure that can track patients across settings and over time. Building these systems is expensive, slow, and contentious. Disputes over which quality measures are clinically meaningful, how to attribute patients to providers in a fragmented system, and how to adjust benchmarks for social determinants of health have occupied policy debates for more than a decade without full resolution.

Despite these barriers, the direction of travel is clear. CMS has set explicit goals for moving Medicare toward value-based payment, and commercial payers have followed. The combination of rising healthcare costs, aging demographics, and the documented failure of FFS to produce commensurate health outcomes has created irreversible pressure for payment reform. For healthcare professionals, administrators, and policymakers, understanding the architecture of value-based care — its models, its incentives, its measurement systems, and its limitations — is no longer optional. It is the vocabulary of the field.

body.message: Value-based care programs have documented early successes in reducing cost and improving quality metrics for defined populations — but evidence on long-term population health impact and equity outcomes is still developing. Not all VBC models reduce health disparities; some early evidence suggests that ACOs serving more advantaged populations outperform those serving high-need, low-income populations, raising important questions about how VBC design can be improved to reduce — rather than widen — health equity gaps.
body.title: Key Limitation of VBC

points: The U.S. spends $5.3 trillion on healthcare annually — more than 2.5x the OECD per-capita average — yet achieves below-average outcomes on most population health indicators, including life expectancy.

The core cause of this paradox is a fee-for-service payment architecture that rewards volume over value, fragmenting care and incentivizing overtreatment while under-incentivizing prevention and coordination.
Value-based care (VBC) is a broad umbrella for payment models that tie financial incentives to quality, outcomes, and cost-efficiency — the central mechanism for realigning the payment system.
The Triple Aim framework — improving patient experience, improving population health, and reducing per-capita cost — provides the conceptual foundation for VBC design.

VBC models exist on a spectrum from low-risk pay-for-performance programs (like MIPS) to full capitation and global budgets; each point on the spectrum involves different degrees of financial risk and structural change.
ACOs are the flagship VBC model in Medicare; the MSSP generated a record $2.1 billion in net savings in 2023 while improving quality metrics — the seventh consecutive year of program-wide savings.

The transition to VBC faces structural, financial, and measurement barriers — but the policy and market direction is clear, making VBC literacy an essential competency for all healthcare professionals.

Capitation replaces the per-service payment with a fixed per-member-per-month amount, fully inverting the FFS incentive: efficient, high-quality care generates margin, while unnecessary utilization erodes it.
