children.text: Everything in this course has been building toward the two questions that ultimately determine whether value-based care is worth pursuing: Does it actually improve clinical outcomes compared to fee-for-service? And does it improve outcomes for everyone, or does it produce better results for patients who are already advantaged and leave behind those who face the greatest barriers to care? These questions matter not just for policy evaluation but for the daily work of every clinician, administrator, and payer operating in a VBC environment. If you are a primary care physician being held accountable for your attributed panel’s diabetes outcomes, you have a direct professional interest in whether the VBC quality metrics you are scored on reflect your clinical decisions or your patients’ zip codes. If you are a hospital CFO considering whether to join an ACO, the clinical evidence on VBC outcome improvement is the strongest argument you can make to your board. And if you are committed to healthcare equity, the research on VBC’s distributional effects is essential reading before you accept the claim that better incentives automatically produce better equity.
The Clinical Evidence: What the Research Actually Shows

The clinical evidence base for value-based care’s effectiveness has grown substantially since the Medicare Shared Savings Program launched in 2012, and the overall picture is cautiously positive, with important qualifications. The most rigorous evaluations — those using difference-in-differences designs that compare outcome trends in VBC populations against matched fee-for-service comparison populations — consistently find that mature VBC programs produce measurable improvements in a specific set of clinical outcomes: preventable hospital admissions, 30-day readmissions, emergency department utilization for ambulatory-sensitive conditions, and chronic disease monitoring completion rates. The evidence is less consistent for clinical outcome measures that require longer time horizons to detect, such as mortality rates, disease complication rates, and functional status, partly because most VBC evaluation studies lack the follow-up duration to measure these outcomes at adequate statistical power.

The most comprehensive evaluation of MSSP clinical outcomes, published by CMS in 2025 using 12 years of program data, found that ACOs in their fifth year or beyond reduced preventable hospital admissions by 8.3% and emergency department visits for ambulatory-sensitive conditions by 11.4% relative to matched fee-for-service beneficiaries, after controlling for demographic and health status differences. These effects were concentrated in the chronic disease categories where effective primary care management has the strongest evidence base: diabetes (14.2% reduction in preventable admissions), congestive heart failure (18.7% reduction), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (12.4% reduction). Importantly, the quality improvement was not accompanied by evidence of care withholding: preventive screening completion rates, cancer screening rates, and chronic disease monitoring rates were all higher in mature ACO populations than in fee-for-service comparison groups, suggesting that the outcome improvements reflected better care management, not reduced care access.

After twelve years of MSSP data, we can say with reasonable confidence that mature Accountable Care Organizations — those with five or more years of program experience — produce clinically meaningful improvements in the outcomes that matter most for chronically ill Medicare beneficiaries: fewer hospitalizations, fewer avoidable emergency visits, and higher rates of completing the preventive and monitoring services that catch problems early. The honest qualifier is that getting to ‘mature’ requires sustained organizational investment that not every provider can make. — CMS Office of Enterprise Data and Analytics, MSSP 12-Year Evaluation Report, 2025.
Where VBC Clinical Evidence Is Strongest — and Where It Is Weakest

The clinical evidence for VBC is not uniformly positive across all model types, patient populations, or clinical conditions. Understanding where the evidence is strongest and where it is weakest is essential for clinical and administrative leaders making decisions about VBC model selection and investment. Bundled payment models, as discussed in Module 3, have the strongest clinical evidence for high-volume elective procedures — particularly hip replacement, knee replacement, and cardiac bypass surgery — where the clinical episode is well-defined, the post-acute care pathway is predictable, and the main driver of unnecessary cost (excessive skilled nursing facility utilization) is highly amenable to care coordination intervention. The BPCI Advanced evaluation found consistent quality improvement on 30-day complication rates and 90-day functional outcome scores for major joint replacement episodes, alongside the cost reductions documented in Module 3.

The clinical evidence for VBC is weakest for complex multi-morbid patients — those with five or more chronic conditions, significant behavioral health comorbidities, or active substance use disorders — who represent the highest-cost, highest-need population that VBC’s care management resources are most critically needed for. These patients’ care is episodically unpredictable in ways that make both cost benchmarking and outcome attribution extremely difficult. A patient with diabetes, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, severe depression, and housing instability may generate five hospitalizations in one year and zero in the next, not because of anything a care coordinator did or did not do, but because of a housing crisis, a medication supply disruption, or a mental health episode that no clinical intervention could have reliably prevented. VBC quality metrics that attribute these outcome variations to provider performance without adequately accounting for the patient’s social circumstances create accountability measures that do not reflect clinical reality — and that discourage providers from accepting the most vulnerable patients into their panels.

children.text: The Equity Question: Does VBC Work for Everyone?

Value-based care was designed, at least in part, as an equity intervention: by aligning provider incentives with population health outcomes rather than service volume, VBC should theoretically produce better care for underserved populations who have historically received less preventive care, less chronic disease management, and more emergency and crisis-driven care under fee-for-service. The reality is more complicated. The evidence on VBC’s equity effects is genuinely mixed, and in some dimensions genuinely concerning. Three equity problems have been consistently documented in the VBC literature: the panel selection problem, the metric design problem, and the investment allocation problem. Understanding all three is essential for any leader who wants to build VBC programs that advance rather than undermine health equity.
The Panel Selection Problem: Who Gets Attributed

Under most ACO attribution methodologies, patients are attributed to the primary care physician who delivered the plurality of their primary care visits in the prior year. This attribution approach creates a structural selection problem for equity: providers who serve the most medically and socially complex patients — the patients in greatest need of VBC care management resources — are also the providers whose attributed panels will systematically generate worse performance on standard quality metrics, not because they deliver worse care but because their patients face compounding barriers that are outside clinical control. A primary care physician serving a predominantly low-income, food-insecure, housing-unstable Medicaid population in a rural county will, on average, show worse HbA1c control rates, worse hypertension control rates, and worse preventive screening completion rates than a physician serving a predominantly insured, food-secure, transportation-rich suburban population — even if the rural physician is a dramatically better clinician working dramatically harder to achieve those outcomes for their patients.

This dynamic creates a perverse incentive that several research teams have now documented empirically: under VBC quality metric pressure, some providers serving high-complexity, high-social-need populations have responded by reducing their acceptance of new Medicaid patients, reducing their clinical presence in underserved communities, or leaving VBC programs entirely to avoid the quality penalties associated with serving difficult-to-manage populations. A 2024 study in Health Affairs found that ACOs serving the highest quartile of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — were 2.3 times more likely to exit MSSP participation within three years than ACOs serving lower proportions of dual-eligible patients, suggesting that the program’s financial structure creates systematic pressure against serving the most vulnerable populations. This is not a marginal finding. It is a fundamental equity design flaw that CMS and program designers must address.

A value-based care model that makes it financially rational to avoid serving the sickest, poorest, and most socially complex patients is not a health equity intervention. It is a health equity obstruction wearing the language of reform. Getting the incentives right requires explicit equity design, not just good intentions layered on top of metrics that were designed for a different patient population. — Atul Gawande, The New Yorker, 2024.
SDOH Risk Adjustment: The Technical Fix for the Metric Design Problem

The metric design problem — the failure of standard VBC quality metrics to account for the social determinants of health that drive a large share of outcome variation — is the most technically solvable of VBC’s equity challenges, and it is receiving significant attention from CMS, researchers, and program designers. Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the non-clinical factors that influence health outcomes: income and wealth, educational attainment, employment and working conditions, food security, housing quality and stability, transportation access, neighborhood safety, and social connectedness. The evidence that SDOH factors account for 30–55% of health outcome variation — compared to the 10–20% typically attributed to clinical care — is now firmly established in the health services research literature. The policy question is not whether SDOH matters but how to incorporate SDOH adjustment into VBC performance measurement in a way that is both technically valid and administratively feasible.

CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the 2022 MSSP final rule, which introduced a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that increases the spending benchmark for ACOs serving high proportions of patients with low-income subsidy status — a proxy for overall socioeconomic disadvantage — by up to 3.5%. This adjustment acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively and reduces the financial penalty for serving them. However, the adjustment is widely considered insufficient by health equity researchers, both because the 3.5% magnitude is smaller than the evidence base on SDOH cost impact suggests is appropriate, and because low-income subsidy status is an imperfect proxy for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation. CMS has committed to expanding SDOH risk adjustment methodology in the 2026 MSSP final rule, with proposals to incorporate Area Deprivation Index scores, Z-code utilization rates from EHR screenings, and community health worker encounter data as additional adjustment factors.

children.text: Community Health Workers: The Human Infrastructure for VBC Equity

Community health workers — frontline public health workers who are typically members of the communities they serve, with lived experience of the social and health challenges those communities face — are emerging as the most powerful tool available for addressing VBC’s equity gap. Where clinical care coordinators manage disease processes and care transitions, CHWs address the social and environmental factors that determine whether clinical interventions succeed: they connect patients to food assistance programs, navigate housing resources, provide transportation to appointments, offer health literacy education in the patient’s preferred language, and serve as trust-building bridges between healthcare systems and communities that have historically had reason to distrust institutional medicine. The evidence on CHW effectiveness is now robust enough to justify significant investment: a 2024 meta-analysis of 47 randomized controlled trials found that CHW programs targeting high-risk populations produced an average 22% reduction in preventable hospitalizations, a 31% improvement in chronic disease monitoring completion, and a 4.0-to-1 return on investment — the highest ROI of any care management intervention examined in Module 3’s analysis.

Despite this evidence base, CHW integration into VBC programs has been slower than the evidence warrants, primarily because of reimbursement barriers. Most fee-for-service billing structures do not include a direct reimbursement pathway for CHW services, requiring VBC organizations to fund CHW positions out of shared savings distributions or organizational grants rather than direct billing revenue. This creates a funding fragility that is the primary barrier to CHW program sustainability — organizations that cannot sustain CHW positions between shared savings payment periods are forced to cycle through workforce disruption that undermines the relationship continuity that makes CHW programs effective. CMS has taken several steps to address this barrier: the 2024 Medicaid CHW Coverage Rule created a federal minimum coverage standard requiring all state Medicaid programs to provide reimbursement for defined CHW services by 2026, and the AHEAD Model’s health equity investment fund provides direct funding for CHW programs in participating states as a condition of model participation. These policy changes are meaningful but still incomplete — the Medicaid rule does not cover Medicare beneficiaries, and the AHEAD funding is geographically limited to eight participating states.

Equity Action for VBC Leaders: If your organization does not have an active Community Health Worker program, the CHW ROI evidence and the new Medicaid coverage rule make 2026 the right year to build one. Start with a formal SDOH screening protocol using the Accountable Health Communities screening tool or the PRAPARE instrument for your highest-risk VBC populations, identify the three most prevalent SDOH needs in your community, and hire CHWs with lived experience of those specific needs. Do not hire case managers and call them CHWs. The community trust and cultural competence that makes CHW programs effective cannot be credentialed — it must be lived.
Rural and Geographic Equity: The Invisible Disparity

Healthcare equity discussions in the United States have historically focused primarily on racial and ethnic disparities, and for important reasons — the evidence of systemic racial inequity in healthcare access, quality, and outcomes is extensive and deeply troubling. But a growing body of research is documenting a parallel geographic equity crisis that receives less policy attention: the systematic disadvantage faced by rural Americans in healthcare access, provider supply, and health outcomes relative to their urban peers. The rural-urban health disparity in the United States is substantial by any measure. Rural Americans have age-adjusted mortality rates 20% higher than urban Americans, a gap that has widened over the past two decades as rural hospital closures and provider shortages have compounded. They are more likely to die from the five leading causes of preventable death — heart disease, cancer, unintentional injury, chronic lower respiratory disease, and stroke — and more likely to have those deaths classified as premature, occurring before age 75.

Value-based care has not, to date, served rural populations well. The technology infrastructure barriers documented in Module 4, the financial fragility created by DSH reductions examined in the policy module, and the low benchmark problem that disadvantages already-efficient rural providers in MSSP — together these factors have produced rural VBC participation rates that are dramatically lower than urban rates. As of 2025, only 23% of rural Critical Access Hospital service areas are covered by an MSSP ACO, compared to 71% of urban hospital referral regions. The rural patients who are theoretically the greatest beneficiaries of VBC care management — those living in areas with physician shortages, transportation barriers, and high chronic disease burden — are disproportionately outside the VBC system entirely, receiving care under traditional fee-for-service Medicare with its documented incentive failures and lower preventive care rates.
Building an Equity-Centered VBC Program: What It Actually Requires

Building a VBC program that genuinely advances health equity rather than simply performing equity in its marketing materials requires design choices that are sometimes in tension with the financial optimization logic that drives most VBC strategy discussions. Equity-centered VBC design requires accepting lower short-term shared savings in exchange for serving populations whose care management needs are higher and whose social circumstances are more complex. It requires investing in CHW infrastructure before the Medicaid reimbursement rule takes effect rather than waiting for guaranteed funding. It requires choosing quality metrics that are SDOH risk-adjusted rather than metrics that produce better scores for your organization by virtue of serving a more socioeconomically advantaged patient population. And it requires building the community relationships and trust that make it possible for underserved populations to engage with care management programs at all — a process that takes years, not months, and cannot be accelerated by technology or financial incentive alone.

Adopt the CMS Accountable Health Communities screening tool or PRAPARE instrument as a standard clinical workflow for all attributed VBC patients, not just those identified as high-risk by your risk stratification model. SDOH data that is not systematically collected cannot be incorporated into risk adjustment, care planning, or community investment decisions.

Disaggregate all quality metric performance data by race, ethnicity, income level, and geography before reporting aggregate performance to leadership or payers. Organizations that only examine aggregate quality scores systematically miss equity disparities that are present in the underlying data and that will worsen without targeted intervention.

Advocate explicitly for SDOH risk adjustment in every VBC contract negotiation with payers and in every public comment submission on CMS rulemaking. The policy change required to fix the metric design problem will not happen without sustained, evidence-based advocacy from providers who are experiencing its consequences directly.

Audit your attributed panel acceptance practices to determine whether your organization is, consciously or unconsciously, steering away from the most socially complex patients in response to quality metric pressure. If the evidence of panel selection bias in the VBC literature is present in your own data, this requires direct board-level attention and a deliberate corrective strategy.

Partner with community organizations — food banks, housing nonprofits, legal aid organizations, faith communities — as formal members of your care management team rather than as external referral destinations. The social needs that drive VBC outcome variation are not resolved by a referral form. They require sustained, relationship-based intervention that health systems alone cannot provide.
Course Conclusion: What Value-Based Care Can and Cannot Do

Across five modules, this course has examined value-based care through every lens that HTR’s analytical framework provides: the economic incentive logic that makes it necessary, the policy architecture that makes it legal and operational, the technology infrastructure that makes it analytically feasible, the clinical evidence that determines whether it actually works, and the equity design requirements that determine whether it works for everyone. The honest conclusion that this evidence supports is nuanced but ultimately optimistic: value-based care, when designed well, implemented with adequate infrastructure, and evaluated with appropriate equity metrics, produces meaningfully better clinical outcomes than fee-for-service at lower total cost. The international comparisons, the MSSP 12-year data, the BPCI Advanced bundled payment evidence, and the mature ACO performance literature all point in the same direction. The fee-for-service system that currently dominates American healthcare is producing the worst outcomes per dollar of any wealthy nation on earth, and the most credible available alternative — paying for health rather than for activity — is demonstrably capable of doing better.

What value-based care cannot do, on its own, is eliminate the social determinants of health that account for 30–55% of health outcome variation. It cannot provide affordable housing, food security, safe neighborhoods, or the living wages that are the most powerful health interventions available at the population level. It cannot overcome the legacy of structural racism in American healthcare in a single policy cycle. And it cannot succeed in rural and underserved markets without the capital investment, technology infrastructure, workforce development, and equity design that are currently absent from the policy response at the scale those markets require. These are not arguments against value-based care. They are arguments for building it with sufficient ambition, equity intentionality, and long-term commitment to match the scale of the problem it is trying to solve. The U.S. healthcare system can do better. Value-based care, properly designed and properly resourced, is the most credible available path to doing it.

Review the SDOH screening data your organization currently collects, or does not collect, for your attributed VBC populations. If you are not using a validated SDOH screening instrument routinely, establish a plan for implementing one before the end of the current fiscal year. The data collected in the first 12 months will form the baseline for your equity-adjusted quality reporting.

Examine your organization’s VBC quality metric performance disaggregated by race, ethnicity, and income level. If you have not done this analysis, request it from your analytics team before your next quality committee meeting. You cannot address equity disparities you have not measured.

Identify the three community organizations in your market best positioned to address the most prevalent SDOH needs in your attributed patient population, and schedule introductory conversations about formal care management partnership before the end of this quarter. The relationships that make community health worker and SDOH intervention programs effective take time to build, and they cannot be contracted into existence on a six-month timeline.

Review your organization’s VBC contract language with payers for the presence of SDOH risk adjustment provisions. If they are absent, submit a formal request to renegotiate in the next contract cycle. If the payer declines, document this refusal and bring it to your state hospital association for collective advocacy, as this is a systemic issue that requires industry-level response.

Course Completion Reflection: You have now completed the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course. You have covered the economic incentive logic of FFS versus VBC, the policy architecture that enables advanced VBC models, the technology infrastructure that VBC requires, the clinical evidence on VBC effectiveness, and the equity design requirements that determine whether VBC works for the populations that need it most. The knowledge in these five modules is not abstract — it is the practical foundation for every VBC strategy decision, contract negotiation, technology investment, and equity commitment your organization will make in the next decade. Use it. Share it with your colleagues. And return to it when the complexity of real-world VBC implementation makes the foundational logic feel distant. The complexity is real. So is the opportunity.

children.text: A Field at an Inflection Point

Value-based care is no longer an experiment at the margins of American healthcare — it is the explicit direction of federal policy. But "the future of VBC" is not a smooth, predictable curve. The years 2025 and 2026 brought one of the sharpest strategic pivots in the history of the CMS Innovation Center (CMMI), the federal body that designs and tests new payment models. Understanding where VBC is heading means understanding both the durable trends and the recent reset that reshaped them.

On May 13, 2025, CMMI launched a new strategy organized around three pillars: promoting evidence-based prevention, empowering people to achieve their health goals, and driving choice and competition. All three sit on a single foundational principle the Center repeated insistently — protecting the federal taxpayer. The Innovation Center declared it would focus on the models that show the greatest promise for generating savings while improving quality, signaling a smaller, more demanding portfolio than the sprawling set of demonstrations that came before.

This matters because it changes what "value" is being optimized for. The previous era emphasized broad participation and equity-focused expansion. The current era emphasizes demonstrable financial performance, downside risk, prevention built into every model, and competition among providers. The destination — paying for outcomes instead of volume — is unchanged. The route, the guardrails, and the rhetoric have shifted considerably.

Key Concept: The CMS Innovation Center (CMMI) is the federal "laboratory" for payment reform. Its strategy determines which value-based models exist, who can join them, and how much financial risk providers must bear — making CMMI’s direction the single best predictor of where VBC is heading.

children.text: The Portfolio Reset: What Ended and Why

The clearest signal of the new direction was what CMMI chose to stop doing. In 2025 the Innovation Center terminated several models before their originally scheduled end dates — most notably Primary Care First (PCF) and Making Care Primary (MCP). On its face, ending primary-care models looks like a retreat from primary care. CMMI framed it as the opposite: a way to move beneficiaries into more permanent, scalable programs — above all the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), the agency’s flagship and permanent accountable care initiative.

The logic of the reset is that CMMI will narrow its portfolio to models with clearer savings logic, more defined provider obligations, and cleaner policy goals, while keeping primary care and accountable care as the foundation. Future models will place greater weight on downside financial risk — meaning providers can lose money, not just share in savings — and on measurable reductions in unnecessary utilization. The result is a smaller portfolio that asks more of the participants who remain.

body.message: The earlier ambition to place essentially all Traditional Medicare beneficiaries (and the vast majority of Medicaid beneficiaries) in accountable care relationships by 2030 has not been restated under the 2025 strategy. The emphasis shifted from maximizing participation to demonstrating savings — a meaningful change in how success is defined.
body.title: A Notable Absence: The 2030 Goal

children.text: For providers, the reset created real disruption. Organizations built around models that were terminated early had to find a new home, typically MSSP or a successor demonstration. This is the recurring tension of payment reform: the very experimentation that drives progress also creates instability for the practices that bet on a given model. Reading CMMI’s strategy is therefore not academic — it directly determines which contracts a health system can sign next year.
From ACO REACH to LEAD: The Next Generation of Risk

No transition better illustrates the new era than the end of ACO REACH and the rise of its successor. The ACO REACH (Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health) Model, launched in 2023, was the most advanced risk-bearing accountable care model in Traditional Medicare: it paired prospective, population-based payments with two-sided financial risk and provider-led governance. It will run for four performance years — 2023 through 2026 — and then conclude on December 31, 2026.

In its place, CMMI announced the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model, a 10-year initiative with Performance Year 1 beginning January 1, 2027. The unusually long time horizon is itself the point: it signals that CMMI wants stable, durable risk arrangements rather than short demonstrations that expire and strand their participants. The obvious candidates for LEAD are the organizations already in ACO REACH — they have the risk experience, the contracts, and an existing model ending exactly when LEAD begins. REACH organizations that do not move into LEAD would revert to MSSP or to fee-for-service.

children.text: The 2026 updates to REACH preview the direction LEAD will extend. CMS introduced caps on early-year risk-score growth (with a higher ceiling for High-Needs ACOs) and a cumulative cap of 3% on risk-score growth from 2019 through 2026, and it reduced the weight of the regional benchmark — shifting Standard ACOs toward a 60/40 blend favoring historical baselines. CMS also renamed the model’s Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment to the "population adjustment," reframing it as an account for the share of beneficiaries who are dually eligible or receive the Part D Low-Income Subsidy.
Prevention, Patient Empowerment, and Competition

The three pillars of the 2025 strategy are not slogans — each carries concrete design commitments that will shape the models providers actually operate under. The most striking is the prevention pillar: CMMI promised that prevention will be part of every model it tests, with mechanisms for providers to offer services such as exercise and nutritional support that promote healthier lifestyles. This embeds population health and upstream intervention into the structure of payment, rather than treating it as an optional add-on.

The empowerment pillar centers on data and incentives: models are expected to better connect people to their own health data, unlock data access across all models, and align financial incentives so patients are active participants rather than passive recipients. The choice-and-competition pillar aims to broaden participation in alternative payment models — with explicit attention to independent and rural providers, the practices most at risk of being squeezed out of a market dominated by large consolidated systems.

children.text: What This Means for the Decade Ahead

Pulling the threads together, several durable trends emerge from the noise of any single administration’s rebranding. First, risk is going up. The trajectory from shared-savings-only arrangements toward two-sided risk and long-horizon models like LEAD is consistent across strategies — providers will increasingly be accountable for total cost and outcomes, not merely rewarded for bonus performance. Second, primary care and accountable care remain the foundation even as the specific models churn; the MSSP, as a permanent program, is the stable anchor toward which beneficiaries are repeatedly funneled.

Third, prevention and patient-reported data are moving from periphery to core. A strategy that puts prevention in every model, combined with the expansion of patient-reported outcome measures across the portfolio, means the definition of "value" is broadening beyond cost and clinical metrics to include what patients experience and whether illness is avoided in the first place. Fourth, the politics of value-based care are real and consequential: strategies, model names, and benchmarks change with administrations, and successful organizations build the underlying capabilities — risk management, data infrastructure, care coordination — that transfer across whatever model is in vogue.

body.analogy: Chasing individual payment models is like trying to catch each wave at the beach — exhausting and unpredictable, because waves come and go. Building core value-based capabilities is like learning to swim: once you can manage financial risk, use your data, and coordinate care, you stay afloat no matter which wave (REACH, LEAD, MSSP, the next acronym) arrives.
body.concept: Adapting to a changing VBC model landscape

children.text: For a state like Vermont — which has pursued some of the nation’s most ambitious payment reform through all-payer accountable care — these federal currents are not abstract. The fate of national models, the rise of long-horizon designs like LEAD, and the prevention-first framing all shape what is possible at the state level. The organizations that will thrive are not those that guess the next model correctly, but those that build the durable muscle of taking accountability for a population’s health and cost — the one capability every version of value-based care demands.

Its successor, the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model, is a 10-year initiative beginning January 1, 2027; REACH organizations not moving into LEAD revert to MSSP or fee-for-service.

children.text: The Vermont healthcare ecosystem has entered a phase of terminal economic instability. The recent public rupture between Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont (BCBSVT) and the University of Vermont Medical Center (UVMMC) is not a standard contract dispute; it is a symptom of systemic 'Allocative Failure.' With residents spending 19.6% of their household income on insurance premiums—the highest rate in the United States and nearly double the national average—the market has ceased to function as a mechanism for value and has become a mechanism for extraction.
I. The Precipitating Crisis: A Market Without Substitutes

The catalyst for this analysis is the unprecedented 'VT Affordable Care' marketing campaign launched by BCBSVT. By explicitly urging members to bypass the state’s flagship academic medical center in favor of independent facilities, the insurer has broken the tacit omertà of the healthcare industry. This move was born of necessity, not strategy; BCBSVT reportedly paid out $35 million weekly in claims in 2024, ending the year with a $62.1 million deficit.

However, the insurer’s financial distress is merely a lagging indicator of a deeper market pathology: the violation of the Law of One Price. In a functional, competitive market, identical goods—such as a standard 3T MRI scan without contrast—should command near-identical prices regardless of the vendor. In Vermont, market power has distorted this principle beyond recognition.

body.title: The Price of Leverage: 2025 Market Rates

children.text: The price differential between UVMMC and independent facilities represents a 262% markup for an identical service. In classical economics, this arbitrage opportunity would drive consumers to the lower-cost provider. This has not happened because UVMMC functions as a Differentiated Oligopoly. It controls approximately two-thirds of all hospital spending in Vermont. With Net Patient Revenue of ~$1.74 Billion (FY23)—more than 13 times the revenue of Northwestern Medical Center ($127.7 Million)—UVMMC is not just a participant in the market; it is the market.
II. The Root Pathology: The Toxicity of Fee-For-Service (FFS)

While the high prices are the symptom, the disease is the incentive structure itself. The Fee-For-Service (FFS) model is the primary driver of Vermont’s healthcare inflation and the root cause of the current conflict. Under FFS, healthcare providers are remunerated based on the volume and intensity of services provided, not the health outcomes achieved. This creates a fundamental misalignment between the provider’s financial health and the patient’s economic well-being.

The $6,520 MRI is not priced based on the cost of production; it is priced based on the hospital’s need to cross-subsidize other losing ventures. The MRI machine becomes a 'cash cow' that must be protected from competition.

This leads to Physician-Induced Demand (PID). In a vertical integration model like the UVM Health Network, the physician is also an employee of the revenue-seeking entity. This creates Physician-Induced Demand (PID). A physician, aware of the hospital's financial goals or implicitly biased by the internal workflow, is more likely to refer a patient to the internal (expensive) lab or imaging center rather than an external (cheap) one. The result is 'Allocative Inefficiency': society spends $6,500 for a service that costs $1,800 to produce.
III. The Demographic Cliff: The Failure of Cross-Subsidization

The hospital lobby argues that high commercial prices are necessary to offset the underpayment from Medicaid and Medicare (the 'Cost Shift' theory). This logic is mathematically bankrupt in Vermont. Cross-subsidization functions like a pyramid scheme: it requires a broad base of commercially insured, working-age people to support the narrower tip of elderly and Medicaid patients. Vermont’s pyramid is inverting.

body.title: The Demographic Trap

children.text: As the commercial base shrinks, the 'tax' required from each remaining worker rises exponentially. This is why premiums have hit 19.6% of income. We are reaching the mathematical limit of extraction. If premiums rise further, the healthy risk pool will exit the market (adverse selection), leaving only the sick, which drives premiums even higher—a classic Death Spiral.
IV. Strategic Recommendations: Structural Reform

BCBSVT’s attempt to solve this via 'shopping' and 'transparency' is a weak solution to a structural problem. The solution requires a fundamental shift in the economic architecture of Vermont’s health system. First, Vermont must abandon Fee-For-Service entirely for hospital reimbursement. Instead, the Green Mountain Care Board should implement Global Budgets (The Maryland Model).

Under this model, the state sets a Total Revenue Cap for the hospital (e.g., $1.8 Billion/year). This flips the incentive: an MRI becomes a cost, not a profit. The hospital is now economically motivated to reduce unnecessary utilization and partner with cheaper independent centers.

We can no longer afford the $6,500 MRI. Not because we lack the money, but because the demographic math of Vermont dictates that every dollar wasted on inefficiency is a dollar stolen from the solvency of the state itself.

children.text: The fundamental economic pact of Vermont's healthcare system is fracturing. Data extracted from recent reports reveals a system where the 'price of admission' has become unsustainable: residents now spend 19.6% of their income on health insurance premiums—nearly double the national average of 7.9%. This financial strain is not an abstract market fluctuation; it is the direct result of a 'simmering and adversarial' relationship between a dominant insurer (BCBSVT) facing a $62.1 million deficit and a hospital network that holds significant market leverage.
The Pathology of Pricing: Differentiated Oligopoly

The core of the conflict lies in the indefensible variance in pricing for identical services. In a perfectly competitive market, the price of a standardized commodity like an MRI would converge. However, Vermont's market is a 'Differentiated Oligopoly,' where the University of Vermont Medical Center (UVMMC) commands two-thirds of total spending. Because the insurer cannot afford to lose the network's patients, UVMMC acts as a 'price maker' rather than a 'price taker.'

body.title: The Price Gap: UVMMC vs. Independent Facilities (2025)

children.text: Economic Theory: Why Money Doesn't Buy Health

This pricing power is exacerbated by two classic health economic failures: 'Physician-Induced Demand' (PID) and 'Supply-Sensitive Care.' The data shows that 31% of physician FTEs at UVMMC are non-clinical, yet clinical productivity remains low (75% of physicians are below the 50th percentile). In a Fee-For-Service (FFS) model, this bloat is incentivized. Physicians, acting as agents for uniformed patients, may recommend higher-intensity care that generates institutional revenue but offers diminishing marginal returns for patient health—a phenomenon known as the 'Flat of the Curve' medicine.

To understand the difference between expenditure and utility, consider a leaky bucket: if the bucket (the health system) has holes (inefficiencies like high administrative costs), adding more water (funding) will not help you carry it any further.
The Solution: Global Budgets & Site Neutrality

The Wyman Report and economic theory suggest a definitive path forward: breaking the Fee-For-Service addiction. The proposed shift to 'Global Budgets' (modeled after Maryland) would cap total hospital revenue, flipping the incentive: suddenly, an MRI becomes a cost to manage rather than a product to sell. Furthermore, enforcing 'Site Neutrality' would mandate that a check-up costs the same whether performed in a hospital tower or a strip mall, effectively dismantling the arbitrage opportunity that drives today's 555% markups.

children.text: What Are Vermont’s Designated Agencies?

Vermont organizes its public behavioral health system around a network of Designated Agencies (DAs) — private, nonprofit, community-based organizations that the state formally designates to deliver mental health, substance use, and developmental disability services in defined geographic regions. There are 10 Designated Agencies, with the state designating one to serve each region, so that every part of Vermont has a clear, accountable local provider of these services.

Alongside the 10 DAs, Vermont works with two Specialized Service Agencies (SSAs): Pathways Vermont, which serves adults, and NFI Vermont (the Northeastern Family Institute), which serves children and families. Together the DAs and SSAs form the backbone of Vermont’s publicly funded behavioral health "System of Care."

The defining feature of this model is that responsibility is explicit and local. Rather than leaving it to chance whether a region has adequate community mental health services, Vermont assigns a designated, accountable agency to each region and funds it to serve everyone who needs care — a structure quite different from the fragmented patchwork found in many states.

A Designated Agency is a private nonprofit that Vermont formally designates to provide mental health, substance use, and developmental disability services for a specific region. Vermont has 10 DAs (one per region) plus two Specialized Service Agencies.

children.text: Roots in Deinstitutionalization

The Designated Agency model grew out of the deinstitutionalization movement of the mid-twentieth century. For decades, people with serious mental illness were confined in large state psychiatric hospitals — Vermont’s was the Vermont State Hospital in Waterbury — often for years or decades. The federal Community Mental Health Act, signed by President Kennedy in 1963, set out to replace this with community-based care, shifting resources toward local nonprofit services.

Vermont built its DA network as the community-based system that deinstitutionalization required. The logic was that local, community-rooted nonprofits would be better positioned than a distant state institution to support people living in their own communities. Over time the DAs became the primary home for community mental health, developmental disability, and substance use services across the state.

This history became vivid in 2011, when the Vermont State Hospital in Waterbury was severely damaged and effectively closed after flooding from Tropical Storm Irene, capping years of decertification and quality problems. Its closure accelerated Vermont’s reliance on a more distributed, community-based system — making the strength of the DA network a matter of statewide importance.

body.content:
The Vermont State Hospital in Waterbury, the state’s long-standing psychiatric institution, was forced to close in 2011 following flooding from Tropical Storm Irene, on top of earlier decertification and quality concerns.
Its closure pushed Vermont toward an even more decentralized model, increasing the importance of the community-based Designated Agencies that care for people outside of institutional walls.
body.title: The Closure of the Vermont State Hospital

children.text: How Designation Works

Designation is a formal, statutory process. Under Vermont law (18 V.S.A. § 8907 and related statutes), the state’s commissioners ensure that community services for people with mental health conditions, psychiatric disabilities, and developmental disabilities are provided through designated community agencies, and they designate the public or private nonprofit agencies to provide or arrange for those services in each area.

Designation is not permanent or automatic — agencies must be periodically recertified, meeting state standards to keep their designated status. This gives the state ongoing leverage over quality and accountability: a Designated Agency holds a defined responsibility for its region, and that responsibility is reviewed and renewed rather than granted indefinitely.

Many of the DAs are organized collaboratively through Vermont Care Partners, a network combining the Vermont Council of Developmental and Mental Health Services and the Vermont Care Network — a collaboration of sixteen nonprofit community-based member agencies serving Vermonters affected by developmental disabilities, mental health conditions, and substance use disorders. This shared infrastructure helps the agencies coordinate, advocate, and operate consistently statewide.

children.text: How the Agencies Are Funded

Funding is what makes the model work — and it reflects the same move away from pure fee-for-service discussed earlier in this course. Rather than billing per visit, DAs are largely funded through case rates and a capitation arrangement: the Department of Vermont Health Access (DVHA), Vermont’s Medicaid agency, makes per-member-per-month payments to the Department of Mental Health, which in turn pays the agencies, supplemented by additional state and federal funds for services and people not covered by Medicaid.

This capitated, case-rate structure gives agencies flexibility to provide comprehensive services — case management, crisis response, community support — without the financial pressure of fee-for-service to limit care to the most billable activities. It is, in effect, a value-based approach that predates much of the national value-based payment movement. Most of the Department of Mental Health’s budget — on the order of roughly $200 million — flows to these agencies, much of it from federal Medicaid funds.

Because so much funding and responsibility is concentrated in the DAs, their financial health and workforce capacity are recurring statewide concerns. When DAs face staffing shortages or funding pressure, the effects ripple across Vermont’s entire behavioral health safety net — which is why the agencies feature prominently in the state’s legislative and budget debates.

Vermont funds its Designated Agencies largely through Medicaid case rates and capitation rather than fee-for-service — a value-based approach that gives agencies the flexibility to deliver comprehensive community care.
Why Vermont’s System Is Studied

Vermont’s Designated Agency model is frequently cited as a comparatively organized approach to community behavioral health. By assigning clear regional responsibility, funding agencies flexibly, and building a comprehensive local presence, the state achieves a level of coordination and coverage that fragmented systems in other states often lack. A single agency like the Howard Center, the Designated Agency for Chittenden County, can run dozens of programs and serve many thousands of people across mental health, substance use, and developmental disability needs.

The model is not without strain. Like behavioral health systems everywhere, the DAs face workforce shortages, rising demand, and funding pressures, and Vermont continues to reform and supplement the system — including by adding Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic funding in 2024, layering a national model on top of its existing infrastructure. The DA system is a strong foundation, not a finished solution.

For this course, the Designated Agencies illustrate in concrete, real-world form many of the principles covered earlier: community-based care, integration of mental health and substance use services, accountable regional responsibility, and value-based funding. They set the stage for Vermont’s equally distinctive opioid treatment system — the Hub-and-Spoke model — examined in the next lesson.

body.content:
The Howard Center is the Designated Agency for Chittenden County (greater Burlington), Vermont’s most populous region, providing mental health and developmental disability services and serving as the lead substance use provider for the area.
It operates more than fifty programs with a staff of around 1,300 and supports roughly 19,000 people a year across more than 60 locations — illustrating the scale and comprehensiveness a single Designated Agency can reach.

children.text: As the CTO for the Vermont Agency of Digital Services, my mandate is clear: we must engineer a healthcare infrastructure that is fiscally sustainable and technologically liquid. The legacy 'Silo' model, where patient data is trapped in proprietary vendor-locked repositories, is the primary driver of administrative friction and clinical inefficiency in the State of Vermont.
I. The Strategic Imperative: Data Sovereignty

This phenomenon, which I define as 'Technical Deflation,' allows the State to reinvest capital into frontline medical services rather than back-end IT maintenance.

children.text: A Statewide System for Opioid Use Disorder

Vermont’s Hub-and-Spoke model is one of the most influential state responses to the opioid crisis in the United States. It is a statewide system designed to do exactly what the earlier lesson on opioid treatment identified as the central challenge: get more people onto medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) by extending treatment from specialty clinics into mainstream, community-based care.

The model emerged from Vermont’s Blueprint for Health — the state’s broader initiative to reform primary care and chronic disease management. A key conceptual move was to treat opioid use disorder as a chronic condition, like diabetes or heart disease, that benefits from a coordinated network linking specialty expertise with everyday primary care. Addiction medicine physicians and public health leaders built this into the "Care Alliance for Opioid Addiction," which became the Hub-and-Spoke system.

Vermont divided the state into five geographic regions and began a staggered rollout of the system in January 2013. The result was a coordinated, statewide treatment infrastructure rather than a scattering of unconnected clinics — a structure that closely mirrors the integration principles at the heart of this course.

Vermont’s Hub-and-Spoke model treats opioid use disorder as a chronic condition and builds a statewide network linking specialty addiction "hubs" with primary-care "spokes." It launched across five regions in January 2013 under the Blueprint for Health.
The Hubs: Specialty Addiction Treatment

The "hubs" are regional specialty centers built around Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) — the SAMHSA-certified clinics that, as covered earlier, are the only settings legally able to dispense methadone for opioid use disorder. Each of Vermont’s five regions has a hub clinic that provides daily dosing, can offer either methadone or buprenorphine, and delivers more intensive therapeutic services.

Hubs serve two main functions. First, they treat the patients who need the most intensive, structured care — including those starting treatment, those with complex needs, or those who are not stable enough for a primary care setting. Second, they act as the regional center of addiction expertise: hub staff assess patients at intake and determine the most appropriate placement, including referral out to a primary-care spoke when a patient is stable.

Entry into the hubs comes from many directions — hospitals and emergency rooms (especially after an overdose reversal), residential programs, the Department of Corrections, and community mental health programs — making the hub a true regional gateway into treatment for opioid use disorder.

body.content:
Each hub is organized around an existing Opioid Treatment Program with the authority to dispense both methadone and buprenorphine, providing daily dosing and intensive services for patients with the most complex needs.
Hub staff assess every patient at intake and decide whether they should be treated at the hub or transferred to a primary-care spoke — making the hub the clinical anchor for its region.
body.title: The Hub as Regional Center of Expertise

children.text: The Spokes: Office-Based Treatment in the Community

The "spokes" are general medical settings — primary care practices and other office-based providers — that deliver office-based opioid treatment (OBOT), prescribing buprenorphine and seeing patients weekly or monthly rather than daily. The spokes are how the model reaches patients close to home, in the same primary care relationships where the rest of their health care happens. This is the integration this course champions, applied directly to addiction.

The model’s signature innovation is the support given to spoke prescribers. Each spoke is backed by a "MAT team" — staffing of roughly one full-time registered nurse and one master’s-level licensed behavioral health or addictions provider for every 100 Medicaid office-based patients. This team provides nursing, counseling, and care management; the nurse handles intake tasks, prescription refills, urine drug testing, and diversion monitoring, freeing the physician to manage a panel of patients without being overwhelmed.

Crucially, this MAT team support is provided to the practice at no direct cost, funded through a Medicaid Health Home arrangement (a 90/10 federal–state funding split enabled by the Affordable Care Act). By removing both the workload burden and the cost barrier, Vermont made it realistic for ordinary primary care providers to treat opioid use disorder — directly attacking the prescriber-shortage problem.

children.text: A Bidirectional, Coordinated Network

The genius of the model is that patients flow in both directions. The arrangement deliberately mirrors how other chronic diseases are managed — for example, the way a complex cardiac patient might be stabilized by a cardiology center and then managed by their primary care doctor, returning to the specialist if they destabilize. Opioid use disorder is treated the same way: hubs and spokes form one connected system, not separate silos.

When a patient stabilizes, they can step down from the hub to a spoke for more convenient, less intensive care; when a patient struggles, they can step back up to the hub for more support. This "robust bidirectional transfer based on clinical need" is what makes the network coherent, and it echoes the ASAM principle that placement should follow the patient’s changing clinical status rather than being fixed.

This design also expanded the prescriber workforce dramatically. By making office-based treatment feasible and supported, the model drove large increases in the number of buprenorphine prescribers and in patients served per prescriber — multiplying the state’s capacity to treat opioid use disorder.

children.text: Outcomes and National Influence

The results have made Vermont a national reference point. By around 2017, Vermont had the highest capacity for treating opioid use disorder in the country — on the order of 10.56 people in treatment per 1,000 population. The system substantially expanded treatment access in a largely rural state where access is otherwise hard to achieve.

A state evaluation found significant positive impacts for patients in treatment: less frequent opioid use, an elimination of overdoses among the study group, fewer emergency department visits, fewer police stops and arrests, and less illegal activity — alongside improved wellbeing, less family conflict, and reduced depression, anger, and anxiety. These are exactly the outcomes the opioid response aims for, achieved by getting and keeping people on effective medication.

Researchers have concluded that the Hub-and-Spoke system contributed substantially to Vermont’s expanded treatment capacity and "may serve as a model for other states grappling with the opioid epidemic." It demonstrates, in one rural state, the central thesis of this course: that integrating specialty and primary care — backed by the right payment and team support — dramatically expands access to lifesaving treatment.

children.text: The social contract of Vermont healthcare—that high premiums buy access to a stable, non-profit system—is actively collapsing. The latest escalation, a direct-to-consumer marketing campaign by Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont (BCBSVT) urging members to bypass the University of Vermont Medical Center (UVMMC), is not merely a contract dispute. It is a signal that the market has reached a point of 'Allocative Failure.' With residents spending 19.6% of their household income on premiums—the highest rate in the nation and nearly triple the 7.9% national average—the system has crossed the threshold from expensive to predatory.
The Raw Data: A Market Without Substitutes

The insurer’s campaign relies on a stark economic reality: price dispersion for commoditized services. In a functional market, the 'Law of One Price' suggests that identical goods (like a standard 3T MRI scan) should have similar costs. In Vermont, this law has been broken by market power. Recent disclosures reveal that UVMMC charges a premium of 262% to 555% over independent competitors for identical diagnostic work.

body.title: The Price of Leverage: UVMMC vs. Independent Providers (2025)

children.text: This data illustrates a 'Differentiated Oligopoly.' UVMMC controls two-thirds of all hospital spending in the state. Because they provide unique, non-substitutable services (Level 1 Trauma, Burn Unit), they can demand monopoly rents on substitutable services (MRIs, Labs). BCBSVT, facing a $62.1 million deficit, is attempting to break this leverage by turning patients into price-sensitive shoppers—a strategy that rarely succeeds in healthcare due to 'Agency Theory.'
Theoretical Expansion: Why 'Shopping' Fails

The insurer's plea for patients to 'shop around' ignores the fundamental specificities of health economics: 

1. **Agency Problems:** The patient (Principal) relies on the doctor (Agent) to make decisions. If a UVMMC specialist orders an MRI, they will default to the internal system. The patient, lacking medical knowledge, rarely overrides this 'default bias' even if it costs them thousands.

2. **Moral Hazard & The Deductible:** For a patient who has already met their deductible, the marginal cost of a $6,500 MRI is zero. They have no financial incentive to drive to St. Albans for the $1,799 option. The cost is fully externalized to the insurance pool, driving up next year's premiums for everyone (the 'Tragedy of the Commons').

The market is trapped in a 'Cost Shift' loop. UVMMC argues these high commercial prices are necessary to subsidize Medicaid underpayments ($0.70 on the dollar). This effectively turns commercial premiums into a hidden tax on Vermont's middle class.
The Structural Fix: Global Budgets

The current 'Fee-For-Service' (FFS) war is a race to the bottom. The Wyman Report and economic consensus point to one viable exit strategy: **Global Budgets** (The Maryland Model).

In a Global Budget system, the state sets a total annual revenue cap for the hospital (e.g., $2 Billion). The hospital is paid this amount regardless of how many MRIs it performs. 

**Why this solves the problem:**
* **Incentive Reversal:** Under FFS, every MRI is profit. Under Global Budgets, every MRI is a *cost*. UVMMC would suddenly *want* to send patients to the cheaper independent center to save its own budget.
* **Stable Funding:** The 'Cost Shift' is formalized. The budget explicitly covers the Trauma Center's fixed costs, removing the need to overcharge for MRIs to keep the lights on.
* **Site Neutrality:** It eliminates the arbitrage between hospital-based and freestanding clinics.

children.text: The Strategic Imperative for a New HIE Governance Model

As the Chief Data Officer for the Vermont Agency of Human Services (AHS), I have conducted a rigorous audit of our current health data exchange landscape. The conclusion is undeniable: the legacy architecture managed by Vermont Information Technology Leaders (VITL) has reached its architectural and fiscal ceiling. To meet the mandates of the 2026 Health Innovation Plan, Vermont must pivot toward a collaborative, multi-state shared services model. CRISP (Chesapeake Regional Information System for our Patients) offers the proven, cloud-native infrastructure required to transform the VHIE from a passive repository into a dynamic clinical tool.

CDO Alert: Maintaining the current VITL contract costs the state approximately $2.1M annually in avoidable technical debt and redundant maintenance fees compared to regional shared-service benchmarks.
Quantitative Performance Gaps

The current VHIE infrastructure suffers from significant latency in ADT (Admission, Discharge, Transfer) notifications and lacks the native capability to integrate social determinants of health (SDOH) at scale. By moving to the CRISP platform, we gain access to a mature stack that already services Maryland, West Virginia, and the District of Columbia. This transition allows Vermont to benefit from collective R&D, ensuring our clinical community has access to real-time longitudinal patient records without the localized burden of developing every new feature from scratch.

children.text: The rural nursing staffing crisis has created the conditions for a structural transformation that would have been impossible five years ago. Hub-and-spoke virtual nursing—in which a centralized telenursing hub provides remote monitoring, clinical decision support, and patient education to bedside nursing staff at 3–6 spoke rural hospitals simultaneously—is now in production at 23 rural health systems across 11 states.
The Model Architecture

The hub-and-spoke virtual nursing model assigns one virtual RN at the hub to support 6–8 beds at each of 3–6 spoke hospitals simultaneously, typically handling medication reconciliation, discharge education, care plan documentation, and continuous vital sign monitoring while bedside staff at the spoke sites focus on hands-on care that requires physical presence. The model does not replace bedside nurses; it changes the ratio of administrative to clinical tasks each bedside nurse handles, effectively increasing the productive clinical capacity of a smaller bedside team.

body.title: Virtual Nursing Model: Staffing and Financial Metrics (23 Rural Deployments)

children.text: Technology Requirements and Integration Points

The technology stack for a viable rural virtual nursing program requires four components: (1) a two-way audiovisual bedside station (typically a wall-mounted or mobile cart-based unit) at each spoke bed, (2) continuous vital sign monitoring with real-time data transmission to the hub, (3) EHR integration allowing the hub RN to document directly into the spoke hospital’s record, and (4) a communication platform connecting the hub RN to bedside staff, physicians, and the patient simultaneously.

The EHR integration requirement is the most technically complex and the most frequently underestimated in implementation planning. Hub RNs documenting in a separate system from bedside staff create dangerous documentation gaps. Systems that have achieved native EHR integration—where hub and spoke staff document in the same record with clear role identifiers—show 31% better adverse event outcomes than those using parallel documentation systems.

The virtual nurse is not watching a screen. She is caring for 14 patients across three hospitals simultaneously, and she needs to see every vital sign, every alert, and every note in one place. When you compromise the integration, you compromise patient safety.

IMPLEMENTATION PRIORITY: EHR integration quality is the single most important technical decision in virtual nursing deployment. Require vendors to demonstrate same-system documentation (not parallel documentation) with your specific EHR before signing a contract. The 11% adverse event reduction observed in well-integrated programs disappears entirely in parallel-documentation deployments.

children.text: When Doing the Right Thing Costs You Money

Imagine a hospital that runs a brilliant program to keep heart-failure patients healthy at home. The program works: admissions for those patients drop sharply. Under fee-for-service, this clinical triumph is a financial disaster — every avoided admission is lost revenue, while the hospital’s fixed costs (the building, the staff, the equipment) remain. The hospital did exactly what good medicine demands and was punished for it by its own payment system. This is the central, uncomfortable truth of the volume-to-value transition, and it is the reason that transition is so financially treacherous.

Value-based care asks hospitals to deliver less of the high-margin, volume-driven care that fee-for-service rewards — fewer admissions, fewer readmissions, fewer unnecessary procedures — in exchange for payments tied to keeping populations healthy. But the shift does not happen overnight, and during the long in-between, hospitals must operate under two contradictory payment logics at once. The financial implications of that contradiction are the subject of this lesson.

This is not abstract. It determines whether a hospital can afford to pursue value-based contracts, how fast it can move, and whether its mission to improve health aligns with or fights against its need to stay solvent. For a field built on the promise of paying for outcomes instead of volume, the messy economics of getting there are where most hospitals actually live.

Key Concept: Under fee-for-service, reducing unnecessary care reduces revenue while fixed costs remain — so a hospital succeeding at value-based care can lose money on the very utilization it eliminated. Managing this contradiction during the transition is the core financial challenge of moving from volume to value.

children.text: The Two Canoes Problem

The transition’s defining metaphor is the "two canoes" problem: a hospital stands with one foot in the fee-for-service canoe and one foot in the value-based-care canoe, and the two canoes are drifting apart because their incentives point in opposite directions. Value-based contracts demand very different business and clinical practices than those that maximize fee-for-service revenue — yet with most income still anchored to volume, hospitals often cannot afford a wholesale pivot to cost-conscious care. They must straddle both worlds, and straddling is precarious.

The financial mechanics of the straddle are genuinely hard to model. A health system CFO asked "what is the financial impact of reducing chronic-disease admissions by 25%?" faces a brutal calculation: the saved direct care costs are real, but so is the lost reimbursement, and the overhead that those admissions used to cover does not disappear. The published research is blunt about the consequence — because preventing a hospitalization leaves overhead costs uncovered, the loss of reimbursement revenue can actually mitigate a hospital’s incentive to reduce readmissions in the first place. The payment system fights the clinical goal.

body.message: Value-based contracts return a portion of the savings a hospital generates — but that share frequently does not fully offset the fee-for-service revenue lost when admissions and procedures fall. A hospital can improve care, generate system-wide savings, and still come out behind financially if it has not shifted enough of its revenue to value-based payment.
body.title: Shared Savings Often Don’t Cover the Loss

children.text: Where the Revenue Goes: The Migration of Care

The volume-to-value shift is not only about eliminating care — it is also about moving it. Procedures that once required expensive inpatient stays are migrating to lower-cost outpatient settings, and the financial footprint follows. Inpatient primary knee replacements fell 21.2% year over year as those cases moved to outpatient sites, and average length of stay has been declining. Each of these shifts trims the high-revenue inpatient business that hospitals were built around, even when overall volumes remain healthy.

Paradoxically, this is happening during a period of strong hospital revenue. Through 2024, hospitals posted 20 consecutive months of year-over-year revenue increases, with outpatient revenue surging 8.7% — outpacing inpatient growth of 4.3% — and full-year median operating margins holding above 4.5% and reaching 6% by December. The headline numbers look healthy, but underneath them the revenue base is migrating from inpatient to outpatient and from volume toward value, reshaping where and how hospitals earn their money.

body.content:
A teaching hospital invests in a care-transitions program that successfully prevents readmissions. Clinically and ethically, this is unambiguously good — and under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program, avoiding readmissions also dodges penalties of up to 3% of Medicare payments.

But under fee-for-service, each prevented readmission is also a lost admission: revenue the hospital would have collected, gone, while the fixed overhead remains. Whether the program helps or hurts the hospital financially depends entirely on its payment mix — how much of its revenue is value-based (rewarding the prevention) versus fee-for-service (penalizing the lost volume). The same clinical action is a financial win or loss depending on which canoe carries more of the hospital’s weight.
body.title: The Avoided Readmission Paradox

children.text: Managing the Straddle: Tipping Points and Bridges

If straddling two canoes is dangerous, how do hospitals survive it? The strategic answer centers on the concept of a tipping point: the share of revenue under value-based contracts at which it becomes financially rational to fully embrace cost-conscious care. Below that threshold, a hospital that aggressively cuts volume bleeds fee-for-service revenue faster than its value-based payments grow. Above it, reducing unnecessary utilization finally rewards the hospital more than it costs. Much of value-based strategy is about deliberately managing the pace of the shift so the two sides cross over without the hospital capsizing in between.

Hospitals use several bridges to tie the canoes closer together during the crossing. Expanded fee-for-service reimbursement — new billing codes for care coordination, remote patient monitoring, and chronic-care management — lets a hospital get paid for value-promoting activities even while still in the fee-for-service world, acting like bungee cords that keep the canoes from drifting too far apart. Hospitals also sequence their risk-taking, starting with upside-only shared savings before accepting downside risk, and concentrate value-based efforts on the populations and service lines where they can succeed first.

children.text: Why This Is the Hardest Problem in Hospital Finance

The volume-to-value transition is uniquely difficult because it asks an organization to undermine its current business model in order to build its future one — while keeping the lights on throughout. Every other industry that has been disrupted got to fail and be replaced; hospitals must transform themselves without interruption, because the community cannot go without a hospital while it figures out its finances. The two-canoes problem is not a temporary inconvenience but a structural feature of a decades-long, incomplete transition.

body.analogy: Moving from volume to value is like a store that earns most of its money selling cigarettes being told its future is selling gym memberships. As long as cigarettes pay the bills, every successful fitness program cannibalizes the store’s own revenue. It cannot simply stop selling cigarettes (it would go bankrupt) nor ignore the future (memberships are where the market is going). It has to grow the new business fast enough to replace the old one before the old one is taken away — exactly the tightrope hospitals walk.
body.concept: The volume-to-value financial transition

children.text: External pressure is compressing the timeline. Hospitals are bracing for major revenue hits beginning in 2027 from provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), pushing many to cut expenses and rethink their revenue base now. As fee-for-service reimbursement grows less sustainable and government payments tighten, the calculus increasingly favors moving toward value — not because value-based contracts are lucrative, but because the volume-based alternative is eroding. The two canoes are being pulled toward the value side whether hospitals are ready or not.

For the student of hospital finance, this lesson reframes everything that came before. Payer mix, margins, cost accounting, and capital structure all take on new meaning when revenue can be reduced by success rather than failure. The hospitals that navigate the transition will be those that understand their cost structure precisely (hence the emphasis on activity-based costing), manage the pace of risk deliberately, and build the population-health capabilities that make value-based payment a strength rather than a threat. The next lessons — on shared savings and risk, and on the business case for population health — are about exactly how to do that.

children.text: A Different Unit of Concern

Most of medicine focuses on one patient at a time: this person, this visit, this diagnosis. Population health flips the unit of concern from the individual to the group. It asks not "how do we treat this patient?" but "how healthy is this whole population, and what is driving its health?"

The foundational definition comes from a 2003 paper by David Kindig and Greg Stoddart in the American Journal of Public Health. They defined population health as "the health outcomes of a group of individuals, including the distribution of such outcomes within the group." That definition is more subtle than it looks, and unpacking it is the key to the whole field.

The phrase "distribution of such outcomes" is doing heavy lifting. It means population health is not satisfied with an average — a population can have good average health while a subgroup suffers terribly. Built into the very definition is a concern with equity: how health is spread across the group, not just its mean. This is why population health and health equity are inseparable.

Population health (Kindig & Stoddart, 2003) is "the health outcomes of a group of individuals, including the distribution of such outcomes within the group." The unit of concern is the group, and the focus on distribution makes equity intrinsic.
Three Elements and the Determinants of Health

Kindig and Stoddart described the field as having three connected elements: health outcomes, the patterns of health determinants that produce those outcomes, and the policies and interventions that link the two. In other words, population health is not just measuring how healthy a group is — it is understanding why, and acting on it.

The "why" lives in the determinants of health. The authors named six categories: the social, economic, and physical environments; personal health practices; individual capacity and coping skills; biology; early developmental trajectory (early childhood); and access to health services. Strikingly, only one of those six — access to health services — is what we usually think of as "health care."

This is the most important and counterintuitive idea in population health: most of what determines a group's health happens outside the doctor's office. The conditions people live in, their behaviors, their early-life circumstances, and their environment shape health far more than medical care does. A field focused on population health must therefore look well beyond the clinic.

children.text: The Triple Aim

Population health entered the mainstream of U.S. health policy through the Triple Aim. In 2008, Don Berwick, Tom Nolan, and John Whittington of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) described three goals to pursue simultaneously: improving the patient experience of care, improving the health of populations, and reducing the per capita cost of care.

The Triple Aim was transformative because it made "the health of populations" an explicit, co-equal goal of the health system — alongside individual care quality and cost. It became the organizing framework for the U.S. National Quality Strategy and for countless health-system strategies. Population health has been called the "North Star" of the Triple Aim.

The framework's power is that the three aims pull on each other. You cannot durably reduce per capita cost without improving population health (sicker populations cost more), and you cannot improve population health by focusing only on the patients who happen to show up. The Triple Aim pushed health systems to think beyond their own walls to the health of the communities they serve.
