children.text: Population Health vs. Population Health Management

A crucial distinction runs through this course: population health versus population health management (PHM). Population health is the broad concept — the health outcomes and determinants of a group, in the academic Kindig-Stoddart sense, which can mean an entire community or nation. Population health management adds a strong, operational management component: it is what a specific health-care organization actually does to improve outcomes for a defined group it is responsible for.

The key word is "defined." A PHM program operates on a defined population — usually the patients attributed to a practice, the members of a health plan, or the employees of an employer. Most PHM models rest on an attribution method that assigns a panel of patients to a provider or organization, which is then accountable for that panel's health.

This distinction matters because this course is mostly about management — the practical work of improving the health of a defined, attributed population. When we say "population health" going forward, we usually mean PHM: a concrete organization, a concrete panel, and concrete interventions, all measured against the Triple Aim.

children.text: Proactive, Whole-Population Care

The defining behavior of population health management is that it is proactive and whole-population, not reactive and visit-based. Traditional care is reactive: it treats the patients who walk in the door. PHM attends to the entire defined population — including the patients who have NOT come in, who are often the ones at highest risk.

This is the logic of "panel management": a practice systematically identifies and tracks the care needs of every patient on its panel, whether or not they are showing up for appointments. The diabetic patient who has not been seen in a year, the woman overdue for a mammogram, the person with rising blood pressure who never schedules a visit — population health is designed to find and reach exactly those people.

This proactive stance is also why population health is bound up with value-based care. Under fee-for-service, there is little incentive to chase the patients who are not generating visits. Under value-based payment, where the organization is accountable for the cost and quality of a whole population, preventing expensive downstream events (an avoidable ER visit, an uncontrolled chronic disease) becomes the whole game. Value-based care is the economic engine that makes population health management worth doing — and the rest of this course builds out how it is actually done.

body.message: The biggest mental shift in population health is attending to the whole defined panel — especially the high-risk patients who are not coming in for care. Reactive, visit-based medicine misses exactly the people who most need outreach. PHM is proactive by design.

children.text: The Money Side of Care

Every time a patient receives care, two things happen in parallel. There is the clinical story — the diagnosis, the treatment, the outcome. And there is a financial story — someone has to be billed, an insurer has to be charged, and the provider has to actually get paid for the work. Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the discipline that governs that second story.

Formally, the revenue cycle is comprised of all the administrative and clinical functions that contribute to the capture, management, and collection of patient service revenue. In plainer terms: it is everything a healthcare organization does to get paid for the care it delivers — from the moment a patient schedules an appointment to the moment the final dollar is collected.

This matters enormously because, in American health care, getting paid is genuinely hard. Care is delivered first and billed later; payment flows through a maze of insurers each with their own rules; and a single error anywhere in the chain can mean the provider is never paid at all. RCM exists to manage that complexity so that providers stay financially viable and can keep their doors open.

Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the set of administrative and clinical functions that capture, manage, and collect the revenue a provider earns for patient care — everything involved in getting paid, from scheduling to final collection.
Why RCM Is Such a Big Deal

The scale of the money and effort involved is staggering. Administrative costs — much of which is billing- and insurance-related work — are estimated to represent roughly 25 to 31 percent of total U.S. healthcare spending. The largest single category of healthcare "waste," about $266 billion a year, comes from administrative complexity.

That complexity translates into real money lost when RCM fails. In 2024, an estimated $262 billion in claims were denied by insurers, and the initial claim denial rate reached about 11.8 percent — meaning roughly one in eight claims was rejected on first submission. Each denied claim costs somewhere between $25 and $181 just to rework.

Unsurprisingly, RCM has become a massive industry in its own right. The U.S. revenue cycle management market is measured in the tens of billions of dollars and growing at double-digit rates, as providers invest heavily in people, software, and outsourced services to capture revenue they would otherwise lose. RCM is not back-office trivia — it is central to whether a hospital or practice survives.

children.text: The Three Phases of the Revenue Cycle

The revenue cycle is conventionally divided into three phases, and this front-to-back structure is the map for the entire course. The first is the front-end: everything that happens before and at the point of care — scheduling, registration, insurance verification, prior authorization, and financial counseling.

The second is the mid-cycle, where clinical care meets the financial process. This is where the care delivered during the visit gets translated into billable form: clinical documentation, medical coding (ICD-10, CPT, HCPCS), and charge capture. The mid-cycle is the bridge — what happens here directly determines how much the provider can bill and how cleanly.

The third is the back-end: everything after the bill is created — claim submission, payment posting, denial management, appeals, accounts receivable follow-up, and patient collections. A useful way to remember it: the front-end sets up the claim, the mid-cycle builds the claim, and the back-end collects on the claim.

children.text: Where Clinical Meets Financial

One of the most important ideas in RCM is that it is not purely a financial function — it is deeply clinical. The mid-cycle makes this explicit: what a clinician documents during a visit directly affects how much the organization gets paid and how quickly. A service that was delivered but not documented, or documented but not coded, simply does not get billed.

This clinical-financial link runs throughout the cycle. A registration clerk who mistypes an insurance ID, a physician who under-documents a complex visit, a coder who selects the wrong code — each is a clinical-adjacent action with direct financial consequences downstream. RCM is therefore a team sport spanning the entire organization, not the job of a billing department alone.

This is also why RCM is increasingly understood as a quality-and-finance discipline together. Accurate documentation and coding are simultaneously about getting paid correctly and about reflecting the care actually delivered. The same data that drives a clean claim also feeds quality measurement, which connects RCM to the broader work of running a health system well.

body.analogy: Think of RCM like a relay race. The front-end runner gets the baton cleanly off the line (correct patient and insurance info). The mid-cycle runner carries it through the hard middle stretch (documentation and coding). The back-end runner sprints to the finish (claims and collections). Drop the baton at any handoff and the whole team loses the race — no matter how fast the other runners are.
body.concept: How the phases of the revenue cycle depend on each other

children.text: Who Does RCM and How It Is Measured

RCM is performed by a wide cast: schedulers and registrars, financial counselors, medical coders, billing specialists, denial and appeals analysts, and accounts-receivable teams, all supported by software and often by outsourced vendors. Many organizations now blend in-house staff with specialized RCM companies and technology platforms.

Because RCM determines whether a provider gets paid, it is measured rigorously. The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) maintains a set of standardized revenue-cycle metrics known as MAP Keys, which establish industry benchmarks for revenue cycle excellence across hospitals, physician groups, and other provider types. Later lessons in this course dive into these key performance indicators in detail.

The goal of all this measurement and effort is simple to state and hard to achieve: get paid the right amount, for the right care, as quickly as possible, with as little waste and rework as possible. Every lesson that follows is, at bottom, about improving one piece of that goal — and this course walks the full cycle from scheduling to collections.

children.text: The Inevitable Reality of Denials

No matter how clean the front-end and mid-cycle, some claims will come back denied. Denial management is the back-end discipline of dealing with that reality, and it begins with a deceptively simple question: why was this claim denied? Understanding the root-cause categories of denials is the foundation for both fixing individual claims and preventing the next batch.

The scale makes this urgent. Initial claim denial rates reached about 11.8 percent in 2024 (with some payer types, like Medicare Advantage and managed Medicaid, running around 15 percent), and roughly $262 billion in claims were initially denied that year. Denials are not an edge case — they are a constant, massive drain that every organization must actively manage.

The single most important fact about denials, though, is hopeful: the Kaiser Family Foundation found that between 86 and 90 percent of denials are preventable. The vast majority of denials trace to fixable, upstream causes — which means understanding the categories is the first step to driving the denial rate down.

Denials are a constant: initial denial rates hit ~11.8% in 2024 (~$262B denied). But 86-90% of denials are preventable, so understanding root-cause categories is the key to both fixing claims and preventing future denials.
Soft Denials vs. Hard Denials

A foundational distinction shapes how a denial is handled: soft versus hard. A soft denial is temporary — it can often be reversed by submitting additional information or correcting and resubmitting the claim. The money is recoverable if the team acts. A duplicate claim or a missing-information denial is typically soft.

A hard denial is final — it generally results in lost revenue and cannot simply be corrected and resubmitted (though some can still be appealed). A denial for a service that was genuinely not covered, or one where the timely filing deadline has irrevocably passed, is typically hard. Hard denials are the ones that become write-offs.

This distinction drives triage. Soft denials should be worked quickly, because they are recoverable with effort; hard denials require judgment about whether an appeal is worth pursuing or whether to write off. Knowing which is which prevents teams from wasting effort on unrecoverable claims while letting recoverable ones age past the point of recovery.

children.text: The Major Root-Cause Categories

Denials cluster into a recognizable set of root causes, and learning them is essential because each maps to a different prevention strategy upstream. Missing or inaccurate information (wrong demographics, missing fields) and prior authorization problems consistently rank as the top causes in industry surveys, followed closely by eligibility/coverage issues.

The other major categories: medical necessity (the documentation did not justify the service — research has found this among the top denial reasons); coding errors (mismatched diagnosis and procedure, wrong modifiers, invalid codes); timely filing violations (the claim was submitted past the payer's deadline); duplicate claims (the same service billed twice); and coordination-of-benefits problems (billed the wrong payer first).

Notice that nearly every category traces back to an earlier lesson in this course: missing info and eligibility to the front-end; prior auth to its own lesson; medical necessity to documentation; coding errors to coding; timely filing to payer contracts. This is the practical proof of the "back-end denial is a front-end failure" principle — the denial categories are essentially a catalog of where upstream processes broke.

children.text: Reading the Denial: CARC and RARC Codes

Payers do not deny claims with a written paragraph — they use standardized codes. The primary one is the Claim Adjustment Reason Code (CARC), which states the reason for an adjustment or denial. CARCs appear on the remittance, telling the provider exactly why the claim was not paid in full. There are roughly 358 CARCs maintained by the X12 committee.

Alongside CARCs are Remittance Advice Remark Codes (RARCs), which provide supplementary explanation and instructions. The rule of thumb: the CARC tells you what happened to your claim, and the RARC adds context or next steps. RARCs are not always present — they appear when extra explanation is needed.

A handful of CARCs account for the majority of denials, so learning the common ones is high-leverage. Examples include CO-16 (claim lacks information), CO-18 (duplicate claim), CO-50 (deemed not medically necessary), CO-97 (service included/not separately covered), and CO-22 (coordination of benefits needed). The "CO" prefix indicates a contractual obligation (provider write-off), while a "PR" prefix indicates patient responsibility — the prefix itself tells you who owes the balance.

body.title: Common CARC Denial Codes

children.text: From Categorizing to Preventing

Categorizing denials is not bookkeeping — it is the engine of prevention. Because 86 to 90 percent of denials are preventable, the path to a lower denial rate runs through systematically tracking which categories and CARCs are driving an organization's denials, then fixing the upstream process responsible.

This is classic root-cause analysis applied to revenue. If "no prior authorization" denials spike, the fix is in the front-end authorization workflow, not the appeals team. If "missing information" denials dominate, the fix is registration data quality. If "medical necessity" denials rise, the fix is documentation. The CARC distribution is essentially a diagnostic readout of where the revenue cycle is leaking.

This is why reducing denials became a top priority for the large majority of organizations — and why denial root-cause analysis sits at the center of the back-end. Understanding why claims are denied is the prerequisite for the next two lessons: building a workflow to work denials efficiently, and appealing the ones that were wrong. But the ultimate goal is always to drive the denial rate down by preventing the categories at their source.

body.message: Fixing an individual denied claim recovers one payment; fixing the root-cause category prevents hundreds of future denials. Because 86-90% of denials are preventable, tracking CARC patterns to find and fix the upstream process is far higher-leverage than working denials one at a time.
body.title: Work the Category, Not Just the Claim

children.text: The Problem Hiding in Plain Sight

For most of the 20th century, American medicine assumed that well-trained doctors working in good hospitals delivered good care, and there was little systematic effort to check. Quality was treated as a matter of individual competence and professional reputation, not something you measured, reported, or improved as a system.

That assumption shattered at the turn of the century, when a pair of landmark reports forced the country to confront how often care fell short. The realization was uncomfortable: the gap between the care people should receive and the care they actually received was enormous, and largely invisible because no one was measuring it.

Clinical quality measurement is the response to that problem. It is the discipline of defining what good care looks like, turning it into standardized metrics, and using the resulting data to hold the system accountable and drive improvement. This lesson explains why that discipline exists and why it matters.
Clinical quality measurement is the systematic practice of defining good care, converting it into standardized metrics, and using the data to improve outcomes and hold the health system accountable.
To Err Is Human: The Wake-Up Call

In November 1999, the Institute of Medicine (IOM) released "To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System." Its central finding stunned the public and the profession: between 44,000 and 98,000 Americans were dying each year as a result of preventable medical errors in hospitals.

To put that in perspective, even the lower estimate would have made medical error the eighth leading cause of death in the United States — killing more people than motor vehicle accidents, breast cancer, or AIDS. The report estimated that medication errors alone accounted for about 7,000 deaths annually, and that the economic cost of preventable adverse events ran to tens of billions of dollars.

Crucially, the report reframed the problem. It argued that most errors were not the fault of bad individuals but of bad systems — poorly designed processes that set up competent people to fail. The solution, therefore, was not to blame and punish, but to measure, learn, and redesign. That insight launched the modern patient-safety and quality-measurement movements.

children.text: Crossing the Quality Chasm: The Six Aims

Two years later, in 2001, the IOM followed up with "Crossing the Quality Chasm: A New Health System for the 21st Century." Where the first report focused on safety, this one widened the lens to the entire quality gap — the chasm between the care we know how to deliver and the care patients actually get.

Its lasting contribution was a definition of quality itself. The report proposed six "Aims for Improvement" that still anchor quality measurement today: care should be safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable. These six aims gave the field a shared vocabulary — any quality measure can be mapped to one or more of them.

The inclusion of equity as a core aim was especially consequential. By naming equitable care — care that does not vary in quality based on personal characteristics like race, gender, geography, or income — as a defining feature of quality, the report planted the seed for the equity-focused measurement work that has become central to the field.

children.text: How Big Is the Gap? The Evidence

The IOM reports made the case conceptually; a landmark study soon quantified it. In 2003, Elizabeth McGlynn and colleagues published a study in the New England Journal of Medicine examining whether adults actually received recommended care.

The researchers reviewed the medical records of nearly 7,000 adults across 12 metropolitan areas, scoring care against 439 clinical indicators for 30 conditions plus preventive care. The headline result: on average, participants received just 54.9 percent of recommended care — barely more than a coin flip.

The variation was striking. Performance ranged from about 79 percent of recommended care for senile cataracts down to just 10.5 percent for alcohol dependence. The study made the abstract "quality chasm" concrete and measurable, and demonstrated exactly why the field needed standardized measures: you cannot close a gap you cannot see.

body.content:
McGlynn and colleagues found U.S. adults received only about 55% of recommended care, with wide variation by condition — from ~79% for cataracts to ~10.5% for alcohol dependence.
Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, it became one of the most-cited demonstrations that the quality gap was real, large, and unevenly distributed — strengthening the case for systematic measurement.
body.title: The McGlynn "Quality of Health Care" Study (2003)

children.text: Why Measurement Drives Improvement

The premise behind quality measurement is often summarized as "what gets measured gets managed." When performance is quantified, problems become visible, comparisons become possible, and attention concentrates where the data points. Measurement creates accountability and transparency that professional good intentions alone cannot.

In practice, measurement now drives improvement through several channels: internal quality improvement teams use it to target their efforts, public reporting lets patients and purchasers compare providers, and value-based payment programs tie reimbursement directly to measured performance. Each channel depends on having trustworthy, standardized measures.

But measurement is a tool, not a guarantee. Measuring the wrong things, or measuring well-intentioned things poorly, can distract clinicians, create administrative burden, and even harm care by encouraging "teaching to the test." The rest of this course is about doing measurement well — choosing meaningful measures, calculating them correctly, and using them to genuinely improve care rather than just generate reports.

body.message: "What gets measured gets managed" cuts both ways. Poorly chosen measures can divert attention from what matters, add documentation burden, and incentivize gaming the metric instead of improving care. Good measurement requires choosing the right measures, not just more of them.

children.text: The Quiet Revolution in How America Covers the Poor

Medicaid is the largest health insurance program in the United States, covering tens of millions of low-income children, adults, seniors, and people with disabilities. But the way most of those people actually receive their care has been transformed over the past three decades, largely out of public view. Today, the dominant model is not the government paying doctors and hospitals directly for each service — it is the state paying private managed care organizations (MCOs) a fixed amount per enrollee to take responsibility for their care. As of July 2024, over 66 million Medicaid enrollees — about 78% of all enrollees — received their care through risk-based MCOs.

This shift from traditional fee-for-service Medicaid to managed care is one of the most consequential and least understood changes in American health policy. It reshaped the relationships among states, the federal government, private insurers, and providers, and it created an entire industry of Medicaid managed care plans operating in most states. Understanding why states made this move — and what they gained and gave up — is the foundation for everything else in Medicaid managed care operations.

The story is not a simple one of cost savings. As we will see, the evidence on whether managed care actually saves money or improves quality is surprisingly mixed. The clearest thing states gained was something subtler but, to a state budget officer, enormously valuable: predictability. This lesson traces the history of the move to managed care and the real rationale behind it.

Key Concept: Medicaid managed care means a state pays a private managed care organization (MCO) a fixed, capitated amount per enrollee to provide their care, shifting financial risk to the MCO — in contrast to traditional fee-for-service Medicaid, where the state pays providers directly for each service.

children.text: From Experiment to Dominant Model: A Brief History

Medicaid began in 1965 as a fee-for-service program: providers delivered care and billed the state, which paid them for each service. By the late 1980s and early 1990s, Medicaid costs were rising sharply, and states began experimenting with more cost-effective ways to deliver care. The answer they reached for was managed care — borrowing the model spreading through private insurance, in which a plan accepts a fixed payment and takes responsibility for managing a population’s care and cost.

The growth was rapid. In 1991, about 2.7 million beneficiaries were enrolled in some form of Medicaid managed care — roughly 10% of the program; by 1996, nearly 40% of Medicaid beneficiaries were enrolled in managed care plans. A key legal turning point came with the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which eliminated the requirement that states obtain a federal waiver before launching mandatory Medicaid managed care programs. That change removed a major bureaucratic hurdle and accelerated adoption, helping push managed care toward the near-universal model it is today.

Before 1997, and still today for certain populations and program designs, states needed federal permission to depart from traditional Medicaid rules — typically through Section 1915 or Section 1115 waivers, which grant exemptions from standard Medicaid guidelines. These waivers remain central to Medicaid managed care and are covered in depth later in this course. The history matters because it shows managed care was not imposed from Washington; it grew from states’ own efforts to control costs, enabled by federal flexibility.

body.title: The Path to Managed Care Dominance

children.text: The Real Rationale: Predictability and Coordination

Why did states embrace managed care so thoroughly? Two rationales are cited most often: increasing the predictability of spending and improving the coordination of care. The predictability argument is the more powerful one in practice. Under fee-for-service, a state’s Medicaid spending is the unpredictable sum of millions of individual claims — if utilization spikes, so does the bill, often after the budget is set. Under managed care, the state pays MCOs a capitated rate per person per month, so it knows its per-enrollee cost in advance. This lets state policymakers predict and manage Medicaid budgets far more reliably.

For a state budget officer, this predictability is enormously valuable. Medicaid is one of the largest items in every state budget, and states (unlike the federal government) must generally balance their budgets each year. Converting an open-ended, volatile fee-for-service liability into a fixed per-member payment transfers the risk of cost overruns to the MCO and gives the state a number it can plan around. The capitation payment effectively caps the state’s per-enrollee exposure.

The second rationale, care coordination, holds that an MCO responsible for a member’s total care — and bearing the financial risk for it — has both the incentive and the tools to coordinate that care, manage chronic conditions, emphasize prevention, and steer members away from costly avoidable utilization. In theory, the same capitation that delivers budget predictability also aligns the plan’s incentives with keeping members healthy. Whether that theory holds up in practice is a separate and contested question.
Did It Deliver? The Honest Evidence

Given how completely managed care has taken over Medicaid, one might assume the evidence for its benefits is overwhelming. It is not. Research has repeatedly challenged whether managed care has delivered on its promises. While states have reliably achieved more predictability in their Medicaid budgets, only a very small number of studies show that managed care has actually helped states lower costs or improve quality. The most confident claim that can be made is about predictability — not savings, and not better outcomes.

Even the predictability gain is more limited than it appears. Research has found that managed care use has been concentrated among the enrollees with the most stable spending — historically healthier children and families — which means the budget predictability gains were smaller than hoped, because the unpredictable, high-cost populations (the aged and people with disabilities) were often kept in fee-for-service. As states increasingly move these complex populations into MCOs, the stakes — and the difficulty — rise.

body.message: Capitated managed care can create an incentive to avoid expensive members. Plans have been criticized for prioritizing cost containment over necessary care and for directly or indirectly selecting healthier enrollees or avoiding patients with complex needs. Guarding against this is a central purpose of the oversight, risk adjustment, and contract rules covered later in this course.
body.title: The Cherry-Picking Concern

children.text: Where Managed Care Stands Today

Despite the mixed evidence, Medicaid managed care is now the dominant delivery model and continues to expand. As of 2024, thirty MCO states covered at least 75% of their Medicaid beneficiaries through MCOs. The populations enrolled tell an important story: children and ACA expansion adults are the most likely to be in comprehensive MCOs (around 90% and 86% respectively), while people eligible through a disability pathway and adults 65 and older have historically been less likely to be enrolled — though states are steadily moving these higher-need groups into managed care too.

body.analogy: A state moving Medicaid to managed care is like a company switching from paying every employee’s medical bills directly to buying a fixed-price health plan for all of them. The company no longer faces a surprise bill when costs spike — it pays a known premium and the insurer absorbs the risk. That predictability is the main attraction. But the company also gives up direct control, and must now watch carefully that the insurer doesn’t skimp on care or shun its sickest workers to protect its own margin.
body.concept: Why states adopt Medicaid managed care

children.text: This trajectory sets up the rest of the course. Because states have handed responsibility for most of their Medicaid populations to private MCOs, the critical questions become operational: How do states choose which MCOs to contract with? How are the capitation rates calculated so they are adequate but not excessive? How do states hold plans accountable for network adequacy, quality, and fair treatment of complex members? Each of these exists precisely because the move to managed care transferred enormous responsibility — and public dollars — to private organizations that must be carefully governed.

The fundamental tension introduced here runs through everything that follows. Managed care offers states budget predictability and the promise of coordinated care, but it does so by giving private plans a financial incentive that can cut against members’ interests. The entire apparatus of Medicaid managed care operations — procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, quality measurement, and value-based purchasing — exists to capture the benefits of the model while guarding against its risks. Understanding why states made this move is understanding why all that machinery is necessary.

points: Medicaid managed care means a state pays private managed care organizations (MCOs) a fixed capitated amount per enrollee to provide care, shifting financial risk to the MCO instead of paying providers per service as in fee-for-service.
It is now the dominant model: over 66 million enrollees (~78%) received care through risk-based MCOs as of July 2024, and 30 states cover at least 75% of beneficiaries in MCOs.

Managed care grew rapidly in the 1990s (from ~10% of beneficiaries in 1991 to nearly 40% by 1996), accelerated by the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which eliminated the waiver requirement for mandatory managed care.

The two most-cited rationales are increasing budget predictability and improving care coordination, with predictability the most powerful in practice because it converts volatile fee-for-service costs into a fixed per-member payment.

Budget predictability matters because Medicaid is a huge share of state budgets that must generally balance annually, so capitation caps the state’s per-enrollee exposure and transfers overrun risk to the MCO.

The evidence is mixed: states reliably gained predictability, but few studies show managed care lowered costs or improved quality, and predictability gains were limited because managed care first covered the most stable-spending populations.
Capitation creates a cherry-picking risk — incentives to avoid expensive, complex members — which oversight, risk adjustment, and contract rules are designed to counter.

The transfer of most Medicaid populations and dollars to private MCOs is exactly why the rest of Medicaid managed care operations (procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, quality, value-based purchasing) is necessary.

children.text: The current war between Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont (BCBSVT) and the University of Vermont Medical Center (UVMMC) is not just a local squabble. It is a textbook example of what happens when a healthcare system gets stuck halfway between two economic models. To understand why your MRI costs $6,500, we first need to understand the three core concepts that govern how money moves in healthcare: The Widget Model, The All-Payer Dream, and The Global Budget Solution.
Concept 1: The Status Quo (Fee-For-Service)

Most healthcare in America, including much of Vermont's commercial market, runs on 'Fee-For-Service' (FFS). Think of this like a grocery store. Every item has a price tag. If you buy an apple, you pay $1. If you buy a steak, you pay $20. The store makes more money the more items you put in your cart.

In healthcare, the 'items' are tests, scans, and surgeries. The hospital (the store) wants to sell you more MRIs (steaks) because they are profitable. The insurer (the shopper) wants to buy fewer items to save money. This creates a natural conflict: The hospital wants high volume and high prices; the insurer wants low volume and low prices.

body.title: Real-World Data: The 'Grocery Store' Markup

children.text: Concept 2: The 'All-Payer' Model (The Failed Dream)

Vermont tried to fix this with the 'All-Payer Model.' The idea was simple: All insurance companies (Medicare, Medicaid, and Blue Cross) should play by the same rules. Instead of fighting 3 different wars, the hospital would have one unified agreement.

However, this model is currently failing in the commercial sector because it hasn't changed the *payment mechanism* for individual services. We have an 'All-Payer' agreement in name, but we are still fighting 'Fee-For-Service' battles in practice. The hospital still needs to sell expensive MRIs to survive, and the insurer still needs to stop them.
Concept 3: The Solution (Value-Based Care & Global Budgets)

This is the 'Subscription Model' (Global Budget). Imagine if instead of paying for every apple and steak, the insurer paid the hospital a flat fee of $1,000 per month to keep you fed and healthy. This is called a Global Budget.
Under this model, the economic incentives flip upside down:

body.title: Comparison: Fee-For-Service vs. Global Budget

children.text: Why This Solves the War

If Vermont moved to a true Global Budget (like Maryland has done), the war over MRI prices would end instantly. Why? Because UVMMC would no longer 'sell' MRIs. They would receive a guaranteed annual budget to care for the population. In that world, UVMMC would happily send you to the cheaper independent center for your scan, because it saves *them* money against their own budget. The incentives of the insurer and the hospital would finally align: Quality up, costs down.

children.text: The social contract of Vermont healthcare—that high premiums buy access to a stable, non-profit system—is actively collapsing. The latest escalation, a direct-to-consumer marketing campaign by Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont (BCBSVT) urging members to bypass the University of Vermont Medical Center (UVMMC), is not merely a contract dispute. It is a signal that the market has reached a point of 'Allocative Failure.' With residents spending 19.6% of their household income on premiums—the highest rate in the nation and nearly triple the 7.9% national average—the system has crossed the threshold from expensive to predatory.
I. The Precipitating Crisis: War in the Open

The conflict began when BCBSVT, facing a $62.1 million deficit after paying out $35 million a week in claims, launched the 'VT Affordable Care' campaign. This initiative explicitly encourages patients to seek care at independent facilities rather than the academic medical center. The insurer's data reveals indefensible price variances that cannot be explained by clinical quality differences alone. For example, a standard MRI costs $6,520 at UVMMC, compared to $1,799 at independent sites. This 262% to 555% markup is the hallmark of a 'Differentiated Oligopoly' flexing its market power.

children.text: II. The Root Cause: Fee-For-Service Incentives

Why does this persist? The culprit is the 'Fee-For-Service' (FFS) payment model. In an FFS system, every procedure is a revenue unit. Hospitals are economically incentivized to maximize volume and intensity. This leads to 'Physician-Induced Demand' (PID), where providers—acting as agents for medically uninformed patients—recommend expensive hospital-based imaging instead of cheaper community alternatives. The data shows that 31% of UVMMC physician time is non-clinical, yet the system demands high throughput to cover its massive fixed costs.

The Fee-For-Service model turns the patient into a 'revenue extraction unit.' The hospital needs the $6,500 MRI to subsidize its other operations, creating a perverse incentive to hoard simple procedures that could be done cheaper elsewhere.
III. The Demographic Death Spiral

The Wyman Report highlights that this model is doomed by demographics. By 2040, 30% of Vermonters will be over 65. The traditional strategy of 'Cross-Subsidization'—charging commercially insured workers high rates to cover the losses from Medicare/Medicaid patients—is failing because the workforce (the subsidy source) is shrinking by 13%. We are running out of 'rich' patients to overcharge.
IV. The Solution: Global Budgets & Site Neutrality

To fix this, Vermont must abandon FFS for **Global Budgets**. Under this model (successfully used in Maryland), the hospital gets a fixed annual revenue cap (e.g., $2.5 Billion) to care for the population. Crucially, this flips the incentive: an MRI becomes a *cost* to the hospital, not a profit. The hospital would suddenly *want* to partner with cheaper independent centers to save its own budget. Combined with 'Site Neutrality' laws (mandating equal pay for equal work regardless of location), this would structurally end the 555% markup arbitrage.

children.text: The fundamental economic pact of American healthcare—that insurers provide access and hospitals provide care—is fracturing. The latest escalation in Vermont serves as a grim bellwether for the national market. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont (BCBSVT), the state's dominant insurer, has launched a direct-to-consumer marketing campaign explicitly advising members to avoid the University of Vermont Medical Center (UVMMC), the state's only Level 1 Trauma Center. This is no longer a contract negotiation; it is an economic blockade.

This conflict represents a classic 'Zero-Sum Game.' In a growth market, stakeholders can compromise by expanding the pie. But Vermont faces a demographic contraction and a stagnant risk pool. Revenue growth for the hospital system can now only come at the direct expense of the payer's reserves or the patient's premiums. There is no 'new money.' This reality has turned the negotiation table into a battlefield, where specific pricing data is weaponized to sway public opinion.
Part 1: The Anatomy of a Price Disparity

The crux of the insurer's argument lies in the indefensible variance in pricing for commoditized services. While complex neurosurgery is difficult to price-shop, diagnostic imaging and standard lab tests are essentially identical products regardless of the setting. Yet, the price tag attached to these services at UVMMC suggests a luxury product. Recent disclosures from the Green Mountain Care Board and the insurer's own marketing reveal disparities that cannot be explained by inflation alone.

For example, a standard MRI at UVMMC is billed at approximately $6,520. That same functional scan, performed on similar equipment at an independent facility less than five miles away, costs $1,799. This is a markup of 262%. For a CT scan of the abdomen, the gap widens further: $5,408 at the academic medical center versus $1,339 independently.

body.title: The Price Gap: UVMMC vs. Independent Facilities (2025)

children.text: These numbers are not abstract. For a patient with a standard High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP)—common among Vermont's self-employed and small business employees—this differential is the difference between a manageable copay and financial ruin. By steering patients away from UVMMC for these services, BCBSVT argues it is performing a fiduciary duty to its members. However, UVMMC argues that this 'cherry-picking' destroys the cross-subsidization model that keeps the hospital doors open.
Part 2: The Provider's Defense (The Cost Shift)

To understand why UVMMC charges $6,520 for a $1,800 MRI, one must look at what that MRI is actually paying for. It is not just paying for the magnet and the technician. It is paying for the Level 1 Trauma Center standby capacity, the burn unit, the pediatric ICU, and the graduate medical education programs that train the state's future doctors. Independent imaging centers do not run 24/7 emergency rooms. They do not treat uninsured trauma victims at 3:00 AM.

This is the 'Cost Shift.' Because government payers (Medicare and Medicaid) reimburse below the cost of care, and because the hospital must maintain money-losing essential services, they load the overhead onto the commercial prices of high-volume, high-margin services like imaging and orthopedics. When BCBSVT successfully steers that volume away, the hospital's 'cash cow' dries up, but the fixed costs of the Trauma Center remain. This forces the hospital to demand even higher rate increases on the remaining services, creating a 'Death Spiral' of rising unit costs.
Part 3: The Weaponization of the Patient

The most disturbing aspect of this zero-sum game is the use of the patient as leverage. BCBSVT's campaign does not merely educate; it instills fear. By publicly labeling the state's primary hospital as 'unaffordable,' they create a psychological barrier to care. Patients may delay seeking necessary treatment for complex conditions because they conflate the price of an MRI with the price of cancer care, or they fear hidden out-of-network costs.

We are witnessing the weaponization of patient access. When an insurer tells a patient to 'shop around' in a market where the next comparable facility is two hours away, they are not engaging in consumerism; they are engaging in denial of care by economic friction.

This 'steering' also fragments care. A patient might get their MRI at an independent center, their blood work at a LabCorp, and their surgery at UVMMC. While cheaper individually, this fragmentation breaks the continuity of the electronic medical record, leads to duplicate testing (when the surgeon cannot access the outside MRI), and increases the administrative burden on the patient to coordinate their own logistics.
Part 4: The Regulatory Failure

Why hasn't the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB) intervened? The regulator is caught in the same zero-sum trap. If they deny UVMMC's rate increase, the hospital cuts services or delays infrastructure investment. If they approve it, insurance premiums spike, and small businesses drop coverage. The GMCB has attempted to cap hospital revenue growth, but they lack the statutory power to force price parity across different sites of service.

The current stalemate suggests that the 'All-Payer' model, once the crown jewel of Vermont health policy, is buckling under the weight of inflation and utilization trends. Without a mechanism to globally budget the entire system—rather than fighting skirmishes over MRI prices—the payer and provider will continue to cannibalize each other until one collapses.

children.text: The social contract of Vermont healthcare is dead. It did not die from natural causes; it was strangled by a toxic economic feedback loop known as the Fee-For-Service (FFS) model.

The current public warfare between Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont (BCBSVT) and the University of Vermont Medical Center (UVMMC) is not a standard contract dispute. It is a symptom of Allocative Failure. When a state’s residents pay 19.6% of their household income on insurance premiums—nearly triple the national average—to fund a system where a single MRI scan costs $6,520, the market has ceased to function as a mechanism for value and has become a mechanism for extraction.
I. The Data: The Price of Leverage

The catalyst for this open conflict is BCBSVT’s unprecedented 'VT Affordable Care' campaign, which explicitly urges patients to bypass the state’s academic medical center. The insurer, facing a $62.1 million deficit and paying out $35 million weekly in claims, has broken the omertà of the healthcare industry to reveal the raw unit prices driving these deficits.

The data reveals a market defined by extreme price dispersion, which violates the Law of One Price. In a competitive market, identical goods (a 3T MRI scan) should command identical prices. In Vermont, they do not.

children.text: Economically, this is not a pricing error. It is the result of Market Power. UVMMC functions as a 'Differentiated Oligopoly.' Because they are the sole provider of essential, non-substitutable services (Trauma, Burn Unit), they leverage this monopoly power to demand exorbitant rents on substitutable services. They effectively say to the insurer: 'If you want access to our Trauma Center, you must pay $6,500 for our MRIs.'
II. The Root Pathology: Fee-For-Service (FFS)

The villain in this story is not a person; it is an incentive structure. Under Fee-For-Service, healthcare providers are paid for volume, not value. Every test, scan, and visit is a billable unit. This creates a fundamental misalignment between the hospital’s financial health and the patient’s financial health.

The Fee-For-Service model turns the patient into a 'revenue extraction unit.' To cover massive fixed costs, the hospital needs the $6,500 MRI to subsidize its other operations, creating a perverse incentive to hoard simple procedures that could be done cheaper elsewhere.

This leads to 'Physician-Induced Demand' (PID). Because of Information Asymmetry, the doctor (Agent) influences the patient (Principal). UVMMC, burdened by a 31% non-clinical administrative load, needs high throughput to survive. Thus, physicians are subtly incentivized to keep care 'in-house,' steering patients toward the $6,500 option rather than the $1,799 independent one.
III. The Demographic Trap: A Pyramid Scheme Collapse

The Wyman Report provides the grim context: Vermont is aging faster than it can pay. Healthcare financing in the US is essentially a Ponzi scheme that relies on a large base of healthy, working-age people paying premiums to subsidize the care of the elderly. By 2040, 30% of Vermonters will be over age 65, while the working-age population shrinks by 13%.

You cannot fund a 'Rolls-Royce' academic medical system on a shrinking, aging tax base using a Fee-For-Service model. As the pool of commercially insured people shrinks, the hospital must charge them even more per unit to maintain revenue. This creates a Death Spiral: premiums rise, healthy people drop coverage, the risk pool gets sicker, and premiums rise again.
IV. The Solution: Global Budgets

The only structural fix is to kill Fee-For-Service and move to Global Budgets (The Maryland Model). Instead of negotiating the price of an MRI, the state sets a Total Revenue Cap for UVMMC (e.g., $2.5 Billion/year).

This flips the incentives entirely. Under a Global Budget, that $6,500 MRI is no longer 'profit'—it is an 'expense' against the fixed budget. UVMMC would suddenly want to partner with the $1,799 independent center to save its own resources. The war ends because the economic reason for the war—volume maximization—is removed.

children.text: I. The Precipitating Crisis: War in the Open

The conflict began not in a boardroom, but on a billboard. As reported by VTDigger, BCBSVT’s 'VT Affordable Care' campaign represents a historic breach of protocol. The insurer is explicitly urging its members to bypass the state’s flagship academic medical center, UVMMC, in favor of independent clinics. This is a desperate move driven by solvency risks: the insurer paid out $35 million a week in claims in 2024, ending the year with a $62.1 million deficit. This is no longer a negotiation; it is a fight for survival.
II. The Data: Anatomy of a Price Disparity

The insurer's argument rests on the 'Law of One Price'—or rather, its violation. In a functional market, identical goods command identical prices. In Vermont, market leverage has distorted this beyond recognition. UVMMC, controlling two-thirds of the hospital market, charges multiples of what independent competitors charge for commoditized diagnostic services.

children.text: III. Theoretical Framework: Why 'Shopping' Doesn't Work

BCBSVT's strategy relies on 'Consumer Directed Health Care'—the idea that patients will vote with their feet. However, standard Health Economics (Bhattacharya et al.) explains why this fails in healthcare markets due to **Agency Theory**. The patient (Principal) delegates decision-making to the physician (Agent). If a UVMMC specialist orders an MRI, the patient rarely questions the location, even if it costs thousands more. Furthermore, **Moral Hazard** dampens the signal: once a patient meets their deductible, the marginal cost of the expensive MRI is zero to them, even as it bankrupts the insurance pool.
IV. The Wyman Report: Structural unsustainability

The Act 167 (Wyman) Report provides the macro-context. Vermont faces a 'Demographic Death Spiral.' By 2040, 30% of the population will be over 65. The working-age population—the ones paying the commercial premiums that subsidize the system—is shrinking. UVMMC argues its high prices are necessary to cross-subsidize the underfunded Trauma and Burn units. However, the data shows inefficiencies: 31% of physician FTEs at UVMMC are non-clinical, and clinical productivity is below national benchmarks.
The state is attempting to fund a Rolls-Royce academic medical system on a rickshaw demographic base. The 19.6% premium burden is the breaking point.
V. The Solution: Global Budgets & Site Neutrality

The only theoretical exit from this zero-sum conflict is to abandon Fee-For-Service entirely. 

1. **Global Budgets (Maryland Model):** If UVMMC received a fixed annual revenue cap (e.g., $2.5 Billion) rather than getting paid per MRI, the economic incentives would invert. An MRI would become a *cost* to the hospital, not a profit center. They would *want* patients to use cheaper independent centers.

2. **Site Neutrality:** Legislation must mandate that a service codes for the same price regardless of the building it is performed in. This removes the arbitrage incentive that drives hospital consolidation.
